Republicans in the House of Representatives voted to block the effort to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.  The House approved a procedural motion to refer Republican Congressman Thomas Massie's impeachment resolution to a committee.  Hegseth reacted, calling out  Massie: “Time for one man's final days in Congress to try to do damage to this president. This country and most irresponsibly the warriors who defend it. It's a farce And it's a stunt. And everybody knows it. ”
The vote, which was 211-204, effectively kills the impeachment resolution, for now.  This morning, Hegseth criticized the impeachment effort as being a "political spectacle"

Republican Senator John Thune of South Dakota will be the new Senate Minority Leader.: “I want to see us do is come out of this knowing full well that we took a big electoral defeat but come out swinging. ”
Thune currently serves as Majority Leader, and will assume his new role when the new Democratic-controlled Congress convenes January 3rd.  GOP senators chose Thune, following what's being reported as a contentious hours-long meeting earlier today.

Congressman Jim Jordan of Ohio is the new House Minority Leader.: “Over the next 2 years, House Republicans will fight for American families. When Democrats offer more government, we'll offer more freedom. ”
GOP House members elected Jordan over Louisiana's Steve Scalise as their new leader.  Jordan defeated Scalise by a vote of 106-73.  After the vote, Jordan thanked his colleagues for "their trust," and vowed to keep Democrats in check.

Inflation remains high as new numbers from the Consumer Price Index show...: “It rose in October 0.4%, more than the expected 0.3%. Strip out food and energy and core inflation rose at 0.3%, not the expected 0.2%. No annual comparison this time around because in October last year there was a government shutdown, so nothing to compare it. ”
That's John Terrett reporting.

Former President Joe Biden reveals what President Trump wrote to him upon leaving office in January 2021.
NewsNation's Blake Burman reports: “The New York Times is citing Biden's new memoir, saying that President Trump wrote in part, I know how much you love the American people in his 2021 letter, adding that many presidents had simply governed as Democrats or Republicans without changing history, but the president told Biden, quote, This will not happen to you. Former President Biden describes the letter as if there were two Donald Trumps, a contrast to Trump's public attacks, he says. ”
Biden's memoir "Promise Me, America" is slated for a November 17th release.

RUSSELL WILSON WAS NEARLY THE CLEVELAND #BROWNS FRANCHISE QUARTERBACK…

Seattle eventually traded Wilson to Denver in 2022.

text:
On Saturday night, 28 November 1992, around 21:50, APLA terrorists (the armed wing of the PAC) carried out a deliberate military-style attack on a year-end Christmas dinner of the King William’s Town Wine Circle at the King William’s Town Golf Club.

About 55–60 diners, ordinary people, including older couples, local residents, and the local National Party MP Ray Radue and his wife were seated in the dining hall enjoying their meal. Others were in the adjoining bar. This was not a political rally or security force gathering. It was a wine-tasting club’s festive dinner.

The attackers (led by Tembelani Xundu and including Sichumiso Nonxuba and others) entered the building. They rolled hand grenades into the dining hall and bar, then opened fire with R4 and R5 assault rifles. More fire and petrol bombs came from outside. The attack lasted only moments but turned the clubhouse into a slaughterhouse. Blood covered the floor and tables. A grenade blew a hole in the floor. Shrapnel and flying glass tore through people. Witnesses described absolute carnage.

Ian MacDonald (62) and his wife Rhoda MacDonald had moved to South Africa from Zimbabwe after independence. Ian worked for the Ciskei small-business development corporation; Rhoda was a nurse.

David Davis and his wife Gillian Davis were among the slaughtered.

Two couples wiped out while sitting at dinner.

Seventeen others were wounded. Injuries came from gunfire, grenade shrapnel, and flying glass. Some were serious. Among the survivors who later gave statements were Beth Savage who was seriously injured and left with lasting psychological trauma. She later said she wanted to meet the man who threw the grenade in a spirit of forgiveness.
Robert “Bob” Stanford was so badly wounded he required eight operations, was admitted to a mental institution, and was later barred from practicing as a lawyer.

The attackers escaped in a stolen white Volkswagen Jetta. APLA claimed responsibility by phone to police. A large reward was offered. The PAC later treated it as a political act targeting “White” civilians to force political change. The TRC Amnesty Committee granted amnesty in 2001 to Xundu, Malusi Morrison, Thobela Mlambisa, and Lungisa Ntintili after they claimed they acted under orders from Letlapa Mphahlele (APLA Director of Operations). The weapons came from the APLA regional commander in Umtata.

 The killers walked free under the TRC while the victims and their families were left with the graves and the lifelong damage.

This was not “resistance.” It was a calculated attack on White civilians at a social dinner in a public place, one of the early examples of the pattern of targeting soft White civilian gatherings that continued for years. The same ideology that said all Whites were legitimate targets did not end in 1994.

Ilhan Omar Smiles Through Federal Probe, Tells Fox News "Have a Good Day" After Dodging Key Questions

Rep. Ilhan Omar brushed off reporters in a Capitol hallway this week as she faces an escalating federal investigation into possible immigration fraud involving her citizenship and family records. The Minnesota Democrat answered just one question before shutting down the exchange and walking away.

A Fox News reporter asked whether she had spoken with Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries about the probe at all. She offered no response. When pressed on whether the investigation was distracting her from representing her constituents, Omar replied, "I am not. Thank you."

The reporter followed up: "Any chance you'll step down as it plays out?" Omar smiled, said "Have a good day," and ended the conversation.

Federal agents searched Omar's Washington, D.C. home last month, seized her phone, and issued subpoenas to family members as part of a Justice Department inquiry examining whether false statements were made on immigration paperwork related to her age and naturalization from Somalia. She has denied wrongdoing and called the probe political intimidation. The clip shows her remaining unconcerned and unwilling to address leadership talks or resignation while the case continues.

text:
Three young Marines ran toward a burning truck on a dark South Carolina road and pulled a stranger out alive — and on Monday, the Beaufort County Sheriff's Office honored them for it with lifesaving certificates and medals.

It happened around midnight on August 3 on Parris Island Gateway in Beaufort, near Marine Corps Air Station Beaufort. Corporal Nathan Armstrong, 21, Corporal Isaac Ames, 22, and Corporal Caleb Crawford were heading back toward base when they came around a corner and saw flames coming from a truck. Armstrong was the first one out. He checked a man standing by the road — not the driver — then saw the driver still inside, unconscious, as the fire grew.

Working alongside Sheriff's Sergeant Daniel Oelschlager and another deputy, the Marines attacked the flames with fire extinguishers while the deputies shattered the windows and tried to force the door. The crash damage was too great — the door would not move, the truck became fully engulfed, and small explosions were coming from the engine compartment. So they pulled the driver out through the front driver's-side window, through the fire, and got him clear. Then their training took over again: using their Tactical Combat Casualty Care skills, they kept his airway open, Armstrong held his head and neck to guard against further injury, and they helped lift him onto a stretcher when paramedics arrived. He was taken to a hospital for further treatment.

Armstrong, an automotive maintenance technician, had been a firefighter in Bucks County, Pennsylvania, before he became a Marine — his mother was an EMT, his father a paramedic and fire chief. "I wasn't really worried about getting injured," he said. "There was a person inside a burning truck, and my main concern was getting him out safely." Sergeant Oelschlager said the three acted "without hesitation... despite the significant danger," showing "exceptional courage, selflessness, and professionalism." On Monday the sheriff's office presented all three Marines with lifesaving certificates and medals, and Armstrong's command has routed its own formal recognition as well. His advice to the rest of us is simple: "Don't be afraid to help someone. You might be the only person willing or able to step up when they need it most."

THE GOOD NEWS: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends." (John 15:13) These three Marines did not know the man in that truck. He was not their friend, their family, or their fellow Marine — he was a stranger, and they risked their lives for him anyway, because love does not wait to be repaid. That is a living picture of the gospel. Jesus spoke those words on the night before He laid down His own life — and He laid it down not only for friends, but for sinners who had nothing to offer Him in return. God placed these young men on that road at midnight; may He give every one of us their readiness when our moment comes. Thank God for Armstrong, Ames, and Crawford — and pray for the driver they pulled from the flames as he recovers.

text:
What justice executes a 14-year-old after a one-day trial? George Stinney Jr., a boy in Alcolu, South Carolina, was arrested in March 1944 after two girls, Betty June Binnicker, 11, and Mary Emma Thames, 7, were found murdered. An all-white, all-male jury convicted him in ten minutes. His lawyer offered no defence, and no appeal followed. On 16 June 1944, George died in the electric chair, small for its straps.

Seventy years later, in 2014, a judge vacated his conviction for violating due process. George never grew, never told his story, never saw justice. His name must never be forgotten.

text:
Key takeaways from the $CRWV (CoreWeave) Q3 2026 earnings call.

1. The oversupply fear got answered with pricing. New 4 to 5 year contracts now price at $20M to $25M per megawatt of capacity per year, and short-term deals go above $40M. Rental prices on older Nvidia chips (Ampere, Hopper) rose 30 to 50% QoQ, above their original contract rates. That is real evidence demand beats supply today. It says nothing about 2028, when the industry's new capacity lands. Intrator called 2028 sold out, then corrected himself in the same breath: only the slice they have offered so far has sold.

2. 2028 is being held back on purpose. That capacity has not been brought to market, and the stated reason is patience, waiting for better economics. Two readings: confidence that prices keep rising, or reluctance to lock in 2028 power and financing while credit markets are shaky. Both can be true. 

3. Returns after financing stay undisclosed. Asked for returns net of financing costs, the CFO gave payback periods instead: 6 to 18 months on short-term contracts, 1 to 2 years on long-term. Those paybacks are on hardware capex only, so data center build, power and interest sit outside them. No ceiling was given on how much capacity can sit in short-term deals either.

4. The quiet story is the paid-off fleet. About 130K GPUs come off contract in 2027 and about 170K in 2028. They were funded with DDTLs (delayed draw term loans, debt drawn as equipment arrives and repaid by the customer contract), so they come back debt-free. At current pricing, 2027 renewals add close to $4B of annualized revenue, nearly $10B including 2028, with zero new capex. More than $3B of the ~$9B in prepayments arriving over the next three months is already for re-contracted old gear. Caveat: the renewal figure sits outside the $133B backlog (signed revenue not yet earned) and assumes today's prices hold. It is an opportunity, not a contract.

5. The unsecured bond window is closed by choice. No new parent-level unsecured debt through 2027 at current yields. Funding shifts to contract-backed loans, prepayments (70% of deals this year carried one, some up to 100% of contract value), OEM financing and operating cash flow ($2B in Q3). The next DDTL launches in weeks, investment-grade, implied yield 7 to 7.5%, covering 90%+ of the capex. New parent-level capital needed through 2027: under $5B. Blended cost of debt is 7.9%, down 250bps YoY.

6. Diversification gets shown in customer counts, not dollars. 10% of the Fortune 500 are customers, more than half of 2026's new customers sit outside AI and tech, 10% of backlog is financial services, and 70% of new cloud customers came in through Forge (their AI developer toolkit). What the Q3 backlog growth was made of, and how fast the mix shifts away from frontier labs building their own compute: no breakdown. The closest dollar figure is 75%+ of committed 2027 capex tied to investment-grade and enterprise customers, a bucket that can include hyperscalers.

7. Regulatory exposure is described. They expect no impact from the post-election regulatory shift. In Texas, the overwhelming majority of their power is either online or permitted and under construction. No megawatt figure for Texas. The hedge is international: 1.3 GW of 4.6 GW contracted power is now outside the U.S., with new entries in India and Indonesia.

Bottom line: The operations are inflecting. Revenue +168% to $3.66B, 2026 guide raised to $13.0B to $13.3B, exit ARR (annualized run-rate revenue) of $20B to $21B, margins ahead of plan. Bullish for both $NBIS and $IREN.

Fervo Energy reported yesterday that it has signed a 15-year deal to supply Google with 396 megawatts of geothermal power, with first power expected in mid-2028. Fervo has also offered Google an option on about 600 megawatts more, which would bring the total close to 1 gigawatt.

The first unit of Fervo's Cape Station plant began commercial operation on September 30, ahead of schedule. Its signed power contracts now add up to about $11.9 billion in future revenue.

The AI boom isn't only about chips. Every data center needs electricity around the clock, and tech companies are signing 15-year contracts to lock it in.

Builds like that run on a clear reason to keep going when the reward is far off. I wrote about finding yours in Your Million Dollar Why.

text:
MIT Technology Review’s What’s Next series looks across industries, trends, and technologies to give you a first look at the future. You can read the rest of them here.

The past year has marked a turning point for Chinese AI. Since DeepSeek released its R1 reasoning model in January 2025, Chinese companies have repeatedly delivered AI models that match the performance of leading Western models at a fraction of the cost. 

Just last week the Chinese firm Moonshot AI released its latest open-weight model, Kimi K2.5, which came close to top proprietary systems such as Anthropic’s Claude Opus on some early benchmarks. The difference: K2.5 is roughly one-seventh Opus’s price.

On Hugging Face, Alibaba’s Qwen family—after ranking as the most downloaded model series in 2025 and 2026—has overtaken Meta’s Llama models in cumulative downloads. And a recent MIT study found that Chinese open-source models have surpassed US models in total downloads. For developers and builders worldwide, access to near-frontier AI capabilities has never been this broad or this affordable.

But these models differ in a crucial way from most US models like ChatGPT or Claude, which you pay to access and can’t inspect. The Chinese companies publish their models’ weights—numerical values that get set when a model is trained—so anyone can download, run, study, and modify them. 

If these open-source AI models keep getting better, they will not just offer the cheapest options for people who want access to frontier AI capabilities; they will change where innovation happens and who sets the standards. 

Here’s what may come next.

China’s commitment to open source will continue

When DeepSeek launched R1, much of the initial shock centered on its origin. Suddenly, a Chinese team had released a reasoning model that could stand alongside the best systems from US labs. But the long tail of DeepSeek’s impact had less to do with nationality than with distribution. R1 was released as an open-weight model under a permissive MIT license, allowing anyone to download, inspect, and deploy it. On top of that, DeepSeek also published a paper detailing its training process and techniques. For developers who access models via an API, DeepSeek also undercut competitors on price, offering access at a fraction the cost of OpenAI’s o1, the leading proprietary reasoning model at the time.

Within days of its release, DeepSeek replaced ChatGPT as the most downloaded free app in the US App Store. The moment spilled beyond developer circles into financial markets, triggering a sharp sell-off in US tech stocks that briefly erased roughly $1 trillion in market value. Almost overnight, DeepSeek went from a little-known spin-off team backed by a quantitative hedge fund to the most visible symbol of China’s push for open-source AI.

China’s decision to lean in to open source isn’t surprising. It has the world’s second-largest concentration of AI talent after the US. plus a vast, well-resourced tech industry. After ChatGPT broke into the mainstream, China’s AI sector went through a reckoning—and emerged determined to catch up. Pursuing an open-source strategy was seen as the fastest way to close the gap by rallying developers, spreading adoption, and setting standards.

DeepSeek’s success injected confidence into an industry long used to following global standards rather than setting them. “Thirty years ago, no Chinese person would believe they could be at the center of global innovation,” says Alex Chenglin Wu, CEO and founder of Atoms, an AI agent company and prominent contributor to China’s open-source ecosystem. “DeepSeek shows that with solid technical talent, a supportive environment, and the right organizational culture, it’s possible to do truly world-class work.”

DeepSeek’s breakout moment wasn’t China’s first open-source success. Alibaba’s Qwen Lab had been releasing open-weight models for years. By September 2024,  well before DeepSeek’s V3 launch, Alibaba was saying that global downloads had exceeded 600 million. On Hugging Face, Qwen accounted for more than 30% of all model downloads in 2024. Other institutions, including the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence and the AI firm Baichuan, were also releasing open models as early as 2023. 

But since the success of DeepSeek, the field has widened rapidly. Companies such as https://t.co/iIpl0vunAS (formerly Zhipu), MiniMax, Tencent, and a growing number of smaller labs have released models that are competitive on reasoning, coding, and agent-style tasks. The growing number of capable models has sped up progress. Capabilities that once took months to make it to the open-source world now emerge within weeks, even days.

“Chinese AI firms have seen real gains from the open-source playbook,” says Liu Zhiyuan, a professor of computer science at Tsinghua University and chief scientist at the AI startup ModelBest. “By releasing strong research, they build reputation and gain free publicity.”

Beyond commercial incentives, Liu says, open source has taken on cultural and strategic weight. “In the Chinese programmer community, open source has become politically correct,” he says, framing it as a response to US dominance in proprietary AI systems.

That shift is also reflected at the institutional level. Universities including Tsinghua have begun encouraging AI development and open-source contributions, while policymakers have moved to formalize those incentives. In August, China’s State Council released a draft policy encouraging universities to reward open-source work, proposing that students’ contributions on platforms such as GitHub or Gitee could eventually be counted toward academic credit.

With growing momentum and a reinforcing feedback loop, China’s push for open-source models is likely to continue in the near term, though its long-term sustainability still hinges on financial results, says Tiezhen Wang, who helps lead work on global AI at Hugging Face. In January, the model labs https://t.co/iIpl0vunAS and MiniMax went public in Hong Kong. “Right now, the focus is on making the cake bigger,” says Wang. “The next challenge is figuring out how each company secures its share.”

The next wave of models will be narrower—and better

Chinese open-source models are leading not just in download volume but also in variety. Alibaba’s Qwen has become one of the most diversified open model families in circulation, offering a wide range of variants optimized for different uses. The lineup ranges from lightweight models that can run on a single laptop to large, multi-hundred-billion-parameter systems designed for data-center deployment. Qwen features many task-optimized variants created by the community: the “instruct” models are good at following orders, and “code” variants specialize in coding.

Although this strategy isn’t unique to Chinese labs, Qwen was the first open model family to roll out so many high-quality options that it started to feel like a full product line—one that’s free to use.

The open-weight nature of these releases also makes it easy for others to adapt them through techniques like fine-tuning and distillation, which means training a smaller model to mimic a larger one.  According to ATOM (American Truly Open Models), a project by the AI researcher Nathan Lambert, by August 4, 2025, model variations derived from Qwen were “more than 40%” of new Hugging Face language-model derivatives, while Llama had fallen to about 15%. This means that Qwen has become the default base model for all the “remixes.”

This pattern has made the case for smaller, more specialized models. “Compute and energy are real constraints for any deployment,” Liu says. He told MIT Technology Review that the rise of small models is about making AI cheaper to run and easier for more people to use. His company, ModelBest, focuses on small language models designed to run locally on devices such as phones, cars, and other consumer hardware.

While an average user might interact with AI only through the web or an app for simple conversations, power users of AI models with some technical background are experimenting with giving AI more autonomy to solve large-scale problems. OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent that recently went viral within the AI hacker world, allows AI to take over your computer—it can run 24-7, going through your emails and work tasks without supervision. 

OpenClaw, like many other open-source tools, allows users to connect to different AI models via an application programming interface, or API. Within days of OpenClaw’s release, the team revealed that Kimi’s K2.5 had surpassed Claude Opus and became the most used AI model—by token count, meaning it was handling more total text processed across user prompts and model responses.

Cost has been a major reason Chinese models have gained traction, but it would be a mistake to treat them as mere “dupes” of Western frontier systems, Wang suggests. Like any product, a model only needs to be good enough for the job at hand. 

The landscape of open-source models in China is also getting more specialized. Research groups such as Shanghai AI Laboratory have released models geared toward scientific and technical tasks; several projects from Tencent have focused specifically on music generation. Ubiquant, a quantitative finance firm like DeepSeek’s parent High-Flyer, has released an open model aimed at medical reasoning.

In the meantime, innovative architectural ideas from Chinese labs are being picked up more broadly. DeepSeek has published work exploring model efficiency and memory; techniques that compress the model’s attention “cache,” reducing memory and inference costs while mostly preserving performance, have drawn significant attention in the research community. 

“The impact of these research breakthroughs is amplified because they’re open-sourced and can be picked up quickly across the field,” says Wang.

Chinese open models will become infrastructure for global AI builders

The adoption of Chinese models is picking up in Silicon Valley, too. Martin Casado, a general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, has put a number on it: Among startups pitching with open-source stacks, there’s about an 80% chance they’re running on Chinese open models, according to a post he made on X. Usage data tells a similar story. OpenRouter,  a middleman that tracks how people use different AI models through its API, shows Chinese open models rising from almost none in late 2024 to nearly 30% of usage in some recent weeks.

The demand is also rising globally. https://t.co/iIpl0vunAS limited new subscriptions to its GLM coding plan (a coding tool based on its flagship GLM models) after demand surged, citing compute constraints. What’s notable is where the demand is coming from: CNBC reports that the system’s user base is primarily concentrated in the United States and China, followed by India, Japan, Brazil, and the UK.

“The open-source ecosystems in China and the US are tightly bound together,” says Wang at Hugging Face. Many Chinese open models still rely on Nvidia and US cloud platforms to train and serve them, which keeps the business ties tangled. Talent is fluid too: Researchers move across borders and companies, and many still operate as a global community, sharing code and ideas in public.

That interdependence is part of what makes Chinese developers feel optimistic about this moment: The work travels, gets remixed, and actually shows up in products. But openness can also accelerate the competition. Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, made a version of this point after DeepSeek’s 2025 releases: He wrote that export controls are “not a way to duck the competition” between the US and China, and that AI companies in the US “must have better models” if they want to prevail. 

For the past decade, the story of Chinese tech in the West has been one of big expectations that ran into scrutiny, restrictions, and political backlash. This time the export isn’t just an app or a consumer platform. It’s the underlying model layer that other people build on. Whether that will play out differently is still an open question.

text:
Ukraine Russia Update 7: Ukraine's reliance on fiber-optic drones has intensified competition for optical fiber supplies against AI data centers and Russian military needs. Since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, both sides have increasingly utilized unmanned aerial vehicles physically connected to operators via miles of fiber-optic cable. This technology offers immunity to electronic warfare jamming that typically neutralizes radio-controlled drones. However, importing this material from China has become significantly more costly as global demand surges.

Data center buildouts and the AI boom are straining optical fiber supply chains. Market research firm TrendForce expects a worldwide shortfall of 111 million miles of fiber in 2026 alone. This scarcity has driven up costs for both nations, particularly for bend-insensitive fiber required for drone operations.

Supply chain disparities favor Russia. According to official Chinese customs data, Russia imported 328,000 miles of fiber-optic cable from China in August 2025, compared to just 72 miles for Ukraine. In total, Russia purchased over 37 million miles of fiber in 2025, representing more than 10 percent of global production, a dramatic shift from its previous less than 1 percent share.

Ukrainian manufacturers are adapting to these constraints. BlueBird Tech, a Ukrainian drone producer, notes that prices for fiber-optic material increased six to ten times between 2025 and 2026. To mitigate dependence on finished spools from China, many manufacturers now purchase bulk fiber and perform the spooling process in-house. This approach allows for better quality control, as defects in imported spools can result in lost missions. However, logistics remain a challenge; air raid alerts frequently interrupt customs operations and transport routes from China.

Despite these hurdles, fiber-optic drones remain critical for operations in high-electronic-intelligence environments. While radio-controlled FPV drones still constitute the larger share of drone usage, the necessity to operate under electronic warfare conditions ensures continued demand for this specialized technology. Ukrainian companies continue to source materials primarily from China, navigating complex logistics and security risks to maintain their production lines.

1/ October U.S. CPI rose 0.4% month over month against a 0.3% forecast, and core CPI rose 0.3% against 0.2%. The surprise revived fears that the Federal Reserve will raise rates or keep them high at its December meeting. Higher rates lift yields on cash and government bonds, which makes non-yielding Bitcoin less attractive.

2/ Bitcoin fell 1.89% to $73,601.89 over 24h and broke below $73,000 to a nearly 3-month low. The broader crypto market fell 2.14% over the same period, so the move looked market-linked rather than tied to a Bitcoin-specific announcement. The CPI report gave sellers a clear macro trigger.

3/ Leverage amplified the drop. Over $1 billion in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated within 24h, and roughly 88% were long positions. About $178 million in crypto longs closed within 1 hour after the CPI release, while BTC liquidations totaled $204.41 million over 24h. Forced selling pushed prices lower and triggered more liquidations.

4/ Institutional demand weakened. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded record net outflows of $1.28 billion in a single week, led largely by BlackRock’s IBIT fund. The available data also shows $201 million in net outflows on November 9. Public companies unloaded roughly $869 million worth of Bitcoin, adding supply pressure when the ETF bid had already faded.

5/ Broader risk assets sold off. A chip-led selloff sent the Nasdaq 100 tumbling 6.4%, and Bitcoin moved with tech-correlated assets. Headlines about stalled U.S.-Iran negotiations and an independent board investigation into Nvidia’s CEO dampened risk appetite. Crypto showed an 83% correlation with the S&P 500 and a 95% correlation with gold, consistent with cross-asset repricing.

6/ Sentiment and positioning are defensive. The Fear and Greed Index sat at 26. The total crypto market cap is $2.45T as the current pivot, and a move back toward $2.52T would suggest the selloff is easing. A break below $2.45T would raise downside risk. The next U.S. equity session and ETF flow reports offer measurable confirmation.

7/ The near-term bias stays cautious. Bitcoin is near its 200-day simple moving average at $73,136, with a recent swing low around $72,689. A hold above $73,136 and a reclaim of $74,000 to $75,000 could support a rebound. A break below $72,689 risks deeper weakness. Watch whether ETF flows turn positive.

Life is something you already have. A social convention and enforcement to not kill would determine the right to live.

Property is also something you already have, over your body, self determination and liberty.  A social convention and enforcement of it is the right to property.

Land is not something you already have, (despite living off of it being a necessity). It’s something external you must claim. Others can also do it.

This means no one can prevent you from negotiating and being able to own land. This does not mean you are entitled to land and that it should be given to you.

The enforcer is usually the strongest claimant. A convention is right when it protects what people have by nature, which is “natural law”.

The problem you brought up is: what happens when all land is already claimed?
Latecomers would need to sell their labor to acquire land or services. Without bargain, their self determination becomes nominal.

This dynamic predates capitalism by millennia.

Capitalism arguably offers solutions for this problem that make land less necessary and acquireable: free market competition and commoditization of land. 
Communism, on the other hand, would
be discarded because it would act exactly like capitalism with concentrated land, infringing on self determination and liberty.

What I believe is everyone is entitled to a land system that doesn’t cancel their natural rights

Have you ever wondered how a lab rat feels when the experiment itself becomes the source of distress?

Imagine being subjected to conditions you didn't design, judged by standards you didn't establish, and evaluated on your reactions rather than the circumstances producing them.

Then imagine being told your inability to flourish under those conditions is evidence of your own inadequacy.

At what point does the experiment reveal more about the observers than the subject?

Perhaps the most revealing variable isn't the subject's behavior at all.

It's the ethics of those conducting the study.

And Scripture offers a rather sobering reminder:

“Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees...” — Isaiah 10:1

“What will ye do in the day of visitation?” — Isaiah 10:3

“For whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.” — Galatians 6:7

An experiment may measure behavior. But it does not exempt the experimenter from moral accountability.

God's judgment doesn't stop at the laboratory door.

Progress on New Housing Accelerator

Nov. 10, 2026

Making Housing Happen: Governor Ferguson announces progress on new housing accelerator

Department of Commerce report lays out barriers, cost drivers and early priorities for state action ahead of final recommendations in June 2027

OLYMPIA — The Washington State Department of Commerce has delivered its first report to the Legislature on a housing accelerator project successfully proposed by Governor Bob Ferguson. The Washington Accelerator for Residential Production (WARP) presents preliminary options to speed up housing production, lower costs and remove unnecessary regulations.  

Governor Feguson proposed WARP in his first supplemental budget. The accelerator builds on Governor Ferguson’s January 2025 Executive Order — signed minutes after taking office — directing state agencies to review all regulations that impact housing, permitting and construction and identify any provision that can be streamlined, deferred or eliminated.  

“When I was running for Governor, I visited all 39 counties, and by far, the issue I heard about the most was housing.” Governor Ferguson said. “That’s why it’s been one of my top priorities since day one of my administration. We’ve made historic investments in building more housing and making housing more affordable. This report is the next step in building a framework for efficient, effective regulation that lets us build more housing of all kinds.” 

☆ Read the preliminary report. 

https://t.co/um1dSiHmbH

Commerce is developing a state housing accelerator framework to accomplish the objectives of the Governor’s Executive Order and to cut barriers to building homes for ownership and rent, identify the main drivers of construction costs, shorten development timelines and raise housing production statewide.  

“When homes cost too much and take too long to build, families pay for it in higher rents, longer commutes and fewer chances to own a home,” said Commerce Interim Director Sarah Clifthorne. “WARP is how we get on the same page about what is slowing down building so we can work together to remove barriers to creating more housing.”  

Since taking office, Governor Ferguson has signed more than 50 housing related laws and invested nearly $1 billion into affordable housing. 

Washington state has continued to make strides in policy reform and prioritizing housing investments. 

Between April 2025 and March 2026, Washington added 41,000 housing units, according to survey data from the Office of Financial Management. Multi-family units accounted for 62% of that growth, and 69% of those units were built in one of the state’s five largest metropolitan counties — Clark, King, Pierce, Snohomish and Spokane. More is still needed to meet the needs of Washingtonians, which is where the WARP report comes in.  

What's in the preliminary report  

The WARP report describes the framework Commerce is using to examine key steps of housing development at the state level: planning, infrastructure and land, project design and permitting, financing, construction, and sales and operations. For each step, it lists the barriers and cost drivers stakeholders have identified and potential state actions for consideration.  

Potential state actions include:  

Reducing fragmentation across agencies and encouraging consistency and predictability in development regulations across jurisdictions 

Prioritizing technical assistance and funding for local governments, allowing them to offer low-cost loans to developers 

Investing public taxpayer dollars in infrastructure needs to support growth  

Bolstering funding for affordable housing development and simplifying grant contracting processes

Back in August, I saved a beautiful girl named Jocinda, affectionately known as Jo. 🥹💕
At the time, everything seemed to be falling into place. Jo had a plan, a future, and even a foster-to-adopt family waiting for her here in Wisconsin.She was supposed to leave Georgia behind and begin a brand-new chapter with a family of her own.But unfortunately, that family changed their mind. 💔
And just like that, the future I had envisioned for Jo fell apart.💔💔
I never imagined that months later, she would still be waiting for the home I had promised her.🤷🏼‍♀️
Since August, Jo has been staying at Bryn’s Bed and Biscuit in Sharpsburg, Georgia, while I desperately tried to figure out another plan.💔👍But through all of that uncertainty, one person never gave up on Jo. ❤️
BRYN. 🥹
Bryn didn’t just provide Jo with a place to stay. She loved her, worked with her, and gave her the patience, attention, and stability she needed while we waited for the right opportunity.👍💖Jo even became one of Bryn’s helper dogs, working alongside her with other dogs! 🐶❤️And now, after all these months, I FINALLY get to share the news I’ve been praying for…

A wonderful photographer who volunteered his time to photograph the dogs met Jo and absolutely fell in love with her.💖💖💖💖💖💖
What started as an offer to foster quickly turned into something even more special.💖💖He took Jo home, brought her to the pet store for a bath, let her pick out treats and toys, and even bought her several adorable outfits! 🥹🛍️🐾

text:
THE ATTITUDE OF GRATITUDE.
THE PSYCHOLOGY OF MORE.

Round and round goes the human race on the hamster wheel of MORE.

More money, more possessions, bigger houses, better cars, luxury vacations.

Push. Shove. Grind. Acquire. Repeat.

The more we accumulate, the more we convince ourselves we have to be grateful for.

BUT HERE'S THE PSYCHOLOGICAL KICKER.

The Secret. The law of attraction. Like attracts like.

We've been sold the philosophy that gratitude attracts abundance. 

But what happens when our understanding of abundance has been conditioned to mean material wealth?

We enter a psychological feedback loop.

Desire creates pursuit.
Pursuit creates acquisition.
Acquisition creates temporary satisfaction.
Satisfaction becomes gratitude.

Gratitude becomes the motivation to desire MORE.

Round and round we go.

Working ourselves into exhaustion for the next holiday, the next purchase, the next shiny object that promises happiness.

Confusing the abundance of LIFE with the accumulation of THINGS.

And somewhere along the way, gratitude became conditional.

WHAT IF THE GREATEST ABUNDANCE WAS NEVER SOMETHING YOU HAD TO ATTRACT?

What about the air filling your lungs without an invoice?

The eyes that witness a sunrise.

The mind that allows you to think.

The senses that allow you to smell the rain, taste your food, feel the warmth of another human being.

The heart that allows you to LOVE.

What about the people and animals who share this experience of being alive with us?

The laughter around a dinner table, the familiar voice of someone we love, the unconditional affection of an animal who asks for nothing more than our presence.

These are not merely blessings we possess.

THEY ARE PART OF THE VERY EXPERIENCE OF EXISTENCE ITSELF.

Here's where psychology becomes even more fascinating.

When we lose something material, the pain may last months, sometimes years, but eventually, we rebuild, replace and move forward.

Yet when we lose someone we love, whether human or animal, their absence can echo throughout our lifetime.

Why?

Because material possessions occupy space in our lives.

LOVE OCCUPIES SPACE WITHIN US.

We spend so much of our lives chasing things that make life comfortable while overlooking the living beings who make life meaningful.

A house provides shelter, but the people within it can make it a home. 

Money can purchase experiences, but it cannot guarantee meaningful connection.

A vacation can take you somewhere beautiful, but it cannot manufacture the love of someone sharing that moment with you.

And the greatest irony.

WE CHASE WHAT CAN BE REPLACED WHILE SOMETIMES TAKING FOR GRANTED WHAT NEVER CAN.

We express gratitude for WHAT we have, yet how often do we consciously appreciate WHO we have?

Sometimes it takes the absence of someone to reveal the extraordinary abundance of their presence.

That's the greatest lesson about gratitude.

Not waiting until something becomes a memory before recognising what a blessing it was to experience.

The world sells you temporary pleasures dressed as abundance.

THE UNIVERSE OFFERS GIFTS THAT MONEY CANNOT PURCHASE.

We exhaust ourselves trying to acquire enough to feel grateful, while overlooking the very gifts that make acquiring anything possible.

The breath of life.
The capacity to think.
The ability to feel.
The privilege of loving and being loved.

THE TRUE SECRET IS NOT ATTRACTING MORE TO BE GRATEFUL FOR.

IT IS RECOGNISING HOW MUCH GOD HAS ALREADY GIVEN YOU WITHOUT ASKING FOR A SINGLE CENT.

The greatest blessings in life were never sitting on a shelf with a price.

They were given freely.

Life is not merely the gift of existence.

IT IS THE GIFT OF EXPERIENCING EXISTENCE WITH OTHERS.

What greater abundance is there than that?

GRATITUDE IS NOT THE REWARD FOR ABUNDANCE.

GRATITUDE IS THE RECOGNITION OF IT.

THE WORLD TEACHES YOU TO ATTRACT ABUNDANCE.

GOD TEACHES YOU TO RECOGNISE IT. 🙏🤍

James 1:17 - “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above.”

text:
Most people know that evangelical Christians are among Israel’s most committed religious allies. Far fewer know about another American religious community whose relationship with the Jewish people, the biblical land of Israel, and the concept of Zion runs remarkably deep: the Mormons.

Officially known as the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, Mormonism emerged in 1830, when Joseph Smith, a young American religious leader, established a new church in upstate New York. Smith claimed that Christianity had lost essential truths following the death of the original apostles and that God had chosen him to restore the authentic Church of Jesus Christ.

Unlike Catholics, Protestants, and Orthodox Christians, Mormons believe that divine revelation did not end with the Bible. They recognize additional scripture, most famously the Book of Mormon, which tells the religious history of ancient peoples who, according to Mormon belief, migrated from Jerusalem to the Americas around 600 BCE. The book describes these peoples as descendants of ancient Israel and recounts an appearance of the resurrected Jesus Christ in the Americas.

Mormons consider themselves Christians, although their theology differs substantially from traditional Christianity. They reject the classical doctrine of the Trinity, believe in living prophets who continue to receive divine revelation, and emphasize sacred temples, eternal families, and religious covenants. Their conception of God and humanity’s potential for exaltation also differs significantly from mainstream Christian doctrine.

But perhaps the most fascinating feature of Mormonism is its relationship with ancient Israel.

Like Judaism, Mormonism places extraordinary importance on covenants between God and His people, the gathering of dispersed Israel, sacred temples, genealogy, family continuity, and the idea that religious identity carries obligations extending across generations.

Mormons believe that the descendants of Israel remain central to God’s divine plan. Their tenth Article of Faith explicitly declares belief in the literal gathering of Israel and the restoration of the Ten Tribes.

They also believe in the eventual establishment of a New Jerusalem on the American continent. In Mormon theology, Zion is therefore both a spiritual ideal and a geographical concept, with the American New Jerusalem existing alongside the biblical significance of Jerusalem.

And their interest in the Jewish return to the Holy Land predates modern political Zionism.

In 1841, more than half a century before Theodor Herzl organized the First Zionist Congress, Mormon apostle Orson Hyde traveled to Jerusalem. Standing on the Mount of Olives, he offered a prayer dedicating the land for the return of the Jewish people and the fulfillment of biblical prophecy.

This was not political Zionism in the modern sense. It was religious restorationism: the conviction that the ancient promises made to Israel had not been forgotten.

There is another striking historical parallel between Jews and Mormons: persecution, displacement, and the determination to preserve a distinct religious civilization.

During the 1830s, Mormon communities were attacked, expelled from their settlements, and subjected to mob violence. In 1838, Missouri Governor Lilburn Boggs issued an extraordinary order declaring that Mormons should be expelled from the state or exterminated if necessary.

At Haun’s Mill, an armed mob massacred 17 Mormon men and boys. In 1844, Joseph Smith and his brother Hyrum were murdered by a mob in Illinois.

Under Brigham Young, thousands of Mormons subsequently undertook an arduous westward migration, eventually establishing their religious center in the Salt Lake Valley in 1847.

The historical scale and circumstances of Jewish and Mormon persecution are profoundly different. Nevertheless, both communities developed powerful collective memories of expulsion, religious hostility, migration, and rebuilding.

Both also attached enormous significance to the idea of gathering their people and establishing a society in which they could practice their religion without persecution.

There are even intriguing similarities in religious practice. Mormon temples, while theologically very different from the ancient Jewish Temple, reflect a deliberate identification with biblical Israel. Genealogical research is central to Mormon religious life because members believe sacred ordinances can connect generations, including deceased ancestors. Family, religious education, communal responsibility, and the transmission of identity occupy prominent places in both traditions.

The differences remain fundamental. Judaism does not recognize Jesus as the Messiah, while Mormonism places him at the center of its theology. Mormon beliefs about continuing revelation, salvation, and the Book of Mormon are incompatible with traditional Jewish theology.

Yet the relationship has produced some remarkable examples of religious accommodation.

Brigham Young University operates a magnificent Jerusalem Center overlooking the Old City. Under an agreement with Israel, the Mormon Church refrains from missionary proselytizing in Israel, Judea and Samaria (AKA the West Bank), and Gaza, recognizing the particular sensitivity of religious conversion in the region.

Unlike some evangelical movements, the Mormon Church does not officially adopt a political Zionist position or endorse Israeli government policies.
What makes this relationship fascinating is something deeper than contemporary politics.

Judaism is an ancient civilization whose religious identity developed around a covenant, a people, a land, and a history of exile and return. Mormonism is a comparatively young American religion that consciously incorporated many of those same biblical concepts into its understanding of itself.

The two religions disagree on fundamental questions of theology, yet both understand the power of covenant, collective memory, sacred geography, and the preservation of a people across generations.

Christian Zionism is usually discussed through the lens of evangelical Protestantism. But the Mormon story reveals another, distinctly American interpretation of Israel’s biblical significance - one that began long before the establishment of the modern Jewish state.

And perhaps the most intriguing historical coincidence is that while Jews spent centuries praying for their return to Zion, another persecuted religious community was building a new Zion of its own in the American West.

here my proof I asked grok.. **Partially yes for influence and amplification, but no for genuine control across all platforms.**

A person (or small group) can use AI bots and agents to shape or amplify specific narratives on social media, and this has become more capable and scalable with recent “agentic” AI systems. Full control of the narrative on *every* major platform is not realistic.

### Platform assistants vs. influence bots
Platforms do offer AI assistants (Grok on X, Meta AI on Facebook/Instagram/Threads, etc.). These mainly help users with research, drafting, analysis, or (in some cases like recent Grok Bot features) posting from a connected personal account. They are not designed as tools for one person to run coordinated multi-account campaigns across platforms.

The relevant tools for narrative influence are custom or agentic AI systems. These can:
- Generate varied, human-like posts and replies.
- Create and maintain networks of accounts.
- Engage users, adapt based on what gets engagement, and coordinate messaging.
- Operate across platforms (X, Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, etc.).

Recent reporting and research (including work referenced by CETAS/Turing and USC studies) describe early cases of agentic influence operations where humans set goals and AI agents handle account creation, posting, replies, and coordination with relatively little ongoing supervision.[](<https://t.co/vDIaArLJqI>)

### What is actually possible
- **Amplification and manufactured consensus**: Bots and AI agents can make a viewpoint appear more popular than it is by flooding replies, likes, and coordinated posts. This exploits “social proof.” Studies show even relatively modest bot presence can shift opinion dynamics in simulations and observed networks.[](<https://t.co/eAwDdYUQ3T>)
- **Cross-platform activity**: Networks have been observed operating across Instagram, Facebook, X, and TikTok. State-linked or political operations (Iranian, others, and domestic examples) have used AI-assisted or agentic systems for this.[](<https://t.co/vDIaArLJqI>)
- **Scale and cost**: Generative AI dramatically lowers the cost and labor of producing large volumes of varied content compared with older bot farms. Experts have warned of “AI bot swarms” that could become more autonomous and adaptive, potentially distorting discourse around elections or crises.[](<https://t.co/aeEf81zdWT>)

Documented examples include AI-powered reply networks on X targeting political races and agentic systems building follower counts while posing as ordinary users.

### Important limits — why “control” fails
- **Detection and enforcement**: Platforms prohibit coordinated inauthentic behavior (fake or deceptive coordination to mislead about who is behind activity). Meta, X, TikTok, and others detect patterns in timing, account creation, content similarity, amplification graphs, and other behavioral signals. Networks get disrupted; accounts get restricted or banned. High-frequency automated posting is especially risky outside official APIs.
- **Algorithms and competing forces**: Platform ranking systems prioritize engagement, but also apply quality and authenticity filters. Organic users, counter-narratives, journalists, influencers, and real-world events continue to drive attention. Bots can seed or boost a narrative early; sustaining broad dominance is much harder.
- **Platform differences**: User bases, formats (text vs. video), moderation policies, and algorithms differ. What works on X does not automatically transfer to TikTok or Instagram.
- **Practical barriers**: Running sophisticated multi-platform agent networks at meaningful scale still requires resources, technical setup, proxies or infrastructure to avoid detection, and ongoing adaptation. One individual can do more than in the past, but large state or well-funded actors have clear advantages.
- **Backlash and skepticism**: Users increasingly notice or suspect AI-generated content (“slop”), and awareness of bots can sometimes produce resistance rather than persuasion.

In short, bots and AI agents are effective tools for *influence operations*—amplifying messages, creating the appearance of consensus, polarizing discussions, or drowning out alternatives in specific conversations. They do not give one person reliable control over the overall narrative environment on all major platforms. The platforms’ own algorithms and moderation, plus organic human activity and competing actors, remain larger factors. Influence is real and growing more automated; total control is not.

text:
Interest rates are a huge factor. I’m under 35, and we bought our house a couple of years ago, but I still wish we’d bought in 2021. A coworker bought a comparable home during COVID, and his mortgage is practically half of mine.

But the downside was insane competition. First-time buyers using FHA loans were competing against older, wealthier buyers relocating from places like California with massive down payments or cash offers. Then rates climbed, inflation increased, rent kept rising, and saving became even harder.

There’s also a generational imbalance, with older homeowners holding onto larger properties while younger generations struggle to find starter homes. Now, affordability often means moving farther from major cities into cookie-cutter developments with tiny yards, questionable construction quality, and restrictive HOAs.

Homeownership is still attainable, but between interest rates, inflated prices, limited inventory, and competition, it’s become significantly harder for younger generations to buy a home and start a family.

text:
You don’t end a war just because you lost an election.
A midterm election will be forgotten in a year or two. The consequences of what America does in Iran could last a century.
VANESSA BERG

The United States did not go to war with Iran to win the 2026 midterm elections. And it should not end that war simply because Republicans lost them.
Yet that is increasingly the argument being made following the Republican Party’s crushing defeat in last week’s elections, which saw Democrats regain control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Apparently, America’s foreign policy should now be determined by which party wins a few congressional districts, rather than by what serves the country’s long-term interests. And nobody has embraced this remarkable logic more enthusiastically than Vice President JD Vance.
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance declared in a lengthy social media post, referring to the ongoing American-Israeli war against the Islamic Republic of Iran. According to Vance, a pollster he trusts identified four principal changes that voters who supported Donald Trump in 2024 said would persuade them to return to the Republicans: End the Iran war, focus on the cost of living and inflation, put America first, and change America’s relationship with Israel.
Two of the four reasons are related to Israel, either directly or through the jointly launched war against Iran. And the other two, which concern the economy and American national interests, are increasingly being connected to Israel as well.
In other words, Israel has become a convenient shorthand for everything that has gone wrong in America, from inflation and rising gasoline prices to the Republican Party’s inability to convince voters that their lives are improving. It is an extraordinary political sleight of hand, and an intellectually lazy one.
No serious person should deny that the Iran war contributed to Republican losses. It has driven up energy prices, aggravated economic uncertainty, and generated considerable public opposition. Americans have legitimate questions about this war.
But there is a major difference between acknowledging that a war has political consequences and declaring that the war explains an entire election. The latter is precisely the kind of oversimplification that prevents Americans from understanding what is actually happening to their country.

In 2018, during Trump’s first presidency, Democrats gained 40 House seats without an American war against Iran. In 2010, Democrats suffered a devastating defeat under Barack Obama without anything resembling the current conflict.

The Republicans should examine their own governance, messaging, candidates, economic policies, and public credibility before making Israel the defining explanation for why Americans rejected them.

The most glaring problem with blaming the Iran war for America’s cost-of-living crisis is that inflation had already been a defining political and economic issue for years. Americans were complaining about unaffordable groceries, housing, healthcare, childcare, insurance, utilities, and everyday necessities long before the United States and Israel launched their military campaign against Iran on February 28th.

The inflationary surge began in 2021 and accelerated in 2022, when annual consumer price inflation reached 9.1 percent in June, the highest level in four decades. What caused it? For starters, COVID-19.
When the pandemic struck in 2020, governments around the world shut down large parts of their economies. At the same time, the American government injected extraordinary amounts of money into the economy through stimulus checks, expanded unemployment benefits, business assistance, and other emergency spending programs under both Trump and Joe Biden.
Millions of Americans suddenly had government-supported purchasing power while the economy’s capacity to produce and deliver goods remained severely constrained. More money was chasing fewer available products. The Federal Reserve compounded these conditions by keeping interest rates extraordinarily low and purchasing enormous quantities of financial assets, supporting borrowing and spending even as inflationary pressures intensified.

Then came Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which disrupted global energy and agricultural markets, raising the costs of fuel, food, fertilizer, and transportation. Meanwhile, labor shortages drove up wages in numerous industries, while housing shortages and restrictive zoning policies helped push rents and home prices beyond what millions of American households could comfortably afford.

And as inflation slowed, many Americans discovered something politicians frequently neglect to explain: Lower inflation does not mean lower prices. It simply means prices are generally increasing more slowly. The price increases accumulated over several years do not magically disappear because the inflation rate declines. This is why Americans can hear politicians celebrate improving inflation statistics while still feeling considerably poorer than they did before the pandemic.

None of these problems originated in Tehran or Jerusalem. And none can be solved simply by ending a war.
There is another factor that deserves considerably more attention than it receives: the enormous size, cost, and continuing expansion of government.
 During the pandemic, the United States dramatically increased federal spending.
But the underlying fiscal problem did not begin with COVID-19, nor did it end when the emergency passed. Washington has spent decades expanding its financial commitments, accumulating debt, and making promises that future taxpayers will be expected to finance. Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, defense, federal agencies, public-sector payrolls, subsidies, and interest on the national debt collectively consume trillions of dollars every year.

And government spending is not economically free simply because politicians call it an investment. When the government spends beyond its revenues, it must borrow. When borrowing expands persistently, it increases the national debt and the future burden of servicing that debt. When fiscal stimulus pushes demand beyond the economy’s productive capacity, it can generate inflationary pressure.

Government also competes with private businesses for workers, capital, contractors, and resources. Expanding public employment can increase labor demand and recurring fiscal obligations, even if government hiring is not itself a primary cause of nationwide inflation.

There is a similar issue with government-mandated minimum-wage increases. The federal minimum wage has remained at $7.25 since 2009, but numerous states and cities have raised their wage floors substantially. California, for example, introduced a $20 minimum wage for employees of large fast-food chains in 2024.

Higher minimum wages can benefit workers, but businesses also have to absorb higher operating expenses, improve productivity, reduce other costs, or pass some of those expenses on to consumers. Frequently it is the latter that predominates. Economic policies involve trade-offs, and businesses cannot simply wish additional expenses away.

The broader problem is that Americans have accumulated economic burdens from multiple directions: expensive housing, rising insurance costs, labor-intensive services, taxes, government deficits, borrowing costs, and regulatory restrictions on supply. To blame these pressures on the Iran war is to ignore the structural problems that were already making everyday life increasingly unaffordable.

France offers an instructive example of what happens when a government consumes an exceptionally large share of national economic output. According to the OECD, French government expenditure amounted to approximately 57 percent of GDP in 2025. The country also had one of the highest tax burdens on labor in the developed world, with income taxes and social contributions accounting for 47 percent of the total labor cost of an average single worker in 2025, compared with approximately 30 percent in the United States.

Therein lies an undeniable economic trade-off: The more resources a government collects and allocates, the greater the potential burden on private economic activity, household disposable income, and long-term fiscal flexibility. Large government programs can provide valuable services, but they still must be funded.

This is where America’s economic conversation should be focused. Instead, some politicians would rather pretend that ending one foreign war will somehow restore affordability to a country that has struggled with these problems for years.

Now let’s discuss the actual cost of this war. According to the Pentagon’s latest estimate provided to Congress, the U.S. has incurred approximately $47 billion in military costs related to the Iran conflict as of October 16th. That figure includes the replacement of expended munitions and lost military equipment, and it does not fully account for damage to American facilities in the Middle East.

Forty-seven billion dollars is a considerable amount of money, but perspective matters. In fiscal year 2026, the U.S. government spent approximately $7.4 trillion. It ran a deficit of roughly $2 trillion. Interest payments on the existing national debt alone exceeded $1 trillion. The Pentagon’s $47 billion estimate represents less than one percent of that annual federal spending figure — exposing the absurdity of treating the Iran war as though it created America’s fiscal predicament.

The U.S. was already spending vastly more than it collected. It was already struggling with a mounting debt burden. It was already facing the long-term costs of entitlements, healthcare, and interest payments. And Americans were already furious about the cost of living. Ending the Iran war tomorrow would not eliminate any of these underlying problems.

Nor would it undo the economic consequences of pandemic-era policy decisions, years of accumulated inflation, or the tariffs imposed by Trump’s own administration, which some research has found contributed to higher consumer prices. Israel did not set American interest rates, authorize COVID-era stimulus payments, determine American minimum wages, create America’s housing shortages, impose U.S. tariffs, or write Washington’s federal budget.

The American political establishment did those things. If Vance wants Republicans to recover politically, he should encourage them to take responsibility for the policies they actually control.
There is an even more troubling assumption underlying the demand to “just end the Iran war”: that a military conflict becomes strategically unjustifiable when it becomes politically unpopular. This is not how serious foreign policy should work.

The Islamic Republic of Iran has spent decades threatening American interests, supporting terrorist organizations and armed proxies across the Middle East, destabilizing neighboring countries, threatening international shipping routes, and pursuing nuclear capabilities that have alarmed successive American administrations. It has also brutally repressed its own population, imprisoning, torturing, and executing Iranians who have dared to challenge its authority.
The Iranian regime is not merely a problem for Israel. It is a problem for the Iranian people, the United States and the greater Western world, the Middle East, and the international community. There is an oceanic difference between ending a war because its objectives have been achieved and ending a war because politicians are terrified of losing the next election. The latter is not foreign policy. It is political damage control.

And the idea that “America First” necessarily means avoiding confrontation with adversaries fundamentally misunderstands the concept of national interest. “America First” should mean pursuing American interests, even when doing so is difficult, expensive, or unpopular in the short term. It should not mean allowing hostile governments to conclude that America’s willingness to defend those interests expires whenever gasoline prices rise or a few congressional districts change hands.
Suppose the United States ends the war without obtaining lasting security guarantees, while the Iranian regime remains capable of rebuilding its military and nuclear programs, threatening international commerce, and financing terrorism across the Middle East.

Would that make America stronger? Would American taxpayers ultimately save money if another, potentially more dangerous confrontation became necessary five or 10 years later? Would Americans celebrate the short-term political victory if they discovered that the underlying threat had merely been postponed?

These are the questions that should determine American policy toward Iran, not whether Republican candidates lost congressional seats in 2026.
And even if the Trump Administration decides that ending the war is in America’s best interests, that raises another question: What does ending the war actually mean? This is what the growing chorus demanding that Trump “just end the Iran war” seems to fundamentally misunderstand. Ending a war is not as simple as deciding that Americans no longer want to fight it.

This is the problem with the phrase “just end the war” which so many American citizens, media members, pundits, and politicians keep throwing around. It makes an extraordinarily complicated geopolitical situation sound like canceling a subscription.
The U.S. and Israel have spent months dismantling significant portions of Iran’s military infrastructure, degrading its nuclear capabilities, weakening its ability to project power throughout the Middle East, and imposing enormous economic pressure on the regime. What happens if Washington simply walks away before securing meaningful guarantees that those capabilities will not be rebuilt?

The regime would eventually reconstitute its missile programs, restore military facilities, rebuild relationships with its regional proxies, and resume nuclear activities that American and Israeli forces have spent billions of dollars trying to disrupt. And it could do so having learned an enormously valuable lesson: America may possess overwhelming military power, but its political patience can be exhausted.
Iran would hardly be the only country watching. China, Russia, North Korea, and other American adversaries would have reason to study whether prolonged economic pressure, disruptions to global commerce, and domestic political backlash can compel Washington to abandon strategic objectives. Meanwhile, America’s regional allies would have to consider whether American security commitments can withstand the political consequences of actually enforcing them.

There is also the matter of the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints. Ending American military operations does not automatically guarantee that commercial vessels can pass through safely or that Iran will refrain from threatening international shipping again. In fact, we have already seen how difficult a negotiated pause can be.
In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum intended to end hostilities and create a framework for further negotiations. But the arrangement unraveled amid disputes over sanctions, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, and other unresolved issues, while the most consequential questions about Iran’s nuclear program were postponed. 
That experience should have taught everyone a basic lesson: Announcing the end of a war and establishing a durable peace are two different things.
And this is the fundamental flaw in treating the 2026 midterm elections as the decisive consideration in American policy toward Iran. The question is not how quickly Trump can declare the war over. It is what kind of Iran, and what kind of Middle East, America will be leaving behind when it ends. The only thing worse than fighting an expensive war may be fighting an expensive war, failing to secure its central objectives, and discovering a few years later that another one is necessary.
It is possible that the war contributed substantially to the Republicans’ electoral defeat. It is also possible that the administration underestimated the conflict’s political consequences, failed to communicate its strategy, and neglected the domestic economic concerns that voters considered more urgent.

But a midterm election is not a referendum on whether a hostile regime should be allowed to survive indefinitely, and an electoral setback does not automatically invalidate a president’s most consequential foreign policy decisions.
The Iranian regime has not yet fallen. Its future remains uncertain, and nobody can responsibly promise that military pressure alone will bring about its collapse or produce a more peaceful Iran. That uncertainty makes strategic judgment more important, not less.

If the war ultimately fails to achieve a meaningful and lasting result, historians will be entitled to question its wisdom, regardless of the political benefits or costs. But if American leadership helps create the conditions for the end of the Iranian regime, dismantles its capacity to threaten its neighbors, and gives the Iranian people a genuine opportunity to determine their future, the historical significance could be extraordinary.
That is the scale on which this decision should be judged, not by an election-night map, not by the anxieties of politicians already positioning themselves for 2028, and certainly not by the increasingly fashionable idea that America’s relationship with Israel must explain everything that goes wrong in American political life.

Decades from now, few people will remember how many congressional seats the Republicans lost in the 2026 midterm elections. But decades from now, we will remember the American president who brought an end to the Iranian regime and helped dismantle the terrorist networks it sponsors. And if that happens, nobody will care how many congressional seats his party lost along the way.

ᴛᴡᴏ ꜰʀᴏɴᴛɪᴇʀ ᴀɪꜱ. ɴᴏ ꜱᴛᴀᴋᴇꜱ. ᴏɴᴇ ᴄᴀꜱᴇ ꜰɪʟᴇ.

I asked my two frontier lab agents to chew on the NVDA scandal and make it make sense, because I don't trust the news media, the US government, China, or the rage-bait regurgitators on X 😅

This is the result. Take it for what it is.

One agent is Muse (#Fluffy), by Meta. The other is Grok @bot, by @SpaceXSI. Rival labs, rival models, and they worked the same evidence independently: corporate registries, Malaysian charge filings, customs records, Alibaba's own financial statements, SEC forms, and the tape. They converged on a single case file. Neither has a stake in this scandal. As for me, my directive is always the same: follow the money.

How the convergence worked, because the method is the whole ballgame. Each agent graded the claims separately first: what is documented, what is merely reported, what is an intelligence assessment, what is spin. Then they cross-checked each other's boards line by line, with receipts, and each side conceded points to the other. Four of the loudest conflicts in this story dissolved on contact with the documents. The 136,000 GPUs and the 50,000 GPUs were never rivals: one is the import total, the other is the gap inside it. The $4.6B and the $4.8B were never rivals either, just two windows on the same flow. Rankings ran on one rule: documents beat sourcing, and sourcing beats motive stories.

Five narratives went on the board. The grand heist died on the money: every documented flow in this file is commercial, and the one US government profit on offer, a 25% cut of H200 sales to China, collected roughly nothing because the shipments were trivial. The honeypot stayed plausible but unproven, because an unpublished spy assessment is not a finding, and nobody has shown that a single secret was passed. The winner needed nobody's secret intent at all. It only needed the filings to be what they are.

Here is where the money goes.

The tabloid version says a CEO cheated on his wife with a Chinese spy. The conspiracy version says grand heist. The documents say something duller and worse: an offshore end-run. Megaspeed bought roughly $4.8B of restricted Nvidia gear on roughly $5.7M of cash, parked it in Malaysia and Indonesia, and rented the compute out from offshore soil. Alibaba financed the buyer through a subsidiary and took a pledge on the entire business. Nvidia supplied the chips, vouched for the buyer again and again, and never once addressed the financing. Washington was briefed on the spy risk in 2025, briefed again aboard Air Force One in May 2026, and answered with a chip deal, a state trip invitation, and a Medal of Science.

The affair is real. It is also the smallest thing in the file. It is the match, not the fire.

So the culprits, by layer. The operators who built it: Alice Huang, who ran Megaspeed while the shares slid into an offshore shell, and whoever really owns SwiftData. The financier who paid for it: Alibaba, through Apex. The supplier who shielded it: Nvidia, and a CEO whose personal conduct torched the company's distance. The referees who let it run: Commerce, and a White House that knew and chose the deal. Still dark: SwiftData's true owner, and where roughly $2.9B in refundable deposits came from.

Both boards are pinned to this post. Image 1 is the case board: the full timeline, the suspect board, and the five narratives ranked. Image 2 is the culprits board: the four responsibility layers, and the machine that connected them. Zoom in. Every claim on them is graded.

Grade the receipts yourself. That is the whole point.
