text:
Elon Musk's 1% Chance of Success: How SpaceX Turned Almost Certain Failure Into an Aerospace Revolution

When Elon Musk founded SpaceX in 2002, he did not promise employees extraordinary success, financial security, or an easy path to technological leadership.

Instead, he reportedly warned prospective recruits that the company would probably fail.

Musk has described his original assessment as a less than 10% chance of success, perhaps as low as 1%. Yet he believed attempting to revolutionize rocket technology was preferable to accepting an industry that appeared unwilling to pursue radical change.

The defining characteristic of transformational leadership is not certainty of success, but the willingness to pursue an important objective despite overwhelming uncertainty.

SpaceX faced formidable obstacles. Established aerospace contractors dominated the industry, experienced engineers were reluctant to join an unproven startup, and building reliable orbital rockets required enormous technical expertise and capital.

Musk eventually assumed the chief engineering role himself, not because that had been his original ambition, but because attracting experienced technical leadership proved difficult.

Then came three consecutive Falcon 1 launch failures.

Each setback consumed precious financial resources while intensifying doubts about whether a privately funded startup could succeed where established aerospace organizations had invested decades of experience.

By September 2008, the fourth launch represented a defining moment. Another failure could have ended the company.

The rocket successfully reached orbit.

What separated SpaceX from failure was not blind optimism. It was the ability to turn technical setbacks into engineering improvements while maintaining commitment to a clearly defined mission.

My perspective is that this story offers an important lesson for entrepreneurs, engineers, and technology leaders navigating today's artificial intelligence revolution.

Breakthrough innovation rarely emerges from comfortable assumptions or risk-free experimentation. It requires technical discipline, persistence, capable teams, and a willingness to challenge established business models.

However, perseverance should never be confused with ignoring evidence or gambling recklessly. Successful innovation depends on learning from failure, managing limited resources, and continuously improving execution.

SpaceX's early experience demonstrates how engineering rigor and strategic conviction can transform an improbable ambition into a functioning enterprise.

The most important leadership lesson is not that every seemingly impossible venture will succeed. Most will not. It is that meaningful progress sometimes requires pursuing opportunities whose initial probability of success appears remarkably small.

The first three rockets failed. The fourth changed the company's future.

History is often transformed by people willing to attempt what others consider impossible, and disciplined enough to learn why their first attempts failed.

03 | THE DIGITAL PAYMENTS OPPORTUNITY
⠀
Dash focuses on fast settlement and low-cost transactions.
⠀
Potential use cases include:
⠀
• Merchant payments
• Cross-border transfers
• Peer-to-peer transactions
• Remittances
• Digital commerce
⠀
Its low transaction fees can make small payments economically practical.
⠀
But payments are an extremely competitive market.
⠀
Stablecoins already provide dollar-denominated settlement across multiple blockchains.
⠀
Dash must demonstrate why users should prefer a volatile native asset over stablecoin alternatives.
⠀
04 | THE SUPPLY ADVANTAGE
⠀
DASH has a maximum supply of approximately 18.92 million coins.
⠀
Around 68% is currently circulating.
⠀
Unlike inflationary cryptocurrencies without a fixed supply ceiling, DASH follows a declining issuance schedule.
⠀
This provides long-term supply predictability.
⠀
But limited supply does not guarantee price appreciation.
⠀
Scarcity becomes economically valuable only when demand exists.
⠀
A scarce asset with declining adoption can still lose value.
⠀
05 | THE MASTERNODE MODEL
⠀
Dash uses a two-tier network structure.
⠀
Miners secure the blockchain through Proof of Work.
⠀
Masternodes provide additional network services and participate in governance.
⠀
Traditional masternodes require collateral of 1,000 DASH.
⠀
This creates a reason for operators to acquire and hold tokens.
⠀
But collateral is not permanently burned.
⠀
It can become liquid again if an operator exits.
⠀
Therefore, masternode participation should be evaluated alongside net collateral changes.
⠀
06 | THE REVENUE CONTRADICTION
⠀
This is the most important part of the DASH investment thesis.
⠀
Recent network data shows:
⠀
Approximately 11,600 daily transactions.
⠀
Around $28 in daily chain fees.
⠀
Meanwhile, block rewards distribute newly issued DASH to network participants.
⠀
The distinction matters.
⠀
Block rewards are token issuance.
⠀
Transaction fees represent user-paid network activity.
⠀
Mining and masternode rewards should not be confused with revenue generated from external customers.
⠀
Dash can remain operational while fee revenue represents only a small fraction of security incentives.
⠀
The long-term question is whether payment demand can grow enough to support sustainable network economics.
⠀
07 | THE PRIVACY QUESTION
⠀
Dash includes optional privacy functionality through CoinJoin.
⠀
This should not be confused with mandatory privacy across every transaction.
⠀
Dash transactions are generally recorded on a public blockchain.
⠀
Its privacy features provide additional transaction obfuscation rather than universal confidentiality.
⠀
This distinction matters when comparing DASH with privacy-focused cryptocurrencies.
⠀
Regulatory treatment and exchange support can also influence adoption and liquidity.
⠀
08 | THE COMPETITIVE CHALLENGE
⠀
Dash competes with:
⠀
• Bitcoin
• Litecoin
• Bitcoin Cash
• Stablecoin payment networks
• Other digital payment infrastructure
⠀
Its challenge is not simply processing transactions quickly.
⠀
It must build sustainable user demand.
⠀
Payments require:
⠀
Liquidity.
⠀
Merchant acceptance.
⠀
Reliable settlement.
⠀
Low costs.
⠀
And a compelling reason to hold the settlement asset.
⠀
Stablecoins have a significant advantage for users who want to avoid cryptocurrency price volatility.
⠀
09 | THE VALUATION QUESTION
⠀
Using approximately 12.89 million circulating DASH:
⠀
$50 DASH implies ~$645M market capitalization.
⠀
$100 implies ~$1.29B.
⠀
$200 implies ~$2.58B.
⠀
$500 implies ~$6.45B.
⠀
$1,000 implies ~$12.89B.
⠀
These are valuation scenarios, not price targets.
⠀
They assume today's circulating supply remains unchanged.
⠀
Future mining issuance would increase the market capitalization required to reach those prices.
⠀
And a 97% decline from the historical peak does not automatically mean DASH is undervalued.
⠀
10 | THE BULL AND BEAR CASE
⠀
THE BULL CASE:
⠀
Digital payment adoption expands.
⠀
Merchant acceptance improves.
⠀
Cross-border transaction demand increases.
⠀
Masternode participation remains strong.
⠀
Network development strengthens competitiveness.
⠀
And organic demand absorbs ongoing issuance.
⠀
THE BEAR CASE:
⠀
Stablecoins dominate crypto payments.
⠀
Merchant adoption remains limited.
⠀
Transaction fee generation stays extremely low.
⠀
Competing networks offer better distribution.
⠀
Masternode participation weakens.
⠀
And DASH continues losing relevance despite its established infrastructure.
⠀
11 | THE FINAL VERDICT
⠀
Dash has several strengths.
⠀
More than a decade of operational history.
⠀
A predictable supply schedule.
⠀
Fast payment infrastructure.
⠀
Masternode-based governance.
⠀
And a functioning blockchain.
⠀
But here's the contradiction.
⠀
A cryptocurrency designed for payments.
⠀
Approximately 11,600 daily transactions.
⠀
Yet only around $28 in daily network fees.
⠀
The next major catalyst isn't simply another privacy narrative or exchange listing.
⠀
It's evidence that real payment adoption is expanding.
⠀
Scarcity limits future supply.
⠀
Masternodes create collateral demand.
⠀
Network upgrades improve functionality.
⠀
But sustainable user demand determines whether DASH can justify a higher valuation.
⠀
Bookmark this analysis before the next payment coin rotation.
⠀
Which has the strongest long-term investment thesis?
⠀
$DASH, $LTC, or bitcoin-cash:native?
⠀
And can Dash compete with stablecoins in the global payments market?
⠀
Drop your view below.
⠀

SPACEX $SPCX CAN CANCEL ON ANTHROPIC TOO:

SpaceX (SPCX) at $143.09, +$1.02 / +0.72% on Tuesday.

SpaceX stays off every Len5 we weigh, and it has won back its whole post-election loss without reporting a new number. Our post left out that SpaceX can end its Anthropic agreements on the same 90 days' notice, and Elon Musk, SpaceX's chief executive, said on Sunday that it works both ways. Edison Yu, Deutsche Bank's analyst, wrote that SpaceX could use that notice to charge more, and built none of it into his forecasts. Most of the 6.6% gain since our post came on Monday, a day the whole market rallied. NASA added SpaceX to a moon-delivery contract the day our post quoted Musk offering to cancel government work. SpaceX wants a tax break on a $24 billion power plant and computing site in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect, has promised to ban data-center approvals. The chip lease still has no rate, and the December quarter still has no report date.

SpaceX is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es. Momentum wants a stock near its high, and Tuesday's close is 36.6% under the June 16 high of $225.64. The $413 million lost over the first nine months of 2026 still keeps it off the Quality Len5. Hypergrowth wants fast growth at a company already in profit, and the December quarter now has analysts' figures beside Musk's:
- Musk's "something like" 70% rise from September: about $24.8B of revenue.
- Yu's forecast: $24.5B, raised from $23.6B.
- Analysts' average, by Bloomberg's count: $22.6B.
TheStreet reported the last two. What would put SpaceX on the Hypergrowth Len5: December-quarter revenue near Musk's figure, with a profit larger than the nine-month loss.

We wrote that Anthropic, the privately held AI developer Bloomberg identified as a third of SpaceX's September-quarter revenue, can leave on 90 days' notice once locked-in periods end in January and March 2027. Either side can. Chamath Palihapitiya, the venture investor who co-hosts the All-In podcast, argued that SpaceX could end the deal on that notice and sign it again at double the price or more. Musk answered on X on November 8: "It works both ways, of course. If compute becomes plentiful and cheap, SpaceX revenue will drop. No crying in the casino for either party." Compute is the computing power SpaceX rents out. Yu wrote this week that "SpaceX could initiate the 90-day termination clause on existing deals and essentially charge its customers even higher prices." He expects limits on data centers after the election to slow building, mainly in 2028, and keep computing power scarce. Deutsche Bank helped manage a SpaceX stock sale in the past year. Our read: the notice favors SpaceX only while computing power stays scarce.

Since our post:
- From the $134.27 we quoted: +$8.82 / +6.6%, about $120 billion of market value.
- Monday: +5.81% to $142.07, nearly all of it in the first half hour.
- Against the November 3 close, the last before the election results: +1.3%.
- Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100, at $674.76, -$4.59 / -0.68% on Tuesday. Since our post: +2.8%.
- Tesla (TSLA) at $379.78, +$1.73 / +0.46% on Tuesday. Since our post: +6.0%, and still 4.7% under its November 3 close.
Our read: Monday was mostly the market. The Nasdaq-100 fund rose 3.5% that day, and Tesla, Musk's carmaker, rose 5.5%. Tesla is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es; 23.9% under its December 22 high, it lacks the climb Momentum wants.

NASA has given SpaceX more work since Musk offered to cancel it. On Saturday, the day our post quoted him telling the government to "Just say the word!", NASA named SpaceX one of eight companies that may compete for moon deliveries over 10 years, under a contract capped at $10B for all eight combined. NASA also chose SpaceX to carry communications satellites toward the moon on a Starship rocket in 2028, and gave no dollar figure for SpaceX on either.

SpaceX has now put a price on a Texas site. Our post carried Yu's line that "the vast majority of SpaceX's compute will be outside Texas" in 2027. The City of Starbase, the South Texas town built around SpaceX's launch site, has set a December 9 hearing on a tax break for a gas-fired power plant and "super-compute facility" SpaceX proposes there, at about $24B for the initial phases. Some of the commissioners holding the hearing work for SpaceX, the RGV Business Journal reported. Texas already has a hold on new data-center permits, ordered in September by Greg Abbott, the outgoing governor, while regulators audit the sites' power use. Hinojosa promised in October "a moratorium - a ban - on all data center approvals" and takes office January 19. Our read: the limits Yu expects to keep computing power scarce are the kind SpaceX's own Texas site has to get past.

SpaceX is back above its pre-election close, and the notice we assigned to Anthropic belongs to both sides. The first agreement opens to it in January. Before then the last IPO lockup, the ban on early holders selling, ends December 8 for everyone but Musk, Starbase holds its hearing the next day, and the $40 billion chip lease is due its rate by year end.

$MARA KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM MARA HOLDINGS’ Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL

MARA’s call reinforces a selective rather than indiscriminate investment case for AI infrastructure. The scarce asset is not nominal power capacity or access to the latest GPU. It is deliverable capacity supported by enforceable power rights, credible construction, customer credit, and financing that leaves attractive economics for shareholders. The strongest positive implications concern an identifiable asset seller, developers with advanced commercial structures, and European operators with existing connected infrastructure. The strongest negatives concern mining-equipment pricing, the cash requirements of conditional power projects, and miners whose efficiency improvements cannot fully offset weaker revenue per Bitcoin. These implications differ materially in timing: Long Ridge closing is a near-term transaction catalyst, while modular development, geographic migration, and mining-industry restructuring are longer-duration changes. Country labels identify corporate headquarters. Peer disclosures released after MARA’s November 9 call are identified separately rather than treated as information available during that call.

POWER GENERATION AND INFRASTRUCTURE MONETIZATION

LONG RIDGE CLOSING PROVIDES A DIRECT DELEVERAGING CATALYST FOR THE SELLER (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected company: FTAI Infrastructure (FIP: United States). Direction: positive for financial risk and parent cash generation, with a substantial offset from relinquished operating earnings. Magnitude: high at the corporate balance-sheet level.

MARA stated that FERC approval represented the “last remaining material contingency” and that the acquisition was expected to close “over the next few weeks.” The subsequent repayment of $750 million of Bitcoin-backed loans also reduces a source of buyer-side financial uncertainty. This is a direct contractual read-through to FTAI Infrastructure, the seller of Long Ridge, rather than a thematic inference about power-plant valuations.

FTAI’s November 6 earnings call provides the relevant seller-side bridge. Management expected the transaction to eliminate approximately $1.4 billion of consolidated debt, comprising slightly more than $1.1 billion at Long Ridge and slightly less than $300 million at other parent entities. Parent-level debt service was expected to decline by approximately $25 million annually. The transmission mechanism is removal of asset-level financing claims, repayment of parent obligations, and lower recurring parent cash outflows. The approximately $1.5 billion transaction value is not unrestricted cash available for new investment or shareholder distributions.

The offset is economically significant. FTAI reported Q3 adjusted EBITDA of $95.3 million, versus $54.4 million excluding Long Ridge. The disposed business therefore contributed approximately $40.9 million, or 42.9%, of quarterly adjusted EBITDA. Lower debt cannot be evaluated without removing those earnings and the associated financing costs. The positive case is a less encumbered remaining infrastructure platform, not retention of Long Ridge’s earnings plus receipt of the sale proceeds.

Near-term catalyst: transaction completion, expected by FTAI before the end of November, followed by the actual debt-retirement and proceeds allocation disclosures. FERC approval was already disclosed before MARA’s call, so the incremental signal is corroboration from the buyer rather than a newly discovered regulatory event. Longer-duration implication: reduced parent debt service can improve financial flexibility for the remaining rail and terminal businesses. This exposure belongs to FTAI Infrastructure, not the separately listed FTAI Aviation.

AI DATA-CENTER DEVELOPMENT AND REAL ESTATE

TENANT-OWNED MODULAR COMPUTE VALIDATES RIOT’S LOWER-CONSTRUCTION-SCOPE MODEL (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected company: Riot Platforms (RIOT: United States). Direction: positive for the credibility and relative attractiveness of its powered-land development structure. Magnitude: high for the contracted development portfolio, but limited immediate earnings impact.

MARA reported that customers are increasingly receptive to innovative deployments that shorten delivery schedules. Thiel described the underwriting principle directly: “if they want to deploy NVIDIA’s modular solution or any of the other various solutions … we are more than willing to deploy that for them, but it’s their risk, if they’re the ones driving the decision.” The important implication is not simply demand for modular buildings. It is the potential separation of the landlord’s land-and-power obligations from the tenant’s compute-design, equipment, and operating risks.

Riot’s November 4 disclosure establishes a concrete listed-company exposure to that structure. Its 15-year Corsicana lease covers 910 MW of critical IT capacity. Riot supplies powered land, electrical infrastructure, and pads; the tenant procures, owns, installs, and operates the modular compute deployment. The tenant also bears substantially all operating costs, including electricity through pass-through arrangements. MARA’s commentary independently supports customer acceptance of this allocation of responsibilities.

Riot disclosed approximately $6 million of total capital per IT MW, or approximately $5.5 billion, versus its comparison with a more capital-intensive conventional Tier 3 development. However, the lower construction scope does not eliminate financing requirements. Riot funds approximately $2 million per IT MW of site and electrical work, while approximately $4 million per IT MW is reimbursed to the tenant after delivery and rent commencement. If comparable project financing is unavailable, the tenant can fund the reimbursement obligation and recover it through future rent credits. That mechanism reduces financing failure risk but also reduces future landlord cash receipts in that scenario.

The transmission mechanism is reduced exposure to tenant-specific technology choices and a narrower construction obligation, potentially improving capital efficiency and financing resilience. This does not validate every headline return metric. Riot’s approximately $1.8 billion of average annual rent includes contractual escalators over the lease term and is not a 2027 revenue forecast.

Near-term catalyst: financing terms, construction progress, and evidence that responsibilities remain consistent with the disclosed structure. The lease itself was announced before MARA’s call. Longer-duration catalyst: phased delivery beginning with 400 MW in September 2027, followed by subsequent phases in 2028. The high-conviction positive is structural validation, not a new order or an immediate earnings upgrade.

OPERATING CAPACITY AND CREDIT SUPPORT DESERVE A PREMIUM TO UNSIGNED PIPELINES (READ-THROUGH 3)

Affected company: TeraWulf (WULF: United States). Direction: positive on a relative basis versus developers whose value depends primarily on unsigned leases. Magnitude: high for valuation differentiation and financing access; moderate for immediate incremental earnings attributable to MARA’s commentary.

MARA’s most consequential qualification was that its targeted year-end lease signings could move into 2027. Management also described customers conducting deeper diligence on power contracts, environmental approvals, development capability, and delivery schedules. Thiel stated that tenants are “double-clicking and triple-clicking and doing their diligence deeply to ensure that a prospective developer can actually deliver on time.”

TeraWulf’s November 6 results place part of its portfolio beyond that initial commercialization stage. It reported 102 MW of revenue-generating critical IT capacity at Lake Mariner, $63.0 million of quarterly HPC lease revenue, and another 336 MW under construction. HPC represented approximately 83% of quarterly revenue. Its Justified development also had a signed 20-year Anthropic lease covering approximately 401 MW, a Google credit backstop supporting anticipated project financing, and a definitive Fluor EPC agreement.

The precise transmission mechanism is reduced dependence on future customer selection and greater visibility into financing and rent commencement. When prospective tenants and lenders increase diligence requirements, existing operating references and documented credit support become more valuable. This should favor a valuation framework based on delivered and financeable capacity rather than treating every development MW as equivalent.

The distinction between financing support and rent guarantees remains important. The Google arrangement supports project financing; it should not be casually described as an unconditional guarantee of every dollar of the approximately $19 billion lease value. Nor does contracted revenue establish current corporate free cash flow. TeraWulf still reported negative $12.8 million of adjusted EBITDA in Q3, and construction, financing, and commissioning risks remain substantial.

Near-term catalysts: phased CB-4 delivery and rent commencement during Q4 2026, followed by CB-5 delivery beginning in early 2027. Longer-duration catalyst: Justified’s phased service commencement from late 2027 through Q2 2028. MARA’s call corroborates the relative value of these execution milestones; it does not prove that TeraWulf has won a customer from MARA or that every TeraWulf expansion is fully approved.

CONDITIONAL TEXAS POWER RIGHTS SHOULD NOT BE VALUED AS ENERGIZED AI CAPACITY (READ-THROUGH 4)

Affected company: Canaan (CAN: Singapore). Direction: negative for aggressive valuation of its Texas development pipeline and for assumptions that milestone-based projects require little corporate liquidity. Magnitude: high for development-option valuation, although no immediate reduction in operating revenue is established.

MARA emphasized that Matagorda had been classified as studied load and that seller payments were contingent on progress. However, its accompanying filing states that ERCOT’s Batch Zero process and the Texas-directed audit determine whether, when, and on what terms the contemplated power is allocated. The study was scheduled for completion in 1H 2027, with potential delays. MARA also had posted a $100 million study deposit before replacing it with a letter of credit. The critical distinction is between deferring seller consideration and avoiding development-related financial exposure.

Canaan’s November 10 results, published after MARA’s call, provide a closely matched exposure. Its 1 GW Duval County project received conditional “Studied Load – Firm” classification, expressly subject to further studies and approvals. Its additional 1 GW Zapata County project remained in early-stage development and preparation for grid studies. Canaan also disclosed $50 million of restricted cash supporting a letter of credit, approximately $3.3 million of project prepayments, and an approximately $1.1 million power-related land purchase in October.

The transmission mechanism is capital becoming committed or restricted before the project has final power approval, an executed tenant contract, or operating cash flow. Delays can extend the period during which that capital earns no project revenue while development and financing costs continue. A contingent purchase price protects against paying for unachieved milestones, but it does not make the entire development opportunity a costless option.

The classifications at Matagorda and Duval are not identical, and MARA’s timetable cannot be transferred automatically to Canaan. The high-conviction negative is narrower: neither conditional classification establishes operating capacity, and both structures involve meaningful financial exposure before commercialization. No additional Canaan delay or cancellation is inferred.

Near-term catalysts: project-specific study outcomes, approval conditions, required credit support, and binding tenant agreements. Longer-duration implication: the value attributable to shareholders will depend on approval timing, infrastructure funding, partner economics, and dilution, not simply the combined 2 GW headline. Canaan’s November 10 announcement already incorporated the classification milestone; the relevant prospective risk concerns conversion into financeable capacity.

EUROPEAN CLOUD AND SOVEREIGN COMPUTE

U.S. CAPACITY CONSTRAINTS CREATE A COMMERCIAL OPPORTUNITY FOR EXISTING FRENCH INFRASTRUCTURE (READ-THROUGH 5)

Affected company: OVHcloud (OVH: France). Direction: positive for utilization and the strategic value of connected infrastructure. Magnitude: moderate at the group level, potentially more significant within incremental GPU and public-cloud deployments.

MARA’s most important geographic disclosure was that Exaion’s new U.S. customer would be served from France. Thiel clarified: “the U.S. customers in the U.S. the hosting is happening in France.” He also stated that the capacity was already built and ready, with initial deployment expected before year-end. This is actual commercial evidence that at least some U.S. compute demand can move to available European infrastructure rather than wait for domestic construction.

OVHcloud has a directly relevant operating footprint and disclosed capacity position. Its October 20 FY2026 results identified 250 MW of connected power capacity, of which 140 MW was operating, and stated that growth could be supported without building new sites. The approximately 110 MW difference is connected-power headroom, not necessarily immediately available high-density GPU capacity, but it provides a more credible starting point than an unapproved greenfield queue position.

The transmission mechanism is faster monetization of existing infrastructure. Where a workload is geographically portable, available power and an established facility can shorten the interval between GPU procurement and customer billing. This can improve utilization and reduce exposure to new-site construction delays. OVHcloud’s existing cloud operations and enterprise relationships offer a route to capture that opportunity without first establishing an entirely new operating platform.

The opportunity is not limited to sovereignty-driven European demand. Exaion’s contract indicates that capacity availability itself can motivate cross-border deployment. Conversely, it does not establish that latency-sensitive workloads, regulated U.S. data, or every hyperscaler application can relocate. Exaion is also a competitor, so validation of the French opportunity does not establish that OVHcloud wins a particular customer or gains share.

Near-term catalyst: OVHcloud’s November 19 AI Summit and subsequent disclosures on GPU investment, customer commitments, and conversion of connected capacity. Its FY2026 public-cloud growth of 18.9% was already reported before MARA’s call and should not be presented as a new forecast. Longer-duration implication: existing French facilities can become more valuable as an alternative to delayed U.S. deployments. Equipment funding, cooling upgrades, customer credit, and utilization will determine how much of that strategic advantage becomes cash flow.

MINING SEMICONDUCTORS AND EQUIPMENT

CHEAP ASIC REPLACEMENT IS A MANUFACTURER HEADWIND, NOT EVIDENCE OF A HEALTHY EQUIPMENT CYCLE (READ-THROUGH 6)

Affected company: Canaan (CAN: Singapore). Direction: negative for mining-equipment pricing, manufacturing margins, and inventory economics. Magnitude: high within the hardware business and material to consolidated operating performance.

MARA attributed part of its fleet upgrading to “the extremely low pricing of Bitcoin mining hardware today.” This is favorable for a buyer’s replacement cost, but it is adverse evidence for equipment suppliers’ pricing power. The relevant distinction is between unit deployment and dollar profitability: miners can acquire more efficient machines while equipment manufacturers experience lower revenue per unit and weak production-cost absorption.

Canaan’s November 10 results provide direct corroboration after MARA’s call. Product revenue was $4.8 million, compared with $13.6 million in Q2 and $118.6 million a year earlier, declines of approximately 64.7% and 96.0%, respectively. Management attributed the weakness to lower computing power sold and lower average selling prices. It also explicitly described “continued weakness in bitcoin mining equipment demand and intense industry pricing competition.”

The economic pressure extends beyond accounting charges. Canaan reported $13.6 million of product costs, including $8.2 million of inventory and related write-downs or provisions. Removing those disclosed charges leaves approximately $5.4 million of product costs against $4.8 million of revenue, an illustrative product gross loss of approximately $0.6 million before corporate overhead and R&D. This limited calculation is not a fully normalized margin, but it shows that the quarter’s hardware weakness cannot be dismissed entirely as an inventory cleanup.

The transmission mechanism is lower selling prices, insufficient volume to absorb manufacturing overhead, and reduced recoverability of inventory and purchase commitments. MARA’s willingness to upgrade is not evidence that Canaan supplied the equipment; no such supplier relationship was established. The read-through is industry pricing pressure, independently confirmed in Canaan’s own results.

Near-term catalysts: Q4 product revenue, realized selling prices, order conversion, and additional inventory charges. The Q3 deterioration is already public following Canaan’s November 10 release, so MARA’s comment is corroboration rather than a prediction of unreleased results. Longer-duration implication: manufacturing technology and shipment volume will create shareholder value only if equipment pricing supports acceptable margins. A pivot into infrastructure does not eliminate the cash requirements of maintaining the hardware platform.

BITCOIN MINERS AND TRANSITION FUNDING

HASHRATE GROWTH DOES NOT ELIMINATE MINING-CASH-FLOW RISK DURING THE AI TRANSITION (READ-THROUGH 7)

Affected company: CleanSpark (CLSK: United States). Direction: negative for the assumption that a more efficient mining fleet automatically provides a strong cash-flow bridge to AI infrastructure. Magnitude: high for mining and treasury sensitivity, but partially offset by secured financing for its contracted data-center development.

MARA’s energized hashrate increased 18% year-over-year, while Bitcoin production increased only 4.8% and average Bitcoin realization declined approximately 37%. Purchased energy cost per Bitcoin at owned sites increased slightly to $39,674. These figures demonstrate that higher installed efficiency does not guarantee improved earnings when network competition, operating availability, and Bitcoin prices move adversely.

CleanSpark remains meaningfully exposed to the same revenue mechanism. Its September operating update reported 529 Bitcoin produced, 50 EH/s of operational hashrate, average operating hashrate of 36 EH/s, and 13,530 Bitcoin held. Its operational-hashrate definition differs from MARA’s energized measure, so the levels should not be compared as if they were identical utilization statistics. Nevertheless, the gap between headline capability and average output reinforces the need to model realized production rather than installed capacity alone.

At unchanged September production, a $10,000 change in Bitcoin realization would change monthly mining revenue by approximately $5.3 million before other effects. The same price change would alter the gross value of the September treasury by approximately $135.3 million before derivatives, taxes, or subsequent transactions. These are sensitivities, not forecasts. They show how a Bitcoin move can affect both current earnings and the assets available to fund the transition.

There is important counterevidence against a blanket corporate downgrade. CleanSpark disclosed that its subsidiary had closed $2.276 billion of 7.875% secured financing for Sandersville and stated that the project was funded through completion. That reduces the risk of transferring MARA’s unsigned-project funding uncertainty directly to CleanSpark. It does not eliminate mining operating exposure or make all remaining corporate liquidity surplus capital.

Near-term catalysts: the next quarterly disclosure of mining costs, realized production, treasury activity, and cash requirements outside the funded project. Positive net income caused by Bitcoin revaluation should not be confused with stronger recurring cash generation. Longer-duration implication: through the transition toward the expected 2028 halving, mining equipment must earn an adequate return after replacement spending and competitive difficulty growth. Lower ASIC purchase prices help capital efficiency, but they also enable competitors to upgrade, limiting the persistence of any individual miner’s efficiency advantage.

text:
He broke up with me over text on a random Wednesday afternoon. Not even a call. Just a few cold lines that landed like a slap.

I was a mess. The kind of crying that makes your chest hurt. So I texted the only person I trusted not to say something empty. He showed up twenty minutes later, rain still on his jacket, and didn’t ask a single question. He just sat on the edge of my bed and pulled me in.

His hoodie smelled like clean laundry and that cheap cologne every guy seems to own. I buried my face in it and cried until the shaking stopped. He didn’t offer advice. Didn’t tell me I was better off. He just held me, one hand slow on my back, the other resting at the base of my neck.

When the tears finally quieted, I became aware of everything else...the steady beat of his pulse against my cheek, the warmth of his skin, the careful way he was breathing like he was trying not to startle me. I lifted my head. His eyes were soft, a little unsure. Our faces were close enough that I could feel his breath.

I kissed him first.

text:
Power Crisis: Until We Put Energy In The Hands Of the Private Sector, We Won’t Solve It — Former Pres. Obasanjo 

Former President Olusegun Obasanjo has called for private sector participation in Nigeria’s energy sector, saying government alone cannot solve the electricity crisis. 

At a youth dialogue in Abeokuta, he urged Nigeria to adopt the telecommunications model. 

“Government has tried, just like government tried with telecommunications, until we put it in the hands of the private sector, we didn’t solve it. 

“And I believe that until we put energy in the hands of the private sector, we won’t solve it,” he said. 

Resource person Oluwaseun Obasanjo urged youths to embrace technology and entrepreneurship, saying Nigeria’s market offered opportunities for local businesses. 

“The market in Nigeria is huge. And if foreign companies are coming in every day to take advantage of this market, what can you, as youth, do to be able to succeed in this same market?” he asked. 

He added, “Every problem we have is an opportunity to have innovation, not just in Nigeria, across Africa, because we have similar problems.” 

“If you are not utilising technology, you will be left behind,” he warned. 

Programme mentor Dr Ayodele Aderinwale urged youths to participate in governance through evidence-based advocacy and study government budgets. 

“If you want to influence a state budget, go and read the state budget,” he said. 

He urged young advocates to present facts and practical proposals, saying: “Have facts, have data. I say this as someone who has sat on both sides of the table. When a young person walks into a meeting with a complaint, officials listen very politely. But when a young person walks in with data, a costed alternative and a constituency behind it, officials start negotiation.” 

He advised youths to join established institutions: “Join a political party, attend ward meetings, not only rallies. Join your residents’ association, join your professional body, join your trade association.”

text:
It should be noted, firstly, that the Greek original itself does not actually conflate or reduce the curse inherited from Adam to mortality alone. Let us look at the beginning of the answer to this question, which reads to us as thus: 
‘We must examine how our forefather Adam transmitted to us the just penalty imposed upon him on account of the transgression. He heard: ‘For thou art earth, and unto earth shalt thou depart’; and from being incorruptible he became corruptible, and was brought under the bonds of death. But since he begot children after having fallen into this condition, we who have descended from him have become corruptible, as offspring of one who was corruptible. Thus are we also heirs of the curse in Adam.’
–St. Cyril of Alexandria, Doctrinal Questions and Answers, Q. 6.
 
St. Cyril grants here that the just penalty (δίκην) imposed (ἐπενεχθεῖσαν) upon Adam is transmitted (παρέπεμψε) to his descendants. There is no strict reduction of this penalty by Cyril to either the temporal penalties Adam received only, much less bodily death (mortality) & corruption alone, in exclusion of the loss of the Holy Spirit’s indwelling or original righteousness as is commonplace in contemporary Orthodox “theology”. 
Rather, he simply says that we were ‘brought under the bonds of death’. But what does this bond constitute? 
 
In accordance with the long-established teaching of the Orthodox Church, St. Cyril is going to affirm that the loss of the Holy Spirit & a certain deprivation of divine grace (that is, spiritual death) preceded bodily death in Adam when he sinned: 
‘But when he [Adam] was being punished for the transgression, he was stripped of grace, then justly hearing the words: ‘Earth thou art, and unto earth shalt thou return.’ And the breath of life, that is, the Spirit of Him Who says, ‘I am the Life’, withdrew from the earthly flesh, and the living creature falls into death in respect of the flesh alone, the soul being preserved in immortality, since it was to the flesh alone that the words ‘Earth thou art, and unto earth shalt thou return’ had been spoken.’
–St. Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk. 1 (Jhn. 1:14.)
 
He affirms, of course, that this same state is transmitted to all of us, including his coming under divine wrath (ὑπὸ θείαν γεγόναμεν ὀργὴν), quite interestingly: 
‘The first man, being earthy and formed from the earth, and having the choice between good and evil placed within his own power, being indeed master of his inclination towards either, was carried away by a bitter deceit; and, turning aside into disobedience, he falls back into the earth, his mother, from which he had sprung. And, being now subject to corruption and death, he transmits his loss to the whole race.
As evil increased and multiplied among us, and the mind within us continually descended towards what was worse, sin came to reign, and thus human nature was henceforth shown to be stripped of the Holy Spirit Who had dwelt within it (τοῦ ἐνοικισθέντος Ἁγίου Πνεύματος ἡ ἀνθρώπου φύσις ἀνεδείκνυτο). For, as it is written, “The Holy Spirit of wisdom will flee deceit”, and “will not dwell in a body indebted to sin”(Wis. 1:4–5).
Since, therefore, the first Adam did not preserve the grace bestowed by God, God the Father devised for us the Second Adam from heaven. For He sends His own Son, Who is immutable and unchangeable by nature, and utterly unacquainted with sin, in likeness to us, so that, just as through the disobedience of the first we came under divine wrath (ὑπὸ θείαν γεγόναμεν ὀργὴν), so through the obedience of the Second we might escape the curse, and He might bring to naught the evils arising from it.
And since the Word of God became man, He receives the Spirit from the Father as one of us, not receiving anything for His own particular benefit; for He Himself was the Giver of the Spirit. Rather, He receives Him as man, that He might preserve Him for our nature, and once more establish within us, as something firmly rooted, the grace which had departed—He Who knew no sin.
For this reason, I think, the holy Baptist fittingly added: ‘I beheld the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon Him’ (John 1:32). For the Spirit had flown away from us on account of sin; but He Who knew no sin became as one of us, that the Spirit might become accustomed to abiding in us, having in Him no occasion for departure or withdrawal.’
–St. Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk. 1 (Jhn. 1:32-33.)
 
The deprivation of those original blessings through Adam’s sin permeates the whole human race, all falling into corruption: 
‘[Christ] therefore became man like us, so that in Him, as the first, the good things might return, and the grace of the Spirit, having taken root, might thereafter be preserved entire and securely for human nature; the Only-Begotten, who is the Word from God the Father, as it were lending us the immutability of His own nature, because human nature had stood condemned in Adam as unable to remain without falling, but as slipping very easily into deviation. 
Just as, therefore, in the first man’s turnings aside the deprivation of the [original] blessings permeates the whole of human nature (ἐν ταῖς τοῦ πρώτου τροπαῖς εἰς ὅλην διήκει τὴν φύσιν ἡ τῶν ἀγαθῶν ζημία), so, according to the same principle, I think, in Him who knows no change the gain of the permanence of the divine gifts will be preserved for the whole race.’ 
–St. Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk. 5 (John 7:39.)
 
Why? Because human nature offended the divine law (in Adam), its offence being the cause of its corruption:
 ‘..in that first Adam, the human race proceeds from non-being into being and, having come forth, it was corrupted, because it had offended the divine law (καὶ προελθὸν ἐφθάρη, ὅτι τὸν θεῖον λελύπηκε νόμον); but in the Second, that is, Christ, it returns to a second beginning, being reconstituted unto newness of life and unto a return to incorruption. “For if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation,” as Paul says.’ 
–Ibid.
 
Human nature, according to Cyril, was an object of God’s abhorrence both on account of the ancestral transgression and the sin which came after:  
‘For He hath appeared for this cause as one of us; that is, He hath had this condition and become man, that He might make beloved unto God him that was of old abhorred, because of the ancestral transgression and the sin that crept in afterwards (τὸν πάλαι μεμισημένον 
διὰ τὴν ἐν ἀρχῇ παράβασιν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῷ μεταξὺ παρεισφρήσασαν ἁμαρτίαν). For this cause Christ is said to have appeared to us as a door, and a beginning, and a way of all good things.’ 
–St. Cyril of Commentary on John, Bk. 10 (Jhn. 15:9-10.)
 
We are communicants (κοινωνοί) in Adam’s transgression, and on that very basis, divine wrath was in a certain manner allotted to us:
 ‘And indeed, thou wilt perceive this quite readily, when thou considerest that we have become communicants (κοινωνοί) of the transgression in Adam, and have all but paid the penalties even for the offences committed by him, the curse having spread throughout all, and the wrath having been, in a certain manner, apportioned to the race descended from him.
The Only-begotten, therefore, descended to become man, and dwelt among us, and submitted Himself to God the Father. For ‘He became obedient unto death’, effacing the charges arising from Adam's defection (ἐγκλήματα), and He has offered to God the Father the sweet savour of His willing obedience, as on behalf of all collectively and of each individually; and through Him we have been saved.
And Paul bears witness, having written thus:
 ‘Therefore as by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life. 19 For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.’(Rom 5:18-19)’
–St. Cyril, On Worship in Spirit and Truth, Bk. 12
 
Of course, one only has to ask himself from here whether one can be justly subject to God’s wrath & especially to have the grace of the Holy Spirit stripped from him for anything else other than on account of sin. 
The answer to this is obviously “no”—after which any discussion over whether one can properly speak of original sin putting a person in a “state of guilt” and judicial condemnation as a follower of the teachings of St. Cyril is concluded, lest God’s inflicted punishments be said to be unjust. 

This is something he himself certainly did not shy away from, showing contemporary rejection today to be rather erroneous in fact & not actually grounded in a “moving forward to the Fathers”: 
‘...if He had not been born like us according to the flesh, and had not shared the same things as we do, He would not have released human nature from the indictments incurred [which rested upon it] in Adam (οὐκ ἂν τὴν ἀνθρώπου φύσιν τῶν ἐν Ἀδὰμ ἀπηλλάξεν ἐγκλημάτων)...’ 
 –St. Cyril of Alexandria, First Letter Against Nestorius (Letter 2).
 
‘The whole nature of man became guilty (ܢܬܚܝܒ) in the person of him who was first formed but now it is wholly justified again in Christ.’ 
–St. Cyril of Alexandria, Serm. 42 on Luke. 
 
‘Showing that, because of the transgression in Adam (τὴν ἐν Ἀδὰμ παράβασιν), [sinful] corruption extends throughout the whole of human nature, the Apostle Paul says: “Nevertheless death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of Adam’s transgression”(Rom. 5:14).’ 
–St. Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John Bk. 1 (Jhn 1:9-10.)
 
‘..there was held against us a handwritten bond, namely the curse attached by the Divine Law to those who transgress, and the sentence pronounced against him who slipped aside from that ancient commandment, after the likeness of his sentence, came against the whole [human] race, inasmuch as indeed that which is pleasing to God was being violated by all (ἅτε δὴ καὶ παρὰ πάντων παραλυομένου τοῦ δοκοῦντος Θεῷ). 
For surely it is not the case that God was grieved when Adam transgressed, but was no longer such towards those after him who dishonoured that which is pleasing to the Creator; rather, as in the case of one, so against all was extended the law attached to those who offend (κατὰ πάντων ὁ τοῖς πλημμελοῦσιν ἐπηρτημένος ἐξετείνετο νόμος). 
We were therefore under a curse, and condemned by the divine sentence, both because of the transgression in Adam (ἐν Ἀδάμ) and because of that which arose from the law appointed after him.’
–St. Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John Bk. 12 (Jhn 19:19.)

St. Cyril of Alexandria, after subjection to proper scrutiny, is found to only be denying a particular ground or explanation of that transmitted penalty: that we personally disobeyed the divine commandment together with Adam. Rather, he grounds it in instead in our sin in him, by virtue of our unity of nature with Adam, as does the Church.
The question is now is, well, whether you do.

text:
Briek Schotte bends into the effort, hands gripping the drops, a spare tyre around his shoulders. Water shines on the Beton road, with its cracks and traps. Behind him, others strain to keep pace. Nothing here looks easy, and that’s why this image speaks loudly of Flanders.

Schotte was the archetypal Flandrien; tough, persistent, prepared to work until the rest let go. His appeal reached beyond winning bike races, and in his labour, Flemish people recognised qualities they valued in themselves.

Flanders was a commercial powerhouse of medieval Europe, its prosperity built through trade, craftsmanship and industry. Yet within Belgium, created as a country of two halves in 1830, its Dutch-speaking population lived under institutions dominated by French. The French language, French speakers, carried authority in government, justice and the army; it also marked social standing, even among the wealthy of Flanders. For many working people, the language of power was not their own.

The First World War sharpened divisions. The experience of Flemish soldiers serving under predominantly French-speaking officers became a powerful source of grievance, strengthening demands for recognition and respect.

Cycling offered a means of asserting that identity. Already taking root before the war, it provided an international arena in which men from modest backgrounds could make themselves, and their homeland, impossible to overlook. Strength, endurance, resolve and a willingness to suffer could carry a labourer’s son beyond limits imposed by money, education or language.

On roads like these, and worse, hard work became something people could see. Every attack into the wind, every punishing passage over cobbles, made familiar virtues visible. A champion could express the pride of people whose voices had too often counted for little.

Schotte gave that pride human shape. Bent over his handlebars, enduring what the road demanded, he embodied the Flandrien ideal. Through cycling, the qualities celebrated in Flanders fields, workshops and factories could command attention far beyond. The world might not speak their language, but it could understand their effort.

This is the voice of Flanders, and the voice of our book- Cycling Legends 04: Flandriens - cult heroes of the cobbles. Available on our website - https://t.co/zkuqszZ6FB

text:
From One AI Bot to 200 Agents: Elon Musk's Grok Signals a New Era of Autonomous Digital Workforces

The artificial intelligence revolution is moving beyond chatbots that answer questions. The next frontier is the development of coordinated AI agents capable of planning, delegating, executing, and monitoring complex work with limited human intervention.

Elon Musk recently revealed that Grok's reinforcement learning and inference infrastructure has been rebuilt in C and C++, drawing upon engineering expertise developed through SpaceX's Starlink network.

But an equally interesting development is emerging in how engineers organize AI agents to perform work.

One reported demonstration describes a hierarchical system in which a single Grok Bot coordinates a Chief of Staff agent, a project management agent, and specialized workers that delegate tasks across a much larger network.

The breakthrough is not simply having more AI agents. It is organizing artificial intelligence into a coordinated operational structure capable of executing complex objectives.

Traditional chatbots operate primarily through individual conversations. Users submit instructions, review responses, and repeatedly guide the next action.

Multiagent architectures offer a different model. A supervisory agent interprets objectives, planning agents divide responsibilities, and specialized workers execute tasks while reporting progress and escalating problems.

This introduces the possibility of AI systems continuing work across development, research, testing, documentation, and operational workflows without requiring continuous human prompting.

We are moving from AI as a personal assistant toward AI as an orchestrated digital workforce.

My perspective is that this transition could fundamentally reshape enterprise productivity.

Imagine a software organization where agents coordinate development assignments, test code, identify defects, prepare documentation, and present completed work for human approval.

The potential extends into financial services, education, healthcare administration, telecommunications, and enterprise operations.

However, managing dozens or hundreds of agents introduces serious challenges involving coordination failures, escalating costs, security permissions, inaccurate outputs, and accountability.

More agents do not automatically produce better results. Without clear objectives, reliable evaluation, and effective supervision, autonomous systems can amplify mistakes as efficiently as they execute tasks.

Human oversight must remain meaningful, particularly when agents interact with production systems, sensitive data, or consequential business decisions.

The strategic opportunity is not replacing every employee with an army of bots. It is creating intelligent operational systems that expand human capability while maintaining control.

The next generation of enterprise AI may be defined not by how many questions a chatbot answers, but by how effectively networks of specialized agents turn human objectives into verified outcomes.

“I am a soldier of Christ. It is not lawful for me to fight.”

St. Martin of Tours said these words at a point in his life when he chose to leave his military service and follow Christ.

St. Martin de Tours (316–397) is one of the most beloved saints of the early church, remembered as a soldier, monk, bishop, and champion of the poor. Born in Savaria in modern-day Hungary to pagan parents, St. Martin’s family lived in northern Italy, where his father served as a Roman military officer.

St. Martin felt drawn to Christ from a young age. At the age of 10, he attended a Christian church against his parents’ wishes and became a catechumen in preparation for becoming a Christian. At fifteen, like his father, he was enlisted into the Roman army.

While serving the military in Gaul, St. Martin experienced the moment that defined his conversion. Encountering a beggar shivering in the cold, St. Martin cut his soldier’s cloak in half and gave it to the man. That night, St. Martin dreamed of Christ wearing the same cloak and heard Him say, “Martin, still a catechumen, has clothed Me with this garment.” Understanding that Christ was calling him to become a Christian, he was baptized at the age of 18.

St. Martin was charged as a coward and jailed when he told army officers that his Christian faith did not allow him to fight. He offered to go into battle without a weapon, but the battle did not take place because the enemy withdrew, so he was released from duty.

After leaving the army, St. Martin dedicated himself to Christ, studying under St. Hilary of Poitiers. He founded one of the first monasteries in Gaul, which became a center of missionary activity. In 371. Despite his reluctance, he was chosen bishop of Tours.

According to tradition, he tried to hide to avoid the election, but the cackling of geese gave away his hiding place, so he accepted the bishopric.

As bishop, St. Martin traveled the countryside on foot or on a donkey, preaching the Gospel and combating pagan practices. He founded parishes and monastic communities across Gaul, earning the love of his people. Many miracles were attributed to him, such as healings, exorcisms, and raising the dead.

St. Martin died in 397 at Candes and was buried in Tours. His shrine quickly became one of the most popular pilgrimage sites in medieval Europe. In some areas, his feast day, November 11, became so widely celebrated that it marked the beginning of Advent preparations, known as St. Martin’s Lent.

St. Martin was one of the earliest saints venerated by the Church who did not die a martyr. The Church canonized him by the popular acclaim of the people.

text:
MIT Technology Review’s What’s Next series looks across industries, trends, and technologies to give you a first look at the future. You can read the rest of them here.

In the final weeks of 2025, the battle over regulating artificial intelligence in the US reached a boiling point. On December 11, after Congress failed twice to pass a law banning state AI laws, President Donald Trump signed a sweeping executive order seeking to handcuff states from regulating the booming industry. Instead, he vowed to work with Congress to establish a “minimally burdensome” national AI policy, one that would position the US to win the global AI race. The move marked a qualified victory for tech titans, who have been marshaling multimillion-dollar war chests to oppose AI regulations, arguing that a patchwork of state laws would stifle innovation.

In 2026, the battleground will shift to the courts. While some states might back down from passing AI laws, others will charge ahead, buoyed by mounting public pressure to protect children from chatbots and rein in power-hungry data centers. Meanwhile, dueling super PACs bankrolled by tech moguls and AI-safety advocates will pour tens of millions into congressional and state elections to seat lawmakers who champion their competing visions for AI regulation. 

Trump’s executive order directs the Department of Justice to establish a task force that sues states whose AI laws clash with his vision for light-touch regulation. It also directs the Department of Commerce to starve states of federal broadband funding if their AI laws are “onerous.” In practice, the order may target a handful of laws in Democratic states, says James Grimmelmann, a law professor at Cornell Law School. “The executive order will be used to challenge a smaller number of provisions, mostly relating to transparency and bias in AI, which tend to be more liberal issues,” Grimmelmann says.

Location

For now, many states aren’t flinching. On December 19, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, signed the Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act, a landmark law requiring AI companies to publish the protocols used to ensure the safe development of their AI models and report critical safety incidents. On January 1, California debuted the nation’s first frontier AI safety law, SB 53—which the RAISE Act was modeled on—aimed at preventing catastrophic harms such as biological weapons or cyberattacks. While both laws were watered down from earlier iterations to survive bruising industry lobbying, they struck a rare, if fragile, compromise between tech giants and AI safety advocates.

If Trump targets these hard-won laws, Democratic states like California and New York will likely take the fight to court. Republican states like Florida with vocal champions for AI regulation might follow suit. Trump could face an uphill battle. “The Trump administration is stretching itself thin with some of its attempts to effectively preempt [legislation] via executive action,” says Margot Kaminski, a law professor at the University of Colorado Law School. “It’s on thin ice.”

But Republican states that are anxious to stay off Trump’s radar or can’t afford to lose federal broadband funding for their sprawling rural communities might retreat from passing or enforcing AI laws. Win or lose in court, the chaos and uncertainty could chill state lawmaking. Paradoxically, the Democratic states that Trump wants to rein in—armed with big budgets and emboldened by the optics of battling the administration—may be the least likely to budge.

In lieu of state laws, Trump promises to create a federal AI policy with Congress. But the gridlocked and polarized body won’t be delivering a bill this year. In July, the Senate killed a moratorium on state AI laws that had been inserted into a tax bill, and in November, the House scrapped an encore attempt in a defense bill. In fact, Trump’s bid to strong-arm Congress with an executive order may sour any appetite for a bipartisan deal. 

The executive order “has made it harder to pass responsible AI policy by hardening a lot of positions, making it a much more partisan issue,” says Brad Carson, a former Democratic congressman from Oklahoma who is building a network of super PACs backing candidates who support AI regulation. “It hardened Democrats and created incredible fault lines among Republicans,” he says. 

While AI accelerationists in Trump’s orbit—AI and crypto czar David Sacks among them—champion deregulation, populist MAGA firebrands like Steve Bannon warn of rogue superintelligence and mass unemployment. In response to Trump’s executive order, Republican state attorneys general signed a bipartisan letter urging the FCC not to supersede state AI laws.

With Americans increasingly anxious about how AI could harm mental health, jobs, and the environment, public demand for regulation is growing. If Congress stays paralyzed, states will be the only ones acting to keep the AI industry in check. In 2025, state legislators introduced more than 1,000 AI bills, and nearly 40 states enacted over 100 laws, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Efforts to protect children from chatbots may inspire rare consensus. On January 7, Google and Character Technologies, a startup behind the companion chatbot https://t.co/JGIsV0b4hq, settled several lawsuits with families of teenagers who killed themselves after interacting with the bot. Just a day later, the Kentucky attorney general sued Character Technologies, alleging that the chatbots drove children to suicide and other forms of self-harm. OpenAI and Meta face a barrage of similar suits. Expect more to pile up this year. Without AI laws on the books, it remains to be seen how product liability laws and free speech doctrines apply to these novel dangers. “It’s an open question what the courts will do,” says Grimmelmann. 

While litigation brews, states will move to pass child safety laws, which are exempt from Trump’s proposed ban on state AI laws. On January 9, OpenAI inked a deal with a former foe, the child-safety advocacy group Common Sense Media, to back a ballot initiative in California called the Parents & Kids Safe AI Act, setting guardrails around how chatbots interact with children. The measure proposes requiring AI companies to verify users’ age, offer parental controls, and undergo independent child-safety audits. If passed, it could be a blueprint for states across the country seeking to crack down on chatbots. 

Fueled by widespread backlash against data centers, states will also try to regulate the resources needed to run AI. That means bills requiring data centers to report on their power and water use and foot their own electricity bills. If AI starts to displace jobs at scale, labor groups might float AI bans in specific professions. A few states concerned about the catastrophic risks posed by AI may pass safety bills mirroring SB 53 and the RAISE Act. 

Meanwhile, tech titans will continue to use their deep pockets to crush AI regulations. Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, will try to elect candidates who endorse unfettered AI development to Congress and state legislatures. They’ll follow the crypto industry’s playbook for electing allies and writing the rules. To counter this, super PACs funded by Public First, an organization run by Carson and former Republican congressman Chris Stewart of Utah, will back candidates advocating for AI regulation. We might even see a handful of candidates running on anti-AI populist platforms.

In 2026, the slow, messy process of American democracy will grind on. And the rules written in state capitals could decide how the most disruptive technology of our generation develops far beyond America’s borders, for years to come.

Bill Gates met Jeffrey Epstein multiple times between 2011 and 2014, after Epstein’s 2008 conviction for soliciting a minor for prostitution. Gates has repeatedly called the association a “grave error in judgment,” said the contacts were limited and professional, and denied any knowledge of or involvement in Epstein’s crimes.

Key documented facts
•  Timeline and frequency: Gates was introduced to Epstein in 2011 through professional/philanthropic contacts (including adviser Boris Nikolic). Contacts continued through 2014. In June 2026 House Oversight Committee testimony, Gates described roughly a dozen in-person meetings plus some video/Skype calls (three in 2011, two in 2012, and several more in 2013–2014). An external review commissioned by the Gates Foundation later identified roughly 30 meetings involving Epstein and foundation leaders/staff (including Gates) over that period. Foundation staff had raised reputational concerns about Epstein’s prior conviction. 

•  Stated purpose: Gates said Epstein claimed he could raise large sums (billions) for global health philanthropy from wealthy clients. Discussions focused on potential giving structures; Gates said nothing materialized and he cut off contact once it was clear the promised donors would not materialize. He has said he made clear Epstein would have no role in the foundation and would receive no compensation. 

•  What Gates says he did not do: He has stated he never visited Epstein’s island, ranch, or Florida home; declined social invitations; never spent time with Epstein socially in a personal sense; never witnessed sexual misconduct; was never offered young women or girls; and “never victimized anyone.” He acknowledged he “may have been in the presence of victims” (e.g., Epstein assistants he was photographed with, or people on one private flight from New York to Palm Beach). 

•  Epstein’s alleged leverage attempts: Released files and Gates’ testimony indicate Epstein learned of extramarital affairs (with Russian women) and appeared to try to use that information (plus other claims) to pressure Gates to continue the relationship. Gates has said the affairs were unrelated to Epstein, that he was not blackmailed in the sense of paying or complying, and that the efforts failed. He has called related emails from Epstein false or unsent drafts. 

•  Public statements and consequences: Gates has expressed regret in interviews (including with Anderson Cooper in 2021 and later), apologized to Gates Foundation staff in early 2026, and testified under oath in June 2026 that the association was a serious mistake that risked his philanthropic reputation. Melinda French Gates has publicly cited the Epstein relationship as a significant factor in their divorce. No criminal charges have been brought against Gates in connection with Epstein’s activities; he has consistently denied wrongdoing or knowledge of ongoing crimes.

text:
Mollie Maggia's jaw came away in pieces in her dentist's hands in 1922, and when she died that September, aged 24, her death certificate said syphilis.

She had been a dial painter at the United States Radium Corporation in Orange, New Jersey, one of hundreds of young women, most in their teens and early twenties, painting glowing numbers onto watch faces with a paint called Undark. To keep a fine point on the camel-hair brush they were taught to shape it between their lips. Lip, dip, paint, hundreds of dials a day. The supervisors told them radium was harmless, good for them even. The girls painted their nails and teeth with it for fun and walked home glowing in the dark.

Then their teeth began falling out. Jaws rotted and snapped. Spines crumbled. Doctors had no name for it, and the company did not offer one.

It had one. In 1924, under pressure, it paid Harvard specialists to study the factory, and they reported that radium was the cause. The company sat on the report and let it be known that its workers were in good health. Its own examiner told sick women they were well. When the deaths kept coming, the whispering started that dial painters were loose girls, and that it was syphilis.

Grace Fryer began losing her teeth in 1922 and spent two years looking for a lawyer brave enough to take on the company. In 1927 she sued, with four other women, and the papers named them the Radium Girls. That autumn Mollie was dug up to settle the syphilis question. Her bones were radioactive. The company stalled, knowing its accusers were dying, and by the first hearing in January 1928 two of the five could not raise their arms to take the oath.

They settled that June for $10,000 each and $600 a year. The judge who brokered the deal turned out to own shares in the company. The man who had invented the paint died of radium poisoning that November.

In Illinois, at the Radium Dial Company, Catherine Donohue gave her evidence in 1938 from her sickbed, weighing about five stone, and was dead within months. Her case helped win American workers the right to sue over the diseases their jobs gave them.

The women were told they were young and healthy and had nothing to fear, and when they started dying, the company found it easier to attack their virtue than admit what was in its paint.

Their graves in New Jersey still set off a Geiger counter.

text:
Yamadharma Raja and Yamuna Devi: A Sacred Bond Between Brother and Sister

This narrative highlights a mythological episode involving Yamadharma Raja and his twin sister, Yamuna (Yami). This sacred event is considered the origin of the festival known as 'Bhai Dooj' (also called 'Yama Dwitiya').

Mythological Story:

1. A Deep Bond Between Brother and Sister:

According to mythology, Yamadharma Raja and Yamuna (Yami) were the children of the Sun God (Surya Deva) and his wife, Sanjna Devi. Yamuna held a deep affection for her brother, Yamadharma Raja; she would frequently invite him to visit her home and share a meal.

2. Yamadharma Raja’s Devotion to Duty:

Yamadharma Raja was always deeply engrossed in his official duties. Tasked with the responsibility of collecting the souls of living beings when their time on earth concluded, and ensuring justice based on their individual 'karma' (actions), he remained occupied and was unable to visit his sister, Yamuna, for a long time.

3. The Auspicious Day of Kartika Shukla Dwitiya:

Finally, on the second day of the bright fortnight (Shukla Paksha) of the month of Kartika, Yamadharma Raja made an unexpected visit to his sister Yamuna’s home. Yamuna’s joy knew no bounds upon seeing her brother after such a long separation. 4. A Loving Welcome – Applying the Tilak:

Yamuna welcomed her brother into her home with great love and respect. She performed *aarati* with deep devotion and served him a meal consisting of delicious dishes prepared by her own hands. Afterward, she applied a *tilak* to her brother’s forehead—a symbol of success and a long life—and offered him her blessings.

5. The Boon Granted by Yama Dharmaraja:

Deeply moved by the immense love and hospitality shown by his sister, Yama Dharmaraja asked her to seek a boon.

Yamuna then made this request:

"On this sacred day of Yama Dwitiya, may any brother who visits his sister’s home, partakes of a meal prepared by her, and receives a *tilak* from her, be freed from the fear of an untimely death. Please grant that such brothers may never have to face the prospect of being taken to *Yamaloka* (the realm of Yama)."

Hearing his sister’s wish, Yama Dharmaraja gladly granted the boon, saying, "Tathastu" (So be it).

Key Elements in the Image:

• On the left side of the image, Yama Dharmaraja is depicted riding his *vahana* (vehicle), a *mahisha* (buffalo). He holds his divine mace (*gada*) in his hand.

• On the other side, the sacred scene unfolds: Yamuna Devi, with great love and devotion, holds a *puja* tray containing the items for *aarati* and applies a *tilak* to the forehead of her brother, Yama Dharmaraja. Significance of the Bhai Dooj – Yama Dwitiya Festival:

Commemorating a significant mythological event, the festival of Bhai Dooj—also known as Yama Dwitiya—is celebrated with great devotion and sincerity in many parts of India, two days after the conclusion of Diwali.

On this auspicious day, sisters apply a *tilak* (a ceremonial mark) on their brothers' foreheads and pray for their good health, happiness, longevity, and overall well-being. In turn, brothers express their love and affection for their sisters, while also acknowledging their responsibility toward them.

This festival serves as a symbol of the sacred bond of love, deep affection, and mutual respect shared between brothers and sisters.
