text:
$BXP Q3 2026 earnings: BXP fills more offices, but a big law firm closes

BXP filled more of its offices again, and then one of its biggest tenants moved to shut itself down. Rent from fuller buildings lifted funds from operations, the profit measure property companies use, to $1.89 a share, above the company's own range. Occupancy reached 89.4%, the level management had planned for December. Chairman Owen Thomas also raised the full-year outlook.

• Profit per share from property operations: $𝟏.𝟖𝟗 (+9% from a year ago)
• Revenue: $𝟗𝟏𝟏.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (+4.6% from a year ago)
• Occupied space in the portfolio: 𝟖𝟗.𝟒% (88.4% three months earlier)
• Full-year profit outlook: 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝟓 𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 (middle of the range $7.07, about 3% growth)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better: the occupancy recovery the plan rests on arrived a quarter early, and the outlook rose again. One caution: Weil, Gotshal & Manges, which pays 1.2% of BXP's rent, is winding down, and the raise fell short of the quarter's beat.

The question now is whether earnings keep growing in 2027, once asset sales and a refinancing bite. One view counts a full year of this year's occupancy plus higher renewal rents; the other counts 1.6 million square feet of expirations and a mortgage resetting near 6%. January's outlook settles it.

Analysis written by Claude Opus 5. Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐎𝐜𝐜𝐮𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐲 𝐇𝐢𝐭 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫-𝐄𝐧𝐝 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲
BXP owns and manages top-tier offices in six large American cities, and rent pays for nearly everything it does. Occupied space across the portfolio reached 89.4% in September, a full percentage point above June.

President Douglas Linde told investors: "Clearly, we have achieved our 89% goal much more quickly than we expected." Leases signed this year on empty space already in service lifted occupancy by 2.4 percentage points; changes to the portfolio supplied the rest.

• Leases signed in the quarter: 74 deals covering 1.2 million square feet
• Property running costs: 36.8% of revenue, 1.3 percentage points less than a year ago
• Signed but not yet paying rent: 1.1 million square feet, about half starting before January

Rent on space the company already built drops almost straight into profit, so every point of occupancy raises earnings without new building. Finance chief Michael LaBelle expects about 90% occupied in December, the level last year's plan set for this year-end.

What to watch: the gap between leased and occupied space, 2.5 percentage points in September after narrowing for two quarters. Without fresh deals on empty space, the fuel for occupancy gains in 2027 runs down.

🟢 𝐑𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐎𝐧 𝐑𝐞-𝐋𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐑𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝐀𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧
When a lease ends, BXP re-lets the space, and the new rent shows what tenants will now pay. In the third quarter those rents landed 9.3% above the expiring ones after costs, and 6.5% above before them.

Midtown Manhattan and Washington drove the gain, helped by a replacement lease at 500 North Capitol Street that raised the rent by almost 30%. LaBelle said the market value of the portfolio's leases has "grown by approximately 10% in the last couple of quarters".

Only about 5% of the space comes up for renewal each year, so better pricing adds to the occupancy story rather than replacing it. Linde said no market is granting larger concessions.

What to watch: the same rent comparison in January, and whether San Francisco turns positive. A second weak reading there would show the recovery still rests on filling empty space.

🟢 𝐀𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐑𝐚𝐧 𝐀𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐎𝐟 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧
A year ago BXP promised to raise $1.9 billion by 2028 by selling land, flats and offices it no longer wants, and to put the cash into new buildings and debt repayment. It has now banked about $1.4 billion.

Two Washington offices went in the quarter for $155 million together. An investor bought 10.55% of the Manhattan tower at 343 Madison Avenue for $50.7 million, which chairman Owen Thomas said closed "at a price above our base", and four more assets sit under contract.

Each sale costs earnings, because the rent leaves with the building, and LaBelle has put a figure on next year's cost. In exchange, the proceeds and a new construction loan sharply cut the equity BXP must still put into its projects under way.

What to watch: the Times Square Tower contract, which Thomas said could close in the first quarter. Finishing it would complete the disposal programme two years early, after which LaBelle expects the remaining sales to add to earnings instead of subtracting.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐖𝐞𝐢𝐥 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐓𝐨 𝐂𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞, 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝟒𝟒𝟕,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐅𝐞𝐞𝐭
Weil, Gotshal & Manges is a global law firm and one of BXP's twenty largest clients. Its management committee recommended an orderly wind-down on 28 October, the day after these results, and the partners have yet to vote. The firm rents about 447,000 square feet at the General Motors Building in Manhattan under a lease running to 2034.

BXP's share of that rent comes to $35.8 million a year, or 1.2% of all the rent it collects. Weil paid its November rent in full, the company said. Should the partnership dissolve, BXP said "we expect we would establish a reserve for the entire straight-line rent balance at that time" — $19.1 million at its share.

The timing cuts against the landlord's own account of its market. Thomas said "BXP delivered another very strong quarter, both operationally and financially", and the building is 99.9% leased, yet one of its largest law-firm tenants is dissolving. Linde said office rent there "is under $150 a square foot", well below what BXP expects at its new tower nearby.

What to watch: the partners' vote, and any reserve in the fourth-quarter accounts. If Weil goes, BXP must re-let a large Manhattan block into a market where asking rents have climbed, so the rent lost could come back higher by 2028.

🔴 𝐀 𝟑.𝟒% 𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐠𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐍𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐉𝐮𝐧𝐞
BXP carries $16.6 billion of debt on its own books, and its cheapest loan is about to get dear. The $2.3 billion mortgage on the General Motors Building, $1.4 billion at BXP's share, pays 3.43% and matures in June 2027.

In August the company sold $700 million of ten-year bonds at 6.05%. LaBelle said lenders have offered to refinance the Manhattan mortgage "for a 10-year term with an all in credit spread in the low 100s", which at today's government yields lands near 6%. Borrowings whose rate moves with the market also rose to 12.2% of the total from 8.7%.

What to watch: the terms BXP signs before June. A rate near 6% on its share would eat a sizeable part of the extra rent that fuller buildings now produce, which is why LaBelle calls this refinancing the main drag on 2027.

🔴 𝐓𝐰𝐨 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐑𝐞-𝐋𝐞𝐭 𝐀𝐭 𝐋𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐑𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬
The portfolio-wide rent gain hides two weak corners. New rents on re-let space came in 11.2% below the expiring ones in San Francisco and 1.5% below in Boston, where one lease at The Quarry in Waltham reset about 28% lower, Linde said.

Los Angeles is worse. Linde said West Los Angeles is the single market in the portfolio where demand has not recovered, blaming consolidation among media companies, and BXP signed only 24,546 square feet there. Its largest 2027 expiry, 175,000 square feet at Colorado Center in Santa Monica, sits in that market.

What to watch: the San Francisco rent comparison, and any new lease at Colorado Center, where Linde said the forecast has "very little sort of reliance on improving our occupancy at Colorado Center in the short to medium term as part of our projection".

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐀𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Five standing worries got no fresh numbers in the release, and the call made two of them bigger. Each one has a disclosure that would settle it, and most arrive with January's results.

• Fitting out space: LaBelle now sees about $550 million of leasing capital this year, after saying $500 million in July
• Free rent: leases signed this quarter grant 356 rent-free days, against 243 days across the nine months
• Debt: BXP's share is $16.3 billion, flat on a year ago, and the leverage goal still has no date
• Sales dilution: deals already done cost about eight cents a share next year, six cents more if Times Square Tower closes
• Rent from AI startups: BXP tracks the share but does not publish it, while technology drives most San Francisco demand
• Next year's expirations: 1.6 million square feet, of which over 1 million is already in talks, Linde said

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝟑𝟒𝟑 𝐌𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐨𝐧 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝟓𝟔% 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐝
BXP is building a 930,000 square foot tower at 343 Madison Avenue beside Grand Central Terminal, which LaBelle said begins to deliver in 2029. A two-floor lease with a business services firm took it to 56% leased, and Thomas said talks on five more floors would carry it to 70%. A $1.2 billion construction loan and the stake sale leave BXP $250 million of equity to fund.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐲'𝐬 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐛𝐲 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟓𝟏𝟒.𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Profit from the buildings, before interest and depreciation, grew 3.7% from a year ago. Boston added 12.9% and New York 9.0%. Los Angeles fell 27.5% and Seattle 25.4%, two small markets that together supply about 5% of the total.

𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭-𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏,𝟓𝟗𝟗.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Rent BXP has booked under accounting rules but not yet collected rose 3.9% in nine months, faster than revenue, because new leases open with free-rent periods. The balance grew $60.6 million this year against $82.1 million last year, so the gap between booked and banked rent widens more slowly.

𝐄𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐨 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: $𝟕𝟒𝟖.𝟐 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
The cash BXP must still put into its six projects fell from about $1.7 billion inside the quarter, after the 343 Madison construction loan closed and an investor bought in. Its share of the total investment is $3.1 billion, and the commercial space is 70% pre-leased.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞: $𝟕.𝟎𝟔 – $𝟕.𝟎𝟖  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $6.99 – $7.05
Raised. The middle of the range moved up five cents, to $7.07 a share, about 3% above 2025. By our math that leaves $1.81 to $1.83 for the fourth quarter, a step down from the third. LaBelle deferred repair costs into that quarter and expects higher interest. Fourth raise in a row: one cent, five cents, five cents.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐝𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 (𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭): $𝟐.𝟑𝟓 – $𝟐.𝟑𝟕  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $2.14 – $2.24
Raised. The middle of the range jumped 17 cents, mostly from gains on the two Washington sales and better results at the properties. Accounting profit swings with sales and write-downs that BXP says it cannot predict, which is why it plans this figure apart from cash earnings. July's version was lower, so this is the biggest move of the year.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐢𝐧 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐛𝐨𝐭𝐡 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬: 𝟐.𝟑𝟓% – 𝟐.𝟕𝟓%  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from 1.8% – 2.6%
Raised. The middle of the range now sits at 2.55%, some 0.35 percentage points above July. LaBelle said pulling occupancy gains into the third quarter did most of it, partly offset by costs moved into the fourth. He expects a materially faster rate in 2027, helped by a full year of this year's leasing.

𝐎𝐜𝐜𝐮𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐲 𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐟 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔: 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝟗𝟎%  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from closer to 90% than 89%
Unchanged. BXP still expects "total portfolio occupancy to reach approximately 90% by year-end 2026", which asks another 0.6 percentage points after September's 89.4%. Linde said 600,000 square feet of signed leases begin paying in the quarter, against 186,000 square feet of leases expiring, so the arithmetic is close to settled.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐲 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐝𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞: $𝟓.𝟎𝟐  ⇒ stable
🠇 cut from $5.10
Cut. The outlook adds back eight cents a share less depreciation than July's did, because BXP sold buildings during the quarter. This line is arithmetic rather than a forecast of trading: it bridges accounting profit to funds from operations, which leave out the cost of ageing buildings.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐰𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐞-𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐬 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞: $(𝟎.𝟑𝟏)  ⇒ stable
🠅 raised from $(0.25) – $(0.29)
Raised. BXP now assumes 31 cents a share of gains and write-downs for the year, against 25 to 29 cents in July, after the two Washington offices sold at a profit. The company subtracts this amount on the way from accounting profit to funds from operations, so it flatters the first and not the second.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐝𝐨 𝐀𝐈 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐮𝐩𝐬 𝐩𝐚𝐲?
Management tracks the figure and has not published it for three quarters, while technology tenants drive most San Francisco demand. Without it, nobody outside the company can size the risk if that funding cools.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐟𝐢𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐬𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐢𝐧 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕?
This year's bill climbed from about $400 million to roughly $550 million. LaBelle says far fewer leases will start next year but has given no figure, and cash available for dividends depends on it.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭?
The aim of cutting borrowing to the lower-seven-times range has been repeated for more than a year with no date attached, while BXP's share of debt has stayed near $16.3 billion.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐝𝐨 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐦𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐧𝐡𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐚𝐧 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐠𝐚𝐠𝐞?
The $2.3 billion loan on the General Motors Building matures in June. LaBelle described the likely credit spread but not the rate built into planning, which decides how much of next year's rent growth survives.

𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐖𝐞𝐢𝐥'𝐬 𝐬𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐚𝐭 𝐚 𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭?
Linde said rent in that building runs under $150 a square foot while newer towers nearby ask far more. Investors need the asking rent and a timetable for re-letting 447,000 square feet.

text:
IRAN WAR - ROUND 3

A return to major combat operations looks increasingly likely and possibly within days to a couple of weeks at most.

November 6th

CENTCOM posts a $20 million Rewards for Justice notice for information on Iran’s nuclear program , the one the U.S. has twice claimed was destroyed. 

The English post put the full offer and clear tip instructions in the text and hit nearly 10 million views. The Farsi post via the Rewards for Justice persian account had the details buried in the graphic, used a much shorter text, and got under 10,000 views. Combined with that gap, it still looks more like messaging aimed at an English-speaking audience than a serious collection effort aimed at people inside Iran.

November 8th

USS Theodore Roosevelt departs Singapore heading for the Arabian Sea. Arrival estimated mid-to-late November.

Parallel: USS Gerald R. Ford reached the theater the day before Epic Fury began.

November 8th

CIA Director John Ratcliffe and DNI Jay Clayton brief the Gang of Eight in a closed session on Iran.

Parallel: First such briefing since February 24 — four days before Epic Fury.

November 9th

Qatar’s Foreign Minister meets Vice President Vance and President Trump in Washington.

Parallel: Oman’s Foreign Minister met Vance the day before the February strikes began.

The sequence is hard to ignore: a public nuclear bounty that functions as a narrative seed, followed within 48–72 hours by the first Gang of Eight briefing since the pre-Epic Fury alongside a third carrier moving into position. It matches the February pattern of intelligence framing, force movement, and last-minute mediation almost exactly.

The only off-ramp is a deal Trump can sell as a clear win, not just a reasonable compromise. He needs concessions he couldn’t get before the war. Iran, believing it is in a stronger position than on February 28 (especially after the midterms), is unlikely to offer that.

Have you ever wondered, what would it take for a humanoid #robot to become part of your everyday working life? 🤖

Unloading a dishwasher without breaking a glass. Handling unfamiliar objects. Completing a full shift safely and reliably. These everyday tasks reveal just how much goes into making physical #AI useful. 🧐

Factories and warehouses offer an important proving ground. Repetitive tasks and controlled surroundings give developers opportunities to test performance, demonstrate commercial value and gather experience that could help robots tackle more complex settings over time. 🏭

We also examine the Greater Bay Area’s role in this development. #HongKong’s research and access to capital, alongside #Shenzhen and Dongguan’s manufacturing expertise, create opportunities to turn advances in AI into machines that businesses can afford to deploy. 🌏

text:
Zimbabwe seeks Russian expertise to expand telemedicine services

Zimbabwe is seeking Russian expertise to strengthen and expand its telemedicine programme as part of efforts to improve access to quality healthcare, particularly in remote communities.

Vice President Dr Kembo Mohadi, who is in Moscow to advance health cooperation agreements between Zimbabwe and Russia, said the country has already introduced remote consultations that allow patients and doctors to communicate from different locations, but is now looking to enhance the system through advanced technology.

Speaking after touring a high-tech medical imaging and radiology centre in Moscow yesterday, VP Mohadi said Zimbabwe was studying Russia's telemedicine and diagnostic systems to identify solutions that could be adapted locally.

He said Russia's model allows medical information from different regions to be transmitted to a central radiology facility for diagnosis, a system Zimbabwe is keen to learn from as it develops its own digital health infrastructure.

VP Mohadi said health specialists accompanying the delegation were assessing the technology and expertise on offer, with a view to facilitating knowledge and skills transfer that would enable Zimbabwe to establish a system tailored to its healthcare needs.

Deputy Minister of Health and Child Care Sleiman Kwidini said Zimbabwe had already begun laying the groundwork for telemedicine through digital equipment supplied by the Ministry of ICT, with the technology currently being used in some hard-to-reach areas.

He said the initiative enables patients in areas without doctors to receive medical guidance and treatment through consultations with practitioners based at referral hospitals. The next phase, he added, is to strengthen digital platforms to allow real-time consultations and faster referrals between clinics and specialist centres.

The visit follows the delegation's tour of the Pharmasyntez-Nord pharmaceutical plant in St Petersburg and forms part of efforts to implement agreements reached between President Dr @edmnangagwa and President Vladimir Putin. The cooperation covers pharmaceutical manufacturing, cancer treatment and digital health, as Zimbabwe seeks to reduce medical tourism and strengthen its healthcare delivery system.

text:
The Project – Longmarsh Data Centre/Solar Farm

EPL Norfolk, a UK company, owned by a Finnish investment company,  is proposing to construct a 1.3Gw Solar Farm on 4,700 acres of valuable, productive farmland in Norfolk. The project is designed to power a large Data Centre, ultimately requiring 1.0Gw power, in this largely rural country.

The economic viability of this project clearly rests on this mega Data Centre. The project also includes a large battery storage facility, though the storage capacity has so far been withheld. Additionally, the Data Centre will be situated close to connections to the national power grid.

It would not be unreasonable to presume that the proximity to the National Grid connection is the key factor and is essential to address those periods when the sun doesn’t shine. Norfolk enjoys sunshine for around 35% of the year. The power requirements of the Data Centre suggest that when the solar farm is requiring full capacity, there will be only a limited capability to charge the batteries.

Data Centres
Data Centres require stable power and to operate 24/7. This Data Centre can only achieve this by drawing power from the National Grid.

Data Centres also require high grade internet bandwidth availability. This is seriously lacking in Norfolk. One reason suggested is that rural Norfolk is outside of the current data pathways and data centre hubs, found in the UK (Docklands, other parts of London, Slough).

Data Centres also require cooling facilities – EPL suggest this will be achieved with a ‘closed-loop system’. The 25M planned height of the Data Centre is unusually high compared to that of other mega centres – in the USA and China. This suggests that such a closed-loop cooling system is untried and untested. A 25M high centre will generate significant heat which will increase successively the higher uo one travels in the building.

Data Centre Tier
It is not clear on what tier will the data centre operate and what is the justification for this selection? Tier IV, which requires 99.995% uptime guarantee, would seem to be out of the question. Such a Tier would require at least two times level of redundancy and a maximum annual downtime of less than 26 minutes.

The Land
4,700 acres of predominantly Grade 1 and 2 agricultural land will be sacrificed for this project. The National Policy document, under which this project will be assessed (EN-3 2.10.21) makes clear that poorer quality land should be preferred to higher quality land avoiding the use of “Best and Most Versatile” agricultural land. EPL’s other major project is called Stonestreet and is at Ahsford in Kent. This 99.9Mw project is to be built on ‘lower grade agricultural land’

Sites of Special Scientific Interest
Islington Heronry – SSSI lies in close proximity to this project. The Consultation Leaflet makes no mention of the potential impact of the project on this important nesting area for herons.  This would include the impact of Infrasonic Low Frequency Noise (ILFN). Noise in the 20Hz to 200Hz range is less impactful on humans though the constant low level ‘humming’ sound is heard to be so at some existing data centres. This ILFN can, studies have found, be heard more than 3,000 feet from their source and can pass around barriers – natural or otherwise. The project’s intention to site the Data Centre at least 300M from housing may mitigate the impact of ILFN on humans but these precious birds and other animals are far less stationary.

National Policy document EN-1 5.4 - 5.4.8. states, development within or outside a Site of Significant Scientific Interest (SSSI), and which is likely to have an adverse effect on it (either individually or in combination with other developments) should not normally be permitted.  The only exception is where the benefits (including need) of the development in the location proposed clearly outweigh both its likely impact on the features of the site that make it of special scientific interest, and any broader impacts on the national network of SSSIs.

Given that the sole purpose of this project is to build and power a Data Centre, the ‘need’ does not justify this development. No Data Centre = no need.

Location
This Data Centre will be located at 52.7 degrees North. There are currently zero operational solar farms of 1Gw or greater located north of latitude 50 degrees North.

Size and location
Fundamentally, given the output of this solar farm is 100% exclusively dedicated for the Data Centre, why is this ‘best and most versatile land’ the chosen site. Surely this could be located anywhere with a similar irradiance exposure level?  Or is it that, because of the proximity to the Walpole National Grid connectivity, the siting is an absolute requirement. That is, the site has to be this close so that, when the sun doesn’t shine and the batteries are exhausted, then the Data Centre – which it is presumed is economically critical to the whole project – can draw power, for its 24/7 requirements, from the National Grid. Put plainly, placing this anywhere else might deprive the Data Centre of power and therefore its reason to exist and deprive the project’s financial investors of economic viability.

This Longmarsh project proposes a solar farm with a capacity of 1.3Gw. The largest currently operating solar farm in the UK is Cleve Hill in Kent, which has a capacity of 373Mw. That is more than 70% smaller than what is proposed for Longmarsh. The other large solar farms in the UK are all at 75Mw or lower levels. That is to say, that the proposal at Longmarsh is significantly out of scale with existing infrastructure.

Indeed, Longmarsh is more than 50% higher in capacity than the recently approved, but not yet constructed and operating, ‘large’ projects elsewhere in the UK. For reference, EPL have recently obtained approval for another large solar farm (Stonestreet) development at Ashford in Kent. This 472 acre site is projected to provide 99.9Mw of energy. The project summary for Stonestreet mentions the ability to power 42,000 homes but also mentions the site’s proximity to local large energy users. Note well that this EPL project is to be built on ‘lower grade agricultural land’

There are currently zero (0) operational solar farms with a capacity of 1 GW or greater located north of latitude 50° N anywhere in the world. Zero!
While solar power is expanding rapidly across higher latitudes, gigawatt-scale "mega" projects require specific geographic, land-use, and economic conditions that have kept them concentrated much closer to the equator.
Where Gigawatt Solar Farms Actually Exist

The Longmarsh project aims to be a 1.3Gw facility. This will be located at roughly 52.7 degrees N.

Virtually all of the world's operational gigawatt-scale solar installations are located between latitudes 10° N and 45° N. They are heavily concentrated in regions featuring vast, low-value desert landscapes, high solar irradiance, and aggressive state-backed infrastructure scaling:

China dominates this space, housing the world's largest installations such as the 5 GW Midong Solar Farm in Xinjiang (~44° N) and the 16 GW Talatan Solar Park in Qinghai (~36° N). Even their northernmost mega-projects, like the Nilka County PV Park (~43.9° N), sit safely south of the 50th parallel.
India holds massive clusters like the Bhadla Solar Park (~25° N).
The Middle East features single-site giants like the Al Dhafra project in the UAE (~24° N).
What Solar Looks Like North of 50°

North of latitude 50° N—an area encompassing the United Kingdom, northern Europe, most of Canada, and Russia—utility-scale solar installations operate on a vastly smaller footprint:

The United Kingdom: The UK's largest operational facility is the Cleve Hill Solar Park in Kent. (~51.3° N), which generates 373 MW (0.37 GW). While there are gigawatt-scale co-located portfolios in the development pipeline, individual operational farms do not yet cross the 1 GW threshold.
Northern Europe: High-latitude nations like Sweden have actively growing markets, but their flagship projects, such as the Hultsfred Solar Farm (~57.5° N), sit at approximately 100 MW (0.1 GW).

o

The combination of lower winter solar irradiance, higher land-use constraints, and decentralized grid infrastructures means that high-latitude green energy relies more heavily on a mixture of offshore wind, distributed rooftop solar, and smaller mid-scale solar arrays.
Ownership
EPL Norfolk Ltd is a wholly owned subsidiary of Evolution Power Ltd.

This is not the whole picture.  Evolution Power Ltd, in turn is owned by Korkia Capital Oy - a Finnish investment company.  Most of the directors of EPL are also directors of Korkia.
In terms of intellectual property and intercompany and parent company loans, it is unclear if will EPL or EVL be subject to any charges from Korkia? Charges that would reduce UK taxable profits and effectively transfer UK-generated revenue offshore and so represent a loss of tax revenue to HMRC. Put bluntly, will the project be adequately capitalized?
Batteries

Given the solar panels will be producing electricity and, someof that will be used to power the data centre, it is currently unclear what i residual power will remain to charge the battery storage capacity.

Related to this, what is the storage capacity of the Battery system.
Following on, it is not clear for how long could the battery storage facility power the data centre. To illustrate. If the Data Centre requires 15Mw, of sustained and stable power to operate, then a 50Mw battery complex would be sufficient to power the Data Centre for just over three hours. Currently the largest battery system in the UK is 99Mw – so a 15Mw Data Centre could be powered for 6.5 hours!

Renewable Energy

The Data Centre once fully operational, will be the sole customer of the solar farm. However, as advised earlier, it is to be expected that the solar farm will supply a maximum of 35% of the Data Centre’s power needs. The remainder will come from a variety of sources – from the National Grid (from Natural Gas, Wind, other solar, and nuclear), from Interconnectors (principally from Natural Gas and nuclear), and from diesel generators. EPL have provided no modelling of the sources for power utilization at the Data Centre? How much from solar? How much from nuclear? How much from wind? How much from natural gas? How much from diesel generators?

Fire Risk
Nearby Suffolk area suffered a significant wildfire in 2026. This took around 12 days to bring fully under control. The presence of potentially dangerous batteries and volumes of diesel give cause for concern as to fire risk. f

Solar Panels
Research suggests this would be between 2.36 and 2.6 million panels. From where would these be sourced? It is worth noting that China is the main global of solar panels. Sourcing from China (the most likely source) will add to the carbon footptint of this project.

Indeed, given that the Longmarsh project is predicated on supplying power to a not yet existing Data Centre, we may reasonably conclude that all of the carbon created by Longmarsh will be an additional net negative position?
Sunlight
Norfolk receives around 1,550 to 1,650 hours of sunlight in an average year.  This suggests a potential target of 35% of available daylight. Or another way, for 65% of the time, these panels would be generating no electricity.  And of course, the battery storage would be equally redundant.   A high panel conversion efficiency rate would be 22% - suggesting that the solar farm would generate electricity of around 350 hours of capacity each year.
Food Security

Information from the Project sponsors is silent on the impact on food security of this project. Specifically, they have offered nothing, by way measurement criteria to compare and assess the criticallity of this project versus its impact on food security and the amenity cost of taking 4,700 acres of prime farmland out of production?
Jobs and Investments

The project suggests there will be £25bn of Data Centre campus investment. Given Norfolk’s predominantly rural nature, we might reasonably expect that very little of this will be spent in the County. Indeed, we might expect that most of this will be spent with overseas chip and server suppliers and therefore impacting Britains trade deficit.
The project suggests that 'over 500 permanent roles'. Will be created and a further 1,500 jobs in the local community. These are small rural communities with a labour pool likely to be lacking in the highly technically skilled personnel. Typical employment levels at current other sites suggest a far lower level of employment.

Norfolk has poor public transport infrastructure, what facilities will be provided to accommodate a large number of single-occupancy private vehicles used by employees (on a 24/7 basis)?
Project Life and De-Commissioning

The stated life of this project is 60 years. EPL’s other project – Stonestreet in Ashford in Kent- has a projected life of 40 years? No explanation for the difference, is provided. This raises the concern that post-project commencement, EPL or other financial investment companies will seek to infill contiguous sites and ‘piggy-back’ off of Longmarsh’s infrastructure.

At the end of the project life – 60 years – EPL has committed to restoring the areas used on the project. And yet nothing is said about whether EPL will be putting up bond to cover the company’s decommissioning obligations. Such a commitment would assuage fears of an abandonment of its obligations by EPL and its foreign owners.

text:
Which project makes money better 
Roadrunners, Layers, or Broilers 

When people ask me "which is the better project in Zimbabwe?", I tell them there is no best project. There is only the project that fits your cash flow, your market, and the land you are standing on.

Before you spend a single dollar, you need to know exactly how we calculate costs and income. Here is the raw math for the three main birds, using current market feed prices.

The Broiler Math (100 Birds)
Costs: You buy 100 chicks at roughly $0.75 each ($75). A broiler eats about 3.5kg of feed over 6 weeks. For 100 birds, that is 350kg. You need 1 bag of Starter ($34), 3 bags of Grower ($99), and 3 bags of Finisher ($96). That is $229 on feed. Add $50 for meds and heating. 
Total cash upfront: $354.
Income: You will lose maybe 5 birds. You sell 95 birds at around $4.80 each (2kg live weight). 
Revenue: $456.
Profit: $102 per cycle.

The Layer Math (500 Birds)
Costs: 500 pullet chicks will cost you around $600. You feed them for 20 weeks before they lay. They eat about 6.5kg of feed each in that time. That is 3,250kg of feed. At roughly $27 per 50kg bag, that is $1,755. Add $300 for meds and housing setup. 
Total cash upfront: $2,655. 
Income: This is where people get it wrong. Layers only start making money when you have a batch big enough to justify the daily effort. With 500 birds at a 90% lay rate, you get 450 eggs a day. Sold at $0.25 each, that is $112.50 a day. 
Daily Costs: Your 500 layers will eat about 55kg of feed a day. That is just over one bag, costing you $29. 
Profit: You make $83 profit per day. Every single day.

The Road Runner Math (100 Birds)
Costs: 100 chicks at $1.00 each ($100). They take 4 to 5 months to mature and eat about 7kg of feed. That is 700kg (14 bags) at $33 per bag. 
Total cash upfront: $562.
Income: You sell 90 birds. If you have a direct market and sell at $9, you make $810. 
Profit: $248.

So, what is the better project?
It depends entirely on your pain tolerance.

Broilers give you fast cash but tiny margins. You are constantly buying feed and living cycle to cycle. 
Layers give you incredible daily income, but you have to survive a $2,600 cash hole for five months before you see a single cent. 
Road runners give you the best margin per bird, but only if you can sell direct.

But here is what nobody tells you about these numbers: your land determines whether you actually keep that profit.

If you put broilers in a poorly ventilated shed or your broiler houses are facing the wrong direction, they will die from heat stress, and your $102 profit becomes a $354 loss.

If you buy 500 layers, but your land doesn't have proper drainage or space, disease will wipe out your $2,600 investment before week 10.

If you buy road runners, but you don't have the land for them to range and scavenge, you are forced to buy 100% of that $562 feed bill. Your profit disappears.

This is why you cannot build a poultry business on a guess. You need a Land Use Plan. You need to know exactly what your land can hold, where your sheds should sit to prevent disease, and how much space you need to make the math work.

Do not spend $2,600 on layers and then hope for the best.

FOR THE FIRST TIME, A CUSTOMER HAS TORN UP A LONG-TERM LNG DEAL WITH QATARENERGY

The buyer is Poland's Orlen.

It filed the notice on Tuesday.

The contract: 1 million tonnes of LNG a year,

signed in 2009,

flowing since 2016,

and supposed to run until 2034.

Its estimated value this year alone was about EUR 570 million.

Orlen's stated reason is the force majeure Qatar declared in March,

after strikes damaged 2 of the 14 production units at Ras Laffan.

QatarEnergy has rolled that notice forward month after month.

The latest one runs to the end of the year.

Orlen says it has received only four Qatari cargoes in 2026.

But there's a second reason in Orlen's own words.

The cancelled deal was priced off crude oil.

Orlen says the market now offers better terms than that 2009 formula.

It also buys gas from Norway and US LNG from Louisiana.

So the deal it keeps with Qatar is the one priced off gas markets, up to 1 million tonnes a year.

Before the war, Qatar shipped about a fifth of the world's LNG.

Buyers long counted it among the most reliable suppliers anywhere.

The cancelled contract stays in force for 60 more days.

The question for Doha is who files next.

Marduk (/ˈmɑːrdʊk/;[2] cuneiform: 𒀭𒀫𒌓 dAMAR.UTU; Sumerian: amar utu.k "calf of the sun; solar calf"; Hebrew: מְרֹדַךְ, Modern: Merōdaḵ, Tiberian: Mərōḏaḵ) was a god from ancient Mesopotamia, patron deity of Babylon. First sparsely attested in the 3rd millennium BC, Marduk slowly rose to prominence before being enshrined as leader of the Mesopotamian pantheon under Nebuchadnezzar I in the 2nd millennium BC. In Babylon, Marduk was worshipped in the Esagila temple.

Believed to have originated as an underworld god, a storm god or an agriculture deity, Marduk came to be worshipped as a god of creation, justice, water, agriculture, MAGIC and medicine. His symbol was the spade and he was associated with the Mušḫuššu.[3] By the 1st millennium BC, Marduk had become astrologically associated with the planet Jupiter. He was a prominent figure in Babylonian cosmology, especially in the Enūma Eliš creation myth.

At the conclusion of the Enuma Elish (Tablet VII), Marduk is bestowed with around fifty names and titles by the assembly of gods. These epithets celebrate his authority, divine acts and supreme status over the Mesopotamian pantheon.[4]

Name and etymology
The name Marduk was solely spelled as dAMAR.UTU in the Old Babylonian Period, although other spellings such as MES and dŠA.ZU were also in use since the Kassite Period. In the 1st millennium BC, the ideograms dŠU and KU were regularly used.[5] The logogram for Adad is also occasionally used to spell Marduk.[6]

Texts from the Old Babylonian period support the spelling Marutu or Marutuk, with the shortened spelling MARTUK or Marduk attested starting from the Kassite period. His name in Hebrew, Merodak, supports the longer version,[7] and First Millennium Assyrian and Babylonian texts employ the long spelling when the circumstances call for the precise form of the name.[8] The personal name Martuku is not to be confused with the god Marduk.[9] Marduk was commonly called Bēl (lord) in the First Millennium BC.[10]

The etymology for the name Marduk is generally understood to be derived from damar-utu-(a)k, meaning "BULL-calf of Utu".[8] Sommerfield suggests this is used to explain the name Marduk in the Enuma Elish as "He is the 'son of the sun[a]' of the gods, radiant is he."[12] While the name may suggest a relationship with Shamash, Marduk has no genealogy with the sun god.[13] However, Babylon was closely associated with the city of Sippar in this period, which may have been the reason for the name.[14]

History
3rd millennium BC
Marduk, along with the city of Babylon, was unimportant[15] and sparsely attested in the 3rd millennium BC. The earliest mention of Marduk comes from a fragmentary inscription, most likely dating to the Early Dynastic II period (ED II). It is left by an unnamed ruler of the city of https://t.co/gvLGzhscLj (likely Babylon[16]) who constructed a temple for Marduk.[17] A text from the Fara period (ED IIIa) seems to mention Marduk without the divine determinative, and a fragment of a contemporary god list from Abu Salabikh contains dutu-ama[r], likely Marduk written with reversed sign order.[18] A dubious reference to Marduk from the subsequent Ur III period comes from the possible personal name "Amar-Sin is the star of Marduk",[19] although Johandi suggests that the god Martu who appeared together with Enki and Damgalnuna in the Ur III period could possibly refer instead to the similarly named Marduk who is otherwise missing in Ur III documentation, as Martu is later attested to have a different parentage (Anu and Urash) and Marduk is later considered the son of Enki/Ea.[20] If so, this could be evidence that Marduk was already part of the pantheon of Eridu during the Ur III period.

Characteristics
Symbol
His symbol is the spade, and he is associated with the Mušḫuššu, a DRAGON-like creature from Mesopotamian mythology.[3]

Original role
Since sources pertaining to Marduk in the early periods are sparse, Marduk's original role is unknown. However, since Marduk appears in the Abu Salabikh list behind three minor deities whose names suggest a possible connection to the underworld, Johandi suggests that Marduk may have been a minor god associated with the underworld.[84] Similarly, Oshima recently proposed that Marduk may have originally had a role similar to Nergal, which may even explain why the logogram dAMAR.UTU is used in Hittite texts to write the name of the god Šanta,[85] who was similar in nature to Nergal.[86]

In the earlier forerunners to the Udug Hul, where both Marduk and Asalluhi appear together in a passage, Marduk, in contrast to Asalluhi, does not help the victim but instead captures him, either because of his powerlessness or because he simply refused to help.[87] Oshima interpreted the passage as supporting the idea that Marduk's original role was illness and death.[88] Similarly, in Sin-iddinam's prayer to Ninisina, Asalluhi (here identified with Marduk) imposes an evil spell on Sin-iddinam (the king of Larsa), causing him to become sick[89] may reflect that Marduk's power to cause illness extended beyond the dominion of Babylon.[90] However Sommerfield, who previously believed that there was little evidence for Marduk being related to magic,[91] more recently suggested that Marduk was originally a god of incantations before his syncretism with Asalluhi.[92]

Jacobsen suggests that Marduk was originally a storm god, based on the storm imagery in the Enuma Elish, wielding the four winds and storms as weapons and assigning to himself the rain and clouds that came from Tiamat's corpse.[93] Abusch, citing Jacobsen, also believes that Marduk was a storm god, and may have been associated with water and vegetation before joining the pantheon of Eridu, as it is improbable to suppose that all of Marduk's traits with water were taken from the circle of Enki.[94]

Bêl (/ˈbeɪl/; from Akkadian: bēlu) is a title signifying 'lord' or 'master' applied to various gods in the Mesopotamian religion of Akkad, Assyria, and Babylonia. The feminine form is Bêlit ('Lady, Mistress') in Akkadian. Bel is represented in Greek as Belos and in Latin as Belus. Belit appears in Greek form as Beltis (Βελτις). Linguistically, Bel is an East Semitic form cognate with the Northwest Semitic Baal with the same meaning.

BEL was especially used for the Babylonian god Marduk in Assyrian and neo-Babylonian personal names or mentioned in inscriptions in a Mesopotamian context. Similarly, Bêlit mostly refers to Marduk's spouse Sarpanit. Marduk's mother, the Sumerian goddess often referred to in the Sumerian language as Ninhursag, Damkina, and Ninmah, was often known as Belit-ili ('Lady of the Gods') in Akkadian.

Other gods called "Lord" were sometimes identified totally or in part with Bel Marduk. The god Malak-bel of Palmyra is an example, attested as a messenger of Bel but existing as a deity separate to Bel/Marduk. Similarly, Zeus Belus mentioned by Sanchuniathon as born to Cronus/El in Peraea is unlikely to be Marduk. Early translators of Akkadian believed that the ideogram for the god called Enlil in Sumerian was to be read as Bel in Akkadian. Current scholarship holds this as incorrect, but Bel is used in referring to Enlil in older translations and discussions.[1]

In Mandaean cosmology, the name for Jupiter is Bil (ࡁࡉࡋ), which is derived from the name Bel.[2]

Bel of Palmyra, Syria
A god named Bel was the chief-god of Palmyra, Syria in pre-Hellenistic times; the deity was worshipped alongside the gods Aglibol and Yarhibol.[3] He was originally known as Bol,[4] after the Northwestern Semitic word Ba'al[5] (usually used to refer to the god Hadad), until the cult of Bel-Marduk spread to Palmyra; by 213 BC, Bol was renamed to Bel.[4] The Temple of Bel in Palmrya, Syria was dedicated to this god. The temple has since been destroyed by ISIS.[6]

Béla Ferenc Dezső Blaskó[a] (October 20, 1882 – August 16, 1956), better known by his stage name Béla Lugosi,[b] was a Hungarian–American actor. He is best remembered for portraying Count Dracula in the horror film classic Dracula (1931), Ygor in both Son of Frankenstein (1939) and Ghost of Frankenstein (1942) and his roles in many other horror films from 1931 through 1956.[1]

Lugosi began acting on the Hungarian stage in 1901, appearing in more than 170 productions. Beginning in 1917, he performed in Hungarian silent films. During World War I, he served as a corporal (in Austrian German: Zugsführer; in Hungarian: szakaszvezető) in the Austro-Hungarian Army from 1914 to 1916. After the failed Hungarian Communist Revolution of 1919, Lugosi chose to immigrate to Germany due to his Socialist party activities. He acted in several films in Weimar Germany, before arriving in New Orleans as a seaman on a merchant ship, then making his way north to New York City and Ellis Island.

In 1927, he starred as Dracula in a Broadway adaptation of Bram Stoker's novel, moving with the play to the West Coast in 1928 and settling down in Hollywood.[2] He later starred in the 1931 film version of Dracula directed by Tod Browning and produced by Universal Pictures. Through the 1930s, he occupied an important niche in horror films, but his notoriety as Dracula and thick Hungarian accent greatly limited the roles offered to him, and he unsuccessfully tried for years to avoid typecasting.

He co-starred in a number of films with fellow horror icon Boris Karloff, including The Black Cat (1934), The Raven (1935), and Son of Frankenstein (1939).

By this time, Lugosi had been receiving regular medication for sciatic neuritis, and he became addicted to doctor-prescribed morphine and methadone. This drug dependence (and his gradually worsening alcoholism) was becoming apparent to producers, and after 1948's Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein, Lugosi experienced a career decline and mostly appeared in low-budget films, some of which were directed by Ed Wood. His collaborations with Wood include a brief appearance in Plan 9 from Outer Space, released posthumously in 1957.[3]

Lugosi married five times and had one son, Béla G. Lugosi (with his fourth wife, Lillian). Lugosi would eventually have four grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren,[4] although he did not live long enough to meet any of them.[3]

Early life
Lugosi, the youngest of five children (one of them died in an early age),[5] was born Béla Ferenc Dezső Blaskó in 1882 in Lugos, Kingdom of Hungary (now Lugoj, Romania) to Hungarian father István Blaskó, a baker who later became a banker,[6] and Serbian mother Paula de Vojnić (Serbian: Паула де Војнић).[7] He was raised in a Catholic family.[8]

Marduk (/ˈmɑːrdʊk/;[2] cuneiform: 𒀭𒀫𒌓 dAMAR.UTU; Sumerian: amar utu.k "calf of the sun; solar calf"; Hebrew: מְרֹדַךְ, Modern: Merōdaḵ, Tiberian: Mərōḏaḵ) was a god from ancient Mesopotamia, patron deity of Babylon. First sparsely attested in the 3rd millennium BC, Marduk slowly rose to prominence before being enshrined as leader of the Mesopotamian pantheon under Nebuchadnezzar I in the 2nd millennium BC. In Babylon, Marduk was worshipped in the Esagila temple.

Believed to have originated as an underworld god, a storm god or an agriculture deity, Marduk came to be worshipped as a god of creation, justice, water, agriculture, MAGIC and medicine. His symbol was the spade and he was associated with the Mušḫuššu.[3] By the 1st millennium BC, Marduk had become astrologically associated with the planet Jupiter. He was a prominent figure in Babylonian cosmology, especially in the Enūma Eliš creation myth.

At the conclusion of the Enuma Elish (Tablet VII), Marduk is bestowed with around fifty names and titles by the assembly of gods. These epithets celebrate his authority, divine acts and supreme status over the Mesopotamian pantheon.[4]

Name and etymology
The name Marduk was solely spelled as dAMAR.UTU in the Old Babylonian Period, although other spellings such as MES and dŠA.ZU were also in use since the Kassite Period. In the 1st millennium BC, the ideograms dŠU and KU were regularly used.[5] The logogram for Adad is also occasionally used to spell Marduk.[6]

Texts from the Old Babylonian period support the spelling Marutu or Marutuk, with the shortened spelling MARTUK or Marduk attested starting from the Kassite period. His name in Hebrew, Merodak, supports the longer version,[7] and First Millennium Assyrian and Babylonian texts employ the long spelling when the circumstances call for the precise form of the name.[8] The personal name Martuku is not to be confused with the god Marduk.[9] Marduk was commonly called Bēl (lord) in the First Millennium BC.[10]

The etymology for the name Marduk is generally understood to be derived from damar-utu-(a)k, meaning "BULL-calf of Utu".[8] Sommerfield suggests this is used to explain the name Marduk in the Enuma Elish as "He is the 'son of the sun[a]' of the gods, radiant is he."[12] While the name may suggest a relationship with Shamash, Marduk has no genealogy with the sun god.[13] However, Babylon was closely associated with the city of Sippar in this period, which may have been the reason for the name.[14]

History
3rd millennium BC
Marduk, along with the city of Babylon, was unimportant[15] and sparsely attested in the 3rd millennium BC. The earliest mention of Marduk comes from a fragmentary inscription, most likely dating to the Early Dynastic II period (ED II). It is left by an unnamed ruler of the city of https://t.co/gvLGzhsKAR (likely Babylon[16]) who constructed a temple for Marduk.[17] A text from the Fara period (ED IIIa) seems to mention Marduk without the divine determinative, and a fragment of a contemporary god list from Abu Salabikh contains dutu-ama[r], likely Marduk written with reversed sign order.[18] A dubious reference to Marduk from the subsequent Ur III period comes from the possible personal name "Amar-Sin is the star of Marduk",[19] although Johandi suggests that the god Martu who appeared together with Enki and Damgalnuna in the Ur III period could possibly refer instead to the similarly named Marduk who is otherwise missing in Ur III documentation, as Martu is later attested to have a different parentage (Anu and Urash) and Marduk is later considered the son of Enki/Ea.[20] If so, this could be evidence that Marduk was already part of the pantheon of Eridu during the Ur III period.

Characteristics
Symbol
His symbol is the spade, and he is associated with the Mušḫuššu, a DRAGON-like creature from Mesopotamian mythology.[3]

Original role
Since sources pertaining to Marduk in the early periods are sparse, Marduk's original role is unknown. However, since Marduk appears in the Abu Salabikh list behind three minor deities whose names suggest a possible connection to the underworld, Johandi suggests that Marduk may have been a minor god associated with the underworld.[84] Similarly, Oshima recently proposed that Marduk may have originally had a role similar to Nergal, which may even explain why the logogram dAMAR.UTU is used in Hittite texts to write the name of the god Šanta,[85] who was similar in nature to Nergal.[86]

In the earlier forerunners to the Udug Hul, where both Marduk and Asalluhi appear together in a passage, Marduk, in contrast to Asalluhi, does not help the victim but instead captures him, either because of his powerlessness or because he simply refused to help.[87] Oshima interpreted the passage as supporting the idea that Marduk's original role was illness and death.[88] Similarly, in Sin-iddinam's prayer to Ninisina, Asalluhi (here identified with Marduk) imposes an evil spell on Sin-iddinam (the king of Larsa), causing him to become sick[89] may reflect that Marduk's power to cause illness extended beyond the dominion of Babylon.[90] However Sommerfield, who previously believed that there was little evidence for Marduk being related to magic,[91] more recently suggested that Marduk was originally a god of incantations before his syncretism with Asalluhi.[92]

Jacobsen suggests that Marduk was originally a storm god, based on the storm imagery in the Enuma Elish, wielding the four winds and storms as weapons and assigning to himself the rain and clouds that came from Tiamat's corpse.[93] Abusch, citing Jacobsen, also believes that Marduk was a storm god, and may have been associated with water and vegetation before joining the pantheon of Eridu, as it is improbable to suppose that all of Marduk's traits with water were taken from the circle of Enki.[94]

Bêl (/ˈbeɪl/; from Akkadian: bēlu) is a title signifying 'lord' or 'master' applied to various gods in the Mesopotamian religion of Akkad, Assyria, and Babylonia. The feminine form is Bêlit ('Lady, Mistress') in Akkadian. Bel is represented in Greek as Belos and in Latin as Belus. Belit appears in Greek form as Beltis (Βελτις). Linguistically, Bel is an East Semitic form cognate with the Northwest Semitic Baal with the same meaning.

BEL was especially used for the Babylonian god Marduk in Assyrian and neo-Babylonian personal names or mentioned in inscriptions in a Mesopotamian context. Similarly, Bêlit mostly refers to Marduk's spouse Sarpanit. Marduk's mother, the Sumerian goddess often referred to in the Sumerian language as Ninhursag, Damkina, and Ninmah, was often known as Belit-ili ('Lady of the Gods') in Akkadian.

Other gods called "Lord" were sometimes identified totally or in part with Bel Marduk. The god Malak-bel of Palmyra is an example, attested as a messenger of Bel but existing as a deity separate to Bel/Marduk. Similarly, Zeus Belus mentioned by Sanchuniathon as born to Cronus/El in Peraea is unlikely to be Marduk. Early translators of Akkadian believed that the ideogram for the god called Enlil in Sumerian was to be read as Bel in Akkadian. Current scholarship holds this as incorrect, but Bel is used in referring to Enlil in older translations and discussions.[1]

In Mandaean cosmology, the name for Jupiter is Bil (ࡁࡉࡋ), which is derived from the name Bel.[2]

Bel of Palmyra, Syria
A god named Bel was the chief-god of Palmyra, Syria in pre-Hellenistic times; the deity was worshipped alongside the gods Aglibol and Yarhibol.[3] He was originally known as Bol,[4] after the Northwestern Semitic word Ba'al[5] (usually used to refer to the god Hadad), until the cult of Bel-Marduk spread to Palmyra; by 213 BC, Bol was renamed to Bel.[4] The Temple of Bel in Palmrya, Syria was dedicated to this god. The temple has since been destroyed by ISIS.[6]

This Monday, NOAA Fisheries published a proposed rule to lift the commercial fishing ban between 50 and 200 nautical miles out from Kalama (Johnston Atoll, Hawaiian name), Ānen Kio (Wake Island, Marshallese name) and Paukeaho (Jarvis Island, Hawaiian name). Pelagic longline and purse seine vessels after tunas and billfish would return to about 1,030,000 square kilometers.

The rule title and 50 CFR part 665 subpart H both name the Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument Expansion. Proclamation 10880 of January 2, 2025 renamed the monument the Pacific Islands Heritage Marine National Monument. The NOAA Fisheries monument page, updated in September, uses the newer name and lists the older one as former.

There are two names on one docket, NOAA-NMFS-2026-2410. Deprecated in a termbase is Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument, with Proclamation 10880 as the authority and January 2, 2025 as the date. Both the President in Proclamation 11035 of June 2026 and NMFS in the CFR subpart have kept the older name.

The economic case in the filing is fees and fuel. NMFS has put purse seine savings on South Pacific Tuna Act access fees at up to $1,367,340 a year across the fleet, with those fees running $10,000 to $13,000 a day. NMFS puts that saving at about 1% of average annual revenue per vessel.

Both the Hawaiʻi longline fleet and the Amerika Sāmoa (American Samoa, Samoan name) longline fleet fall under the analysis, which counts up to 224 longline vessels. The Hawaiʻi fleet earned $109M in 2025.

NMFS rests its finding of negligible effects on cultural resources on a permit count. Zero cultural practitioners have sought a Special Use Permit since the expansion, the rule says. The Pacific Islands Heritage Coalition opposes the change and disputes that finding.

NMFS calls notice and comment not legally required and offers it out of caution, citing the 2025 Kapaʻa v. Trump ruling in federal court. Comments go in online through the federal rulemaking portal or by mail to the Pacific Islands Regional Office in Honolulu until December 9.

text:
The New York Times: Why U.S. Business Deals Are Unlikely to Get Putin to Give Any Ground. President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia has shown a willingness to endure a high price to get what he wants in Ukraine, and he sees little reason to stop fighting now, analysts say. For a year and a half, as the United States engaged Russia in on-again, off-again peace talks, the Trump administration held off on cutting any business deals with Moscow, insisting that the Kremlin first take concrete steps toward ending the war in Ukraine.

That all changed this fall. President Trump brokered a deal to waive sanctions and import Russian diesel ahead of the midterm elections. U.S. officials held talks on a range of possible deals, including the sale of the international assets of the Russian energy giant Lukoil and the resumption of Russian gas exports to Europe.

U.S. officials argued that the frenzy of potential deal-making could build good will and help compel the Kremlin to stop fighting. But the inducements have done little to curb President Vladimir V. Putin’s central demands on the war, which include placing limits on Ukraine’s defenses and alliances and broadly reordering the security architecture in Europe.

Those demands are at the center of peace talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Mr. Trump’s envoys, are convening on Tuesday and Wednesday in the United Arab Emirates. The talks, the first since February involving all three countries, will address thorny topics like how to put in place an eventual cease-fire and whether a compromise can be reached on territory, U.S. officials said.

Top security advisers have flown in from European countries and NATO as momentum builds for Europe to become more directly involved in the peace process. The European officials will meet with the Americans and the Ukrainians, with a view toward fostering more direct discussions between European and Russian leaders in the future, the U.S. officials said.

But to pull Mr. Putin toward compromise, it is going to take a lot more than business deals, analysts say.

“It’s not going to entice him to make compromises on Ukraine,” said Eric Green, who served as senior director for Russia on the U.S. National Security Council under President Joseph R. Biden Jr.

Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner, both real estate investors, have dealt with Russian oligarch types. Mr. Green said that the two men most likely went into the talks thinking: “We have a common language with these guys. They are interested in money. If we offer them various deals, that will persuade them to compromise in Ukraine.”

Mr. Green added, “It may be true of the oligarchs, but it is not true of Putin, who has different metrics that he is thinking about.” Those include political and security objectives — such as a ban on NATO membership for Ukraine and limits on the scope of its military — that would give Russia leverage over Ukrainian national policy.

Mr. Putin has demonstrated a stubborn willingness to endure a high price at home to get what he wants in Ukraine. He angered much of Russia’s business elite by choosing to invade Ukraine, and despite botching the initial invasion, he doubled down as war costs mounted.

Just before the Abu Dhabi talks, two hacking groups banned by the Kremlin as extremist organizations released pilfered data from the state statistics service, Rosstat, that they said showed that between 390,000 and 450,000 Russian troops had been killed in the war. The numbers could not be independently verified.

Despite the human and economic losses, the Russian leader may see little reason to stop fighting now, analysts say. Though Russia’s progress on the battlefield has stalled, Ukraine is running out of air defenses ahead of perhaps the most perilous winter of the war. Moscow appears to believe that a brutal campaign against Ukrainian cities will increase its negotiating advantage in the coming months.

On top of this, Europe’s resolve to back Ukraine is beginning to fray. The far-right politician Marine Le Pen, who opposes support for Ukraine, is leading the polls ahead of France’s presidential election next spring. And the far-right Alternative for Germany party, which also wants to end Ukraine aid, is on the rise in Germany.

It was Russia that first injected the possibility of business deals into peace talks days after Mr. Trump returned to office.

To appeal to the real estate mogul president, Mr. Putin dispatched Kirill Dmitriev, the Stanford- and Harvard-educated former McKinsey executive who runs the Russian government investment fund, to sketch out all the ways that the United States could make money by re-engaging with Russia.

In Moscow’s ideal world, a Russia-friendly Trump administration would press ahead with energy deals, begin lifting sanctions and normalize relations with Russia, all while forcing the Kremlin’s preferred terms on Ukraine to end the war.

Just as the Trump administration believes that Mr. Putin can be swayed by business deals, the Russians believe that such deals can also sway the Americans, Mr. Green said.

“On the Russian side, they are using the same logic, ‘These guys are just interested in money. If we dangle enough deals in front of them, they are going to coerce Ukraine into doing what we want,’” Mr. Green said.

But Mr. Trump has not gone nearly so far as to hand victory to Russia in Ukraine. Domestic pressures have constrained the president in delivering what the Kremlin most desires, and Europe has continued sending billions of dollars and buying American weapons to keep Ukraine in the fight.

Ukraine still has bipartisan support in Congress, and once the Democrats control the House and the Senate with large majorities beginning in January, lawmakers could move more aggressively to curb any deals Mr. Trump strikes that are seen as overly favorable to Russia.

Thomas Graham, who served as senior Russia adviser on the National Security Council under President George W. Bush, said Mr. Putin had misread the domestic political situation in the United States.

“The idea was if he dangled those deals, the Trump people would jump on them, lean on the Ukrainians and this would be over on Russia’s terms,” Mr. Graham said. “But it turns out it’s not that simple; there is a domestic political context here.”

While commercial deals on their own are not sufficient to move Russia toward serious concessions, Mr. Graham said, it makes sense to include them as part of the broader negotiations.

American officials, he said, should broker deals and sanctions relief packages that would entice the Russians but act on them only when Moscow commits to concrete steps to de-escalate the war. Those steps, he said, could include cease-fires on energy infrastructure and on shipping in the Black Sea.

The inducements for Russia should also be paired with additional U.S. support for Ukraine that pressures Moscow simultaneously, Mr. Graham said, including more air defenses.

Mr. Putin has rejected any broad cease-fire before the full specifics of a peace deal are worked out, worrying that the minute Russia puts down its weapons, it will lose leverage in the talks.

But the idea of brokering every last detail of a peace deal before a cease-fire is unrealistic, Mr. Graham said. He argued that the parties should be shooting for a “framework agreement” that lays out the fundamentals of a deal in exchange for a cease-fire.

Officials could then work out the details of carrying it out afterward.

“If Putin’s position is no cease-fire until everything is signed, then that is a recipe for a forever war on the Russian side,” Mr. Graham said. “And Russia can’t sustain that.”

text:
On Monday, the Council of Ministers was unable to reach a unanimous compromise on the Tobacco Tax Directive. Had it adopted the compromise text promoted by the Irish Presidency - and, even more forcefully, by the European Commissioner - the European tobacco market would have been distorted for years to come.
The Commission and the Presidency billed the proposal as needing to bring new nicotine products within the scope of the Directive setting minimum rates in many cases well above national rates. Contradicting its objectives, the outcome of the final compromise is that only the minimum rates for niche traditional European products such as pipe tobacco, nasal snuff, and chewing tobacco are now disproportionately high.
These niche traditional products are manufactured in Europe by small and mid-sized European companies, with, according to the Commission ‘insignificant market shares’ and no need to assess the impact of the proposal on these.  Europe’s heritage SMEs would therefore have been placed at a competitive disadvantage, even though the Directive itself states that it must ensure neutral conditions of competition.
The Presidency could have put a better compromise on the table had it simply listened to Member States. Differentiated taxation is a cornerstone of the Directive, whilst concerns on uptake have apparently now become a relevant parameter as well. Logically, this should mean that pipe tobacco and traditional smokeless products are taxed at lower rates because sales are continuously decreasing, and its consumers are mainly older adults. Yet the compromise on the table does exactly the opposite.
If illicit trade is a concern, then it must be acknowledged that raising tax rates will lead to more illicit trade unless smokers are offered more affordable alternatives, including hand-rolling tobacco. If neutral conditions of competition are to be ensured, this should be achieved not only by removing Swedish snus from the Directive’s scope, but also by excluding Bavarian nasal snuff and traditional chewing tobacco. At the very least, their tax rates should be set at the same level as those for new nicotine products.
Instead, the compromise became reactive rather than principled. The compromise is riddled with inaccuracies and contradictions simply to get a compromise over the finish line – any compromise.
That a compromise is necessary is clear. But throwing internal-market principles over-board and Europe’s small and medium-sized companies under the bus demonstrates, once again, that for all the talk on Europe’s competitiveness, better regulation and SME tests, the reality is that those are merely afterthoughts and not guiding principles.
More than 120,000 people are employed as a result of the tobacco businesses of ESTA’s small and mid-sized member companies. They deserve a better compromise - one that does not unnecessarily put their jobs at risk.

Marduk (/ˈmɑːrdʊk/;[2] cuneiform: 𒀭𒀫𒌓 dAMAR.UTU; Sumerian: amar utu.k "calf of the sun; solar calf"; Hebrew: מְרֹדַךְ, Modern: Merōdaḵ, Tiberian: Mərōḏaḵ) was a god from ancient Mesopotamia, patron deity of Babylon. First sparsely attested in the 3rd millennium BC, Marduk slowly rose to prominence before being enshrined as leader of the Mesopotamian pantheon under Nebuchadnezzar I in the 2nd millennium BC. In Babylon, Marduk was worshipped in the Esagila temple.

Believed to have originated as an underworld god, a storm god or an agriculture deity, Marduk came to be worshipped as a god of creation, justice, water, agriculture, MAGIC and medicine. His symbol was the spade and he was associated with the Mušḫuššu.[3] By the 1st millennium BC, Marduk had become astrologically associated with the planet Jupiter. He was a prominent figure in Babylonian cosmology, especially in the Enūma Eliš creation myth.

At the conclusion of the Enuma Elish (Tablet VII), Marduk is bestowed with around fifty names and titles by the assembly of gods. These epithets celebrate his authority, divine acts and supreme status over the Mesopotamian pantheon.[4]

Name and etymology
The name Marduk was solely spelled as dAMAR.UTU in the Old Babylonian Period, although other spellings such as MES and dŠA.ZU were also in use since the Kassite Period. In the 1st millennium BC, the ideograms dŠU and KU were regularly used.[5] The logogram for Adad is also occasionally used to spell Marduk.[6]

Texts from the Old Babylonian period support the spelling Marutu or Marutuk, with the shortened spelling MARTUK or Marduk attested starting from the Kassite period. His name in Hebrew, Merodak, supports the longer version,[7] and First Millennium Assyrian and Babylonian texts employ the long spelling when the circumstances call for the precise form of the name.[8] The personal name Martuku is not to be confused with the god Marduk.[9] Marduk was commonly called Bēl (lord) in the First Millennium BC.[10]

The etymology for the name Marduk is generally understood to be derived from damar-utu-(a)k, meaning "BULL-calf of Utu".[8] Sommerfield suggests this is used to explain the name Marduk in the Enuma Elish as "He is the 'son of the sun[a]' of the gods, radiant is he."[12] While the name may suggest a relationship with Shamash, Marduk has no genealogy with the sun god.[13] However, Babylon was closely associated with the city of Sippar in this period, which may have been the reason for the name.[14]

History
3rd millennium BC
Marduk, along with the city of Babylon, was unimportant[15] and sparsely attested in the 3rd millennium BC. The earliest mention of Marduk comes from a fragmentary inscription, most likely dating to the Early Dynastic II period (ED II). It is left by an unnamed ruler of the city of https://t.co/gvLGzhsKAR (likely Babylon[16]) who constructed a temple for Marduk.[17] A text from the Fara period (ED IIIa) seems to mention Marduk without the divine determinative, and a fragment of a contemporary god list from Abu Salabikh contains dutu-ama[r], likely Marduk written with reversed sign order.[18] A dubious reference to Marduk from the subsequent Ur III period comes from the possible personal name "Amar-Sin is the star of Marduk",[19] although Johandi suggests that the god Martu who appeared together with Enki and Damgalnuna in the Ur III period could possibly refer instead to the similarly named Marduk who is otherwise missing in Ur III documentation, as Martu is later attested to have a different parentage (Anu and Urash) and Marduk is later considered the son of Enki/Ea.[20] If so, this could be evidence that Marduk was already part of the pantheon of Eridu during the Ur III period.

Characteristics
Symbol
His symbol is the spade, and he is associated with the Mušḫuššu, a DRAGON-like creature from Mesopotamian mythology.[3]

Original role
Since sources pertaining to Marduk in the early periods are sparse, Marduk's original role is unknown. However, since Marduk appears in the Abu Salabikh list behind three minor deities whose names suggest a possible connection to the underworld, Johandi suggests that Marduk may have been a minor god associated with the underworld.[84] Similarly, Oshima recently proposed that Marduk may have originally had a role similar to Nergal, which may even explain why the logogram dAMAR.UTU is used in Hittite texts to write the name of the god Šanta,[85] who was similar in nature to Nergal.[86]

In the earlier forerunners to the Udug Hul, where both Marduk and Asalluhi appear together in a passage, Marduk, in contrast to Asalluhi, does not help the victim but instead captures him, either because of his powerlessness or because he simply refused to help.[87] Oshima interpreted the passage as supporting the idea that Marduk's original role was illness and death.[88] Similarly, in Sin-iddinam's prayer to Ninisina, Asalluhi (here identified with Marduk) imposes an evil spell on Sin-iddinam (the king of Larsa), causing him to become sick[89] may reflect that Marduk's power to cause illness extended beyond the dominion of Babylon.[90] However Sommerfield, who previously believed that there was little evidence for Marduk being related to magic,[91] more recently suggested that Marduk was originally a god of incantations before his syncretism with Asalluhi.[92]

Jacobsen suggests that Marduk was originally a storm god, based on the storm imagery in the Enuma Elish, wielding the four winds and storms as weapons and assigning to himself the rain and clouds that came from Tiamat's corpse.[93] Abusch, citing Jacobsen, also believes that Marduk was a storm god, and may have been associated with water and vegetation before joining the pantheon of Eridu, as it is improbable to suppose that all of Marduk's traits with water were taken from the circle of Enki.[94]

Bêl (/ˈbeɪl/; from Akkadian: bēlu) is a title signifying 'lord' or 'master' applied to various gods in the Mesopotamian religion of Akkad, Assyria, and Babylonia. The feminine form is Bêlit ('Lady, Mistress') in Akkadian. Bel is represented in Greek as Belos and in Latin as Belus. Belit appears in Greek form as Beltis (Βελτις). Linguistically, Bel is an East Semitic form cognate with the Northwest Semitic Baal with the same meaning.

BEL was especially used for the Babylonian god Marduk in Assyrian and neo-Babylonian personal names or mentioned in inscriptions in a Mesopotamian context. Similarly, Bêlit mostly refers to Marduk's spouse Sarpanit. Marduk's mother, the Sumerian goddess often referred to in the Sumerian language as Ninhursag, Damkina, and Ninmah, was often known as Belit-ili ('Lady of the Gods') in Akkadian.

Other gods called "Lord" were sometimes identified totally or in part with Bel Marduk. The god Malak-bel of Palmyra is an example, attested as a messenger of Bel but existing as a deity separate to Bel/Marduk. Similarly, Zeus Belus mentioned by Sanchuniathon as born to Cronus/El in Peraea is unlikely to be Marduk. Early translators of Akkadian believed that the ideogram for the god called Enlil in Sumerian was to be read as Bel in Akkadian. Current scholarship holds this as incorrect, but Bel is used in referring to Enlil in older translations and discussions.[1]

In Mandaean cosmology, the name for Jupiter is Bil (ࡁࡉࡋ), which is derived from the name Bel.[2]

Bel of Palmyra, Syria
A god named Bel was the chief-god of Palmyra, Syria in pre-Hellenistic times; the deity was worshipped alongside the gods Aglibol and Yarhibol.[3] He was originally known as Bol,[4] after the Northwestern Semitic word Ba'al[5] (usually used to refer to the god Hadad), until the cult of Bel-Marduk spread to Palmyra; by 213 BC, Bol was renamed to Bel.[4] The Temple of Bel in Palmrya, Syria was dedicated to this god. The temple has since been destroyed by ISIS.[6]
