text:
On Remembrance Day, a day when we honour the fallen who gave their lives for our freedom, the Woman of the Day can only be “The Poppy Lady from France”, teacher and humanitarian Anna Guérin (1878-1961) from Ardeche.

She campaigned for all WW1 Allied Countries to use poppies made by French widows and orphans as a symbol of remembrance and to raise money for the families of the fallen and those who had survived.

In 1911, Anna was living with her family in England and delivering lectures on behalf of the Alliance Française, an international organisation that promotes French culture and language. Soon after Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914, she left Liverpool on the Lusitania bound for New York. While delivering lectures to American audiences on behalf of the Alliance Française, she quietly raised funds at the end of each lecture for those made destitute by war, sending all donations directly to the American Red Cross.

Once the USA entered the war, Anna was free to raise funds openly. She returned to France each summer throughout the war and was halfway across the Atlantic at the 11th hour on the 11th day of the 11th month of 1918: Armistice Day.

In 1915, Canadian surgeon Lt Colonel John McCrae had famously written “We shall not sleep, though poppies grow, in Flanders fields”, which inspired Moina Michael of Georgia to persuade the American Legion Auxiliary to adopt the poppy as their symbol in 1921 but Anna had already started promoting the poppy as the symbol of Remembrance two years before after the French government formed "La Ligule des enfants de France et d'Amerique" with the poppy as its emblem and asked her to travel to the USA to form the American branch.

From 1919, Anna raised funds for the war orphans of France by holding Poppy Days in every American state she visited, distributing paper poppies in exchange for donations. Women and girls wearing sashes bearing the words "In Flanders Fields the poppies grow” sold them. It was then that Anna devised a plan for holding an Inter-Allied Poppy Day, a day when all WW1 Allied countries could use poppies as a symbol of remembrance and to raise humanitarian funds.

The USA decided to go its own way and follow the American model so Anna turned her attention to the Commonwealth, starting with Canada and Newfoundland (not part of Canada then). Both signed up to her idea so she travelled to the UK, arriving in Liverpool in August 1921.

Anna brought samples of her French-made poppies to the British Legion and offered to fund the manufacture of a million poppies in France, an offer the British Legion accepted. She also persuaded the Legion of the value of recruiting women as volunteers to form a distribution and collection network.

Australia and New Zealand followed suit and the Inter-Allied Poppy Day became established.

When Earl Haig announced in October 1921 that 11 November would be known as Remembrance Day or Poppy Day, the British Legion contributed a further eight million poppies made in Britain to Anna’s one million French poppies.

All nine million poppies sold.

Today, over 45 million poppies are distributed by the British Legion in the UK and many more are created at home by volunteers for civic remembrance displays. #LestWeForget

text:
Grok Bot shipped a dozen updates this week. Four of them touch your money or your logins.

Matt Palmer from the Grok Bot team covered them in a 7.5-minute video. Here's the minute that matters.

1. It makes your phone calls. It waits in the queue, gets through the phone tree and hands you the call with a live transcript. In the demo it cancels an internet plan and turns down a 10%-off retention offer. US only, not in Washington or Illinois.

2. Checkout cards got longer and more honest. Totals now include shipping, tax and promo codes, and you get 6 hours to approve a purchase instead of 30 minutes. His reason: "I always get to the checkout and then I get some hesitation."

3. Team bots got permissions: whoever creates a shared bot decides who can change its memory. Plus a new "hours saved" chart.

4. Hidden-instruction warnings. If a page or a chat tries to slip commands to your bot, it tells you: "the page had hidden instructions for AI agents, and I didn't follow them."

The video below is those four.

Number 2 is the one I'd think about. A 6-hour window is great when you're unsure. It's also 6 hours where an approved charge is one tap away on your phone.

Paste this into Grok Bot:
"List which of this week's new features can spend my money, call someone or change a bot's memory. For each one, tell me what it can do without asking me first. Show me first, change nothing until I confirm."

Which one would you turn on first: the phone calls or the 6-hour checkout?

“The Philistines now mustered their army for battle and camped between Socoh in Judah and Azekah at Ephes-dammim. Saul countered by gathering his Israelite troops near the valley of Elah. So the Philistines and Israelites faced each other on opposite hills, with the valley between them. Then Goliath, a Philistine champion from Gath, came out of the Philistine ranks to face the forces of Israel. He was over nine feet tall! He wore a bronze helmet, and his bronze coat of mail weighed 125 pounds. He also wore bronze leg armor, and he carried a bronze javelin on his shoulder. The shaft of his spear was as heavy and thick as a weaver’s beam, tipped with an iron spearhead that weighed 15 pounds. His armor bearer walked ahead of him carrying a shield. Goliath stood and shouted a taunt across to the Israelites. “Why are you all coming out to fight?” he called. “I am the Philistine champion, but you are only the servants of Saul. Choose one man to come down here and fight me! If he kills me, then we will be your slaves. But if I kill him, you will be our slaves! I defy the armies of Israel today! Send me a man who will fight me!” When Saul and the Israelites heard this, they were terrified and deeply shaken. Now David was the son of a man named Jesse, an Ephrathite from Bethlehem in the land of Judah. Jesse was an old man at that time, and he had eight sons. Jesse’s three oldest sons—Eliab, Abinadab, and Shimea—had already joined Saul’s army to fight the Philistines. David was the youngest son. David’s three oldest brothers stayed with Saul’s army, but David went back and forth so he could help his father with the sheep in Bethlehem. For forty days, every morning and evening, the Philistine champion strutted in front of the Israelite army. One day Jesse said to David, “Take this basket of roasted grain and these ten loaves of bread, and carry them quickly to your brothers. And give these ten cuts of cheese to their captain. See how your brothers are getting along, and bring back a report on how they are doing.” David’s brothers were with Saul and the Israelite army at the valley of Elah, fighting against the Philistines. So David left the sheep with another shepherd and set out early the next morning with the gifts, as Jesse had directed him. He arrived at the camp just as the Israelite army was leaving for the battlefield with shouts and battle cries. Soon the Israelite and Philistine forces stood facing each other, army against army. David left his things with the keeper of supplies and hurried out to the ranks to greet his brothers. As he was talking with them, Goliath, the Philistine champion from Gath, came out from the Philistine ranks. Then David heard him shout his usual taunt to the army of Israel. As soon as the Israelite army saw him, they began to run away in fright. “Have you seen the giant?” the men asked. “He comes out each day to defy Israel. The king has offered a huge reward to anyone who kills him. He will give that man one of his daughters for a wife, and the man’s entire family will be exempted from paying taxes!” David asked the soldiers standing nearby, “What will a man get for killing this Philistine and ending his defiance of Israel? Who is this pagan Philistine anyway, that he is allowed to defy the armies of the living God?” And these men gave David the same reply. They said, “Yes, that is the reward for killing him.” But when David’s oldest brother, Eliab, heard David talking to the men, he was angry. “What are you doing around here anyway?” he demanded. “What about those few sheep you’re supposed to be taking care of? I know about your pride and deceit. You just want to see the battle!” “What have I done now?” David replied. “I was only asking a question!” He walked over to some others and asked them the same thing and received the same answer. Then David’s question was reported to King Saul, and the king sent for him. “Don’t worry about this Philistine,” David told Saul. “I’ll go fight him!” “Don’t be ridiculous!” Saul replied. “There’s no way you can fight this Philistine and possibly win! You’re only a boy, and he’s been a man of war since his youth.” But David persisted. “I have been taking care of my father’s sheep and goats,” he said. “When a lion or a bear comes to steal a lamb from the flock, I go after it with a club and rescue the lamb from its mouth. If the animal turns on me, I catch it by the jaw and club it to death. I have done this to both lions and bears, and I’ll do it to this pagan Philistine, too, for he has defied the armies of the living God! The Lord who rescued me from the claws of the lion and the bear will rescue me from this Philistine!” Saul finally consented. “All right, go ahead,” he said. “And may the Lord be with you!” Then Saul gave David his own armor—a bronze helmet and a coat of mail. David put it on, strapped the sword over it, and took a step or two to see what it was like, for he had never worn such things before. “I can’t go in these,” he protested to Saul. “I’m not used to them.” So David took them off again. He picked up five smooth stones from a stream and put them into his shepherd’s bag. Then, armed only with his shepherd’s staff and sling, he started across the valley to fight the Philistine. Goliath walked out toward David with his shield bearer ahead of him, sneering in contempt at this ruddy-faced boy. “Am I a dog,” he roared at David, “that you come at me with a stick?” And he cursed David by the names of his gods. “Come over here, and I’ll give your flesh to the birds and wild animals!” Goliath yelled. David replied to the Philistine, “You come to me with sword, spear, and javelin, but I come to you in the name of the Lord of Heaven’s Armies—the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. Today the Lord will conquer you, and I will kill you and cut off your head. And then I will give the dead bodies of your men to the birds and wild animals, and the whole world will know that there is a God in Israel! And everyone assembled here will know that the Lord rescues his people, but not with sword and spear. This is the Lord’s battle, and he will give you to us!” As Goliath moved closer to attack, David quickly ran out to meet him. Reaching into his shepherd’s bag and taking out a stone, he hurled it with his sling and hit the Philistine in the forehead. The stone sank in, and Goliath stumbled and fell face down on the ground. So David triumphed over the Philistine with only a sling and a stone, for he had no sword. Then David ran over and pulled Goliath’s sword from its sheath. David used it to kill him and cut off his head. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they turned and ran. Then the men of Israel and Judah gave a great shout of triumph and rushed after the Philistines, chasing them as far as Gath and the gates of Ekron. The bodies of the dead and wounded Philistines were strewn all along the road from Shaaraim, as far as Gath and Ekron. Then the Israelite army returned and plundered the deserted Philistine camp. (David took the Philistine’s head to Jerusalem, but he stored the man’s armor in his own tent.) As Saul watched David go out to fight the Philistine, he asked Abner, the commander of his army, “Abner, whose son is this young man?” “I really don’t know,” Abner declared. “Well, find out who he is!” the king told him. As soon as David returned from killing Goliath, Abner brought him to Saul with the Philistine’s head still in his hand. “Tell me about your father, young man,” Saul said. And David replied, “His name is Jesse, and we live in Bethlehem.””

This is the same Pannun who has threatened bomb attacks against India’s Parliament and the Red Fort, issued threats of aviation terrorism against Air India, warning passengers that their lives could be in danger. He has also called for sabotage of the Indian Railways infrastructure, encouraged Sikh soldiers in the Indian Army to mutiny and offered financial rewards, including Rs 11 crore to soldiers who would prevent Prime Minister Narendra Modi from hoisting the Tricolour at the Red Fort. He has announced monetary rewards for acts of desecration of the Indian national flag and for Khalistani flag-raising campaigns targeting Indian institutions.

These are not simply separatist slogans or political provocations. Pannun’s entire profile is built around threats of bombings, assassination, sabotage and armed insurrection against India. He has repeatedly threatened India’s elected leadership, including Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

And now the US government wants to give this man 20 minutes at an American court, effectively elevating him to the position of a victim whose voice deserves special accommodation. Washington is prosecuting an Indian national over an alleged plot against Pannun while extending a platform to a man who has himself spent years openly threatening violence against India. text:
Verdun, 1916

> germany masses 140,000 men, over 1,200 guns and 2.5 million shells, brought in on 1,300 trains
> the french have 34 battalions in the sector. the germans attack with 72
> falkenhayn's plan is to make the french army bleed to death defending it
> 21 february, a 380 mm naval gun fires the first shell into verdun from about 20 miles out
> over a million shells fall in the opening bombardment
> bois des caures. lt col driant, 60 years old, holds the wood with 1,200 chasseurs
> a full german division comes at them behind 230 guns and mortars
> they hold for almost two days, much of it hand to hand
> cut off, driant and about 80 men beat back two more assaults
> driant is killed on the 22nd. about 110 of the 1,200 make it back
> 25 february, fort douaumont falls. pétain takes command the same day from a sickbed
> he turns one 72 km road into the army's lifeline. a truck every 14 seconds, every 5 at the peak
> any truck that breaks down goes in the ditch. the column never stops
> he rotates divisions out before they're wiped out. about two thirds of the french army fights at verdun
> 10 april, pétain's order of the day: "courage! on les aura!" (courage, we'll get them)
> fleury-devant-douaumont is taken and retaken 16 times in two months
> june, fort vaux. the fort has no artillery
> major raynal's garrison fights the germans inside the fort's own tunnels with grenades and bayonets
> the cistern gauge is broken. the water is nearly gone
> 4 june, raynal sends his last bird with the message "this is my last pigeon"
> le vaillant flies through gas, delivers it and dies. the only pigeon of the war given the légion d'honneur
> 7 june, out of water, raynal surrenders
> his sword is lost in the ruins, so he offers a private's bayonet: "this weapon is worth an officer's sword"
> the german crown prince is so impressed he gives him an officer's sword
> nivelle takes over: "ils ne passeront pas" (they shall not pass)
> they don't
> 24 october, colonial infantry from morocco, senegal and somalia retake fort douaumont
> general anselin, who volunteered to lead the assault, is killed that day
> 2 november, the germans abandon fort vaux
> 18 december, it ends near where it started. verdun never falls
> 300 days. between 40 and 60 million shells fired
> about 70% of the casualties come from artillery
> france: 163,000 dead, 216,000 wounded
> germany: 143,000 dead, 190,000 wounded
> nine villages are wiped out and never rebuilt. they still have mayors
> the douaumont ossuary holds the bones of about 130,000 unidentified french and german soldiers

text:
I increasingly believe that certain American political forces and media organizations have turned the phrase “Chinese spy” into a universal weapon. The moment China becomes remotely connected to a story, it can be repackaged as a national security incident. Anyone maintaining ordinary contact with China can suddenly find themselves under a spotlight of suspicion.
The Chris Cash case is a revealing example.
A British parliamentary researcher became embroiled in a serious espionage allegation because of his connections with individuals in China. Thousands of private communications were scrutinized, while politicians and media outlets repeatedly amplified warnings about Chinese infiltration. Yet the prosecution eventually withdrew the charges and offered no evidence.
So who takes responsibility for the political hysteria and media coverage that came before?
Now look at the Jensen Huang controversy.
A private relationship has been transformed, through sensational reporting and anonymous intelligence sources, into a story involving Chinese intelligence operations, semiconductor technology leaks and national security.
The most troubling aspect of this narrative is the attempt to make the public accept an absurd principle: whenever China is involved, ordinary relationships become suspicious and unverified allegations become believable.

I reject that logic.
China has a vast technology sector, a comprehensive industrial ecosystem and substantial innovation capabilities. The competitiveness of Chinese companies in international markets comes from long-term investment, the dedication of engineers, industrial coordination and technological progress—not espionage stories invented by American politicians.
When Washington struggles to address its own industrial challenges through legitimate competition, portraying China as a security threat is apparently much easier than examining its own policy failures.
The irony is that the United States demands market access and respect for international commercial rules while increasingly politicizing legitimate business relationships with China, even dragging private relationships into national security narratives. This damages individuals and companies while undermining the trust required for normal international engagement.
I support lawful investigations into genuine espionage. But such investigations must be based on evidence, not nationality; facts, not political positions; and judicial procedures, not media trials.
America cannot preach the rule of law while allowing anonymous allegations to substitute for evidence. It cannot claim to support free competition while portraying Chinese competitors as spies. And it cannot turn everyone and everything connected to China into a target of political witch-hunts.

China has every right to develop its own technology, participate in global commerce and reject malicious accusations unsupported by facts.
China does not need American media's approval to establish its innocence, nor will it abandon legitimate development and international engagement because of fear manufactured in Washington.
If the United States genuinely has evidence, let it present that evidence for scrutiny. Stop using espionage stories as substitutes for proof, political propaganda as a substitute for justice, and smears against China as a substitute for genuine competition.

text:
There exists a better way to govern, but your local despot isn't willing to give up his turn at the trough to make it happen.

Decentralization is an institutional technology for producing better governance, and history proves it.

Switzerland offers the clearest running experiment. The Swiss canton system, which predates the 1848 federal constitution by centuries, gave each canton genuine fiscal and legal autonomy. Cantons compete. Appenzell Innerrhoden ran its affairs differently from Zurich, and both had to live with the consequences of their own choices. Tax policy, spending, local regulation: all accountable to populations small enough to hold officials personally responsible. When a canton governor failed, residents noticed immediately. Exit was real and cheap. Cross the border, pay lower taxes, keep your capital. That threat disciplines governments in a way that no constitutional clause ever manages.

Pre-unification Germany made the same point, often uncomfortably for German nationalists. The patchwork of hundreds of principalities, free cities, and minor kingdoms that made up the Holy Roman Empire and later the German Confederation produced fierce jurisdictional competition. Hamburg grew wealthy as a free city because it kept commercial law light and bureaucratic interference minimal. Frankfurt became the financial center of continental Europe for the same reason. Bismarck's 1871 unification consolidated power upward and, within a generation, Berlin was micromanaging what Hamburg had run perfectly well on its own.

Smaller jurisdictions cannot hide fiscal failure behind monetary expansion or transfers from distant taxpayers. A canton that overspends runs visibly short. A German principality that harassed merchants watched them relocate. The feedback loop is tight and fast. Large centralized states break that loop. Washington, Brussels, and Berlin all collect taxes from populations too dispersed and too diverse to coordinate effective pushback. The spending continues, and the bureaucracy expands, insulated from consequence.

You end up paying the price of centralization every time a uniform federal regulation destroys a local arrangement that worked. The canton system worked because Appenzell could not impose its preferences on Zurich. 

Brussels hasn't learned that lesson yet, and Europeans are paying the tuition.

text:
SOMALILAND IS NOT SOMALIA: SENATOR TED CRUZ PUTS SOMALILAND’S INDEPENDENCE AT THE CENTRE OF A U.S. SENATE HEARING

A powerful moment for Somaliland’s diplomatic cause as Senator Ted Cruz presses President Trump’s ambassadorial nominee on why the United States has yet to formally recognise the Republic of Somaliland.

During the November 10 Senate Foreign Relations Committee confirmation hearing for Devin Kennington, President Donald Trump’s nominee for U.S. Ambassador to Somalia, Senator Ted Cruz made Somaliland’s distinct identity, sovereignty and long-standing independence aspirations a central issue.

Cruz invoked President Trump’s own description of Somaliland as “a totally different country”, making clear that Somaliland should not simply be treated as part of Somalia.

The senator emphasised Somaliland’s remarkable record of self-government since 1991, its democratic elections, peaceful political transitions, functioning institutions and distinct political and security realities.

He also challenged the nominee on the difference between practical engagement with Somaliland and the much bigger question of formal diplomatic recognition. Although Kennington acknowledged Somaliland’s distinct circumstances and the importance of engagement, he stopped short of explicitly endorsing recognition.

Cruz made his position unmistakable: the State Department should follow the President’s guidance, and he made clear that the issue would have implications for the nominee’s confirmation.

WHY SOMALILAND MATTERS

Somaliland is not merely a diplomatic question. It is a strategically important partner in the Horn of Africa.

- Three decades of self-government: Since restoring its independence in 1991, Somaliland has built its own government, institutions and security forces largely through its own efforts, while Somalia has depended heavily on international aid, foreign intervention and external support to rebuild its state.

- Democratic credentials: Somaliland has held multiple multiparty elections and peaceful transfers of power. In contrast, Somalia has yet to establish a fully functioning system of direct national multiparty elections and continues to face constitutional disputes and political deadlock.

- Strategic geography: Somaliland effectively administers its strategic coastline along the Gulf of Aden, including Berbera Port, near the vital Red Sea shipping corridor. In contrast, Somalia struggles to exercise effective federal authority over significant parts of its strategic territory and coastline.

- Security partnership: Somaliland maintains its own security institutions and offers opportunities for cooperation in counterterrorism, intelligence and maritime security. Somalia, meanwhile, continues to rely heavily on foreign military forces and international security assistance while struggling against Al-Shabaab.

- Geopolitical significance: Somaliland maintains strong relations with Taiwan and seeks closer strategic cooperation with the United States. Somalia, meanwhile, maintains strong diplomatic relations with China and supports Beijing's One-China position, including opposition to Taiwan's international engagement.

Formal recognition would be a significant foreign-policy decision, but Somaliland's case deserves serious consideration on its own historical, democratic and strategic merits.

A MESSAGE OF APPRECIATION TO SENATOR TED CRUZ

A heartfelt thanks to Senator Ted Cruz @SenTedCruz @tedcruz  for continuing to champion Somaliland’s identity and legitimate aspirations for international recognition. Your words, “Somaliland is not Somalia,” mean so much to our people. We deeply appreciate your support and commitment to keeping Somaliland’s cause alive in Washington.

Thank you, Senator Cruz, for keeping Somaliland's cause firmly on the American diplomatic agenda.

SOMALILAND IS NOT SOMALIA. RECOGNITION IS THE NEXT DIPLOMATIC QUESTION.

text:
A $12.5 million house in Georgetown is standing empty this week. Its owner is the man running America's economic war on Iran.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has moved onto a US military base after Iranian threats against his life. The New York Times broke it on Tuesday night, 10 November. Reuters confirmed it with two people familiar with the matter.

He is not the first. Newsweek counts him as the third serving Cabinet member in military housing, after Marco Rubio and Pete Hegseth at Fort McNair.

But Bessent is the one whose move tells us the most.

Since August he has run "Operation Economic Outcast". Sanctions on Middle Eastern bank branches and financial firms that touch Iranian money. Restrictions on trade routes.

All of it sits on top of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The aim, per the Times, is to cut cash to the Revolutionary Guard. The hope is that this spares Washington from resuming major combat.

On Tuesday in Paris, Rubio said exactly that: "The economic campaign is so devastating that right now there is no need for major combat operations."

So the man holding the main weapon now sleeps behind a guarded gate.

US officials told the Times that Iranian plotting against current and former officials had reached "a more advanced stage", partly on intelligence about Bessent himself.

How serious the specific threats are remains unclear, the Times and Reuters both stress.

Iran has denied plotting attacks on US soil. US officials also note its capacity for large-scale attacks abroad is limited.

The same evening, though, the Justice Department unsealed an eight-count indictment against three men it says worked for the IRGC and Kata'ib Hizballah.

Prosecutors tie them to nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks in Europe and the US, including a September plot at RAF Fairford in England.

CBS reports the plan involved vans filled with fuel. Only one defendant is in custody.

A source told Reuters that concern grew after the Wall Street Journal published an aerial photo of the Georgetown house, allowing it to be geolocated.

Now set Washington's message beside the sea.

On Tuesday, the IRGC said three tankers were burning after using an "unauthorized route" through Hormuz. ADNOC said one of its vessels was damaged in UAE waters.

UKMTO logged a projectile strike 19 nautical miles off Limah, Oman.

The Washington Institute counts 37 ships attacked in October, the most of the war, and 10 so far this month.

Brent rose 71 cents to $92.20 early Wednesday, CNBC reported, off a two-month low.

Tehran's line is consistent. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says the two-day Hormuz reopening offer stands, but only if sanctions, the blockade and asset freezes go.

Security chief Mohsen Rezaei says there are no talks at all.

Iran is answering a financial war with a personal one. Pressure on the economy is met with pressure on the people who design it.

Trump speaks of "positive momentum". Treasury says Bessent "will not be deterred".

Maybe so. But a strategy sold as the alternative to fighting has just sent its architect to live on a base.

The Georgetown house is the cleanest measure of how far this war has travelled from the Gulf.

7. The bigger pattern  when delivery apps meet sacred prices.

The Costco hot dog isn’t the only iconic low-price item being resold at massive markups:

In-N-Out burgers: Southern California delivery drivers reselling $4-5 burgers for $20-100+ through Facebook Marketplace and TaskRabbit. In-N-Out doesn’t offer delivery. The markup fills the gap.

Chick-fil-A (on Sundays): the internet routinely jokes about what people would pay for Chick-fil-A on Sundays when the chain is closed. Third-party reselling of Saturday purchases for Sunday consumption has been documented.

Trader Joe’s specialty items: limited-run products resold on Amazon and eBay at 3-5x retail.

The pattern: any beloved product that the original company restricts  by location, by delivery, by hours, by membership  creates an arbitrage opportunity for someone willing to bridge the gap.

The delivery economy equation:

Convenience has a price. That price is the markup between what the product costs at the source and what someone will pay to not go to the source.

For a $1.50 Costco hot dog: the convenience premium is $16.50. A 1,100% markup. On paper: outrageous. In practice: people are paying it. Because the alternative  driving 20 minutes to Costco, parking in a crowded lot, navigating the warehouse, waiting in the food court line, and driving 20 minutes back  costs time. And for an office on a deadline: time costs more than $16.50.

The hot dog costs $1.50. Your time costs whatever No Tip charges for you to not spend it.

text:
"Andrew Zywiec, M.D., argues that low vitamin K at birth is an intentional, adaptive physiological state across all mammals rather than a flaw or “deficiency” requiring routine medical correction. He contends that “nature doesn’t make a mistake” and that the modern push for intramuscular (IM) vitamin K prophylaxis represents a loss of common sense in medicine, driven more by institutional inertia or profit motives than pure biology.
Core physiological rationale he offers
He proposes that the reduced clotting capacity serves the transition from fetal to neonatal life:
•Birth itself is an inflammatory process. Lower vitamin K-dependent clotting factors help maintain a more fluid blood-flow pattern, reducing the risk of unwanted clotting, stasis, or “sludging” during the stresses of labor and delivery.
•This fluidity may facilitate the free circulation and distribution of stem cells through the vascular circuit at a critical developmental window.
•It supports the rapid normalization of vascular pressures and the remodeling of cardiac structures as the newborn shifts from placental to pulmonary circulation (closure of fetal shunts such as the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale).
In his view, artificially flooding the system with a large pro-coagulant dose disrupts these processes. He specifically links the injection to hemolysis (breakdown of red blood cells), circulatory stasis, and subsequent jaundice—claiming that most cases of neonatal jaundice are caused or worsened by the vitamin K shot rather than being purely physiological.
Critique of the risk–benefit narrative and data
Zywiec highlights the high number needed to treat (NNT). He places it around 15,000, meaning thousands of healthy newborns must receive the injection to prevent one case of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB). He argues this unfavorable ratio does not justify universal administration, especially when safer options exist.
He also questions the attribution of bleeding events solely to vitamin K status. Potential confounders he lists include:
•Labor induction drugs
•Epidural anesthesia

text:
Thyrocare: 25% growth, a specialty diagnostics bet and a strategic exit. Is the business entering its next phase?

1/ The growth engine is firing on multiple cylinders

Q2 FY27:
Revenue: ₹271 Cr | +25.1%
EBITDA: ₹89.3 Cr | +24.9%
Normalised PAT: ₹60.2 Cr | +25.7%
EBITDA margin: 33%

H1 FY27 revenue grew 24.7%, while EBITDA and normalised PAT grew 29.2% and 29.7%, respectively.

This is not a one-quarter spike. Management says the company has sustained around 20% growth for nine consecutive quarters, with the latest two quarters above 25%.

2/ The most interesting operating metric is not revenue growth. It is testing intensity.

Q2:

Tests conducted: 61.6 million | +27.4%
Patients: 5.7 million | +13.4%
Tests per patient: 10.9 | +12.3%
Revenue per patient: ₹433 | +9.8%
Revenue per test: ₹39.8 | -2.3%
Tests are growing much faster than patients.
Existing customers are using the platform for more tests. That is a positive sign for customer engagement and wallet share.

But there is a catch: revenue per test is declining.

Growth is currently being driven more by volumes and testing intensity than by pricing. Sustaining margins while scaling volumes will be important.

3/ The franchise network is becoming a formidable distribution advantage.
Thyrocare added around 1,180 franchisees in Q2 — its highest quarterly addition in three years.

The active network now stands at 12,911.
Franchise revenue grew 27% to ₹159 Cr.
But the bigger insight is the maturity curve.
Management indicated that franchisees added around two years ago are now contributing meaningfully. Today's additions could therefore become an important revenue driver in FY28–FY29.

The metric to watch is not just franchisee additions. It is productivity, survival and revenue contribution per franchisee.

4/ The B2B partnership business is another growth engine.

Partnership revenue grew 28% to ₹84 Cr.

This includes health-tech platforms, online aggregators, insurance, corporate wellness and institutional customers.

API integrations allow partners to tap into Thyrocare's laboratory infrastructure.

The opportunity is attractive: partners bring customer access, while Thyrocare provides the diagnostic backbone.

However, there is a trade-off.

Around 95% of pathology revenue comes through franchisees and partnerships. This provides reach and scale, but also makes the business dependent on external distribution partners.

5/ Specialty diagnostics could change the quality of the business.

This is perhaps the most important long-term strategic development.

Thyrocare is moving beyond routine pathology into:

Genomics and NGS
Oncology markers
Allergy diagnostics
Molecular diagnostics
Histopathology
Advanced coagulation testing

Specialty diagnostics currently contribute around 4% of pathology revenue.

Management wants this to reach 10–15% over the next 3–5 years.

Why does this matter?
Specialty testing can potentially improve realisations, deepen relationships with doctors and hospitals, and make the platform more differentiated.

But this is still in execution mode. 

Specialised equipment, reagents, skilled personnel and physician adoption all come at a cost. Higher revenue does not automatically mean higher margins.

6/ An interesting consumer experiment: the pregnancy test kit.

Thyrocare has launched an at-home pregnancy test kit.

Five-minute results
MRP of ₹60
Distribution across 10,000+ pharmacies
Confirmatory Beta hCG blood test offered at ₹399

The distribution partnership with API Holdings provides access to PharmEasy and Ascent's network.

The potential funnel is interesting:

Home test → Confirmatory blood test → Thyrocare laboratory.

This could create a direct consumer entry point into the diagnostics ecosystem.

But distribution reach is not the same as consumer demand. Actual sales, repeat usage and conversion into laboratory testing will determine whether this becomes meaningful.

7/ Jaanch is growing, but still small.
Jaanch, Thyrocare's curative and chronic-care testing initiative, grew 58% YoY.
It currently contributes around 2.5% of pathology revenue.

The opportunity lies in recurring testing for chronic conditions such as diabetes, thyroid and kidney disorders.

Promising growth, but the small base means investors should wait for material revenue contribution.

8/ The proposed NHL exit could be a sensible capital-allocation decision.

Thyrocare proposes selling its entire stake in Nueclear Healthcare (NHL) to Trovera for approximately ₹141.4 Cr.

The consideration includes:

₹81.9 Cr cash, subject to working-capital adjustments

₹59.5 Cr in compulsorily convertible preference shares, representing around 4.5% equity on a fully diluted basis

Why exit?

The difference in business economics is striking:

Pathology ROCE: 34.9%

NHL ROCE: 6.95%

NHL has also faced revenue pressure and requires substantial investment in ageing equipment.

Management estimates that NHL reduced consolidated revenue growth by around 2 percentage points and EBITDA margin by approximately 1 percentage point.

The strategic logic is clear: focus capital and management attention on the higher-return pathology business.

However, the transaction is still subject to approvals. Completion and deployment of the proceeds remain important monitorables.

9/ Don't misread the reported PAT.

Q2 reported consolidated PAT was just ₹15.2 Cr, compared with normalised PAT of ₹60.2 Cr.

The difference largely reflects a ₹45 Cr non-cash goodwill impairment related to NHL.

For H1, reported PAT was ₹66.6 Cr versus normalised PAT of ₹111.5 Cr.

Investors should distinguish the exceptional impairment from underlying operating performance — while also recognising that the impairment reflects a real reassessment of the value of the radiology investment.

10/ Cash generation remains a major strength.

H1 operating cash flow: ₹132.8 Cr.

H1 normalised PAT: ₹111.5 Cr.

Cash conversion is therefore approximately 1.19x.

The company also has:

Zero borrowings

Cash equivalents of ₹21.9 Cr

Investments of ₹141.7 Cr

Other bank balances of ₹42.6 Cr

H1 capex was ₹33.2 Cr, including eight new labs and additional equipment. Similar capex is expected in H2.

This is a healthy balance sheet, but investors should track returns on incremental capital as the network and specialty capabilities expand.

11/ What could go wrong?

The growth story is attractive, but there are important risks:
a) Revenue per test is declining despite strong volume growth.
b) Heavy dependence on franchisees and B2B partnerships.
c) Specialty diagnostics may take longer to scale or may not deliver expected margins.
d) New labs and equipment need to generate adequate returns.

The pregnancy kit needs to demonstrate actual consumer traction.

NHL divestment must be completed on acceptable terms.

And finally, valuation matters. A good business can still be a poor investment if expectations are already priced in.

12/ What should investors track over the next 4–6 quarters?

Can pathology revenue growth sustain 20–25%?
Will revenue per test stabilise?
Are new franchisees becoming productive?
Can partnership growth continue without excessive concentration?
Does specialty diagnostics move meaningfully beyond its current 4% contribution?
Are EBITDA margins maintained around 32–33%?

Does the NHL transaction close, and how is the capital redeployed?

My takeaway

Thyrocare is no longer just a routine pathology testing story.

Its core franchise and partnership network provides distribution scale. 

Higher testing intensity is driving volume growth. Specialty diagnostics offers a route towards a more differentiated business. 

The proposed NHL exit could improve capital allocation.

But the transformation is not complete.

The core business is already delivering. The next phase is about proving that specialty diagnostics and consumer initiatives can add meaningful, profitable growth.

The key question for investors: Can Thyrocare convert its distribution scale into a higher-quality diagnostics platform — without sacrificing the margins and capital efficiency that made the business attractive in the first place?

I mean, businesses are already siphoning money out of us depleting our assets to get to where they are. Why would a company offer a superior product if Americans are too poor to buy it? Basically all that’s gonna be outsourced outside of our country for sales to other nations where their citizens have more purchasing power I would assume. 

I don’t know. I still don’t understand how this hypothetical scenario of automating everything is gonna fix any of this without destroying our democracy. I mean, if the only solution presented is to have a universal basic income for all the jobs lost to AI and robots we’ve essentially reached the climax of corporate capture of our government when the corporations are directly paying the government and the government’s handing money to us. 

And at that point if everyone’s just getting a check, where’s the incentive for innovation from everyday American people? It’s like we’re just being treated as commodities. 
Sounds kind of depressing to be honest. I wish the government would start talking about this and figuring out what’s gonna happen moving forward if there is a Tech boom because I don’t hear anyone talking about it.  I mean, if people are just given a basic stipend essentially from the government, they have no way to make their life better through hard work, their spirit and drive die. Goodbye American Dream. 

I mean, what’s the long-term plan here because it sounds like we’re just turning into China. The more this administration wants to compete with a communist country in the tech race. It’s just like a money loop and then the government controls and restricts our ability to rise above the low or middle class. It creates a wall that can’t be overcome. I’m just having a hard time wrapping my head around how this creates abundance for everyday people and not just abundance for just the big tech companies.

text:
Re: Mauricio Pochettino and Manchester United. From the United States of America to the United States of Disrepair. Managerial churn may have short-term gain but problems remain as Pochettino will discover if/when he leaves USMNT for United. Michael Carrick is the Red Man Walking. So you can understand why the risk-averse board would go for Poch. United were linked with Pochettino in 2016, 2019, 2024. It seems destined. 

Pochettino is “gettable”, with that £7m release clause, but United must also take into account the cost of recruiting his staff. United’s board is not currently known for operating with respect – as its shameful handling of Carrick’s exit highlights - but it also must be mindful of Pochettino’s important work with USMNT over the next week: the Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti in Miami on Saturday and then Cincinnati on Wednesday.

He is a very good manager, just below elite level (Luis Enrique, Jurgen Klopp, Carlo Ancelotti, Mikel Arteta, Pep Guardiola, Unai Emery etc and the rising Fabian Hurzeler). Pochettino knows English football and has a reputation for playing good football, promoting youth and living with budget restrictions – all qualities attractive to the board. 

"Poch" is a very engaging character (as are his staff) and will receive a largely warm welcome from the media he has always got on with. But Pochettino has a point to prove that he is not past his peak and will need to convince many sceptical United fans. They will back the new man, because that’s what United’s remarkable match-going faithful do. Many would prefer Antonio Conte to come in and shake up the dressing-room and boardroom and challenge the not-best-in-class Jason Wilcox, the director of football who badly let down Carrick in the summer. But Poch it is. 

He needs better players. Pochettino favours a high press, far more intense than the half-hearted press offered by some United players. His tactics involve a high line - good luck with that with Harry Maguire, Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt at centre-back. He likes to play out from the back, risky with some of the defenders. 

He’s worked with top strikers like Harry Kane and Kylian Mbappe. He’ll find the No 9 wearing No 30 and in the treatment room. Pochettino likes to play (often) with a double pivot. Kobbie Mainoo is certainly good enough and has the quality in possession but would need a more defensive force alongside - which is Carlos Baleba, a player deemed surplus to requirements at Brighton. Poch likes attacking full-backs who can also defend well. United need to sign some. Good luck to Pochettino - he'll need it. #MUFC

text:
OPEN BRIEF: ASOCIAAL? WIE?
Open brief aan politici, politieke bestuurders, topambtenaren en topbestuurders

Geachte dames en heren,

“Asociaal om alleen in zo’n groot huis te zitten.”

Die uitspraak van een gastheer staat in een advertentie van Takecarebnb. Hij koos ervoor zijn huis te delen. Zijn gastvrijheid verdient waardering. Maar het gebruik van het woord ‘asociaal’ in een wervingscampagne roept ook een vraag op: aan wie stellen we zulke morele eisen?

Ik richt mij tot degenen onder u die burgers oproepen ruimte te maken voor opvang, integratie en solidariteit.

Hebt u zelf ruimte in huis? Bent u bereid tijdelijk een statushouder te ontvangen?

Dit is een serieuze uitnodiging. Wie anderen vraagt hun dagelijks leven aan te passen, kan geloofwaardigheid winnen door zelf het voorbeeld te geven.

Mijn aanbeveling is concreet: begin een campagne onder de naam BESTUURDERS GEVEN THUIS. Nodig politieke ambtsdragers, topambtenaren en topbestuurders uit om te onderzoeken of zij gastgezin kunnen worden. Zoek daarvoor samenwerking met een organisatie als Takecarebnb, met aandacht voor een passende kennismaking, begeleiding en de wensen van alle huisgenoten.

Vraag uw eigen organisatie deze uitnodiging onder de bestuurlijke leiding te verspreiden. Laat geïnteresseerden zich aanmelden. Deel vervolgens, met instemming van gast en gastgezin, wat u ervaart en welke lessen dat voor uw werk oplevert.

Juist wie invloed heeft op wonen, opvang en integratie kan leren van het samenleven met iemand die opnieuw moet beginnen. Van de formulieren, het wachten en de onzekerheid. Van de behoefte aan rust, zelfstandigheid en een eigen plek.

Uw deelname ontslaat u uiteraard niet van de verantwoordelijkheid om goed beleid te maken. Een logeerkamer lost de woningnood niet op. Zij kan u wel dichter brengen bij de mensen over wie u besluiten neemt.

Ook u mag persoonlijke redenen hebben om geen gast te ontvangen. Gezondheid, gezinsomstandigheden, mantelzorg en privacy kunnen zwaar wegen.

Gun burgers diezelfde afweging. Een vrije slaapkamer bewijst niet dat iemand ruimte heeft in zijn leven. Alleen wonen is geen bewijs van onverschilligheid.

Asociaal wordt het wanneer mensen met macht offers van anderen verlangen en zichzelf zonder uitleg buiten die verwachting plaatsen. Wanneer de bereidheid tot delen uitsluitend bij de burger wordt gemeten.

Wie het woord ‘asociaal’ gebruikt, moet bereid zijn dezelfde maatstaf op zichzelf toe te passen.

Ik vraag u daarom: onderzoek wat u zelf kunt bijdragen, geef daar waar mogelijk het voorbeeld en wees terughoudend met het moreel beoordelen van mensen wier omstandigheden u niet kent.

Laat uw oproep tot solidariteit beginnen bij uw eigen mogelijkheden.

Misschien begint dat met een gesprek thuis.

Misschien met een vrije kamer.

Met vriendelijke groet,

Max von Kreyfelt
￼

text:
I got fired from my job over $18,600 that went missing from the company's financial records, and the worst part is that I was completely innocent.

I had worked as an operations supervisor at a distribution company in Ohio for almost five years. I wasn't making crazy money, but the job paid my bills, covered my mortgage, and allowed me to take care of my family. I had never received a serious disciplinary warning, so I never imagined things would end this way.

It all started on a Friday afternoon when my manager called me into his office.

"Close the door for a minute. We need to talk."

I sat down, and he turned his computer screen towards me.

"Do you recognize this transaction?"

I looked at the screen. It was an $18,600 payment recorded under my department's authorization.

"Yes, that's one of our vendor payments. What's the problem?"

He folded his arms.

"The vendor says they never received the money, but our system shows that it was approved using your credentials."

I immediately became uncomfortable.

"That's impossible. I didn't authorize that payment. Check the approval history."

He looked at me and said, "Are you suggesting someone used your login?"

"I'm telling you that's exactly what could have happened."

I was asked to surrender my work laptop temporarily while the company investigated. I cooperated because I genuinely believed the truth would come out.

A week later, HR scheduled a meeting.

When I walked in, there were three people sitting around the conference table. Nobody even offered me coffee.

The HR director started reading from a document.

"Following our internal investigation, we've determined that you violated company financial policies. Your employment is terminated effective immediately."

I stared at her.

"Excuse me? You're firing me without giving me an opportunity to explain what happened?"

She responded, "We have sufficient evidence to support management's decision."

I became emotional.

"I've worked here for five years. I have never stolen from this company. You're willing to destroy my career over a transaction you haven't even properly explained to me?"

My manager finally spoke.

"We trusted you, and you let us down."

I looked at him and said, "You don't even know whether I did this. You're just looking for someone to blame."

Security escorted me out of the building that afternoon. Some of my colleagues watched through the glass doors as I carried my personal belongings to my car.

I sat in that parking lot for almost 40 minutes, trying to understand how my life had changed so quickly.

My wife called.

"Hey, babe. Are you still at work?"

I couldn't even speak properly.

"No. They fired me."

"What? Why?"

"They said I stole money. Money I never touched."

She went quiet before asking, "But you didn't do it, right?"

I replied, "You know me. I didn't do it."

Three weeks later, something unexpected happened. A former colleague called me and told me the company had discovered that the payment was actually redirected to a fraudulent vendor account after an employee's email was compromised.

My login had been accessed from a different device, and the investigation had apparently failed to establish who actually initiated the transaction.

I immediately contacted HR.

Their response?

"The company considers this matter closed. We are not discussing individual personnel decisions."

I was furious.

text:
ATRICURE $ATRC FORECAST ALLOWS A LOSS THIS QUARTER:

AtriCure (ATRC) at $56.26, -$1.52 / -2.63% on Tuesday.

AtriCure, the Mason, Ohio maker of heart-surgery tools, is off the Momentum Len5, where it was #4 in our November 6 post, and it passes the Quality Len5. It lost that seat without the close we said would cost it. The shares are down 5.4% since our post, after four lower closes in a row. We tied its November 4 jump to its report, and medical-device stocks as a group rose almost as much that day. Our post gave the December-quarter forecast for adjusted profit, which leaves out one-time costs, and not the one for reported profit, which counts them and runs from breakeven to a loss. Angie Wirick, AtriCure's chief financial officer, calls the forecast cautious, and a heart-surgery trial is due to finish signing up patients this quarter.

AtriCure is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es. Momentum wants months of gains with the price near its peak, and Tuesday's close is 14.8% under the November 4 high of $66.02. We said a close under $52.84 would knock it off the Momentum Len5. We were factually incorrect about that line: AtriCure has not closed under $56 since, it was out of the top five by November 7, and it is off the Len5 now. What would put it back on the Momentum Len5: closes climbing back toward that high. Quality wants a profitable business with debt under the owners' stake; AtriCure earned $14.9M over its past four quarters and owes $61.0M against $533.2M of equity. What would knock it off the Quality Len5: a 2026 that ends in a loss. At about 190 times that profit it offers the value Len5es no discount. Hypergrowth wants sales multiplying, and AtriCure's grew 15% in the September quarter. It pays no dividend, which keeps it off the Income Len5.

Since our post:
- From the $59.45 we quoted: -$3.19 / -5.4%.
- Tuesday's close: the lowest since October 19, and $4.15 under the $60.41 close before the report.

iShares U.S. Medical Devices ETF (IHI) at $58.07, -$0.50 / -0.85% on Tuesday. The fund holds a basket of device makers, so no Len5 applies. We wrote that AtriCure's 8.5% jump on November 4 came on its report. Our premise was faulty: that was the day after the midterm elections, and device makers rose together. Reuters reported hospital operators and health insurers rallying that morning on the Democrats' sweep of Congress, and hospitals are AtriCure's customers.
- At the November 4 open: AtriCure 3.9% under its prior close, the device fund 2.8% above its own.
- November 4, the full day: AtriCure +8.5%, the device fund +6.7%.
- From the November 3 close through Tuesday: AtriCure -6.9%, the device fund +2.9%.
Our read: most of AtriCure's gain that day was the group's, and since its report it has trailed other device makers by almost ten percentage points.

Our post said the new forecast leaves 4 to 10 cents a share of adjusted profit for the December quarter. AtriCure also forecasts reported profit, the figure under standard accounting.
- 2026 reported profit, forecast: 21 to 27 cents a share.
- Earned through September 30: 27 cents.
The top of that forecast leaves nothing for the December quarter, and the bottom leaves a 6-cent loss. AtriCure earned 4 cents a share in the December quarter of 2025. The gap between the two forecasts for the quarter is about 10 cents a share of one-time costs. In the September quarter that kind of cost was a $4.5M milestone payment under an agreement to co-develop pulsed field ablation technology, which treats the irregular heartbeat with electrical pulses. The same forecast has sales growing more slowly.
- Revenue growth it leaves for the December quarter: 11.5% to 14.4%, against 15.0% in the September quarter.

Wirick told analysts on November 3 that AtriCure sets its forecast ranges with "a pathway to a beat," meaning room to do better. She pointed to a full quarter of costs from a new manufacturing plant, to faster spending on new products, and to a clinical trial called BoxX-NoAF. The trial tests AtriCure's clamps and clips in heart-surgery patients who have never had atrial fibrillation, the irregular heartbeat its tools treat. Michael Carrel, the chief executive, said more than 880 patients are enrolled, fewer than 100 short of the total, with first results due in spring 2027. This year AtriCure gave early fourth-quarter revenue on January 12, five weeks before its full report.

AtriCure is off the Momentum Len5 at a price above our line, and its own forecast has this quarter ending at breakeven or worse. September's 8 cents a share, repeated in the report tentatively set for February 16, would put the year well above the top of that forecast.

Not investment advice.

Fewer cases and smaller penalties, but more money back to investors. That is the shape of the SEC’s fiscal 2026 enforcement results.

Civil penalties fell to $343 million from $1.3 billion, while the agency returned $731 million to harmed investors and added units targeting retail fraud and accounting misconduct.

The agency’s case list carries a message for advisers who recommend private offerings. In one settled order, a North Carolina adviser representative steered clients into more than $50 million of private real estate deals. He collected nearly $1.5 million from the sponsors and did not adequately disclose it. In another, the SEC censured the manager of a set of tender-offer funds that lost about $300 million after a liquidation deal went wrong.

A bipartisan group of US lawmakers comprising 91 members of the congress have sent a letter to Republican and Democratic leadership in the House of Representatives asking them to formally invite Pope Leo XIV to address a joint session of Congress next year. Addressed to House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana, and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-New York, the letter was signed by 91 Republican and Democratic members of Congress.

“The election of Pope Leo XIV serves as a sign of great pride for millions of Americans. As the first ever American-born Pope, his unique perspective, and ties to our country, would serve as a unifying force for members of Congress,” the bipartisan members wrote in the letter.

“Following a divisive election, Pope Leo’s unifying message of service, compassion for fellow mankind, and the importance of human dignity would be especially timely,” the letter added. The Congress representatives also said that a visit from the Holy Father “would offer a much-needed outlook as we navigate complex foreign and domestic issues.”

Citing the “undeniable historical significance and cultural impact of Pope Francis’s address to Congress in 2015”, the lawmakers urged the leaders to work to schedule a joint address as soon as possible in the beginning of the 120th Congress with the first American-born Pope.

"Someone with 5 billion to expenditure is very different from one with twenty million and no loan facilities to explore"

Since we are on the topic of Agriculture/cattle rearing, 👇👇

Loans are available to farmers and cattle rearers through the following;

1) FarmerMoni Programme (GEEP / NSIPA) which provides collateral free and interest free loans of up to ₦300,000 for smallholder farmers across all 774 LGAs

2) Bank of Agriculture (BOA) offers a government backed loan facility which provides microcredit, crop production loans, animal husbandry/livestock financing, equipment leasing, and specialized programs for women and youth in agriculture.

3) Commercial Agriculture Credit Scheme (CACS): A joint initiative by the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Federal Government offering large scale commercial agricultural loans up to ₦2 billion at a capped single digit interest rate (around 9%) with a tenor of up to 7 years.

4) National Agricultural Development Fund (NADF) with it's loan focus across crop and aquaculture sectors 

5. Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme Fund (ACGSF) managed by the Central Bank of Nigeria, this fund guarantees 75% of loans granted by deposit money and microfinance banks for crop production and animal husbandry, covering loans up to ₦100,000 (non collateralized) and up to ₦50 million (collateralized).

6) Sterling Bank Agribusiness Support offers structured commodity finance, SWAY AgFin (for women and youth), broiler finance facilities, and modern agricultural asset/equipment loans.

7) Keystone Bank Agric Finance provides agricultural value chain financing, including specialized aggregation schemes like the Modified Paddy Aggregation Scheme (M-PAS) for rice millers and Maize Aggregation Schemes (M-MAS).

8) Wema Bank Agric Finance offers agricultural production loans (for seeds, fertilizers, and pesticides), farm development finance, and agricultural finance leases for machinery and tractors.

On a final note...know what is happening in your country. This will enable you take advantage of opportunities and not missing them through ignorance and then becoming not only an eternal nag but also an eternal pessimist.

text:
A launch post describes the company a founder intends to build. The disclosure at the bottom of the same page describes the company that exists.

@marblegroupxyz launched on 10 November with an $11M seed led by Polychain, alongside Maven 11, Ripple, Susquehanna Crypto, Lattice and Blockwall. New York. It is run by Matt Ballensweig, previously BitGo, Genesis and Bridgewater, and Leon Marshall, previously Galaxy, Genesis, Trafigura and Apollo. That is about as serious a founding pair as this market produces, and the capital came from people who can read a balance sheet.

The pitch is two businesses. Marble Markets covers OTC and electronic spot trading strategies, borrowing and lending against assets you already hold, and derivatives to hedge or express a view. Marble Compute is institutional private credit for AI infrastructure, lending against GPUs and contracted offtake to neoclouds and GPU operators.

Now the footer, in their own words. Marble does not currently provide any services to the public. It buys, sells and holds digital assets solely for its own account, at its own risk and with its own capital. It does not act as an intermediary, broker, dealer, market maker, exchange or money transmitter, does not accept or custody assets for anyone else, and does not match or facilitate orders between others.  It is not registered or licensed with the SEC, the CFTC, FinCEN, the New York Department of Financial Services or any state money transmission regulator, and may offer services in future only after obtaining any required registrations. 

Both of those are on the same website. One page sells lending against your holdings and derivatives to hedge exposure. The footer says they cannot custody an asset for you or match an order between two people, which is what both of those products require.

That gap is not a scandal, and it is not unusual. A firm launching before its licences will say so in the only place a lawyer insists on. The UK notice is the same instinct, blocking anyone who isn't an investment professional or a high net worth company under articles 19 and 49 of the Financial Promotion Order, with no retail access.

The thing worth watching is what happens to the marketing pages between now and the first licence. If they stay up unchanged while the firm trades only its own capital, then the site was selling access it did not have.

Verdict: a funded, credible team with a disclosure that is more honest than its product pages.

Reader rule: when a financial firm launches, read the footer before the homepage. The footer is written to be survived and the homepage is written to be shared.
