Flock, the police-tech giant known for its network of some 120,000 automatic license plate readers around the US, announced some changes to its platform last Thursday. The updates are meant to prevent officers from using the platform for illegal or illegitimate purposes. 

That includes stalking. The Washington Post recently identified 50 cases in which officers misused systems from Flock and its competitors, often to stalk and harass women. One woman in Wisconsin alleged that her officer ex-boyfriend searched for her car 179 times. Another woman was being stalked by the chief of police, with nobody to report him to.

Flock has responded with practices aimed at ensuring that officers have a proper cause for every search, like using software to flag abnormal searches and requiring searchers to enter a criminal case number.

The changes come with big loopholes, though. For example, officers can enter bogus case numbers, just as they’ve lied to get around other Flock safeguards. The policies also don’t address some of the broader concerns from civil liberties and privacy groups that Flock is turning what was sold as a crime-stopping tool into a mass surveillance network. These criticisms have led to a growing backlash that already has some cities canceling contracts and some states trying to pass laws to limit or ban license plate readers entirely. 

Amid all this, there have recently been several arguments defending Flock: If these cameras help solve crime, what’s the big deal? On a good day they might help catch a kidnapper, and if not, they’re simply snapping pictures of my car that nobody will bother to look at. 

Putting aside the unanswered question about the extent to which Flock’s systems actually do solve or prevent crime, this all skips over a more important question: What kind of crime-fighting system has Flock chosen to build? Its network works the way it does because of a series of decisions about what information to collect, who can search it, how long to keep it, and how widely to share it. Those decisions set the terms of the bargain between security and civil liberties. Believing that technology should play a role in solving crime should not mean blindly accepting the terms of that bargain.

Consider, for example, its new requirement that officers enter a case number before running a search on Flock’s platform. This is meant to ensure that searches have a legitimate purpose. But Flock confirmed to MIT Technology Review that it doesn’t verify those case numbers, so an officer can simply enter fake information. One could imagine a system that instead requires case numbers that match the police department’s records—a more intrusive integration, perhaps, but also a far stronger safeguard and one that leaves a more useful audit trail.

Or what about finding people who have been kidnapped or have gone missing, the use case that Flock cites more than any other? Efforts to solve these crimes would hugely benefit from Flock’s nationwide network of cameras. But if Americans want officers to tap into that network only for this purpose, we could design it that way: Searches tied to an active Amber Alert, or a similar emergency, could perhaps access larger amounts of data from surrounding cities. That would preserve the network’s value in emergencies without requiring people to accept mass surveillance.  

Finally, there’s the question of how much data Flock collects and how long it’s kept. Flock mostly operates as a national network: Police in one city or state can search data collected in another, and agencies can retain that data for months or years. Yet Flock itself says 90% of searches happen within a week of an incident. That suggests another possible bargain: Keep and share data only as widely and for as long as it’s actually useful for solving crimes. (The company recently changed its recommended retention time to seven days, but in reality agencies can hold onto data for as long as they like or local laws permit.)

In short, Flock could design its surveillance to be much narrower. If it did, some of the company’s critics might not cease. Chad Marlow, a senior policy counsel at the ACLU, half-joked to me that the most acceptable Flock contract by his standards is “one that is never signed” and emphasized that the best way to set limits on surveillance isn’t with new Flock guidelines but with new laws. (Flock CEO Garrett Langley, for his part, said he’ll “probably always have a different view than the ACLU.”) 

And narrowing the scope of its technology would threaten the company’s entire pitch to police departments. License plate readers have been around since the 1990s, used for tolls and ticketing. Flock’s business model—and recent $8 billion evaluation—relies on instead leveraging its cameras into a massive network that collects rich amounts of data and offers police departments a modernized way to make sense of not just their own but others’. 

Flock’s hand might soon be forced. Cities have canceled contracts with the company. Some have gone to competitors, while others are taking a beat as residents ponder how they want this tech to be used and write new rules for police to abide by. The result might be that communities drive their own bargains about how technology can be used to solve crime and how much surveillance people should have to accept for it to do so.

In October 2018, auctioneer Dan Dotson of Storage Wars sold the unit in Southern California.

Dotson heard the story from a woman at a charity event in Indio.

A second specialist succeeded, revealing millions in cash.
Then an attorney representing the previous owners contacted the buyer, seeking the money's return.
The initial offer was $600,000, but the buyer rejected it.
The owners reportedly doubled their offer to $1.2 million, and a deal was reached.
The buyer returned $6.3 million and kept the agreed reward.
His identity was withheld for privacy and safety concerns.
After his original $500 purchase, he reportedly emerged $1,199,500 ahead.

text:
A man in Southern California is buying Costco’s $1.50 hot dog combo  and reselling it for $18.

That’s an 1,100% markup. On a hot dog. From a food court.

His name is Jack Chen. His delivery startup is called No Tip. The business model is simple: you order a Costco food court meal through his app. Someone walks into Costco, stands in line, buys it with their membership, walks out, and delivers it to your door.

The famous $1.50 hot dog and drink combo? $18 delivered.
Chicken tenders? Marked up.
Pepperoni pizza? Marked up.
Cookies? Marked up.

Every item on the Costco food court menu  a menu that has been a symbol of unbeatable value for 40+ years  is being resold at 5-12x the in-store price.

Customers are furious. The internet is losing its mind. Costco hasn’t responded.

And the wildest part? People are paying it.

Chen told SFGate his customers are mostly offices ordering lunch on company expense accounts. “It’s the company’s money,” he said.

The $1.50 hot dog combo  unchanged since 1984, defended by a CEO who once said “if you raise the effing hot dog, I will kill you”  is now an $18 delivery item on an app that turns Costco’s biggest loss leader into someone else’s profit margin.

text:
7. The bigger pattern  when delivery apps meet sacred prices.

The Costco hot dog isn’t the only iconic low-price item being resold at massive markups:

In-N-Out burgers: Southern California delivery drivers reselling $4-5 burgers for $20-100+ through Facebook Marketplace and TaskRabbit. In-N-Out doesn’t offer delivery. The markup fills the gap.

Chick-fil-A (on Sundays): the internet routinely jokes about what people would pay for Chick-fil-A on Sundays when the chain is closed. Third-party reselling of Saturday purchases for Sunday consumption has been documented.

Trader Joe’s specialty items: limited-run products resold on Amazon and eBay at 3-5x retail.

The pattern: any beloved product that the original company restricts  by location, by delivery, by hours, by membership  creates an arbitrage opportunity for someone willing to bridge the gap.

The delivery economy equation:

Convenience has a price. That price is the markup between what the product costs at the source and what someone will pay to not go to the source.

For a $1.50 Costco hot dog: the convenience premium is $16.50. A 1,100% markup. On paper: outrageous. In practice: people are paying it. Because the alternative  driving 20 minutes to Costco, parking in a crowded lot, navigating the warehouse, waiting in the food court line, and driving 20 minutes back  costs time. And for an office on a deadline: time costs more than $16.50.

The hot dog costs $1.50. Your time costs whatever No Tip charges for you to not spend it.

3. The internet’s reaction  outrage, humor, and uncomfortable economics.

The internet’s reaction split into three camps:

Camp 1  Pure outrage:

“1,100% markup on a $1.50 hot dog is criminal.”
 “Jim Sinegal would kill this guy.”
 “This is everything wrong with the gig economy.”

The emotional response: someone is profiting from a product that Costco deliberately sells at a loss to serve customers. The markup feels parasitic  extracting profit from a company’s intentional generosity.

Camp 2  Grudging respect:

“The man saw a gap in the market and filled it.”
 “Nobody is forcing anyone to pay $18. If they’re willing to pay, that’s the market.”
 “This is just capitalism doing capitalism things.”

The economic response: No Tip provides a service (delivery of food court items) that Costco doesn’t offer. The $16.50 markup covers labor, transportation, time, and profit. Nobody is being deceived  the price is listed before you order.

Camp 3  The comparison makers:

One X user pointed out that this isn’t new. In Southern California, rogue delivery drivers have been reselling In-N-Out burgers for $20-$100+ per order through Facebook Marketplace and TaskRabbit. The Costco hot dog is just the latest item to get the unofficial delivery treatment.

The pattern: any beloved food item that a restaurant won’t deliver becomes a delivery arbitrage opportunity for someone willing to stand in line and charge a premium.

What a load of bollocks. The idea that the BBC is “pro-Israel” is laughable. 

NewsCord is openly and explicitly partisan on Israel-Gaza. It grew directly out of the Tech for Palestine (T4P) coalition in the months after 7 October 2023.

This analysis is flawed because the “Israel would say” phrasing is a routine journalistic device, not evidence of bias. When a guest makes a strong accusation - such as genocide or deliberate targeting of civilians - and the other side is not in the studio, interviewers commonly put the official counter-position. Those accusations have been widely contested: the ICJ issued provisional measures but has never ruled that genocide is occurring, and multiple governments and military analyses reject the claim given Hamas’s documented use of civilian infrastructure and human shields.

The raw counts also need context that the charts do not provide. Far more on-air claims criticised Israel’s conduct than defended it, so presenters naturally offered the Israeli response more often. 

Normalising for the volume and severity of claims, or for the mix of guests, would be required before concluding systemic bias. A short “Israel would say it disputes those figures” is not equivalent to a sustained challenge.

The graphs themselves are clean visualisations of the categories the author chose to code. Whether those categories and inclusion rules were selected because they produce a dramatic disparity, or were applied neutrally, is the key methodological question. Anyone can examine the linked data and recode a sample to test how robust the imbalance remains under different criteria.

The numbers exist; the interpretation that they demonstrate editorial capture does not follow automatically once the nature and volume of the claims are taken into account.

The BBC Israel Would Say Files. The full results are in for both broadcast and articles.

Analysis of 267 broadcast interviews between October 2023 and October 2026:

- BBC presenters put Israel's case, in Israel's name, to guests criticising Israel's conduct in Gaza in 252 separate interviews.

- They put the Palestinian case, in its name, to guests defending Israel's conduct in 15.

- To better portray this disparity, our compilation of the BBC defending Israel in their own words now runs at 48 mins 12 secs. Our compilation of the BBC defending Palestinians in their own words runs at 2 mins 38 secs.

- The plainest form, “Israel would say”, was put to critics in 75 interviews. “Palestinians [or any Palestinian group] would say” was put to defenders in 4.

- 10 of the 15 Palestinian cases came in the first six weeks after 7 October 2023, and 5 in the three years after. Presenters were still putting Israel's case to critics in 2026.

- The above point suggests an editorial shift to stop conveying what Palestinians are saying, but to continue conveying what "Israel would say".

Analysis of 1,618 written articles, from October 2023 to October 2026:

- When an article reported criticism of Israel's conduct in Gaza, the BBC added Israel's position 49% of the time (1,771 of 3,648 claims).

- When an article reported Israel's claims, the BBC added a Palestinian or UN position 38% of the time (914 of 2,431). A Palestinian position alone: 25%.

- Put the two official sides side by side. When the authorities in Gaza made a claim against Israel, the BBC added Israel's position 58% of the time (334 of 575). When Israel's government or army made a claim, the BBC added a Palestinian or UN position 39% of the time (855 of 2,165).

- Article by article: 71% of the articles reporting criticism of Israel gave Israel's position at least once. 53% of the articles reporting Israel's claims gave a Palestinian or UN position.

- In other words, in almost half of the articles where Israel makes a claim, it goes completely uncontested.

The full report, including every single broadcast and article in the corpus, can be found here, completely free of charge: https://t.co/qEYyFnMyCV

WWE Unreal Season 3 will be released on July 21.

WWE Unreal Season 3 will have five 50-minute episodes.

Netflix News

Here's the latest Netflix news as of mid-January 2026!

The streaming giant is kicking off the year strong with a packed slate of new releases, ongoing buzz around major deals, and continued subscriber growth.

Major Highlights

Netflix is reportedly in the midst of a blockbuster acquisition: the company has agreed to buy Warner Bros. in a massive deal valued at around $82.7 billion (with some reports citing $72 billion in equity value).

This move aims to supercharge its content library with iconic franchises like Harry Potter and classic films.

However, there's drama — Paramount Skydance has launched a competing hostile takeover bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, adding some high-stakes industry intrigue!

Netflix ended 2025 with over 301.6 million global subscribers, solidifying its position as the top streaming platform.

What's New & Coming in January 2026

January is loaded with fresh originals, from thrilling mysteries to romantic adaptations and long-awaited returns.

Here are some of the standout releases that are lighting up the charts and generating buzz right now:

People We Meet on Vacation — A charming rom-com adaptation of the Emily Henry novel, starring Emily Bader — it's been topping the charts as one of the biggest new movies of the year so far!

The Rip — This high-octane action-thriller directed by Joe Carnahan reunites Ben Affleck and Matt Damon — it's one of the most anticipated films dropping mid-month, perfect for fans of intense heist vibes!

His & Hers — A gripping mystery series starring Tessa Thompson and Jon Bernthal, following estranged spouses racing to solve a murder. It's been climbing the Top 10 with strong buzz around its twists.

Bridgerton Season 4 — The Regency-era drama returns later in the month (Part 1 premiering around Jan 29), with plenty of masquerade glamour and romance — the premiere events are already making waves!

Stand-up specials and reality shows keeping the variety flowing.

(In Case You Missed It)

WWE Unreal

WWE Unreal is a professional wrestling documentary and reality series on Netflix that provides an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the creative process and internal operations of WWE.

WWE Unreal

Show Overview

Genre: Reality television / Documentary series.

Premise: The series follows WWE Superstars and executives, notably Paul "Triple H" Levesque, as they plan storylines in the writers' room and manage the "Gorilla Position" during live broadcasts.

Production: A collaboration between WWE, Omaha Productions (Peyton Manning), NFL Films, and Skydance Sports.

Seasons & Episodes

The series has released two seasons as of January 2026:

Season 1: Premiered July 29, 2025. It chronicled the lead-up to the debut of WWE Raw on Netflix and WrestleMania 41. Notable segments included a look at John Cena's high-profile storyline turns and the return of Charlotte Flair.

Season 2: Released January 20, 2026. This five-episode season focuses on the "Road to SummerSlam 2025" and features superstars like Seth Rollins, Becky Lynch, Rhea Ripley, and Cody Rhodes.

It delves into real-life drama such as R-Truth's contract negotiations and Naomi's previous walkout from the company.

Season 3: Confirmed to be in development, expected to focus on John Cena's retirement tour.

Key Personalities Featured

Executives: Paul "Triple H" Levesque (Narrator), Peyton Manning (Executive Producer).

Superstars: John Cena, Roman Reigns, Cody Rhodes, CM Punk, Rhea Ripley, Becky Lynch, Seth Rollins, and Bianca Belair.

🧭 CORNICHE BEIRUT | TRAVEL ESSENTIALS

📍 Getting There
Beirut’s Mediterranean promenade stretches through Ain el Mreisseh and Manara toward Raouché. From central Beirut, taxis or ride-hailing services provide convenient access. Start at Ain el Mreisseh for a longer coastal walk, or head directly to Raouché for the famous sea views.

🗺️ What to Explore
Follow the waterfront past the Manara lighthouse toward the Pigeon Rocks viewpoint. For a shorter visit, focus on Raouché, where the limestone formations can be admired from the public promenade without taking a boat.

⏱️ Time & Costs
Allow 1–3 hours for walking and sightseeing. Public access and views are normally free, while cafés and optional boat excursions charge separately. Early mornings and late afternoons offer more comfortable temperatures, particularly in summer.

⚠️ Travel Planning Alert
As of November 2026, several governments advise against travel to Lebanon due to ongoing security risks. Leisure travel is best postponed until conditions improve. Visitors already in Beirut should verify local restrictions, transport availability and official travel advisories before planning an outing.

#MPF4Plus
#Origami turns a flat sheet into a vessel for memory, transformation, protection, and desire. These ten scenes bring the folding languages of distinguished Asian origami artists into dialogue with European and American oil painting, from the Renaissance to Pop Art. Each paper construction inhabits the painted world through shared light, perspective, texture, and emotional atmosphere.

Here, MPF‑4+ serves as a compositional framework linking light, geometry, palette, and materiality, enriched by symbolism, psychological tension, explicit camera perspective, and time of day. Each prompt brings these elements together in one cinematic scene.

The Fold Before Flight [Sandro Botticelli — Florentine Renaissance Allegory] (Ultra‑Max): At dawn, an ivory origami crane shaped through Akira Yoshizawa’s sensitive folding language rests between a young woman’s open palms within a Sandro Botticelli–inspired oil painting of a secluded coastal garden. An intimate, eye-level medium-wide view aligns its triangular wings with the distant geometry of sails; pale rose light passes through thin washi edges, revealing fibers beneath the sharply compressed creases. Myrtle branches articulate dark arabesques against celadon water, while translucent flesh glazes and delicately brushed gold embroidery surround the paper’s quiet whiteness. One wing leans toward the sea, the other toward her breast: peace and longevity suspended between the desire to release and the terror of abandonment.

The King Beneath the Table [Albrecht Dürer — Northern Renaissance Precision] (Ultra‑Max): In the cold light of an early winter morning, a tawny paper lion conceived through Hideo Komatsu’s sculptural origami vocabulary stands beneath an astronomer’s oak table inside an Albrecht Dürer–inspired oil painting. A low-angle, floor-level wide shot makes its folded mane echo the radiating divisions of an abandoned celestial instrument overhead. Amber glazes disclose the lion’s interlocked planes, minute paper abrasions, and compressed angular paws; beyond it, pewter, fur, walnut, and leaded glass receive distinct, exacting surfaces. A pale sun illuminates the empty chair without reaching the animal’s face. The tiny sovereign guards a broken compass, its meticulously folded strength confronting a universe that refuses to remain measurable.

The Guest at the Last Candle [Caravaggio — Baroque Tenebrism] (Ultra‑Max): At midnight, a crimson origami devil inspired by Jun Maekawa’s geometric ingenuity sits beside an unpaid coin on a tavern table in a Caravaggio–inspired oil painting. An intimate, low-angle close-up places its pointed horns against a young gambler’s half-lit throat; one guttering candle draws a diagonal through wine-dark space, exposing folded knuckles, scarred wood, greasy fingerprints, and the brittle white interior of a damaged paper edge. Dense umber shadows swallow the other players, while vermilion and lead-white highlights concentrate around a hand poised to retrieve the figure. The devil’s shadow touches the gambler before his fingers touch the paper, making temptation appear less like an invitation than an agreement already signed.

A Rose Kept Unopened [Johannes Vermeer — Dutch Domestic Intimacy] (Ultra‑Max): At nine in the morning, a single folded rose inspired by Toshikazu Kawasaki’s spiral geometry lies upon a sealed letter in a Johannes Vermeer–inspired oil painting of a quiet Delft interior. An intimate three-quarter view from just above the tabletop lets the rose’s concentric folds answer the elliptical mouth of a blue-and-white porcelain jug. Cool window light gathers along cream paper ridges, sinking into a muted carmine center; restrained oil glazes distinguish granular plaster, yellow satin, soft bread, and the fraying blue cloth beneath the envelope. A woman pauses with her hand suspended above the seal. The flower promises permanence, yet its flawless closure makes tenderness feel inseparable from something withheld.

The Water Remembers Wings [Claude Monet — Impressionist River Light] (Ultra‑Max): Beneath the last lavender light of a summer evening, a wet-folded paper swan inspired by Hoàng Tiến Quyết’s flowing origami forms drifts among reeds in a Claude Monet–inspired oil painting of a sheltered river bend. A water-level panoramic view stretches its curved neck across trembling reflections of willow branches, while the softened geometry of its wings catches apricot light. Broken strokes of cobalt, mauve, jade, and pale gold dissolve the banks without dissolving the swan’s tactile paper seams; darkened fibers at the waterline betray its gradual saturation. An empty skiff waits beneath the trees. The swan advances with ceremonial calm toward the sinking sun, carrying an impossible wish for beauty to survive the element that sustains it.

The Eagle That Cannot Leave [Vincent van Gogh — Post-Impressionist Emotional Landscape] (Ultra‑Max): At late-afternoon harvest time, an enormous folded-paper eagle inspired by Nguyễn Hùng Cường’s intricate origami construction grips a splintered fence within a Vincent van Gogh–inspired oil painting. A low-angle dramatic wide shot drives the diagonals of its pleated wings against a turbulent ultramarine sky; ocher handmade paper bears visible fibers, taut creases, and tiny tears where the talons tighten around the wood. Thick chrome-yellow wheat strokes surge toward violet hills, while orange impasto catches the bird’s angular breast. Its wings spread fully, yet a single loose paper strip remains caught beneath the fence rail. Freedom dominates the silhouette; one almost invisible attachment commands the entire body.

The Dragon Behind Her Shoulder [Gustav Klimt — Viennese Symbolist Ornament] (Ultra‑Max): Under the amber glow of evening lamps, an emerald origami dragon inspired by Fumiaki Kawahata’s figurative folding language coils along the back of a woman’s chair inside a Gustav Klimt–inspired oil painting. A frontal, waist-up portrait compresses the room into tessellated fields of ocher, malachite, black, and burnished gold pigment, while the dragon’s folded scales remain unmistakably fibrous paper. Its angular tail repeats the spirals embroidered across her robe; warm flesh emerges through thin, luminous glazes against densely patterned upholstery. Her jeweled hand rests beside its delicately articulated claws. The dragon appears to guard her, yet its encircling body follows the chair so closely that protection and captivity become the same ornament.

The Owl in the Empty Afternoon [René Magritte — Philosophical Surrealism] (Ultra‑Max): At three in the afternoon beneath an immaculate blue sky, a monumental paper owl inspired by Kyohei Katsuta’s precise origami animal forms occupies an ordinary dining chair in a René Magritte–inspired oil painting. A restrained, eye-level wide shot frames a suburban room whose open doorway reveals the same room again, perfectly empty. Smooth, measured oil passages describe gray walls, polished floorboards, and a white tablecloth; the owl alone carries intricate folded planes, feather-like pleats, and the faint tooth of charcoal-colored paper. Sunlight gives every object a consistent shadow except the chair, whose shadow resembles a standing person. Wisdom has taken the occupant’s place, but the room offers no evidence that anything has changed.

The Hour That Burned Without Fire [Salvador Dalí — Surrealist Metamorphic Desert] (Ultra‑Max): At the instant before sunrise, a vast origami phoenix inspired by Satoshi Kamiya’s supercomplex folding architecture rises from an overturned hourglass within a Salvador Dalí–inspired oil painting. An extreme low-angle panoramic view makes its intricately pleated wings span a mineral desert of pink limestone, turquoise distance, and elongated violet shadows. Vermilion paper feathers sharpen into hundreds of articulated folds; their edges glow with reflected dawn rather than flame, while individual grains of sand cling to the fibrous breast. A solitary figure shelters beneath one wing, holding an unbroken egg. The phoenix casts the shadow of a collapsed bird: rebirth ascends visibly while exhaustion remains fastened to the earth.

The Gift Nobody Opens [Roy Lichtenstein — Pop Art Domestic Drama] (Ultra‑Max): At noon, a modular origami box inspired by Tomoko Fuse’s interlocking geometric structures sits between two estranged lovers in a Roy Lichtenstein–inspired oil painting. A sharply cropped, high-angle cinematic view turns the kitchen table into a confrontational arrangement of diagonals, scarlet rectangles, lemon-yellow surfaces, and blue-black shadows. Crisp painted contours and carefully articulated dot fields surround the box’s tangible paper facets, slightly crushed corners, and alternating red-and-white modules. Window light casts its nested geometry across an untouched cup; a woman’s hand approaches the lid while a man’s fingers retreat beyond the frame. The box contains no visible lock, but its perfect assembly makes opening it feel like destroying the only thing still holding together.

CRITERIA: Most engagement on X (past 24 hours)

SpaceX

Super Heavy V3 Booster 22 rolls to Starbase pad; Starlink Mini 2 unveiled; major solar cell contract for Starmind

SpaceX moved Booster 22 (first Super Heavy V3 planned for tower catch) to the launch pad at Starbase for final catch testing, including a suspended squeeze test. Flight 15 remains targeted as early as November 13 for a dual catch attempt (booster + ship), pending regulatory approval. Separately, Starlink introduced Mini 2, a next-gen portable unit with quick-swap battery offering up to 4.5 hours runtime (or USB-C), Wi-Fi 6, IP67 rating, and ~1.6 kg weight including battery; US invitation preorders are open with deliveries expected to start in December. SpaceX also signed a major supply contract with Germany’s SINGULUS for heterojunction (HJT) solar cell manufacturing equipment supporting >100 GW to accelerate Starmind satellite production in Bastrop, Texas; first line targeted for H1 2027. Source: @SpaceX, @Starlink, Elon Musk (@elonmusk)

SpaceXSI

Starmind solar scale-up highlighted as SpaceX orders 100 GW/year HJT equipment

The SINGULUS partnership (detailed above) is explicitly tied to powering Starmind orbital superintelligence satellites. Elon Musk framed the order as enabling “a sentient sun.” SpaceXSI (the rebranded former xAI / SpaceXAI unit focused on Grok models, Colossus compute, and related apps) continues to underpin these efforts, with prior mentions of space-based compute plans from 2027 onward. No major new product announcements or financial disclosures appeared in the past 24 hours. Source: SpaceX, elonmusk

X-corp

Quiet day. No high-engagement, on-topic English posts from official or primary accounts on product, legal, or operational developments for X Corp in the past 24 hours that met criteria (excluding memes, giveaways, and pure opinion). Source: N/A

Tesla

Unplugged Performance offers to take Cybertruck line; Robotaxi registrations edge past Waymo in Texas

Aftermarket specialist Unplugged Performance publicly offered to assume Cybertruck production (plus proposed CyberSUV and CyberCargo variants) via an investor consortium, at no cost to Tesla floor space/headcount/focus, in exchange for a license fee plus FSD/Robotaxi network revenue per vehicle. This follows reports that Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck output at Giga Texas around mid-2027 to prioritize Cybercab; Tesla has also slimmed orderable trims to primarily the higher-priced Cyberbeast. Separately, trackers showed Tesla surpassing Waymo in total robotaxis registered in Texas (roughly 1,302 vs. 1,297), with recent Model Y additions. No formal Tesla response to the Unplugged offer was noted. Source: @UnpluggedTesla, @SawyerMerritt (and related reporting)

Grok

Grok Bot adds Tailscale private-network access; Musk comments on Grok 5 timeline vs. Claude Opus

Grok Bot announced it can now join personal or company Tailscale tailnets for secure access to private MCP servers, internal tools, and network apps. Elon Musk stated that current Grok is “not as good” as Claude Opus 5.5 (which he called a masterpiece) but that Grok 5 should exceed it, potentially in 2–3 months with continued acceleration. Additional minor Grok Bot feature notes (phone calls, share sheet, shopping, team bots, etc.) circulated in video form. A SpaceX VP comment (quoted earlier) about Grok outperforming humans on foreign-object debris detection in parts also received attention. Source: Grokbot, elonmusk

Neuralink

New early-feasibility study (PRIME2) registered including chronic ischemic stroke patients

A newly registered ClinicalTrials.g early feasibility study (N1-EFS-300 / NCT07929792) lists Neuralink’s N1 implant and R1 robot for up to 10 participants with severe arm/hand weakness from chronic ischemic stroke, spinal cord injury, or ALS. University of Miami is listed as a recruiting site; primary results expected around November 2027. Engagement was moderate rather than peak, and the company account itself was quiet; details come from secondary reporting of the registry entry. Broader discussion of future Optimus-limb + Neuralink concepts continued at lower volume.
Source: Secondary X posts citing ClinicalTrials.g

$AKAM KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM AKAMAI TECHNOLOGIES’ Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL

Akamai’s November 5 call supports a selective investment conclusion: AI infrastructure spending is broadening beyond GPUs, but the associated economic benefits accrue to different companies at different stages. Component suppliers and manufacturing partners can receive orders and cash well before cloud operators recognize revenue or earn acceptable returns on invested capital. The approximately $30 million deployment-related revenue deferral does not establish weaker underlying demand; the planned $1.7 billion component purchase illustrates that procurement can accelerate while customer billing slips. The highest-conviction implications concern customer-funded manufacturing, server memory, established CPU suppliers, PC input-cost pressure, CDN pricing discipline, application security, and available colocation capacity. Several relationships were disclosed before this earnings call, making November’s contribution confirmation of execution rather than an entirely new order announcement.

ELECTRONICS MANUFACTURING AND SERVER SYSTEMS

CUSTOMER-FUNDED COMPONENT INVENTORY IMPROVES JABIL’S EXPOSURE TO THE AI BUILDOUT (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected company: Jabil Inc. (JBL: US). Direction: positive. Magnitude: meaningful program-level opportunity and favorable working-capital protection; the incremental consolidated earnings contribution remains undisclosed.

Call evidence: Akamai reiterated that it expects to spend approximately $1.7 billion in Q4 2026 to “secure and pre-purchase critical supply chain components, notably memory.” Management also stated that approximately 70% of the hardware, memory, and other components required for the latest Anthropic agreement had been secured.

The decisive supplier connection appears in Akamai’s September contractual disclosure. Jabil was authorized to purchase approximately $1.7 billion of memory components, with Akamai paying the corresponding supplier invoices when Jabil receives the components. Pending use, Jabil holds the inventory on consignment for Akamai and repurchases it at cost as it is consumed in production.

The transmission mechanism is therefore more attractive than a generic increase in contract-manufacturing orders. Akamai funds the advance component stockpile, reducing Jabil’s exposure to carrying that inventory during the interval before server assembly. Jabil retains manufacturing, integration, warranty, spare-parts, and repair opportunities without necessarily financing the entire early procurement requirement. This structure transfers an important portion of the inventory-financing burden toward the infrastructure owner.

The $1.7 billion authorization is equivalent to approximately 4.7% of Jabil’s roughly $36 billion fiscal 2026 revenue, demonstrating the program’s scale. It is not evidence of $1.7 billion of immediate incremental Jabil revenue, nor should Jabil’s corporate operating margin be applied to that amount. Component pass-through, consignment accounting, manufacturing fees, and shipment acceptance determine the actual revenue and profit contribution.

Near-term catalyst: component receipts, funding, and subsequent manufacturing conversion during Q4 2026 and early 2027. The agreement preceded Jabil’s September 30 fiscal 2027 outlook, so adding the entire procurement amount to existing guidance would risk double counting. Longer-duration implication: customer-funded procurement can make selected manufacturing exposures economically preferable to owning the infrastructure itself, particularly when cloud billing and returns are back-end-weighted.

LENOVO HAS A VERIFIED MULTIYEAR SUPPLY RELATIONSHIP, NOT MERELY THEMATIC AI EXPOSURE (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected company: Lenovo Group Ltd. (0992: China, Hong Kong-listed). Direction: positive for Infrastructure Solutions Group. Magnitude: potentially meaningful account-level contribution, but a moderate consolidated read-through rather than a transformational group-level earnings event.

Call evidence: Akamai has contracted the required space and power for the $11.6 billion Anthropic agreement and secured approximately 70% of its necessary components. Management expects the large agreements to reach full revenue run rate by the end of 2028.

Akamai’s September disclosure identifies Lenovo as a contractual supplier of hardware, software, and related services under a statement of work with a 7-year term. This establishes a direct commercial relationship. It is materially stronger evidence than assuming that every major server vendor benefits from Akamai’s capital budget.

The transmission mechanism runs through hardware procurement, system deliveries, and associated services during the deployment period. Supplier revenue can be recognized before Akamai’s customer revenue, subject to Lenovo’s contractual delivery and acceptance provisions. The call’s procurement progress consequently supports delivery visibility even though Akamai’s own service-recognition schedule has slipped.

The opportunity is significant but must be scaled appropriately. Lenovo’s latest reported Infrastructure Solutions Group quarterly revenue was $8.5 billion, while its disclosed AI server pipeline was $54 billion. Akamai is therefore a credible contributor to an already large infrastructure business, not sufficient evidence for a company-wide growth step-change by itself. Neither the $11.6 billion customer commitment nor Akamai’s full infrastructure spending plan belongs entirely to Lenovo.

Near-term catalyst: evidence of deliveries and conversion into recognized infrastructure revenue during late 2026 and 2027. Longer-duration implication: CPU-heavy, distributed AI deployments expand server demand beyond the most visible GPU clusters. The principal offset is Lenovo’s substantial PC exposure, which faces the same memory-cost inflation discussed below. The positive conclusion is strongest for the infrastructure division, not an assumption that every Lenovo business benefits equally.

SEMICONDUCTORS AND CLIENT HARDWARE

AI MEMORY DEMAND IS BROADER THAN HBM, WITH ADVANCE PROCUREMENT SUPPORTING CONVENTIONAL SERVER MEMORY (READ-THROUGH 3)

Affected companies: Micron Technology Inc. (MU: US), SK hynix Inc. (000660: South Korea), and Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. (005930: South Korea). Direction: positive for server-memory demand and supplier bargaining power. Magnitude: moderate sector-level confirmation; the direct earnings allocation among suppliers is unknown.

Call evidence: Akamai plans approximately $1.7 billion of purchases concentrated in memory and other critical components, while stating that “well over 90%” of the servers being deployed are CPUs. The latest Anthropic agreement also includes a pricing-adjustment mechanism for components not yet ordered.

The important conclusion is not simply that AI consumes more memory. It is that economically significant AI infrastructure demand extends beyond accelerator-associated HBM into the memory supporting CPU execution, agents, application workloads, and distributed services. Akamai’s disclosure does not specify the exact DRAM, NAND, or module mix, so the entire purchase cannot be classified as DDR5 or attributed to a particular manufacturer.

The transmission mechanism is procurement competition. Infrastructure operators seeking delivery certainty commit capital earlier, reducing the availability of uncommitted supply and supporting firmer contract negotiations. Akamai’s ability to adjust customer pricing for remaining component purchases makes its future procurement less sensitive to cost increases than that of a buyer unable to pass those increases through.

This interpretation is corroborated by the memory producers’ own recent disclosures. SK hynix reported increased server DDR5 sales and long-term agreements covering more than 50% of 2027 and 2028 production capacity. Samsung described server demand as supporting higher memory prices across applications and identified server DRAM and SSDs as expansion priorities. These disclosures support a broad memory-market mechanism rather than an unsupported assumption about Akamai’s vendor allocation.

Near-term catalyst: Q4 component deliveries and subsequent disclosures on contract pricing, allocation, and customer prepayments. Longer-duration implication: AI demand can support conventional server-memory economics even when investor attention remains concentrated on HBM. The limiting factor is timing: advance procurement pulls purchases forward and must not be modeled as an additional recurring $1.7 billion annual order. Micron and SK hynix offer more concentrated memory exposure; Samsung’s consolidated outcome also reflects its substantial non-memory businesses.

THE SAME PROCUREMENT CYCLE IS A HEADWIND TO HP’S PC MARGIN RECOVERY (READ-THROUGH 4)

Affected company: HP Inc. (HPQ: US). Direction: negative for Personal Systems margins and confidence in a rapid recovery. Magnitude: potentially material at the segment level and moderate at the consolidated level.

Call evidence: Akamai is committing approximately $1.7 billion to secure scarce components and protecting the unpurchased portion through customer pricing adjustments. Management explicitly discussed rising component costs and the ability to charge higher prices on subsequent cloud contracts.

The transmission mechanism differs sharply for a PC manufacturer. Large infrastructure customers can reserve memory well in advance against multiyear revenue commitments. PC manufacturers must recover higher component costs through device pricing, product mix, redesigns, or cost reductions while selling into a more price-sensitive market. Server and client memory are not perfectly interchangeable, but shared manufacturing resources, supplier allocation decisions, and broader DRAM pricing connect the markets.

HP’s August results demonstrate the exposure. Personal Systems revenue was $11.8 billion, approximately 75% of group revenue, with an operating margin of 4.6%. PC units declined 16% even as segment revenue increased 18%. Management attributed revenue performance partly to pricing and mix, illustrating why revenue growth alone does not establish healthy unit demand or improving economics.

At that revenue level, an illustrative 100-basis-point margin change represents approximately $118 million of quarterly operating profit, or roughly 22% of the segment’s reported operating profit. This is a sensitivity, not a forecast of an additional 100-basis-point decline.

Near-term catalyst: HP’s fiscal 2026 closing results and fiscal 2027 guidance, particularly the conversion of higher-cost inventory into cost of goods sold and the response to further pricing actions. Longer-duration implication: sustained AI-driven memory tightness can redistribute profits from device assemblers toward memory producers.

The negative conclusion is not that Akamai’s purchase alone causes an HP earnings miss. It is that the call provides additional customer-side evidence against assuming rapid component-cost normalization. HP’s sourcing improvements, premium mix, and productivity measures remain meaningful offsets.

AMD HAS AN ESTABLISHED ROUTE INTO CPU-HEAVY AI INFRASTRUCTURE (READ-THROUGH 5)

Affected company: Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD: US). Direction: positive for EPYC demand visibility and the breadth of the server-CPU opportunity. Magnitude: strategically meaningful, with the direct consolidated revenue contribution unquantifiable from the disclosed information.

Call evidence: Akamai said that “the vast majority of servers that we’re deploying, well over 90%, are CPUs.” Management emphasized application execution, enterprise workloads, post-training, selected inference, and agents rather than frontier-model training.

AMD is a verified incumbent, not an inferred supplier based solely on processor architecture. Akamai’s published G8 dedicated-compute offering uses 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors, and AMD separately identifies Akamai as an EPYC customer. The exact processor allocation for the new Anthropic agreements remains undisclosed.

The transmission mechanism is broader paid demand for CPU-based compute surrounding AI models. Agents require orchestration, application execution, data access, networking, and other general-purpose processing. Those workloads can expand CPU capacity requirements even when the underlying model relies heavily on accelerators. Akamai’s commitments provide evidence that this surrounding infrastructure can become a substantial commercial category.

Near-term catalyst: server deliveries and subsequent disclosures identifying the hardware configurations used in the 2027 deployment ramp. Longer-duration implication: AI infrastructure investment can support both accelerators and merchant server CPUs rather than producing a simple substitution between them.

The boundary is important. More than 90% of server units being CPUs does not mean more than 90% of spending or revenue is attributable to CPUs. Nor does Akamai’s established AMD relationship prove that AMD wins every new deployment. Management’s emphasis on 7-year contractual revenue and long equipment life also argues against extrapolating the initial buildout into a rapid recurring replacement cycle. This is a positive CPU-market read-through, not evidence of falling GPU demand.

INTERNET INFRASTRUCTURE AND CYBERSECURITY

AKAMAI’S CAPITAL REALLOCATION SUPPORTS CDN PRICING DISCIPLINE, BENEFITING FASTLY (READ-THROUGH 6)

Affected company: Fastly Inc. (FSLY: US). Direction: positive for pricing resilience and selective customer acquisition. Magnitude: potentially material because network services remain the majority of Fastly’s revenue.

Call evidence: McGowan stated, “We’re probably holding pricing better now than we have for a long period of time.” Leighton added that Akamai is avoiding very low-priced delivery contracts and large traffic spikes where the economics do not justify the capacity, because the associated capital can earn better returns in CIS.

The transmission mechanism is reduced incentive for a major incumbent to compete aggressively for marginal delivery traffic. When Akamai prioritizes capital returns over maximizing delivered volume, competitors face less pressure to match uneconomic bids. Fastly can benefit through better renewal economics and opportunities to win appropriately priced workloads.

Fastly’s November 4 results provide relevant exposure and corroboration. Network Services revenue was $138 million, approximately 73% of total revenue, and increased 16% year over year. Non-GAAP gross margin reached 65.8%, versus 62.8% a year earlier. Akamai’s commentary is consistent with a healthier competitive environment, although it does not prove that Akamai’s decisions caused Fastly’s performance.

An illustrative 1% improvement in realized revenue across Fastly’s quarterly Network Services base equals approximately $1.38 million before associated costs. That is approximately 4.4% of Fastly’s $31.2 million quarterly non-GAAP operating income, demonstrating the sensitivity to relatively small changes in pricing or monetization.

Near-term catalyst: renewal pricing and traffic monetization through Q4 2026 and early 2027. Fastly had already reported Q3 before Akamai’s call, so this is corroboration rather than a prediction of that completed quarter. Longer-duration implication: disciplined incumbents can improve CDN economics even if aggregate traffic growth remains unexceptional. The caveat is that rejected traffic is not automatically attractive traffic; taking structurally unprofitable contracts would reverse the benefit.

APPLICATION-SECURITY DEMAND CAN MONETIZE AI WITHOUT FINANCING LARGE COMPUTE CLUSTERS (READ-THROUGH 7)

Affected companies: Cloudflare Inc. (NET: US) and Fastly Inc. (FSLY: US). Direction: positive for application-security demand and platform attachment. Magnitude: moderate for the relevant businesses, with a potentially attractive capital-efficiency profile; no immediate company-wide estimate increase is established.

Call evidence: Akamai’s security revenue increased 10% in constant currency, supported by web application protection, API security, and segmentation. Management cited more sophisticated AI-enabled attacks, agents interacting with applications, sensitive information entering AI tools, and bots becoming harder to distinguish from legitimate users. Leighton also emphasized that security “doesn’t take a huge amount of CapEx.”

The transmission mechanism is an expanding security problem at the application boundary. More APIs, automated users, agents, and execution environments increase the requirements for discovery, authentication, traffic inspection, abuse prevention, and policy enforcement. Providers already positioned in application traffic can sell additional protection without owning the customer’s entire AI compute estate.

Cloudflare and Fastly have directly relevant application-security and edge-platform offerings. Fastly’s November results reported 32% security revenue growth and additional AI firewall, runtime-control, and API-security capabilities. Cloudflare’s November 5 results showed 39% overall revenue growth and described continued demand for protection as digital threats escalate. Cloudflare’s consolidated growth should not be misrepresented as a security-only growth rate, but the disclosures support the broader adoption environment.

Near-term catalyst: security attachment, enterprise expansion, and paid adoption of AI-specific controls over subsequent reporting periods. Both companies had already reported by the information cutoff, so the call confirms a demand mechanism rather than revealing an undisclosed earnings beat.

Longer-duration implication: security can capture part of AI’s economic value with substantially less infrastructure ownership than large dedicated-compute contracts require. The offset is stronger competition from Akamai itself. The high-conviction conclusion concerns expanding demand and the monetization opportunity, not guaranteed market-share gains or automatic margin expansion for every vendor.

DATA-CENTER REAL ESTATE

AVAILABLE, POWERED COLOCATION CAPACITY BENEFITS BEFORE THE CLOUD TENANT REACHES FULL UTILIZATION (READ-THROUGH 8)

Affected companies: Equinix Inc. (EQIX: US) and Digital Realty Trust Inc. (DLR: US). Direction: positive for available-capacity leasing, interconnection, and the scarcity value of suitable existing facilities. Magnitude: moderate sector-level confirmation; no specific Akamai contract award or quantified earnings uplift is established for either company.

Call evidence: Akamai stated that all necessary space and power for the latest Anthropic agreement had been contracted. Leighton emphasized deployment across “a lot of spaces that are much smaller,” rather than dependence on a small number of very large construction projects. McGowan explained that colocation costs arrive ahead of the corresponding cloud revenue and that long-term agreements include escalators.

The transmission mechanism favors landlords with suitable powered space available on the required schedule. Distributed CPU deployments create demand for smaller increments of capacity, connectivity, and geographically diverse locations, broadening the addressable opportunity beyond the largest GPU campuses. Lease commencement can also precede the tenant’s full customer-revenue ramp, allowing the property owner to begin monetizing capacity while the cloud operator is still absorbing startup costs.

Recent landlord disclosures corroborate the mechanism. Equinix reported strengthening pricing, record annualized gross bookings of $533 million, and 10% interconnection revenue growth. Digital Realty reported record bookings in its 0-to-1-megawatt plus interconnection category and 11.8% cash renewal-rate increases. These results preceded Akamai’s call and should be treated as independent confirmation, not revenue caused by this specific announcement.

Near-term catalyst: lease commencements and delivery of already-contracted capacity through 2027. Longer-duration implication: existing power access, network density, and operational readiness can be more valuable than land or theoretical future capacity alone.

Several limits prevent overstatement. Neither company was identified on the call as the landlord for the new agreements. Signed leases do not immediately become cash rent, and part of Akamai’s reported colocation pressure reflects noncash straight-line accounting. The disclosed approximately $2.2 billion mature revenue opportunity at $22 million per contracted megawatt implies only roughly 100 megawatts across the large-deal portfolio. The opportunity is attractive within distributed colocation, but it does not justify converting Akamai’s contract value into a giant new electricity-load forecast. Site-level locations were not disclosed, so no high-conviction utility-specific or regional power-demand trade follows from the call.

THE POT THAT NEVER BOILS DRY The Story of Shrimp Congee with Salted Egg and Mushrooms
Somewhere in the world, at this very moment, a person is doing the one thing every rice teacher warns against: they are boiling rice until it falls apart on purpose.

They are not making a mistake. They are standing at the end of a road that is at least three thousand years long, stirring a pot that has fed emperors and beggars, monks and sailors, newborns and the dying. The grains are swelling, bursting, surrendering their starch into the water until the whole pot turns into something silky, white and quietly luminous. In a few minutes, a handful of pink shrimp will be dropped in, a salted duck egg will be cracked open to reveal a yolk the color of a setting sun, and dried mushrooms that smell like a forest after rain will be stirred through. And what comes out of the pot will taste like comfort itself.

This is the story of that bowl. It does not belong to one inventor, one village or one century. It is a bowl built from four separate stories, each one older than most nations, which happened to meet in the same pot.

THE ACCIDENT THAT FED A CIVILIZATION

Let us begin with the plainest ingredient, and the most underestimated one: water and rice, cooked for too long.

Nobody knows who made the first congee, because nobody was writing things down when it happened. But we can guess the moment with some confidence. Rice was being grown along the Yangtze River valley more than seven thousand years ago, and archaeologists have dug up the charred remains of ancient paddies, along with clay pots sturdy enough to sit over a fire. Once you have grain, water and a pot, porridge is not an invention. It is an inevitability. Someone forgot the pot on the fire. Someone added too much water. Someone had too many mouths and too little rice, and discovered that a handful of grain, boiled long enough with enough water, could be made to feed a whole family.

That last point matters more than any other, because it tells you what congee is. Before it was a delicacy, before it was a medicine, before it was a breakfast, congee was an act of arithmetic. It is the food of people who need to make a little go a long way. In years of famine, in the cold months before the harvest, in the lean spring when the granary was nearly empty, the thin rice porridge stretched a single cup of grain into a meal for six. In Chinese history, the phrase for a hard season could almost be measured by how thin the congee had become.

Chinese tradition, of course, prefers a grander origin. An old text from the Zhou era, preserved in a collection of ancient writings, credits the legendary Yellow Emperor himself, a figure somewhere between king and myth, with being the first person to steam grain into rice and to boil it into porridge. Historians treat this the way they treat most such stories: as a charming way of saying that congee is so old that nobody can remember a world without it. Which, in its own way, is the more impressive claim.

What we can say with more certainty is that by the Han dynasty, more than two thousand years ago, congee had moved from the poor man's pot into the physician's bag. The famous court doctor Chunyu Yi, whose case histories were recorded by the great historian Sima Qian, is described using a preparation of congee as part of his treatments. Think about how strange and wonderful that is. At a time when medicine was a swirl of herbs, needles and incantations, one of the remedies a doctor could reach for was simply a bowl of rice that had been cooked until soft. The logic was simple and, as it turns out, sound: when the body is weak, give it food that asks nothing of it. Congee is already half digested by the time it reaches the mouth.

That idea, congee as the gentlest food in the world, has never left. Ask almost anyone raised in a Chinese household what they ate the last time they were sick, and you will hear the same answer. A parent sat on the edge of the bed with a bowl of porridge and a spoon. It is one of the most universal acts of care in the entire culture, and it has been repeated, with variations, for centuries.

A WORD THAT TRAVELED THE WORLD

Here is a small puzzle that tells you how far this dish has wandered. The English word "congee" does not come from Chinese at all.

Chinese has its own words for the dish. In Mandarin it is zhou, in Cantonese it is jjuk, the sound that English speakers hear when they say "jook." But the word congee, most often traced by linguists to the Tamil word kanji, meaning rice water or the water in which rice has boiled, took a very different route. European traders and sailors met the dish on the coasts of southern India, borrowed the local word, and carried it with them as their ships moved east along the spice routes. By the 1600s it had appeared in English travel writing, attached to the rice porridge that sailors were served in ports from Malabar to Canton.

So when you say "congee," you are speaking a word with the whole monsoon trade wind in it. It is a word assembled from Tamil kitchens, Portuguese ships and English ledgers, used to describe a dish that is deeply and unmistakably Chinese. It is exactly the sort of linguistic accident that mirrors the dish itself: a humble, flexible thing that every culture it touched made its own.

And touched, it did. Rice porridge appears across Asia under a dozen names. In Japan it is okayu, served at the New Year in a ceremonial seven-herb version. In Korea it is juk, and in Vietnam, cháo. Thailand has jok, the Philippines has the Chinese-influenced arroz caldo and lugaw, and the Teochew communities of southern China and Southeast Asia have muay, a thin porridge served with a parade of small salty dishes.

THE MONASTERY AND THE MORNING BOWL

If the physicians gave congee its reputation as medicine, it was the monks who gave it a soul.

Buddhist monasteries spread across China in the centuries after the religion arrived from India, and with them came a way of eating built on simplicity, restraint and gratitude. Congee fit that philosophy perfectly. It was cheap, it was filling, it could be cooked in enormous quantities, and it asked for nothing but rice and water. In many monasteries, a bowl of porridge became the standard morning meal, and monks developed a kind of quiet devotion around it. Some old monastic teachings praise congee for ten virtues, among them that it gives strength, brings clarity, and settles the stomach. Whether or not you take the list literally, the sentiment is clear: this was food to be eaten slowly, with attention.

The most famous expression of that tradition is a festival still observed today. On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, in the dead of winter, Chinese households and temples cook Laba congee, a thick porridge studded with grains, beans, nuts and dried fruit. According to tradition, the day marks the moment the Buddha, weakened after years of severe fasting, accepted a bowl of rice porridge from a village girl and found the strength to sit beneath the bodhi tree and reach enlightenment. By the Song dynasty, the custom had spilled out of the temples and into ordinary life. Imperial palaces, wealthy families and neighborhood monasteries all handed out bowls of Laba congee to the hungry, and the porridge became a symbol of charity as much as of devotion. Eating it was a way of keeping warm in the coldest part of the year and of remembering that somebody, somewhere, was colder.

The scholars and poets noticed, too. In the Song dynasty, a literary age that was passionate about food, writers began to praise the humble bowl with surprising tenderness. The great poet Lu You, who lived to the astonishing age of eighty-five, wrote verses suggesting that a bowl of congee in the morning was the closest thing an ordinary man could find to an elixir of immortality. Another Song writer, Zhang Lei, composed a short essay arguing that an empty stomach in the early morning, filled with warm porridge, soothed the whole body in a way no medicine could. These were men who ate richly and traveled widely, and they still came back to the pot. That says something. Congee is the rare food that is loved equally by the poor, who rely on it, and by the wealthy, who could afford anything else.

And here is where our story begins to narrow toward the bowl in front of you. Because once congee became beloved, people began to do what people always do with a beloved blank canvas. They began to add things.

The earliest additions were practical: a few greens, a little ginger, a scrap of pork. But over the centuries, as trade routes expanded and Chinese regional cuisines grew more ambitious, congee became a stage. In the north, it stayed closer to its grain-and-bean origins. In the Yangtze delta, it picked up sweet and salty pickles. And in the far south, in the humid, seafood-rich province of Guangdong, it was transformed into something extraordinary.

THE EGG THAT WAITED

Now we meet the first of the toppings that make our bowl so distinctive, and it is perhaps the most surprising: an egg that was deliberately left to rot, or so it might seem, but was actually made immortal.

Before refrigerators, the problem of eggs was the problem of time. A hen, or in much of southern China a duck, lays far more eggs in the spring and summer than a household can eat. Those eggs spoil quickly in the heat. So Chinese cooks, over a thousand years ago, worked out a beautiful solution: salt.

Salting duck eggs is documented early. The Qimin Yaoshu, an agricultural encyclopedia compiled around the sixth century, describes methods of preserving eggs in brine, a technique that, with local variations, has barely changed since. You submerge whole duck eggs in a strong salt solution, or pack them in a paste of salt and clay or ash, and then you wait. Over several weeks, salt seeps slowly through the porous shell and begins to transform what is inside. The white becomes sharp and saline. And the yolk, the glorious part, does something remarkable: it firms, shrinks and releases its fat, turning from pale yellow into a deep orange-red, dense and sandy, glistening with its own golden oil.

Duck eggs are the perfect material for this because they are larger and richer than hen eggs, with a higher fat content in the yolk. The best-known salted eggs in China come from Gaoyou, a small city in Jiangsu province, surrounded by lakes and waterways where ducks have been raised for centuries. The eighteenth-century gourmet and writer Yuan Mei, who wrote one of the most famous cookbooks in Chinese history, praised the eggs of Gaoyou as the finest of all, noting that their yolks ran red and oily when cut open. In Gaoyou, salted eggs are tied to a festival too: during the Dragon Boat Festival in early summer, children traditionally wear little woven nets holding eggs around their necks, and the family eats them together at the table. An egg, a net and a child. It is hard to imagine a gentler image of food as love.

So how did a preserved egg end up in porridge? Almost certainly through necessity. Salted eggs are intensely salty, and plain rice is intensely bland. Put the two together and each solves the other's problem. A little bit of egg, mashed into hot porridge, seasons the entire bowl. In many Chinese households, plain congee with a salted egg and a few pickles was, for generations, the standard breakfast of ordinary working people. There was nothing glamorous about it. It was cheap, it kept for months, and it made a whole pot of nothing taste like something.

THE MUSHROOM FROM THE MOUNTAIN

The next ingredient comes from the mountains, and the story attached to it is one of the best in Chinese food history.

The mushroom in question is the shiitake, called xianggu, "fragrant mushroom," in Chinese, and donggu, "winter mushroom," when it is harvested in the cold months. Today it is one of the most widely eaten mushrooms on earth. But for centuries it was a wild forest treasure, gathered with luck and patience from fallen oak and chestnut logs.

According to local tradition in the mountains of Zhejiang province, around the Song dynasty, a man named Wu Sangong, a woodcutter or farmer from the Longquan area, was the first to figure out how to grow them on purpose. The story goes that he noticed mushrooms sprouting thickest on trees that had been struck, scarred or chopped with an axe. From this observation, he developed a method that villagers later called "cutting the flowers": he would slash the bark of felled logs, leave them in the damp shade, and wait for mushrooms to appear. Whether Wu Sangong was one man or a composite of generations of mountain farmers, the technique spread, and Zhejiang's hill villages grew prosperous on it. To this day, some of them hold ceremonies honoring his memory. It was among the earliest recorded forms of mushroom cultivation anywhere in the world.

The mushroom later became an obsession in Japan, where the name shiitake comes from shii, a type of oak the logs were cut from, and take, meaning mushroom. But in Chinese kitchens, the dried version is what has always mattered most. And there is a good reason for that.

When a shiitake is dried in the sun or in a low oven, something chemical and magical happens. The slow dehydration changes its flavor compounds, concentrating its aroma and, crucially, boosting a compound called guanylate, one of the molecules responsible for the savory taste known as umami. When you soak the dried mushroom back in water, you are left with two treasures: a chewy, meaty mushroom, and a dark, fragrant broth that cooks have always treated as liquid gold. Pour that soaking water into your congee and the whole pot deepens, as though someone had quietly turned up the volume on the rice.

This is not just folk wisdom. Modern food science has confirmed that umami compounds work in partnership. Glutamate, found abundantly in shrimp, seafood and many vegetables, and guanylate, found in dried mushrooms, do not simply add together. They multiply. Taste them together and the savory sensation is far stronger than either could produce alone. Chinese cooks had been exploiting that synergy for centuries before anybody had a name for it. Shrimp and shiitake in the same pot is not a coincidence. It is an old secret hiding in plain sight.

THE SHRIMP AND THE LUCKY SOUND

Which brings us to the shrimp, and to the place where our dish truly comes alive: the warm, wet, restless south.

Guangdong, the region around Canton, now called Guangzhou, sits at the mouth of the Pearl River, where fresh water meets the South China Sea. For thousands of years, it has been one of the greatest seafood kitchens on the planet. And the Cantonese, more than any other regional cuisine in China, are devoted to freshness. A fish should still be alive when it reaches the table. A shrimp should be so fresh that it snaps between the teeth.

There is also a linguistic joke that gives shrimp a special place in Cantonese culture. The Cantonese word for shrimp, ha, sounds like the sound of laughter, "ha ha." Shrimp therefore appears at celebrations, weddings and the Lunar New Year, as a sort of edible wish for a happy life. A dish of shrimp is a dish of laughter.

Shrimp also happens to be among the best foods in the world for congee. The reason is partly texture. Raw shrimp dropped into a pot of piping hot porridge cook in a minute or two, staying tender and sweet, in a sharp contrast to the soft, yielding rice around them. But the reason is also flavor. Shrimp heads and shells are packed with savory compounds, and cooks who understand this know to simmer them first, or fry them in a little oil until they glow orange and fragrant, before straining them out. That orange oil, stained by the shell's natural pigment, can be stirred into the congee, carrying the entire taste of the sea into every spoonful.

THE BOAT PEOPLE AND THE BIRTH OF THE LUXURY BOWL

So now all the ingredients are on the table: rice from the river valleys, eggs from the duck ponds, mushrooms from the mountains, shrimp from the sea. But how did they come together? Here the trail becomes less certain, and I will be honest with you: there is no document that says "On this date, in this kitchen, shrimp congee with salted egg and mushrooms was invented." Dishes like this are almost never born in a single moment. They accrete. They are assembled by thousands of cooks who each add one ingredient they happen to love, until one day the combination feels so natural that nobody can imagine it any other way.

But we can trace the atmosphere in which this kind of bowl became possible, and it is a fascinating one.

Along the Pearl River and in the harbors of southern China lived communities of boat dwellers, often called the Tanka, who spent their entire lives on the water. They fished, they traded, they raised their children on the decks of small wooden boats, and they cooked on tiny stoves wedged between nets and baskets. According to widely repeated tradition, the famous sampan congee of Guangzhou, a porridge cooked with fish slices, squid, peanuts, crisp fried dough and scallions, was born in this world. Floating vendors would row their little boats alongside larger pleasure boats and sell steaming bowls of porridge to the people on board. It was food for night owls and travelers, quick, hot and generously seafooded.

This is the cultural setting for our dish. Cantonese congee grew into something very different from the plain porridge of the north. It became silky and thick, almost creamy, with the rice grains cooked until they completely dissolved. And it became a vehicle for seafood, dried delicacies and cured ingredients, a bowl you could dress up or down depending on who was eating.

FROM HONG KONG TO SINGAPORE: THE BOWL GOES GLOBAL

In the twentieth century, the Cantonese congee tradition crossed borders with the people who loved it. After the upheavals of war and revolution, waves of migrants left southern China for Hong Kong, Southeast Asia and eventually each continent. They carried few possessions, but they carried recipes, and congee was the first thing they rebuilt.

In Hong Kong, congee shops became part of the city's rhythm. Some stayed open all night, feeding taxi drivers, shift workers and revelers. A good congee master was a respected craftsman: he cooked the rice base for hours, often longer than you would believe, until every grain collapsed into a smooth, glossy cream. The toppings were then added to order, never cooked in advance, so that each bowl arrived with its own freshness. Fish, beef, pork liver, century egg with lean pork, shrimp, scallops, mushrooms: the menu on the wall could run to dozens of choices, but the ritual was the same. A bowl of congee was ordered, a long fried dough stick arrived alongside it, and the world slowed down for a few minutes.

Meanwhile, in Singapore, Malaysia and the other Chinese communities of Southeast Asia, the dish was taking its own path. Teochew families served plain, watery rice porridge with a table full of side dishes, and salted duck egg was nearly always among them, along with preserved radish, braised peanuts, steamed fish and stir-fried greens. Here the salted egg kept its role as the great seasoner. But the region's cooks were also beginning to experiment with the yolk alone.

In the 2010s, Singapore and Malaysia fell in love with salted egg yolk in a way that surprised even the locals. Salted egg yolk prawns, a dish in which shrimp are fried until crisp and then tossed in a sandy, buttery, curry-leaf-scented sauce made from crushed cooked yolks, had been a staple of local seafood restaurants for years. Suddenly, the flavor was everywhere: on potato chips, fish skins, croissants, even ice cream. The reason is simple and delicious. A cooked salted yolk offers saltiness, richness, sweetness, and a faint toasted, almost cheesy depth all at once. It is an umami bomb with a grainy, melting texture. And when it meets shrimp, the two foods, one from the sea and one from the pond, recognize each other like old friends.

This is the modern context in which shrimp congee with salted egg and mushrooms makes the most sense. It is a dish that sits at the crossroads of every tradition we have walked through. It has the thick, soothing Cantonese porridge. It has the Teochew devotion to salted egg. It has the monk-and-scholar reverence for a humble morning bowl. It has the mountain mushroom, the sea shrimp, the duck-pond yolk. And it has a new generation of cooks, in home kitchens from Guangzhou to Toronto, who understand that a good dish does not need an inventor. It needs only to be loved by enough people for long enough.

WHAT HAPPENS INSIDE THE POT

Before we finish, it is worth understanding why this combination works so well, because the story is not only cultural. It is also physical.

When rice is cooked in a large amount of water, usually eight to ten times its volume for a proper congee, the grains absorb liquid and swell. As the temperature climbs past about 60 or 70 degrees Celsius, the starch granules inside begin to gelatinize: they take in water, burst, and release long, tangled starch molecules into the surrounding liquid. The longer you cook and the more you stir, the more starch escapes, and the thicker and creamier the porridge becomes. This is why great congee cooks are patient, and why many of them swear by small tricks: soaking the rice first, rubbing it with a little oil and salt, or even freezing the grains overnight so that the ice cracks them and they bloom faster in the pot.

Into this silky base go the other ingredients, each at precisely the right moment. The mushrooms and their soaking liquid go in early, so their flavor has time to spread. The shrimp go in last, for only a minute or two, so they stay sweet and tender. And the salted egg, mashed or crumbled, goes in at the end or on top, where its fat melts into the heat and sends ribbons of gold through the white. A shower of scallions, a few threads of ginger, a drizzle of sesame oil or a crack of white pepper finishes the bowl.

The result is a dish with nearly every dimension of taste and texture. There is sweetness from the shrimp, savoriness from the mushrooms, saltiness and richness from the egg, and the clean, quiet backdrop of the rice. There is softness, there is bite, there is a sandy crumble and a silken pour. It is complex, and yet when you eat it, it feels like nothing at all. It feels like being taken care of.

THE LAST SPOONFUL

There is a reason this dish endures when so many fashionable ones disappear. Congee is not trying to impress anyone. It is a kind of promise: that whatever kind of day you have had, there is a pot somewhere that is warm, and that someone has been patient enough to let it become soft.

Think of everything that has gone into your bowl. The rice grown in terraced paddies, whose ancestors were planted in the Yangtze valley when the pyramids were still unbuilt. The duck egg that sat in brine for weeks while salt did its slow, silent work. The mushroom that a mountain farmer in Zhejiang learned to coax from a wounded log. The shrimp that came from a sea whose Cantonese name for it sounds like laughter. The monks who ate porridge at dawn, the poets who praised it, the sick who were saved by it, the migrants who rebuilt their lives around it. Every single one of them is in the spoon.

So the next time you stand over a pot of rice that is boiling far longer than any teacher would advise, stirring gently as the grains dissolve and the kitchen fills with the smell of mushrooms and the sea, remember that you are not breaking a rule. You are keeping one, perhaps the oldest one there is: that the simplest food, cooked with care and shared with someone, is the closest thing to magic that most of us will ever make.

Make the congee. Crack the egg. Watch the gold spread. And eat it slowly.
