📷 FROM THE DESK OF SISTER MARY CATHERINE
EDITORIAL: THE LORD WORKS IN MYSTERIOUS WAYS, BUT SOMETIMES HE MAKES HIMSELF PERFECTLY CLEAR.

📷 Convent of Our Lady of Perpetual Exasperation | Bureau of Divine Intervention & Political Repentance | 3:47 AM

My dear children,

I have spent sixty-three years in the service of the Lord, and in that time I have witnessed enough foolishness to fill the Vatican Library twice over.

I have survived seven popes, twelve parish priests, four bishops, three renovations of the convent kitchen, and one particularly unfortunate incident involving Father O'Malley, the altar wine, and the Easter Vigil.

But nothing, and I mean NOTHING, prepared me for the spectacle of American politics this past week.

For the first time in history, we have a pope who has actually participated in an American election before ascending to the Chair of Saint Peter.

And what happens?

The Republican Party suffers an electoral calamity of biblical proportions.

Now, I am not suggesting that His Holiness personally arranged the results. The Church has very strict rules about attributing miracles, and frankly, the Vatican has enough paperwork without opening an investigation into the disappearance of Republican congressional seats.

But I am suggesting that when the Almighty sends a message, it might behoove certain people to put down their golden idols and listen.

For years, I have watched politicians wrap themselves in Christianity while treating the teachings of Jesus Christ like optional reading material.

They quote Scripture when convenient, ignore it when expensive, and invoke the Lord's name whenever a camera is within twenty feet.

They proclaim themselves defenders of Christian values while demonstrating a remarkable inability to remember what those values actually are.

Blessed are the poor?

Apparently, only if they can provide proof of employment and a valid photo ID.

Love thy neighbor?

Terms and conditions apply.

Welcome the stranger?

Certainly, provided the stranger has completed the appropriate immigration paperwork and doesn't require medical attention.

Thou shalt not bear false witness?

My children, if I enforced that commandment on modern political television, I would wear my ruler down to a toothpick before the first commercial break.

And then came election night.

As the returns rolled in, I watched certain television personalities stare at their electoral maps with expressions normally reserved for discovering that the parish bingo money had been stolen.

Texas was causing palpitations. Kansas was raising blood pressure. And Fox News appeared to be approaching the theological equivalent of the Seven 
Stages of Grief, occasionally managing three simultaneously.

At one point, I turned to Sister Agnes and said, "My dear, I haven't seen that many frightened Republicans since someone suggested taxing church-owned private jets."

She laughed so hard her dentures landed in the holy water.

But I digress.

The lesson here is not that God is a Democrat.

God is not registered with either political party, despite what certain televangelists would have you believe.

The lesson is that Christianity is not a campaign accessory, the Bible is not a political prop, and faith is not something one wears on Sunday before discarding it on Monday.

If you insist upon claiming divine endorsement for every political ambition, you must be prepared for the possibility that Heaven may eventually request a change in management.

And to those declaring that these results represent some terrible punishment from above, I offer a simple theological observation:

Perhaps it was not divine punishment.

Perhaps it was divine performance evaluation.

After all, even the Lord must occasionally look down upon His creation and wonder why the people shouting His name the loudest seem to have read so little of His work.

Now, if you'll excuse me, I have morning prayers to attend, a chapel to prepare, and Sister Agnes to retrieve from the confessional, where she has been laughing uncontrollably since Tuesday.

May the Lord bless you, keep you, and grant you the wisdom to distinguish between the Sermon on the Mount and a campaign rally at Mar-a-Lago.

And remember, my children:

The Lord giveth, the Lord taketh away, and apparently, every now and then, the Lord checks the electoral map.

In Christ's service, with a rosary in one hand and a ruler in the other,

Sister Mary Catherine
Convent of Our Lady of Perpetual Exasperation

Unofficial White House Disinformation Desk

text:
I’m Rachel, twenty-seven years old, and I teach literature at Horizon Prep, a private middle school in Seattle.

I genuinely enjoy my career. Seventh graders can be unpredictable bundles of teenage emotions, but watching them discover a passion for reading makes the difficult days worthwhile.

Five years earlier, shortly after graduating from college, Mom offered me an arrangement that seemed almost too generous to refuse.

“Rachel, remember Aunt Margaret’s apartment?” she asked one evening while preparing tea.

We were standing in the kitchen Aunt Margaret had also left to Mom in her will.

Of course I remembered the apartment.

I’d spent countless childhood afternoons there, listening to Aunt Margaret reminisce about the theatrical community she’d once belonged to.

Her place occupied an old brick building downtown. It had two bedrooms, unusually high ceilings, and large windows overlooking a peaceful courtyard.

Even better, Horizon Prep was just a ten-minute walk away.

Mom proposed renting it to me rather than finding an unfamiliar tenant.

She would charge $1,000 monthly instead of the usual $1,500 because I was her daughter.

For an apartment in central Seattle, that sounded extraordinary.

I accepted immediately.

For the following five years, I paid Mom every month while comparable homes in the neighborhood rented for at least $500 more.

But I did much more than occupy the apartment.

I invested my savings, time, and energy into transforming it into a beautiful home.

One room at a time, I replaced outdated features and made improvements.

I installed genuine hardwood flooring instead of laminate, repainted every wall, and upgraded the plumbing.

I purchased the furnishings gradually, saving between paychecks.

Eventually, my home contained a large leather sectional, a substantial wooden dining table, a king-size bed with a memory-foam mattress, and an enormous television for movie nights.

Every purchase represented money I’d personally earned.

Mom visited every couple of months to inspect her property, as she liked to describe it.

She would admire the improvements, occasionally running her hand across the kitchen’s quartz countertop.

“You’re a magician,” she’d sigh. “Aunt Margaret would be so happy to see this place now.”

Her approval meant something to me then.

I’d spent enough on renovations and furniture to purchase a respectable secondhand car, but I considered the investment worthwhile.

This apartment was my sanctuary after exhausting days teaching adolescents.

There was only one continuing source of trouble in my otherwise comfortable life.

My younger sister, Kayla.

At twenty-three, she still lived with our parents.

Mom described her as someone who was finding her direction in life.

In reality, Kayla generally slept until noon, spent hours scrolling through social media, and avoided employment whenever possible.

I loved my sister, but I’d already rescued her financially far too often.

When she exhausted her credit card buying clothes, I cleared the balance.

When she decided she desperately needed a girls’ vacation in Miami, I supplied the money.

The previous year, she spent weeks complaining about her outdated phone.

“Ra, please,” she begged. “Everyone has the 14 Pro, and I’m walking around like a loser with my old one.”

The replacement cost $1,400.

Seeing how delighted she was when I gave it to her, I convinced myself the expense had been justified.

Recently, however, our Sunday family dinners had become increasingly uncomfortable.

During one meal, Kayla complained while pushing her salad around her plate.

“I’m so sick of mom and dad treating me like a child,” she announced. “I’m 23. I want my own place.”

“Then get a job and move out,” I suggested without intending any insult.

“It’s not that simple. You don’t understand,” she replied irritably.

Dad cleared his throat awkwardly.

text:
The Musée d'Orsay in Paris is currently hosting an important exhibition dedicated to Mary Cassatt, the American artist who became part of the Impressionist movement. Despite her significance, France's national museums had never previously devoted such a major exhibition to her. Visitors can discover her work until January 31, 2027.

Born near Pittsburgh in 1844, Cassatt moved to Paris as a young woman with the ambition of becoming a professional painter, a path that remained difficult for most women at the time. Edgar Degas eventually invited her to exhibit alongside the Impressionists, making her the group's only American woman. She spent most of her life in France, where she died in 1926, exactly a century ago.

Titled "Mary Cassatt. The Independent," the exhibition reflects the spirit of a woman who lived on her own terms. She never married, supported herself through her artwork, and made independent choices in a society largely dominated by men. Almost 80 works are featured, including paintings, pastels and prints. Among them are her celebrated portraits of mothers and children, as well as prints influenced by Japanese art.

The final gallery explores Cassatt's involvement in the women's suffrage movement. In 1915, her paintings were included in a New York exhibition organised to raise funds for women's right to vote.

Beyond her own artistic achievements, Cassatt also encouraged American collectors to purchase Impressionist masterpieces. Many of the works acquired through her recommendations eventually found their way into museums such as New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art, where visitors can admire them today.

The Musée d'Orsay occupies a former railway station on Paris's Left Bank, directly across the Seine from the Louvre. The museum closes on Mondays but offers extended opening hours on Thursday evenings.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On the morning of November 11, 1864, the engines of destruction began to turn in Atlanta. The city that had once pulsed as the Confederacy’s great inland arsenal now lay under the hard hand of William Tecumseh Sherman. Captured two months earlier after a brutal summer of maneuver and battle, Atlanta was no longer a prize to be held. It was an asset to be erased.

Sherman had already ordered the civilian population out. Now Captain Orlando Poe, his chief engineer, set the engineers and pioneers to work with cold precision. Railroads that had fed the armies of Lee and Hood were torn from the earth; the iron rails were heated over burning ties and twisted into the grotesque shapes that would forever be known as Sherman’s neckties. Foundries, machine shops, car sheds, and warehouses were battered down or prepared for the torch. The order was clear: nothing that could again serve the Confederate cause was to remain. Fire was to be held back until the last moment, lest the flames leap the bounds of military necessity. But the bounds did not hold.

By nightfall the first unauthorized fires were already flickering. Soldiers who had lived for months on hardtack and the edge of the bayonet began to light private homes and commercial blocks that had never appeared on Poe’s maps. Officers posted guards at the churches and offered rewards for the arrest of arsonists, yet the discipline that had carried the army through the Atlanta campaign was fraying in the emptied streets. Over the next four days the controlled wrecking and the uncontrolled burning ran together. When Sherman’s columns finally stepped off on the fifteenth, nearly forty percent of the city—its industrial heart and much of its commercial core—lay in smoking ruin. Behind them rose the black pall that Sherman himself would later recall hanging over the shattered town.

This was not the accident of battle. It was the deliberate opening stroke of a new kind of war. Sherman meant to make Georgia howl, to strip the Confederacy of its remaining capacity to feed, arm, and move its armies, and to break the will of a people who had already endured three years of invasion. The March to the Sea that followed would carry the same logic two hundred and eighty-five miles to Savannah: live off the land, destroy what cannot be carried, and leave the civilian population to taste the cost of continued resistance. Atlanta’s ruin was the proof that the Union would no longer fight only armies; it would fight the society that sustained them.

In the long memory of the South the day remains a scar. In the North it was celebrated as the necessary hammer that helped end the bloodiest war in American history. Both judgments contain their portion of truth. What cannot be denied is the scale and the method. On November 11 the systematic dismantling of a Confederate city began in earnest, and the age of hard war arrived with it.

text:
ICYMI O/N — November 11th, 2026

MACRO:

Anthropic’s bankers expect to raise its IPO price above the filed $70–78 range after strong demand, potentially valuing it at $1.5tn or more and lifting proceeds above $100bn (including $26bn cornerstone investment), people familiar told the FT. (FT)

OpenAI grew revenue by roughly 50% to $10 billion from the second to the third quarter, but continued to report heavy operating losses, showing mixed results in its effort to catch up with industry leader Anthropic. (WSJ)

OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar called it a “blockbuster” quarter. Said OpenAI’s enterprise business doubled q/q and now accounts for half of revenue. Consumer revenue grew 20%. Said wider distribution through third-party cloud providers could be a significant 2027 tailwind. (Yahoo Finance)

Politico reports citing lawmakers, congressional aides and lobbyists close to the debate, the revelation that Jensen Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy has significantly raised the chances that Congress will enact chip export limits this year as part of a must-pass defense package, known as the National Defense Authorization Act. (Politico)

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang should resign, Republican Senator Kevin Cramer told Politico, citing what he characterised as potential blackmail exposure. (RTRS)

Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence agent was flagged to Lutnick in a classified warning before Trump’s May China visit, Axios reported. (Axios)

Nvidia H200 chips reached China’s blacklisted Northwestern Polytechnical University through a local supplier, Reuters found. The university bought two chips for CNY874,700 in October; the investigation does not establish a direct sale by Nvidia. (RTRS)

Democratic Senator Michael Bennet has written to the State, Commerce and Justice departments asking for an update on its probe into Megaspeed, Semafor reports, citing a letter it has seen. Asked for the departments to consider “specific punitive measures against Megaspeed”. (Semafor)

US ambassador David Perdue described relations with China as “bumpy” following the Nvidia controversy, stressing that economic and national security are intertwined. He also said US companies have waited months for important Chinese rare-earth shipments. (BBG)

Banks are increasingly using credit insurance to hedge AI infrastructure and data center loan risks and stretch internal lending limits, the FT reported, citing sources. Insurers are charging annual premiums equivalent to 50–70% of banks’ potential earnings on the insured portion of data-centre loans. (FT)

Global equity hedge funds have cut risk at the fastest pace in more than a decade, Morgan Stanley prime brokers said in a Tuesday note. Long-short funds’ gross market value has fallen 10.7% since late June; US net leverage dropped five percentage points to 42% in one session. (BBG)

Treasury yields could face further near-term upward pressure, Capital Economics said in a fresh note. It expects a reversal if the equity rebound fails, but sees less scope for Fed easing after an AI bust than after the dotcom crash. (WSJ)

The dollar’s growing dependence on equity inflows could encourage foreign investors to increase currency hedges, Deutsche Bank strategists warned. A weakening tendency for the dollar to offset US stock losses is reducing the benefit of leaving those holdings unhedged. (BBG)

Bessent said Washington and Beijing are establishing a channel to flag serious AI incidents and exchanging practices for evaluating models before release. His prepared remarks detailed implementation of the AI dialogue announced earlier, rather than a new overarching agreement. (US Treasury)

Speaker Mike Johnson backed tighter AI-chip export controls in the year-end defence bill, adding support for congressional licence reviews and tracking requirements to deter smuggling. These remain legislative proposals. (Politico)

Fed’s Goolsbee called October CPI “borderline disturbing” in a PBS interview and said inflation is moving in the wrong direction. Asked about a larger rate increase, he declined to restrict the Fed’s options before its meeting. (BBG)

Fed’s Paulson backed further gradual rate increases, saying she would accelerate if inflation expectations, wages or underlying inflation strengthened. “Right now, that’s not what I’m seeing,” she said at Tuesday evening’s event. (WSJ)

Goldman Sachs added a March 2027 Fed hike to its forecast following the hot CPI report. David Mericle’s team still expects a 25bp December increase, followed by another 25bps in March. (BBG)

Deutsche Bank’s Matthew Luzzetti now expects quarter-point increases at each of the Fed’s next three meetings, he told WSJ. He considers larger moves more likely only if officials decide substantially more tightening is necessary. (WSJ)

Incoming Senate Appropriations chair Patty Murray wants a short-term funding extension into January, giving Democrats control over full-year spending negotiations. She said Democrats are considering using December’s funding deadline to end the Iran war. (Politico)

Amid a wave of high-level departures from the Department of Justice, a senior political official on Monday warned U.S. attorneys across the country to either get on a “wartime footing” for President Donald Trump’s final two years or consider leaving, according to sources cited by MS NOW. (MS NOW)

Trump’s Russian-diesel import initiative has produced no new US deliveries, WSJ reports. Four originally US-bound tankers changed course or discharge plans; executives cited buyer reluctance over legal, sanctions and reputational risks. (WSJ)

API reported a 9m-barrel increase in US crude stocks and a 1.5m-barrel rise in distillates last week, according to Bloomberg. Official inventory data is due Thursday. (BBG)

Developing economies face an 800m jobs shortfall over the next 15 years, World Bank president Ajay Banga said at COP31. About 1.2bn people will reach adulthood, against approximately 400m expected new jobs. (BBG)

Japanese manufacturers' sentiment rose to its strongest level in more than five years in November as booming semiconductor demand underpinned broad-based optimism, while the non-manufacturers' mood hit its highest in over eight years, a Reuters monthly poll showed. (RTRS)

Private-sector members of the Japanese government's top economic panel said on Wednesday that hitting the central bank's 2% inflation target is not an end in itself, stressing that higher incomes and productivity were needed for a lasting exit from deflation. (RTRS)

The PBOC surveyed lenders about a possible 25% tax on government-bond interest income, people familiar said. No decision or implementation timetable is established; 30-year bond futures fell as much as 0.47% after Bloomberg’s report. (BBG)

US ambassador David Perdue said China is using its anti-foreign-sanctions regulation, State Decree 835, against two European companies and their employees. He called it the most onerous escalation he has encountered during his decades working in the region. (BBG)

China's copper fabricators are operating on a hand-to-mouth basis due to a surge in domestic prices, only buying raw material after securing an order for a finished product. (BBG)

South Korea’s competition regulator imposed a record 1.63tn won ($1.2bn) fine on banks and brokerages for collusion in sovereign-bond auctions. KB Securities received the largest penalty, at 332.2bn won. (BBG)

South Korea’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate fell to 2.5% from 2.6% in October, matching its lowest since May 2023. Employment declined by 50,000 month-on-month, with the lower jobless rate largely reflecting people leaving the workforce. (BBG)

Australian new home-loan values fell a record 15.5% in Q3, almost twice the expected decline. Investor lending dropped 32.3% and first-home-buyer owner-occupier lending fell 8%. (BBG)

New Zealand's NIESR said Bank Rate should reach about 5% next year and forecast inflation peaking at 4.4% in February. Under a 4.25% rate path, it warned inflation could remain above target until 2030. (WSJ, BBG)

RBC BlueBay’s head of market strategy argues in the FT that eventual UK rate cuts may need to be unusually deep and rapid. Fixed-rate mortgages could delay relief to borrowers while savers’ interest income falls immediately, weakening the effect of modest cuts. (FT)

The Bank of England will not succeed in returning inflation to target before 2030, driven by second-round effects on wages caused by the Iran war, according to forecasts from a leading academic think-tank which also nudged up its outlook for growth. (RTRS)

German economic growth will accelerate this quarter as Europe's largest economy recovers faster than expected, even if deep structural challenges continue to hold it back, Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel said on Wednesday. (RTRS)

Brussels plans to propose rules targeting addictive online design, manipulative sales techniques and influencer marketing. The draft Digital Fairness Act would permit fines of up to 6% of worldwide annual turnover and requires approval by EU governments and Parliament. (FT)

Vanguard’s Ales Koutny warned that weak growth, high spending and rising financing costs were putting France and Belgium on course for deficits approaching 6% of GDP. Bond managers told the FT that fiscal concerns increasingly distinguish these borrowers from other eurozone sovereigns. (FT)

Higher German drug prices would increase costs in both Germany and the US, a study commissioned by Germany’s statutory health insurers concluded. A hypothetical 25% increase would add roughly €5.5bn to German spending and reduce projected annual Medicaid savings by about $300m. (BBG)

Spain’s main unions began a nationwide housing strike ahead of the November 29 election, with disruption expected across the country. Pickets formed at bus stations Wednesday, while Cadena Ser reported police clashes at Madrid’s wholesale food market. (BBG)

Lula’s economic team is preparing a fiscal package for Congress as soon as next week, people familiar said. Spending restraints under discussion could produce a 50bn–60bn real adjustment in 2027 relative to this year’s budget. (BBG)

Broad-based economic growth and resilience to the energy supply shock from the Iran war prompted credit rating agency Moody's to raise its India growth forecast to 7% from 6.5% for the fiscal year ending March 2027. (RTRS)

India’s wind industry is discussing a plan with governments to upgrade about 8GW of older turbines, potentially lifting capacity at those sites by almost 50%. The proposal would increase output without requiring additional land, the manufacturers’ association told Bloomberg. (BBG)

IRAN:

Iran will not remove “a single atom” of enriched nuclear material from country, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaee said in an interview with Al Mayadeen. Said Iran has informed Russia that its enriched material will remain in the country and be used for domestic purposes. Also warned any US attack would trigger strikes on US military bases, including those far away. (BBG)

Rubio told G7 ministers Trump had chosen sustained economic pressure and the naval blockade over renewed major strikes or a deal on Iran’s current terms, according to three attendees. Rubio said the pressure has “no end date,” Axios reported. (Axios)

Araghchi rejected Rubio’s argument that economic hardship would eventually force Iran to change course, describing US policy as driven by delusions. (Araghchi)

Turkey, Iraq and Pakistan fear US demands to stop business with Iran—including halting flights or closing borders—could destabilise their countries, a US official told Axios. (Axios)

Qatar’s prime minister told G7 ministers he wants China and European countries to guarantee a potential US–Iran deal, to address Tehran’s fear that Washington could resume the war, Axios reported. (Axios)

Trump offered to replace some of China’s Iranian oil purchases with US crude, ambassador David Perdue told Bloomberg Television. (BBG)

Treasury Secretary Bessent moved from his Washington-area home to a military base amid Iranian threats, the New York Times reported. The report notes US intelligence indicates that Iran’s hard-line leadership is determined to hold on to power at nearly any cost, which suggests economic pain alone may not lead to regime change. (NYT)

In a letter dated Tuesday and reported overnight, Iran’s FM Araghchi asked the UN and IAEA to condemn the US offer of up to $20m for information on Iran’s nuclear programme. He warned it could endanger scientists and undermine safeguards. (Mehr)

The House voted 211–204 to refer Hegseth’s impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee, blocking an immediate vote on the charges. Massie was the sole Republican opposing referral; 11 Democrats did not vote. (House Clerk, FT)

Hakeem Jeffries said he would discuss another Hegseth impeachment effort with Democrats in the next Congress after Tuesday’s procedural defeat. (Hugo Lowell)

Massie said he had no plans to reintroduce his Hegseth impeachment articles. Separately, Massie said he would try to force another war-powers vote before leaving Congress. (WSJ, Avani Kalra)

Iran’s hardline Kayhan newspaper called for threatening US bases in Germany, Britain, Albania, Greece and Cyprus with missiles. This was a newspaper editorial, not an announced military operation. (Iran International)

GEOPOLITICAL:

Russian, Ukrainian and US officials began a second day of peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, resuming meetings which Kyiv and Washington depicted on Monday as constructive but produced no early signs of a breakthrough. (RTRS)

Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia issued overnight drone alerts that were subsequently withdrawn, with NATO fighters activated. Lithuania reported an attempted interception, but whether the drone was hit remained unclear. (RTRS)

Finland imposed temporary aviation and maritime restrictions in the eastern Gulf of Finland as a precaution against possible drones. Reuters reported that the restrictions were later withdrawn. (Finnish Defence Forces, RTRS)

Zelensky said Russian negotiators were presenting an inaccurate picture of their territorial gains in Abu Dhabi, while the US side backed Ukraine’s battlefield assessment. He renewed his call for talks at leaders’ level. (Zelensky)

France is pressing Germany to align its long-range missile doctrine with French nuclear strategy, fearing conventional strikes could inadvertently provoke a nuclear response. A senior German official said Berlin supported a shared escalation framework and that talks were gaining momentum. (FT)

Britain and Germany are discussing whether France could join their programme to develop weapons with ranges exceeding 2,000km, a senior British official told the FT. (FT)

US' Perdue denied that a $14bn US weapons package for Taiwan had been delayed. He said nothing was being held up and that Trump controls the timing and composition of arms sales. (BBG)

EQUITIES:

Coreweave (+12%) squeezing higher after forecast beating figures/guidance and bullish commentary on compute pricing, it also firmed up its capex guide (after the IREN cut). But crucially it provided investors with a funding roadpath. Now its shut out of unsecured debt markets it is now leaning heavily on customer prepayments, secured funding (it expects to secure a new facility shortly), and "parent level" capital raises (share issuance). (CoreWeave)

GE Vernova said SoftBank’s turbine-order changes had “no negative or positive impact” on its business, responding to WSJ’s reporting on the cancellations. The report notes Softbank "opted to cancel its excess reservations" after ordering an excess for its Ohio plant and data centre. (WSJ)

SoftBank Group had reserved well over 13GW of turbines, largely from GE Vernova, before cancelling excess reservations and unwinding some more advanced orders, people familiar told WSJ. These are new details behind its previously disclosed equipment charges. (WSJ)

Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez said the company faces a daily fight to secure computing capacity, pushing back against concerns about AI overbuilding. He told Bloomberg in Tokyo that more energy, facilities and chips are needed to relieve supply shortages. (BBG)

JPMorgan Chase considered buying credit insurance against lending exposure in recent weeks but decided against it, people familiar with the discussions told the FT. (FT)

Rigetti Computing (-1%) reported Q3 revenue of $1.4mn (exp. 3.5mln), operating profit -33.2mln (exp. -29.1mln) and $497.1mn of cash and investments, with no debt. Its approximately $20mn FY26 revenue outlook depends on Q4 acceptance and recognition of the $8.4mn Indian C-DAC contract. (Rigetti, Barron’s/Dow Jones)

Barrick Mining filed to list a minority stake in American Barrick Gold on the NYSE, covering its North American gold assets. The filing proposes a $1.25bn base annual dividend and shareholder returns from proceeds; offering size and pricing remain unspecified. (SEC filing, WSJ)

Nintendo said its Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time sold more than 5.2mn copies in four days, including 810,000 in Japan—its strongest four-day Switch 2 launch. (Nintendo)

Nissan reported a quarterly net loss of ¥43.5bn versus ¥15.57bn profit expected; operating profit of ¥2.12bn missed ¥49.3bn consensus. It cut annual vehicle-sales guidance to 2.97–3.00mn from 3.15mn while retaining its ¥20bn net-profit forecast. (WSJ, BBG)

China's memory player Yangtze Memory Technologies is targeting a Shanghai Star-board IPO as soon as Q1 2027, people familiar said, countering last week’s report that the flotation was on hold. The previously planned fundraising was 33bn yuan ($4.9bn). (BBG)

Samsung Display and LG Display plan to raise monitor OLED panel prices and have reduced their original 2027 shipment targets, according to Sigmaintell research reported by The Elec. Higher material costs are the cited pressure; these are reported plans rather than company-announced price increases. (The Elec)

SK Hynix secured industrial functional-safety certification for LPDDR5X and certification of its automotive cybersecurity management process. The company said the approvals support expansion into robotics, edge AI, smart factories and autonomous vehicles. (SK Hynix)

TSMC executive Kevin Zhang said AI computing demand had grown “parabolically” over nine months. Speaking at a Nikkei forum in Tokyo, he highlighted power and substrate constraints alongside chip supply. (Commercial Times / CNA, WSJ)

Taylor Wimpey expects annual operating profit at the bottom of its £262m–£299m range, with approximately 10,500 completions excluding joint ventures. Higher mortgage rates and living costs have weakened autumn trading, while its forward order book fell year-on-year. (BBG)

Barclays recently bought credit insurance to hedge AI infrastructure loans, the FT newly reported, citing a person familiar with its programme. HSBC has also explored using credit insurance to manage its AI infrastructure lending exposure. (FT)

Siemens Energy AG said profit margins will swell to as much as 22% by 2030, driven by booming demand for gas turbines and power-grid equipment that more than doubled earnings last year. (Siemens Energy, WSJ, BBG)

ABN Amro lifted annual commercial net-interest-income guidance above €6.9bn from €6.8bn after quarterly profit rose about 52%. Higher rates and the NIBC acquisition supported income; annual cost guidance remains approximately €5.5bn. (BBG)

E.ON reaffirmed annual guidance after quarterly adjusted net profit of €278mn beat €268mn expected. It retained planned annual investment of €8.7bn and adjusted EBITDA guidance of €9.4–9.6bn. (WSJ)

Volkswagen’s namesake brand reported record Chinese EV and hybrid deliveries of more than 28,000 in October, up 350% year-on-year. It expects continued growth and aims to become one of China’s top 10 new-energy-vehicle brands next year. (BBG)

US ambassador Andrew Puzder will meet European Investment Bank president Nadia Calviño this week as Washington presses for details of its €3bn Airbus loan. Brussels maintains that the financing complies with the transatlantic trade agreement. (FT)

AkzoNobel and Axalta Coating Systems face an in-depth UK Phase 2 investigation unless they offer undertakings addressing the CMA’s competition concerns. The warning adds regulatory risk to their proposed $25bn merger. (WSJ)

Petrobras earnings missed estimates in the third-quarter despite record oil and gas production and a favorable backdrop of high crude prices and strong refining margins. It raised 2026 capital-expenditure guidance to $24bn–$25.5bn from $19.4bn. (BBG)

[...]
These plans may seem fantastical, but to historian and sociologist of science M. Susan Lindee of the University of Pennsylvania, the CIA’s assassination schemes read less like spy fantasy and rather more like a familiar product of Cold War America. The inspector general’s report, she suggests, offers a bleak window into a political culture shaped by intense patriotism and a belief that the stakes were existential. “For many experts, helping the United States defeat ‘godless communism’ was a patriotic duty,” Lindee says. “The stakes seemed so high.”
The premise, Lindee notes, was blunt: only one superpower would survive.
That outlook fits what University of Minnesota Twin Cities historian Elaine Tyler May calls the post–World War II “era of the expert.” Allied victory in World War II—and the atomic bomb that ended it—had elevated scientific authority into a source of national legitimacy. Scientific expertise promised security, power, and modernity—part and parcel of the American way of life. In that climate, technical solutions to political problems often appeared rational and forward looking rather than alarming. Officials increasingly viewed geopolitical threats as problems that could be managed through scientific means.

🇨🇳 Northwestern Polytechnical University — an institution with deep ties to the PLA — bought two Nvidia H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an Oct 21 procurement record on its website.

Northwestern is a member of the "Seven Sons of National Defense" group of Chinese universities under US sanctions and ⁠with a history of conducting defense-related research for Beijing.

The chips were purchased for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia.

Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five contracts for rented computing capacity from Chinese companies, procurement records show.

Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related to military aircraft, missiles and satellites. The US Commerce Department added the university to the Entity List in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research. It tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licences for exports of controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances.

Northwestern Polytechnical's purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them.

A review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services that use such chips through domestic suppliers. Several had close ‌links to China's ⁠defence industry or military research.

In addition to the management school's outright purchase of the two H200 chips, procurement records show the university's cybersecurity school awarded two seven-month contracts in Jan for access to servers containing eight H200 chips each. The contracts, worth 441,700 yuan and 441,000 yuan, covered fine-tuning AI models and reinforcement-learning training.

It also rented access to servers containing 8 Nvidia A100 chips and 8 A800 chips. The A100 and A800 are banned from ⁠export to all Chinese entities, though the H200 is the most advanced of those cited in Northwestern Polytechnical's procurement records.

In April, another university institute bought computing services requiring at least 24 A100 chips in a 375,000 yuan contract for structural and fluid-dynamics simulations.

The awards went to several little-known Chinese technology suppliers. The records offered scant information about where the processors originated or where the rented servers operated.

Under Chinese law, public procurement agencies must verify that suppliers can fulfil orders before announcing winning bidders and signing contracts.

The procurement records show a wider market for restricted Nvidia AI chips and computing services ⁠at Chinese universities.

Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors, another high-end Nvidia AI chip banned by the US, for 769,800 yuan in Sep. Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an H100 chip for 355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips in a separate 344,000 yuan purchase.

Beihang University, another of the Seven Sons of National Defense universities, bought four A800 processors for 489,000 yuan in April. Beihang has close ties to China's aerospace and defence industries and conducts research for military aviation and space programmes.

Two government procurement announcements in ⁠July and Sep named suppliers selected to provide computing services using Nvidia H800 and A800 chips restricted from export to China to the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences. One listed H800 access at 10 yuan per chip-hour. A separate January procurement award named a supplier of six A100 chips worth 484,800 yuan for a Shenzhen-based public institution.

THE BLUEPRINT | Part 23 of 24

THE DEMOCRATS' PROJECT 2029: The Second Envelope

Democrats spent 2024 warning voters about Project 2025. 

Now some of them are building their own. Same rules as every other part of this series: what they say, what they've done and what they haven't told you.

📘 WHAT THEY SAY

🔹 Who: Chaired by Andrei Cherny, former president of the journal Democracy, and run by Chad Maisel, a former Biden White House domestic policy aide. It's an initiative of a nonprofit called ReForm America.
🔹 The goal: a book-length agenda for a Democratic president to use from day one in January 2029. Maisel says it will be "bigger and bolder than what people have been offered before," drawing from across the party, not just the center-left or the left.
🔹 On Project 2025: It calls that plan "a sweeping, if deeply destructive, agenda," and calls its own name "a wake-up call."

🔍 WHAT THEY'VE RELEASED

"Kids Over Clicks" (June 2026): limits on social media for children under 16, phone bans in schools from bell to bell, limits on collecting children's data, a ban on AI companies training on personal data without consent, and a narrower Section 230. 

Backers include Sen. Cory Booker, New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill and teachers' union president Randi Weingarten.

The "annoyance economy" (July 2026): Developed with Stanford economist Neale Mahoney. It targets junk fees, robocalls and spam texts, including political fundraising texts. It proposes "click-to-cancel" rules for subscriptions and restoring the option to press zero to reach a human. The authors estimate these hassles cost families "at least $165 billion" a year.

The full book: due in 2027.

🕳️ THE PART YOU MISSED

Who's writing it is secret. 

About 200 people sit in its working groups, and their names aren't released unless they author a proposal. 

Project 2025 printed its authors' names in the book. 

Neither Heritage nor ReForm America discloses its donors.

The missing pillars. 

So far, Project 2029 is policy papers. 

A personnel database, training academy or 180-day playbook, the parts that made Project 2025 work, hasn't been reported.

It overlaps with the right. 

Narrowing Section 230 was also in Brendan Carr's Project 2025 chapter. Critics warn that age limits on social media could mean ID checks for everyone online.

It isn't the only one. 

New Consensus, the group behind the Green New Deal, has its own plan for 2029, called "Moonshot 2029."

Not every Democrat has signed on. 

Possible 2028 contenders Gavin Newsom and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez haven't publicly endorsed its first proposals. 

Strategist Max Burns says it misreads why Project 2025 worked and lacks a clear ideological vision.

🛡️ THE CASE FOR

Supporters say Democrats lost in 2024 partly because they ran against an agenda without offering one. 

Publishing ideas early lets voters judge them before the election, the same argument Heritage made. And the first proposals, like ending junk fees and protecting kids online, target problems that frustrate voters in both parties.

📌 Next, Part 24: The Finale. Two blueprints, one inauguration day.

text:
How an Ex-NBA player tried to join the WNBA

This is Enes Kanter Freedom.

He spent 11 years in the NBA. 
Then he tried to enter the women’s league. 
He got rejected.

2011–2022: The NBA
@EnesFreedom Drafted 3rd overall by the Utah Jazz in 2011. 
6’10”, 250-pound center. 
Played for the Jazz, Thunder, Knicks, Trail Blazers, and Celtics. 
Career averages: 11.2 points and 7.8 rebounds per game.

His NBA career ended in early 2022. He has said criticism of the Chinese government shortened it.

August 2026: The announcement
On August 7 he publicly declared for the 2027 WNBA Draft.

He said that if simply declaring who you are is enough under the current rules, then he qualified. 
He stated he identified as a woman.

On August 10 he signed and posted a formal letter to the league notifying them of his intent to enter the draft.

August 23: Courtside
He attended the Indiana Fever vs. Chicago Sky game wearing a black T-shirt that read:
“WOMAN noun. adult human female.”

Late in the third quarter, after celebrating a Sophie Cunningham three-pointer, he got into a heated confrontation with Sky guard Natasha Cloud. 

She approached his seat yelling. He stood with arms outstretched. Security escorted him out.

He posted that he had been kicked out “for supporting WOMEN.” 
The Sky banned him from their home games. 

The WNBA did not issue a league-wide ban.

The rejection
Within days, league sources said he and Royce White were not eligible for the draft.

In mid-October, after members of Congress asked the league how it defines “women,” Commissioner Cathy Engelbert replied in a letter:
“Only women are eligible to play in the WNBA and the individuals you cite in your letter are both men.”

Freedom responded that she could not clearly define what a woman is but was certain he was a man. 

He said he would drop the entire effort if the league explicitly limited eligibility to biological females. 

He also said he identified as a woman and wanted that identity respected.

October: The Finals
He bought seats for Game 3 of the WNBA Finals. The arena offered him a private suite instead, citing safety concerns. 

He refused and insisted on sitting in the seats he had paid for. He was not allowed entry and was escorted out.

After the season
He continued to say he would show up for the 2027 WNBA Draft if the rules did not change.

The WNBA’s CBA still says only women are eligible. It does not define the term further. No transgender woman has ever played in the league.

He tried to join by declaring himself eligible under the rules as written. 
The league said he is a man. 
He got rejected.

Was he wrong to try, or should he have been eligible?

text:
$NNI Q3 2026 earnings: Nelnet's reported profit falls, but its loan business earns more

Nelnet, which services student loans and lends to consumers, reported lower profit but earned more from its loans. Net profit fell 29%, because a year ago it booked one-off gains, including a $33 million government contract payment. Without those items, profit almost doubled by our math. Interest income from its loans kept growing, and loss charges took a smaller share of it.

• Profit excluding one-offs: $𝟕𝟎.𝟗𝐌 ($37.3M a year ago, by our math)
• Net profit: $𝟕𝟔.𝟐𝐌 (−29% from a year ago)
• Department of Education borrowers serviced: 𝟏𝟎.𝟕𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (10.68 million last quarter)
• Quarterly dividend: 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 $𝟎.𝟑𝟔 ($0.33 last quarter)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better, because profit from Nelnet's loans now makes up for weaker servicing, and servicing stopped losing government borrowers. Nelnet Bank also more than doubled its profit. One caution: losses on Pay Later debts, short-term consumer loans Nelnet buys from an unnamed partner, still run far above a year ago.

The question now is whether the Pay Later debts stay profitable after their losses. If losses hold steady, the program keeps adding profit; if they climb as the debts age, the gain could disappear. The fourth-quarter write-off rate will tell.

[Model: Claude Opus 5.5. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐋𝐨𝐚𝐧 𝐉𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭 𝐕𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐍𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐈𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞
Beside the loans on its own books, AGM (Asset Generation and Management), Nelnet's lending arm, owns stakes in joint ventures that buy and manage loan portfolios. Those stakes cover about $1.21 billion of loans, the company said.

• Joint-venture income, third quarter: $12.4 million, against $4.5 million a year ago
• Joint-venture income, first nine months: $36.4 million, against $9.6 million
• AGM profit after tax: up 22% from a year ago

This matters because the ventures earn money without the Pay Later partner that supplies AGM's short-term consumer debts, so AGM depends less on one contract. But Nelnet reports only its share of their profit, so readers cannot see the ventures' own loan losses.

What to watch: joint-venture income in the fourth quarter. A figure near $12 million again would show that the stakes give AGM a steady source of profit beside its own loans.

🟢 𝐍𝐞𝐥𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐁𝐚𝐧𝐤'𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐃𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐝
Nelnet Bank, the group's online bank in Utah, lends to students and consumers and funds those loans with deposits. Nelnet said "operating expenses have stabilized while loan and deposit balances have continued to expand".

• Profit after tax: $12.0 million, against $4.6 million a year ago
• Own new loans: $73 million, against $20 million last quarter

Part of the growth came from inside the group: AGM handed the bank $64 million of old student loans. But the bank also lent on its own and, since June, relied less on costly deposits bought through brokers. Its net interest margin, what its assets earn after deposit costs, still slipped to 2.66% from 3.32%.

What to watch: the bank's own new lending in the fourth quarter. Steady lending would show that it wins its own customers and does not just take over the group's loans.

🟢 𝐂𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐝𝐚 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐚 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐖𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧 𝐍𝐞𝐥𝐧𝐞𝐭'𝐬 𝐂𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐚𝐬𝐞
Nelnet bought businesses abroad this year. NDS Canada, bought in February, services student loans for Canadian governments. Chief executive Jeff Noordhoek described the deal for Entab, a school software provider in India, as "expanding our education technology business internationally".

• Canadian servicing revenue: $16.5 million in the quarter
• Canadian borrowers: 2.8 million
• Servicing revenue without Canada and one-off payments: $118.0 million, against $118.2 million, by our math

So Canada supplied all of the servicing division's growth, while the US business stood still. Entab serves more than 1,000 schools, Nelnet said, and its three software deals this year cost $30.9 million together.

What to watch: Canadian servicing revenue in the fourth quarter. A figure above $16.5 million would show that the deal keeps adding revenue while US government work shrinks.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐋𝐨𝐚𝐧 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐲 𝐅𝐚𝐫 𝐀𝐛𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐋𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫
Since last August, AGM, Nelnet's lending arm, has bought Pay Later receivables: short-term consumer debts it buys at a discount from a partner it does not name. These purchases lifted AGM's loan spread, what its loans earn above funding costs, to 2.40% from 1.27%.

Nelnet says losses climbed because it bought more debts and the loans aged, and that the rise was "not indicative of a deterioration in credit quality".

• Net write-offs on consumer loans outside the bank: 8.78% a year, against 5.75% a year ago
• Loans 31 days or more late: 3.2% of that book, against 1.3%
• Reserve for future losses: 7.55% of that book, against 5.11% in December

The write-off rate matched the second quarter's, so losses held steady over the summer. But by our math, the $33.7 million loss charge on these loans topped the $31.2 million that the discount and late fees earned. The partner also stays unnamed, so outsiders cannot judge how long the income lasts.

What to watch: the write-off rate on these loans in the fourth quarter. A rate above 8.78% would show losses still rising as the debts age, which Nelnet's explanation does not cover.

🔴🔴 𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐚𝐬 𝐁𝐨𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐏𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝
"We delivered strong operating performance this quarter, with continued progress diversifying our products and customer base," chief executive Jeff Noordhoek said. The servicing division, NDS, which collects student-loan payments for the US Department of Education and others, does not fit the first half of that claim.

• Profit before tax at NDS: $16.5 million, against $46.3 million a year ago
• Margin excluding one-offs and deal amortisation: 10.0%, against 11.0%
• Other costs, mainly software and professional fees: 14.7% of revenue, against 7.2%
• Department revenue excluding one-off payments: down 4%, by our math

One part did improve. The Department borrower count rose to 10.78 million from 10.68 million, the first gain after six quarterly declines. Nelnet said it "does not expect to transfer additional volume to this servicer", meaning the new servicer that took its borrowers in 2025.

What to watch: the Department borrower count in the fourth quarter. A second rise would show the losses have stopped, but the contract's five-year base period still ends in 2028.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Four standing risks got little new evidence in this quarter's filings, so each item below names the reading that would move it.

• Solar tax-credit partnerships: Nelnet's own share of losses shrank to almost nothing, but it has not restated its 2025-2030 income target; the annual report will show it.
• School payments and software (NBS): margin excluding interest income reached 22.0%, against 20.8%, but education services revenue fell 6%; the fourth quarter will show if the gain holds.
• Interest-rate mismatch: swaps that cover $1.15 billion of student loans against a gap between two rate benchmarks expire in November and December; the next filing will show replacements.
• Funding lines: Nelnet cut its student-loan warehouse line to $475 million and still relies on Union Bank, a related party holding $532 million of loan stakes; renewal terms will show the risk.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐍𝐞𝐥𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐋𝐚𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐚 𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐒𝐜𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐚𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 𝐓𝐚𝐱 𝐂𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐬
In October Nelnet announced FACTS Compass, which chief executive Jeff Noordhoek said will "help scholarship granting organizations support students in public and private schools" under the new Federal Scholarship Tax Credit. Its BenefitEd unit offers employers a payroll deduction option for the program. Nelnet gave no revenue figure, so nobody can yet judge what the product earns.

𝐋𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐍𝐞𝐥𝐧𝐞𝐭'𝐬 𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐁𝐢𝐥𝐥
Falling market rates helped Nelnet's lending this quarter. Its interest expense dropped 11% from a year ago, because it owed less debt and paid lower rates, the company said. But lower rates also trimmed interest on its cash and investments, to $42.4 million from $43.2 million.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟑𝟓.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Nelnet keeps cutting its share count: 35.4 million shares at September 30, 1.6% fewer than a year ago. It spent $53.1 million on buybacks in the quarter, about twice the year-ago sum. Another $37.0 million followed by November 5, and 3.8 million shares remain under its authority.

𝐁𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐧𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟔.𝟕𝟕 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Debt keeps shrinking: bonds and notes payable fell 13.5% from a year ago. The old student loans pay off, and the bonds backed by them go too. Nelnet Bank now funds $781 million of moved loans with deposits instead. The $435 million unsecured credit line stays unused.

𝐑𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐢𝐮𝐦𝐬 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐝 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟒𝟒.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
The reinsurance arm, which takes on part of other insurers' property and casualty risks, almost doubled its premiums, up 92%. Growth with existing carriers and a smaller share passed to other reinsurers drove it, the company said. Losses and costs took 80% of premiums, against 86% a year ago.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐄𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐱 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞, 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔: 𝟐𝟐.𝟓%–𝟐𝟒.𝟓%  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from 22.5%–24.5%
Unchanged. Nelnet still expects a tax rate of 22.5% to 24.5% for the rest of the year. Its third-quarter rate came in at 24.57%, just above that range. So the plan points to a lower rate in the fourth quarter. Nelnet measures the rate on profit before its solar partners' share of losses.

𝐅𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡-𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝: $𝟎.𝟑𝟔 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞  ⇗ accelerating
New. The board raised the quarterly dividend 9%, to $0.36 a share, payable on December 15. Nelnet paid $0.33 in each of the last four quarters. That makes this the second increase in five quarters, and the payment still takes a small part of quarterly profit.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐨 𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐍𝐞𝐥𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐏𝐚𝐲 𝐋𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭𝐬, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐠?
One unnamed partner supplies most of the consumer debts that lifted AGM's earnings. The contract's length and volume commitments decide how long that income lasts, and Nelnet has not disclosed them.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭 𝐦𝐢𝐱?
Nelnet says the reserve rose because it bought riskier non-Pay Later loans and because Pay Later debts aged. It has not split the two, so readers cannot test its claim that credit quality held.

Leslie Kershaw, Chief Information Security Officer at @IonQ_Inc, is featured in Forbes. In a piece published on November 9, Heather Wishart-Smith brings her in on what leaders need to do before a quantum computer can break today's encryption (Q-Day).

Before IonQ, Kershaw was Chief Information Security Officer at Capella Space, now an IonQ company. Earlier, she held cyber leadership roles in the U.S. Space Force and at the National Security Agency.

Her first step, as Forbes reports it: make a list of every lock (the cryptography) a company uses and where. Only that list shows which locks to change first. She worries that AI is taking much of the attention and budget away from that work.

IonQ applies it to itself. Through Kershaw, Forbes reports that IonQ is implementing quantum key distribution (QKD) internally, keys sent on particles of light so any interception shows up, across a company that has acquired 11 businesses in the past three years. On October 26, IonQ had already shown a live quantum-safe network protecting its own data between Geneva and Seoul.

Her view reaches beyond security: "I look forward to the ability to cure diseases. I think quantum will allow us to unlock things with medicine that we haven't been able to do before," she said.

She spoke on October 8 in Tysons, Virginia, at Uniting Women in Cyber, the one-day conference of The Cyber Guild, a nonprofit, on a panel alongside Verisign's CTO Burt Kaliski.

That list is exactly where IonQ's offer starts, as laid out at Investor Day and with Elisity:
→ Map where a customer is exposed to a quantum attack
→ Add the cryptography each device runs and the risk it carries to Elisity's IdentityGraph (planned), to rank upgrades by business risk
→ Move to post-quantum encryption (PQC) or quantum keys (QKD)
→ Wall off older machines that can't be upgraded, like factory controllers or medical devices, until they are replaced

text:
Today is a day of national mourning in Bulgaria. 11 people died on the Trakiya motorway yesterday, in the fog that comes every November. More than 50 people were injured and were airlifted or taken by ambulance to hospitals in Sliven, Yambol and Burgas. Thousands of people helped, many of them donating blood and filling up blood banks across the country.

Grief first. Then the question every Bulgarian is asking: why do our roads remain among the deadliest in the EU, year after year?

When will the responsible parties face the music?

When will Boyko Borissov and GERB answer for how our motorways were built? The Trakiya Highway was built and repaired under GERB-led governments, with years of criticism over quality and cost. Billions in EU funds went into our roads. Where did that money go, and why were they built as cheaply as possible?

And why did the state scrap an EU-co-financed project for 40 electronic fog-warning signs on the Trakiya Highway? The road agency changed where the signs would go, the cost rose, the ministry refused to cover it, and the contract was simply cancelled. Yesterday, there were no signs to warn anyone.

When will Delyan Peevski, sanctioned by both the US and the UK for corruption, face the consequences? How much of that corruption reached the contracts for building and maintaining our highways?

When will Rumen Radev and Progressive Bulgaria take responsibility? He has an absolute majority and carte blanche to fix the issues Bulgaria is facing, including maintaining the highways properly and installing warning systems. Instead, he is busy with populist policies, backing a backwards law to “safeguard” the Bulgarian language by removing English from our signs, and scaring away investors our economy needs.

When will Kostadin Kostadinov and “Revival”, the authors of that language law and of a “foreign agents” bill, face consequences for stirring up hatred in Bulgarian minds? While the President of the European Commission came to Varna to support our defence, he declared that “Ursula brought death to Bulgaria”. In the meantime, Ursula von der Leyen came to Varna to support our defence and offer €10 million for our rescue teams. Revival stood in the street telling her to “go home”.

The EU answered with solidarity: flags were lowered to half-mast at the European Parliament, the Commission and the Council, in solidarity with the Bulgarian people. If Russia is supposed to be our “brotherly nation” (which it obviously isn’t), did Moscow lower a single flag?

This is yet another example out of many. We need to wake up. Fully. We need to create our own government, one that is functional, effective and accountable. This should mark the dawn of a new Bulgarian movement, one that will finally change things once and for all.

Good morning, friends. As dawn breaks on this November 11, 2026, the words of Psalm 63:11 offer a gentle yet powerful invitation: "But the king shall rejoice in God; all who swear by him shall exult..." These ancient lines remind us that true joy and celebration come when we anchor our lives in the Lord, no matter what surrounds us.

Many of us wake today carrying heavy loads. Veterans Day stirs memories of service and sacrifice, while ongoing global tensions, economic pressures, and personal worries about health or family relationships can make the morning feel overwhelming. It is tempting to let fear or frustration set the tone for the hours ahead. Yet the psalm points us toward a different path, one where rejoicing flows not from perfect circumstances but from the simple act of trusting and swearing by God.

Picture the quiet strength of those who have served our nation. Their commitment mirrors the steady faithfulness we are invited to offer the Lord each day. In homes across the country, people rise to face uncertain jobs, strained conversations with loved ones, or the ache of loneliness. Swearing by Him means choosing to place our hope in His unchanging character rather than the shifting news cycle or our own limited strength. That choice opens the door to exultation, a deep gladness that steadies the heart.

This morning, let the verse settle into your routine. When headlines feel alarming or your schedule presses in, pause and remember that kings and ordinary people alike find their greatest joy in God. He sees every hidden struggle and every small act of courage. As we move through the day, may we carry this hopeful outlook, sharing encouragement with coworkers, neighbors, and family. The Lord remains near, turning ordinary moments into opportunities for quiet praise.

May your morning be filled with peace and the quiet confidence that comes from resting in Him. Whatever lies ahead, we can face it together with hearts that rejoice.
