text:
Every dog owner is fighting three small wars at home, and most of us have been losing them for so long that we forgot we were at war.

Not the dramatic kind. Nobody makes a documentary about these. There is no siren, no rescue crew, no stranger holding a flashlight. Just a Tuesday. A black sweater that turns grey the moment you sit on the couch. A damp spot on the floor that you discover with a sock. A walk that feels less like a walk and more like being towed by a very enthusiastic tugboat.

You call it normal. That is the trick. Anything you endure daily long enough gets filed under "the price of loving a dog," and once it is filed there, you stop looking for a way out.

Here is the uncomfortable part. A lot of that price is optional.

Not all of it. Dogs shed. Dogs have accidents. Dogs pull toward the squirrel with the force of a small hydraulic press. Those are not bugs in the system, they are the system. But the distance between "this is part of having a dog" and "this is part of having a dog that nobody ever showed me how to handle" is a lot wider than most people think.

I want to talk about three of those gaps. Three problems that almost every dog household shares, three places where people quietly overpay in money, in time, in patience, or in the relationship itself. And one short video that puts all three in front of you in under a minute, which is the real reason I am writing this at all.

But first, the problem with problems.

The first war is the one you can see from across the room.

Hair.

Anyone who has lived with a double-coated dog knows the seasonal event that happens twice a year, when the dog appears to be manufacturing a second, smaller dog out of loose fur and leaving it in installments. You vacuum in the morning and by evening the floor looks like nobody has vacuumed since the previous administration. It collects in the corners. It migrates into the car. It finds its way into a sandwich you swear you made in a closed kitchen.

And the standard response is a kind of grim loyalty. You brush a little. You buy a lint roller in bulk. You accept that every piece of dark clothing you own is now a two-species garment.

Meanwhile there is a second cost that most people never connect to the first one: the professional route. Grooming is skilled work, and it is worth paying for. The people who do it well are doing something genuinely difficult, with a living animal that does not understand why it must stand still. Nothing here is a complaint about them. But skilled work has a price, and a dog that sheds constantly can turn a luxury into a standing obligation. Somewhere between the brush that does not quite reach and the appointment that costs more than you planned, a quiet question starts forming in the back of your head.

Is there something in the middle?

Most people never ask it out loud, because the question feels disloyal. As if wanting an easier time with the fur meant wanting less of the dog.

It does not. It means the opposite. A dog who gets brushed regularly, comfortably, without a battle, is a dog whose coat, skin, and mood all benefit. The owner who dreads grooming day is the owner who postpones it. And the owner who postpones it is the owner whose dog ends up matted, itchy, and miserable. Make something easier and people do it more often. That is not laziness. That is how every good habit in human history actually got built.

Keep that idea in your pocket. It is going to matter in the next two sections.

The second war is quieter, and it is fought at floor level.

Accidents.

There is a particular kind of dread that belongs only to people who own dogs, or who are raising a puppy, or who are caring for a dog that is getting older and slower and no longer quite as certain about timing. It is the dread of walking into a room and not yet knowing what you will find. The dread has a smell. It has a temperature. It has a dozen cleaning products and enzyme sprays and old towels that never really go back to being just towels.

And here is what almost nobody says out loud: accidents are rarely about discipline. A puppy has a bladder the size of a walnut and no concept of the calendar. A senior dog may have a body that simply no longer cooperates. A dog recovering from surgery, a dog in a new home, a dog who is anxious, a dog who ate something unusual yesterday. The list of reasons is long, and almost none of them are the dog being bad.

So the real question is never "how do I stop this forever, today." It is "how do I make the cost of this smaller while the dog learns, ages, or heals."

That is a boring question. It is also the one that determines whether the home stays calm.

Think about what a surface does. A floor either forgives or it does not. A rug either survives or it becomes a permanent record of the worst week of your year. The difference between a household that handles accidents with a sigh and a household that handles them with a meltdown is rarely the dog. It is the material under the dog.

Which is a strange thing to realize. That a major source of tension between people and their pets might come down to what the floor is made of, and whether the thing on top of it can be tossed in a machine and returned to normal.

And yet that is what many owners discover, usually after years. Somebody mentions it in passing. A friend, a neighbor, a groomer, a stranger in a comment section. And the response is always the same: wait, that exists?

That is the pattern worth noticing. Not that the solutions are secret. They are not. It is that nobody tells you, because nobody thinks of it as something worth telling.

The third war is the one that happens outdoors, in public, with witnesses.

The leash.

There is a version of this that every owner knows by heart. The dog sees something. A bird, a bike, another dog, a wrapper blowing across the sidewalk. The body changes. The ears go up, the weight shifts forward, and suddenly a thirty-pound animal can pull with a force that feels completely out of proportion to its size. Your shoulder remembers. Your wrist remembers. Your sense of calm absolutely does not survive.

And the thing about leash pulling is that it is not a character flaw. It is physics and instinct. Dogs move faster than we do. They are built to follow their noses. When a dog pulls and the walk continues in that direction, the dog has learned something very clear: pulling works. Every time it works, it gets stronger. Many owners are not failing at training. They are accidentally rewarding the exact thing they are trying to stop.

So we reach for equipment. And here is where the stakes turn more serious than the hair or the floor, because the wrong choice is not an inconvenience. It can be uncomfortable for the dog. It can be harmful. It can make a nervous dog more nervous, and a reactive dog more reactive.

There is a reason trainers and behaviorists argue about this at length. There is also a reason that a lot of owners drift toward whatever was on the shelf at the store, never realizing there is a gentler, more thoughtful option sitting one aisle away. Or one video away.

I will not pretend that any single piece of gear is a miracle. Anyone who tells you a gadget replaces patience, practice, and a dog who trusts you is selling something. But gear can change the conversation. It can shift where the pressure goes, how much control you have, and how the dog experiences the walk. And when that conversation changes, the dog changes too.

Which brings me to the thing I keep coming back to.

Why do smart, caring people live with these problems for years?

I have a theory, and it has nothing to do with money.

It is that dog owners are some of the most conditioned problem-tolerators on earth. Think about what we put up with. We wake at dawn because a creature needs to go outside. We step in things. We apologize to strangers for enthusiasm. We schedule our vacations around a being who cannot read a calendar. We do all of it cheerfully, and we are right to, because what we get back is enormous.

But that same cheerful tolerance has a shadow side. If you are used to absorbing inconvenience in the name of love, you stop distinguishing between inconvenience that is meaningful and inconvenience that is just friction. The two feel identical from the inside. A sleepless night with a sick puppy and a weekly battle with a vacuum cleaner both get the same shrug and the same sentence: that is just how it is.

Friction, though, is not love. Friction is friction.

And friction compounds. A tiny irritation repeated daily for years is not tiny anymore. Take the leash as an example. A walk that starts with tension tends to carry that tension through every block. The owner tightens up. The dog feels the tightening. The dog gets more alert, and more reactive, and the owner tightens again. Two living creatures bounce a mood back and forth along a strip of nylon. After a few weeks of that, some owners start walking less. Not because they love the dog less. Because the walk stopped being pleasant.

Now picture what that does to the dog. A dog that walks less is a dog with more energy and less outlet for it, and that energy goes somewhere. The couch. The shoes. The window at three in the afternoon. A small leash problem becomes a household problem, and nobody connects the two.

The same chain runs through the other wars. Hair that is hard to manage becomes grooming that happens less. Grooming that happens less becomes a coat in worse shape. Accidents that feel catastrophic make an owner short-tempered with a dog who did not choose to have them, and dogs read tone far better than they read words.

So the stakes are not really about fur, floors, and straps. The stakes are about the daily emotional climate of a home with an animal in it. Reduce the friction, and the relationship gets more room to be what it was supposed to be in the first place.

That is a much bigger claim than "here are some handy products," and I want to be careful with it, because the internet is full of people who inflate small things into life-changing revelations. Most gadgets are not life-changing. Most are fine. Some are a waste of money. A few are quietly excellent.

The skill is telling the difference. And that is where I get skeptical on your behalf.

Here is the filter I would apply to anything that claims to make life with a dog easier.

First: does it solve a problem you actually have, or one that a marketing team invented for you? A lot of pet products are built to make an owner feel like a better owner, not to make the dog's day better. If you cannot name the specific daily pain it removes, skip it.

Second: does it make things better for the dog, or only for you? The best answer is both. If the benefit lands entirely on the human side and the dog quietly pays for it, that is not a solution, it is a transfer of discomfort.

Third: does it get used? The graveyard of dog gear is enormous. Closets and garages everywhere are full of things that sounded wonderful in the store and demanded too much effort at home. A good solution is one so easy that it disappears into the routine. If it needs a ceremony, it will not last a month.

Fourth: is it honest about what it cannot do? Anything that promises to end shedding, end accidents, or end pulling forever is lying to you. The honest ones promise something smaller and more believable. Less hair on the floor. Less to clean when things go wrong. Less strain on both ends of the leash.

Run any product through those four questions and most of the hype falls away. What is left is a short list of things that genuinely earn their place in a house with a dog.

Which brings us back to the short video.

I am going to be careful here, because I do not want to turn this into a walkthrough. The whole point of a good short clip is that it does something text cannot. It shows rather than argues. It lets you see, in a few seconds, whether something looks like it would fit in your life. If I explained every detail in advance, I would be doing you a disservice and spoiling the thing that makes it worth watching.

So I will say only this about it.

It touches all three wars. Hair, mess, leash. Not as a lecture, not as a sales pitch with a countdown timer, but as a quick, practical look at ways other dog owners have found to make those three daily frictions smaller. The kind of thing that makes you pause and think, huh, I never considered that, followed immediately by, why did nobody tell me this years ago?

And that second reaction is the interesting one.

Because it points at something larger than any single item. Knowledge about living well with animals travels in a very strange way. It does not move through institutions or textbooks. It moves sideways. Neighbor to neighbor. Groomer to client. One owner holding a leash at a park telling another, you know, there is a different way to do that.

Most of the best practical dog knowledge on earth was passed along this way, almost casually, by people who had already been through the problem and did not want anyone else to suffer through it as long as they had.

That is a lovely tradition. It is also wildly inefficient. How many owners are right now, this minute, struggling with a problem that someone two doors down solved years ago? Thousands upon thousands. Not because anyone is hiding the answer, but because the right sentence never found the right person.

Short video is, in a sense, a way of speeding up that tradition. A stranger with a camera leans over the fence and says, here, look at this. Sometimes it is nonsense. Sometimes it is the best two minutes of your week.

I want to talk about why the format works so well for this specific subject, because it is not an accident.

A dog problem is a physical, sensory, in-the-moment problem. Reading about it feels abstract. A paragraph describing a pulling dog does not convey the way the whole body of the walker leans back like someone waterskiing. A description of a mess does not carry the dread. But a few seconds of real life does, instantly, because you recognize it. You have been there. Your own history walks into your head and sits down next to what you are watching.

That recognition is the engine. It is why people who would never read a product review will happily watch thirty seconds of a stranger solving their exact problem. Recognition creates trust faster than any argument.

And trust is the scarce resource here. We live in an age when every recommendation might be an ad, every enthusiastic voice might have a discount code attached, and every "genius" product might have been named by someone with a quarterly target. People are tired. They have learned to flinch at the word "genius."

So I will be honest about my own flinch. A title that promises three genius things you wish you had known sooner is, on its face, the kind of thing a sensible person scrolls past.

The reason it is worth stopping for is the same reason it is worth being skeptical of. The bar is low, which means the ones that clear it are easy to spot. If something is genuinely useful, you do not need to be convinced. You just need to see it once and think about your own kitchen floor, your own couch, your own walk, and your own dog.

Watch it with that in mind. Not as entertainment, but as a quick audit of your own home.

There is another layer to this that rarely gets discussed, and it concerns who these small fixes actually serve.

We tend to frame dog products as conveniences for people. Less vacuuming. Less scrubbing. Fewer sore shoulders. All true. But look at each of the three wars from the dog's side of the room, and the picture shifts.

Start with grooming. A dog does not understand why it is being brushed. It only understands what the experience feels like: being held, being handled, sometimes tugged at a tangle, often for longer than it would choose. If the tool is gentle and the process is quick, the dog can learn that this is a calm, even pleasant routine. If the process is slow, awkward, and stressful for the human, the dog absorbs that stress too. The method matters because the mood of the person doing it travels straight down the arm and into the animal.

Move to the floor. A dog who has an accident and is met with a sigh learns very little. A dog who has an accident and is met with a sharp voice, a flinch, or frantic scrubbing learns something else entirely: that the person it trusts most becomes unpredictable at certain moments. Dogs do not connect the scolding to the puddle the way we imagine they do. They connect it to the face above them. So anything that lowers the stakes of an accident for the owner protects the dog from the owner's worst reaction. The humble surface under the dog is, in a roundabout way, a piece of emotional safety equipment.

And then the leash, where the dog's experience is the most direct of all. Equipment sits on a body. It presses somewhere. It redirects something. A dog cannot tell you that a piece of gear feels wrong, so you have to learn to read it from posture, from pace, from how willingly the dog goes out the door. Some of the most important sentences in dog care are the ones the dog says without words, and a good fit is one that makes those sentences calmer.

Seen from this angle, the idea of "making life easier" changes character. It is no longer about convenience. It is about reducing the number of moments in a dog's week when the person it depends on is tense, frustrated, or hurting it by accident.

That is a better reason to care about any of this than saving an afternoon.

Let me make a slightly bolder claim, and then walk it back to something defensible.

The bold version: the quality of a dog's life is largely decided in the boring moments. Not the vacations, not the birthday treats, not the photogenic hikes. The boring moments. The way the morning goes. What the evening walk feels like. Whether the person is relaxed or braced.

The defensible version: that is not the whole story, and I cannot prove it. Dogs have temperaments, histories, health, and breed traits that no gadget will touch. A dog with deep anxiety needs real behavioral help, and no piece of gear stands in for a good trainer or a good vet. If your dog is hurting, frightened, or showing signs of something serious, the answer is a professional, not a product.

But within the wide territory of ordinary daily life, the ordinary mornings and ordinary walks, small improvements compound just as small irritations do. A household that runs smoothly is a household in which the dog is met more often with ease than with strain. Over years, that is a very large number of moments.

Now let me turn to the person who is reading this and does not currently own a dog at all.

If that is you, you might be here for the video and nothing else, and that is completely fine. But there is something in this that applies to anyone who has ever cared for something that cannot speak for itself. The pattern is the same for a child, for an aging parent, for a houseplant, for a rescue cat that hides under the bed. We pour in effort, we adapt, we endure, and we rarely stop to ask whether the effort could be spent better.

There is a kind of martyrdom in caregiving, and it is not always healthy. People take pride in how much they absorb. They wear the exhaustion as proof of devotion. And sometimes the exhaustion is simply the result of doing something the hard way for no reason, because nobody ever suggested a different way.

Care that costs less is not care that means less. If a tool lets you give the same love with half the strain, the love is not diminished. You just have more of yourself left over to give.

That is worth sitting with, especially if you are someone who tends to feel guilty about wanting things to be easier.

Let me also say something to the people who have been doing this for a long time.

If you have lived with dogs for decades, you may read all of this with a raised eyebrow. You have your methods. You have your tricks. You have survived puppyhood, adolescence, shedding seasons, and farewells. You do not need a stranger telling you how to run your house, and you certainly do not need a clip with a catchy title.

I understand. The experienced owner is often the most skeptical audience, and often for good reason. You have seen fads come and go. You have watched trendy equipment fall out of favor, and you remember the ones that did harm.

But I would offer one gentle thought. Experience builds habits, and habits are very good at making a method feel like the only method. The owners who stay curious across decades are the ones who keep learning from newcomers, from different breeds, from strange little ideas that turn out to be better than the old way. Curiosity is the thing that keeps long experience from hardening into stubbornness.

So even if you are certain you know everything about your own dog, a short look at how other households handle the same three problems costs you almost nothing. The worst outcome is that you nod and move on. The best outcome is that you steal one idea.

And there is a quiet generosity in stealing ideas from strangers. Every good practice in the world began as somebody's improvised fix for an annoying afternoon.

Let me close the loop on the three wars, because they deserve a proper ending.

Hair is a war about time. It is fought in small daily skirmishes, and it is won not by eliminating shedding, which cannot be done, but by making the cleanup so light that it stops feeling like a war at all. A coat that sheds is a coat that is alive. The goal is not a spotless home. The goal is a home where fur is a minor weather condition instead of a recurring crisis.

Mess is a war about composure. It is won not by a dog who never has accidents, which does not exist, but by a home that absorbs them without drama. The measure of success is not the absence of puddles. It is how you feel standing next to one.

The leash is a war about trust. It is won not by a dog who never pulls, but by a walk in which both ends of the line are calmer than they were last month. The measure of success is small and wonderful: a dog who looks back at you, as if to check that you are still coming.

Notice that none of these victories is dramatic. That is exactly why they matter. Nobody gets a medal for a quiet morning. Nobody throws a parade for a floor that stayed clean or a walk that did not hurt. But those are the victories that a life with a dog is actually made of, repeated a thousand times, until one day you realize the whole house feels lighter and you cannot remember when it changed.

And that is the question I would leave you with, because it is the one that really matters.

What is the thing you have stopped noticing?

Every household has one. The small, daily, endured thing. The corner you avoid. The chore you dread. The moment in the walk where your shoulders rise toward your ears. You have lived with it so long that it has become scenery, and scenery does not feel like a problem. It feels like home.

Somewhere there is a person who solved the exact thing you are quietly putting up with. They are not smarter than you. They were not luckier. They just happened to see the right thing at the right moment, and it changed their week.

Maybe that moment is one short video away.

I will not tell you which of the three will hit closest to home. It is different for everyone. For some it is the fur, for some the floor, for some the strain on the other end of the lead. It is entirely possible that none of it is new to you, and you will watch it with a knowing nod.

But it is also possible that one small moment in it makes you say, out loud, to nobody, to the dog lying on the rug next to you: how did I never know that?

And the dog will look up, tail tapping once against the floor, perfectly happy, having never been the problem at all.

One more thought, for the skeptics who made it this far.

You do not have to buy anything. That may sound strange at the end of a post about products, but it is the honest position. Watching is free. Noticing is free. Asking yourself which of your three daily frictions is the heaviest is free. A good idea does not become worthless because you decided not to spend money on it. Sometimes the best outcome of seeing how someone else solved a problem is simply realizing that your own problem has a name, and that it has a solution, and that you can choose the timing.

Dogs live fast. The years with them are shorter than any of us want, and the daily routine is where most of those years are actually spent. A little less friction in that routine is not a trivial thing to want. The routine is where the love actually lives, and it deserves to feel good for both of you, the one with two legs and the one with four. Small daily kindnesses build a good life with a dog, and the best ones go unnoticed.

Go and see it for yourself.

text:
The morning after my father died, I was getting ready to leave for his funeral when my husband suddenly asked, "Who's going to prepare dinner for my mother and the rest of the family?"

I stood by the entrance with my bag packed and my mourning clothes ready.

Me: "We discussed this yesterday. I told you I'd be staying at my parents' house from today."

Husband: "I know, but tomorrow is Mom's birthday."

Me: "And I already told you I wouldn't be attending."

He opened the refrigerator and said, "Can't you at least prepare something before leaving? Fried chicken and a few dishes shouldn't take more than a couple of hours."

Me: "My father just died. I want to see him before the funeral."

Husband: "He's already dead. Arriving a little later won't change anything."

I slowly put my bag down.

Me: "What did you just say?"

He looked irritated. "I have plans with living people too. My sister and her children are coming tomorrow."

Me: "Then you can cook for them."

Husband: "I've never prepared food for ten people."

Me: "Neither had I when your family first started visiting. I learned."

We had been married for seven years. Every holiday, birthday, and family gathering, he invited relatives over because eating at home was cheaper. I did all the shopping, cooking, and cleaning.

My father had only visited our house once. After my husband complained that he didn't want to spend his days off entertaining my family, I started meeting my father elsewhere.

Just then, the doorbell rang. It was my mother-in-law.

When she saw my black mourning clothes, she offered her condolences before asking, "I'm sorry about your father, dear. But can you please arrange tomorrow's food before leaving?"

Me: "I can't."

She looked disappointed. "Everyone is looking forward to your cooking."

I replied, "My father was also looking forward to seeing me."

She turned toward my husband and told him to talk some sense into me.

He picked up my bag, and I thought he was finally going to help me leave. Instead, he carried it back into the bedroom.

"Fine. Just return tomorrow evening after the wake. You'll have nothing else to do by then."

I went inside, collected my bag, and walked toward the door.

He shouted, "If you walk out now, don't bother coming back!"

I put on my shoes and said, "Fine."

.. Of course, there are a couple of problems with Senate Democrats’ proposal, mainly that if you put a price control on interest rates, you’re very quickly going to find that poorer Americans and those with bad credit increasingly find credit out of reach.

Higher interest rates are used to compensate banks for the risk of lending. Cap what banks can charge without reducing that risk, and they may simply stop lending to riskier borrowers, until, of course, Democrats push another bill to force risky lending, and then we could be looking at another recession.

text:
One mother. A crowd of lives so small you could lose a hundred of them in the crease of your palm.

And it all happens in a stretch of time shorter than the average ad before a video.

I have watched this clip more times than I want to admit, and every time I catch myself doing the same thing: holding my breath, as if exhaling too loudly might scatter something that has no right to be this fragile and this stubborn at the same time.

Ten seconds. That is the whole runtime. Ten seconds is not enough time to understand what you are looking at, which is exactly why you will press play again.

Let me explain why this one hit me differently, without spoiling what you will see for yourself.

Most of us are trained to think of strength as something big. A roar. A wingspan. A horn, a claw, a jaw. We build our admiration around size because size is easy to measure and easy to fear.

This clip is about the opposite end of the scale. It is about what happens when life decides that bigness is overrated, and that the real power is in arriving in numbers that make the arithmetic dizzy.

There is a kind of motherhood that never appears on posters or in greeting cards. It does not cradle. It does not hover. It does not teach. It carries, it releases, and it trusts a system far older than any of us to do the rest.

Is that less love? Or is it love in a language we never learned to read?

I honestly do not know. That is why I keep watching.

Here is the thing about animals we file under "food" or "farm stock" or "seafood": we almost never meet them as individuals. We meet them as a plate, a price per kilo, a line on a menu. The word "shrimp" has been so thoroughly absorbed into the vocabulary of dinner that most people have never once asked what a shrimp's beginning looks like.

Not the grocery-store beginning. The real one.

The one that starts with a single female and ends, in a heartbeat of footage, with a scene your brain refuses to file under "normal."

I am not going to tell you what happens in those ten seconds. I will tell you what it did to the part of my head that likes to believe it understands how the living world works.

It humbled it.

There are moments in nature footage where you stop being an audience and start being a witness. The camera did not do anything clever. There is no music swelling, no narrator with a velvet voice telling you how to feel. Just a small animal doing something it has done for longer than humans have had language, in a place most of us would walk past without a glance.

And yet.

If you have ever wondered what it looks like when a single life becomes many, this is the closest thing I have seen to an honest answer. No metaphor. No poetry layered on top. Just the thing itself.

Let me ask you something before we go further, and I want you to answer honestly, even if only in your head.

How many animals have you ever seen being born?

Not hatched in a documentary. Not in a time-lapse with orchestral strings. Actually, physically, in front of you, in real light, with no framing device telling you it was a miracle.

For most people the answer is zero, or close to it. Birth is the most universal event in biology and one of the least witnessed by the people who eat, wear, and live off its results. We have outsourced the beginning of life to places we never visit and then act surprised when we feel nothing at the end of it.

This clip puts the beginning back in front of you. Uninvited. Unfiltered. Unreasonably small.

Now, a few things I can say with confidence, because they are simply true of this kind of animal and have nothing to do with embellishing anything.

Shrimp mothers carry their young before those young ever meet the world. Depending on the species, a single female can carry anywhere from a few hundred to tens of thousands of eggs. She keeps them with her, tucked against her own body, for as long as it takes. She fans them, cleans them, keeps them moving through the water. Not because anyone told her to. Because every one of those specks is a possibility, and possibility is the only currency evolution has ever accepted.

Think about the labor in that.

Weeks of carrying something that is not yet anyone, protecting a future you will never be able to supervise.

That is what lives behind the scene you are about to watch. Not just a moment. A long, quiet wait that ends in a few seconds nobody planned to film.

And that is where the strangeness begins, because what comes after the wait does not look like anything you have been taught to call a "birth."

I want to slow down here, because the gap between what we expect and what we get is where this whole video lives.

We have a template for new life. Something small is born, something larger watches over it. The large one shields, the small one shivers, and we fill in the emotions ourselves because the script is so familiar we could recite it asleep.

This clip tears up the template and leaves the pieces on the ground.

There is no single baby. There is no gentle hand-off. There is no moment where you can point and say, there, that is the one she is looking after. Instead there is a scale of arrival that makes the word "litter" look embarrassingly modest.

Do you know what that does to a viewer? It forces a question that the usual birth story lets you dodge.

What does it mean to be loved when you are one of thousands?

The usual answer is that it cannot mean much. Love, we assume, needs a ratio. One parent, one or two children, attention divided gently. Once the numbers climb, the feeling must thin out into something statistical.

But watch how the animal on screen behaves, and I mean really watch it. Whatever you decide it is doing, it is not behaving like a creature performing a chore. Whether you call that instinct, devotion, or something we lack a word for, the effect on the viewer is the same: you lean closer.

And then you notice the tiny ones.

I will not tell you what they do. I will tell you that the first time I saw it I said "no" out loud, alone in a room, to no one.

That small, involuntary word is the best review I can give this video.

Let me pull the camera back for a moment and talk about stakes, because there is more riding on those ten seconds than it first appears.

Everything about this moment is a gamble taken at an almost absurd scale. The mother is betting that enough of these will survive. The young, if we are generous enough to credit them with anything, are betting on nothing at all, because betting requires knowing there is a table. They simply arrive, and the world either accommodates them or it does not.

Biologists have a blunt name for this strategy. They call it producing many and investing little in each, and they contrast it with the strategy we are more comfortable with: producing few and investing everything. Neither is better. They are two answers to the same question, which is how a living thing turns its own short existence into something that outlasts it.

We tend to romanticize the second answer. We tend to look away from the first.

But here is a thought that has been following me around since I saw this: the first strategy is not the absence of care. It is care performed at a scale that makes it invisible to us. The effort of building a body that can carry thousands of futures at once is not nothing. The patience of keeping them safe until the right moment is not nothing. The release itself, whatever that looks like, is not nothing.

We just do not have a vocabulary for tenderness this large.

And so we call it biology and move on.

I do not think we should move on.

Think about what it takes to be that small. A creature that begins life too slight to be seen properly without leaning in. Too light to disturb the surface it lands on. Too numerous to be named, counted, or individually mourned.

Now think about the odds those creatures are born into.

Open water is not a nursery. It is an enormous, indifferent, hungry place. Almost everything in it is either looking for food or being food. The idea that a new arrival, barely formed and almost weightless, could hold its own in that arithmetic should sound ridiculous.

And yet here they are.

Here is where I will put my one honest limit on this post, because I respect you too much to bluff. I cannot tell you what happens to them afterward. I do not know the name of the animal, the place, the owner of the water, or the story behind the person holding the camera. The file I was given carries only a handful of words in its title and ten seconds of footage, and I refuse to invent a backstory to make this more dramatic than it is.

What I can tell you is that the footage does not need one.

It is the rare kind of clip where the less you know going in, the harder it lands.

So let me tell you what to bring with you, instead of what to expect.

Bring patience for the first second. It looks like something ordinary. It is not.

Bring your full attention, because this is not a video that rewards half-watching on a commute with the sound off. The movement in the frame is the story, and it is subtle enough that a distracted eye will treat it as texture.

Bring a willingness to be a little unsettled. I mean that in the best possible way. Some beauty is comfortable. Some beauty makes the back of your neck prickle because it reminds you how little of the world you actually understand.

And bring a second viewing. The first pass is for shock. The second is for meaning.

Let me tell you a small story about attention.

When I was learning to notice things, the best advice I ever got was embarrassingly simple: look at the smallest thing in the room and assume it is more important than it seems. Not because it always is. Because the habit of assuming it might be trains your eyes to stay open.

Most of the world's great dramas are small. A seed splitting. A cell dividing. A decision made by a creature with a brain the size of a grain of rice. We keep waiting for the grand scenes in nature to happen on grand scales, with thunder and migration and teeth, and we miss the fact that the real engine of the planet runs on moments exactly like this one.

Quiet. Brief. Easily scrolled past.

Which is the actual reason I am writing this at such length. Not to inflate a ten-second clip into an epic. To argue that ten seconds can hold more than we usually give them credit for, if we agree to stop moving long enough to find out.

There is a version of you that will see this post, think "shrimp," and keep scrolling. I understand that version. I was that version.

But consider what you would be skipping.

You would be skipping an animal most people reduce to a single word and a single use. You would be skipping a scene that sits at the boundary between something we call a farm and something we call a wild thing. You would be skipping the one situation in the whole animal kingdom where a single parent might be responsible for more beginnings than a small town has residents.

You would be skipping the evidence that the thing on your plate once had a first day.

That is not a guilt trip. I am not here to tell you what to eat, what to buy, or what to feel about either. I am saying something more modest and, I think, more durable: the more you know about where a living thing starts, the harder it becomes to be careless about the world it starts in.

And that holds whether you eat shrimp every week or have never touched one in your life.

There is another contrast hiding in this clip, and it is the one that kept me up that night.

On one side: a mother, a body, a lifetime of instinct, doing something that cannot be taught or rushed.

On the other side: a crowd of arrivals who have no idea what any of this means. They do not know she exists in the way you know your own parent exists. They do not know the water is dangerous. They do not know they are small.

Between those two sides sits the entire emotional weight of the video. One party knows what is at stake in the way an animal can know anything. The other knows nothing at all.

Is that tragic? Is it beautiful? Is it just how the world is built?

Different people will tell you different things, and I would genuinely like to hear yours.

I know what I felt. It was something close to vertigo. The sense that I was looking at a hinge in time, the exact place where one chapter closes and a thousand new ones open, and nobody involved had any idea I was watching.

It reminded me that I am surrounded, constantly, by moments like this that happen without an audience. Right now, somewhere, hundreds of them are unfolding in ponds, tanks, rivers, tide pools, and puddles. Nobody is filming. Nobody is writing threads about them. They happen anyway, with a regularity that should humble every one of us.

The only reason this one reached you is that somebody pointed a lens at the right place and held still.

Think about how rare that is. Think about how many seconds of the living world go unrecorded for every one that gets captured. Then think about the decision to hold still instead of reaching in, instead of narrating, instead of doing anything at all except letting the moment be what it was.

There is restraint in that. A kind of respect.

And the footage rewards it.

Now let me say something that may sound like a tangent, but it is not.

Every system humans build tries to reduce uncertainty. We insure, we schedule, we forecast, we back up. We spend an astonishing share of our lives making sure that outcomes are predictable and losses are small.

The animal kingdom mostly runs on the opposite principle. It accepts enormous loss as the price of continuity. It does not try to save every individual. It tries to make sure that, in aggregate, something gets through.

Seen from our side of the glass, that feels cold. Seen from the other side, it may be the most hopeful design ever invented. Because it says: you do not need guarantees. You need enough chances.

Watch the clip with that idea in mind and something shifts. What looks like a spectacle of fragility starts to look like a spectacle of nerve.

Nerve is the word I keep landing on.

It takes nerve to carry that much life and let it go. It takes nerve to enter a world that was not built for you. It takes nerve, from the other direction, to stand behind a camera and let a scene play out without intervening, even if some part of you is dying to step in.

That last one matters more than it sounds.

We live in an era of constant intervention. See a problem, fix it. See a gap, fill it. See a silence, talk over it. The reflex to manage everything is so strong that watching something unfold on its own terms feels almost radical.

This video is an exercise in not managing.

You are not told what to feel. You are not guided. You are simply placed in front of an event and trusted to bring your own humanity to it. And I think that trust is the reason the clip travels so well. People do not share things that tell them what to think. They share things that make them feel like they noticed something on their own.

So here is my honest prediction. You will watch it, and your first reaction will be some version of "wait, what." You will watch it again to make sure you saw it right. Then you will think of one specific person you need to send it to, and you will already know who it is.

That is how a ten-second video becomes a conversation.

A few questions I would love you to carry into it, not as homework but as lenses.

What does it mean for a parent to give life to more than it could ever personally protect?

Where does responsibility begin when the one you are responsible for is too small to ask for it?

If you could see how many futures start in a single body, would you treat the idea of "one life" differently?

And the one I cannot shake: how much of what we call indifference is really just distance?

Because that is the quiet accusation underneath all of this. Not anger. Not blame. Just the observation that the creatures we see least are the ones we think about least, and that this is a fact about our eyesight, not about their worth.

A video like this closes the distance, if only for a few seconds. And once the distance is closed, it is very hard to pretend it was ever as wide as we claimed.

I want to be fair to the skeptics, because there are good reasons to be skeptical of posts like this one.

Maybe you think I am making too much of a small animal. Maybe you think shrimp are shrimp, and no amount of careful writing will change that. Maybe you think nature footage is overhyped and every other clip claims to be a revelation.

All fair.

My only request is that you test it. Do not take my word for any of this. I could be wrong about how it will land for you. I could be overreading a handful of frames and a title I cannot even fully translate into a story.

But if I am wrong, you lose ten seconds.

And if I am right, you gain a moment you will describe to someone else tomorrow, probably badly, probably with your hands, probably saying "you just have to see it."

That is the best trade the internet has ever offered me.

Here is something I have noticed about the clips that stay with me for years. They are almost never the loud ones. They are the ones that do something unexpected with scale. A giant thing that moves gently. A tiny thing that moves in a way that makes you rethink what "tiny" means.

This is the second kind.

It takes an animal most of us have stopped really seeing and turns it, for ten seconds, into a reason to look again.

And what you find when you look again is not cute and not horrifying. It is something harder to name. A sense that you have walked in on a process that has been running longer than any of our institutions, any of our religions, any of our stories about ourselves, and that it will keep running long after we have stopped paying attention.

That is a humbling thing to feel on a Wednesday.

Here is a thought experiment, and it is the last one I will ask of you.

Imagine you could only keep one image from an entire year of watching the internet. Not the funniest, not the loudest, not the most shared. The one that actually rearranged something in your head.

Most people, if they are honest, would not pick a spectacle. They would pick a quiet frame that made them feel the size of the world for half a second, and then slipped away before they could explain it.

That is the category this clip belongs to.

It is not trying to win an argument. It is not selling a cause. It is not asking for money, outrage, or a follow. It simply exists, small and strange and entirely sincere, and it leaves a mark anyway.

I think the reason is that sincerity has become scarce. When something shows up with no angle at all, we do not know what to do with it, so we do the one thing we can: we pay attention.

Give it ten seconds of that.

Let me widen the lens one more time, because the clip raises a question that has nothing to do with shrimp and everything to do with us.

How do we decide which births deserve our attention?

We celebrate certain beginnings loudly. Human babies, puppies, the occasional panda cub with a publicist. Those arrivals come wrapped in ceremony, because we have decided they matter.

Then there are the beginnings we never think about. The ones that happen in the dark, in the water, in the margins. They outnumber the celebrated ones by a factor that would embarrass a statistician, and they are every bit as real.

Is it possible that the ranking is ours alone? That the planet itself sees no difference between a birth with a name and a birth without one?

I do not have a tidy answer. I have a feeling, and the feeling is that the more of these quiet beginnings I let myself witness, the less I trust my own ranking system.

There is a line of thought in ecology that says the health of a habitat is measured not by its largest animals but by the abundance of its smallest. Where the small things flourish, everything above them can. Where they vanish, the whole structure starts to wobble.

Seen that way, a scene like this is not trivia. It is infrastructure. It is the base layer of a living system doing exactly what it exists to do.

And we are watching it on a phone, in a pocket, between a meeting and a message.

That contrast alone should make us pause.

Because here is the strange truth about our moment. We have access to more footage of the natural world than any generation before us, and we are arguably worse at paying attention to it. We swipe past things that would have stopped a naturalist in their tracks a century ago. We treat wonder as content and content as disposable.

I am not scolding. I do it too. I did it right before I found this clip.

What stopped me was not a headline or a thumbnail. It was an almost physical reaction to the scale mismatch, the sense that the frame contained more than a frame should be able to hold.

If you want to understand what I mean, there is only one way. You have to see it for yourself, and you have to let it run without scrolling.

I promise I am not selling you a miracle. I am describing a small, strange, real thing and telling you that it moved me more than most of the carefully engineered content I scroll past in a day.

Real things have that advantage. They do not need to be optimized.

They just need to be noticed.

One more angle, because it is the one most people miss.

We talk about survival as if it were a single event. You survive or you do not. But for the smallest animals, survival is a relay. It is handed from the egg to the first hours, from the first hours to the first week, from the first week to a body that can finally outswim its own fear. Every handoff is a separate gamble with its own odds, and almost nobody is there to cheer at any of them.

That is what makes the opening seconds so loaded. They are not the end of a story and they are not quite the beginning. They are the first handoff, the one where a private, hidden, carried thing becomes a public, exposed, independent thing. Everything after it depends on that moment going the way nature needs it to.

I find that unbearably tender, and I cannot fully explain why.

Maybe it is because we all remember, somewhere beneath memory, what it was to be exposed for the first time. Maybe it is because the scale makes the vulnerability impossible to ignore. Or maybe it is simply that a crowd of anything, when it is this small and this alive, bypasses the argument part of the brain and goes straight to the part that just feels.

Whatever the reason, it works.

And it works without a single word of narration.

Some practical notes before you go, written plainly.

Watch it with the sound on if you can. Not because there is dialogue, but because the absence of it is part of the experience.

Watch it full screen. The scale is the point, and a thumbnail steals it.

Watch it once without thinking, and once while asking yourself what, exactly, you are looking at and what it asks of you.

Then ask yourself whether it changes anything.

For me, it changed the way I think about a word I used to use without a second thought. A small word, a common word, a word I have typed hundreds of times. It now arrives with a little more weight than it used to, and I think that is a good thing.

Weight is what attention gives to the things we used to treat as weightless.

If you are the kind of person who likes to know exactly what you are getting before you press play, I understand, and I am sorry. I have decided to withhold the details on purpose. Not out of cruelty, but because the experience depends on you arriving without a script.

What I can promise is that nothing in it is staged for effect, nothing in it is cruel, and nothing in it will ask you to feel something you do not feel on your own.

It is simply a piece of the living world, shown at close range, for ten seconds, without apology.

There is a kind of person who will watch it and shrug. That is fine too.

But I suspect most people will not shrug. I suspect most people will do what I did.

They will lean in. They will whisper something. They will play it again.

And somewhere in the second viewing, they will feel the thing that is very hard to describe and very easy to recognize: the quiet jolt of realizing that the world is far more generous, far more crowded, and far more astonishing than the version of it we carry around in our heads.

A last honest note. I wrote this without knowing the name of the animal, the pond, or the person who held the camera, and I think that gap is a gift. It means nothing about the clip has been decided for you in advance. No caption can tell you whether to smile, wince, or go quiet. Whatever you feel will be yours. I would rather you trust your own eyes than my adjectives. Ten seconds, no more.

So press play.

Let the ten seconds happen to you.

And when they are over, ask yourself what you just saw, and who you want to show.

𝗜 𝗠𝗘𝗧 𝗔 𝗠𝗔𝗡 𝗪𝗛𝗢 𝗛𝗔𝗗 𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞𝗘𝗗 𝗙𝗢𝗥 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗡𝗜𝗚𝗘𝗥𝗜𝗔𝗡 𝗚𝗢𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗡𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗙𝗢𝗥 𝟯𝟮 𝗬𝗘𝗔𝗥𝗦. 𝗪𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗛𝗘 𝗧𝗢𝗟𝗗 𝗠𝗘 𝗧𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗘𝗗 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗪𝗔𝗬 𝗜 𝗟𝗢𝗢𝗞 𝗔𝗧 𝗢𝗨𝗥 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗡𝗧𝗥𝗬.

I was returning from an engagement one Saturday afternoon when I stopped at a small roadside restaurant to have something to eat.

An elderly man, probably in his early 60s, was sitting at the table beside mine. He had a small nylon bag beside him and kept checking his phone.

He ordered a plate of rice and stew. When the food arrived, he ate a few spoons, stopped and asked the woman serving him to package the remaining food.

A few minutes later, she brought his bill.

It was ₦2,500.

The man searched his pockets, brought out a few crumpled ₦500 notes and started counting.

He had only ₦1,500.

He looked at the woman and said quietly,

"My daughter, please, can you allow me to transfer the remaining ₦1,000 when I get home?"

The woman declined, explaining that she needed cash.

I immediately offered to pay the bill. 

He thanked me and insisted on knowing why I had decided to help a complete stranger.

I smiled and told him it was nothing.

But what he said next caught my attention.

"My son, I used to be a civil servant. I worked for the government for 32 years. I retired believing that the country I had served would at least allow me to live comfortably in my old age."

I listened.

He continued.

"Today, my pension is not enough to buy my monthly medication. My wife has been sick for months, and my children are struggling to survive too."

He paused, looked at me and asked:

"My son, what exactly did I do wrong?"

I couldn't answer.

Then he brought out his phone and showed me his pension account. His arrears had remained outstanding for several months.

He had left home that morning hoping to buy food and return with enough money for his wife's medication.

Before leaving, he held my hand and said something I will never forget.

"When politicians need our votes, they remember the poor. When they get into office, they suddenly forget that we exist."

I stood there quietly.

On my way home, I kept thinking about how many Nigerians are going through similar experiences.

How many pensioners are waiting endlessly for what they worked for?

How many parents are choosing between medication and feeding their children?

How many young graduates are unemployed despite having the qualifications?

How many families are one medical emergency away from financial ruin?

These are not just statistics. They are human beings.

Nigeria cannot continue like this.

We cannot keep rewarding incompetence because a politician belongs to our preferred party, speaks our language or shares our religion.

𝗚𝗢𝗢𝗗 𝗚𝗢𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗡𝗔𝗡𝗖𝗘 𝗜𝗦 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗔 𝗟𝗨𝗫𝗨𝗥𝗬. 𝗜𝗧 𝗜𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗔𝗥𝗘 𝗠𝗜𝗡𝗜𝗠𝗨𝗠 𝗧𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗖𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗭𝗘𝗡𝗦 𝗗𝗘𝗦𝗘𝗥𝗩𝗘.

Our votes must become instruments of accountability, not rewards for political loyalty.

Vote for competence. Vote for character. Vote for accountability.

Above all, 𝗩𝗢𝗧𝗘 𝗙𝗢𝗥 𝗚𝗢𝗢𝗗 𝗚𝗢𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗡𝗔𝗡𝗖𝗘.

Nigeria belongs to all of us.

End.

text:
“What is that? It’s a hand. There’s a body!” Police searched the woods with flashlights, and what they found raised a terrifying question: “Are we dealing with a serial killer?”

Tallahassee, Florida, June 2020. 19 year old activist Toyin Salau is waiting at a bus stop when a man in his 40s sits down beside her. They talk for almost an hour. Then 75 year old Victoria Sims pulls up and offers them both a ride. Known for helping people, Victoria has no idea who she is letting into her car.

Days later, Victoria’s daughter calls 911. Her mother is missing, the apartment door is wide open, and her car is gone. Suspicion turns to Victoria’s grandson Rusty, who is in jail at the time. A neighbor tells investigators that 15 people once stormed Victoria’s home while Rusty stood against a wall smiling. Rusty gives police the name of his friend, 49 year old Aaron Glee.

When officers arrive at Glee’s property, they find Victoria’s car. Nearby, a phone starts ringing inside a trash can. It belongs to Victoria, and her family is still trying to reach her. SWAT officers enter the house and discover Victoria’s body with her hands and feet bound. That night, a police dog leads officers into the woods, where they find a second body. It is Toyin Salau.

Glee had nine felony convictions dating back to 1992. Just days before the killings, he had been arrested twice for battery. He manages to leave town on a bus while police are looking for him, but officers eventually catch him at the bus station in Orlando. During interrogation, Glee confesses to both murders.

In 2023, Aaron Glee pleaded guilty and was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. During the court proceedings, Victoria’s grandson Rusty addresses the man who killed his grandmother: “I forgive you, man, and I hope that you have a blessed day.” Those were the same words that appeared in the strange message connected to the beginning of the investigation.

Do you think Rusty knew more about the murders than he told police?

Georgian Dream propagandist Giorgi Gvimradze, head of the analytical department at Georgia’s Public Broadcaster, has called for Georgia to embrace the Russia-backed 3+3 regional format and seek security guarantees from Russia, Iran and Turkey rather than relying on Western powers.

Speaking on Georgian Public Broadcaster’s First Channel, Gvimradze argued that Georgia should not merely participate in the format but offer Tbilisi as its permanent meeting place.

“Not only should we participate in the 3+3 format, we should propose Tbilisi as its centre. These countries should gather here,” he said.

Gvimradze presented Russia, Iran and Turkey as the dominant powers in an emerging regional order encompassing the South Caucasus and Central Asia.

“I think it is already clear that these three will not allow anyone else into this region,” he declared, arguing that Georgia should help the three powers negotiate the region’s rules.

He also suggested that Georgia’s neutrality and security should be guaranteed by Moscow, Tehran and Ankara.

“Who should give us security guarantees if not our neighbours? Unless these three states guarantee our neutrality and security, it is impossible for us either to declare neutrality or to feel safe,” Gvimradze said.

text:
The most interesting thing about Jon Ossoff becoming the 2028 favourite isn't his age, his fundraising or even that Georgia result. It's the particular Democratic problem he seems capable of solving.

Democrats need someone who can make the party feel younger and more combative without making it feel more ideological. Ossoff has the ability to do both.

Donald Trump won Georgia in 2024. Two years later, Ossoff won his Senate race with roughly 59% of the vote. More importantly, he improved on Kamala Harris's 2024 performance in every county in the state and almost every precinct. He also flipped a dozen counties Trump had carried.

That matters because this wasn't simply a case of Democrats turning out more Democrats. Ossoff won roughly two-thirds of independents and made substantial gains with white voters, while still performing strongly with younger voters and the Democratic base.

That starts to look like the coalition Democrats need to take the White House in 2028. Not a candidate who wins the argument inside the party. A candidate who expands the party.

Ossoff is interesting because he combines things Democrats usually struggle to find in the same politician. 
- He can attack Trump hard without sounding permanently online. 
- He can talk about corruption, healthcare and cost of living in language that travels beyond the progressive base.
- He is young enough to embody generational change without asking voters to sign up to an ideological revolution.
- And he has spent six years building a fairly conventional Senate record rather than becoming defined by one faction of the party.

What Ossoff offers that is different to other potential candiates is generational change without an ideological revolution.

He will be 41 in 2028. That matters less because America needs a young president and more because the Democratic Party badly needs to look like it has moved into a new political era.

Biden represented restoration. Harris represented continuity with that administration. The next Democratic nominee may need to represent a break.

But the danger is that “break” becomes shorthand for moving sharply left or fighting another internal ideological battle. Ossoff offers a cleaner version of change. Different generation. Different communication style. Different energy. But without asking swing voters to accept a dramatically different Democratic Party.

2026 was a good Democratic year. His Republican opponent had serious weaknesses. Winning a Senate race in Georgia is not the same as surviving a presidential primary. But presidential candidates usually become serious because they appear to solve a problem their party has not yet worked out how to solve.

For Democrats, that problem may be becoming clearer. How do you fight Trumpism without making Trump the centre of everything? How do you recover independents without depressing the base? How do you look like change without frightening swing voters? 
How do you bring younger voters back without sounding like politics designed exclusively for younger voters?

Ossoff has just run a campaign that appears to have done all four. It may be an early signal that Democrats are beginning to work out what they want their next candidate to look like.

Not a return. Not a revolution. A reset.

Facade of St Peter's
Designed by Carlo Maderno (1608-1614) The inscription (1m letters) states:
"Paul V Borghese, Roman, Pontiff, in 1612, the seventh of his pontificate, [built] in honour of the Prince of Apostles
On February 10, 1608 the first stone of the Facade was laid and on July 21, 1612 most of the work was completed. It took another two years for the ornamentation, and the basilica was finally consecrated by Urban VIII on November 18, 1926.

From the central balcony, called the Loggia of the Blessings, the new pope is announced with "Habemus Papum", and gives the Urbi et Orbi blessing (to the city and to the world) upon his election and at Christmas and Easter. The relief under the balcony, by Buonvicino, represents Christ giving the keys to St. Peter. The facade is 114.69 metres (376.3 ft) wide and 45.55 metres (149.4 ft) high and is built of travertine.

Above the basic structure is an attic, with eight square windows decorated with small pilasters, surmounted by a balustrade and 13 statues in travertine. The statues on the balustrade represent Christ the Redeemer (19 feet high), St. John the Baptist and 11 Apostles. St. Mathias is included because he is associated with the other "Eleven" in bearing witness to Christ's Resurrection. St Peter is not included because his statue is below in the Square.

When Carlo Maderno started to build the facade, he was bound to the already existing Michelangelo's wings. He just put the attic all around the building, as planned by Michelangelo. That creation looks mighty and dynamic along the west side of the Basilica but is disharmonious in the facade. For this reason, at the far sides of the facade, Maderno planned two bell towers which lightened and soared the building. In 1621, at the death of Paul V, the ground subsided and the building of the two bell towers had to be stopped.

In 1646, Bernini tried to erect the bell towers again, but had to demolish the left-hand side bell tower because of cracks in the facade. Only the bases of the bell towers remain, two archways at the sides of the facade that seem to form part of it while they should have been separated. This was remedied in 1790 by the installation of two clocks designed by Giuseppe Valadier.

The eight gigantic columns of the facade are almost 10ft wide and 90 feet high.

The restoration of the facade and the 13 statues, begun in April 1985, was concluded on November 30, 1986. The original copper cross (1613) in the arms of the statue of the Redeemer, which was replaced by a new one during the work, was given to the Knights of Columbus in recognition of their support for the restoration.

Above the basic structure is an attic, with eight square windows decorated with small pilasters, surmounted by a balustrade and 13 statues in travertine. The statues on the balustrade represent Christ the Redeemer (19 feet high), St. John the Baptist and 11 Apostles. St. Mathias is included because he is associated with the other "Eleven" in bearing witness to Christ's Resurrection. St Peter is not included because his statue is below in the Square.

When Carlo Maderno started to build the facade, he was bound to the already existing Michelangelo's wings. He just put the attic all around the building, as planned by Michelangelo. That creation looks mighty and dynamic along the west side of the Basilica but is disharmonious in the facade. For this reason, at the far sides of the facade, Maderno planned two bell towers which lightened and soared the building. In 1621, at the death of Paul V, the ground subsided and the building of the two bell towers had to be stopped.

In 1646, Bernini tried to erect the bell towers again, but had to demolish the left-hand side bell tower because of cracks in the facade. Only the bases of the bell towers remain, two archways at the sides of the facade that seem to form part of it while they should have been separated. This was remedied in 1790 by the installation of two clocks designed by Giuseppe Valadier.

The eight gigantic columns of the facade are almost 10ft wide and 90 feet high.

The restoration of the facade and the 13 statues, begun in April 1985, was concluded on November 30, 1986. The original copper cross (1613) in the arms of the statue of the Redeemer, which was replaced by a new one during the work, was given to the Knights of Columbus in recognition of their support for the restoration.

“Hey bud, got a flat tire. Can you help me?” An officer stopped to help a stranded driver. Seconds later, he was shot. He had no idea the man standing in front of him was a killer.

New Mexico, Interstate 40, March 15, 2024, around 5 a.m. 35 year old officer Justin Hare is finishing his night shift. Waiting at home are his two young daughters and pregnant wife. One final call comes in. A man is stranded on the roadside with a broken down car.

“Hey bud, got a flat tire. Can you help me?” Hare kindly offers him a ride into town in his patrol car. Seconds later, gunshots ring out. The attacker pushes the wounded officer into the passenger seat and steals his cruiser.

Despite his injuries, Hare manages to press his emergency alarm. Fellow officers give chase, but the patrol car crashes off the road. All they find inside is blood on the seat. For nearly an hour, officers search along the highway before finally finding Justin near an exit. “Brother, hang in there! You're still breathing. Keep fighting!” But he cannot be saved. He has suffered two gunshot wounds to the head and one to the neck.

Investigators soon discover that the BMW abandoned on the roadside belonged to 52 year old Phonesia Machado Fore, a paramedic from South Carolina who had disappeared two days earlier. Her body is found behind an abandoned house, her hands bound and a gunshot wound to the back of her head. The killer is her neighbor, 33 year old Jaremy Smith. He had recently been released from prison after serving eight years for armed robbery and hostage taking.

For two days, police search across the state. A gas station employee in Albuquerque recognizes Smith. His former girlfriend lived there, and he had promised her he would come back. After a chase through residential backyards, officers finally capture him, shooting him four times.

In 2025, Smith pleaded guilty to killing Justin Hare and was sentenced to life in prison. In September 2026, he also pleaded guilty to Phonesia's murder and received a second life sentence without the possibility of parole.

After a case like this, should police officers still stop to help strangers stranded on the road?

text:
The Planet That Vanished—Because Its Neighbor Made It Wobble

For seven years, a scorching gas giant roughly 1,000 light-years away regularly slipped in front of its star, dimming the light just enough for NASA’s TESS telescope to notice. Then, in 2026, the transits simply stopped.

The planet hadn’t been destroyed. It had tilted out of view.

TOI-2535 b is a classic “hot Jupiter”—a Jupiter-sized world racing around its star in only 8.25 days, ten times faster than Mercury orbits the Sun. Its transits were never perfectly regular; they arrived up to six hours early or late, and grew steadily shorter and shallower until they vanished altogether.

UCLA astronomers Samuel Yee, Erik Petigura, and their team realized an unseen neighboring planet is to blame. The two worlds are gravitationally locked in a strong interaction that makes both of their orbits wobble like a spinning top. As TOI-2535 b’s path tilts, it no longer crosses our line of sight—exactly the same geometry that makes total solar eclipses on Earth rare instead of monthly.

“This is the most extreme example we’ve seen,” Yee says. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching.”

The planet is expected to swing back into view in 30 to 50 years. Its hidden companion may appear sooner. The discovery also offers a clue about how the hot Jupiter got so close to its star: the presence of a nearby neighbor suggests it migrated inward more gently through the disk rather than being violently flung onto an eccentric orbit.

It’s a rare, real-time view of planets actively reshaping each other’s paths—proof that planetary systems are not fixed clockwork, but dynamic and ever-changing.

As someone still navigating life in the UK and a new parent whose child is just starting school, I’m genuinely surprised by how the school application process works here.

If you’re applying for a state school in England, you have to apply through your local council, list your preferred schools in order of preference and wait to find out which school your child is offered a place at.

You don’t automatically get a place in the school you choose, even if it’s your first preference.
