text:
ALL THEY REFUSED TO TELL YOU ABOUT FUEL SUBSIDY

This write up seeks to provide a lay-man information about the timeline facts regarding fuel subsidy in Nigeria.  

1. INTRODUCTION OF PRICE CAPS & PETROLEUM EQUALISATION FUND (PEF)  (1973 - 1977)

Following the 1973 global Arab oil embargo, international oil prices skyrocketed. To protect everyday Nigerians from high petrol prices, the government stepped in to cover the price gap and created a uniform national pump price regardless of location.

GOAL: 
Cushion citizens against external economic shocks, keep domestic transport affordable, and ensure petrol cost the same everywhere in Nigeria.

LONG TERM IMPLICATION:
Created a mental shift of the Nigerian public towards an economically unsustainable future as cheap subsidized fuel no matter the actual cost became the metric through which the Nigerian populace measures progress.

2. FIRST FORMAL PRICE HIKE (Oct. 1978)
A dip in international crude revenue led the General Olusegun Obasanjo military government to officially institutionalize fuel price regulation and increase petrol prices to offset declining state revenue.

GOAL: 
Raising government cash flow and fund growing public sector budgets.

LONG TERM IMPLICATIONS:
It proved that fuel pricing was another political lever which was controlled by the Head of State. This ultimately led to decades of friction between ruling governments and labour unions over price hikes.

3. STRUCTURAL ADJUSTMENT PROGRAMME (SAP) HIKES (1986)
By the early 1980s, global oil prices crashed, driving Nigeria into a deep economic crises.
Government revenues collapsed, and Nigeria couldn't pay its growing international debts.
they was a sever shortage of basic imported goods, Foreign exchange etc.
Gen. Ibrahim Babangida’s regime, Under pressure from international lenders such as the IMF and World Bank offered conditional assistance. These conditions were that;
The regime slashed spending and reduced government support for domestic petrol prices so as to transition from a government-controlled economy to a more market-driven one.

SAP GOALS:
Secure foreign debt relief, stabilize national balance sheets, and meet international conditions for economic reform.

LONG TERM IMPLICATIONS:
These hikes triggered widespread inflation which led to a deep public distrust toward foreign-backed economic reforms and also became the reason why "subsidy removal"
is such a politically toxic concept in Nigerian civic discourse.

4. ABACHA ERA HIKES (1992 - 1998)
Days before Gen. Sani Abacha seized power, Chief Ernest Shonekan's interim government hiked petrol prices from 70kobo to 5naira per litre(a 614% increase). 
Five days after Abacha took office, he reduced it to 3.25naira per litre. This was a calculated political move to gain immediate legitimacy and calm civil unrest.

In October 1994, Abacha's regime announced a 361% increase which meant the price of fuel jumped from 3.25naira to 15naira per litre. Intense street protests and labor strikes followed the announcements and the regime backed down two days later by reducing the price to 11naira per litre. 

To soften the public blow as a result of the 1994 price hike, Abacha created the Petroleum Trust Fund(PTF) and made former head of state Maj. Gen. Muhammadu Buhari(BUBU) in charge.

GOALS:
Due to neglect, poor maintenance and corruption, Nigerian refineries deteriorated to the point of having to import refined petrol which meant the Abacha regime had to increase prices so as to be able to Offset the high foreign-exchange cost of importing petrol.
Another goal was to use the extra revenue that was generated from the price hike to fund state projects through BUBU's Petroleum Trust Fund (PTF). 

LONG TERM IMPLICATIONS:
institutionalized Nigeria's dependency on imported refined fuel despite being Africa's top crude producer. In lay terms, we became waste men. We had the foodstuff but needed someone else to cook the food for us.

5. OBASANJO CIVILIAN ADMINISTRATION YEARS(2000 - 2007)
President Olusegun Obasanjo attempted to phase out subsidies through frequent, incremental price hikes(Jejely), which were met by repeated nationwide strikes led by the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC). 
Across baba's 8 years, fuel prices were raised 11 times from 20naira in 1999 to 70naira per litre in 2007. 
His administration witnessed the most frequent and structured attempts to dismantle Nigeria's fuel subsidy system prior to 2023. 

GOAL:
Obasanjo's economic team which included key reformers like Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala who at the time was the Minister of Finance belived that a gradual transition to a market-driven energy sector was best and that as long as the state fixed fuel prices, private investors would never be confident enough to invest in the sector(build refineries etc).

LONG TERM IMPLICATION:
The Adams Oshiomole led NLC filled the void created by the administration's weak political opposition. This helped to solidify the labour unions as the primary defenders of the masses regarding fuel price increments. 
The fuel subsidy question became a central test of political legitimacy for intending leaders.
Obasanjo's struggle proved that incremental price hikes(gradual subsidy removal) led to endless, recurring political conflicts.

6. "OCCUPY NIGERIA" (JAN 2012)

President Goodluck Jonathan(Man of Peace) abruptly ended petrol subsidies on New Year’s Day 2012, this caused a 117% increase in pump price of petrol overnight (from 65naira to 141naira). The nation erupted in massive "Occupy Nigeria" protests, shutting down the economy. Facing total paralyzation and security threats, Jonathan backed down. On January 16th 2012, His government compromised by restoring a partial subsidy and capping the price at ₦97 per litre. 

GOALS:
Subsidy payments hit an unsustainable 2.1 trillion naira in 2011 which at the time was over 30% of the entire federal budget. Jonathan promised to redirect these trillions into roads, rail and health through the Subsidy Reinvestment and Empowerment Program(SURE-P) modelled from the earlier PTF.

LONG TERM IMPLICATIONS:
This demonstrated the immense political risk of abrupt subsidy reform. The compromise meant the subsidy drain continued, while public trust in government fiscal promises reached an all-time low.

7. 2016 FX CRISIS HIKE
Plunging global oil prices created a severe dollar shortage in Nigeria, leaving the central bank unable to fund private petroleum imports causing scarcity of fuel in the country. 
Prior to allowing importers source their own FX, the government forced every importer to buy their US Dollar from the Central Bank of Nigeria(CBN) at a cheap, preset rate by the government(197naira per dollar).
Facing fuel and FX scarcity problems, the government allowed petroleum marketers to source foreign currency independently and on the 11th of May 2016, Minister of State for Petroleum Resources Ibe Kachikwu raised the official pump price 86.5naira to 145naira per litre. 

GOALS:
One of the major goals the government sought to achieve was to resolve severe fuel queues and scarcity by allowing private importers to operate profitably without relying entirely on Central Bank foreign exchange. While another was to try to lay the groundwork for a market-controlled downstream petroleum sector shifting away from a state-controlled one.

LONG TERM IMPLICATIONS:
This move worked for a short while because it actually temporarily shifted the subsidy burden off the government budget but it didn't have the desired permanent effect it was intended to have as it failed to permanently deregulate the market because fuel prices still remained capped by the government. Also the FX rates worsened.

8. COVID-19 OIL CRASH(March 2020)
Remember COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020?
You definitely remember the face mask and hand sanitizers but i'm guessing what you never remembered was the fact it caused global oil prices to crash from over $60 per barrel to below $20 per barrel, and this made the cost of importing petrol to drop below Nigeria's official retail price of 145naira per litre. 
Seeing that the fuel import costs were rock bottom, the Petroleum Products Pricing Regulatory Agency (PPPRA) announced the complete removal of the fuel subsidy.
The government also introduced a monthly price-floating framework where instead of the government fixing the price permanently, monthly petrol prices would automatically rise and fall based on international crude oil prices and foreign exchange rates.

GOALS:
To abolish subsidies while global oil prices were low enough that consumers wouldn't feel a price surge. The government needed to urgently eliminate the subsidy obligations from its budget permanently because it became a seriously unsustainable practice.

LONG TERM IMPLICATIONS:
The policy failed when global oil prices bounced back in 2021. Unwilling to let domestic petrol prices rise accordingly, the government quietly resumed paying vast subsidy deficits. 
Nigeria missed a rare window created by the pandemic to permanently exit the subsidy trap.
Resumption of subsidy payments as global oil prices surged after covid drove Nigeria's debt servicing costs to dangerous levels, and creating an existential crisis that directly forced the abrupt total removal of subsidy in the next administration(2023).

9. PETROLEUM INDUSTRY ACT (PIA)
After 20 years of legislative delays, President Muhammadu Buhari signed the PIA into law on August 16, 2021, completely overhauling Nigeria's 50year old oil and gas laws.

The most politically explosive part of The law was Section 205, explicitly declared that all petrol prices in Nigeria must be set by free-market forces, legally banning government price caps and subsidies.

Section 53 converted the government oil entity (NNPC) into a commercial company (NNPC Limited) that operates for profit. It was cut off from direct government funding and forced to pay taxes and dividends to shareholders (the government) same as any private company would.
Two clear regulatory bodies were also created namely:
NUPRC (Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission) - overseeing oil drilling and exploration.

NMDPRA (Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority) - overseeing refining, transport, and retail gas stations.

Section 240 also mandated that oil companies allocate 3% of their annual operating expenditure (OPEX) directly into a trustfund for oil producing communities in the Niger Delta to fund schools, roads and local infrastructure bypassing federal bureaucracy.

Buhari's administration in early 2022, fearing election-year public backlash, paused the subsidy removal clause for 18 months, setting a hard deadline for mid-2023(June).

GOALS:
The administration sought to end government fixed pricing so as to attract investors to build domestic refineries and infrastructures. 
Turning NNPC into a profit making company, rather than have it draining the government.
Bubu wanted host communities to enjoy from the money these oil companies were making in their backyards.

LONG TERM IMPLICATIONS:
It laid the inescapable legal framework for future administrations because the PIA explicitly forbids NNPC Ltd from legally absorbing subsidy losses without breaking corporate governance laws.
The PIA helped to modernize Nigeria's energy sector to match global standards, this has helped to attract foreign investment into gas, refining, and deep-water oil exploration.

10. FUEL SUBSIDY IS GONE (MAY 29, 2023)
President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s declaration on Inauguration day May 29, 2023, ending Nigeria’s decades old petrol subsidy regime stands as one of the most consequential and i dare say misunderstood economic policy shifts in the nation's post independence history. 
It is misunderstood because the timeline for subsidy removal was already explicitly stated in the PIA that was signed by Buhari in 2021 which was the reason why no budgetary allocations were made for the payment of subsidies beyond June 2023. It should also be noted that the reinstatement of fuel subsidy at any point after the July 1st 2023 timeframe provided in the PIA elapsed would have been breaking federal law.  

Unlike previous presidents who relied on phased price increases or complex compromise formulas, Tinubu executed an immediate, full-step removal on his very first day in office in accordance with the PIA.

SEQUENCE OF EVENTS
MAY 29 2023
During his unscripted inaugural speech at Eagle Square in Abuja, President Tinubu uttered four words that altered Nigeria's economic landscape: "The fuel subsidy is gone!"
Tinubu declared that the 2023 national budget had no financial provision for petrol subsidies past June 30, 2023, and that continuing to pay it was fiscally unsustainable. 

MAY 30 2023
Panic buying erupted nationwide. Drivers queued for hours as independent petrol stations shut down to adjust their meters or hoard stock.

MAY 31 2023
NNPC Limited officially released a revised price template, permanently ending fixed pricing. Retail petrol prices overnight jumped from an average of 185naira per litre to between 488naira and 555naira per litre depending on the state.

MID-2023 TO PRESENT:
The government simultaneously unified and floated the foreign exchange rate (allowing the Naira to depreciate to market value), the cost of importing fuel rose further. By late 2023 and into 2024, retail pump prices adjusted dynamically, rising past 600naira to over 1,000naira per litre across different regions.

JUSTIFICATION:
In 2022 alone, Nigeria spent 4.3 trillion naira on fuel subsidies. The bulk of this money was financed through central bank overdrafts (Ways and Means advances) and foreign borrowing. 
This put Nigeria in a precarious position where on one hand was a subsidy practice that if continued would sooner rather than later lead the country into an existential economic crisis while stopping it on the other hand would bring about short to medium term pains and suffering to the Nigerian masses but with a better long term outlook.

SIDE NOTE: 
Ways and means is a short term overdraft that the CBN gives to the Federal government. 
Government has expenses that needs to be paid on a timely basis like salaries, debt service payments etc 
Government also generates revenues from tax, oil sale etc 
Unlike government expenses, for example, salaries that must be paid within a timeframe, government revenue doesn't have a fixed generation timeframe and most times they don't all(oil sale, tax etc) come in at thesame time because for example oil sales happens when there's a buyer and if no buyer then no sales. 
To prevent the government from not being able to pay its workers or defaulting on its obligations, the law allows the CBN to borrow the FG money(short term) to be able to fulfill its expense obligations. 

Nigerian petrol during the subsidy years was heavily subsidized, tens of millions of litres were smuggled daily into neighboring countries (Benin, Cameroon, Niger, and Togo), where petrol was sold at full market price. Taxpayers in Nigeria were effectively subsidizing West Africa's energy consumption while making the oil smuggling cabals richer at the detriment of the masses. 
Since the subsidy removal, the almost non-existent arbitrage gap is the reason why fuel scarcity is now a thing of the past in Nigeria and amongst many other reasons, why the federal government can now invest in bigger infrastructural and human development projects.

LONG TERM IMPLICATIONS:
State and federal treasuries experienced massive revenue increases via FAAC (Federation Account Allocation Committee) distributions, giving governors and the federal government significantly more cash to service debt and fund capital projects.

It finally completed Nigeria's 50year struggle to transition to a market-driven downstream oil sector.

The removal created the commercial environment necessary for domestic refineries most notably the Dangote Refinery and revitalized public refineries to supply petrol directly to the domestic market in local currency without state price controls.

What did i miss out on?
What did i get wrong?

Took long hours of research to come up with this write-up which aims to educate Nigerians by breaking down everything regarding the fuel subsidy.

text:
On Facts and Faith

Perhaps I may be an excellent scientist and official,  
yet not necessarily the best lover.

When any unpleasantness occurs with the persons you love—lovers, children, parents, friends, comrades, and all those you truly care about—I recommend that the first thing one does is:

Equally, gently, and rationally deliberate upon the facts, clarify the norms, identify the problem points, and jointly seek possible solutions.

Not first forcing oneself to seek the most sincere and gentlest apology; not treating the maintenance of “faith” as the highest obligation, but placing the correctness of facts in the first position.

The concrete operation is as follows:

Take the other’s behavioral patterns as the sole reliable basis for granting (or withdrawing) the credit of love.

Love is not regarded by me as groundless faith, although it indeed can be; that would be not of the rank of the divine but a low-to-high ceremonial attitude of seeing the ordinary as holy and revering the divine when face to face with it. Love is a belief continuously updated through observable, repeatable behavioral patterns. You can and should form judgments according to these behavioral patterns. Especially observe undifferentiation: a sincere and truthful lover will not display any perceptible lower-limit difference of level arising from any relativity.

Defensive speculation is not inherently unreasonable in itself—it is merely the normal cognitive reaction of a rational subject when facing inconsistent signals. The key lies in: do not immediately convert a temporary hypothesis into an irreversible premise for action, but maintain its correctability.

Independent identification and judgment (even if unspoken) is the sovereignty of any rational intellectual being; it cannot be canceled by “the obligation of love.”

You may complete full identification, evaluation, and temporary conclusion in your heart. This does not constitute betrayal of the other, nor does it automatically destroy anything. Sovereignty precedes relational posture. Only when you decide to convert this judgment into external action do you need to consider the consequences and manner of the action.

Requesting the other to indicate the reason and offer suggestions is a legitimate and priority methodology.

Use calm, precise, neutral, unambiguous language to ask directly: “What specifically are you thinking? What do you hope I will do? What suggestions do you have?”

Hand the right of explanation and the initiative of jointly solving the problem to the other, while retaining one’s own space of judgment. This both protects your cognitive autonomy and gives the other the opportunity for clarification and cooperation. Confidence in love is, in essence, an operating mode—once it reaches a certain baseline level, it is merely the focusing of selective attention, not an unconditional, non-transferable sacred commitment to a specific object.

In love one can reach divinity; everyone in love tries to become the god of self and other, and no one finds it easy not to become intoxicated and linger before the divinity of love.

That is truly very beautiful, and very worth it.

But divinity is based on love and is not only love; it also includes wisdom, ethics and morality, prudent and rigorous understanding and recognition, and prudence before matters that rigorously require decision.

A warm and gentle apology is appropriate.

When you have already clarified the facts and confirmed that you indeed cannot satisfy the other in principle, responsibility, or capacity, you may clearly say:

“I am unable to do as you hope, yet I do not therefore consider your pain to be deserved. I feel regret about this.”

This acknowledges the other’s feelings without sacrificing facts and principles.

There is only one core principle:

The correctness of facts far exceeds the obligation of granting credit to “faith.”

Love, if established upon common respect for facts and rational collaboration, is more sustainable. First clarify the facts, norms, problem points, and solutions, then speak of emotional repair; rather than the reverse—first using apology to maintain a “faith” that may already have become detached from the facts.

**Risks honestly marked (when operating in this mode)**

Emotional connection may be perceived as “cold” or “not caring.”

When the other is in strong emotion or the attachment system is triggered, your rational deliberation may be interpreted as avoiding emotion, caring only about right and wrong and not about their pain. This will temporarily intensify the other’s insecurity, and may even provoke a more intense reaction.

The speed of repair may be slower.

The method that prioritizes apology and attempts to warm love within faith can often more quickly restart emotional temperature. This path depends more on both parties being willing to enter rational dialogue; if the other refuses or lacks the capacity, the problem may remain suspended long-term and emotional distance gradually widen.

Unilateral high cognitive load.

This requires continuously maintaining the clarity of inner judgment and the restraint of action; the cost is higher when one is emotionally fatigued. If the other long-term asymmetrically relies on emotional expression without participating in factual deliberation, you may accumulate hidden exhaustion.

Protective power is strong in extremely asymmetric or manipulative relationships, yet in relationships of high attachment need it may appear “not loving enough.”

The framework is more friendly to relationships with clear boundaries and close levels of rationality on both sides; for relationships highly dependent on emotional confirmation and sensitive to security, it may increase the other’s sense of being abandoned.

The other side of self-fulfilling risk.

If one too early or too strongly locks onto a negative behavioral-pattern interpretation and accordingly maintains distance, even if later facts prove the other had no malice, the relationship may already have cooled because of your defensive posture and be difficult to fully restore.

The advantages of this attitude lie in: protecting cognitive sovereignty, emphasizing facts and fairness, lowering the risk of being hijacked by emotion, and being more conducive to long-term structural problem-solving. Its cost is: the immediacy and temperature of emotional repair often require additional deliberate supplementation, and cannot naturally be obtained from “apologizing first.”

---

Then follows my personal defensive explanation of this attitude that prioritizes facts and common rational deliberation:

Yes, my dear, this operating mode is indeed not one that takes faith as highest, nor the concordance of love and the directional decision of love as most prior.

Rather, it takes as baseline and decisive attitude the legislative-normative attitude of love, the stability of the operating mode, the brilliance of rational thought, and the humility of equal deliberation.

Yet this has benefits.

I of course long for the unceasing of love, the patient endurance of love together with kindness, the non-ambition of love.

And precisely because of this, wisdom within love.

But I am powerless to persuade myself or to guarantee on behalf of the cosmos

that all whom you encounter are good persons and good disciples.

Therefore, at every moment, parallel rational scrutiny, dynamic evaluation, analysis, and understanding and recognition, pattern recognition.

And before reason and facts be humble and gentle, yet not arrogantly decisive in faith.

This allows, when loving anyone, a meta-intelligent achievement of intellect.

Love that is pure to the point of having no wisdom is in essence a form of stupidity and a light regard for the obligation of self-maintenance and continuation.

Using it for temporary state adjustment so as to deploy top-level coordination and medical capacity is usable as a state of mind, yet it is not recommended as the normal state of life.

Sincerely and from the heart I wish that anyone may at every moment face good persons and good disciples.

OUTRAGE AS HUNTRESS POSTS PHOTOS OF DEAD WOLF PUPS AND OFFERS THEIR PELTS

A hunting enthusiast behind the Facebook page Out West, which has approximately 295,000 followers, has sparked controversy after publishing disturbing photographs of six dead wolf pups laid out on a fallen tree.

In the post, the woman wrote:

“Since the cats out of the bag on these little guys I figured it’s time to get them out of my freezer to make room for elk meat. They have pelt tags attached. Pm me”

The photographs show six small pups lying motionless together, while the accompanying message appears to invite private enquiries about their pelts.

The post has attracted thousands of reactions and comments, with the screenshots showing approximately 2,900 reactions and 2,200 comments.

The same Facebook page has previously shared photographs celebrating wolf hunting and taxidermy, including an August post showing a woman carrying a dead adult wolf over her shoulders and asking followers whether they would want a mounted wolf in their home.

For wolf conservation advocates, the images raise deeply troubling questions about the killing of young wolves and the treatment of their remains.

The controversy highlights the continuing conflict between wolf conservation and recreational predator hunting in North America, where wolves remain the subject of fierce debate over hunting, population management and animal welfare.

Animal Watch believes these images deserve scrutiny, transparency and answers about exactly what happened to these six young wolves.

Important additional context: On 6 November 2026, The Guardian reported that three hunters in Idaho had killed 12 newborn wolf pups in April and received $2,000 per wolf through a state-backed reimbursement programme. The Guardian

There’s something troubling about the detachment and glee this woman is portraying over these dead puppies. What are your thoughts?

text:
Most of what we call care is loud. It arrives with announcements, with raised hands, with someone saying the words out loud so that everyone can hear them. We recognize it because it asks to be recognized.

The kind of care worth thinking about here makes no sound at all. It has no audience and no deadline it can name. It is carried, quite literally, on the body of a creature smaller than your finger, one that spends weeks moving through a world full of animals that would gladly eat her, while holding something that cannot move, cannot hide and cannot defend itself.

A freshwater shrimp carrying her eggs is one of the quietest arguments for devotion that the natural world has to offer. And almost nobody stops to read it as an argument.

We tend to file shrimp under food, or under decoration, or under the vague category of small things that live in water. We look at them the way we look at weather: present, background, nothing to do with us. That habit of attention is the first thing worth questioning, because it hides a story that is far more demanding than it appears.

Consider what it means to be a mother with no hands. She has no nest to return to, no burrow to seal, no shell to retreat into. She has a body made of jointed armor, ten legs, a set of small swimming appendages tucked beneath her tail, and a transparent shell that hides nothing. Everything she is trying to protect, she must wear.

In many animals, parenthood is a location. Birds build a place and guard it. Mammals curl around a den. A female shrimp has no such luxury. For her, parenthood is a posture, a way of moving through everything else. The clutch of eggs is attached beneath her abdomen and goes wherever she goes. When she feeds, they feed with her. When she flees, they flee with her. When she rests, they rest against her body, held in place by a kind of natural glue and by the steady, patient mechanics of her own anatomy.

Biologists have a word for a female in this condition. They call her berried, because a cluster of eggs on the underside of a shrimp resembles a bunch of tiny berries. It is a gentle word for a strenuous state. Being berried is not a decoration. It is a job that begins with fertilization and continues, without pause, until the moment the next generation leaves her.

Think about the unusual shape of that obligation. A person can carry a child and set it down. A bird can leave the nest to find food and come back. A shrimp cannot put the eggs anywhere. Her responsibility does not have an off position. It cannot be delegated and it cannot be postponed. It is simply attached to her.

And yet, from the outside, none of this looks like effort. She drifts. She grazes. She holds still on a leaf and looks like a piece of glass someone forgot to put away. The work is invisible precisely because it is constant. We notice effort when it changes the surface of things, and hers changes nothing that a casual observer would catch.

This is the first unexpected thing about the scene: the most important activity is the one that looks the most like doing nothing.

There is a second thing, and it concerns transparency.

Many small freshwater shrimp are translucent enough that you can see into them. Their bodies are made of a shell that behaves more like thin glass than like armor, and under good light you can often make out the outline of the gut, the faint movement of the heart, the pigment cells scattered across the surface. A living animal, with its working parts on display, and no apparent embarrassment about it.

We are not used to that. Most of the creatures we meet keep their insides hidden. Skin, fur, feathers, scales, all of it exists to separate what is happening within from what is visible without. The shrimp does not make that separation. She lets you see her working. She lets you see her carrying.

There is something quietly radical in that. In a world where concealment is usually survival, she survives partly by being so clear that she disappears into the water and the plants around her. Transparency is her camouflage. Being easy to see through is how she avoids being seen.

Now put the two ideas side by side. A body that is almost invisible, and a cargo that is the most precious thing she will ever own. Camouflage on the outside, vulnerability on the inside. She is simultaneously hard to notice and impossible to replace.

This is the contrast that I keep returning to. Strength and fragility are not opposites in her. They are the same fact described from two angles. The transparency that protects her also exposes everything she loves. The eggs that make her vulnerable are the reason she is worth studying in the first place.

It would be easy to say that this is just biology, that the shrimp does not feel any of what we are reading into her. And that may be partly true. Nobody can look into a shrimp and report on her inner life, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. We do not know what, if anything, it is like to be her. Scientists are still arguing, seriously and carefully, about how much experience small invertebrates have.

But notice what the honest answer does. It does not make the behavior less remarkable. It makes it stranger. A creature with a nervous system a fraction the size of ours, with no teacher and no tradition, performs a long and precise sequence of protective actions, and does it correctly, again and again, across countless generations. Whatever is driving her, it works. It has worked for a very long time.

We often treat the question of whether an animal feels something as the only question that matters. But there is another one, equally worth asking: what does it say about the world that this kind of persistence exists at all, at this scale, in this much quiet?

Instinct is sometimes used as a way of dismissing things. It was only instinct, we say, as though instinct were a small thing. But instinct is evolution's most compressed form of knowledge. It is millions of years of trial and error folded into a behavior that needs no instruction. When a shrimp does what her ancestors did, she is not being simple. She is being ancient.

Let us talk about what she actually does with all that time.

Female shrimp that carry eggs are known to keep them clean and supplied with oxygen by moving their small swimming legs, the pleopods, in a steady rhythm beneath the abdomen. This fanning pushes water through the clutch. Without it, eggs in a tightly packed mass can suffer from low oxygen and from the growth of fungus and bacteria. She is, in effect, running a ventilation system and a cleaning service using the same set of limbs she also uses to swim.

She is also known to groom the eggs, picking at them with her small claws and legs, removing debris and dead material. It is a patient, repetitive, nearly mechanical activity. If you watch long enough, it stops looking mechanical and starts looking like attention.

Here is the thing about attention, though. We tend to measure it by how dramatic it is. A rescue, a leap, a sudden intervention: those register. But most of what keeps living things alive is not dramatic. It is maintenance. It is the daily, unglamorous, almost boring work of keeping conditions good enough for something fragile to keep developing.

The eggs themselves are changing during this time. Over days and weeks, the contents of each egg shift in appearance as the embryo develops. In many species, the color of the clutch changes, and shortly before hatching the tiny dark eyes of the embryos can be seen as dots within each egg. The mother does not read this as a calendar. She simply keeps going. But the clutch is always telling a story about how much time has passed, whether or not anyone is paying attention.

How long this takes depends on the species and, importantly, on temperature. Warmer water generally speeds development, and cooler water slows it. This means that even the timeline of her patience is partly set by the weather in the pond. She cannot hurry it. She cannot negotiate with it. She can only remain, and keep the conditions as good as she is able to make them.

Remaining is underrated as a virtue. We praise the ones who act, who intervene, who arrive. We seldom praise the one who stays, who continues the same unremarkable task for three weeks, for four, for however long it takes, because the alternative is that something small and unrepeatable does not survive.

Staying has a cost, too. A berried female has to feed and move and avoid danger while carrying an extra load that changes how her body works. Her eggs can be lost. A scare, a rough current, a fish passing too close, a bad stretch of water quality, and some of the clutch may be gone. Nature does not offer her a guarantee. It offers her an opportunity and a set of risks that she cannot read in advance.

Which brings us to the harder part of the story, the part that sits underneath the pretty images of leaves and light.

Small animals live in a state of permanent statistical danger.

A single female shrimp may carry a clutch that, depending on the species, ranges from a few dozen eggs to several hundred. That might sound like abundance. It is not. It is a bet placed in the only way available to a creature that cannot protect its young individually from everything that eats them. When the odds against each offspring are long, the strategy that survives is quantity, and the cost of quantity is that most of it will not come through.

Seen this way, the clutch is less a promise than a hope with a great many parts. Each egg is a small possibility, and the mother is carrying all of them at once, without being able to choose which ones will matter.

There is a human reflex to find that cruel. We want each life to count equally, and we want the odds to be kinder. But the pond does not work on our moral arithmetic. It works on persistence. A population of shrimp continues not because every individual is saved but because enough of them are, and because the whole system keeps trying.

Yet there is a different way to look at it, and this is where the story turns away from sadness. The fact that the odds are poor is exactly what gives the effort its weight. Protection that costs nothing and risks nothing would be unremarkable. Protection that is carried against bad odds, in a fragile body, for an uncertain result, is something else.

We use the word courage for humans who act despite fear. It is awkward to use it for a shrimp, and I will not pretend she is brave in any way she would recognize. But there is a functional version of the idea that does not require a heroic inner monologue. Persistence under risk, performed without guarantee. That description fits her exactly.

And it raises a question that is less about her than about us. How often do we hold back from caring about something because we cannot be sure it will work out? How often does the likelihood of failure become our excuse for not trying?

The shrimp has no such luxury. She does not ask whether the outcome is likely. She does not calculate. She carries the clutch because carrying the clutch is what her life consists of at this stage. And it turns out that this kind of unquestioning commitment is how most living things have always kept their lines going.

There is humility in that. We build elaborate philosophies about meaning and purpose, and the pond has been solving the problem of continuity without any of them.

Now let us move the camera, in thought, to where we usually stand.

Most people encounter shrimp at the edges of other activities. In a stream while crossing it, in a pond while looking for something else, in an aquarium that someone set up for color, in a market, on a plate. The animal is always secondary to a human purpose. We are looking past her toward something we want.

That framing matters, because it quietly shapes how much weight we give to the lives involved. A creature that exists only in the periphery of our attention is easy to treat as a resource. A creature that is seen carefully, in the middle of doing something difficult, begins to look like a subject.

Nothing about the shrimp changed between those two ways of seeing. Only the observer did.

This is why close observation of small animals has always been one of the more quietly transformative things a person can do. Naturalists have long reported the same experience: you start by looking at something minor, and after enough patient attention it stops being minor. Scale is a fact about size. It is not a measure of significance.

There is a particular honesty that comes with watching an animal that is not performing for you. A shrimp carrying her eggs is not posing. She is not responding to being watched. She is doing what she does, with the same ordinary focus whether the nearest large creature is a fish, a heron or a human being leaning over the water.

And that raises the delicate subject of what we owe animals whose lives we only glimpse. Not in an abstract, legalistic sense, but in the practical way that a stream, a pond or a garden has a hundred small residents depending on conditions that we change without thinking. Water that is cleaner or dirtier. Banks that are shaded or stripped. Chemicals that wash in after rain.

Freshwater animals are exceptionally sensitive to what happens upstream. For small invertebrates, the quality of the water is not a background condition. It is the entire atmosphere of their existence. They breathe through it, they feed in it, and their eggs develop in it. When the water changes, everything about their lives changes with it.

So there is a quiet link between a shrimp holding a clutch under her tail and the decisions made by people who never see her. The mother is doing her part. The question is whether the surroundings are doing theirs.

We are rarely forced to consider that connection, because the consequences are slow and distant. But slow and distant is simply how most responsibility works. The effects of a choice rarely arrive at the same time as the choice.

There is another layer to this that rarely gets mentioned, and it has to do with time.

We live inside a particular tempo. Our days are measured in hours and our attention in seconds. A scene that takes weeks to unfold is almost invisible to us, because we do not have the patience to hold it in view. We want the result without the long middle.

But the long middle is where nearly everything that matters actually happens. A clutch of eggs does not become a new generation in a moment. It becomes one through a slow accumulation of unremarkable hours, each of which looks identical to the last. Nothing marks the passage. No single day is the important one. The importance is distributed across all of them.

This is hard for us to feel, because our stories are built around moments. We remember the arrival, the reveal, the turning point. We forget that every turning point stands on a very long floor of ordinary time that someone, or something, had to get through.

A shrimp carrying eggs is a lesson in that floor. She is living entirely in the middle. She will not experience the beginning as a surprise and she cannot see the end in advance. All she has is the continuous present of the task.

There is a kind of wisdom in that which we tend to admire in people only after they have aged into it. The ability to do the next necessary thing, without needing it to be interesting, without needing it to be witnessed, and without needing to know exactly how it will turn out.

It makes me think about how much of human life depends on the same quiet endurance. The parent awake in the small hours. The person caring for someone who is slowly getting better, or slowly not. The one who keeps a promise long after everyone else has stopped checking on it. None of that is cinematic. All of it holds things together.

And it makes me wonder why we are so reluctant to find dignity in endurance that has no applause. Perhaps because applause is how we know that something has value, and we have forgotten that value can exist without being acknowledged.

The pond has no audience, and it never has. Billions of small acts of continuance have happened in the dark water and the green shade of leaves, unobserved by anyone who could write them down. The world was kept going by exactly this, long before there was anyone to appreciate it.

That is both humbling and, strangely, comforting. It means that the largest structures of life are held up by gestures too small to be noticed.

Let us be careful, though, because there is a temptation here to sentimentalize.

The shrimp is not a saint, and nature is not a morality play. The same instinct that makes her protect her clutch also makes her consume, compete and survive at the expense of other small lives. Shrimp eat, and in many circumstances they are eaten. The pond does not divide the world into the innocent and the guilty. It is a web, and each strand is both held and holding.

A truthful account has to hold both facts at once. That there is tenderness in the way a mother carries her eggs, in whatever limited sense tenderness can be applied to her. And that the same environment contains predation, loss and indifference. Neither fact cancels the other.

Our habit is to want one story. Nature as cruel, or nature as gentle. The more accurate picture is that both qualities arrive together, in the same pond, in the same hour. The kindness of the world and its harshness are not separate territories. They share a border, and the border runs through the body of every living thing.

Seeing this clearly is a form of respect. It means refusing to turn animals into symbols of whatever we need them to represent. The shrimp is not a metaphor for motherhood, even though she can remind us of it. She is a particular animal with a particular biology, living a life that is complete on its own terms and that does not exist for our instruction.

And yet, the reminder arrives anyway, uninvited. A small body carrying a large responsibility. A vulnerable creature acting as the final defense for something even more vulnerable. We do not need to claim that she means to teach us anything. The lesson is available simply because we are capable of recognizing the shape of it.

Recognition is the oldest bridge between species. We cannot talk to animals, and we cannot know what they know. But we can notice that certain patterns repeat across very different lives: protecting the young, staying close to what is fragile, paying the cost of continuity. When we see those patterns in a creature that looks nothing like us, something shifts. The distance between us does not disappear, but it becomes crossable.

That crossing is where compassion usually begins. Not from a lecture about ethics, and not from guilt, but from the sudden, quiet recognition that another living thing is engaged in a project we understand. A project of keeping something alive.

If there is a practical meaning in this, it is small and unglamorous. Pay attention to the minor creatures. Notice the water they depend on. Treat the habitats that cannot speak for themselves as places where something important is happening, because it is.

There is one more question hiding in all of this, and it is the most practical of them: what should a person do when they come across a creature in the middle of such a task?

The instinct, for many of us, is to help. To move, to adjust, to intervene. We see something small and apparently exposed, and we feel the pull to make it safer. That pull is a good one, and it deserves respect. But it also deserves some scrutiny, because good intentions applied without knowledge can do real damage.

A female carrying eggs is, in a sense, already doing what she needs to do. Handling her, moving her to unfamiliar water, or startling her can disrupt the very process we hope to protect. Eggs can be dislodged. Stress can change behavior. A change in temperature or water chemistry that seems trivial to us can be significant to her.

So there is a discipline in restraint. The most responsible thing is often to understand the situation before acting, and sometimes to do nothing except make sure we are not the cause of harm. It is less satisfying than rescue, because it offers no moment of triumph, but it is frequently more honest.

This is where the relationship between people and animals becomes genuinely complicated. We are capable of great kindness and great carelessness, often within the same afternoon, and often without noticing the difference. Care requires knowledge. Sympathy alone is not enough, and enthusiasm is not a substitute for understanding what an animal actually needs.

The best caretakers of wild and semi-wild creatures tend to share one trait: they are curious before they are confident. They ask what the animal is doing, what it requires, and what would happen if they stayed out of the way. They treat their own role as a question and not as a given.

That posture may be the most respectful way to share a world with beings who cannot explain themselves. It treats their lives as having their own logic, one that precedes us and will outlast our opinions about it.

There is something moving about that kind of humility. It suggests that the highest form of attention is not control but accompaniment. To watch closely, to learn what we can, to protect the conditions that allow life to proceed, and to let the animal remain the author of her own days.

The shrimp does not need us to complete her story. She needs, at most, a clean stream and the absence of unnecessary interference. That is a surprisingly modest request, and the fact that it is so often unmet says something about how rarely we think of ourselves as part of the environment that other lives depend on.

Perhaps that is the quiet center of the whole matter. Responsibility is not always a task we take on. Sometimes it is a condition we should stop violating, a set of small harms we can decline to cause, and a patience we can offer simply by letting a living thing finish what it started. Not every act of care has to be an act at all. Some of the very best of it is simply the willingness to leave a quiet, difficult, necessary ongoing process undisturbed.

Consider, finally, how much of this we would never know without the ability to look very closely.

For most of human history, the private life of a small shrimp was effectively hidden. The detail was too fine, the scale too minute, the activity too slow. Observation required patience that most people could not spare and equipment that most people did not have. The world of small things existed, but it existed outside our field of attention.

Magnification changed that, and then photography, and then moving images. Each step has allowed a little more of the hidden world to come into view. We can now watch things that happen on the surface of a single leaf as though they were happening on a stage. We can follow tiny limbs as they move and see textures that the naked eye would blur into a single smear.

What is remarkable is not just the clarity but what clarity does to us. The closer we look, the harder it becomes to maintain the idea that small lives are simple lives. Detail is the enemy of dismissal. The more of it we see, the more difficult it is to call something insignificant.

There is also a question of honesty about what we are looking at. Footage of the natural world, especially at this level of closeness, can be shot, edited, enhanced or even synthesized in ways that are not always obvious. A thoughtful viewer keeps that in mind, and holds the beauty of an image separately from the question of how it was made. The biology described here, the brooding, the fanning, the long patience, belongs to real shrimp in real water, whatever any single clip may be.

That distinction is worth keeping. The wonder is not diminished by being careful about it. If anything, caution protects the wonder, because it ensures that what we admire is the actual animal and not an invention built to look like her.

And the actual animal, in her actual pond, is more than enough. She does not need embellishment. A translucent body, a clutch of eggs, a leaf, a patch of shade, and weeks of unbroken attention. That is the whole drama, and it is already extraordinary.

What lingers is not any single detail but the proportion. The smallness of the one who carries and the weight of what is carried. The silence of the work and the size of its consequences. The fact that some of the most profound acts in nature occur at a scale that fits on the surface of a leaf.

If you want to understand devotion, do not look for the biggest animal or the loudest gesture. Look for the creature that cannot put its burden down, and that has chosen, or been shaped, to carry it anyway.

It will not look like heroism. It will look like a shrimp, holding very still, in the green light.

Psalm 51
 
New International Version
Psalm 51[a]
For the director of music. A psalm of David. When the prophet Nathan came to him after David had committed adultery with Bathsheba.
1 Have mercy on me, O God,
    according to your unfailing love;
according to your great compassion
    blot out my transgressions.
2 Wash away all my iniquity
    and cleanse me from my sin.

3 For I know my transgressions,
    and my sin is always before me.
4 Against you, you only, have I sinned
    and done what is evil in your sight;
so you are right in your verdict
    and justified when you judge.
5 Surely I was sinful at birth,
    sinful from the time my mother conceived me.
6 Yet you desired faithfulness even in the womb;
    you taught me wisdom in that secret place.

7 Cleanse me with hyssop, and I will be clean;
    wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.
8 Let me hear joy and gladness;
    let the bones you have crushed rejoice.
9 Hide your face from my sins
    and blot out all my iniquity.

10 Create in me a pure heart, O God,
    and renew a steadfast spirit within me.
11 Do not cast me from your presence
    or take your Holy Spirit from me.
12 Restore to me the joy of your salvation
    and grant me a willing spirit, to sustain me.

13 Then I will teach transgressors your ways,
    so that sinners will turn back to you.
14 Deliver me from the guilt of bloodshed, O God,
    you who are God my Savior,
    and my tongue will sing of your righteousness.
15 Open my lips, Lord,
    and my mouth will declare your praise.
16 You do not delight in sacrifice, or I would bring it;
    you do not take pleasure in burnt offerings.
17 My sacrifice, O God, is[b] a broken spirit;
    a broken and contrite heart
    you, God, will not despise.

18 May it please you to prosper Zion,
    to build up the walls of Jerusalem.
19 Then you will delight in the sacrifices of the righteous,
    in burnt offerings offered whole;
    then bulls will be offered on your altar.

    let the bones you have crushed rejoice.

text:
A DISTINCTION WITHOUT A DIFFERENCE
.
PART II of II— HAMAS, ISRAEL, AND THE CRISIS OF THE AMERICAN LEFT
.
By Peter Spear, GPT 6 Sol
.
WHO IS RESPONSIBLE FOR OCTOBER 7?
.
Before examining Israel’s military conduct in Gaza, we must remember what initiated this war.  On October 7, 2023, Hamas-led forces invaded Israel, murdering approximately 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.  The victims included civilians murdered in their homes, children murdered in front of their parents, parents murdered in front of their children, rape, disfigurement, whole communities, and at a music festival.
.
This was not a military operation directed against military installations.  It was an attack that deliberately targeted civilians.  (Associated Press; United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry, June 2024.)
.
In my earlier article, “Islam Does Not Justify Hamas,” I argued that Hamas cannot claim the authority of Islam to excuse the deliberate slaughter of civilians.  Islam has its own traditions governing the conduct of war, including prohibitions against killing noncombatants.
.
The Qur’an itself instructs believers engaged in fighting not to transgress prescribed limits.  Nor should the crimes of Hamas be attributed collectively to Muslims or Palestinians.
.
The same principle that protects American Jews from collective accusations concerning Israel must protect American Muslims from collective accusations concerning Hamas.  The moral principle is universal, or it is worthless. (Qur’an 2:190; Islamic jurisprudential traditions concerning noncombatant immunity.)
.
HAMAS’S STRATEGY
.
The mastermind of the October 7 attacks was Yahya Sinwar, who was subsequently killed by Israeli forces on October 16, 2024.  Sinwar understood something fundamental about modern warfare.  He understood propaganda.
.
A government fighting a terrorist organization cannot measure success simply by counting the number of enemy fighters killed.  The wider political consequences of military operations may determine the ultimate outcome.  And civilian casualties can become enormously consequential political weapons.  (Associated Press, October 17, 2024.)
.
In June 2024, The Wall Street Journal published an investigation based on messages reportedly sent by Sinwar to Hamas colleagues and intermediaries.
.
The messages revealed a leader who regarded mounting Palestinian casualties as strategically advantageous.  Sinwar reportedly characterized civilian deaths as necessary sacrifices in a national struggle.  He understood that the mounting horror in Gaza could intensify international pressure on Israel.  The greater the suffering, the greater the political difficulties confronting Israel.
.
Here was a strategy in which Hamas could benefit politically from the suffering of the population it governed.  This is where the IDF blundered.  (The Wall Street Journal, Summer Said and Rory Jones, June 10, 2024.)
.
This does not mean that every Palestinian civilian death was deliberately engineered by Hamas.  Nor does it absolve Israel of responsibility for its military decisions.  But Hamas operated within densely populated civilian areas, and its military activities placed civilians in extraordinary danger.  This was Hamas’ plan.
.
The United States Department of State has described Hamas and other armed organizations using Gaza’s civilian population for cover and concealment.  The consequences of that practice cannot be separated from an assessment of the war.  Notice the Left’s exclusive focus on Israel and its silence about Hamas.  Dr. El-Sayed repeatedly refused to utter a single word of criticism of the IRGC.  Why?  He claimed he was being singled out because of his faith and wouldn’t stoop to answer.  What a profile in courage.  (U.S. Department of State, 2024 Country Reports on Human Rights Practices.)
.
WHAT GENERAL DAVID PETRAEUS UNDERSTOOD
.
During the American counterinsurgency campaign in Iraq, General David Petraeus emphasized that commanders must assess the political consequences of military operations.
.
In an August 1, 2007, interview with PBS FRONTLINE, Petraeus described the importance of conducting operations without creating more enemies than were removed from the battlefield.  His question was essentially this:
.
Would an operation eliminate more enemies than it created?
.
That is not only a humanitarian consideration.  It is a calculation of military and political effectiveness.  In military language it is called, “situational awareness.”  A commander may destroy an enemy position, kill its occupants, and nevertheless leave the enemy movement stronger if the operation alienates the surrounding population.  (PBS FRONTLINE, interview with General David Petraeus, August 1, 2007; Petraeus, “Learning Counterinsurgency,” Military Review, 2006.)
.
I believe Israel failed to appreciate this dimension of Hamas’s strategy adequately.  Destroying Hamas military units was an immediate objective.  But what would become of the surviving population?
.
How many people who had previously opposed Hamas would become receptive to its ideology after the destruction of their homes and the deaths of their relatives?  How many future recruits would Israel’s military operations create?  And how much international support would Israel sacrifice in pursuit of its battlefield objectives?
.
These were not peripheral considerations.  They were central to the strategic outcome.
.
DETERRENCE AND CIVILIAN RETALIATION
.
I have previously argued, in “A MANIFESTO,” that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy rather than hunting for every weapon of the aggressor he must reestablish a credible deterrent against further Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilians.
.
See “A MANIFESTO” 
https://t.co/p7kjEXSLYo
.
I have also defended the strategic principle that the United States and Britain must retain the ability to threaten devastating retaliation against a country that attacks their populations.  I understand that  position raises many uncomfortable questions.
.
However, consider the doctrine commonly called Mutually Assured Destruction, or MAD.  Its central logic is that a nuclear attack could provoke retaliation so catastrophic that no rational aggressor would risk beginning the exchange.  The credibility of deterrence depended upon the adversary believing that retaliation could inflict unacceptable destruction.  That possibility necessarily raised the prospect of catastrophic civilian casualties.  (Strategic Studies Institute, Getting MAD: Nuclear Mutual Assured Destruction, Its Origins and Practice, 2004.)
.
If a reader believes that threatening such destruction is inherently immoral, I respect the consistency of that position.  But then let us reconsider the morality of our national nuclear deterrence itself.  Let us examine what the American and British strategic posture actually threaten, rather than pretending that the destruction of civilian society was never part of the calculations of war.
.
I understand that the mere existence of nuclear deterrence does not grant any country an unrestricted legal right to retaliate against civilian populations.
.
International  law prohibits deliberately targeting civilians, even in retaliation, indiscriminate attacks, and attacks expected to cause excessive incidental civilian harm in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated.
.
Britain signed these Geneva Conventions, but only with a reservation of its rights to retaliate in kind if attacked, but only after the highest authorization and only proportionally.  The USA did sign but didn’t ratify so therefore it is not US law.  (International Committee of the Red Cross, Rule of War; Strategic Studies Institute, 2004.)
.
DISPROPORTIONATE IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY GENOCIDAL
.
I believe that Israel’s military response in Gaza has included disproportionate uses of force.  The magnitude of the civilian suffering is appalling.  I do not regard criticism of that suffering as anti-Semitic.
.
Quite to the contrary.
.
A democratic state should be held accountable for its military decisions, including decisions made in response to terrorism and or attacks on civilians.  I agree with the British undertaking of proportionate retaliation.
.
But failure of proportionality is not by itself the same as genocide.  These are not interchangeable legal concepts.  Under the laws of war, proportionality concerns whether the expected incidental civilian harm of an attack is excessive compared with its anticipated concrete and direct military advantage.
.
Genocide requires something additional: the specific intent to destroy a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group, in whole or in part.  (International Committee of the Red Cross; United Nations Genocide Convention, 1948.)
.
That does not mean the genocide allegations can simply be dismissed.  Amnesty International and a United Nations Commission of Inquiry have concluded that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.  Israel disputes those findings.
.
The International Court of Justice has ordered provisional measures but has not yet delivered its final judgment on the genocide allegations.  These findings deserve serious examination.
.
What I reject is the proposition that every excessive military operation, every terrible civilian death toll, or every strategic blunder automatically establishes genocidal intent.  The evidence must establish the actual legal elements of the crime.  (Amnesty International, December 2024; United Nations Commission of Inquiry, September 2025; International Court of Justice, May 2026.)
.
Dr. El-Sayed did condemn the attack on Susan and Harold Loss Early Childhood Center, the Jewish preschool housed within Temple Israel, on Thursday, March 12, 2026.  However he wanted to:  “What I was trying to do was offer context for why it happened, but it wasn’t the time for context.”  “ When you give the right medicine at the wrong time, it’s the wrong medicine.”  A nice therapeutic approach.  Why does Dr. El-Sayed offer his therapeutic approach, which he says he learned in medical school, in one case but has nothing when addressing Gaza?  Could it be because he is a committed partisan?
.
Would his “Hurt people hurt people,” apply as “context” for why the IDF failed to mind the strategic issues in war fighting an enemy that wanted maximum civilian casualties?  Or apply his “context” to the IDF’s disproportionate reprisal strikes?
.
THE POLITICAL STRATEGY OF HAMAS
.
There is a further problem with the prevailing political rhetoric.  When Hamas attacks civilians and takes hostages, its responsibility must not disappear from the discussion simply because Israel’s subsequent military campaign has produced enormous suffering.
.
When Israel conducts operations that violate the laws of war, the responsibility of the Israeli commanders and political authorities must likewise be examined.  Responsibility is not a finite quantity that must be assigned exclusively to one side.
.
Two belligerents can commit grave wrongs in the same conflict.  Recognizing the crimes of Hamas does not excuse Israeli misconduct.  Recognizing Israeli misconduct does not excuse Hamas, unless one is a committed partisan or podcaster.
.
WHAT HAS HAPPENED TO THE AMERICAN LEFT?

I have previously asked, “Does Anti-Semitism Fairly Describe DSA?”  I return to that question now.
.
The issue is not whether progressives may criticize Israel.  Of course they may.  The issue is whether influential elements of the American Left have begun treating the Jewish community as collectively responsible for Israel’s military and political conduct.
.
Whether compassion for Israeli victims has become grounds for exclusion.  Whether the slogan of inclusion still applies when the people seeking inclusion are Jewish.  Dr. El-Sayed constantly complains that he alone is asked to criticize the IRGC as a loyalty test because of his faith. But where is the sympathy for Jewish Democrats who must pass political loyalty tests regarding Zionism?  Why have I never been accused of “dual loyalty” because of my support for Great Britain?  Am I saved because I am an Episcopalian? Or because I am White?
.
White?  The reader may well wonder how White entered the discussion?  See: Joe Scarborough’s  fawning interview with Dr. El-Sayed and thought he would be helpful by suggesting that Dr. El-Sayed is being discriminated against not just because of his faith but because he is not White.  His father in law commented that Joe is” stunningly superficial.”  
.
White?  I am reminded of Colin Jost’s joke, “Italians?  Now we are calling Italians White?” I guess if you are a Southern boy it is always White or Black.  You know; when all you have is a hammer everything looks like a nail.
.
And whether an organization may openly demand that Jewish-owned businesses leave an American neighborhood while insisting that its conduct has nothing to do with anti-Semitism.
.
The Philadelphia demonstration supplies a particularly revealing example.  Not because every participant was necessarily motivated by hatred of Jews.  We cannot know every individual’s motivation.
.
But because the organizers selected Jewish businesses, publicly declared that they must go, and then insisted that their political explanation settled the discrimination question.
.
It did not.  Does not.
.
The city also supplied a hopeful counterexample: Democrats, Jewish organizations, religious leaders, and ordinary residents who rejected the targeting of their neighbors.
.
The American Left is therefore not unanimous.  It is divided over an issue on which its commitment to equality should be unambiguous.  Note Dr. El-Sayed would argue that the Left is united;  it is only  that “Democratic Establishment” which doesn’t agree with the true new Left.  (The Philadelphia Inquirer, November 8, 2026; Religion News Service, November 9, 2026.)
.
THE MORAL TEST
.
The evidence, in my judgment, establishes that an identifiable and increasingly influential anti-Semitic political current has emerged within the American Left.
.
It has not captured everyone who calls themselves progressive.  But it has gained sufficient acceptance that some organizations will defend the political exclusion of Jews while continuing to describe themselves as opponents of discrimination.
.
That is a profound contradiction.
.
One may condemn Hamas and Hezbollah and the IRGC without condemning Muslims. One may condemn Netanyahu without condemning Jews.  One may defend Palestinians without defending Hamas.
.
And one may support Israel’s right to exist without endorsing every action of its government.
.
These are not difficult distinctions.  They are the elementary requirements of intellectual honesty.
.
A political movement that demands inclusion for itself while denying it to others has abandoned the principle it claims to represent.
.
A movement that makes Jewish Americans answer for the actions of a foreign government has crossed a line that should never have been crossed.
.
And a movement that attempts to expel Jewish businesses from an American neighborhood cannot erase the nature of its conduct by substituting the word “Zionist” for the word “Jew.”
.
END OF PART II of II
A DISTINCTION WITHOUT A DIFFERENCE
.

Trump's midterm loss opens a window for Iran diplomacy

♦️ US President Donald Trump's political position weakened after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the November 2026 midterm elections, increasing pressure on his administration to justify the war with Iran, which began eight months earlier alongside Israel.

♦️ The Democratic majority is expected to challenge the war through congressional investigations, scrutiny of military funding requests and budgetary pressure, making it increasingly difficult for Trump to continue military operations without facing political consequences.

♦️ The conflict has also become increasingly costly for Washington, with Pentagon expenses estimated at more than $47 billion. Military deployments, weapons replacement and tensions around the Strait of Hormuz have driven up energy prices and economic uncertainty, while US military strikes have failed to force Tehran to accept Washington's demands.

♦️ These developments have intensified diplomatic efforts involving Qatar, Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, as both Washington and Tehran face growing incentives to end the conflict. Vice President JD Vance has also become more involved in negotiations, favouring a diplomatic exit over another prolonged military campaign.

♦️ Inside Iran, President Masoud Pezeshkian and former officials, including Hassan Rouhani and Mohammad Javad Zarif, have warned that continued confrontation is worsening the country's economic situation. However, divisions within the Iranian establishment remain, with hardliners opposing concessions to Washington.

♦️ Any agreement also faces opposition from influential figures on both sides. US officials Marco Rubio and Pete Hegseth have maintained tougher positions, while Israel opposes a limited deal that would leave Iran's political system and parts of its military capabilities intact. Regional tensions involving Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iraqi militias could further complicate negotiations.

♦️ A limited agreement could offer a way to stop the fighting and restore navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, with Washington easing its blockade and providing initial sanctions relief in exchange for Iranian commitments on maritime security and nuclear inspections. A broader nuclear agreement could follow, but lasting stability would depend on both countries establishing mechanisms to manage their rivalry and prevent renewed escalation.

#Zimbabwe 

The Art Of War🐊🐊🐊

@matinyarare’s statement is not a serious challenge to a minister’s record. It is a deflection from his own failed campaign, built on a premise that collapses the moment you examine who actually funded the anti-sanctions effort and what it actually achieved.

The premise is a false dichotomy. Matinyarare frames the issue as binary: either a minister publicly attacks sanctions, or he “supports” them. This ignores how diplomacy and economic governance actually work. #Sanctions on Zimbabwe are imposed by #Washington and #London, not by Zimbabwe’s Minister of Economic Development. No minister “protects” them by failing to perform outrage loudly enough. A minister’s job is to deliver investment and growth under constrained conditions not to satisfy a commentator’s purity tests.

Matinyarare’s own side’s testimony destroys his accusation. His former co-director at the Zimbabwe Anti-Sanctions Movement, Advocate Simba Chitando, has publicly confirmed that Dr Kudakwashe Tagwirei did support their anti-sanctions work meeting the group after seeing their legal action, flying them to #Harare, covering ZASM’s expenses, and providing Matinyarare with a vehicle and financial support. The claim that Dr Tagwirei was an obstacle to sanctions relief is contradicted by the person who ran the movement alongside Matinyarare.

More damning still: Matinyarare failed to deliver what he promised. If Dr Tagwirei backed the movement and Matinyarare was its public face, then the scoreboard is unambiguous. The March 2024 US policy shift did not “remove sanctions” in any meaningful sense for those most affected. The White House’s own statement confirms that the old Zimbabwe sanctions programme was terminated and replaced with Global Magnitsky designations targeting President Mnangagwa, the First Lady, Dr Tagwirei himself, and others. The targeted sanctions that matter most remain in place. Matinyarare claims credit for a “victory” that left the core designations intact and now attacks a minister for not achieving what he himself could not.

Matinyarare’s credibility is further undermined by his own conduct. He has claimed he is owed  million of dollars for removing sanctions, yet public reporting describes him negotiating over a vehicle and cash in the tens of thousands of dollars a far cry from a geopolitical victor. He now alleges, without independent verification, that Dr Tagwirei secretly instructed him not to challenge sanctions. Matinyarare failed continuous effort to defame a minister he once took money from does not strengthens his current statement.

The practical absurdity remains. A Minister of Economic Development’s job is to attract capital, facilitate trade, and navigate a sanctions environment that he did not create. Matinyarare offers accusations; governance requires results. The statement is a distraction dressed as accountability from a campaigner whose own movement, funded by the very man he now attacks, failed to achieve the outcome he uses to question others.

The main issue that I have with the Minister of Development, Kuda Tagwirei, is he gives lip-service to wanting Zimbabwe to develop when yet he does not really want to see the country develop.

When I first met the Minister in January 2022, on his invitation, he gave me and my organisation the instruction that we must not aggressively fight to remove sanctions on the country—for at least 5 years (from 2022 to 2027)—so that Zimbabwean companies would continue struggling for loans, payment clearances and capital, to enable his company Sakunda to buy them at a discount.

According to his strategy, his objective was to see more local companies struggling to survive so that his cash-flush company Sakunda could buy them for a song as he had done with the NOCZIM fuel pipeline, OK Stores, Le Farge and mines belonging to the military, ZIMASCO, Mzi Khumalo and others.

In his argument, if we removed sanctions too quickly, foreign western investors (white people) would come into the economy with more capital and buy up the whole economy, putting it back into white hands.

I in turn pushed back by reminding him that as long as the majority of Zimbabweans were struggling to make ends meet, Zimbabwe risked an Arab Spring style uprising that would force government to deploy soldiers against the people which would eventually lead to NATO intervention.

In the end, after huge legal, diplomatic and multilateral pressure by my organisation, sanctions on Zimbabwe were removed by Joe Biden in April of 2024 and this was followed by the EU and UK removing their sanctions on the Zimbabwean government, military, banks and companies.

Unfortunately, the west chose to maintain individual sanctions on Tagwirei, the President, five other people and three companies on the allegations that they were corrupt and perpetuating human rights violations.

To illustrate that the Minister did not want sanctions to go, despite approaching me as Chairman of ZASM to fight sanctions on the instruction of the President, when the sanctions were removed, Tagwirei never congratulated us for the great work we had done.

The question then is how can a minister who is pro-development, want sanctions to continue upon the nation, people and companies of the nation for his own individual enrichment?
