text:
The Pork That Fed Eighty-Three People

A story of meicai kourou, and the winter nobody was supposed to survive

By every rule of arithmetic, eighty-three people should have died inside the Lin family roundhouse in the winter of 1947.

The grain was nearly gone by January. The well froze solid in the first week of the new year. The soldiers outside the only gate had been told to wait, and they were very patient men. They had boots, blankets, and a supply wagon that came up the valley every ten days. The people inside had walls of rammed earth and a great deal of stubbornness, which, as any soldier will tell you, is not edible.

And yet eighty-three people walked out of that gate in March. Not one of them was buried in the courtyard.
My grandmother, who was nine years old that winter, used to say the arithmetic was wrong because nobody had counted the pork. Then she would go quiet, cook us a bowl of it, and refuse to say another word until we had eaten every grain of rice underneath.
This is the story she told me, a piece at a time, over a great many bowls.
I. The People Who Never Owned the Good Land
To understand why the pork saved them, you first have to understand the Hakka.
The word means guest families. For a thousand years the Hakka were the people who arrived second. They came down from the north in waves, fleeing wars and floods and tax collectors, and each time they reached a new valley the good rice land was already taken. So they climbed. They settled in the high, stony hills of Guangdong and Fujian, and they built their houses the way you build when you do not trust your neighbors: great circles of earth and timber, four stories tall, with one gate, one courtyard, and one well. Whole clans lived inside a single wall. Outsiders called them tulou, earthen buildings. The people inside simply called them home.
A people who are always the last to arrive learn one lesson above all others: nothing is allowed to spoil. The Hakka salted what they could salt, dried what they could dry, and fermented the rest. Their pantries held jars within jars. They had a saying, which my grandmother repeated in a deep, grave voice: A good cook feeds the family. A great cook feeds the family in the year it cannot be fed.
The Lin roundhouse stood at the top of a long valley above Meizhou. It had a hundred and eight rooms, an ancestral hall, a pig yard, and, in the cellar, a hundred and forty clay jars of meicai.
Meicai is a mustard green. Fresh, it is bitter and rough. But every autumn the Lin women cut it by the cartload, wilted it on bamboo racks in the sun, rubbed it with coarse salt until their hands cracked, and packed it into jars. Then it was dried, steamed, and dried again, until each leaf was black and fragrant like a bundle of old tea. Packed tight, it would keep for years. Some jars in the cellar were older than the children who were forbidden to touch them.
Most of it was sold at the Meizhou market. The rest was saved for the New Year, when the clan cooked its great dish: pork belly braised with meicai, steamed for hours, then turned out of its bowl onto a plate, so that the dark glistening slices sat crowned with black leaves. Kou means to turn a bowl upside down. Meicai kourou. A dish for weddings and births and the arrival of a new year.
It had never occurred to anyone in the Lin family that it might also be a weapon.
II. The Gate
The trouble came in the eleventh lunar month, in the last gold days of November.
A new commander had arrived in the district. He was not a Meizhou man, and he had a map and a quota. The quota was grain and young men, and the map said the Lin roundhouse held plenty of both. He sent a polite letter. The elders sent a politer reply, which said no. He sent a second letter that was not polite at all. The elders did not answer.
On the morning of the fourteenth day, my grandmother woke to a sound she had never heard: the sound of two hundred men not talking.
She climbed to the third-floor gallery with the other children and looked over the wall. The soldiers had spread across the valley floor in a neat ring. Smoke rose from their cooking fires. They were not going to storm the walls; the walls were two meters thick and had been built for exactly this. They were simply going to sit there and let winter do the work.
Down in the courtyard, the clan head, Uncle Fu, was already shouting. He was a big man with a big voice, and he believed every problem could be solved by being louder than it. He wanted to send the young men over the wall at night. He wanted to burn the supply wagon. Above all he wanted not to be the man who opened the gate.
“We have food,” he kept saying. “We have a well. We have walls. We can wait them out.”
The man who answered him was not an elder. He was Teacher Chen, a thin, nervous schoolmaster who had boarded in the roundhouse for six years because nobody else would hire him. He had a piece of chalk and a rice-sack cloth, and he had spent the morning in the granary.
“Eighty-three people,” he said quietly. “I have counted every sack. At the rate we eat, we have six weeks of rice. A little more, if the children eat less.”
“Six weeks is plenty,” said Uncle Fu. “They will give up in a month.”
“Will they?” Teacher Chen looked at the ring of smoke outside the walls. “They are fed. We are not. Who gives up first?”
Nobody had an answer. The courtyard went silent. And in the silence, from the corner near the kitchens, a small cracked voice said:
“You have counted the rice. Did you count the pigs?”
III. Great-Aunt Qiu
Great-Aunt Qiu was seventy-four that winter, and according to my grandmother she was the smallest and most frightening person in the roundhouse. She was barely taller than the children. She carried a bamboo stick, which she used less for walking than for tapping people on the ankle when they disappointed her. She had been born in a drought and widowed in a flood, and in between she had survived two sieges and one famine. She never talked about any of it. But what she had learned was written, in some private shorthand, into the way she cooked.
She tapped her way across the courtyard and stopped in front of Teacher Chen.
“Eleven pigs,” she said. “Fat ones. How much grain do they eat each day, Teacher, by your chalk?”
Teacher Chen blinked at his cloth. “Two jin each.”
“Twenty-two jin a day,” said Great-Aunt Qiu. “More than a quarter of what you just counted. You have been feeding the people’s rice to pigs and calling it arithmetic.”
Uncle Fu found his voice. “Those are the New Year pigs. If we kill them now there will be no feast, no offering to the ancestors—”
“If we do not kill them now,” said Great-Aunt Qiu, “there will be no New Year. There will be a gate, and a man outside it, and some very quiet people inside.” She turned and looked at the whole clan. She did not raise her voice; she never did. “I will tell you how we will live. I will say it once. You may argue, and then you will do it anyway, because I am old and you are afraid.”
And she did.
All eleven pigs would be killed in a single day, while the weather was cold enough to hold the meat. Nothing would be wasted: not the blood, not the bones, not the ears or the trotters. The lean meat would be salted and hung. The bones would go into the great iron pot for broth. The fat would be rendered into lard and poured into crocks.
And the belly, the thick, striped, trembling belly, the best part, the New Year part, would be cooked. Not a little. All of it. As meicai kourou, in batches so large the kitchen would need every steamer in the building. And each bowl, once steamed, would not be turned out onto a plate. It would be left in its bowl, covered with a finger’s thickness of hot white lard, and sealed.
“Fat keeps,” said Great-Aunt Qiu. “Fat holds out the air. Under fat, in the cold, pork will last until spring. You will not eat it yet. You will treat it as I treat my own name: with respect, and with rarity.”
“But why meicai?” asked Shui, who ran the kitchens. “Why not simply salt the pork?”
Great-Aunt Qiu looked at her for a long moment, as though deciding whether a secret was worth giving away.
“Because of the sailors,” she said.
Nobody understood. Only years later, when my grandmother had read many books, did she realize what the old woman meant: the sickness that takes besieged armies and ships at sea, the swollen gums and loosened teeth, the slow bleeding that comes when people live for weeks on rice and salted meat and nothing alive. Great-Aunt Qiu had never heard the word vitamin. She had simply watched, in a famine long ago, who got the sickness and who did not. The ones who did not had eaten something sour and fermented every day.
“Sour keeps the mouth from bleeding,” she said. “I do not know why. I only know it does. Every person in this house will eat meicai every day until the gate opens, even if it is only a leaf.”
IV. The Day of Eleven Pigs
The killing took one day, and it was the loudest and the quietest day of the winter. Loud, because eleven pigs do not go quietly, and the soldiers outside could hear every squeal and wondered what the Lin family was celebrating. Quiet, because afterward, when the work began, nobody spoke. The roundhouse had become a single machine. Men hauled and scalded and scraped. Women cut. Children carried. Teacher Chen, who was no good with a knife, kept a tally of every cut on his cloth with fierce, trembling precision.
The kitchen smelled of soy and scorched sugar and ginger. The method was the old one, passed from mother to daughter for as long as the Hakka had owned any recipes at all. The belly was boiled until just cooked, then dried. The skin was pricked all over with a bundle of needles, a thousand tiny holes, so that it would blister in hot oil. It was rubbed with dark soy and fried skin-side down until it puffed and darkened and crackled like parchment. Then it was cooled, cut into thick slabs, and laid skin down in a bowl, in overlapping rows.
Over this went the meicai: a thick black blanket of it, rinsed and chopped and stir-fried with rock sugar and rice wine, sweet and sour and salty at once. A star anise. A knob of ginger. A spoon of soy. Then two hours or more in the steamer. By the end of the first afternoon, sixty bowls were waiting their turn, the steamers stood a dozen high, and the air itself had become thick enough to chew.
My grandmother stood in the kitchen doorway, staring. She was nine, and she had never smelled anything so wonderful or so unbearable. It was the smell of the New Year, the smell of every good thing the family owned. And she was not allowed to eat it.
“Not yet,” said Great-Aunt Qiu, appearing out of the steam like a very small ghost. She tapped my grandmother on the ankle. “You are not eating dinner, little Lan. You are eating February.”
The bowls were cooled, topped with white lard, sealed with oiled paper and a cloth tie, and carried down to the cold stone cellar beneath the ancestral hall, where the temperature never rose above a shiver. Sixty bowls. Then eighty. Then, by the end of the week, one hundred and four, standing in long silent ranks in the dark like soldiers of a different army.
Teacher Chen stood among them with his chalk and did the arithmetic again. He finished. He frowned. He did it again.
“What is it?” Uncle Fu demanded.
“I had been counting wrongly,” said Teacher Chen. “Rice fills the stomach, but it burns away in an hour. But this—” He waved his chalk at the bowls. “All that fat. One slice of this belly holds more strength than a full bowl of rice, and it will keep. If we eat it carefully, once a day, with only a little rice to carry it, I think we could last until spring.”
Uncle Fu stared at him. Then, to everyone’s astonishment, he laughed, one great booming laugh that echoed off the cellar walls, and bowed deeply to a very small old woman who was already walking away.
V. How to Eat a Winter
There is a way of eating that you do only when you are trying to survive, and it is nothing like the way you eat at a feast. Great-Aunt Qiu taught it to the whole roundhouse.
Breakfast was a thin gruel, so thin you could see the bottom of the bowl, eaten slowly with a leaf of plain meicai. Lunch was nothing; you drank hot water and stayed busy. Dinner, the one real meal, was the pork.
But it was never a bowl of pork. Each person received two slices of belly, laid over a bowl of gruel, with a spoonful of the dark sweet meicai and its sauce. The sauce was the secret. Salty, sour, rich with melted fat, it turned every grain of gruel into the taste of the whole bowl. A little went a very long way.
The children were given the skin. It was Great-Aunt Qiu’s rule, and nobody argued. The skin was the softest, richest, most melting part, and it went down easily into small stomachs that had begun to ache. The elders took the lean slices. The men on night watch, in the bitter cold, got a third slice and a cup of hot bone broth. And every single person, from the oldest to the infant, had to swallow one leaf of meicai at the end of the meal. They called it the leaf. A boy who refused it was made to stand in front of the bamboo stick until he changed his mind.
By mid-December the roundhouse had settled into a strange routine. Everyone was hungry, but nobody was starving. They were thin and slow, and the children no longer ran in the courtyard. But their eyes were clear. Their gums did not bleed. Their skin held its color.
“It is hunger that kills the spirit,” said Great-Aunt Qiu, “long before it kills the body. So at dinner, we will eat as though we were rich.”
And they did. No matter how little was on the table, the clan sat together in the great hall and ate as if it were a feast. They said the old blessings. They passed the dishes. Uncle Fu told long and ridiculous stories about his youth. The children licked their bowls clean.
My grandmother said that was the real miracle of the winter: not the pork, but the dinners. For one hour every evening, eighty-three people forgot there were soldiers outside.
VI. The Well, the Fire, and the Smell
Then came the cold.
It arrived in the first week of January, a deep, dry, merciless cold the valley rarely saw. One morning a boy went to the well and came back with an empty bucket: the well had frozen from the top down. A person can live for weeks without food but only days without water, and to melt ice you need fire, and fire needs fuel, and the fuel was running low.
They burned the spare beams from the storerooms first. Then the chairs from the schoolroom, which pained Teacher Chen. Then the old wooden opera stage in the courtyard, which several old men mourned like a dead relative. By the second week, Shui came to Great-Aunt Qiu with a stricken face.
“There is enough wood to melt water,” she said. “Or to steam the bowls. Not both.”
Great-Aunt Qiu thought for a long time, leaning on her stick.
“What is steam?” she said at last.
Shui looked at her. “Hot water.”
“Then it is the same fire. One pot beneath, one pot above. The water that boils for the steamer is the water we drink. The steam that warms the pork warms the kitchen. A fire that does all three is a fire we only have to build once.”
From that day the roundhouse ran on a single fire. A great iron cauldron of melted ice sat at the bottom, and above it rose a leaning tower of bamboo steamers, each holding a bowl of pork warming gently in the rising steam. Not a stick of wood was wasted. The kitchen became the heart of the roundhouse, and in the evenings the old people dragged their stools in and sat breathing the steam like a blessing.
It was in the kitchen that Great-Aunt Qiu had her last and strangest idea.
“Open the roof vents,” she said one afternoon.
“What?” said Uncle Fu. “It is freezing. We will lose the heat.”
“A little heat,” said Great-Aunt Qiu. “And a great deal of smell.”
For the smell of meicai kourou is not an ordinary smell. It is deep and savory and sweetly sour, soy and caramel and rendered fat and dark fermented leaves. On a still night in a cold valley, it travels. It rose from the roofs of the roundhouse and drifted across the frozen paddies, across the long ring of silent soldiers sitting by their fires over cold, thin, rationed rice.
“They think we are starving,” said Great-Aunt Qiu. “Every morning the commander looks at our walls and thinks: today, perhaps, they will open the gate. Let us give him something else to think about.”
So each evening at dinner time the vents were thrown open, and the smell of eighty-three people eating well poured out into the night.
My grandmother never forgot standing on the third-floor gallery in the dark, watching the soldiers’ fires flicker across the valley and thinking: they can smell us. The soldiers could not have known the feast was two slices a person. They could only smell it. And a smell is a very difficult thing to argue with.
VII. The Thief of the Seventh Row
Hunger finds the weakest place in any wall.
In late January, a bowl in the seventh row of the cellar was found open, its seal broken, two slices gone, the lard smeared at the edges by small fingers. The roundhouse went very still. A clan can survive many things, but not a secret thief. Trust is the only wall that matters, and that wall had cracked.
Uncle Fu wanted a trial. Several elders wanted a harsh, public punishment, so that nobody else would try. Great-Aunt Qiu said nothing. She went down to the cellar and looked at the broken bowl for a long time. Then she went to find my grandmother’s cousin Bao.
Bao was eleven, thin even by the standards of that winter, and growing too fast to ever be full. He was sitting alone behind the kitchen with his arms around his knees, shaking. Great-Aunt Qiu sat down beside him on the cold stone, the only time my grandmother ever saw her sit on anything that was not a chair.
“How many slices?”
“Two,” Bao whispered. “Just two. I could not—”
“I know,” said Great-Aunt Qiu. “When I was your age I stole an egg. I have never told anyone. It is not the stealing that is the sickness, Bao. It is the secret. A secret in the dark is a worm in a jar.” She tapped his ankle, very gently. “Here is what you will do.”
The next morning, in the great hall, she announced that the cellar needed a keeper: someone who knew every bowl and every row, who would keep a chalk ledger of every portion taken and owed, so that nobody could ever take in secret again.
She appointed Bao.
There was a murmur of astonishment. Bao went white, then red. He stood up and said, in a voice that cracked: “I took two slices from the seventh row. I am sorry. I will keep the ledger.”
Nobody laughed. And then, from the back of the hall, a very old man began to clap, slowly, once, twice, three times. Others joined. It was not applause exactly. It was something older: the sound of a clan deciding to remain a clan.
Bao counted every bowl twice for the rest of the winter, and would not take an extra slice even when it was offered. Years later he became a banker in Hong Kong, and then an old man who told this story at every New Year’s dinner, always ending the same way: “I was the thief of the seventh row. And they made me the keeper.”
VIII. The Child Named Kou
On the third of February, at four in the morning, a baby was born in the roundhouse.
Her mother, Mei, had spent the last months of her pregnancy on gruel and two slices of pork a day. By every measure she should have been weak, and the midwives were afraid: a birth in the middle of a siege, in the coldest week of the winter, was the kind that ended in funerals. But the pork and the fat and the sour leaves had held her up. The baby came after eleven hours, small but loud, with a full head of black hair and a furious wavering cry that echoed through the whole building. The soldiers outside, my grandmother said, must have heard it.
The clan argued for two days about a lucky name: Spring, Plum, Jade, Harvest. In the end it was Mei herself, propped on her pillows with the baby on her chest, who settled it.
“Kou,” she said.
“Turned upside down?” said Uncle Fu doubtfully.
“Turned over. Like the bowl. When you turn the bowl over, everything hidden inside comes out onto the plate. They told us we would be turned out of our home. But we have not been. We have turned them over.” She smiled down at her daughter. “Her name is Kou. She is what came out of the bowl.”
Little Kou grew up to be a doctor and delivered a great many children of her own. But that is another story.
IX. The Last Bowl
By the third week of February, the cellar was nearly empty. Bao’s chalk marks told the story plainly: a hundred and four bowls had become eighty, then fifty, then twenty. The rice was long gone. The broth had been boiled so many times it was barely hot water with a memory of bones. Yet the clan was alive, the soldiers were still outside, and the snow had begun, at last, to thin on the hillsides.
On the morning of the twentieth day of the month, there were three bowls left.
“If we eat as we have been, it is five more days,” said Teacher Chen, ashen. “Perhaps six. And then there is nothing.”
Great-Aunt Qiu sat very still in the warm steam of the kitchen, her hands folded over her stick.
“What day is it?”
“The twentieth of the first month. Tomorrow is—”
“The Lantern Festival,” said Great-Aunt Qiu. “The end of the New Year.”
Everyone had forgotten. The New Year had come and gone in the middle of the siege, and nobody had marked it. No firecrackers, no red papers, no feast.
“We have not had our New Year dinner,” said Great-Aunt Qiu.
“Aunt,” said Uncle Fu gently, “we do not have the—”
“We have three bowls. A people who cannot have a New Year dinner have already surrendered. Tomorrow night we will eat the last of the pork. All of it. Properly. On plates.”
“And after?”
“After, we will see what the new year brings.”
It was either the bravest or the most foolish thing anyone had ever said, and the whole clan knew it. And yet, one by one, they nodded. For the first time in three months the roundhouse felt something that had nothing to do with hunger: the feeling of a decision made together.
The next evening the three last bowls were steamed one final time, over the last timbers of the opera stage. Shui lifted the first from the steamer, set a wide white plate over its mouth, and with a single practiced motion, turned it over. The bowl lifted. And there it stood: a dark, glistening, trembling dome of pork, its skin a burnished mahogany, its slices fanned like the petals of a heavy flower, and crowning it all, black and sweet and shining, a mountain of meicai.
No one spoke. Eighty-three people stood around the long table in the flickering light of a few precious candles. The children’s eyes were enormous. The old men had tears on their faces.
Then Great-Aunt Qiu said, in her small cracked voice: “Eat.”
And they did. Every plate was cleaned. Every drop of sauce was drained into the last of the gruel. Nobody was greedy. They passed the plates the way the Hakka always have, the old first, the young second, themselves last. And when the pork was gone there was a long, contented, exhausted silence, and then someone began to laugh. And then everyone was laughing.
Uncle Fu climbed onto a bench with an iron ladle and a cooking pot and began to bang them together. Others joined: pots, pans, bowls, spoons. The sound grew into a great wild ridiculous racket that rolled off the courtyard walls and out through the open roof vents, over the frozen valley, across the dying fires of the soldiers’ camp.
It was the loudest New Year the Lin roundhouse had ever had, and it was made entirely of kitchenware. And outside in the dark, two hundred soldiers listened to a sound that no starving people could possibly make.
X. The Man at the Gate
The commander came to the gate on the second of March.
There was no army behind him. In the last weeks the valley had been emptying. First a handful of men slipped away at night. Then a dozen. Then, one cold morning, an entire squad simply walked down the valley road and did not come back. The supply wagon stopped coming. A letter from the district government recalled the unit to the coast. What the commander had left was a coat, a cough, and a sergeant holding his horse.
He knocked: an absurd, formal little knock, three raps against a gate that could have withstood a cannon. Uncle Fu, who had waited for this moment for a hundred and eleven days, stepped out through the small door.
The two men looked at each other. The commander was gaunt. Uncle Fu was thin too, but his eyes were bright, his color was good, and when he opened his mouth to speak, his teeth were white and whole.
“I have come to ask a question,” said the commander, visibly struggling. “By every calculation you should have starved by January. My sergeant counted your grain from the hill. I know what you had. And yet at night we would smell—” He stopped. He looked down at his own hands. “I would like to know what you ate.”

📡Today, we focus on the article 'Ukrainian Intelligence’s Use of Telegram in Wartime' by 𝗣𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗦𝗰𝗵𝗿𝗶𝗷𝘃𝗲𝗿, researcher at the Faculty of #Military Sciences of the #Netherlands Defence Academy in Breda. He is a lieutenant colonel in the Netherlands Army and has been deployed to Bosnia-Herzegovina and Afghanistan.

🛜Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of #Ukraine in 2022, the Main Directorate of Intelligence (#HUR) has adopted a structured, public-facing #communication strategy on #Telegram that diverges from conventional #intelligence practice. This approach integrates three recurring functions: 
1. projecting #institutional legitimacy
2. targeting the adversary through disclosure, and
3. mobilizing domestic publics.

📱In doing so, the HUR turned intelligence communication into an ongoing process of public engagement rather than episodic outreach, underpinning an emerging concept of participatory intelligence communication. 

🌐The HUR’s case demonstrates how, under high-intensity conflict, a state intelligence service may use #digital platforms to coordinate narrative control, reinforce legitimacy, and enlist the public as contributors. While grounded in Ukraine’s specific #wartime conditions, these findings extend existing frameworks of intelligence communication and offer broader insight into how intelligence agencies may reconfigure their public role in wartime.

The Battle of Carrhae (Latin pronunciation: [ˈkar.rʰae̯]) was fought in 53 BC between the Roman Republic and the Parthian Empire near the ancient town of Carrhae (present-day Harran, Turkey). An invading force of seven legions of Roman heavy infantry under Marcus Licinius Crassus was lured into the desert and decisively defeated by a mixed cavalry of armoured cataphracts and light horse archers led by the Parthian general Surena. On such flat terrain, the legion proved to have no viable tactics against the highly mobile Parthian horsemen, and the slow and vulnerable Roman formations were surrounded, exhausted by constant attacks, and eventually crushed. Crassus was killed along with most of his army. It is commonly seen as one of the earliest and most important battles between the Roman and Parthian Empires and one of the most crushing defeats in Roman history. According to the poet Ovid in Book 6 of his poem Fasti, the battle occurred on 9 June.

Crassus, a member of the First Triumvirate and the wealthiest man in Rome, had been enticed by the prospect of military glory and riches and decided to invade Parthia without the official consent of the Senate. Rejecting an offer from the Armenian King Artavasdes II to allow Crassus to invade Parthia via Armenia, Crassus marched his army directly through the deserts of Mesopotamia. His forces clashed with Surena's troops near Carrhae. Surena's cavalry killed or captured most of the Roman soldiers. Crassus was killed when truce negotiations turned violent, and his death ended the First Triumvirate.

Honoring Our Veterans

Today, we honor the men and women who have served in the United States Armed Forces. With grateful hearts, we thank our veterans for their service and sacrifices, and we remember the families who have stood beside them.

As a community of faith, we pray especially for veterans carrying wounds both seen and unseen. May they find healing, friendship and the support they need.

✝️ Venerable Father Emil Kapaun offers a powerful example of faith and service. A Kansas priest and U.S. Army chaplain in World War II and the Korean War, he chose to remain with wounded soldiers rather than escape capture. As a prisoner of war, he cared for the sick, found food for fellow prisoners and led prayers, bringing hope amid terrible suffering.

Father Kapaun died in captivity in 1951 and was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor in 2013. Declared Venerable in 2025, his cause for sainthood continues. In the October/November EOC magazine feature, we share a new book for younger audiences that recounts Father Kapaun's story.  https://t.co/HroZEytL89

Across the centuries, others who served in the military - including St. Martin of Tours, St. Ignatius of Loyola and St. Francis of Assisi - also became examples of lives transformed by Christ. Their stories remind us that God is present in every chapter of our lives, including service, hardship, recovery and new beginnings.

🙏 Lord, bless our veterans and their families. Grant them strength, healing and peace. Help us express our gratitude through prayer, friendship and faithful care.

Is there a veteran you would like us to remember in prayer? Share their name in the comments below.

- His citation: “ … As the battle raged, CPL Rubin was severely wounded and captured by the Chinese … Choosing to remain in the prison camp despite offers from the Communist Chinese to return him to his native [then Communist controlled] Hungary, CPL Rubin disregarded his own personal safety and immediately began sneaking out of the camp at night in search of food for his comrades. Breaking into enemy food storehouses and gardens, he risked certain torture or death if caught. CPL Rubin provided not only food to the starving soldiers, but also desperately needed medical care and moral support for the sick and wounded of the POW camp. November 11th is Veterans Day. It is a time to honor and extend our deepest gratitude to all the brave men and women who have served in the United States Armed Forces. Originally established as Armistice Day to mark the end of World War I, this day serves as a powerful reminder of the immense sacrifices made by our veterans to protect our freedoms and preserve peace.

Behind the grand history of operational military triumphs are the deeply personal, interior lives of the individuals who served. This Veterans Day, Time's Tin Cup is honoring that legacy by looking closely at a tangible piece of living history: a WWII Protestant Episcopal Church's Army and Navy Commission prayer book.

This compact, khaki cloth pocket edition offered comfort, prayers, and hymns to service members during wartime, serving as a lasting testament to the resilience of the Greatest Generation.

Visit Time's Tin Cup in Downtown Denville to explore this piece of history. To our veterans: thank you for your service. 🇺🇸

text:
#RadioMoskva

Hobson’s choice for Zelenskiy in Abu Dhabi

You have to feel sorry for Zelenskiy. He faces a historically horrible Hobson’s choice in Abu Dhabi: take the Russian deal or watch what is left of Ukraine’s economy be utterly destroyed.

He is being asked to give up the Donbas in exchange for a US-backed security deal to end the war. The issue is: how “real” is that deal? At stake is Ukraine’s future as a sovereign nation. If he does the deal then he is being asked to trust both Putin and Trump will keep their word.

Putin started with his Pandora’s box campaign in August and it is now into a total war of destroying everything that is left. “I will destroy all of Ukraine’s basic infrastructure,” he said last week – and he is not kidding. And he can. In fact, he is, as there is already not much left of the power sector; Ukraine’s biggest steel mill just closed down; and the grain is rotting in the field as the Odesa port has been closed for months.

The lack of interceptor missiles saga has moved into a farcical phase: Germany said last week it’s out of interceptors and can only send some in 2027. Portugal has some, but they are not available until 2028. And Trump’s offer to sell Ukraine 500 interceptors (which the EU still has to pay for) doesn’t kick in until mid-2030.

I'm just finishing off a piece that tries to calculate how many men there will be left in the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) in 2030 and the preliminary worst-case estimate, based on current attrition rates + desertion, says Ukraine will reach the “fight to the last Ukrainian” zero-point in April 2029.

In the meantime, Zelenskiy is getting 12 rockets a month – it can fire one every three days. Russia has a stockpile of 200 ballistic missiles and is making 50 new ones a month. That is not counting drones, other missiles and the massive FAB3000 glide bombs it used to flatten a school and kill 55 people last week – including first responders in a double-tap strike. (Oddly a story that got relatively little play in the international media.)

Zelenskiy has spent months touring the world (he was still on the road in Denmark yesterday) trying to get more money and missiles, with little success. It’s now clear that he is facing defeat in the face as the deadline of the first snows is now on us.

That has led to a clear change of tone amongst the Western allies as I wrote yesterday. Now suddenly everyone has gotten pragmatic. One aspect where this is clearest is in the reopening of the lines of communication between Europe and Moscow – which to be clear has happened far too late, as with everything Europe has done in this war.

Macron got roasted when he first suggested this last year, but now everyone is doing it, following the Stubb-Store-Putin call initiative last week. The UK said it too yesterday: “maybe it would be a good idea to re-establish communication, and not just at diplomatic level but at the military-to-military level as well…” Even Zelenskiy added his voice to the Kremlin’s yesterday (!), saying Europe should “hurry up” and appoint an interlocutor to deal with the Kremlin.

Guys, the talks have already started. Deep winter is only about 40 days away. You have failed to give Zelenskiy anything he needs to continue the war. And you want to start the outreach now, but still haven’t appointed anyone to do it? It has been perfectly obvious what will happen in December to Kyiv since July. Have the military planners been asleep all this time – hibernation in reverse? This late in the game, ex-Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder is now the only one that could literally be sent tomorrow and buys some time, but that’s never going to happen.

So, given the appalling situation Zelenskiy finds himself in – he has not been asleep, which is why he has sounded so desperate for months – he needs to do a deal in Abu Dhabi – or at least lay down the groundwork for the now inevitable meeting with Putin to decide on territories. That is what this whole discussion will boil down to, in a repeat of the proposed Istanbul deal mechanics.

It is a very simple trade off: Zelenskiy gives up the Donbas - and everyone involved, including Stubb is very clear about this point – in exchange for a really tough security deal.

Despite all Trump’s very obvious flaws, the White House has actually stepped up and promised “Article 4 and Article 5-like” security promises – presumably at bilateral level although Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Kremlin have both now changed tack and both are now saying “Europe has to be involved”. That is new, as until now both of them have done everything they can to exclude Europe.

Kushner said last month if Zelenskiy agrees to give up Donbas then “the deal is done.”

So, is it all agreed?

Not so fast.

Zelenskiy posted a whinge on X yesterday that highlights his dilemma.

"Ceding Ukrainian land for peace is just abstract words. It's not only about reality, even more about philosophy… This is why when Americans ask, 'Can you exchange Donbas for security?'
I said right there, 'Can you tell me what it means? What security? Nato?'
'Not Nato, but similar to Nato.'
'Similar? But you don't want the answer about Donbas to be 'similar'. You want a clear answer about Donbas. This is your goal. And this is Putin's goal for today. What will you do if we have security guarantees but not Nato?' …
“Nobody trusts Putin to stop if we leave Donbas. He will pause. Then he will come back in one year, two years, or five years. And who will be guilty?"
You can see that he is scared of being sold up the river. What exactly does “Article 5-like" mean? Remember that Article 5 does not automatically trigger military action, but only consultations where the members then take action “deemed necessary.”

What Zelenskiy wants, and needs, is a security deal that will automatically trigger WWIII if Russia invades for a second time. Anything less means that Russia could restart the war in two years’ time and walk all the way up to Dnipro, taking half of Ukraine in the process, which they would never get back.

Now put these US promises into the context of the new “Donnie Doctrine” of the National Security Strategy (NSS) released last December, where the Trump administration made it crystal clear that it was pulling back from Europe and that Russia was “Europe’s problem now.”

Moreover, this is not idle chat. In the same month, in another under-reported story, the Pentagon issued a “hard deadline” for Europe to take over responsibility for its own conventional forces' security by 2027. What that means in practice is the US will withdraw its logistical support for Europe – which is currently under the sole control of one US general. Countering a Russian invasion doesn’t work with a committee of 30 members running the show. Which is where we are now. European Nato has done nothing to prepare for this change, apart from one meeting in Budapest earlier this summer.

So, Trump’s security deal is pretty meaningless as it seems likely that the Pentagon will immediately default to Europe to respond to a second Russian invasion – as it has already done since Trump took over.

In this case what has Europe offered Zelenskiy to bolster the security deals on offer? So far, nothing.

There is starting to be lots of talk from the Europeans that Ukraine will have given up land, but while people like Rubio are clearly talking about security deals, people like Stubb pointedly failed to mention it at all. “Give up land and… [on security, silence].”

That means we are still at Macron’s suggestion of a “reassurance force” (force de reassurance) to ensure Ukraine’s security – a band of some 7,000 European troops living in a hut on the Polish border that are mandated to stay as far away from the Russians as possible. The Russians were almost laughing out loud when this was first suggested as it’s so ridiculous and promised to target them first anyway should it come to blows. Half a dozen FAB3000 bombs in an afternoon would probably do the trick.

Zelenskiy is looking at all this and has to decide if he is willing to take the gamble: take the US at its word; hope the EU will actually say something sensible about security… today…; and believe any promises Russia makes to get this deal over the line.

It’s not very reassuring is it?

But that was what Hobson’s choice was: take the horse by the stable door, or take nothing.

The one ray of hope in this otherwise gloomy story is there is a chance that Putin will stick to his word if he does the Russian security deal that is part of the package. If peace with Ukraine comes, that clears the way for the Kremlin to do the so-called $12 trillion-worth of deals in the Dmitriev package. That is a ton of money – six times the value of the Russian economy. It’s not guaranteed that Putin will do these deals, but Kirill Dmitriev is serious about them. As the head of the Russia Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) sovereign wealth fund, that is what he does and I have watched him do billions of dollars-worth of deals with the Chinese and Arabs over the last ten years.

Ironically, this would give the White House real leverage over the Kremlin, which have dramatically improved relations with both Riyadh and Beijing. Putin’s incentive to do a lot more business with the US also provides him with some leverage over Beijing, which he actually badly needs. And if he is in business with the US, that will provide him with a strong incentive not to rock the boat by invading Ukraine a second time as a second time round US sanctions would actually mean something. But this remains a pipedream for now and doesn’t help Zelenskiy one bit.

It is my firm belief that business is a more powerful force to bring countries together than the threat of violence. Surely the lesson of Germany’s transformation from pariah and hated enemy during WWII to the lynch pin of the EU thanks to its prosperity proves the point. And the fact that the EU has been willing to gut its own sanctions on Russia for the sake of the profitability of its own companies on highlights how powerful this force is.

text:
NQ / NASDAQ — PRE-OPEN REGIME RADAR
CoreWeave Reignites the AI Rally as Nasdaq Futures Surge Despite Hot CPI and Fed Tightening Risks — 11 November 2026
11 NOVEMBER 2026 | REPORT CUT-OFF: 12:45 SWITZERLAND (CET) | 05:45 CHICAGO | 06:45 NEW YORK
FIRST REPORT OF THE DAY — US PRE-OPEN / VETERANS DAY
LATEST SYNCHRONISED US FUTURES SNAPSHOT VERIFIED: 11:04 SWITZERLAND / 05:04 NEW YORK — REUTERS

MAIN CONCLUSION
The Nasdaq-100 begins Wednesday with a powerful technology-led rebound after CoreWeave reported accelerating AI cloud revenue, a substantial contracted backlog and higher full-year guidance. At 05:04 New York / 11:04 Switzerland, Reuters recorded Nasdaq-100 E-mini futures up 1.67%, S&P 500 E-mini futures up 0.74% and Dow futures up just 0.03%. Nvidia rose about 4% pre-market, with Marvell and Micron gaining almost 7% each. That represents a meaningful reversal from Tuesday's inflation-driven selling, but the forces responsible for the previous decline have not disappeared: October CPI exceeded forecasts, Treasury yields surged and the market expects further Federal Reserve tightening. Today's Veterans Day bond-market closure adds an unusual limitation to cross-market confirmation.

KEY CONFIRMATION / RISK
CoreWeave reported quarterly revenue of $3.661 billion, up approximately 168% year on year, and backlog of around $132.5 billion. It also recorded a $709 million GAAP net loss, $846 million of net interest expense and guided 2026 capital expenditure to $37–39 billion. The results confirm rapid demand growth without establishing that debt-funded infrastructure expansion has become financially risk-free. The central question for NQ is whether the US cash market validates the chip-led futures advance after 15:30 Switzerland, particularly with the cash Treasury market closed and the latest CPI surprise still influencing the expected path of rates.

TUESDAY'S CLOSE — AN INFLATION-DRIVEN RETREAT
The US equity session ended lower on 10 November after October inflation exceeded economists' forecasts. The S&P 500 closed at 7,520.93, down approximately 0.38%; the Dow Jones Industrial Average finished at 52,231.89, down 0.30%; the Nasdaq Composite closed at 25,065.87, down 0.74%; and the Russell 2000 fell roughly 0.69% to 2,821.38. These are final cash-index values, not NQ futures prices.

Tuesday's closing losses were smaller than some intraday declines, showing that buyers absorbed part of the earlier pressure. Nevertheless, a weaker close followed the previous day's strong relief rally. The problem was not an announced collapse in computing demand. It was a higher cost-of-capital outlook and renewed concern about the valuation of companies whose most substantial expected cash flows may be years away.

WEDNESDAY FUTURES — TECHNOLOGY LEADS, NOT THE DOW

REUTERS | 05:04 NEW YORK / 11:04 SWITZERLAND:

NASDAQ-100 E-MINI FUTURES (NQ): +465.25 POINTS | +1.67%.

S&P 500 E-MINI FUTURES (ES): +55.75 POINTS | +0.74%.

DOW E-MINI FUTURES (YM): +15 POINTS | +0.03%.

These observations are time-stamped and were not verified again at the 12:45 Swiss report cut-off. They establish the strongest relative participation in Nasdaq futures, not the live value of the contract. No current NQ level, opening range, VWAP, POC or support/resistance number is asserted without a matching quotation.

The divergence with the Dow is particularly useful. Tuesday's sell-off affected growth-sensitive companies; Wednesday's initial recovery is concentrated in businesses associated with computing and AI infrastructure. That is more consistent with a sector-specific reassessment after earnings than with a uniform improvement across all US equities.

COREWEAVE — WHAT THE COMPANY ACTUALLY REPORTED
CoreWeave's third-quarter earnings release provides unusually clear evidence of both opportunity and financial strain:

Q3 REVENUE: $3.661 BILLION, versus $1.365 billion a year earlier, approximately +168%.
GAAP OPERATING INCOME: $207 MILLION, a 6% operating margin.

GAAP NET LOSS: $709 MILLION, versus a $110 million loss a year earlier.
NET INTEREST EXPENSE: $846 MILLION, versus $310 million a year earlier.

ADJUSTED EBITDA: $2.256 BILLION; adjusted EBITDA margin 62%.
ADJUSTED OPERATING INCOME: $379 MILLION; adjusted operating margin 10%.

REVENUE BACKLOG: approximately $132.5 BILLION at 30 September.

2026 REVENUE GUIDANCE: $13.0–13.3 BILLION, raised by management.

2026 CAPEX GUIDANCE: $37–39 BILLION.

EXPECTED Q4 INTEREST EXPENSE: $1.05–1.15 BILLION.

The figures explain why shares reacted strongly. The business is scaling rapidly and improving some operating measures. At the same time, financing is consuming a very large amount of cash and the company remains loss-making under GAAP. An attractive growth story and a demanding balance-sheet story can both be true.

COREWEAVE BACKLOG — CONTRACTED DEMAND IS NOT IMMEDIATE CASH

The $132.5 billion backlog includes remaining performance obligations and other contracted amounts expected to be recognised over future periods, subject to service availability and delivery requirements. It should not be described as cash already received, guaranteed profit or revenue that will necessarily arrive immediately. Delivery schedules, customer commitments, funding and operating costs determine how backlog converts into realised earnings and cash flow.

Management also referred to approximately $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected over the next three months. Those anticipated inflows may support liquidity, but the precise timing and contractual obligations still matter. For NQ, this is an important difference between stronger demand visibility and a fully resolved financing question.

THE INFRASTRUCTURE BUILD-OUT — GROWTH AT AN EXCEPTIONAL SCALE

CoreWeave reported more than 1.7 gigawatts of active power capacity and over 4.6 gigawatts of contracted power. It expects more than 1.85 gigawatts of active power by year-end. These numbers illustrate the physical scale of the AI investment cycle: advanced processors require buildings, electricity access, cooling, networking and substantial construction expenditure.

The company reported issuing about $4.2 billion of convertible senior notes and closing a $2.6 billion financing facility. Its capital plan includes an at-the-market equity programme. These are mechanisms for financing growth, not evidence that the cost of capital has become irrelevant. The market will continue assessing debt service, potential equity dilution, utilisation and the returns ultimately generated by new infrastructure.

PROFITABILITY EXPECTATIONS — AN IMPORTANT QUALIFICATION

Reuters reported that CoreWeave expects to become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028. That is forward-looking management guidance and does not mean the company has already achieved positive GAAP net earnings. The distinction between adjusted profitability, GAAP profitability, positive operating cash flow and free cash flow is essential when evaluating an infrastructure operator with very high capital expenditure and financing costs.

The pre-market rally shows that investors found the earnings and outlook reassuring. It does not eliminate the possibility of sharply different interpretations once the wider US cash market opens.

NVIDIA — SHARP REBOUND AFTER TWO DIFFICULT SESSIONS

Reuters recorded Nvidia approximately 4% higher in Wednesday pre-market dealing after a two-session decline that erased around $480 billion in market value in its observation. The company has been affected by reports concerning its chief executive and an alleged foreign-intelligence connection. Nvidia's board has announced an independent investigation and stated that it had no reason to believe corporate secrets or national-security interests had been compromised.

Allegations are not confirmed investigative findings. The immediate financial issue is how investors price unresolved company-specific uncertainty at a business with exceptional index influence. A rebound in Nvidia can strongly support NQ, but the cash-market response and the behaviour of other chipmakers are needed before declaring a sustainable recovery.

MARVELL, MICRON AND THE SEMICONDUCTOR HANDOVER

Marvell Technology and Micron were indicated nearly 7% higher in Reuters' early Wednesday pre-market snapshot. This wider semiconductor response is constructive because it extends beyond Nvidia itself. The prior correction showed how quickly the AI trade can become concentrated in selling. Today's initial rebound suggests buyers are returning to several points in the semiconductor supply chain.

However, strong pre-market moves are not the same as confirmed regular-session breadth. A higher-quality recovery would involve sustained buying across chip designers, memory suppliers, equipment companies and large technology platforms after the opening. The relevant relationship is NQ versus ES and the participation of SOX constituents, rather than one percentage gain in isolation.

OCTOBER CPI — THE NEGATIVE MACRO BACKDROP HAS NOT DISAPPEARED

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported October headline CPI up 0.4% month on month, compared with a 0.3% market forecast, and core CPI up 0.3%, compared with an expected 0.2%. Headline inflation slowed from September's 0.6% monthly rise, but not by as much as economists anticipated. Core monthly inflation did not decelerate from September.

Shelter increased 0.3%, food rose 0.5% and energy increased 0.7%. A decline in crude oil prices during November cannot retroactively change October's measured inflation. For most categories the BLS cannot provide the normal twelve-month October rate because the October 2025 federal shutdown disrupted the historical comparison. Today's analysis therefore uses official monthly observations rather than presenting an unofficial annual rate as fact.

FEDERAL RESERVE — DECEMBER TIGHTENING REMAINS CENTRE STAGE

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said that a monthly core CPI reading of 0.3% could justify discussing a 50-basis-point increase at the December meeting. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan also argued for further rate increases; other policymakers have indicated concern about persistent inflation. These are individual policy views, not an announced Federal Open Market Committee decision.

Reuters reported the market as effectively pricing a quarter-point December increase, with roughly an 11.5% implied chance of a half-point move in its Wednesday morning observation. Those probabilities can change throughout the day. The key issue for high-valuation technology is whether interest rates remain elevated long enough to reduce the present value of future earnings and make new infrastructure funding more expensive.

TREASURY MARKET — VETERANS DAY LIMITS LIVE CONFIRMATION

Wednesday is Veterans Day. The US cash equity markets are scheduled to open normally, but the US Treasury and dollar fixed-income cash markets are closed. Consequently, Tuesday's sharp increase in Treasury yields remains essential background information without an ordinary live cash-bond market to validate the latest equity rally.

Reuters reported the US two-year yield rising around 18 basis points on Tuesday and the ten-year trading near 5%. Those are previous-session references, not current Wednesday cash-market yields. Some Treasury futures or related instruments may have contract-specific holiday hours; they should not be substituted automatically for normal, fully liquid cash-Treasury pricing. Traders should check CME and their broker for the precise instrument schedule.

DOLLAR — RATES EXPECTATIONS STILL SUPPORT THE CURRENCY

In Reuters' international-market observation, the dollar index was around 102.45, up approximately 0.2% on Wednesday after Tuesday's advance. A firmer dollar alongside stronger technology futures shows that currency and equity markets can move differently when earnings and monetary-policy news compete for attention.

Dollar strength may tighten conditions for some international borrowers and influence overseas earnings translation. It does not provide a reliable one-variable forecast for NQ. The dollar's relationship with growth equities depends on the wider reason for the movement and the behaviour of actual corporate earnings expectations.

ASIA — THE REBOUND HAS INTERNATIONAL PARTICIPATION

Reuters observed South Korea's Kospi up around 2.6%, Taiwan's benchmark up about 3.6% and Japan's Nikkei up around 1.3% in its Wednesday global-market report. The wider Asia-Pacific equity measure rose approximately 1.5%. The gains followed CoreWeave's report and a renewed willingness to take exposure to technology and AI-related businesses.

This is meaningful international confirmation of better sentiment, not proof that the US cash session will finish higher. Asian exchanges, currencies and index constituents differ from NQ. Their closing moves should be treated as observations from a separate trading session.

EUROPE — AN EQUITY RECOVERY AGAINST A HAWKISH BOND BACKDROP

The pan-European STOXX 600 advanced approximately 0.4% by 10:24 Switzerland in Reuters' observation, approaching an earlier record. European technology companies participated, but value and other sectors also attracted interest. German benchmark government yields remained under scrutiny after the sharp US rate repricing, while Japanese yields climbed.

The global picture is therefore not simply risk-on or risk-off. Earnings have encouraged equity buying, while inflation has left bond investors wary of further tightening. That divergence is precisely why the opening US equity reaction needs to be observed rather than inferred from an overnight futures gain.

OIL AND GEOPOLITICS — A PARTIAL REBOUND FROM RECENT LOWS

Brent crude was around $91.60 per barrel, modestly higher in Reuters' Wednesday international-market observation after earlier declines. Traders continue weighing diplomatic efforts and shipping risks involving Iran and the Strait of Hormuz. Lower oil compared with recent highs may help future inflation expectations, but energy remains exposed to sudden geopolitical news.

For AI operators, power availability and long-term electricity costs matter more directly than an isolated intraday move in Brent. The scale of physical investment in computing capacity means that energy and grid constraints remain relevant even in a day dominated by an encouraging cloud earnings release.

GOLD AND DEFENSIVE ASSETS — A DIFFERENT RESPONSE

Gold recovered to about $4,049 an ounce, up 0.4% in Reuters' international-market snapshot after falling approximately 2.6% on Tuesday. These movements reflect a combination of interest-rate expectations, currency conditions and defensive demand. They provide useful background, but should not replace direct evidence about NQ futures, chip participation or corporate financing.

ANTHROPIC — PUBLIC-MARKET VALUATIONS REMAIN UNDER SCRUTINY

Investors are also evaluating Anthropic's proposed flotation at an indicated valuation of up to roughly $1.4 trillion, according to Reuters. A proposed offering is not a completed capital raise. The terms, timing and final valuation can change. Its significance is that public investors may soon have another major AI company against which to compare revenue growth, spending requirements and longer-term profitability assumptions.

Large AI valuations can attract interest even as funding markets become more demanding. The two conditions are not mutually exclusive. The central question remains whether growth can justify the capital and risk being committed.

TODAY'S ECONOMIC CALENDAR — A QUIETER DAY FOR US DATA

WEDNESDAY, 11 NOVEMBER — VETERANS DAY.

There is no major Bureau of Labor Statistics inflation or employment release scheduled for today. The central information event has already occurred: CoreWeave's results. The US Treasury cash market is closed, but regular NYSE and Nasdaq equity trading is expected to proceed.

15:30 SWITZERLAND / 08:30 CHICAGO / 09:30 NEW YORK — US STOCK-MARKET OPENING. Observe how much of the overnight technology rally survives the cash opening and whether buying extends beyond AI-linked stocks.

22:00 SWITZERLAND / 15:00 CHICAGO / 16:00 NEW YORK — REGULAR US EQUITY CASH CLOSE. The closing breadth, semiconductor participation and comparison between Nasdaq and S&P 500 performance will help establish the quality of today's recovery.

US futures and options products may observe distinct holiday arrangements; use the current CME contract-specific schedule for trading hours rather than extrapolating from the NYSE or cash Treasury calendar.

THURSDAY — CLAIMS AND SUPPLY-CHAIN EARNINGS

THURSDAY, 12 NOVEMBER, 14:30 SWITZERLAND — US INITIAL AND CONTINUING JOBLESS CLAIMS. After strong October payrolls and a hotter CPI, the claims figures can offer another view of labour-market resilience. The market response will depend on how they affect the expected pace of monetary tightening.

THURSDAY, 12 NOVEMBER, AFTER THE CASH CLOSE — CISCO AND APPLIED MATERIALS EARNINGS. Cisco can provide evidence on networking orders and AI-related infrastructure demand; Applied Materials can shed light on semiconductor equipment spending and manufacturing-capacity investment. Applied Materials has confirmed its conference call for 22:30 Switzerland. Those results are future events at the cut-off of this report, not known outcomes.

FRIDAY — OCTOBER PRODUCER PRICE INFLATION

FRIDAY, 13 NOVEMBER, 14:30 SWITZERLAND — US PRODUCER PRICE INDEX. The BLS has confirmed the official release time. After Tuesday's consumer-inflation surprise, PPI will provide another reading on producer costs and pricing pressures. A benign report might alter the balance of concerns; another unfavourable surprise could reinforce expectations of tighter policy. Neither outcome guarantees a predetermined NQ direction.

CROSS-MARKET CONFIRMATION FRAMEWORK

NQ VERSUS ES — Is the Nasdaq continuing to outperform the broader equity market after the opening?

NVIDIA, MICRON AND MARVELL — Are pre-market gains sustained and spreading through semiconductor constituents?

COREWEAVE, DATA-CENTRE OPERATORS AND POWER SUPPLIERS — Does the earnings response spread across the infrastructure chain, or remain company-specific?

NASDAQ BREADTH AND SOX — Does the cash market provide genuine sector participation?

DXY AND OIL — Are currency and energy markets reinforcing or complicating risk appetite?

US GOVERNMENT YIELDS — Tuesday's closing conditions are reference points, not a normal live cash-bond series today because of Veterans Day.

VIX AND EXECUTION CONDITIONS — Is the rebound occurring alongside reduced volatility or large, abrupt changes in price?

None of these references is an automatic entry instruction. No unsupported contract-level signal is presented.

BULLISH SCENARIO — CONDITIONS FOR CONFIRMATION

A constructive case would be strengthened by sustained buying after 15:30 Switzerland, broadening semiconductor participation and continued support for data-centre operators following CoreWeave's results. Lower volatility and evidence that buyers can absorb profit-taking would make the recovery more convincing. The strongest confirmation would come from the cash market, not from assuming that a large pre-market gain must continue.

BEARISH SCENARIO — CONDITIONS FOR A RENEWED SELLOFF

The negative case remains grounded in Tuesday's inflation surprise, the expected Federal Reserve tightening and the cost of capital required for very large AI projects. It would gain support if chip gains fade, Nasdaq breadth deteriorates or investors refocus on CoreWeave's net loss, debt burden and expenditure plans. The absence of a normal cash Treasury session can make interest-rate confirmation less reliable than usual. Sharp intraday reversals remain possible even in a constructive pre-market environment.

ANALYTICAL EDGE

TECHNOLOGY-LED PRE-MARKET RECOVERY / VERIFIED AI REVENUE GROWTH / UNRESOLVED FINANCING COSTS / HAWKISH FED BACKDROP / LIMITED BOND-MARKET CONFIRMATION.

The strongest evidence is the relative NQ futures advance and the company-specific information behind it. The most important remaining uncertainty is whether cash-market participation validates the advance after the opening. This is a discretionary assessment of observed conditions, not a calibrated probability of the next futures move.

CURRENT REGIME

POST-CPI TECH REBOUND / COREWEAVE EARNINGS SUPPORT / SEMICONDUCTOR BUYING / VERY HIGH AI CAPITAL EXPENDITURE / STRONGER DOLLAR / FED TIGHTENING RISK / VETERANS DAY BOND-MARKET CLOSURE.

OPERATIONAL CONCLUSION

Today's pre-market strength offers useful information about buying interest following a technology correction. It does not by itself establish a lasting trend change. In leveraged NQ and MNQ trading, the relevant decisions remain actual market structure, position size, protective stop, realistic transaction costs and maximum acceptable loss. The closure of the cash Treasury market makes it especially important not to draw conclusions from missing or stale bond quotations.

FINAL ANALYTICAL VIEW

WHAT CHANGED: Tuesday's hot CPI and negative Nasdaq close were followed by strong CoreWeave results and a renewed technology-led futures recovery. Reuters recorded NQ futures +1.67% at 11:04 Switzerland, against ES +0.74% and Dow +0.03%.

WHAT COREWEAVE ADDED: Quarterly revenue grew approximately 168% to $3.661 billion and backlog reached $132.5 billion, but the company remained GAAP loss-making and expects $37–39 billion in 2026 capex. Strong demand and significant funding risk coexist.

WHAT MATTERS TODAY: The 15:30 Swiss-time US cash opening, the breadth of chip-sector buying, the response of Nvidia and data-centre operators, and the limitations of trading on Veterans Day without normal cash Treasury pricing.

WHAT MATTERS NEXT: Thursday's claims and Cisco/Applied Materials results, followed by Friday's October PPI at 14:30 Switzerland.

The AI investment cycle has demonstrated strong revenue demand. Today's question is whether investors will pay higher valuations for that growth despite elevated financing costs and unresolved monetary-policy risk.

Frank Scott, 48, who had 54 previous convictions for 91 offences, has been jailed for 22 years after pleading guilty to three counts of rape against two vulnerable victims in Manchester between June and November 2025.

Scott approached his first victim in Manchester's Gay Village after she became separated from friends on her way home. The woman was struggling with a bereavement and had been using alcohol and crack cocaine. Scott offered her directions and access to his crack pipe before taking her to a secluded car park on Chorlton Street, where he was sleeping rough. He pinned her down, forced her to drink vodka, raped her and subjected her to oral rape.

When she tried to escape, Scott dragged her along the ground and smashed her head against the concrete. She eventually fought him off and fled naked, striking him over the head as she escaped, before members of the public came to her aid.

Scott was arrested but, despite the victim suffering 67 injuries and his previous convictions for assaults on emergency workers, threatening behaviour and arson, he was released on police bail while further enquiries continued.

In November 2025, while still on bail for the first attack, Scott targeted a second vulnerable victim, a man sleeping rough in Sackville Gardens, close to the location of the first assault. He offered the man what he believed was a cigarette, but it contained crack cocaine. After the drug impaired his awareness, Scott sexually assaulted him and subjected him to oral rape. The victim later reported the attack and Scott was arrested four days afterwards. He initially denied the allegations, claiming the sexual activity was consensual, but eventually pleaded guilty.

On 9 November 2026, Scott was sentenced at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court by Judge Jenny Lester-Ashworth. Both victims described the lasting psychological effects of the attacks. The woman reported panic attacks and sleepless nights, while the male victim said he had developed PTSD and was constantly on edge. Scott received 22 years in prison, followed by an eight-year extended licence.

The circumstances surrounding Scott's release on police bail were also raised by the judge, who described his subsequent offending as being "of considerable public concern". She said it was not for her to make findings but suggested the circumstances should be reviewed to establish whether lessons could be learned.

It is a special time set aside to proudly recognize acknowledge their sacrifices, dedication, and patriotism in defending our freedom and country.

Mamdani just told NYC property owners who gets first dibs on their buildings. 

See you in court, commies.

Today he signed COPA, the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act.

It covers about 2,100 apartment buildings across the city.

Owners must notify the city and "approved" nonprofits before they sell.

And guess who decides what nonprofits get approved? 

The city does. The Department of Housing Preservation.

So, the mayor's own agency picks who gets first crack at these buildings. 

Those groups get months to make an offer before anyone else can buy.

Turn them down? 

They can still match any other buyer's deal for a full year.

Eric Adams vetoed this bill last year. 

The Council brought it back.

It takes effect November 2027. 

Expect landlord groups to sue the minute it does.

Their case is ready-made: Cedar Point Nursery v. Hassid (2021).

There the Supreme Court ruled that when government takes away an owner's right to control their own property, that's a taking.

Under the Fifth Amendment, the government has to pay for a taking.

A year-long right to hijack any sale looks a lot like taking control from the owner.

Private property means the owner decides. 

Not City Hall. 

Not Mamdani's friends.

San Diego, California, November 2026. An 8-year-old Haitian boy and third-grader in San Diego was taken into federal custody by ICE after a routine immigration check-in with his uncle. Video captured agents escorting the child away alone. The boy and his uncle had attended the scheduled meeting at the federal building in San Diego to comply with immigration rules, where agents separated the child, classified him as an "unaccompanied alien child," and transferred him to the Office of Refugee Resettlement. The boy had been cared for by his uncle and cousins following his father's 2025 deportation and the earlier termination of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians.
 
The explanations offered for this appalling sequence of events only deepen the outrage. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson claimed the uncle could not verify legal guardianship, prompting protective custody under anti-trafficking laws, yet the San Diego Unified School District and the Haitian Bridge Alliance noted the uncle is an authorized school caregiver, arguing the father's sudden deportation hindered formal paperwork. California Senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff, alongside four House Democrats, launched a congressional inquiry on November 10, 2026, and lawmakers and school officials are demanding details on the boy's status and his immediate return to family. That a third-grader should be ripped from his family and put through this ordeal, separated, labeled, and processed alone, is a damning indictment of an immigration system that treats children as collateral damage.

text:
"HERE TO STAY FOR THE USA": THREE MONTHS LATER, MAURICIO POCHETTINO HAS HIS BAGS BY THE DOOR

On August 3, U.S. Soccer posted six words alongside the news that Mauricio Pochettino had signed a new contract through the 2030 World Cup: "Here to create a culture. Here to stay for the USA."

Fourteen weeks later, the culture is still under construction, and the man who was here to stay is reportedly agreeing terms with Manchester United.

Let's be precise, because the story is moving fast. Michael Carrick is still United's head coach as of Wednesday morning, but the BBC, The Athletic, the Guardian, the Telegraph and Sky Sports all report that the club is preparing to sack him and has lined up Pochettino as his replacement. David Ornstein reports that United are "finalising" a deal and that terms are being done with his camp. The BBC says he is "ready to accept an offer" and sees it as a "serious opportunity." The only thing missing is a phone call to U.S. Soccer, which, according to every reliable outlet, hasn't happened yet. A release clause of around $10 million is reportedly all it takes.

Nobody is pretending Pochettino owes the federation his whole life. But it's worth remembering what he said when he signed that deal, because he said it so well. "Every time we sign a contract, it's to go to the last day of the contract," he told reporters in August. "If we don't believe in that process, if we don't believe in that journey, why sign [for] four years? Only to be sure that we are going to receive a salary at the end of the month? That is not nice."

No, it isn't.

He did leave himself a door ajar ("In life, nothing is sure. Less in football"), and the escape clause suggests his lawyers left a wider one. Legally, then, this may well be clean. Morally, it's harder to dress up. You don't get to deliver a speech about believing in the journey, accept a four-year brief that covers youth development, coaching education and the whole national-team pathway, and then start working out personal terms with another employer before the first competitive camp of the cycle is over.

And look at the timing. The USMNT face Haiti in a Nations League quarter-final on Saturday in Miami and again next Tuesday in Cincinnati. It's the first official competition on the road to 2030, the cycle he signed up to lead. Instead of selling a vision, he'll spend Friday's press conference dodging questions about Old Trafford. Antonee Robinson says the players see it as "outside noise." That's admirably professional of them. It's also a job their head coach is supposed to be doing for them.

To be fair to him, the record is real. He won the group at a home World Cup, delivered the first USMNT knockout win since 2002, and won all four games in the autumn window. He has also never hidden his longing for the Premier League. As recently as September he told Sky that his "dream now is to be in the USA for four years, but after that, why not?" The trouble is "after that" seems to have arrived about three and a half years early.

There's also the small matter of what he'd be swapping it for. United are 18th after ten games, their worst start in four decades, and he'd be their third manager of 2026. That isn't ambition in any forward-looking sense. It's the oldest pull in football, the badge, the stadium, the Premier League spotlight, beating a project he described as building a legacy "beyond results on the field."

American soccer has spent years asking to be taken seriously by the game's elite. It finally hired one of them, gave him a four-year mandate and philanthropic backing to match, and heard him promise he believed in the journey. If he walks now, the lesson isn't that the USMNT aimed too high. It's that, for some coaches, the national team is a very well-paid waiting room.

Loyalty's a two-way street, and it looks like Pochettino has just found the exit.

Should U.S. Soccer let him go, or make United pay every cent of that clause?

text:
Fixed-rate credit could be the next big leg of DeFi lending 💎

Aave’s risk stewards reported stablecoin borrow rates of 10-36% APR during late-October liquidity stress.

A week later, Aave Labs bought a team building fixed-rate loans.

That’s why I’m paying attention to the Avon deal.

@aave already had $33B+ in deposits and $13B+ in active loans when it announced the acquisition.

Now it has Avon’s team, fixed- and floating-rate lending tech, and an onchain order book.

> TL;DR

A fixed-rate, fixed-term loan sets your interest rate and repayment date upfront.

Borrow $100K for 90 days at 8% simple APR and you know you’ll owe about $1,973 in interest before fees.

The lender knows what they stand to earn if the loan is repaid.

In a variable-rate pool, your borrowing cost can change as more people borrow or depositors pull liquidity.

Why I think DeFi needs it?

When I look at a 90-day stablecoin loop, I care about what I’ll earn after borrowing costs.

I can buy a @pendle_fi PT that yields 10% to maturity. If my floating borrow rate moves from 6% to 12%, the annualized spread on the borrowed portion goes from +4 to −2 percentage points before fees.

Fixing both rates for the same term lets me price that spread upfront. I still need to manage collateral and repay or refinance at maturity.

For protocols, the opportunity goes beyond loops.

– A business waiting 90 days on a receivable can borrow for 90 days and know its financing cost.

– A vault can allocate to loans with known repayment dates and earn interest in return for committing capital.

The hard part is liquidity. Each maturity needs enough lenders and borrowers, and a vault offering daily withdrawals needs liquid assets or a way to sell loans early.

This is where the macro angle gets interesting to me.

If I can compare 30-, 90-, and 180-day USDC loans against the same collateral and liquidation terms, I can see what borrowers are paying for longer funding.

I’d judge that yield curve by the rates I can actually get for a $1M loan.

Where I see the opportunity?

→ $AAVE - distribution.

I’m watching whether Avon’s tech makes it into Horizon, where institutions already borrow stablecoins against tokenized assets.

For scale, even 1% of Aave’s reported loan book would be about $130M. The metric I want after launch is outstanding fixed-rate loans by maturity.

→ $MORPHO - live fixed-term credit.

Midnight had ~$92M in active loans on Nov 9. DeFiLlama tracked ~$524K in borrower interest over 30 days and $0 in protocol revenue.

Coinbase already uses Midnight for fixed-rate BTC-backed USDC loans.

The next catalyst is the planned Q4 adapter that lets curators allocate from @Morpho’s ~$5B vault base into Midnight.

→ $PENDLE / Boros - fixed yield and rate trading.

I’d use PTs to compare fixed yields across maturities. For traders running a perp basis trade, Boros lets them swap floating funding for a fixed rate.

It has ~$149M in swap open interest and ~$56K in 30-day protocol revenue. Pendle V2 fees fund PENDLE buybacks.

Boros currently retains its revenue for operations.

→ $EUL - benchmark-based borrowing.

@eulerfinance’s Treehouse market uses an ETH staking benchmark to set the WETH borrow rate for most of each month.

The rate rises to 50% APY for up to 24 hours on the final day to encourage repayment.

I’d watch whether borrowers renew after repricing. Euler’s protocol fee is currently 0%, while curators can charge vault-level fees.

→ solana:KMNo3nJsBXfcpJTVhZcXLW7RmTwTt4GVFE7suUBo9sS - fixed-rate financing for RWAs.

@kamino’s ONyc market showed ~$60M borrowed from its fixed-rate USDC reserve.

It also offers 30-day fixed-rate borrowing against AUTO, which gives holders exposure to US consumer auto credit.

I’m watching whether borrowers keep rolling these positions once the first term expires.

One early project on my radar is IRIS, which targeted Nov 10 for its SparkLend launch.

Borrowers choose their term, and competing solvers quote a fixed rate while taking on the difference against SparkLend’s floating rate.

I’m curious how much solvers will charge for 90 days of that risk.

For now, I’d track Morpho for fixed-rate loan growth, Boros for swap OI and fees, and Aave for distribution.

The number I’ll come back to is how many borrowers refinance into another fixed term when the first one ends.
