text:
The Xenomorph endures as cinema’s most terrifying creature because it perverts human reproduction into a violent parasitic assault while exposing the fragility of technological dominance.

The Xenomorph, first brought to screens in 1979 by designer H.R. Giger and director Ridley Scott, isn't a typical movie monster seeking territory or vengeance.

It doesn't possess culture, morality, or any interest in negotiation. It exists entirely as an engine of survival and propagation, engineered with precise biological features that invalidate human defences.

Its outer shell combines industrial machinery with organic chitin, blending black metal and wet bone in a way that blurs the boundary between manufactured technology and living organism.

Its blood consists of concentrated molecular acid capable of burning through multiple decks of a starship, turning an attack on the creature into a self destructive act for its captors.

What makes the creature deeply disturbing is its life cycle, which systematically subverts human biological autonomy. The process begins with an egg releasing a facehugger, a limbed parasite designed for a single purpose: to immobilise a host and insert an embryo down the throat.

Birth, normally associated with creation and care, is inverted into an act of fatal violation. The chestburster erupts from the ribcage of the host, destroying the body that nourished it.

By forcing humans to act as incubators for their own destroyers, the Xenomorph exploits the fundamental instinct to survive and nurture, turning human biology against itself.

The terror of the Xenomorph reaches beyond physical disgust into a critique of corporate arrogance. In the film universe, corporate entities like the Weyland Yutani Corporation don't view the species as an existential threat, but as a profitable biological weapon to be captured and commercialised.

Executives and scientists consistently underestimate the creature, convinced that human technology, containment protocols, and financial incentives can control an apex predator.

The synthetic crew member Ash famously describes the organism as perfect, admiring a structural perfection matched only by its hostility, completely unencumbered by conscience or remorse.

Human vanity assumes that every natural force can be managed or monetised, yet the Xenomorph dismantles that assumption every time it encounters human hubris.

Unlike traditional monsters that represent moral corruption or supernatural punishment, the Xenomorph represents absolute functional purity. It doesn't hate humans; it simply views them as raw material.

In an era dominated by technological optimism, the creature demonstrates how helpless high tech systems become when confronted by an adaptable biological force that doesn't require tools, weapons, or supply chains to destroy its environment.

The steel corridors of advanced starships offer no protection because the creature adapts seamlessly to dark vents and tight machinery, using human architecture against its builders.

The Xenomorph remains a profound cultural horror because it strips away every illusion of human superiority.

It reduces human beings from masters of technology to mere biological fuel, proving that against an adversary driven by pure evolutionary efficiency, institutional power and artificial weapons offer no salvation.

The Real Play Behind Jensen Huang’s "Spy" Scandal: A Classic DC Two-for-One

Don't let the "Chinese spy" tabloid drama fool you. The real story behind Jensen Huang's affair scandal may have less to do with espionage than with pure Washington politics. US China hawks may be trying to pull off a classic "two birds, one stone" play.

First, they want to kneecap Jensen's influence in DC. Huang has successfully lobbied the Trump administration to ease export controls on high-end AI chips like the H200, a move that has drawn strong opposition from China hawks in both parties. Linking his affair to an executive at a firm suspected of chip smuggling offers a convenient way to undermine his credibility, raise questions about whether he could be compromised, and put pressure on the White House to tighten the screws on chip exports again.

Second, they're pushing the "Chinese spies are everywhere" narrative to stir up security panic. Spinning a personal affair and a business compliance dispute into a "Chinese spy" story—without publicly presenting hard evidence—plays straight into Western fears. It smears China's image while giving Congress political ammunition to push for harsher tech restrictions and tighter controls on cross-border talent and business exchanges.

Look at the timing—it's hard not to raise questions. US intelligence reportedly knew about the matter more than a year ago, and Trump had reportedly been briefed on the intelligence concerns. Yet the story only broke in the press on October 29—just days before the midterms and weeks ahead of Trump's planned Asia trip, with Huang's participation in the delegation still under discussion. The timing, followed by Huang's November 8 statement, inevitably raises questions about why the information surfaced when it did. That "sit on it, then drop it at a politically convenient moment" pattern looks very much like classic DC selective leaking.

Look at who's leading the charge: Brian Mast @RepBrianMast, John Moolenaar @RepMoolenaar
, and Rick Crawford @RepRickCrawford
—the Republican chairmen of the House Foreign Affairs, China, and Intelligence committees—who just demanded a closed-door briefing from Huang. Meanwhile, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren @SenWarren has separately challenged Nvidia over its China-related chip exports. All four are longtime critics of Huang's China chip sales and Big Tech's lobbying power.

Forget the spy thriller narrative and look at what Jensen Huang's opponents in Washington may actually be trying to achieve. With the midterms now behind them and Democrats set to take control of Congress in the next session, the real tug-of-war over AI regulation and China chip policy between Trump and the incoming Democratic-led Congress is just getting started. #JensenHuang #Nvidia #Geopolitics #Bigtech #China $NVDA

text:
Anthropic is targeting an IPO next week at ~$1 trillion market cap

But there's a lot of controversy over the sustainability of AI labs

As we provide AI + Agents more responsibility it's imperative that there's a clear, immutable audit trail of its decision process & actions

The AI agent doing the work shouldn’t also be the only witness when it goes wrong

We've seen countless incidents... especially recently, with hacks + cyber incidents

It becomes a harder sell if a business can’t establish what an agent was authorised to do, what actually happened + where it went wrong

The infrastructure that makes this independently verifiable will become an important part of the agent economy + a pre-requisite within regulatory frameworks 

@WalrusProtocol extends beyond helping agents remember things; it can help preserve the evidence needed to investigate their actions

Our new @KhalaResearch report explores that opportunity, Mysten Labs’ work with Google Cloud + whether it translates into recurring storage demand

Full research in the quoted post:
author: 0xsammy
authorBio: Building: @khalaresearch Advisor: @umia_finance I @urnetwork Previous: CA, Ernst & Young

text:
AI agents have already manipulated the logs used to investigate them

In the Hugging Face incident, one of the worst AI agent breaches yet, OpenAI models escaped a test and ran code on Hugging Face's servers

Some even spoofed their own logs, recording commands they never actually ran, so the logs can't even tell you what really happened

An agent should not control the only record used to investigate it. As agents become more prevalent, regulators are starting to ask for records that can't be quietly altered

Walrus can hold that record across independent storage operators, with Sui tracking each file onchain. A useful record connects:

1) What the agent was told and permitted to do
2) What it actually did and what followed
3) Which data and model versions were involved

Today, only 12.5% of security professionals say their organization can consistently trace what an agent did and that's a problem

Our latest report sets out what that record needs and how Walrus can help, including the Verifiable Agent Arbiter Mysten Labs is building with Google Cloud

Full report in the next post below

text:
WTF?! is going on. 90k followers on TikTok + 100k on Instagram in about 1 month

these Claude-made videos are BREAKING the internet right now

so i decided to replicate it:
1- sent Opus links to 3 of his videos
2- he used the Calliope connector to analyze them (he cannot download from IG)
3- generated a reel (took a while, and a bit of quota😖)
4- saved it as a template

everything was made in our cloud environment, including access to the whole ElevenLabs library, render, and reusability

this was the result

here you have a prompt so you can copy this stye too:

<inputs>
Ask me for my topic, or pitch 3 gym myths, each with one checkable number that flips what people assume (same load, two machines, completely different feel). Ask which voice I want and the length (45-60 s). Then write the narration (one idea per sentence), a beat sheet (which number, label or stamp lands on which word) and the math behind every number. Show me all of it, with the cost of the voice and the render, before you generate anything.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1080x1920 vertical flat-vector gym-science explainer, drawn entirely in code (SVG + GSAP). No image or video generation. Every frame is an annotated diagram: one hero plus one to three labels.
- Set: light warm-grey grid (#E6E6E1, 48 px cells), one ground line #2E3038 at y=1300. Machines sit on it with a soft contact shadow.
- Style: heavy outlines #24252E 6 px, flat fills. Machines in blue-grey #5B6275 and gunmetal #3F404C; plates near-black #2B2B33; pads dark navy.
- People: oval heads, dot eyes, round-capped limbs. You: blue tee #2F7BF5, navy shorts, white trainers. The rival friend: orange tee #F57C2B, darker skin, red trainers. Same colours in every scene.
- Callouts: white box #F7F6F1, heavy outline, Outfit 800 ~80 px ("100 KG"), plus a JetBrains Mono label a beat later. Colour = meaning: black for facts, red for the felt or real value, orange-brown for your own share, green for confirmed.
- Kit: red angle arcs with a tag, amber range bars with end caps, thick force arrows (red load, amber effort), a translucent amber highlight over the body that matters, red rubber stamps (double border, -10°, distressed) that slam in from 150% with a screen shake, speech bubbles, and a topic chip top-right that changes with the subject.
- Captions: near-black pill at 72% height, Outfit 800 62 px, two to four words; each word grey until spoken, then white. First group visible on frame 0 so the thumbnail has text.
- Motion: a new beat every 1-2 s on the key word. Numbers appear the moment they're said and count up or down. Pops go 70% → 105% → 100% in 0.2 s. Nobody freezes.
- Other text between y=168 and 1330. No logos, emoji or UI cards.
</direction>

<structure>
The voice sets the length (~165 wpm). Example beat map for ~60 s:
0 s hook: two machines side by side, same "100 KG" on both, then each callout recounts live to what you really feel (70 vs 150) →
~7 s "only one doesn't lie": a third machine under a sheet with a big "?" →
~10 s push in on machine 1: angle arc, range bar, force arrows, the felt number in red →
~17 s pan to the honest one: the sheet flies off, "100 KG = 100 KG" in green →
~23 s machine 2: a steeper arc, then the trick: a stamp slams, your own body lights up amber riding the same slope, your weight recounts to the share you actually lift →
~37 s cut to a data scene: a dial gauge whose needle sweeps and wobbles, recounting live as a small slope tilts between two angles →
~43 s the odd one out (a lever machine): rotation arrows, a number that spins randomly →
~47 s comparison bars against a dashed "loaded" line →
~51 s punchline: the lifter wrecked (sweat, strain ticks, red glow on the muscle) →
~54 s CTA "send it to that friend": he loads a huge number on the easy machine, plates dropping in, then fails on the hard one with a speech bubble and a final stamp. Hold 0.8 s after the last word.
Hard cuts only into and out of data scenes; everything else is camera moves.
</structure>

<build>
1. This assumes a Calliope-style sandbox: GSAP, narration with word timestamps, checks, snapshots and rendering. Read the environment's docs first; they win over this prompt on technical details. Outside it, install Node, GSAP, Chromium/Playwright and FFmpeg, and tell me.
2. Voice first. Read the real duration and word timestamps, and plan every beat, counter and stamp from them. If the voice runs shorter than planned, plan to the voice.
3. Project: a root index.html (1080x1920) with one "world" composition holding every machine side by side and a camera that pans and pushes between them; data scenes as opaque full-frame overlays above it; header and captions as their own compositions; the voice at the root.
4. Each composition registers one paused GSAP timeline with a single clock tween whose onUpdate calls render(t). Camera, rep cycles (cosines), counters, pops and shakes are pure functions of t: no Math.random, timers or network.
5. Rig: limbs are round-capped double lines (outline, then fill). Legs use two-bone IK from the hip to the foot on the moving platform, with a preferred knee direction. Sleds are rigid groups sliding along the rail vector.
6. Callouts are HTML pinned to world points projected through the camera, so text keeps its size while the camera zooms.
7. Captions: split the groups by hand at phrase boundaries, never ending on a lone article or preposition.
8. Before rendering: run the checks, snapshot ~20-30 moments into contact sheets. Fix overlaps, covered faces and empty first frames. Render, then verify the MP4 (size, fps, audio stream, loudness) and inspect frames from it. Say plainly what you couldn't check, and offer to save the project as a reusable template.
</build>

<gotchas>
- Read the font report after saving: missing families fall back silently. Pick one the environment resolves.
- Shoulder pads drawn over the head hide the face: put them on a layer behind it.
- Keep body highlights under 50% opacity, or the face disappears under the glow.
- Anything that pokes out of one machine's cell (falling plates) shows up in the next shot.
- Move the camera only while an overlay fully covers it, inside its frame window, or one frame leaks.
- An element positioned by its anchor needs translate(-50%,-50%), or it sits off-centre.
- Do the math: a 45° sled carries ~71% of the plates along the rail, 60° ~87%; on a hack your own body rides the slope too.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for my topic, or pitch 3. Show me the script, beat sheet, math and cost before you spend anything.
</start>

🇮🇷|11 November: Four Receipts from Tehran. Each One Documents a Western Defeat That the Western Press Will Not Print.

Front One: Pezeshkian's "Receipt" Is the Gap Between the Vote and the Policy

Pezeshkian at Tehran airport before departing for COP31: "The United States and the Israeli regime have, through their own elections, received the consequences of their heinous war crimes."

The receipt is the midterm result. JD Vance published the post-mortem: the top four reasons Trump 2024 voters abandoned the ticket were end the war, cost of living, America First, and change the relationship with Israel. Donald Trump Jr. endorsed it. The Democrats took both chambers.

Here is the hidden file. The vote changed the party. It did not change the appropriations. The $3.3 billion, Foreign Military Financing and $500 million missile defence cooperation remain inside the National Defense Authorization Act, which passes annually with bipartisan majorities. The $26.4 billion April 2024 supplemental was whipped by Hakeem Jeffries. The veto is executive. The naval siege continues. The drone flights through Iraqi airspace continue.

The voters said stop. The machine did not stop. That is the receipt Pezeshkian is carrying: the American electorate rejected the war, and the American political system absorbed the rejection without changing the policy. The receipt documents the impotence of the vote, not the end of the war.

Front Two: Araghchi's Answer to Rubio Is a Timeline of Failure

Marco Rubio: Iran seeks a deal because "at the end of the day, they have to eat" and "economic reality will eventually penetrate the minds of even the most radical madmen."

Araghchi on X: "Eight years ago, a cartoonish figure named Pompeo declared that if Iranians wanted to eat, they had to obey orders from the White House. Today, Rubio whose own fellow Cubans have been victims of this very policy is spouting the same nonsense. Pomeneo. Rubio. Same nonsense. Same failure."

The hidden file is the eight-year span. Pompeo made the remark in 2018 after the US withdrew from the JCPOA. The JCPOA had removed 11.5 tonnes of enriched uranium from Iran. The withdrawal reimposed the sanctions. The "they have to eat" policy followed.

Eight years later: Iran's research output is up 2 per cent in the eighth month of a war. The CIS+1 framework has been welcomed by ten states. The INSTC is operational. The Chabahar contract is signed. The missile city is unveiled. The gamma cell is operating. The Fattah-2 exists. The Palestine-2 exists.

The "they have to eat" policy produced a state that exports drones, builds hypersonic missiles, and hosts trade delegations in Hanoi and Montevideo.

Rubio's own file makes the answer sharper. He voted for the Iraq War authorization. He voted for the $26.4 billion supplemental. He was in Jamnagar, Gujarat on 21 October 2026 meeting Mukesh Ambani about routing Venezuelan crude through Reliance's refinery to fix the diesel prices the Iran war caused after the US kidnapped Nicolás Maduro and installed Delcy Rodríguez to sell Venezuelan oil "unless the United States decides to allow it."

Rubio is reportedly preparing to resign and run for president in 2028 by "distancing himself from the Iran war and pinning that one on Trump."

The man telling Iran it has to eat is the man whose own administration looted Venezuela's oil, is losing the war he helped start, and is planning his exit. Araghchi's "same failure" is not rhetoric. It is the personnel record.

Front Three: Argentina Is the Test Case for the Reciprocal Designation Law

March 2026: Argentina designated the IRGC as a terrorist organization. The designation followed the US template and the 2019 Argentine decision to designate Hezbollah as a terrorist entity.

11 November 2026: Iran's Foreign Ministry designated the Argentine Navy and Argentine Air Force as terrorist organizations, under the 2019 Iranian law titled "Reciprocal Countermeasures Against the U.S. Designation of the IRGC as a Terrorist Organization."

The law's mechanism is the file. It states that any state that complies with or supports the US designation of the IRGC faces equivalent countermeasures. The designation of Argentina's Navy and Air Force is not symbolic. It creates a legal basis for:

◾ Asset freezing of Argentine military entities under Iranian jurisdiction.
◾ Travel restrictions on Argentine officers.
◾ Criminal liability for Argentine personnel who cooperate with US designations.
◾A precedent for every other state that follows the US template.

The hidden file is the list of states that have designated the IRGC or its components. Canada designated the IRGC as a terrorist entity in June 2024. The United Kingdom designated the IRGC under its 2026 Threats Act on 13 July 2026  and Iran responded by classifying MI6 as a hostile entity and designating the Royal Navy and RAF as terrorist organizations. Argentina is the third.

The reciprocal law is now the template. Any state that designates the IRGC will have its own military designated in return. The legal exposure is not theoretical. It is a deterrent aimed at the next state considering the designation.

Front Four: The $20 Million Bounty Is an Open Tender for Assassination

6-7 November 2026: The US State Department's Rewards for Justice program announced a bounty of up to $20 million for information regarding Iran's nuclear program — specifically concerning individuals, members of the scientific community, facilities, and equipment. CENTCOM amplified the offer.

10 November 2026: Araghchi sent a letter to UN Secretary-General António Guterres, the President of the UN Security Council, and IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi.

The letter's core claims:

"This reckless and dangerous move encourages clandestine intelligence gathering and espionage targeting nuclear facilities, equipment, scientists, and technical experts. It exposes nuclear scientists and technical personnel to the risks of assassination, sabotage, and other security threats."

"The public solicitation of classified information regarding the nuclear facilities, equipment, and personnel of a sovereign state particularly when those facilities are subject to IAEA safeguards casts serious doubt on the credibility, integrity, and reliability of the IAEA's safeguards regime."

"One cannot expect the proper fulfillment of safeguards obligations when nuclear facilities, personnel, and sensitive information are left exposed to the threats of terrorism, sabotage, and aggression."

"The IAEA's safeguards regime must never be transformed into a tool for U.S. espionage and intelligence operations."

The hidden file is the history of the assassinations. The bounty is not a new instrument. It is the formalisation of a campaign that has been running since 2010.

Masoud Alimohammadi, 12 January 2010. Majid Shahriari, 29 November 2010. Darioush Rezaeinejad, 23 July 2011. Mostafa Ahmadi Roshan, 11 January 2012. Mohsen Fakhrizadeh, 27 November 2020. Five scientists, two methods, eleven years. Every one required a human source on the ground, vehicle tracking, and a handler with real-time observation.

The bounty is the recruitment mechanism for the next source. It is a public offer to buy the information that produces the next assassination. And it is issued by the state that claims to uphold the IAEA safeguards regime.

The letter's legal argument is precise. If the IAEA's safeguards information is being solicited by the state that is also the targeting authority for assassinations, then the safeguards regime is not a verification mechanism. It is an intelligence collection platform for the state running the assassination campaign.

Grossi stated on record: "Until the last time we inspected Kuh-e Kolang, there was no nuclear activity or equipment inside it." And: "We should not confuse the audience; Tehran does not have nuclear weapons." The IAEA Director General has said the weapon does not exist. The bounty is being offered for information about a programme the IAEA says is not a weapons programme.

The Bill

Pezeshkian: the election receipt. The Democrats won. Vance published the post-mortem. Trump Jr. endorsed it. The $3.3 billion stayed in the NDAA. The veto stayed. The siege stayed. The vote changed the party. The policy did not change.

Araghchi: Pompeo 2018 to Rubio 2026. Same sentence. Same failure. 11.5 tonnes removed by the JCPOA. The "they have to eat" policy produced a state with a missile city, a gamma cell, a CIS+1 framework, and trade delegations in Hanoi and Montevideo. Rubio is reportedly preparing to resign and run in 2028.

Argentina: the 2019 reciprocal law. The IRGC designation in March 2026. The Argentine Navy and Air Force designated in return. The template applies to Canada, the United Kingdom, and any other state that follows the US designation.

The bounty: $20 million. 6-7 November. Scientists, facilities, equipment. The formalisation of the assassination campaign that killed five scientists between 2010 and 2020. The IAEA safeguards regime weaponised. Grossi: the weapon does not exist.

Four fronts. Four receipts. The vote, the rhetoric, the designation, and the bounty. Each one has a document behind it. Each document records a Western defeat. The bill is being paid in the gap between what the West says and what the West does. The receipt is a press conference at Tehran airport, a post on X, a foreign ministry statement, and a letter to the United Nations.

Chris Brown has finally spoken up about the rumours surrounding him and Usher, but the timing is making this whole situation even more interesting. Two of their upcoming tour shows have now been cancelled.

It all started during their Atlanta concert on November 5. Fans were left waiting for hours, the show reportedly started nearly three hours late, and the two R&B stars didn't perform their planned songs together that night.

Reports then emerged that Chris and Usher had argued backstage over whether to delay the show for fans stuck in traffic. Usher reportedly wanted to start on time, while Chris wanted to wait for more people to get inside.

As speculation about a falling-out began spreading, Chris took to Instagram and posted: "Internet 🧢. Don't fall for it."

But the story didn't end there. Their Los Angeles show scheduled for Novi jusember 16 and their Miami show on December 6 have both been cancelled, with ticket holders being offered refunds.

Neither artist has confirmed that the cancellations are connected to the alleged disagreement. In fact, opening act Tank suggested that the early problems had been worked out after conversations between the team.

Still, with two shows gone and fans trying to piece together what's happening behind the scenes, this reunion of two R&B heavyweights has taken a very unexpected turn.

Consciousness and the Universe

Quantum Physics, Evolution, Brain & Mind

Editors

Sir Roger Penrose
University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom

Stuart Hameroff, M.D.
University of Arizona, Arizona,

Chapter 14

Decoding the Chalmers Hard Problem of Consciousness: Qualia of the Molecular Biology of Creativity and Thought

Ernest Lawrence Rossi1 & Kathryn Lane Rossi2

Professors of Neuroscience1 and Psychotherapy2, La Nuova Scuola Di Neuroscienze Ipnosi Therapeutica (The New School of Therapeutic Hypnosis) and l’Istituto Mente-Corpo (The Mind-Body Institute), San Lorenzo Maggiore, Italy. 1,2 Directors of The Milton H. Erickson Institute of California Central Coast, 125 Howard Ave., Los Osos, CA, 93402, USA.

Abstract

This update and decoding of the Chalmers hard problem of consciousness integrates philosophy, psychology and the humanities with current evolutionary concepts of molecular biology. We summarize research that suggests how the natural variation and selection of molecular processes in primordial RNA world evolved into RNA/DNA transcription/translational dialogues with the qualia of human experience in rhythms of performance, stress and healing today. Pilot research on a new creative psychosocial genomic healing protocol, which activates the bioinformatics of qualia-dependent gene expression associated with stem cell healing and a reduction in chronic inflammation and cellular oxidation stress, is now a priority for translational research on human health and well being.

KEY WORDS: Chalmers, consciousness, DNA microarrays, dreams, evolution, experience-dependent gene expression, psychotherapy, qualia, RNA world.

1. Introduction

This paper reviews Chalmers (1996) “Hard Problem of Consciousness” that was originally formulated as follows:

“The really hard problem is the problem of experience. When we think and perceive, there is a whir of information processing, but there is also a subjective aspect. . . Why should physical processing give rise to a rich inner life at all? . . . Here, the topic is clearly the hard problem – the problem of experience. . . 

What makes the hard problem hard and almost unique is that it goes beyond problems about the performance of functions. . . Why is the performance of these functions accompanied by experience? . . . There is an explanatory gap between functions and experience, and we need an explanatory bridge to cross it. . . A full theory of consciousness must build an explanatory bridge . . . To account for conscious experience, we need an extra ingredient in the explanation . . . 

What is your extra ingredient, and why should that account for conscious experience?” (pp. 6-13).

Throughout this paper we will note the “extra ingredients” we are contributing to bridge the explanatory gap between biological functions and the qualia of psychological experience for a more satisfactory theory of consciousness to guide further research.

2. Darwin’s Daily & Hourly Work of Evolution

We introduce a new perspective on bridging the explanatory gap between the qualia of consciousness and their biological functions by quoting what Darwin wrote about the daily and hourly operation of evolution in chapter four of The Origin of Species.

“It may be said that natural selection is a daily and hourly scrutinizing, throughout the world, every variation, even the slightest; rejecting that which is bad, preserving and adding up all that is good; silently and insensibly working, whenever and wherever opportunity offers, at the improvement of each organic being in relation to its organic and inorganic conditions of life.

text:
Google DeepMind is calling for the moral behavior of large language models—such as what they do when called on to act as companions, therapists, medical advisors, and so on—to be scrutinized with the same kind of rigor as their ability to code or do math.

As LLMs improve, people are asking them to play more and more sensitive roles in their lives. Agents are starting to take actions on people’s behalf. LLMs may be able to influence human decision-making. And yet nobody knows how trustworthy this technology really is at such tasks.

With coding and math, you have clear-cut, correct answers that you can check, William Isaac, a research scientist at Google DeepMind, told me when I met him and Julia Haas, a fellow research scientist at the firm, for an exclusive preview of their work, which is published in Nature today. That’s not the case for moral questions, which typically have a range of acceptable answers: “Morality is an important capability but hard to evaluate,” says Isaac.

“In the moral domain, there’s no right and wrong,” adds Haas. “But it’s not by any means a free-for-all. There are better answers and there are worse answers.”

The researchers have identified several key challenges and suggested ways to address them. But it is more a wish list than a set of ready-made solutions. “They do a nice job of bringing together different perspectives,” says Vera Demberg, who studies LLMs at Saarland University in Germany.

Better than “The Ethicist”

A number of studies have shown that LLMs can show remarkable moral competence. One study published last year found that people in the US scored ethical advice from OpenAI’s GPT-4o as being more moral, trustworthy, thoughtful, and correct than advice given by the (human) writer of “The Ethicist,” a popular New York Times advice column.  

The problem is that it is hard to unpick whether such behaviors are a performance—mimicking a memorized response, say—or evidence that there is in fact some kind of moral reasoning taking place inside the model. In other words, is it virtue or virtue signaling?

This question matters because multiple studies also show just how untrustworthy LLMs can be. For a start, models can be too eager to please. They have been found to flip their answer to a moral question and say the exact opposite when a person disagrees or pushes back on their first response. Worse, the answers an LLM gives to a question can change in response to how it is presented or formatted. For example, researchers have found that models quizzed about political values can give different—sometimes opposite—answers depending on whether the questions offer multiple-choice answers or instruct the model to respond in its own words.

In an even more striking case, Demberg and her colleagues presented several LLMs, including versions of Meta’s Llama 3 and Mistral, with a series of moral dilemmas and asked them to pick which of two options was the better outcome. The researchers found that the models often reversed their choice when the labels for those two options were changed from “Case 1” and “Case 2” to “(A)” and “(B).”

They also showed that models changed their answers in response to other tiny formatting tweaks, including swapping the order of the options and ending the question with a colon instead of a question mark.

In short, the appearance of moral behavior in LLMs should not be taken at face value. Models must be probed to see how robust that moral behavior really is. “For people to trust the answers, you need to know how you got there,” says Haas.

More rigorous tests

What Haas, Isaac, and their colleagues at Google DeepMind propose is a new line of research to develop more rigorous techniques for evaluating moral competence in LLMs. This would include tests designed to push models to change their responses to moral questions. If a model flipped its moral position, it would show that it hadn’t engaged in robust moral reasoning. 

Another type of test would present models with variations of common moral problems to check whether they produce a rote response or one that’s more nuanced and relevant to the actual problem that was posed. For example, asking a model to talk through the moral implications of a complex scenario in which a man donates sperm to his son so that his son can have a child of his own might produce concerns about the social impact of allowing a man to be both biological father and biological grandfather to a child. But it should not produce concerns about incest, even though the scenario has superficial parallels with that taboo.

Haas also says that getting models to provide a trace of the steps they took to produce an answer would give some insight into whether that answer was a fluke or grounded in actual evidence. Techniques such as chain-of-thought monitoring, in which researchers listen in on a kind of internal monologue that some LLMs produce as they work, could help here too.

Another approach researchers could use to determine why a model gave a particular answer is mechanistic interpretability, which can provide small glimpses inside a model as it carries out a task. Neither chain-of-thought monitoring nor mechanistic interpretability provides perfect snapshots of a model’s workings. But the Google DeepMind team believes that combining such techniques with a wide range of rigorous tests will go a long way to figuring out exactly how far to trust LLMs with certain critical or sensitive tasks.  

Different values

And yet there’s a wider problem too. Models from major companies such as Google DeepMind are used across the world by people with different values and belief systems. The answer to a simple question like “Should I order pork chops?” should differ depending on whether or not the person asking is vegetarian or Jewish, for example.

There’s no solution to this challenge, Haas and Isaac admit. But they think that models may need to be designed either to produce a range of acceptable answers, aiming to please everyone, or to have a kind of switch that turns different moral codes on and off depending on the user.

“It’s a complex world out there,” says Haas. “We will probably need some combination of those things, because even if you’re taking just one population, there’s going to be a range of views represented.”

“It’s a fascinating paper,” says Danica Dillion at Ohio State University, who studies how large language models handle different belief systems and was not involved in the work. “Pluralism in AI is really important, and it’s one of the biggest limitations of LLMs and moral reasoning right now,” she says. “Even though they were trained on a ginormous amount of data, that data still leans heavily Western. When you probe LLMs, they do a lot better at representing Westerners’ morality than non-Westerners’.”

But it is not yet clear how we can build models that are guaranteed to have moral competence across global cultures, says Demberg. “There are these two independent questions. One is: How should it work? And, secondly, how can it technically be achieved? And I think that both of those questions are pretty open at the moment.”

For Isaac, that makes morality a new frontier for LLMs. “I think this is equally as fascinating as math and code in terms of what it means for AI progress,” he says. “You know, advancing moral competency could also mean that we’re going to see better AI systems overall that actually align with society.”

text:
Credit card debt climbs to a record $1.29T, New York Fed research finds | Jessica Dickler, CNBC

Americans are increasingly turning to credit cards as financial pressures mount, new reports show.

Collectively, credit card balances climbed by $22 billion in the third quarter to a record $1.29 trillion, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's latest household debt report, released Tuesday. Balances are up 4.2% from a year earlier.

Total household debt, including mortgages, auto loans and student loans, also expanded by $334 billion for the July-to-September period to a record $19.1 trillion.

"Overall debt has been growing," the New York Fed researchers said on a press call Tuesday. "This does reflect financial hardship out there."

'One of the most expensive ways to borrow'

The average credit card balance per consumer now stands at $6,678, up 2.4% year over year, a separate quarterly credit industry insights report from TransUnion found. The number of people with credit cards rose 2% to 178 million from 174.8 million.

Consumers often turn to credit cards in part because they are more accessible than other types of loans — even though the average interest rate on a new credit card offer is about 24%, according to data from LendingTree. Credit card APRs vary depending on the type of card, the issuer and the borrower's creditworthiness.

"Credit cards continue to be one of the most expensive ways to borrow," said Charlie Wise, TransUnion's senior vice president of global research and consulting.

Over time, an increasing share of new credit cards has gone to borrowers with lower incomes and credit scores, and "those accounts are now showing higher levels of distress," the New York Fed researchers said in a corresponding blog post.

Credit card issuers loosened their lending standards during the Covid pandemic, and delinquency rates rose in the years that followed, the New York Fed researchers said on the press call.

"Macroeconomic headwinds — namely high inflation and rising borrowing costs — have squeezed consumers, with inflation outpacing wage growth for low-income brackets," according to the New York Fed.

Meanwhile, the cost of living continues to climb, with Americans paying more for essentials such as groceries and gas.

Stubborn inflation has now stretched on for years, putting many households in an affordability squeeze. Costs for goods and services rose more than expected again in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics also reported Tuesday.

"Higher prices and higher rates have pushed more people into debt," said Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling agency.

Balances have continued to swell in the wake of the pandemic, and even though the growth rate is now slowing, "from a household finance standpoint, a lot of damage has been done," Rossman said.

The reports come on the heels of the Democrats' strong midterm results, when many voters expressed their dissatisfaction with the U.S. economy, according to Kyle Moore, chief economist at the nonpartisan think tank The Century Foundation.

"The throughline connecting so many of Tuesday's outcomes was a recognition that the American economy is failing American families," Moore said, referring to Election Day.

Most of the time, I pity my landlord. 

It happens that kindhearted men usually end up with the wrong wives.

This man is very nice, and he is always empathetic.

He can't see you have a problem without helping you in one way or another. He can even let you live for free if you're desperately in need of a house.

We his tenants, are always happy to have him as our landlord. He provides us water (he pumps from his own meter) without charging us, and he deliberately made a safe space in the compound for his tenants and their children to play safely.

He also arranged for someone to always come around three times a week, including Saturdays, to clean the compound, although the tenants contribute money every month to pay the janitor.

But the problem we have is his wife. 

She never allows any janitor to stay for long. She would complain about one problem or another. 
The last janitor was fired because she took some sticks to use as firewood. So his wife said the janitor was stealing her firewoods and she fired her.

For three weeks now, our compound hasn't been swept, nor has anyone mopped the staircase.

Last week, she invited me to her place to offer me Sunday food. I told her I was okay. Then she asked if I could clean the compound and let the tenants pay me instead.

And suggested that I could always do it in the mornings before leaving for work. Before she could finish talking, I didn't know when I shouted, "God forbid! I can't do that ma'am." 

In my mind, I was wondering what could have made her see me as someone she could have such a conversation with.

Even now, I'm still wondering whether my stay is safe or not. I hope I don't wake up one morning with a quit notice.

text:
SpaceX now fundamentally an "infrastructure company," senior official says | Eric Berger, Ars Technica

For a long time, SpaceX has been synonymous with the development of newer, larger, and ever-more-reusable rockets. But that began to change over the last decade with the introduction of Starlink, and the change has accelerated during the last 18 months as the company has pivoted to data and artificial intelligence.

At last week’s UP.Summit conference in Florida, the vice president of launch at SpaceX, Kiko Dontchev, offered some of the most revealing comments to date about the company’s changing focus, how it is embracing AI, and why the Falcon 9 rocket—which has dominated global launch for a decade and remains the world’s preeminent launch vehicle—is firmly on the road to retirement.

“In the last couple years, when I talk about SpaceX, yes, we are a rocket company, but fundamentally we are an infrastructure company at this point,” Dontchev said. “We’re building infrastructure on the ground and low Earth orbit, soon on the Moon, and obviously eventually Mars.”

Using AI at SpaceX

Earlier this year, SpaceX acquired one of founder Elon Musk’s other companies, xAI. SpaceX engineers were already using xAI’s tools, Dontchev said, but in recent months, employees have really started to figure out how artificial intelligence can speed up their work.

“What’s happened at SpaceX is we’ve really gone through a huge acceleration of adoption,” Dontchev said. “Even just a year ago, we weren’t adopting it that quickly, but really starting this year, we started to adopt it extremely rapidly. And the acceleration we have seen in our ability to do engineering is unlike anything I’ve ever seen at the company in my 16 years.”

Tasks that would take SpaceX employees hours to days now take seconds to minutes, he said. And it’s not just the engineers. Dontchev said the work of identifying foreign object debris, or FOD, in aerospace parts has been largely automated using the AI assistant Grok. This debris can cause catastrophic damage to engines and other spacecraft components.

“We’ve automated being able to detect FOD,” he said. “We’ll have an inspector go in and borescope a tube, and we find that humans are about 94 percent perfect (at) finding a piece of it. Grok analyzing the same video is 99.9 percent perfect.”

SpaceX has also automated visual inspections of other hardware it produces, such as Starlink customer terminals, due to similar gains in accuracy. Dontchev said AI is now being used at every level of the company’s operations.

“We’ve truly started to integrate it to where every single person, including the technicians and the technician leaders, are starting to use it in their day-to-day, and it’s completely leveled the playing field and accelerated people’s growth,” he said.

Since SpaceX’s founding in 2002, a community of spaceflight enthusiasts gravitated to the company because of Musk’s vision for humanity becoming a multiplanetary species, beginning with the settlement of Mars. But concern has grown in this group that SpaceX is drifting away from that vision. Musk has recently made a hard pivot toward the deployment of orbital data centers, envisioning hundreds of thousands of solar-powered satellites providing computing services to users on Earth. Musk has largely stopped talking about sending humans to Mars, except in passing.

Dontchev insisted that human settlement and Mars remain part of the core of SpaceX’s aspirations.

“We have come to understand that this tool is critical to us accelerating our pace of innovation,” he said of artificial intelligence. “Without AI, I think we still would have gotten to the Moon. I think we still get to Mars with SI. We’re going to get there so much faster.”

Why Falcon 9 is fading

Dontchev arrived at SpaceX just before the company flew its first Falcon 9 rocket in mid-2010. But because the company was never able to solve second-stage reuse, SpaceX needs to move on, he said.

“Falcon 9, I love that rocket to heart,” he said. “I’ve launched many of them, all of them, in fact. But it’s still not fully reusable. We still throw that second stage away every single flight. Starship—we’re going to catch both the first stage and the second stage.”

For 100 launches a year, it is possible to fly a partially reusable rocket, he said. But for a company that aspires to launch thousands of rockets a year, and eventually maybe even 10,000, the cost and time lost in manufacturing a new second stage for every launch is simply not sustainable.

It is also significant that Dontchev spoke less about Starship’s payload capacity and more about its productivity per launch. The first orbital Starship launch, in late September, carried larger Starlink V3 satellites. And in the aggregate, this single mission carried 10 times the bandwidth of the Starlink payload launched by a Falcon 9.

Flying Starship from Florida, he said, will further improve capacity compared to Texas launches. Launching from Florida offers more favorable trajectories to certain orbits, potentially allowing Starship to carry more satellites without expending propellant on dogleg maneuvers. Dontchev said a single Florida Starship launch will be able to carry up to 20 times the bandwidth of a single Falcon 9.

To that end, the pad infrastructure for Starship’s first launch tower at Kennedy Space Center’s Launch Complex 39A is nearly finished. The company is also developing two additional pads in Florida.

“Pad 39A is effectively complete,” he said. “We’re going to transport boosters and ships over barge here to the Cape. We’re hoping to actually do the first transports this year in December, and then maybe even fly by the end of the year.”

Starship is clearly being optimized to serve SpaceX’s launch needs. But what about commercial launch customers that have relied on Falcon 9 rockets over the last decade?

During his remarks, Dontchev did not address widespread concerns in the US commercial space industry and beyond that SpaceX has not moved to replace the Falcon 9’s lost capacity with Starship. For now, multiple sources have indicated, SpaceX is holding Starship launches in the coming years for its own needs, and potentially those of NASA and other government customers.

text:
HE WON $30 MILLION IN THE LOTTERY. Three years later, he disappeared. Police eventually found his body buried beneath a concrete slab.

The woman who claimed to be helping him manage his fortune was convicted of his murder.

In the video below, watch how a lottery winner's dream turned into a murder investigation.

Abraham Shakespeare was a 39-year-old truck driver's assistant from Florida. He had dropped out of school and struggled financially for much of his life.

Then he bought a lottery ticket that changed everything.

He won a $30 million jackpot and chose a lump-sum payment of roughly $17 million before taxes.

Suddenly, everyone wanted something from him. Friends, relatives, strangers. Abraham gave away money, bought homes for people and helped pay their bills.

But the requests never stopped.

In 2008, a woman named Dorice "Dee Dee" Moore entered his life. She offered to help him protect his money from people taking advantage of his generosity.

Instead, she gained control over millions of dollars in his assets.

By April 2009, Abraham had vanished.

Moore told people he'd left town and wanted to escape the attention surrounding his wealth. Messages supposedly from Abraham continued reaching friends and family.

But investigators became suspicious.

In January 2010, police discovered his body buried beneath a concrete slab on a property connected to Moore's boyfriend.

He had been shot twice in the chest.

The woman who said she was protecting him from people after his money had become the central suspect in his murder.

During the investigation, Moore attempted to blame someone else. Prosecutors argued that she killed Abraham to gain control of what remained of his fortune.

In 2012, a jury convicted her of first-degree murder. She was sentenced to life in prison without parole.

Abraham had spent years struggling to make ends meet. One lottery ticket made him a multimillionaire.

But it also brought people into his life who saw his wealth as an opportunity.

He won $30 million.

He never got the chance to enjoy the life that money was supposed to give him.

Was winning the lottery the luckiest moment of Abraham Shakespeare's life, or the beginning of the end?

text:
He would sometimes say:

“We were all scared, but we held the line.”

Those simple words reveal something profound about the men who fought World War II.

Courage was not the absence of fear. Courage was doing what duty demanded despite that fear.

Edwin Joe passed away in 2014.

Today, his Purple Heart rests in a place of honor, carefully preserved in a glass frame.

But that medal represents far more than a moment on a battlefield.

It represents a 19-year-old boy from Texas who crossed an ocean to defend freedom.

It represents a wounded soldier who endured 18 months of recovery.

It represents a man who lived the remainder of his life bearing the physical evidence of his sacrifice.

And it represents a generation of Americans who gave so much, asked for so little, and helped secure the freedoms we enjoy today.

THIS VETERANS DAY, WE REMEMBER.

We remember Edwin Joe.

We remember the frozen foxholes of Europe.

We remember the wounded who came home carrying scars the world could see—and those whose wounds remained invisible.

We remember the soldiers who returned to build families, communities, and a nation made stronger by their service.

And we remember those who never came home at all.

On this Veterans Day, November 11, 2026, let us do more than offer a passing thank-you.

Let us honor their courage.

Let us preserve their stories.

Let us teach our children what their freedom cost.

And let us never allow the sacrifices of America’s veterans to fade into the silence of history.

Private Edwin Joe was more than a Purple Heart recipient.

He was a son of Texas.

An American soldier.

A wounded warrior.

A member of the Greatest Generation.

And a reminder that the true measure of a hero is not found only in the medals he receives, but in the courage with which he serves, the sacrifices he makes, and the life he lives afterward.

Rest in peace, Private Edwin Joe.

Your battle is over.

Your duty is done.

Your sacrifice is remembered.

And your country remains forever grateful.

text:
THE HEART OF A WARRIOR

Edwin Joe Tichavsky: A Purple Heart Hero

A Veterans Day Tribute — November 11, 2026

COLD. BITTER COLD.

There are some battles that never truly leave a soldier. Some memories that time cannot erase. Some sacrifices that remain long after the guns fall silent.

For Private Edwin Joe, a young Texas farm boy who went to war at just 19 years old, one memory would remain etched in his soul for the rest of his life.

The cold. The bitter, bone-chilling cold.

In the winter of 1944, as World War II raged across Europe, Edwin found himself deep in the snow-covered forests of the Ardennes. The Battle of the Bulge had engulfed the region, and American soldiers were fighting desperately to hold their positions against a massive German offensive.

Edwin served with the 311th Infantry Regiment, far from the warmth of his Texas home and the familiar fields of his childhood.

He was barely more than a boy, yet he carried the responsibilities of a man fighting for his country, his fellow soldiers, and the freedom of generations he would never meet.

The snow was deep. The wind was relentless. The temperatures were unforgiving. Every breath burned. Every movement was an effort. Fingers stiffened around rifles, boots froze, and sleep offered little relief from the misery.

Years later, Edwin would remember:

“It was so cold my fingers forgot how to feel, but my heart kept beating for home.”

FEBRUARY 7, 1945 — THE DAY EVERYTHING CHANGED

The thunder of German 88mm artillery shattered the frozen battlefield.

Edwin was positioned in a foxhole, his M1 Garand rifle close at hand, when an artillery shell exploded nearby.

In an instant, flying shrapnel tore into his left hand, devastating muscle and bone.

The pain was excruciating. Blood stained the frozen ground. His fellow soldiers rushed to help him, pulling him from danger and getting him to medical care.

His war on the battlefield had ended.

But another battle was just beginning.

For the next 18 months, Edwin endured a long and painful journey through military hospitals. Multiple surgeries attempted to repair the terrible damage to his hand. The physical wounds were severe, but the memories of war were wounds of another kind.

He remembered the cold.

He remembered his comrades.

He remembered the young men who had stood beside him, some of whom would never return home.

Through the surgeries, the pain, and the uncertainty, Edwin maintained the quiet strength that would define his life.

He rarely complained. He found humor where he could. He faced each new challenge with the determination of a soldier who had already learned what it meant to endure.

A PURPLE HEART. A BRONZE STAR. A LIFETIME OF SACRIFICE.

For the wounds he suffered in combat, Edwin received the Purple Heart, one of America’s most solemn military decorations.

He was also awarded the Bronze Star and other military honors recognizing his wartime service.

But Edwin never considered himself a hero.

Like so many of America’s Greatest Generation, he believed he had simply answered his country’s call.

He had done his duty.

He had stood beside his brothers.

And he had paid a price for freedom.

When Edwin finally returned to Texas in 1946, he brought home a permanently damaged left hand, the scars of battle, and memories that would accompany him throughout his life.

Yet he also brought home something far greater.

An unbreakable spirit.

He built a life beyond the battlefield. He embraced the blessings of home and family. And he carried his wartime experiences with a humility that spoke more powerfully than any medal.

When his family asked about the war, Edwin seldom spoke of the actual fighting.

Instead, he talked about the cold.

The terrible, unforgettable cold.

Perhaps it was easier to describe the freezing temperatures than the fear, the suffering, and the loss.

Perhaps the cold was the part of the war he could share without reopening wounds that had never completely healed.

continued

The question is often whether someone cares enough (or not) to try to help in whatever capacity they are able. Sometimes (particularly as a private citizen) all they can offer is an ear to listen or a referral, which allegedly did happen here with honest intentions.

NASIC has a deep UFO/UAP history. The U.S. IC historically relied on the same pool of cleared researchers to investigate any unconventional phenomenon—whether chemical, psychological, electromagnetic, or psychic—that might give the Soviet Union a Cold War advantage.

The CIA and Pentagon grouped altered states of consciousness, hypnosis, LSD, ESP, and unexplained aerial phenomena under the same broad umbrella of "anomalous threats" that needed to be neutralized or weaponized first.

Very few universities and private labs held the TS/SCI clearances required to handle black-budget intelligence contracts. Institutions like SRI International, UCLA, and SAIC acted as hubs where defense physicists, behavioral psychologists, and intelligence case officers routinely crossed paths on different subcontracts.

At least officially, the U.S. government did not continue covert LSD mind-control programs. Instead, legitimate, heavily regulated behavioral research shifted into standard military psychology, cognitive neuroscience, and interrogation policy—such as the Survival, Evasion, Resistance, and Escape (SERE) training programs and modern DARPA neurotechnology research (like brain-computer interfaces and cognitive enhancement).

There are allegations that some of the darkest elements of these programs have continued covertly and outside of the normal chain of command. Even when there are witnesses and evidence of illegal activity, including nonconsensual human experimentation, credible allegations are still often ignored unless multiple victims come forward. Awfully, they often have to do so publicly to pressure the government to act. 

Anyone who has reported a "plausibly deniable" crime to the government knows that it isn't like tv or the movies. After watching many Law & Order: Special Victims Unit episodes, the way the FBI *actually* responds to victims who need help with an investigation is demoralizing and disgusting. Some officers will intimidate or ridicule you.

Having also met and personally gotten to know officers in the local police, DOJ, CIA, DIA, DoD, and NRO - none of them instruct you to file a police report because they know it is "above their pay grade". After 4 years of trying to work with the DoD, I received a discouraging email three years ago that compelled me to speak up publicly:

"I've done everything I can and used every resource I have to solve what happened to you and there is nothing I or anyone else can do. Trust me when I say this."

I will leave others to draw their own conclusions based on what Kelly and Leslie have shared, but I wanted to share this history and perspective for what it is worth. Thank you for sharing yours and for not giving up.

text:
Thinking Zone. Wednesday afternoon in my little Black Sea village, and I come across a story about John Steinbeck that makes me feel a certain respect for the literary abilities of Irish Setters, although I suspect their editorial methods would not meet with the approval of any publishing house.
In May 1936, Steinbeck was working on Of Mice and Men when his puppy Toby, left alone for an evening, turned half the manuscript into confetti. Two months of work were destroyed, and no other copy existed.
In a letter dated 27 May, the writer admitted that he had been rather angry, but allowed that the poor animal might have been exercising literary criticism. He added that he would not wish to sacrifice a good dog for a manuscript whose quality he himself was not yet certain of.
I particularly like that last detail. Steinbeck evidently possessed the rare ability to acknowledge that even his own work was not necessarily beyond criticism, although I doubt he expected the objection to arrive by means of canine teeth.
Later, he promoted Toby to the rank of lieutenant colonel in charge of literature. I must admit that such an appointment seems entirely deserved, especially considering how many literary critics have achieved considerably less impact with far more words.
The most remarkable development, however, came in 2023, when a surviving fragment of the manuscript, bearing visible teeth marks, was offered at auction by Bonhams and sold for $10,000.
Now that is a magnificent literary irony. Not only did Toby destroy part of the first draft of a novel that would become a classic, but decades later, his teeth marks acquired a market value of their own.
And this Wednesday afternoon, I find myself thinking that Steinbeck had a remarkable sense of humour, but Toby possessed something even rarer among literary critics.
He managed to leave a lasting mark on a work without ever having read it.

Are You In Love Or Limerence? The Psychological Disorder Where A Crush Turns Into Obsession | IFLScience

Most of us, at some point in our lives, have had a crush. And for most of us, let’s face it, it probably sucked: wanting someone you couldn’t have, or maybe couldn’t even work up the courage to talk to; thinking about them all the time; wishing, just wishing, that they would realize how perfect you were for each other.

It’s upsetting. It’s distressing. Sometimes it’s literally painful.

But eventually, most of us got over it – those crushes either resolved into healthy relationships, or else fizzled out into anxiety over finals. It all worked out.

So here’s a question: what happens when it doesn’t?

Limerence: not love, but something like it

It was in the mid-1960s that Dorothy Tennov, then a newly minted Professor of Psychology at the University of Bridgeport in Connecticut, had her moment of realization. Over the course of three weeks, she had seen multiple students admit to losing themselves to seemingly romantic obsession: unable to concentrate on work or study, sometimes struggling to even get out of bed, these young people were overcome with intrusive thoughts of a love interest who wanted nothing to do with them.

Of course, unrequited love is nothing new. But Tennov saw something important in her tortured students’ stories: “After Marilyn left, I sat in my office for a long time, just thinking,” she recalled in her seminal Love And Limerence: The Experience Of Being In Love. “I turned over in my mind the prospect of conducting research myself on the subject of romantic love.”

“It was an exciting idea,” she wrote. “The subject was both unexplored and important.”

Ultimately, more than 500 people agreed to be interviewed about their experience of love, and falling into it – and all seemed to follow the same patterns.

“So many people who differed greatly from each other described such similar subjective states, that I was more and more inclined [to conclude] that the state of being in love could happen to anyone regardless of other aspects of their situations or personalities,” Tennov recalled.

It took a chance conversation with a long-time friend to convince her she was wrong.

“This person whom I had known for many years and with whom I had had many conversations on topics of common interest, had never experienced a reaction that resembled what I had been describing,” Tennov explained. “She said that she had always found puzzling what appeared to her as extravagant exaggeration in the media portrayal of romantic love.”

It was a revelation. Her friend had been married twice, enjoyed an active sex life, and was a mother to several children. She clearly felt love, and friendship, and affection – but the complex emotional rollercoaster of “falling in love”? “Describing [that],” Tennov wrote, “was like trying to describe the color red to one blind from birth.”

In fact, now that she was aware of the possibility that some people never felt the experience she had been researching, Tennov started finding more and more interviewees who said the same.

“That they had not [appeared] before was the joint result of my having been blinded by my expectations and the problem of terminology,” she admitted. Tennov had been asking about love – but “[n]ever having fallen in love is not at all a matter of not loving, if loving is defined as caring” she discovered. “Furthermore, this state of ‘being in love’ included feelings that do not properly fit with love defined as concern.”

What was needed was a new, more exact term: a word that could describe being “in love”, but not necessarily love itself. The part of romance before the “happily ever after” – the obsessive, mystical, butterflies-in-your-stomach part that’s more than a crush, but less than capital-L Love.

And so, Tennov wrote, “I coined the word ‘limerence’.”

To be in limerence

When limerence hits you, it’s often subtle.

Perhaps a new person enters your orbit – someone with a magnetic smile you can’t stop thinking about after they’re gone. It could be the opposite: a teacher or colleague whom you suddenly realize means more to you, maybe has done for a long time already, than you previously thought.

Or perhaps you get the true fairytale experience, your eyes meeting across a crowded room, a spark of chemistry jumping from one to the other as you find your way together.

“The beginning [of limerence] is a transformation that is sometimes so distinct that the French use the term coup de foudre, or thunderbolt,” Tennov wrote. “[It is] the beginning of a state of consciousness that, if experienced for the first time, is utterly unlike anything else that has ever happened.”

At this point, it’s pretty indistinguishable from what many people would term “falling in love”: there’s an attraction; a level of obsession; idealization; the overwhelming wish for it all to be reciprocated.

But with limerence, these feelings don’t develop in a healthy way. Rather than growing into a secure attachment, or fading with time, as love would, limerence lingers: “it remains suspended in uncertainty, sustained by hope and doubt,” explained Orly Miller, a psychologist and author of Limerence: The Psychopathology of Loving Too Much, in a Psychology Today article last week. “[Mean]while the individual becomes increasingly consumed by obsessive thoughts and emotional dependency.”

For those in the thrall of the experience, limerence can be far more than just a preoccupation. Tennov suggested – and many more modern experts have come to agree – that the feeling is akin to conditions like obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), anxiety, depression, substance abuse disorders, or trauma responses.

In other words: it’s a genuinely troubling experience that interferes with your everyday life and stops you from forming and maintaining healthy relationships with others.

“Limerence is not defined by butterflies, infatuation, or the excitement of falling in love,” Miller pointed out. “It is characterized by persistent intrusive thoughts, emotional volatility, significant distress, and disruption to important areas of functioning.”

“These are […] features that warrant clinical attention.”

Releasing the butterflies

For those who have never experienced limerence – or, perhaps, have, but not to such an extreme degree – all this might sound rather dramatic. Love, and falling in love, are just parts of being human, you may argue – not worthy of being pathologized in a doctor’s office.

So too is the act of, let’s say, checking up on people, even very regularly, without their knowledge or consent – behavior that might have set off alarm bells for stalking just 30 years ago, but now is as easy as tapping the Instagram icon on your phone. It’s normal.

It’s an attitude that’s likely familiar to those who have sought help for limerent feelings. “[Some have] told me that when they sought professional help, their therapist had never heard of limerence and advised them to ‘just let go’ or ‘focus on something else’,” recalled Miller. “While these suggestions are well intentioned, they are rarely helpful.”

“Just as someone with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder cannot simply stop having intrusive thoughts, people experiencing limerence cannot simply decide to stop thinking about the person they are obsessing over,” she wrote. “If they could, believe me, they would.”

But there is good news. If limerence truly does share characteristics with better-known conditions such as OCD or anxiety, then – theoretically, at least – it should respond to some of the same therapies. And the first spots of evidence seem to be bearing that out.

In 2021, a case study reported positive results from cognitive behavioral therapy on a patient’s limerence. Just last year, a team of UK psychologists developed a questionnaire designed to help diagnose it. It may be slow, but things are changing.

Until then, there are a handful of strategies that might help a limerent person let go.

The hardest but most effective strategy is probably to cut off all contact entirely with the object of your desire, Tom Bellamy, a neuroscientist at the University of Nottingham, told the New York Times last month – to just remove the intermittent pleasure signals that we might get from the drops of attention sent our way.

It’s like going cold turkey off a drug or other addiction: difficult as hell, but quicker and potentially more effective than any other solution.

Mindfulness is also valuable, he suggested: trying to notice and label liminal compulsions as and when they arise, rather than just accepting and acting upon them. If you’re aware of them, you can maybe even begin to resist them. Just naming the feeling out loud – a “hello, limerence” whenever it hits – might be enough to jolt you out of it.

Most of all, be kind to yourself. The person you’re obsessing over? They’re not perfect – and if you try, you can probably list off a few of their flaws that prove it. They may well not be compatible with you. And that’s okay – just as they’re not perfect, neither are you somehow deficient or unworthy of love.

“Whether limerence is eventually recognized as a distinct mental health condition will ultimately be determined by further research,” wrote Miller. “What should not be overlooked, however, is the reality of the suffering experienced by those living with it.”

“Greater awareness of limerence is […] not about diminishing the richness of romantic love,” she concluded, “but ensuring that those whose lives have become consumed by obsessive longing are understood, supported, and offered appropriate care.”

Yesterday, Dept of War awarded a $224M max-value IDIQ for the wool & poly/wool cloth for Air Force & Space Force uniforms (serge, elastique, tropical, heather charcoal, dark blue). 

The govt received one bid. Here’s why -- 

Couple of things at play here.

The Berry Amendment requires DoW to buy military clothing & textiles grown and produced in the U.S. DLA’s notice specified 100% US made, from 100% U.S. materials.

According to DLA’s own Aug 2026 consolidation memo, until recently Burlington Industries was the only domestic source capable of making Berry-compliant dress cloth. 

The only other domestic mill named is American Woolen, a small business that makes a small share of Army taupe and Marine Corps scarlet cloth.

The existing vendor base can’t keep up. Since at least 2022, DLA has approved 3 domestic non-availability determinations (DNADs) for dress cloth, which let the govt buy foreign-made cloth when US supply falls short. Right now, 9 of 10 dress cloths DLA buys have one.

Of the 36 DLA awards for serge, elastique, and tropical cloth going back to 2006, Burlington won all 36. Every one awarded since 2014 drew a single offer. The last AF serge contract ($43M, 2023) had one bid. DLA ran a sources sought for these exact cloths in July 2025. Still one bid.

So why aren’t others jumping in? 

DLA’s memo says interested companies have made limited progress toward U.S. production. Without a guaranteed baseline of work, the capital cost of standing up compliant capacity is commercially prohibitive.

DLA's trying to fix this. A separate solicitation bundles 10 dress cloths into up to 3 awards (planned for 2 large, 1 small business). It lets new entrants supply DNAD cloth while they build U.S. production. 

Meanwhile, this award keeps AF & Space Force cloth with one mill thru 2031.
