"Hopes of a Prisoner Exchange" Is the Lede. The Lede Is the Anesthetic. The Surgery Is the Assets.

The headline says nine months of deadlock, talks resumed in Abu Dhabi, first day raised hopes of a prisoner exchange, major differences remain. Read that sentence as a product. It has a hook, a villain, and a resolution arc. It is designed to make you feel that something is happening.

What is actually happening is that three men who owe their fortunes to the Gulf are sitting in a Gulf capital, dividing a country they do not represent, while the war that produced the division continues on the ground.

The Prisoner Exchange Is the Emotional Hook

Every negotiation needs a human story. The prisoner exchange is the human story. It is the thing that makes the reader feel that the talks are worth something.

Ask who benefits from the exchange. The belligerents, Russia and Ukraine, exchange prisoners. The lists are drawn up by the military and intelligence services of both sides. The exchange happens at a border crossing or a neutral venue.

The negotiators in Abu Dhabi do not control the exchange. They announce it. The announcement is the product. The exchange is the work of the militaries.

The exchange is real. The families are real. The relief is real. But the exchange is not the reason the talks are happening. It is the proof of life for the talks. It is the thing that lets the headline say "hopes raised."

Nine Months of Deadlock: What Was Actually Happening

The talks were suspended for nine months. During those nine months:

◾The US-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund was signed on 30 April 2025, giving the United States a 50 per cent share of revenue from every newly issued Ukrainian mineral, oil, and gas extraction licence.
◾ The €210 billion at Euroclear was taxed at 99.7 per cent on the windfall profits.
◾ The €90 billion EU loan was approved, two-thirds earmarked for weapons.
◾The Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive was amended by Directive (EU) 2026/806 and the CMDI package was published in April 2026, codifying the bail-in order.
◾Medinsky was appointed to lead the Russian delegation.
◾Witkoff and Kushner were appointed to lead the American side.
◾The UAE was selected as the venue.

The deadlock was not a pause in the war. It was the period in which the financial architecture was built. The talks resumed when the architecture was ready to be signed.

Who Is at the Table and Who Is Not

At the table: Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, the UAE Foreign Minister.

Not at the table: Europe. Medinsky said: "We did not communicate with the European representatives. We do not really understand in what capacity they are here."

Not at the table: Ukraine's actual negotiators. The Ukrainian delegation is present, but the decisions are being made between Washington and Moscow.

Not at the table: Russia's actual foreign ministry. Medinsky is a cultural figure and a former minister, not a career diplomat. He is there to sign, not to negotiate.

Not at the table: the European Union, which paid €130 billion in security assistance and is now being told it is present without a defined capacity.

The table is a three-sided arrangement: the US, Russia, and the host state. Europe is in the corridor. Ukraine is in the room but not at the table.

What "Major Differences Remain" Actually Means

The headline says major differences remain over ending the war and Europe's role in the talks. Read those two items separately.

Ending the war: the difference is between a ceasefire and a settlement. A ceasefire freezes the line. A settlement divides the assets. The US wants a settlement. Russia wants a ceasefire that recognizes the territorial reality on the ground. Ukraine wants a ceasefire that preserves its legal sovereignty. The three positions are not compatible.

Europe's role: the difference is whether Europe is a party or a creditor. The US and Russia agree that Europe is a creditor. Europe insists it is a party. Medinsky's statement is the answer: Europe is not a party.

The "major differences" are not a negotiating gap. They are a structural incompatibility. The talks cannot resolve them because the parties are not negotiating the same thing.

The Real Estate Deal Behind the Talk of Peace

Read the minerals deal against the "hopes" of the talks.

The US-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund was signed in April 2025. It gives the US a 50 per cent share of revenue from every newly issued Ukrainian mineral, oil, and gas extraction licence. It is managed jointly by the US International Development Finance Corporation and Ukraine's PPP Agency.

Trump, July 2026: "We can go in there at any time we want to take pretty much whatever we want. That was a pretty good deal."

The fund has no security guarantee. It has no reconstruction obligation. It has a claim on the revenue.

The talks are not about whether the fund exists. The fund exists. The talks are about when the extraction can begin. The extraction can begin when the ceasefire is signed. The ceasefire is the closing condition for the fund.

Kushner's $2 Billion and the Gulf Venue

Jared Kushner runs Affinity Partners. The firm's capital: $2 billion from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, approved in 2021 over the objections of the PIF's own advisers. Add money from Lunate, an Abu Dhabi fund, and from Qatari sovereign entities.

Kushner is the son-in-law of the President. He has no diplomatic credential beyond the family tie. He has a $2 billion Gulf-funded investment firm and a seat at a table negotiating the fate of Ukraine.

The venue is Abu Dhabi. The host is a Gulf monarchy that hosts Al Dhafra Air Base and Jebel Ali port, that is on the Zero Hour target list, and whose adviser said "confidence has been shaken."

The talks are being held in the capital of a state that is renegotiating its own exposure while hosting the negotiations. The host is not neutral. The host is a party to the regional architecture the talks are meant to stabilize.

The Istanbul Precedent

The deal that would have ended the war was on the table in Istanbul in April 2022. Ukraine's written proposals included neutral, non-aligned status and a pledge not to host foreign weapons, including nuclear arms.

Boris Johnson flew to Kyiv on 9 April 2022. Yulia Mendel, Zelensky's former press secretary, said Johnson "intervened and influenced Zelensky, saying he could become a hero and could continue this war." David Arakhamia, head of the Ukrainian delegation, said Johnson told them: "We won't sign anything with them at all."

The neutrality that is now being discussed in Abu Dhabi was on offer four years ago. It was destroyed by a British prime minister acting on instructions from Washington and London.

The talks in Abu Dhabi are not new. They are the resumption of a negotiation that was sabotaged in 2022. The sabotage cost hundreds of thousands of lives. The talks are now picking up where the sabotage left off.

The Bill

The headline: nine months of deadlock, talks resumed, hopes of a prisoner exchange, major differences remain.

The hook: the prisoner exchange. Real, but not the reason for the talks. The reason for the talks is the assets.

The nine months: the period in which the minerals fund, the frozen assets architecture, the bail-in directive, and the reconstruction contracts were built.

The table: Witkoff, Kushner, the UAE Foreign Minister. Not Europe. Not Ukraine's actual negotiators. Not Russia's actual foreign ministry.

The major differences: a ceasefire versus a settlement versus legal sovereignty. A structural incompatibility, not a negotiating gap.

The real estate deal: the 50 per cent claim on Ukrainian extraction revenue. Trump's "take pretty much whatever we want."

The venue: Abu Dhabi. A Gulf monarchy renegotiating its own exposure.

The precedent: Istanbul 2022. The deal was on the table. Boris Johnson said no. Mendel and Arakhamia confirmed it.

The talks are not about stopping the war. They are about who owns the wreckage. The war continues because the wreckage is not yet fully priced. The ceasefire is the closing condition. The prisoner exchange is the anesthetic. The "hopes" are the product. The bill is being paid by the dead, and the receipt is a communiqué from Abu Dhabi.

text:
A country once generated wealth from what it owned: land, infrastructure, utilities, energy, transport networks and national industries. These assets produced revenue that could fund public services and reduce the burden on taxpayers. This land originally belonged to the people. 

Then came privatisation. Assets built over generations, often with public money, were sold off for short-term cash. The Government and Monarchy received a one-off payment, while private owners inherited the income streams. The public lost the assets, the future revenue and, in many cases, control over the very infrastructure upon which society depends.

Now the bills keep coming, but the income-producing assets are gone. Governments must increasingly squeeze revenue from the people who have already paid to build the country in the first place.

In this dystopian model, you own less, pay more and depend on private corporations for the essentials of life. Your wages are taxed before you receive them. Your purchases are taxed when you spend them. Your home is taxed because you own it. Your energy, water and transport costs rise because the infrastructure belongs to someone whose primary obligation is to shareholders, not citizens.

And when the cost of living becomes unbearable, the solution offered is another tax, another levy, another charge, another scheme supposedly designed to save you.

The ultimate dystopia is a state that sells the nation's wealth, transfers its income to private interests, then turns to its own citizens to make up the shortfall.

The people are left owning the debt, paying the bills and financing a system in which they increasingly own nothing.

And the final twist?

The Government still claims that it is doing all this, "for your benefit".

You are no longer a citizen sharing in the wealth of your country. You are a revenue stream to be harvested by a state that has sold off the means of generating wealth for itself.

We NEED to take it all back, using any means necessary.

Marine Le Pen: the estranged daughter tied to a very public life
The brutal breaking of bonds with her father has hung over the horse-hugging hardliner’s run for the French presidency
Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
Fri 14 Apr 2017 04.12 EDT

Backstage at a rally in southern France in the early days of the presidential race, Marine Le Pen took a puff on the electronic cigarette that has replaced her two-packets-a-day tobacco habit. “I’m going to run a joyful campaign,” she smiled.

Le Pen, controlled and image-conscious, has always a walked a tight line between denouncing the system and trying to be part of it. Her life has played out in the public eye ever since, aged six, she was photographed being tucked into her bed in a bedroom incongruously wallpapered with Front National election posters about fighting the “Marxist cancer”. The Le Pen family dynasty was always something of a national soap opera, with the blond clan living together – including the three Le Pen daughters well into their 30s – in a 19th-century manor house perched on a hill outside Paris, watched over by dobermans.
Le Pen wanted to soften her harsh image and “soothe” voters – she had posed for pictures hugging horses and pet kittens – but also to offer a hardline programme she believed would “reassure” a French population despairing of decades of mass unemployment and a persistent terrorist threat.

The aim, as always for the far-right Front National founded by her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, in 1972, was keeping France for the French. There would be a referendum to change the constitution so that “national priority” would be given to French people over non-nationals in jobs, housing and welfare. There would be another referendum to leave the European Union. Le Pen promised an immigration clampdown and a ban on religious symbols, including the Muslim headscarf, from all public places in France.

Marine Le Pen, 48, is the closest she has ever been to the French presidency – with a chance of making it to the final runoff in an election that is impossible to predict. In the six years since she took over the party from her father, she has steadily increased her party’s vote in every local and European election. If her ex-paratrooper, Holocaust-denying, provocateur father was content to be a protest vote,
@MLP_officiel

  wants power and political office.

But the troubled father-daughter bond – and the brutal public breaking of it – has hung over her presidential campaign. Marine Le Pen’s election strategy has been to broaden her voter base by sanitising the party’s image, moving it away from the racist, jackbooted and antisemitic imagery of the past. The problem was that Papa Le Pen felt left out. In 2015, he deliberately wrecked her plans by repeating the Holocaust denials that had landed him a series of convictions for hate speech and contesting crimes against humanity. After a bitter public feud, she expelled him from the party. He publicly disowned her and they haven’t spoken since.

But the ghosts of the second world war persist in French politics. Marine Le Pen was asked on a radio programme this week about a major wartime roundup of Jews in Paris. She said France as a nation was not responsible, only “those who were in power at the time”, sparking fury from Jewish organisations. Le Pen argued that modern France should not be locked in permanent repentance and that the “real” France was Gen de Gaulle’s resistance, not the “illegal” Nazi-collaborationist Vichy regime. “If you’re trying to say Marine Le Pen is a Nazi, come out and say it but that will make everyone laugh to the rafters because it’s simply not credible,” her chief strategist, Florian Philippot, angrily told a chatshow host. Le Pen slammed what she called a pointless controversy.

Marion Anne Perrene Le Pen – swiftly nicknamed Marine – was born west of Paris in 1968, the youngest of three daughters. Her father showed off his children in the press. But their home life was more disjointed than it seemed. In the Le Pens’ first Paris apartment building, the children lived separately from their parents, in a flat upstairs with a nanny. Jean-Marie Le Pen and his wife, Pierrette Lalanne, would go off on holiday or long sailing trips around the world on their own, sometimes missing Christmas.

It was only when the eight-year-old Marine woke up in her nightdress amid shards of glass and a blown-away bedroom wall, after a bomb attack aimed at killing her father, that she realised his political role and the extent of hatred towards him. “As an eight-year-old girl, I was suddenly made aware of death,” she told me when she took over the Front National leadership. “But maybe that gave me a distance, a kind of armour, that’s useful when you’re aiming for positions of responsibility.”

The family surname was a burden – she recalled teachers at school referring to her sisters as “daughters of a fascist” – but she constantly stood up for her father. When, in 1985, the paper Libération revealed that Le Pen Sr had engaged in torture during the Algerian war, he denied it and advised the teenaged Marine Le Pen to take the day off school. She refused and went in defending him.

In the 1980s, as he gained political prominence, Le Pen Sr commissioned a biography from a journalist who spent time at the family’s manor house. One day, Marine , then 16, was surprised to find one of her older sisters waiting outside school. “Mum’s gone,” she said. Without telling anyone, Lalanne had taken all her possessions and left with Le Pen’s biographer to set up a new life. She didn’t see or speak to her daughters for more than 15 years. Marine , the youngest and most attached to her mother, was left alone with her distant and distracted father. She said she waited every day for some kind contact from her mother, but none came.

“Marine Le Pen grew up in a very odd atmosphere, a family that appeared close but was actually very distant,” said David Doucet, who co-authored a biography of her early years, La Politique Malgré Elle. “She lived almost 20 years without her mother. Her father hardly knew her. She was brought up by nannies and governesses, left to her own devices.”

A vicious, public divorce battle followed. Jean-Marie Le Pen rebuffed Lalanne’s maintenance claims, saying she should work as a cleaner. As revenge, Lalanne posed naked in French Playboy scrubbing kitchen floors.

Marine Le Pen occasionally accompanied her father out campaigning as a teenager as a way to spend time with him and win a little attention. But she didn’t initially set herself up for a political career. She told me once: “My father says I’m like Obelix. I fell into the magic potion of politics when I was young.” In fact, she had tried to escape the party by studying law. To make extra income beyond her law firm jobs, she worked for six years as a state-appointed duty lawyer, defending illegal immigrants facing deportation. “They are human beings who have rights,” she said recently in a TV interview. “We don’t blame immigration policies on them. It’s not their fault.”

At 30, she won her first role as regional councillor for the Front National in Henin-Beaumont, a depressed, former coal-mining town in the north, which she later made her political laboratory, a place to reinvent herself as a “defender of the people”. She recognised that France’s northern industrial belt, which had traditionally voted left, could turn to the Front National if the party stood not just against immigration, which remained its chief selling point, but for the victims of deindustrialisation and the financial crisis. “It used to be called her laboratory, but now it’s the place she still has an apartment, the region I think she feels most at ease in,” said Sébastien Chenu, who ran her northern campaign in the last regional elections. “She’s easy to approach. That’s why it works for her in the north. She likes the contact.”

Le Pen keeps her old friends close. “If anyone tried to betray her, they couldn’t stick around,” Chenu said. The Front National party-funding corruption cases currently under investigation – including allegations of misusing European public funds to pay French party workers, and false-accounting in election funding – have seen some of Le Pen’s closest childhood friends placed under formal investigation. They and the party deny all charges. But the cases showed how she had placed people she met at college in positions of trust.

Le Pen protects her children from the public exposure she had a child. Twice married and divorced from men who were active in the Front National, she had three children in the space of one year – a daughter immediately followed by twins. Her current partner is the party deputy, LOUIS Aliot.

The Latin word mare ('sea') was a pun upon the name Mary, and the phrase Stella maris is an mistranslation of the Hebrew form of her name, Miriam.

Mary as a star, giving guidance to sailors on a stormy ocean, became a popular metaphor for the help she gave to mankind on earth. The great fourteenth-century Italian poet Petrarch, wrote a powerful lyric on the subject:

Bright virgin, steadfast in eternity /
Star of this storm-tossed sea, /
Trusted guide of every trustful pilot, /
Turn your thoughts to the terrifying squall /
In which I find myself, alone and rudderless...

Interestingly, Stella maris was originally an epithet of the goddess Isis in Roman religion. Like Mary, Isis was a divine mother with a very popular cult, and representations of her with her baby son Horus in Egyptian art to some extent influenced the way early artists showed the Virgin and Child.

Mary or Miriam: Was the Mother of Jesus Jewish?
By Joseph Goodenough
14 min read
Posted November 21st  2024
 Hebrew Words,  Messianic Bible Teachings

Miriam or Mary? (or Maria?)
While some question whether Mary and Miriam are the same name, there are important linguistic and historical factors we need to consider.

The New Testament was written in Greek, and many of the names were translated or transliterated from Hebrew or Aramaic into Greek. The Hebrew name “Miriam” became Miryam or Maryam in Aramaic.
Jesus and his contemporaries would have spoken Aramaic, a language closely related to Hebrew. The Gospels use the form Maria, which then became Mary in English. Since Greek female names often end in -a/-ah, and that is likely how Maryam became Marya.

It is worth noting that the name “Miriam” was prominent in the land of the Bible, and it is not surprising that several women were named Mary/Maryam/Miriam in Jesus’ circles. It confirms the popularity of the name among Jewish women of the time.

Interestingly, while the Western churches use the name Mary or Maria for the mother of Jesus, the Eastern Orthodox Church still often refers to her as “Miriam” in their liturgy.

The Meaning of Miriam: A Name of Struggle and Hope
To understand the depth of Mary’s identity, we must start with her name. Her Hebrew name was Miriam (מִרְיָם), the same name as that of Moses’ sister, a woman who played a pivotal role in Israel’s deliverance during the Exodus.
Thus, this name carries layers of meaning tied to the story of Israel and God’s redeeming plan. Scholars often debate its precise etymology, but there are two primary interpretations:
“Bitterness” or “Rebellion”: Derived from the Hebrew root מרר (marar), meaning “to be bitter,” the name reflects the sufferings and struggles of the Jewish people.

Vatican Diary: Reflections on Pope Leo and the Revolution in France
September’s papal visit to the ‘eldest daughter of the Church’ highlights a faith revival in secularized France.
Francis X. Rocca
October 2, 2026
Pope Leo XIV’s pastoral visit to France last week (Sept. 25-28) produced a wealth of memorable images: the Pope blessing a girl with multiple disabilities; 80,000 young people cheering Leo in the national stadium; and priests hearing confessions on Paris sidewalks along the papal motorcade route.

The most indelible emblem of the trip is likely to remain the aerial view of 800,000 people filling the Place de la Concorde and the Champs-Élysées, the symbolic heart of the French capital, during Leo’s open-air Mass on Sept. 26. That outpouring seemed to defy the widespread image of France as a bastion of secularism.

International papal travel as we know it today, inaugurated by St. Paul VI with a visit to the Holy Land in 1964, is still a new practice by the standards of a 2,000-year-old Church. Paul’s successors have embraced this powerful form of communication. Dozens of journalists from different countries accompany the pope on these trips, which typically feature enthusiastic crowds in photogenic settings, not to mention the drama of local controversies, either within the Catholic fold or between the Church and wider society. A pastoral visit is therefore not only a missionary expedition but also a global showcase.

In this case, the big revelation for many readers and viewers around the world was the evidence that Catholicism in France is not dead and may even be undergoing a revival.

The stereotype of a secular France has a basis in reality. According to France’s national demographic institute, more than half of adults ages 18 to 59 have no religious affiliation. Twenty-nine percent identify as Catholic, but only 8% of Catholics say they regularly attend a place of worship.

Yet France has been experiencing a surge in adult baptisms in recent years. More than 20,000 adults and adolescents have been baptized so far this year, a roughly 20% increase over the previous record set in 2025, which itself represented a 45% increase from 2024.

Pope Leo noted the trend with hope and satisfaction, but not triumphalism. It is by no means clear that the numbers of new Catholics in France augur anything like a wholesale re-Christianization of French society rather than the growth of a vibrant subculture that will keep the flame of faith alive in the expectation of an eventual renaissance. The current Pontiff did not quote Pope Benedict XVI’s idea that “creative minorities” of Catholics can live as appealing witnesses to the majority of nonbelievers, but that could be what the world saw on display, in a highly concentrated and energized state, during the papal trip.

The Pope in France touched on politically sensitive questions, including immigration, a signature issue for him, as it was for Pope Francis. Yet, coming after his dramatic portside appearances with migrants over the summer in Spain and the Italian island of Lampedusa, and his statements of opposition to mass deportation in the U.S., Pope Leo’s approach to the matter in France was strikingly low-key, conciliatory and hopeful.

That was probably a reflection of just how incendiary a subject immigration is right now in France, which is holding presidential elections next year, with the anti-immigration politician Marine Le Pen currently the front-runner. The Vatican is generally careful to avoid any appearance of partisanship in national politics, especially so close to a vote.

2. WAS IT THE CANAL THAT WAS NATIONALISED IN 1956? OR THE COMPANY THAT BUILT IT AND HAD A CONCESSION TO RUN IT UNTIL 1968? AND WHY DOES IT MATTER?

Entirely admirable as is David Runciman’s broad sweep of history linking Suez, Hungary and the US presidential elections in 1956, I cannot avoid feeling that, in focusing on the interplay of these three dramas, he subordinated the drama of Suez 1956 to his overriding thesis about the end of illusion in the old world, and to his notion that “we continue to live in the world that these events created.”

How deeply did he delve into the detail of the nationalisation? The second part of his series, “Oil”, says that Nasser’s nationalisation happened on 25 July in Cairo. In reality, it happened on 26 July in Alexandria.

The series asserts that the Canal, described as the shared “property” of Britain and France, was nationalised. It also speaks of the Canal as “acquired by Britain in the course of building its colonial empire.”

Strictly speaking, the Canal was always regarded as Egyptian. What was nationalised in 1956 was the Universal Company of the Suez Maritime Canal, steeped from its very origins in the internationalism of its “universality”, under the concessions granted by the ruler of Egypt, Said Pasha, in 1854 and 1856, when Egypt was part of the Ottoman Empire.

It was twenty years later, in 1875, that Britain acquired its 44 per cent shareholding in the Company when Said’s successor, Ismail Pasha, was on the brink of bankruptcy. And seven years after that, in 1882, that the British occupation began, establishing what became known as the “veiled protectorate”, while Egypt remained formally part of the Ottoman Empire.

In August 1956, John Foster Dulles, the American Secretary of State, questioned the legality of President Nasser’s nationalisation, a view shared by Britain, France and others. The compatibility of Egypt’s action with the 1888 Convention governing the Canal was also disputed.

At the first London Conference, which aimed to find a peaceful resolution to the Suez conflict, Dulles said:

“The United States does not believe that the Egyptian Government had the right to wipe out the Convention establishing the rights of the Universal Suez Canal Company until 1968 (the end of the Company’s concession to operate the Canal). This arrangement has the status of an international compact… The Government of the United States questions that the Government of Egypt had the right unilaterally to take that action.”

Australia’s Robert Menzies was even more outspoken:

“If at any time and for any reason of real or supposed self-interest, a nation could claim that its sovereign rights entitled it to set treaties aside or violate international contracts, all talk of, or of reliance on, international law would become a sham.”

These were contemporary arguments, not a definitive legal judgment. But they demonstrate that the dispute was about more than the ownership of shares or the principle of nationalisation.

Mr Runciman suggests that British politicians understood that nationalisation was not necessarily illegal, particularly if shareholders were compensated.

Yet the Opposition Leader, Hugh Gaitskell, raised a rather different concern in a Commons debate, while broadly supporting the Government’s attempts to seek a peaceful resolution and accepting the need for precautionary military preparations:

“How can he (Nasser) at one and at the same time both keep the Canal going… pay the compensation… to the shareholders, and also find the money for the Aswan Dam?”

Mr Runciman further argues that the Conservatives had accepted the previous Labour Government’s nationalisation of significant proportions of British industry.

But the reality is that the Suez Canal Company was not anything like an ordinary national public utility. It had acted almost like a state in creating not merely what is now a vital waterway for Egypt’s economy, but also the freshwater canal that helped transform the surrounding desert, and in developing new towns in what became the Suez Canal Zone.

And while Mr Runciman speaks of “deception”, he does not, other than referring to the de Lesseps code word, examine President Nasser’s nationalisation speech in any detail, or the extent to which its claims might well have reinforced British suspicions of Egyptian intentions.

This is all the more significant because, while Mr Runciman refers to British forces leaving Egypt in 1954, that was the year in which the withdrawal agreement was signed. The withdrawal itself was completed in 1956, just one month before President Nasser’s nationalisation.

While  this series records that Britain and America had withdrawn their offers of financial support for the Aswan High Dam the week before nationalisation, it does not point out that it was America’s Foster Dulles who, arguably, lit the fuse — not so much by withdrawing the funding, but, as Nasser later explained, by the “insulting” manner in which he did so.

And that raises a question which is not explored in this series: did President Nasser deliberately provoke the crisis that resulted in nationalisation?

Shortly after the Suez War, President Tito of Yugoslavia reportedly disclosed that Nasser had already told him, on 5 February 1955, that he would have to nationalise the Canal one day because Egypt, as an independent country, could not tolerate foreigners exercising authority on its territory. It was only a matter of time.

Incidentally, that meeting happened just a fortnight before Nasser’s meeting with Anthony Eden, who had made a genuine attempt at that time, in 1955, to establish a new basis of cooperation with Nasser, in line with the Suez Canal Base Agreement of 19 October 1954, which spoke of the desire to establish Anglo-Egyptian relations on a new basis of firm friendship.

Dulles himself wrote to Eisenhower on 30 October 1957:

“President Nasser has since said that he planned for nearly two years to seize the Suez Canal Company, but was waiting for a good occasion.”

If these accounts are accepted, Nasser had contemplated nationalisation long before the Aswan Dam funding dispute. That does not prove that he deliberately engineered the ensuing crisis. But it certainly does raise questions about the conventional account of nationalisation as an essentially spontaneous response to the withdrawal of Western financial assistance.

So why does all this matter?

It matters, in my view, because of the ease with which the historical narrative of Suez as an episode of colonialism and imperialism became the accepted orthodoxy, with Mr Runciman speaking of Suez and Hungary as “two virulent imperialist excursions”.

That interpretation is not without foundation. But it is not the whole story.

There were competing considerations of sovereignty, international obligations, freedom of navigation, economic security and the intentions of the protagonists themselves. Indeed, the United Nations Security Council recognised in October 1956 both Egypt’s sovereignty and the principle that the operation of the Canal should be insulated from the politics of any country. That, in my view, is an important point.

Now, seventy years later, as the familiar narrative is seemingly reinforced in 2026, there are historical counterweights — including Selwyn Lloyd’s memoirs and the contemporary diplomatic record — which, I would argue, have not received sufficient attention.

Thirty seconds. One monkey. A street that does not seem to care.

The clip opens high above the ground, on a stretch of blue tarpaulin stretched over a market stall. A small brown monkey is standing on it, and the video's editor has stuck a red arrow on the animal, which tells you something before you have even processed the scene: whoever made this knew you would lose it. The monkey is the same colour as the road, the shadows and half the cargo in the frame. Below it, a working market is doing exactly what a working market does at that hour. Fruit carts. Steel pots stacked like armour. Scooters nosing through foot traffic. Pigeons working the pavement. A cycle rickshaw with passengers settled into the seat.

Nobody in the frames I examined is looking up.

That is the first thing worth sitting with, before any of the symbolism that people will inevitably pile onto this video. A monkey is moving through the roofline of a crowded street, and the street is carrying on as though a traffic light had changed. There is no scattering, no shouting that I can make out from the footage, no sudden gap opening in the crowd. If you have only ever met monkeys in documentaries, where they are either cute or catastrophic, this register will feel strange. This is a third register: ordinary.

The route is the first story. The animal does not wander. It drops from the awning to the ground, and from there the clip becomes an exercise in watching something move through a place with a kind of fluency that a visitor would never have. It passes people who are standing still. It passes a rickshaw. It passes motorbikes parked at angles. Then it keeps going, along the same street, in a direction that, once you know where it ends, begins to look less like drifting and more like commuting.

I want to be careful with that last word, and I will be careful with it for the rest of this piece, because the single most dangerous thing you can do with a video like this is let a satisfying story outrun the evidence. What the footage shows is a monkey travelling a considerable distance through a busy market and arriving at one specific spot. Whether that is habit, hunger, curiosity, memory, or some mixture, the camera cannot tell you. But the arrival is the reason this clip exists, and it is a better arrival than most.

Where the monkey ends up is a small, whitewashed shrine built into the side of the street. It has an arched niche, carved edges, a brass bell hanging from the arch, and inside the niche a seated figure painted a deep orange-red. In front of the figure, on a flat stone platform about the height of a doorstep, someone has laid out a small arrangement: bright orange flowers, small dishes, what look like fruit pieces. A man in a checked shirt and a blue lungi, with a red-checked cloth draped over his shoulder, is standing right beside it.

The monkey climbs up onto that platform and sits down.

I am going to stop describing there, deliberately. What happens in the next several seconds is the part you have to see for yourself, because it depends on timing, posture, and the way two living things share a very small piece of space, and none of that survives being translated into sentences. What I can do is tell you what it means that this is happening where it is happening, and why this very ordinary place is one of the more loaded locations in the world for a monkey to be sitting.

THE ORANGE FIGURE

Start with the obvious question, because the answer is partly a matter of tradition and partly a matter of honesty. Who is the figure in the niche?

The title attached to this clip invokes Rama, and in the tradition that surrounds that name, there is one deity who is almost always found in small street shrines like this one, painted in this colour, with a bell overhead and flowers laid at his feet: Hanuman. A vermilion or orange-red finish is a very common way of rendering him. A bell at a shrine entrance is common across temples in general, there to mark the arrival of a worshipper. I cannot confirm the statue's identity from a thirty-second video shot from above, and I do not want to state it as fact. But the context makes it a reasonable reading, and it is the reading that gives this clip its weight.

Hanuman, in the Ramayana, is the great devotee of Rama. He is the one who crosses the sea to find Sita, the one who is sent for medicinal herbs and, in the story, returns carrying an entire mountain because he could not identify which plant was needed. He is strength, loyalty and service combined into a single figure. And he is a monkey, or something close enough to a monkey that, for many people, the distinction is not the point.

That last detail is the hinge of the entire clip.

If the shrine belongs to Hanuman, then a monkey sitting on its platform is not merely an animal that has found a convenient ledge. To many of the people who walk past, the animal sits inside a frame of meaning that was prepared long before this particular monkey was born. Researchers who have spent years studying how people and rhesus macaques live together in Indian cities describe exactly this layer: for many Hindus, the monkeys are felt to be living representatives of the god, and that feeling shapes how people treat them, where they are allowed to be, and what happens when they take food.

And here is the part that I find the most interesting, and the part I would hold on to while watching: the monkey, as far as anyone can tell, knows none of this.

One ethnographer who studied macaques and people in two Indian cities noted that the monkeys do not seem to have any special awareness of Hanuman's resemblance to them, nor of the moral weight that humans attach to them. The animal on that platform is not performing devotion. It is not auditioning for sainthood. It is a macaque doing macaque things in a place where macaque things are tolerated, and on some days rewarded.

So the clip contains two stories that are happening in the same few square metres, and they do not need each other in order to be true. One is the story that the animal is living. The other is the story that the people around it are reading into it. The most compelling thing about the video is that they overlap, and that you can feel the seam where one meets the other.

A MARKET IS A MAP

Now look at the monkey as a monkey.

From the colouring, the build and the way it carries itself, this looks like a rhesus macaque, the species most people in northern and central Indian towns mean when they say "the monkeys". I cannot be sure from a vertical video, and there are other macaques and langurs in India that look different enough to matter to a specialist, so I will say "appears to be" and move on. If it is a rhesus, it belongs to one of the most successful non-human primates on the planet when it comes to living beside people.

Ecologists have a word for this: commensal. It describes an animal that lives alongside humans and benefits from the arrangement without being domesticated. Rhesus macaques have a large geographic range among Indian primates, a flexible diet, and a habit of making use of whatever a human settlement produces. Fruit stalls. Temple offerings. Food scraps. Kitchen windows. The market in this video is not an obstacle to that animal. It is closer to a pantry with a very complicated door system.

This is where the route starts to look different.

Primates, including macaques, are generally understood to remember where food is, and to learn when it tends to appear. A town is full of such information, and it has rhythm. Stalls open and close. Vendors shoo or ignore. Some people hand over fruit. Some people lunge. A monkey that survives in a place like this has to read the street the way a courier reads traffic: where the quick gaps are, which walls are climbable, which corners are risky, and which spots reliably produce something to eat. I cannot tell you what this particular monkey knows. But the first thirty seconds of this clip are what that kind of knowledge looks like from above.

Look at how the animal uses vertical space. It begins on the awnings, above head height, where people rarely look and where a monkey is, in practical terms, invisible to the street. Then it comes down at a moment of its own choosing. When it joins the people at ground level, it does not appear to be negotiating with them. It is moving through them, and in the stretches I could make out, the crowd is returning the favour. Most of the time, a human crowd that does not flinch is a crowd that has seen this many times before.

That is not a trivial observation. Researchers who studied rhesus macaques in a northern Indian hill town found that animals living with more frequent human contact behaved differently from those with less. In the study I reviewed for this piece, monkeys exposed to higher rates of human interaction spent shorter periods on grooming, a basic social and hygienic activity, and were more vigilant. In plain terms: living in the middle of us costs them something, even when the arrangement looks relaxed to a person with a phone in hand. The calm of the street, from the monkey's side, may not be calm at all. It may be a state of constant, practiced alertness that looks like ease.

I raise this not to spoil the mood of the video, but because it changes how the shrine reads. If the street is a place where a monkey has to stay alert, a shrine platform might be a different sort of place. It is raised. It is stone. It is edged by a wall on one side and presumably a little apart from the stream of feet. It has food on it. And it belongs, symbolically, to something that people are not supposed to chase away.

You do not need any mystical explanation to see why a monkey might choose it. You also do not need to dismiss the mystical explanation to see it works. Both readings land in the same place.

WHAT IS ON THE PLATFORM

The offerings are the second reason the shrine works as a destination, and it is the part of the story that makes people uncomfortable once they notice it.

The things laid out in front of a figure like this are, in many cases, edible or adjacent to edible. In this clip I can make out bright orange flowers, small dishes, and what appear to be pieces of fruit. I will not claim to know what each item is, because the resolution and the angle do not permit it. But one thing is plain enough: a small arrangement of fruit and flowers has been set down on a surface that a monkey can reach.

Across India, giving fruit to monkeys, bananas above all, is widely treated as an act of merit at religious sites. A number of researchers who study human and macaque interaction describe it as a common form of devotion, with monkeys found in high densities around temples as a result. A study of how people provision macaques at tourist and religious sites also treats the link to Hanuman as a central reason for the behaviour among Hindus.

So the platform in this video sits where two economies meet. In one, a person places something at a shrine as an act of reverence. In the other, an animal discovers that shrines are reliable and relatively unguarded places to find food. Neither economy has to be cynical for them to reinforce each other. A devotee feels a quiet satisfaction. A monkey learns a location. The next day, the location is more likely to be visited again.

That is how a place turns into a habit.

It is also how a place turns into a problem, and I will come to that. For now, the thing to notice is the quality of the ambiguity. If you watch a monkey sit at an altar and handle what has been laid there, you can see tenderness in it. You can see theft in it. You can see two things that are both true: a creature meeting a need, in a space that a human community has set aside as sacred.

The video does not choose between those readings, and neither do the people in it. That is what gives it its charge.

THE MAN BESIDE THE SHRINE

There is a person in the frame who deserves more attention than he is likely to get, because he is the clearest evidence of what this place means to the people who actually live near it.

He is standing next to the platform, a man in a checked shirt and a blue lungi, with a red-checked cloth over one shoulder. I do not know who he is, and nothing in the footage tells me, and I would not try to find out. He is a private individual who happened to be standing in a shot someone else was taking, and the right way to treat him is as part of the scene, not as a character to be hunted down. What matters is what he does, and what he does not do.

He does not wave the monkey off. He does not step back. As the clip goes on, other people join the edge of the frame, and in one of the later moments his hands appear to come together in front of his chest, in what looks like the gesture that usually accompanies a greeting or a prayer. I say "appears" because the footage is shot from a distance and above, and I would not want to put words or feelings in the mouth of someone I cannot see clearly.

But even if you refuse to read anything devotional into that gesture, the ordinary facts are striking enough. A wild animal is sitting a short distance from a stranger at a place of worship, and the stranger is standing his ground, in calm. That tells you something about how people in this street understand what a monkey on that platform means. It tells you, at the very least, that this is not an emergency.

Think about how unusual that is on a global scale. In many parts of the world, a wild primate within arm's reach of a person would be a crisis, or at least an incident, a phone call to someone with a uniform. Here, a few seconds of footage show it being absorbed into the day. Not forgiven, not celebrated, just absorbed. A skill that cultures take generations to develop, and that visitors tend to notice only when it is missing.

THE PART THE CAPTION LEAVES OUT

Clips like this travel with a promise attached. The version of this video that circulates under its title implies that what you are about to see will touch your heart, and it might. I am not here to take that away from anyone. But a responsible account of what the footage shows has to include the other side of the same coin, because the people who live with monkeys every day know it well, and because it is the reason this scene is more complicated than it looks.

The same species that sits quietly on a shrine platform in a thirty-second video is, in other contexts, at the centre of a long-running argument in Indian towns and cities. The facts are not in dispute. Rhesus macaques are legally protected under India's Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972, which makes keeping or using them a punishable offence. They are also widely regarded as a nuisance in cities in the north of the country, where bites, snatched food and damage to property are a regular part of the news. One article reported nearly eighteen hundred monkey bite cases a year in the capital alone. I would treat a figure like that as an illustration of scale rather than a precise measurement, but nobody involved in the debate pretends the problem is imaginary.

Researchers who work on this do not frame the conflict as the monkeys' fault. A wildlife protection specialist writing about the problem argues that the underlying drivers are largely human: poor management of solid waste, restaurants dumping leftovers, residents leaving food out, habitat fragmentation, and wildlife managers who are not resourced to prevent problems before they start. The same writer makes the point that this is not a problem that can be "solved" in the simple sense of the word, only managed, and that well-meant feeding is part of what keeps the cycle going. When a lone macaque or a small group first appears in a neighbourhood, he notes, many residents respond by offering fruit or leftovers as a gesture of kindness or devotion, and that gesture is the beginning of dependence.

There is a legal edge to this too. A Delhi High Court order years ago told people not to feed monkeys in public places, and feeding is discouraged, and in some places prohibited, around temples and tourist sites. The reason is not cruelty. It is that monkeys who learn that people are food sources become bolder, and bolder monkeys get into more conflicts, and the conflicts tend to end badly for the monkeys.

I raise all of this because it would be easy to watch a video like this and conclude that the lesson is simply to go and offer a banana. It is not. The thing the clip shows is delicate. A fruit offering on a shrine platform, left by a person who is acting out of faith, can be a beautiful act and also the seed of a habit that is hard on both species. People who work on coexistence tend to favour arrangements that do not make wild animals dependent on handouts, however kindly meant.

Nothing in the video asks you to resolve that, and I would not try. Hold both facts: a monkey on a platform at a quiet moment, and a country-wide argument about what to do with an animal that lives in so many places that cities were built for people. The clip is a gentle slice of the quieter half of that tension.

WHAT THIRTY SECONDS CANNOT PROVE

Every clip that goes around the internet arrives wearing a story, and the story is usually bigger than the clip. This one is no exception, so here is a plain accounting of what is known and what is not.

What is visible: a monkey, probably a rhesus macaque, on a market awning at the start. It travels through a busy street at ground level, with people, scooters, a cycle rickshaw and pigeons all around. It reaches a small whitewashed roadside shrine with a bell and an orange-red figure, climbs onto the stone platform in front, and spends the end of the clip there, among flowers, small dishes and what look like pieces of fruit, while a man stands close by and, later, more people arrive nearby. The video is vertical, about thirty seconds long, filmed from a high vantage point, and the fingers of the person holding the phone appear at the edge of the frame in the later part. The red arrow that follows the animal was added by whoever edited the clip.

What is not known: where this is, beyond what the scene suggests. Who any of the people are. Whether this monkey comes to this shrine every day or has never been there before. Whether the route was a purposeful trip or a series of opportunistic moves that happened to end at the shrine. What the monkey ate, if anything. What the man beside the shrine felt. Whether anything before or after the thirty seconds changes how the footage should be understood. Nothing in what I could examine points to staging, and I have no reason to suspect it, but I have no means of verifying that, and so I will not claim it either way.

One more limit: the file carries audio, but I could not reliably interpret it, so nothing in this account depends on what is said or played in the clip. If there is speech or music that changes the picture, that is something you will hear and I cannot report.

This matters because the temptation with a video like this is to supply the missing information with feeling. It is a very human reflex. A monkey sits at a shrine, a man stands by with his hands together, and the mind fills in a tale of mutual understanding that the footage does not strictly contain. I think that is a perfectly natural response, and I do not think it is wrong to feel moved. I do think it is worth knowing which part of the feeling is coming from the screen and which part is coming from us.

Primatologists have a word for the habit of reading human intention into animal behaviour, and the word is not always an insult. Anthropomorphism can be a lazy shortcut, but it can also be a starting point for good questions. What I would suggest is a middle path: treat the monkey as an animal with its own reasons, which we cannot access, and treat the people as people with their own reasons, which we should not guess. Then enjoy the fact that those two sets of reasons, whatever they are, have produced a scene so quiet and so strange that it stops a thumb mid-scroll.

There is also a smaller point about vantage that I find hard to let go of. The person filming is above the street, looking down, with a hand intruding on the corner of the frame. That is not a neutral position. From above, the whole route is legible: the awning, the street, the crowd, the destination. At ground level, in the middle of the market, very little of it would have been. You would have seen a monkey pass at knee height and been gone. The video works because someone had the right window at the right time and the instinct to keep the camera on a small brown animal rather than on the more obviously photogenic parts of the street.

That is an underrated kind of skill, and it is part of why the clip holds together.

WHAT TO WATCH FOR

If you are going to watch it, and I think you should, here is how I would approach it. Not as a list of things to check off, but as a handful of questions the footage answers better than words can.

First, find the monkey before the arrow does. The animal is small and its colouring is close to the street's. See how long it takes you to lock on without help. Then watch what happens to that effort when the camera pulls across the market, because the street is busy enough to hide it, and that difficulty is part of the point.

Second, watch the people and not the animal. This is the part a transcript can never give you. Count how many faces turn toward the monkey as it crosses the street. Notice what the crowd does with its hands, its feet, its attention. The reaction, or the absence of one, is the real subject of the first half.

Third, pay attention to the change in tempo when the monkey reaches the shrine. The first half of the clip is movement: roofs, pavement, bicycles, bodies. The second half is almost the opposite. Something slows down, and the question is who slows it, the animal or the place.

Fourth, look at the stone platform and what is on it. I have told you what it appears to hold, and I have told you what I think it means, but I have deliberately not told you what the monkey does with it, or how the man beside the shrine responds, or what the last few seconds look like. That is the part where my account runs out and the footage takes over.

There is a quieter detail in the first half that is easy to miss. The monkey is not the only animal living off this market. Pigeons crowd the pavement among the feet, picking at the ground, rising and settling as the crowd shifts. A street like this feeds several species at once, and most of them have worked out where they fit. Seen from up above, a market is an ecosystem as much as a shop. The monkey is simply the one that ends up at the shrine.

Finally, watch it twice. The first time, you will follow the animal. The second time, look at everything else: the bell, the carved edge of the niche, the steel utensils stacked at the neighbouring stall, the pigeons that rise and settle as the street shifts around them, the way people pass the shrine without breaking stride, as if it were part of the architecture. It is a very small piece of a very large place, and it rewards the second look.

THE QUIET PART

Strip away the title, the arrow and the music that may or may not be on the track, and what remains is something rare for a clip of this length: a plain record of two kinds of life sharing a corner of a street without much fuss.

It does not resolve whether the monkey is a pilgrim, a thief, a regular or a stranger. It does not settle whether the offerings on that stone are an invitation or an accident of geography. It does not tell you whether the man beside the shrine is praying, greeting, watching, or just standing where he always stands. It gives you a route, a destination, and a few seconds of closeness, and leaves you to decide what you saw.

That is why I would send you to the video itself rather than ask you to take my word for any of it. Everything above is context, and context is only worth anything if it sharpens your eyes. The part that actually matters is a small animal on a stone ledge, in front of an orange-red figure and a hanging bell, with a man at arm's length and a market carrying on behind them, and what the animal does in the moments after it sits down.

One request, if you pass it along. The people in this footage did not choose to be in it. Please leave the man by the shrine and the others at the edge of the frame alone, and resist the urge to work out who they are or where exactly they live. Credit whoever filmed it if you know who that is. And if the clip makes you want to feed a monkey the next time you meet one, remember that the kindest thing, for the animal, is usually to keep your distance and your banana.

I have told you everything I can about why that spot is loaded. I have not told you what happens on it. That bit belongs to the footage.

text:
There is something I would like to say to those of you who currently support Restore Britain or Reform UK.
First of all, I understand why many of you support these parties. Like many people, you are frustrated with the political establishment, disillusioned with traditional politics and desperate to see meaningful change in our country.
You want Britain to regain control of its borders, restore a sense of national pride, address the cost of living, tackle the problems facing our communities and put ordinary people before political interests.
I share many of those concerns.
However, I would ask you to keep another political organisation in mind: The Alliance for Democracy and Freedom (ADF). Maybe as your second option? IF you feel politically homeless, maybe as your first?
Not necessarily because I expect you to abandon your current political allegiances, but because I believe we should always have alternatives.
What happens if the parties we currently support fail to deliver what they promise? What happens if their actions eventually prove very different from their words? And what happens if, once in positions of power, they turn out not to be quite what we thought they were?
No political party deserves unquestioning loyalty. We should support policies and principles, not personalities or party rosettes.
RESTORE BRITAIN – WHERE I AGREE AND WHERE I HAVE RESERVATIONS
I like Rupert Lowe. I appreciate his willingness to challenge the political establishment, and I recognise that many people see Restore Britain as an opportunity to take the country in a different direction.
However, I do have reservations about some of Restore Britain's more Thatcherite economic and social policies.
My concern is that, while certain policies may be intended to tackle waste, dependency and those who exploit the system, their consequences could potentially reach much further.
I worry that some of those who genuinely need help and assistance, particularly disabled people and those who are unable to support themselves, could end up being left behind.
We must be careful not to confuse people who genuinely need the safety net of the state with those who deliberately exploit it.
This is one of the reasons I believe the ADF deserves consideration.
The ADF believes in means-testing benefits across the board. Everyone claiming benefits should be subject to fair and consistent assessments of their entitlement.
This isn't about singling out disabled people, the vulnerable, immigrants or those who genuinely need assistance. Quite the opposite.
I want a system that identifies those who genuinely qualify for support and ensures that public money reaches them, rather than being lost through abuse, exploitation or payments to people who are not entitled to receive them.
Immigration status and eligibility must also be properly considered, in accordance with the law.
Those who genuinely need assistance should not be punished because others exploit the system.
Benefits should be a safety net, NOT a way of life. But that safety net must be there when people genuinely need it.
That, to me, is fairness.
BRITISH IDENTITY, INTEGRATION AND EQUALITY
There is another issue I feel strongly about.
I believe Restore Britain is attracting the odd person who holds ethno-nationalist views. In the same way, I believe our own Belmont Accord, is a possible target for the disingenuous, although as with Restore, I'm sure it's just the odd person. I appreciate that very few who support the party share those views.
However, I think it is important that we are honest about the kind of country and political movement we want to build.
The Alliance for Democracy and Freedom was until recently led by Dr Teck Khong, a Malaysian-born man who has given around forty years of service to the NHS in this country.
Yet there are people who believe that someone should not be entitled to political office because of their ethnicity or birthplace.
I find that attitude completely unacceptable.
Why should somebody who has devoted decades of their life to serving this country be judged by their ethnicity rather than their character, contribution and commitment?
The ADF rejects that kind of discrimination, and so do I.
I believe that if you are proud to be British, or proud to make Britain your home, respect British law, and respect the cultures, traditions and values that make up our country, built on Christianity, whether you're a Christian or not. You should be welcomed, if you wish to contribute.
Integration, mutual respect and shared civic responsibilities matter.
You do not have to share the same ancestry to share a commitment to this country.
Racism and discrimination have no place in the Britain I want to see.
REFORM UK – WHY I HAVE GREATER RESERVATIONS
Reform UK is a different proposition altogether, and I have considerably more reservations about its political direction.
I have concerns about its leadership's historical positions on mandatory vaccination for health workers during Covid, and statements supporting, in my opinion, war criminal, Tony Blair's involvement as a vaccine tsar.
For me, this raises fundamental questions about bodily autonomy.
I believe that full bodily autonomy is a basic human right. What happens to individual freedom when governments believe they can override that right?
This is not a small political disagreement for me. It is a matter of principle. I believe it is a right worth fighting for.
I also disagree with Reform's approach to the war in Ukraine and its support for the position taken by NATO and the wider Western alliance. I believe these matters deserve much more scrutiny and independent thought. How we can give money to Ukraine when we have homeless veterans on our streets and children in food and energy poverty, I just don't understand. Especially as I believe that Putin, isn't a direct threat to us, as long as NATO, stops poking him.
I am also concerned about the willingness to welcome former Conservative politicians into the party.
After fourteen years of Conservative government, many people feel that the country was badly let down. We saw failures to adequately address illegal migration, and legal migration levels that raised serious questions about infrastructure, integration and social cohesion.
Why should people automatically trust politicians who were part of that political establishment simply because they have changed their party allegiance?
There are also questions surrounding Reform's approach to Net Zero.
I believe we should be investing in technology that delivers cleaner air and a more sustainable future, rather than pursuing policies that risk imposing unnecessary costs on ordinary people. Nuclear energy and technological innovation should be central to that conversation.
I also have concerns about the financial interests and backgrounds of some of Reform UK's donors.
There is publicly available information concerning connections between some financial donors, George Soros and previous financial support for the Conservative Party. One donor in this category who also funds gb nEWS. maybe that's why Rupert Lowe and Tommy Robinson are never allowed to appear?
I am not suggesting that any particular donor controls Reform UK. That isn't my argument.
My concern is about transparency, influence and whether a party can genuinely present itself as an outsider challenging the political establishment when some of the people financially supporting it have connections with that very establishment.
These are questions I believe voters have every right to ask.
If we are serious about changing British politics, we should be looking beyond the party leaders and examining the wider networks of financial support behind them.
How can we expect an establishment party to challenge the establishment if some of its financial supporters have previously supported the very political interests it claims to oppose?
Having said all that, I am a realist.
If I lived in an area where a Reform UK candidate had a genuine opportunity to defeat a candidate representing the political establishment, and the ADF had no realistic prospect of winning that seat, I would seriously consider voting Reform as the best available option of a bad bunch.
I would do the same with Restore Britain, with a much less heavier heart and a lot more enthusiasm.
I would rather see some movement towards change than simply stand by while the same political failures continue.
But that doesn't mean I have to abandon my principles.
THE ADF – A POLITICAL HOME FOR PEOPLE WHO FEEL THEY HAVE NOWHERE TO GO
This is where I believe the Alliance for Democracy and Freedom deserves an opportunity.
The ADF offers the possibility of a political home for people who feel that neither the traditional left nor the current right-wing alternatives fully represent their views.
People who want controlled immigration, responsible public spending, individual liberty, equality before the law, protection for those genuinely in need, and a government that puts the interests of the country and its people first.
One policy I particularly welcome is the proposal to reintroduce the Right to Buy scheme for council and social housing tenants.
However, there is an important distinction in how I believe this should work.
Money raised through the sale of social housing should go directly towards building replacement and additional social housing, rather than being diverted elsewhere.
We have to learn from the mistakes of the past. Selling social housing without adequately replacing it has contributed to the shortage of affordable homes.
If people have the opportunity to own their own homes, that is something worth supporting. But we must also ensure that future generations and those who cannot afford to buy still have access to decent, affordable social housing.
We need to build, not simply sell.
I also want to see a political movement that genuinely believes in individual freedoms, bodily autonomy, democratic accountability and the right of citizens to question those who govern them.
UNITY DOES NOT MEAN AGREEMENT ON EVERYTHING
I should also be clear about something.
I do not personally agree with every individual or organisation associated with the Belmont Accord. Nor would I necessarily agree with every position taken by every partner.
I have concerns about some of the ethno-nationalist views that exist within certain political circles, and there are people whose outlook I could not personally work with.
However, I recognise that the original idea behind Dr Teck Khong's initiative was admirable: to encourage smaller right-wing and centrist political parties to communicate, cooperate and potentially work together where they share common ground.
As I understand it, approaches to discuss cooperation were made to a number of parties, including Reform UK, SDP, Heritage Party, Advance UK, Restore Britain, UKIP and Reclaim.
Those approaches did not result in the wider cooperation that had been hoped for.
It makes me wonder: so much for uniting the right?
If parties cannot even find common ground on issues where they share concerns, how can they expect to bring about meaningful political change?
We do not have to agree on everything to work together on things that matter.
But there must be some basic principles: democracy, freedom, equality before the law, respect for others and rejection of racism.
WHY I WOULD STILL STAND, EVEN IF I HAD LITTLE CHANCE OF WINNING
I am considering standing as a candidate in an area where Restore Britain has little prospect of winning.
Realistically, the ADF might not have much chance of winning either.
Some people might ask why I would bother. Why risk losing the £500 election deposit when the chances of success might be so small?
My answer is simple.
Sometimes standing is about more than winning.
It is about making a stand, giving people a choice and offering a voice to those who feel they have no political home.
There may be people who agree with much of what Restore Britain says but are uncomfortable with some of its economic policies.
There may be people who agree with Reform UK on immigration and national sovereignty but cannot reconcile themselves with its other positions.
There may be people who simply do not feel represented by any of the established parties.
Those people deserve a choice too.
I would rather stand, make the case for what I believe in and give people an alternative than sit back and complain that nobody represents them.
If elected, I would want to represent the people of my area to the very best of my ability, regardless of how they voted, where they came from or what their personal circumstances might be.
That is what representative democracy should be about.
IS THE BALLOT BOX ENOUGH?
I will admit that I sometimes question whether meaningful change can still be achieved through the ballot box alone.
There is an old saying: "If voting changed anything, they wouldn't let you do it."
I don't necessarily accept that as an absolute truth, more in hope of avoiding civil war and civil unrest, that I believe is coming, but I understand why people feel that way.
Having attended council and general election counts, I have personally witnessed things that have left me questioning aspects of the process. Either I can't count or on occasions, I don't personally believe that they can.
I have seen things that made me wonder about the accuracy of the figures being announced, particularly when compared with what I believed I had counted myself.
I also don't believe in boxes stored overnight and counted the next day and postal voting/ Don't get me started !
Some may disagree with my interpretation, and that is their right. But I am entitled to draw attention to what I have personally experienced and to ask questions.
I believe citizens should be able to question the systems that govern them without being dismissed or ridiculed.
Democracy requires scrutiny, transparency and accountability. If people lose confidence in the process, those concerns deserve to be taken seriously.
We cannot afford to lose faith in democracy itself. We need to make it work better, make it more transparent and ensure that every legitimate vote is counted fairly.
The answer to political disillusionment should be more accountability, not abandoning democratic participation. Although Government after government, set of liars, after set of liars, make it increasingly harder not to abandon the ballot box.
I sometimes wonder how far removed those at the top of politics have become from the everyday lives and struggles of ordinary people. Actually, I don't wonder. I know. I doubt greed fuelled psychopaths and their puppets really care about you or me, in truth.
Too many people feel that their voices are ignored until somebody wants their vote.
That has to change.
ONE DAY, THERE COULD BE A GENUINE ALTERNATIVE
I believe that if we can grow the Alliance for Democracy and Freedom, spread the word and encourage people to become involved, we could eventually build a genuine political alternative.
Not necessarily overnight. Not necessarily at the next election.
But one day.
Imagine a political movement where people from different backgrounds and political traditions can come together around shared democratic principles.
A movement where people are not expected to agree with every policy, but where they can trust that individual freedoms, democratic accountability, fairness and the interests of ordinary citizens matter.
A movement where disabled people are not abandoned, where benefits are properly means-tested, where immigration is controlled, where public money is spent responsibly, where housing is built and where people are treated equally under the law.
A movement that does not demand blind loyalty and does not expect its supporters to stop asking difficult questions.
I want to see a Britain where citizens stand together against abuses of power, authoritarianism and the erosion of our freedoms.
I want a country where our political representatives remember that they work for us, not the other way around.
And I believe the Alliance for Democracy and Freedom could, with the right people and the right principles, become a home for those who want something different.
MY APPEAL TO YOU
So, if you support Restore Britain, I am not asking you to stop supporting Rupert Lowe.
If you support Reform UK, I am not asking you to change your mind overnight.
I am simply asking you to keep the Alliance for Democracy and Freedom in mind.Maybe for the future or sign up and support the ADF Party, even if you are going to vote Restore or Reform, if you can see the potential.
Look at its policies. Read what it stands for. Ask questions. Challenge it where you disagree. Don't take my word for it.
And if the day comes when the party you currently support fails to deliver, compromises on the principles you believed in, or turns out to be something different from what you expected, remember that there may be another political home available to you.
We should never become so attached to a political party that we are afraid to question it.
Our loyalty should be to democracy, freedom, fairness and the people of this country – not to any particular political leader or party.
If you feel that there is room for a genuinely different political voice in Britain, I invite you to take a look at the Alliance for Democracy and Freedom.
Visit the website, read the policies, get involved, ask questions and, if you believe in what it is trying to achieve, consider joining or showing your support.
I don't expect everyone to agree with everything I have said. I don't even agree with every position taken by every organisation within the wider political alliances.
But I do believe we need more choices, more honest debate and more people prepared to stand up for what they believe in.
We may not have the numbers today. We may not win seats tomorrow.
But every political movement starts somewhere.
Perhaps it is time we started building a political home for people who feel politically homeless.
Perhaps one day people will finally put their party rosettes aside and recognise that there are bigger things at stake than party loyalty.
A country where we, as citizens, can stand together against tyranny, the erosion of our freedoms and the loss of democratic accountability.
Alliance for Democracy and Freedom. A voice for those who want a choice.
Because Britain belongs to all of us, and its future should never be left exclusively in the hands of any one political party.   https://t.co/TnYgqyGxmP

text:
Scripture never presents the Lord’s Prayer as a ritual formula that must be performed with specific postures under the direction of a priest. Jesus gave it as a model of how we are to pray, not as a liturgical act that requires regulated gestures to be valid.

True worship is not bound to the traditions of men or to the rules of a human hierarchy. Jesus said the hour was coming when true worshippers would worship the Father in spirit and in truth (John 4:23-24).

That worship is made possible because Jesus has finished the work. He offered Himself once for all, and by that one offering He has perfected forever those who are sanctified (Hebrews 10:14).

We do not re-present that sacrifice. We do not need a priest to stand in the place of Christ and perform prescribed actions so that we can approach God. We have boldness to enter the Holiest by the blood of Jesus (Hebrews 10:19).

The Catholic insistence on controlling every detail of posture and gesture in the Mass is simply another layer of tradition added to what God never required. The finished work of Christ still stands.

Believers pray the Lord’s Prayer, or any other prayer, directly to the Father through Jesus. That is the liberty of the gospel. No man, no posture, and no liturgy can add to or restrict what Jesus has already accomplished.
