text:
The cage is already in the first frame.

Nobody carries it in later. Nobody runs for it after a surprise. In the very first second of this clip it is standing behind the man, a little left of center: a round wire dome with a small ornamental knob on top, set down on the leaf litter like a prop waiting for its cue.

Hold onto that detail, because the title attached to this video promises an accident. The wording is roughly: unexpectedly, under the brooding chicken, there was a bird's nest. Everything in that sentence leans on one word. Unexpectedly. A surprise is something nobody prepared for. And yet somebody, apparently, prepared a cage.

I am not saying that to spoil the clip. I am saying it because the clip gets more interesting, not less, once you notice what it is actually doing. On the surface it is a quiet, almost sleepy scene at the edge of some dry woodland: a man in a mustard-yellow shirt and a checked wrap around his waist kneels on a bed of what look like rice husks, and in front of him a small, strikingly patterned hen sits behind a heap of brown eggs. A sprig of green leaves is tucked in near his face, and it sways in front of his eyes for the entire video. I caught myself watching that sprig more than I expected to.

Under the surface there is a small puzzle with three layers.

Layer one: the scene is built to look like a discovery, but several details suggest it was arranged before the camera started.

Layer two: the thing being "discovered" is not a nest in any ordinary biological sense, at least not as far as the footage shows.

Layer three: the birds that eventually appear are doing something that nestlings simply cannot do, and that single behavior changes what the whole clip is about.

All three layers are visible in nineteen seconds of vertical video, and none of them requires guessing anything about the man, his character, his location, or his motives. This is a story about what can be seen, what can be reasonably inferred, and what the footage honestly leaves open. Please keep that distinction in mind, because I will try to keep it too.

Start with the hen, because she is the easiest part of this video to love and the easiest part to misread.

THE HEN WHO ANSWERS NOTHING

She is small. Next to the eggs she looks almost ornamental, a bird dressed for a show rather than a nest. Her feathers carry a crisp pattern of dark, glossy centers edged in white, so that she looks as if she has been drawn by someone with a very fine pen. Her tail is fanned and lifted. The comb on her head is small and red. The markings resemble the silver-laced bantam type, a family that includes breeds such as the Sebright, though I cannot confirm a breed from a short clip, and I would not trust anyone who claims to.

She sits at the back edge of a heap of roughly a dozen or more brown eggs, with the eggs banked up in front of her like a low wall. Her posture reads, to anyone who has kept chickens, as calm. She is not fleeing, not flapping, not shrieking. For a few seconds she simply occupies the scene the way a hen occupies a nest.

That calm is the first thing worth pausing on, because of what the title wants you to feel. The word "brooding" is doing quiet work here. It lets you imagine a devoted mother who has been sitting patiently for days, unaware that something is happening beneath her. It is a lovely picture. It is also a picture the footage does not support, for reasons I will lay out one at a time.

A small technical point first, since this is the kind of detail that makes a viewer look twice. In strict poultry language, a hen sitting on eggs is incubating. Brooding is what she does after the chicks hatch, when she keeps them warm under her body. In everyday speech people say "brooding hen" for both, and the title does the same, so nobody is being deceptive by using the word that way. But it helps to know the difference, because the whole phrase "brooding chicken" quietly promises that a long, patient process has been going on. A genuine incubation lasts about three weeks for chicken eggs. Three weeks of sitting is a very different story from a hen placed on a pile of eggs for a camera.

I do not know which of those two situations this is. The video does not say. What I can say is what an actual broody hen tends to do, so that you can compare it with what you see.

WHAT A REAL BROODY HEN DOES

A hen that has genuinely gone broody is one of the more stubborn creatures on a farm. The state is driven by hormones, with prolactin usually named as a key player, and it changes her behavior in ways that are hard to miss. She stops laying. She spends most of the day and night on the nest. She puffs her feathers out so she looks twice her size, and she may growl, hiss, or peck at a hand that comes near. Many keepers describe the experience of reaching under a broody hen as a small act of courage.

She also works. A hen on eggs does not lie still like a lid on a pot. She shifts, rolls, and rearranges the eggs with her beak and body many times a day, which helps keep the temperature even and keeps the developing embryo from sticking to the inside of the shell. She leaves the nest only briefly, usually once or twice a day, to eat, drink, and relieve herself, and then she goes straight back. The target temperature for chicken eggs is generally given as about 37.5 degrees Celsius, around 99.5 degrees Fahrenheit, and a broody hen holds that range with nothing but her own body.

Now compare that with what you see here. The hen in the clip does not puff, growl, or defend. She is moved aside by a hand without any visible protest, then walks out of the way. I want to be careful here, because hens differ and a single video cannot diagnose a bird's state of mind. Some very tame hens tolerate handling, and a short moment of calm is not proof of anything. But the absence of the classic defensive display is one more small reason the "devoted mother, patiently incubating" picture feels borrowed from somewhere else.

THE EGG PROBLEM

Here is a detail most people will not catch on a first viewing. The hen is a small bantam-type bird. The eggs look large.

Bantams are miniature chickens, and their eggs are typically noticeably smaller than the eggs of a standard-size hen. The eggs in this clip, set next to her body, look like ordinary full-size brown eggs. I cannot measure them from a video, and perspective can fool the eye, so I will not claim a mismatch as proven. But a little hen sitting on a pile of what appear to be full-size eggs is a visual note that, in my view, belongs in the "worth noticing" column.

There is also a simple capacity question. A hen can only cover as many eggs as fit under her body, and a small bantam can usually cover fewer eggs than a large hen. A heap of a dozen or more eggs, spread out in the open, is more than a small hen could comfortably keep warm. Real incubating hens often lose eggs to the edges of the nest, which cool down, and experienced keepers limit a small hen's clutch for exactly that reason.

None of this makes the scene impossible. It makes it look arranged, the way a table in a restaurant window is arranged. Everything is placed neatly, everything is visible to the lens, and nothing looks quite like the messy, tucked-away, camouflaged thing that a real nest tends to be.

THE HAND THAT RESETS THE SCENE

Watch what the man does in the first few seconds. He does not look surprised. He leans in, puts a hand near the hen, and she is gone from the picture, her fanned tail disappearing at the edge of the frame. With her out of the way, the heap of eggs sits alone on the husks, a tidy mound.

Then he works on the eggs with both hands.

I am going to be deliberately restrained about this part, for two reasons. First, the video does not explain it, and I will not invent an explanation. Second, whatever happens here, it is the one stretch of the clip where the footage shifts from a calm tableau to something that takes up a lot of the frame and a lot of the viewer's attention. What I can say plainly is this: the eggs begin the sequence whole and numerous, and they end it as scattered, empty shell halves lying on the husks. In the frames I examined I do not see chicks. I do not see a hatch. I do not see anything that would explain what became of the contents.

That matters for one reason I will return to later. If these were fertile, incubated eggs, then what happens to them is more than a camera trick. If they were ordinary eggs from a kitchen, then the "brooding hen" is even more of a stage prop. The video gives no way to tell, and I will not pretend it does.

What I can tell you is that the heap, which was the visual center of the first seconds, ceases to be the point. By the time the shell halves are strewn around, the camera has already started moving toward the next object of interest, which is not the eggs and not the hen.

It is the ground.

THE FLAT PIECE OF BARK

Look at the husks to the side of the egg mound, a little way down the frame. Under the loose layer there is something flat and pale, roughly the shape and finish of a slab of bark or a thin piece of wood. It lies level with the surface, dusted with husks, so that at a glance it blends into the ground.

The man's hand finds its edge and lifts it.

This is the moment the whole video was built to reach. Under the slab there is a hole in the earth, a dark opening with soil walls, sitting a short distance from where the hen and her eggs had been arranged. The caption's promise is that this hole is, or contains, "a bird's nest." The camera obliges by dwelling on it.

Here is where the first layer of the puzzle, the staging, becomes hard to ignore. Ask yourself a plain question. If a nest hole were hidden under a hen's eggs and discovered by accident, why would it be covered by a flat, loose, hand-liftable slab that blends into the surface? Wild nests are camouflaged by nature. They are not usually fitted with lids. A lid is a human tool, and a lid that sits flush and is dusted with husks is a lid somebody put there on purpose.

And then there is the cage.

THE CAGE, AGAIN

Remember the dome standing at the back of the opening frame. Now, with the hole open, a hand lowers it. The wire dome settles over the opening like a bell jar over a specimen, and the cage's bottom rim presses into the husks.

This is the piece of the video that changes its genre. Before the cage comes down, the scene is a mystery: what is in that hole? After the cage comes down, the scene is a procedure. Cover the hole, let whatever is inside come out, and keep it from going anywhere.

I want to be exact about what I am and am not claiming. I am not claiming anything about anyone's intentions. I am not claiming this is illegal, and I do not know where it was filmed, so I could not say. What I am saying is that a cage placed beside the hole before the "surprise," then lowered over the hole once it is uncovered, is a sequence with a very legible logic, and that logic is not "we were astonished by what we found."

THE DETAIL INSIDE THE HOLE

With the cage in position, the camera looks down through the bars, and there is one more thing worth your attention. At the mouth of the hole there is a small, slatted wire panel, like a miniature gate or flap. It carries a little coil spring, the kind you find in a mousetrap or the hinge of a spring-loaded gate. In the close frames I examined it is clear enough to see the coil and the slats.

What I think it is, and I am hedging deliberately because I cannot test it, is a one-way entrance: a spring-loaded wire gate that lets a small animal in and then closes behind it. That is a common basic principle in small traps and in the entrances of some bird and rodent cages. But I did not see it work, so the honest version is this: the hole contains a manufactured wire fitting with a spring, which is not something a bird builds into a nest.

I will say this as clearly as I can. A hole fitted with a wire gate, covered by a flat lid, with a cage waiting beside it, does not look like a nest that was stumbled upon. It looks like a prepared setup. And the title's word "unexpectedly" starts to sound like something other than a report of events.

THE BIRDS

And then the birds appear.

They come out of the dark opening, a few at first. They are small, in a muted brown-and-gray coloring that makes them hard to separate from the shadows, and they are not hatchlings. This is the third layer of the puzzle, and for me it is the best part, so let me slow down.

A newly hatched bird comes in one of two broad types. Some species hatch as chicks that are covered in down, have open eyes, and can run within hours. Chickens and quail are like that. They are called precocial. Other species hatch naked, blind, and helpless, and stay in the nest for days or weeks while their parents feed them. Those are called altricial. Many small songbirds are altricial.

The birds in the cage are neither. They are fully feathered. They beat their wings. They launch from the ground, hit the top of the cage, and flutter against the bars. In the moment the cage fills with motion, they look less like the occupants of a nest and more like adult or near-adult birds, in a wire dome, trying to leave.

This matters for what the video is. A "nest" implies eggs and dependent young. A hole holding several flighted birds is better described as a refuge, a roost, or a shelter. What exactly it was, in this case, the footage does not say. It could have been an actual burrow they used. It could have been something prepared. The honest answer is: I do not know, and anyone who tells you with certainty is guessing.

I counted at least three birds, and at moments it looks like four. They move fast, they overlap, and the bars of the cage break up the image, so the exact number is hard to pin down. That, to me, is one of the strongest reasons to watch the clip rather than read about it. A count is a number. The fluttering is a motion. They are not the same thing.

HOW NESTS REALLY WORK, AND WHY THE CAPTION STILL SOUNDS PLAUSIBLE

It would be unfair to say the idea of a bird's nest near a hen is absurd. Birds nest in surprising places, and the caption's premise is not nonsense. It just does not match the specifics.

Plenty of birds nest on or in the ground. Quail, partridges, pheasants, larks, and nightjars all place their eggs on or very close to the surface, often with no more than a scrape lined with a few leaves. Their eggs are usually patterned so they vanish against soil and litter, and the parents often sit so tightly that a walker nearly steps on them before noticing.

Other birds nest in holes. Kingfishers and bee-eaters dig tunnels into earth banks. Sand martins do the same. Burrowing owls use burrows originally dug by mammals. Puffins nest in burrows on grassy cliffs. A bird in a hole in the ground is nothing new.

And chickens do live near wild birds. Small birds do enter chicken runs, nest in sheds and barns, and share the feed. Chickens and wild birds are not strangers.

So a bird's nest near a hen is possible. What would be unusual is the specific combination the caption sells: a nest hidden under a hen's own eggs, discovered by accident, containing fully flighted birds, in a hole fitted with a spring gate, under a flat lid, next to a cage that was already waiting. Each of those items has a normal explanation if you take it alone. Put together, they are a recipe.

WHAT THE RECIPE MAKES YOU THINK OF

There is a genre of short animal videos that gets millions of views. Its titles use the same few words again and again: unexpectedly, amazing, you will not believe. Journalists and animal welfare groups have reported that some videos in this broad category are staged, with animals placed in situations created for the camera, rescues arranged in advance, and "discoveries" prepared. I am not saying this clip belongs to that group, and I cannot know the intentions of whoever filmed it. I am saying that if you have seen a lot of this material, the pattern may feel familiar, and the details I listed above are the kind that people who study such videos tend to look for.

The point is not to be cynical. The point is that a good viewer can enjoy a video and also look at it with open eyes. The staging, if it is staging, does not make the footage boring. It makes it a different kind of object. A magic trick is not less fascinating because the rabbit was in the hat all along. You watch it differently, with your attention on the hands.

In this clip, the hands are the whole story. The man's hands lift the hen out of the way. His hands work the eggs. His hands raise the slab. His hands lower the cage. His hands reach in, at the end, toward the fluttering birds. If you want to understand what this video is, watch the hands.

A NOTE ON WHAT IS NOT KNOWN

Here is what I do not know, so that nobody mistakes my observations for facts.

I do not know who filmed this. I do not know when or where. I do not know the species of the hen or the birds. I cannot confirm that the eggs were fertile. I cannot confirm what happened to their contents. I cannot confirm that the wire fitting is a trap. I cannot confirm that the birds were wild. I do not know what happened to them after the final frame.

I also did not identify the man, and I will not. He is a private person who appears in a short video, and whatever the clip is, nobody gains anything from turning it into a hunt for his name or location. If you are reading this and feel tempted to dig him up, please do not. The video can be examined perfectly well without knowing who he is.

THE WELFARE QUESTION

There is one part of this clip I would be uncomfortable skipping, because it is the part that sits beneath the entertainment.

The birds in the final seconds are confined. They are inside a wire cage that is sitting on bare ground, and they are visibly panicking, beating against the bars. That is what captured wild birds do. It is not cruelty by itself, because people handle and capture birds for many legitimate reasons, including research, rehabilitation, and licensed work. Rules about capturing wild birds vary a great deal from one country to another, and in many places the capture of wild birds is regulated or restricted. I do not know the rules where this was filmed, so I make no claim about legality.

I will make a smaller claim. Watching a group of fully feathered birds beat against the bars of a cage is not the same as watching a charming nest discovery, and the caption's cheerful tone hides that difference. If part of why this clip works is the viewer's delight at "baby birds" or "a secret nest," it is worth knowing that what the footage shows is closer to a captured group of capable flyers.

And the eggs. Whatever happened, the shells scattered over the husks are not the setting for a happy hatch. If anything in this video should give a viewer pause beyond the question of staging, it is that stretch. I would rather say so in plain words than let it slide past under the cheerful title.

NINETEEN SECONDS, BUILT FOR A THUMB

The file itself tells a small story. It runs just over nineteen seconds. It is vertical, shot for a phone held upright, at a high frame rate, so motion looks smooth and every flutter has detail. That format is designed for one thing: a viewer scrolling quickly, who will decide in the first second whether to stay.

Look at how well this clip serves that viewer. The opening frame has a visible hen, a visible heap of eggs, and a visible person, which is a lot of reasons to stop. The middle has hands, motion, and a hidden-hole reveal. The end has birds. Every stretch has something moving, and nothing is explained, which keeps the viewer filling in the blanks. That is precisely the kind of structure that a caption promising an "unexpected" discovery can sit on top of.

I find that fascinating even if the premise is shaky. A video does not have to be a spontaneous event to be well made. But it helps to know which one you are watching, because the experience changes. If you think you are watching luck, you feel wonder. If you think you are watching a procedure, you feel curiosity about the procedure. The second feeling is less pure, but it is more durable.

A SECOND VIEWING CHECKLIST

If you watch this clip, try it twice. The first time, let it wash over you. The second time, look for these small things, which are easy to miss at full speed.

First, find the cage in the opening frame, and then find where it is when the camera next looks that way. It is the one object that changes meaning without changing appearance.

Second, watch the sprig of leaves near the man's face. It hardly changes between shots, which, together with the unbroken sense of continuity, suggests the video is one long take rather than a stitch of separate takes. I cannot be sure, and some cuts may be hidden, but that is how it reads to me.

Third, watch the moment the hen disappears from the frame. Her posture, her tail, and the way she leaves are not the behavior of an animal who was just disturbed from a nest she has been defending.

Fourth, look at the shells. Look at how they are broken, how many there are, and how they lie. I told you I will not interpret them, and I won't, but your eyes may notice something that my words cannot hold.

Fifth, look at the slab. Notice how flat it is and how it sits. Then look at the hole's edges. Ask yourself whether the soil around them looks like a place a bird dug or a place someone prepared.

Sixth, look at the wire gate in the hole. See the spring. See how it sits against the opening.

Seventh, watch the birds. Count them if you can. Watch what they do when they hit the top of the cage. Watch the way their wings move in a space too small to use them.

Finally, watch the last second, and see what the man's hand does.

WHAT THE CLIP DOES WELL, AND WHAT IT COSTS

It is possible to be fair to this video and still be honest about it.

It does well what short-form video does best. It uses a clean visual hook, a patterned hen on a ring of eggs. It uses suspense, a lifted slab over a dark hole. It uses a payoff, a cage full of motion. It keeps its own explanation out of the picture, so the viewer's mind supplies a story, and the title supplies the story the creator wants.

What it costs is trust. A viewer who later learns that the "unexpected" nest was a prepared setup is likely to feel a little tricked, and that feeling does not stay in one video. It spreads to the next clip, and the next, and what started as wonder becomes suspicion. That is a real loss, and not only for the creator. It is a loss for the honest wildlife videos that share the same feed, because viewers learn to doubt everything.

I would rather give you the version where you know what you are looking at and still want to look.

IF YOU SHARE IT

A short note, because it matters on a platform where clips travel.

If you repost this video, it costs nothing to avoid presenting it as a verified discovery. You can say what you actually know: it is a short clip, the caption claims an unexpected nest, the footage shows a hen, eggs, a hole with a wire fitting, a cage, and several flighted birds, and the circumstances are unconfirmed. That is more accurate and, honestly, more interesting.

And please do not turn the man in the video into a target. He appears in nineteen seconds of footage. Nobody needs his name, his village, or his account. If the clip has a problem, the problem is a caption, not a person to be hunted.

HOW I CHECKED WHAT I TOLD YOU

Everything above about the footage comes from the file itself: its length, its vertical format, and a careful look at frames taken from the beginning, the middle, and the end, including enlarged crops of the hole and the birds. I did not rely on outside claims about where or why it was filmed, because I found none I could trust. Where I offered general facts about chickens and wild birds, they are widely documented basics, and I kept them general on purpose.

WHERE THE STORY ACTUALLY LIVES

By now I have given you most of the facts. I have told you about the cage in the first frame, the hen that does not behave like a defender, the eggs that look too large, the lid that looks too neat, the wire gate with its small spring, and the birds that fly where a nest would only hold the helpless. I have told you what I do not know.

What I have not given you is the thing that no paragraph can: the sequence in motion. The way the calm of the first seconds sits against the rush of the last. The moment the slab comes up and the hole is simply dark. The odd stillness of the husks under all that panic.

You can read about a magic trick. You cannot read your way into watching it.

So look at the first frame, and then look at the last. Between them is the distance between an accident and a plan, and nineteen seconds is exactly enough time to see how it is crossed.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) estimated that Iran possessed 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to 60% before the June 2025 attacks on its nuclear facilities. How much of that material remains is currently unclear.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told G7 allies in Paris on Tuesday that U.S. sanctions and the naval blockade of Iranian ports are hurting Iran’s economy so badly that President Trump has no need to resume major combat operations, according to the State Department transcript and Reuters. He said the military stands ready if Iran crosses red lines.

Rubio pushed back on reporters who called it a stalemate. “The economic pressure is going to get even worse,” he said, adding that once the last Iranian oil that slipped past the blockade is gone, almost all of Iran’s oil revenue will dry up. Reuters reported Trump said Monday he would hold off on strikes after appeals from countries in the region, including Qatar’s prime minister.

Tehran isn’t budging yet. France 24 reported Iran says its offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days still stands, but only if Washington ends the blockade, lifts oil sanctions and unfreezes its assets. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told IRNA the conflict won’t be resolved by military means or by more sanctions.

Choking off the money beats sending our troops into another shooting war. Iran can reopen the Strait any time it wants. Until then, keep the squeeze on.

text:
Will open source AI keep up for long? | Sharif Kazemi MATS Fellow Joseph Levine Development Economist & Google DeepMind, Voxdev

Open source AI is likely further behind closed-source than current benchmarks indicate. If this gap grows, which is certainly possible, it would limit the usefulness of open source AI across a broad spectrum of capabilities that will be important for LMICs.

Every few months, there’s a ‘moment’ when open source AI (OSAI) seems to be ‘catching-up’ to the frontier, and this triggers widespread speculation about the comparative advantages of open- and closed-sourced models. The most memorable in the past two years may be the release of Deepseek R1, which demonstrated stunning reasoning capabilities comparable to the leading (closed) model at the time, OpenAI’s o1.

In July 2026, we had another burst of excitement from Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3. At 2.8 trillion parameters, the open-weight release is 75% larger than the previous largest open release in Deepseek’s V4 Pro, and the scaled size as well as training refinements have yielded a model with comparable capabilities to many closed frontier models – ranking #3 in Artificial Analysis at the time.

Similar to the Deepseek ‘moment,’ this has created anxiety about non-Chinese OSAI falling behind which led to widespread support for a letter by the CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, on the importance of keeping model weights open - which was later followed up by an announcement in September 2026 that Nvidia would acquire the open source repository Hugging Face.

Given all this news, it’s not surprising that many governments are betting big on the future of open source, and designing strategies explicitly around it.

Within days of R1's release in 2025, India's IT minister announced that DeepSeek would be hosted on domestic servers, with Indian user data processed locally on a new state compute facility of nearly 19,000 GPUs offered at 42% below market rates. By the time global leaders gathered in New Delhi for the AI Impact Summit in February 2026, the rhetoric supporting open weight models was shaping action: Mozilla pledged its billion-dollar reserves to open source AI, with its CTO describing the commitment as “a hard-headed investment in sovereignty, resilience, and democratic legitimacy,” set against the “digital rents paid to foreign entities” that come with typical access to proprietary models.

Think tanks are often promoting the same message. Carnegie greeted R1 as proof that world-class AI can be developed affordably and adapted for Swahili, Hausa, or Amharic; authors at CSIS commended open models to the Global South on the logic that LLMs are “expensive to build but relatively cheap to fine-tune,” pointing to nascent hubs in Kenya and Nigeria. The Gulf states were one of the first movers and invested heavily: Saudi Arabia's ALLaM, an Arabic model first post-trained on open source Llama 2 and now folded into Humain, the kingdom's $100 billion AI venture, and the UAE's open-weight Falcon models both showed that national projects could begin to build atop open foundations. Where all of these efforts have since gone is far less clear, and mapping that uncertain trajectory is where we'd like to focus on for this piece.

What if open source keeping up is a moment, rather than a trend?

There is a plausible scenario in which open source, rather than keeping up, falls too far behind to be a key pillar of a national AI strategy.

The current commentary around the latest AI model release, as exciting as they can be, are not useful for clear policy thinking – we are being trained to have the reflexes of spectators at a horserace. Breathless tracking of AI’s capabilities tells us to watch the yawning and closing gap between models in the horse race, with the distance often measured by months. This gives a false impression that fluctuations in the gap are likely to continue oscillating.

However, it may be deeply unrealistic to consider the breeds of horses in this race to be equally matched. One outcome could instead be a widening capability gap, durable for long enough to limit the utility of OSAI across a range of domains.

To argue why these dynamics should be taken seriously, we will:

- Offer a few reasons for why the current gap in the horse race could be understated and an artefact of temporary dynamics.

- The structural advantages of fast following fall away in an arms race due to technical, economic, and security dynamics.

- Make the case that across varying scenarios, including an arms race, some benefits of OSAI may still be worth capturing (covered in greater detail in a subsequent post).

These dynamics run counter to the common discourse about the utility of OSAI for LMICs, which typically assert that OSAI will be ‘good enough’ and accessible - meaning that countries can enjoy strong AI capabilities from OSAI without compromising on sovereignty to gain frontier access. The implications of these trends are serious enough that they should inform policy planning today, rather than simply hoping that fruitful futures for OSAI are the default path.

The horse race: Reasons why we think the gap is understated

Benchmarks are currently being used as the go-to measure of the race between open- and closed source AI – whether measured in months or indices. But there are reasons to believe that OSAI’s gap with the frontier may be understated.

This is likely for two main reasons:

- Benchmark performance may have overstated present capabilities.

- The source of growing capabilities has primarily been fast following rather than innovation.

What exactly do we mean by these? Well, for the first, benchmark performance overstates present capabilities in three key ways:

1. Open source models have often spent far more tokens than closed-source variants to tackle the same benchmarks

Allowing the models to think for longer costs more but gives open source models an advantage in performance which is under-reported. Even though token cost is often lower for open source models, price per question was found to be higher for Kimi K3 than GPT-5.6 Sol because the open source Kimi spent far more tokens on answering questions across the measured benchmarks. Some of these benchmark-hacking practices could shift in the near future. For instance, Inkling, an open source model developed by Thinking Machines, trained in the ability to control thinking efforts which reduces cost.

2. Open source models consistently fall short on private benchmarks

This shortfall compared to their performance on public benchmarks implies deliberate training, as noted by EpochAI in their methodology (May 2026). The "questions" on private benchmarks are not available for labs to train their models on, and therefore serve as less hack-able tests of a model’s capabilities. The recent Kimi K3 is an extreme example. On GPQA Diamond – public since 2023, with its questions and answers freely downloadable – K3 scores 93% against the best closed model's 95%. On FrontierMath, whose questions Epoch AI keeps secret so that no model can study for the exam, the same race is not close: 72% against 89% on the standard tiers, and 39% against 88% on the hardest problems. This pattern holds generally. Measured on public benchmarks, the open–closed lag reads as roughly four to six months; on private benchmarks this lag roughly doubles. This effect likely compounds with release taxes (outlined below) as developers publishing later have more opportunities to assess which aspects of frontier models were improved on to achieve benchmark gains.

3. The adoption gap between open and closed models

Although there is a capabilities gap, it’s unclear how much this explain the high adoption gap between open- and closed-source models as reported in Demirer, Fradkin, and Tadelis (2026), or by vast price differentials depending on inference provider (up to 5x), or by just general lack of knowledge about open source AI (four years post-ChatGPT is still very early days for adoption and diffusion as per past general-purpose technologies that have taken decades – approximately 80 years for electricity).

Now, in terms of the fast following versus innovation debate, it’s clear that fast following is much easier than pushing the frontier. It’s certainly the case that many of the improvements in OSAI are the result of genuinely brilliant advancements which achieve gains at high efficiency. Deepseek’s GRPO is a classic example, and it seems Kimi’s K3 has deployed similarly novel architectures through Stable LatentMoE. However, that these headlines focusing on ‘catching-up’ are so attention-grabbing proves the rule that OSAI has still never pushed the frontier on capabilities.

There are a number of factors that give fast following the edge. First, iterating on working formulas is much easier than pure innovation. Schumpeter also observed the same dynamic in capitalist economies: the pioneer's success is a signal that draws swarms of imitators to compete the profit away. Second, developers of frontier models also incur an additional release tax through the additional safety tests and high R&D costs of exploring paths in the frontier. Third, distillation, the extraction of model components by training on another model’s outputs, is reported to have aided many laggard developers – we explore this last point using available evidence in the next section.

The arms race: We shouldn’t expect this gap to remain stable, and it could easily grow further

The size of the gap between the best open and closed models is less important than whether it is growing or shrinking – measuring in ‘months behind’ obfuscates the capability dynamic. The most careful analysis of the gap found that it is growing over time. It was smallest just after the release of DeepSeek R1 in January 2025, and has grown since. Not every indicator agrees (UK AI Security Institute empirically measured a narrowing gap on cyber, although the results from the Kimi K3 update made somewhat different claims), and any of these series are noisy over such a short period of time. After all, we are only talking about, at most, three to four years. Any claims about the trend in the gap, therefore, should rely on structure: why might the fast-following strategy that produced the small gaps of the past years become harder, and how fragile will the supply of high-capability open models turn out to be.

Three factors may prove pivotal in the supply of high-capability open models: technical dynamics for fast-following, the economics of open sourcing AI, and securitisation.

To begin, we turn to an important technical tool for fast-following – distillation. This is a means of training new models to imitate the outputs of a stronger model, so that the student model inherits capabilities without repeating the full and expensive training process. Distillation on its own is a common exercise within labs to train their own models, particularly smaller versions which can then be hosted on more edge devices common in LMICs (this is a key adaptation pathway). The specific practice of extractive distillation, or illicit distillation, is what has been conjectured to be a key factor in fast following: the practice of training on a stronger model’s outputs without the approval of the original model’s developers, in order to ride the coattails of the frontier.

The practice of extractive distillation is apparently widespread, as can be inferred from its fingerprints. A statistical comparison of raw outputs across models placed Kimi K3's responses unusually close to Fable's. A simpler experiment is just asking the model for its name: both Kimi K2 and K3 call themselves Claude at rates far beyond chance. But in spite of its recent rise in prominence within the discourse on AI, there are reasons to believe that the potential of distillation may have already peaked.

First, the benefits of distillation are likely to fall. The method works by extracting what is visible in a model’s outputs, and a growing share of frontier capabilities are invisible through outputs only. The current frontier models are built on reinforcement learning within curated task environments, such as screen-recordings of developers or specialised sandboxes, and in proprietary post-training pipelines. While distilled models can imitate what better closed models say in the final output, they cannot imitate the environment they were trained in or the interim steps taken to generate that output. Apple's study of distillation scaling laws finds that imitating a model beats training from scratch only while the imitator model's compute budget is small – spend enough, and ordinary training overtakes it. Another condition is that the imitator model has to start from a capability base close enough to the model it’s trying to distil. If the imitator model is too far behind it stops benefiting from the teacher's strength at all. Distillation will likely remain an effective tool for building good, cheap models, but its strength fails as capabilities advance to accomplish more complex tasks, where less of the work is visible.

Second, AI labs are improving their defense against distillation. One of the more valuable inputs to distilled models were the reasoning traces, which show how a model is thinking about answering your prompt. Increasingly, labs are hiding these traces. Some labs have gone further, “poisoning” their models’ outputs when they suspect that it is being used for training outside models. Google, for example, says it "continuously detects, disrupts, and mitigates model extraction activity to protect proprietary logic and specialised training data, including with real-time proactive defenses that can degrade student model performance." These defenses are increasingly being layered on commercial and legal barriers, such as rate limits and contract terms. While none of these are decisive, there appears to be a defensive bias against distillation attacks.

Third, while distillation has been one of the most reliable tools for fast-following open models, it is not the only one. Large gains were made in 2024 by improvements in training techniques, such as DeepSeek’s reinforcement-learning innovations before R1 which we highlighted in the previous section. Such algorithmic improvements enable smaller companies to keep up with larger companies even as the cost of compute for a frontier model doubles every eight months. Eventually, however, capital constraints on these smaller companies will make it more and more difficult to keep up and innovate. Staying within touching distance of the frontier will increasingly involve paying escalating costs.

Partly because of this, there are very few companies releasing open models, and they are concentrated in China. The supply of frontier open models today comes entirely from a few Chinese firms – DeepSeek, Moonshot, Alibaba, https://t.co/GBdSBxHbvh – after Meta, the standard bearer for open weights, retreated. These companies release open models as part of a market-access strategy, seeking to gain global distribution, developer usage, and leverage against the American incumbents. This strategy may change at any time, and the economic conditions of Chinese AI labs could soon force a pivot away from open-weight releases: one analysis tabulated American AI firms raising 24x more equity funding than their Chinese lab rivals, and the gap in annualised rate of revenue for 2025 was even higher at over 50x.

Beyond economics, there are also signs of greater securitisation. In June 2026, the US government ordered Anthropic to suspend all foreign access to its newest model on national-security grounds. Although these restrictions were later lifted, it’s evidence that Washington is beginning to treat frontier models as securitisable assets. Soon after, Reuters reported that China's Ministry of Commerce had held talks with Alibaba, ByteDance and https://t.co/GBdSBxHbvh about restricting overseas access to their most advanced models, including open-weight releases and as yet unreleased models. This fits with a tiered logic already circulating in Chinese legal debate: basic tools released freely, frontier capability kept at home. Admittedly, this is hard to square with recent public announcements by Xi Jinping that have placed OSAI at the centre of China’s global AI strategy – these are uncertain times.

Another pressure that might constrain open source is on the safety side. Open weight models are far easier to misuse as their safeguards are more vulnerable to jailbreaks or fine-tuning, enabling bad actors to commit cyberattacks or assist in terrorist activity – misuse categories that would be monitored under API-based access. As OSAI increases in capability alongside the frontier, the capacity for harm through misuse goes up asymmetrically to the frontier given the lack of monitoring. As a result, proposals for pre-release capability review would bind open models far more tightly than closed ones, since a released weight file cannot be recalled. If implemented, this would create a release tax for open models which had historically enjoyed the opposite advantage to closed source models, and it was reported on August 13th that the US government would require such higher evaluations for more capable OSAI releases.

Finally, even if the gap between open and closed models does not increase, its effects will become more pronounced. The gap is conventionally quoted in months: how long ago the frontier matched what open models can just do today. As the speed of capabilities improvements increases, an unchanged lag of four to eight months between closed and open models represents a growing gap in capabilities, with no deterioration in the ability of fast-followers. If frontier AI companies succeed in speeding up their own research even more, through internal recursive self-improvement, the gap will increase even faster, while even less of it can be poached through distillation.

Many of the mechanisms above are uncertain. New distillation techniques may be discovered, governments may choose to support rather than oppose open models, scaling laws may slow down, or the Nvidia and Hugging Face consortium could herald a new era of OSAI. However, it is clear that the supply of near frontier-level open models is dependent on the continued strategic patience of a handful of firms in a single jurisdiction, whose government is actively debating whether that patience serves the national interest. This single point of failure may be sufficient to foreclose the hopes of many open model advocates for indefinite access to near-frontier capabilities that can power intelligence infrastructure. With such vulnerability, arguably the worst course of action for LMICs would be to pin all of their hopes on the high-risk prospects of OSAI remaining accessible and competitive on capabilities.

Facing these uncertainties, how can LMICs prepare for the future

Given the variety of possible futures on offer, it is tempting to conclude that no policy chosen today can be optimal across all of them. Perhaps the technical, economic, and security dynamics we have described will combine to sideline OSAI entirely. Or maybe a new distillation technique, or a change of heart in Beijing or Washington, will restore the fast-followers to touching distance. Our projection seems to introduce more uncertainties than we started with.

But there is another gap which overshadows this uncertainty for the future: the capability gap is measured in months, yet the policy response is measured in years. Everything an LMIC would need in any of these futures, whether its compute procurement, data infrastructure, technical teams capable of post-training and auditing a model, or the regulatory capacity to govern one, takes years to build and cannot be improvised on the day a given future arrives. A government that waits for the race to resolve will discover that the hard part is the capacity to act on that future.

The sound strategy is to identify no-regret investments: policies that pay off whether the gap widens, narrows, or holds. Even as the horse race keeps producing its 'moments', and the commentary keeps calling the gap. Our next post will take each scenario in turn as we assess which policies enacted today could survive different tomorrows.

Yeltsin was a terrible leader, but Russia’s disastrous state in the 1990s was the result of its own leadership and domestic policies, not the West. Closer alignment with Western democracies wouldn’t have hurt Russia.

And no, Russia didn’t preserve Artsakh. The geopolitical circumstances simply allowed Armenia to maintain it. If Azerbaijan had believed it could retake it earlier, it would have tried, and Russia wouldn’t have lifted a finger, just as it did nothing for Serbia in Kosovo or Bosnia.

Armenia isn’t ungrateful for refusing to maintain an alliance that no longer serves its interests. Russia abandoned Armenia when it needed support. Exploring relations with the West isn’t betrayal, it’s pursuing national interests.

By your logic, Serbia should be grateful to NATO simply because it wasn’t completely flattened and occupied during the Yugoslav wars. It should have accepted whatever terms Washington offered and considered itself lucky to have survived. Do you realise how absurd that sounds? The irony of a Serb making this argument is almost laughable if it wasn’t sad. Serbs probably understand better than most what it means to be politically isolated, abandoned by supposed allies and treated as a geopolitical inconvenience by greater powers. You, of all people, should understand why Armenia might want to pursue its own interests rather than blindly depend on Russia. 

But I suppose I understand. You don’t live in Serbia, so perhaps you’re somewhat removed from the reality of Serbian political isolation and the sentiment that has surrounded Serbian society for decades. Radovan Karadzic himself once remarked that the Serbs have only two friends: God and the Greeks. Perhaps it’s worth remembering why that sentiment exists before lecturing other nations about gratitude towards their supposed allies.

@atensnut see this is great repost 🇺🇸
On Jeopardy the other night, the final question asked: “How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb of the Unknown?”

All three contestants missed it.

Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

1. How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb and why?

He takes 21 steps — symbolizing the 21-gun salute, the highest military and foreign tribute.

2. How long does he pause before turning to walk back and why?

He waits 21 seconds, again in honor of the same tradition.

3. Why are his gloves damp?

They are lightly moistened to ensure he never loses his grip on his rifle.

4. Does he keep his rifle on the same shoulder, and if not, why?

He always carries it on the shoulder farthest from the Tomb. After each crossing, he performs an about-face and moves it to the outside shoulder.

5. How often are the guards changed?

Every 30 minutes, 24/7, 365 days a year.

6. What are the physical requirements for a Tomb Guard?

Applicants must be between 5'10" and 6'2" and have a waist no larger than 30".

Other expectations of the Guard:

They devote two years to the Tomb, live in the barracks beneath it, and must refrain from drinking alcohol on or off duty for the rest of their lives.

They can never swear in public or dishonor the uniform or the Tomb.

After two years, they earn a wreath pin signifying their service — fewer than 400 are currently worn.

If they violate the code, they must relinquish the pin.

Their shoes have thick soles to protect against extreme temperatures and metal heel plates that create the crisp click when they halt.

Uniforms must have zero wrinkles or lint and are inspected in a full-length mirror.

For the first six months, guards do not speak to anyone and do not watch television.

Their off-duty time is spent studying the 175 notable individuals buried at Arlington National Cemetery, memorizing who they are and where they rest.

Among them: President Taft, Joe E. Lewis, and Audie Murphy, the most decorated WWII soldier.

Every guard spends five hours daily preparing their uniform.

ETERNAL REST GRANT THEM, O LORD, AND LET PERPETUAL LIGHT SHINE UPON THEM.

When Hurricane Isabel approached Washington, D.C. in 2003, Congress shut down for two days. The guards were offered permission to suspend duty due to danger.

They replied: “No way, Sir!”

Drenched and marching through the storm, they insisted that guarding the Tomb is the highest honor, not just a task.

The Tomb has been continuously guarded — day and night — since 1930.

God Bless and Keep Them

I don’t often encourage sharing posts, but I would be honored if this one reached as many people as possible. We should always feel proud of the men and women who serve, wherever they are stationed.

text:
The students stared at her. Several exchanged uncertain glances, while others remained openly suspicious. Neville, who had endured her insults for years, seemed particularly taken aback. Whatever they had expected from Draceana Malfoy, it certainly wasn't an apology, much less one delivered with her head bowed before the people she had once considered beneath her.
"I don't care if you believe me or not," she continued, "but we genuinely didn't know there was a resistance here. Our mission came directly from Professor Dumbledore, and we have to finish it before anything else. Harry can't afford to waste any more time."
Her voice remained steady, although the hand resting against her stomach had tightened against the fabric of her clothes.
"So please, I'm begging you. Listen to what Harry has to say. He needs your strength. Please, help him."
Draceana remained bowed after finishing, her platinum-blonde hair falling forward to conceal her face.
For a moment, the Room of Requirement fell silent. The students looked at one another, uncertain how to respond.
Harry was the first to move. He couldn't help smiling as he approached Draceana, feeling a quiet pride in how far she had come. He knew she wasn't particularly good at admitting she was wrong, much less apologizing to an entire room of people who had every reason to despise her. Yet she had done it, and without asking for anything in return.
He gently took her hand, prompting Draceana to straighten. She looked up at him in surprise, but Harry merely gave her fingers a reassuring squeeze and remained beside her.
Neville watched them for a moment. His expression was difficult to read, particularly when his eyes settled on their joined hands.
"You're sure about her, Harry?"
"Yeah," Harry answered without hesitation. "I trust her."
"She's helped us, Neville. More than once," Hermione added.
"Yeah," Ron agreed. "Believe me, I never thought I'd be saying that about Malfoy."
Neville looked between the three of them. If Harry alone had defended Malfoy, he might have suspected there was something else going on. But Ron and Hermione agreeing with him? That was considerably harder to dismiss. It still didn't make Neville any more comfortable with the girl standing beside Harry, though.
Harry seemed to understand his hesitation. "Look, I'm sorry too. I had no idea how bad things had become here, or how hard you've all been fighting. But everything Draceana said is true. Dumbledore left us an important mission, and we've got to finish it first." He glanced around at the others. "I promise I'll help you fight back. I will. Just give us a chance to do what we came here for."
Neville considered his words before giving a reluctant nod. "All right, Harry. If you trust her, that's good enough for me. For now."
Seamus still looked unconvinced, and a few students began whispering again. Neville's willingness to trust Harry had settled the matter for him, but it was clear that not everyone was prepared to follow so readily.
Ginny, meanwhile, had yet to say another word.
She had expected Malfoy to answer her accusations with something spiteful, perhaps even try to turn the blame upon everyone else. An apology had been the last thing on her mind. For a moment, she had almost forgotten what she intended to say next, and she was still rather irritated with herself for it.
But surprise was hardly the same as forgiveness.
She looked at Harry, who was standing beside Draceana with an expression of unmistakable affection. Ron and Hermione had spoken up for her too, which was perhaps even more astonishing. Ginny couldn't begin to imagine what had happened during their absence to bring about such an unlikely arrangement, but she knew all three well enough to recognize that they weren't being foolish.
Still, she found herself looking at Draceana once more. The girl had finally straightened, although the reddened mark on her cheek remained plainly visible. Ginny felt a brief, uncomfortable twinge at the sight before firmly putting it aside.
Honestly, Malfoy. Of all the times to choose to grow a conscience.
Her gaze returned to the students. She recognized their expressions well enough. They were angry, suspicious, and frightened of what might happen if they trusted the wrong person. After everything the Carrows had done, Ginny could hardly blame them.
But none of that changed the reason they had gathered here in the first place.
"Oh, for goodness' sake," she said, stepping forward. "Nobody's asking you to like Malfoy. I certainly don't."
Draceana glanced at her, evidently surprised by the interruption.
"But Voldemort's still out there, isn't he?" Ginny continued, looking around at the others. "And Harry's come back because Dumbledore left him something important to do. We can settle our differences with Malfoy later. Right now, Harry needs our help, so can we please stop arguing about her and get on with it?"
Seamus opened his mouth, apparently ready to object, but stopped when Neville gave him a small nod. Ginny and Neville had spent much of the year helping keep Dumbledore's Army together, and the other students had learned to rely upon their judgment. There were still doubtful faces among the crowd, but the argument had finally begun to lose its urgency.
Draceana watched Ginny with a faint frown. She hadn't expected any kindness from the younger Weasley, and Ginny certainly hadn't offered her any. Nevertheless, she had just told the very people who despised Malfoy to put aside their grievances and help Harry.
Perhaps that was enough.
"Of course, Harry. What do you need from us?"
Luna Lovegood smiled pleasantly at him, apparently satisfied that the matter had been settled. Her easy acceptance drew a few uncertain looks from the students nearby, but Luna seemed entirely untroubled by them.
"Draceana won't bite, you know," she added, looking toward Neville with the same serene expression. "She's actually quite nice. And Harry's Harry. Everyone knows that, don't they?"
Neville gave a small, helpless shrug. He plainly didn't share Luna's opinion of Malfoy, but he had already given Harry his answer.
Ginny turned toward Harry. "Well? What do you need us to do?"
Harry looked around the room. Several students still regarded Draceana with suspicion, but nobody was demanding that she leave anymore. For the first time since his arrival, he could finally speak without being interrupted.
"If you've come back to Hogwarts," Ginny added, "whatever Dumbledore left you to do must be important enough to help end this war. Isn't that right, Harry?"
"Er... uh, yes," Harry answered, caught slightly off guard by her confidence in him.
A sharp jab to his ribs made Harry flinch. He turned to find Draceana withdrawing her elbow, her lips pressed into a thin line as she glanced from Ginny back to him. When their eyes met, she gave him a pointed look before turning away, though her hand remained firmly clasped in his.
Ginny noticed the exchange between Harry and Draceana but chose not to comment. Instead, she folded her arms and regarded Harry with the same determined expression she had worn throughout their conversation. "I'm still expecting answers when this is all over, Harry." Her gaze shifted toward Draceana. "From you too, Malfoy."
"Whatever, Weasley," Draceana replied, turning her head away. Yet despite the dismissive words, a faint smile tugged at the corner of her mouth. Ginny noticed it, and for the briefest moment, their eyes met. Neither said anything further.
"Now then, Harry," Luna asked pleasantly, apparently satisfied that the argument was over. "What exactly do you need our help with?"
Harry took a moment to consider his answer. He was grateful that everyone had finally agreed to listen, although that presented another difficulty: how much could he actually tell them? The Horcruxes were still a secret, and explaining why Voldemort might have hidden one inside Hogwarts would raise far more questions than he could afford to answer. Still, he needed a starting point, and the students who had spent the past year living in the castle might know something he didn't.
"I'm looking for something that belonged to Rowena Ravenclaw," he began, watching the faces around him. "Something valuable, very old, and unique to her. Something she might have been famous for."
"Oh, that's easy," Luna replied almost immediately, as though Harry had asked her something ordinary. "You must be looking for the diadem of Rowena Ravenclaw."
Harry stared at her. He had expected the Ravenclaws to suggest several possibilities, perhaps even argue over obscure pieces of their founder's history, but Luna had produced an answer before he had finished gathering his thoughts. For the first time since arriving in the Room of Requirement, he felt that they might actually be getting somewhere.
Unfortunately, the Ravenclaw students standing nearby were considerably less enthusiastic.
"Luna, the diadem's been lost for centuries," Cho Chang pointed out, stepping forward. Her expression was apologetic, as though she regretted having to dampen Harry's sudden optimism.
"Lost?" Ron repeated, looking thoroughly dismayed.
"Nobody knows what happened to it," another Ravenclaw explained. "Some people aren't even sure it really existed. It's more of a legend than anything else."
Harry frowned. It can't be lost. Not if Voldemort brought it here. He had seen Hogwarts through Voldemort's eyes, and everything pointed toward another Horcrux being hidden somewhere inside the castle. The thought that the object might have disappeared centuries ago was impossible to reconcile with what he knew. Perhaps nobody had recognized the diadem for what it was. After all, if Voldemort had gone to such lengths to conceal it, he certainly wouldn't have left it somewhere obvious.
"Isn't there anything we can use?" Harry asked, unwilling to let the matter end there. "A picture, a description, some sort of clue? We don't necessarily need to know where it went. We just need to know what we're looking for."
"Well, there's a statue of Rowena Ravenclaw in our common room," Cho offered after a moment's thought. "She's wearing a replica of the diadem. It won't tell you where the real one is, but at least you'll know what it looks like."
That was enough for Harry. He couldn't afford to waste time searching blindly, and even a replica might help him recognize the genuine article. Turning toward Cho, he asked, "Can you take me there?"
"No, definitely not her!"
The objection came from two voices at precisely the same moment.
Harry blinked, looking first at Ginny and then at Draceana. Of all the people he had expected to disagree about something, those two had been near the top of the list. Yet here they were, apparently united in their objection to Cho Chang.
Ginny and Draceana exchanged startled glances of their own. The moment of agreement seemed to surprise them just as much as it had surprised Harry, although neither appeared particularly inclined to reconsider.
"Lovegood, you take him," Draceana said, turning toward the Ravenclaw beside her before Harry could protest.
"Yes, Luna would be much better," Ginny agreed at once, nodding with rather unnecessary enthusiasm. "Wouldn't you, Luna?"
Luna looked from Ginny to Draceana, then toward Cho, who appeared equally confused by the sudden change of arrangements. Whatever had prompted the objection seemed to have escaped Luna entirely.
"I don't quite understand," she admitted, "but all right. I can take Harry."
Harry glanced between Ginny and Draceana once more. Neither looked interested in explaining herself, and he had the distinct impression that asking would only lead to another argument. Considering how much time they had already lost, he decided it was probably wiser to accept Luna's offer and leave the matter alone.
"Oi, mate. Can we have a moment?"
Ron had stepped closer, interrupting the discussion with a gesture toward a quieter corner of the room. Hermione stood beside him, looking as though she had something equally important to say.
Harry glanced toward Luna. "Just a minute."
He followed his friends away from the gathering, but before they had gone far, Hermione turned and beckoned toward Draceana.
"You too, Malfoy."
Draceana raised an eyebrow at the invitation, but followed without argument. She could still feel several pairs of eyes upon her as she crossed the room. Apparently, being allowed to stay was not quite the same as being welcomed, though she could hardly expect otherwise.
The four gathered near the wall, keeping their voices low enough to avoid being overheard. This did not stop Fred and George from taking an immediate interest in the private conversation. The twins exchanged curious looks and began edging closer, only for Ginny to intercept them with a warning glare. Whatever protests they might have had, they evidently decided that irritating their younger sister was best left for another occasion.
"What is it, Ron?" Harry asked.
"The cup, mate," Ron replied. "Surely you haven't forgotten about that?"
"Of course I haven't." Harry reached into his belongings and produced the golden cup they had taken from Gringotts. "We've still got to find the diadem, though."
"And we still need to get the fangs," Hermione reminded him. "There's no point carrying the cup around forever if we can't destroy it."
"Then what do you suggest, Granger?" Draceana asked.
"We split up," Ron answered before Hermione could reply. "One team goes down to the Chamber for a fang, and the other goes with Luna to investigate Ravenclaw Tower."
Harry considered the suggestion. It would certainly save time, but splitting up meant travelling through a castle occupied by Death Eaters. They had barely managed to reach the Room of Requirement without attracting attention.
"Hold on." He glanced toward Neville, who was speaking with several students nearby. "Neville! How many Death Eaters are in Hogwarts at the moment?"
"Three, Harry," Neville called back. "Snape and the two Carrows."
"Thanks, Neville."
Three. Harry had expected more, although the thought of running into Snape was unpleasant enough without considering the Carrows. He turned back toward the others, lowering his voice once more.
"Well, there's that. And we've only got one Invisibility Cloak."
"Which isn't exactly ideal for moving around in a group," Hermione added. "We learned that much at Gringotts."
"Exactly why we need to split up," Ron replied, evidently encouraged that Hermione had understood his reasoning. "Hermione and I can deal with the cup, while you and Malfoy go after the diadem."
He reached over and took the golden cup from Harry's hand.
Harry, Hermione, and Draceana stared at him.
"Ron," Hermione began slowly, "do you know Parseltongue?"
"No, but I've heard Harry speak it in his sleep. And I heard him use it to open the locket."
"Bloody idiot," Draceana muttered.
"Parseltongue is a magical language, Ron," Hermione explained, already sounding exasperated. "You can't simply imitate a few sounds and expect it to work."
"Well, how do you know it won't?" Ron protested. "I heard him clearly enough!"
"That isn't the point!"
"Then what do you suggest we do?"
Ron and Hermione immediately began arguing, the former insisting that his imitation would be convincing enough while the latter questioned whether he even remembered the sounds correctly. Harry opened his mouth to intervene, but a gentle squeeze around his hand stopped him.
"Harry, go with them," Draceana said.
He turned toward her. "And you?"
"I'll go with Lovegood." Her eyes flickered toward Ron, who was still trying to defend his rather questionable plan. "It's certainly better than letting that idiot Weasley stand outside the Chamber hissing at a wall."
Harry almost smiled. He couldn't deny that she had a point, but the thought of separating from her was another matter entirely. He had expected them to search for the diadem together, and although Neville had reported only three Death Eaters, that hardly made the castle safe.
Draceana met his gaze, apparently recognizing his reluctance. Her fingers trembled ever so slightly in his, though she maintained her usual composure. She wasn't particularly eager to part ways either, but they both knew Harry was the only one who could reliably open the Chamber of Secrets.
He trusted her ability to look after herself. That had never been the problem. Yet after everything they had survived together, he had grown accustomed to keeping her close, and the thought of letting her venture through Hogwarts without him was unexpectedly difficult.
After a moment, Harry nodded. "All right. You're right."
He reached into his belongings and drew out his Invisibility Cloak, offering it to her.
"Take this. You'll need it."
Draceana looked down at the familiar silvery fabric. She knew how valuable the cloak was to Harry, particularly now that they were moving through a castle controlled by their enemies.
"Are you certain?"
"Yeah. Ravenclaw Tower's a fair distance from here, and you and Luna will have more of the castle to cross. Ron, Hermione, and I should be able to find a quieter route down to the Chamber."
Draceana accepted the cloak, carefully folding it over her arm. "Thank you."
For a moment, she remained beside him, reluctant to release his hand despite having been the one to suggest separating. At last, she gave his fingers one final squeeze.
"Be safe, Potter."
"You too."
A pointed cough interrupted them.
"We're still here, mate," Ron reminded him.
Harry turned toward his best friend. "Oh, right. Nearly forgot about your big mouth, Ron."
"Very funny."
Hermione shook her head at the two boys before turning toward Draceana. "Then it's settled. Harry will come with us, and you'll go with Luna." She hesitated briefly, as though the next words still felt somewhat unfamiliar. "I can't believe I'm saying this, but... good luck, Malfoy."
Draceana looked at her in surprise. Not so long ago, receiving such a remark from Hermione Granger would have been unthinkable, much less returning it sincerely. But they had come a long way since then, and for once, she found no reason to hide behind an insult.
"You too, Granger."
Hermione returned the small nod, and neither felt the need to elaborate.
"Lovegood!" Draceana called, turning toward the waiting students. "Come here, will you?"
Luna approached at her usual unhurried pace, seemingly undisturbed by the urgency surrounding the others.
"Yes, Draceana?"
"We're going to Ravenclaw Tower. You're taking me there."
"Oh, lovely," Luna replied with a smile.
Draceana was about to turn away when she remembered something. Looking back toward Harry, she reached for the wand she had been carrying.
"Harry. The wand."
She held it out to him, intending to giving it before they separated. Harry, however, shook his head.
"Keep it for now. You might need it more than me."
Draceana hesitated. He had already given her the Invisibility Cloak, and now he was insisting that she keep the wand as well. She looked at him for another moment, then nodded and tucked it away.
Harry turned toward the students gathered inside the Room of Requirement. Most were watching them with varying degrees of curiosity and concern, having heard little of the conversation that had taken place in the corner.
"Everyone, we'll be back in a jiffy!" he announced.
With that, Harry hurried toward the door with Ron and Hermione, while Draceana and Luna followed close behind. The four exchanged a final glance before heading off toward their respective destinations.
The remaining students watched in bewilderment as the two groups disappeared into the castle. They had understood that Harry was in a hurry, but none had expected him to leave quite so abruptly, without so much as an instruction about what they should do next.
Neville and Seamus exchanged uncertain glances. A few students continued staring at the door through which Harry had vanished, while others looked toward Ginny, apparently hoping she might have some idea what Harry expected of them.
For several moments, nobody seemed quite sure whether they were supposed to follow or stay where they were.
The Room of Requirement, so full of noise and anticipation only minutes earlier, was left in an awkward silence.
******
The corridors of Hogwarts had grown unusually quiet by the time Draceana and Luna made their way toward Ravenclaw Tower. Hidden beneath Harry's Invisibility Cloak, the two girls proceeded cautiously, moving quickly through the deserted stretches of the castle while slowing whenever distant footsteps or voices threatened to betray someone's approach.
It didn't help that sharing an Invisibility Cloak with Luna Lovegood was proving to be an experience of its own.
"I swear, it stinks in here," Draceana whispered, wrinkling her nose as she adjusted the silvery fabric over her head. "When was the last time that bloody Potter washed this thing? Honestly, once all this is over, I'm going to make him give it a proper scrub."
Luna giggled softly beside her. "You've changed, Draceana."
Draceana glanced sideways at the Ravenclaw, although there was little she could see of her beneath the cloak. "You've already told me that, Lovegood. At Shell Cottage, remember?"
"You can call me Luna, you know."
"I will not. And you still haven't explained yourself."
"Oh, I said that because you've changed again."
Draceana frowned. She had never quite understood how Luna Lovegood's mind worked, and the girl's cheerful insistence was beginning to test her patience. "In what way, exactly? And what makes you such an expert on me?"
"Well, you apologized."
"People apologize all the time, Lovegood. It's hardly an extraordinary achievement."
"Not you, though," Luna replied matter-of-factly.
Draceana opened her mouth, then closed it again. As irritating as the observation was, she couldn't exactly argue with it.
"And you looked as though you were having fun with Ron and Hermione," Luna continued. "Not just Harry."
"I most certainly was not."
"Oh, I think you were. You even seem quite comfortable arguing with them now."
"Lovegood, I have been arguing with those two since our first year. That hardly makes us friends."
Luna appeared to give this some thought as they rounded another corner. "Perhaps. But it feels different now."
Draceana rolled her eyes, though Luna was unlikely to see it. She had no intention of discussing her relationship with the other two Gryffindors, particularly with someone who seemed capable of drawing the most ridiculous conclusions from perfectly ordinary conversations.
"And there's something else," Luna added.
"Oh, Merlin. What now?"
"Whenever you're with Harry, you sometimes look as though you've gone somewhere else entirely. Almost like you've wandered into a little world of your own, even when everyone else is still there."
Draceana nearly missed a step.
"What on earth are you talking about?" she whispered sharply, feeling warmth creep into her cheeks. "Honestly, Lovegood, I haven't the faintest idea where you get these things."
Luna merely smiled.
"I really don't understand you, Luna," Draceana complained.
"Thank you."
"That wasn't a compliment!"
Draceana stopped herself.
Luna's smile widened beneath the cloak. "Oh, and you called me Luna."
Draceana stared at her, momentarily at a loss for words. How had she managed that? She had been quite determined not to give the Ravenclaw the satisfaction, yet somehow the name had slipped out without her noticing.
"Shut up."
Luna giggled again, apparently taking the response in good humour.

Strict Fast today, no meat, dairy & eggs, no fish, no oil, no wine.

Martyr Menas of Egypt
Commemorated on November 11

The Holy Great Martyr Menas (Mēnás), an Egyptian by birth, was a military officer and served in the Kotyaeion region of Phrygia under the centurion Firmilian during the reign of Emperors Diocletian (284-305) and Maximian (305-311). He was praised and admired for his bravery in battle, his patience, and his self-discipline.

In 298, the Emperors published an edict ordering everyone to worship the idols. Those serving in the Legions were ordered to capture and persecute Christians. As soon as Saint Menas heard this impious decree he threw down his soldier’s belt (a sign of military rank) and withdrew to a mountain above Kotyaeion, where he lived an ascetical life of fasting and prayer. He spent a long time in the wilderness, suffering great privation and laboring in feats of prayer, fasting, and nocturnal vigils. Thus, the Saint purified himself of every passion of soul and body.

When his heart was strengthened with godly zeal, and his soul aflame with love for God, divine grace came upon him and he had a vision. He regarded this as a sign that he was to follow the path of martyrdom. Therefore, he left the mountain and went into the city, where the people were celebrating a pagan festival.

At that time, Saint Menas was approximately fifty years old. Standing in the midst of the crowd, he shouted: "There is only one true God, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Your "gods" are demons, and your idols have been fashioned by craftsmen. These inanimate objects are nothing but metal, wood, and stone."

Those who heard his voice left their dancing and their games and went to see who had disrupted their idolatrous festival, marveling at his boldness. They seized and beat him, then brought him before Pyrrhus, the City Prefect. When he saw Menas he asked him who he was, and why he was creating a disturbance. The Saint replied, "I am an Egyptian, a servant of Jesus Christ, the Ruler of all things. I was a soldier and I served in the Imperial Army for most of my life. But since the Emperor has chosen to follow the path of idolatry, and to persecute Christians, I chose to dwell with the wild animals in the wilderness rather than obey the impious commands of those who do not know God."

When the Prefect heard this he became enraged and had the Saint thrown into prison.

The next morning, Pyrrhus urged Saint Menas to return to the Army, offering to restore his former rank if he would offer sacrifice to the pagan "gods." Menas refused, and so he was subjected to many cruel tortures. The Prefect urged him to submit to the edict and offer sacrifice to the idols, but the Martyr remained firm in his Faith, saying that he would never deny Christ. Pyrrhus ordered further torments, but seeing that he could not persuade Saint Menas, he ordered that he be taken outside the city and beheaded. As he was being led to the place of execution, he asked his friends (who were secret Christians) to take his body back to Egypt for burial when the persecution had ceased. These friends gathered Martyr’s relics at night and hid them until the persecution was over. Later, they were brought to Egypt and placed in a church dedicated to Saint Menas southwest of Alexandria.

Saint Menas received the crown of martyrdom in the year 304. By God's grace he continues to work miracles for those who entreat him with faith and love. He is known for healing various illnesses, delivering people from demonic possession, and is a protector, especially during times of war.

In 1942, General Erwin Rommel had conquered almost all of North Africa, and was heading toward Alexandria. The Nazis had reached El Alamein,1  where they camped for the night, intending to attack Alexandria in the morning. Saint Menas, however, did not allow this to happen. At midnight (October 23-24), certain people noticed Saint Menas coming out of his ancient church leading camels into the German camp. Overcome by panic, weakness, and confusion, Rommel's troops fled. The battle ended on November 4th with the enemy in full retreat. It is regarded as a turning point in the whole war. Later, Winston Churchill said: "Before Alamein we never had a victory. After Alamein we never had a defeat."

The Allies offered that place to Patriarch Christophoros of Alexandria so that the church of Saint Menas could be rebuilt.

We pray to Saint Menas to ask for his help in finding lost objects.
