text:
This being Veterans Day, I thought I’d reissue this. This New Internet Thing isn’t a WW II book, but it does begin with Len, a member of the Greatest Generation, recounting his and his brother’s experiences in the war. It jumps forward to 1992 when Len discovers the online world!

Many men and women served without holding a gun. Len’s brother joined the Merchant Marine, carrying supplies to Russia, and the merchant sailors actually sustained greater casualties (1 in 26 were killed) than any other service. Len himself kept the industrial machine running back home, which is the real reason the Allies won. Many, or even most of the men & women who wore the uniform never fired a gun or had one fired at them, but every one sacrificed for our country.

I wrote a book (This New Internet Thing). The publication date was May 29, 2024 (if you’d rather not deal with Amazon, your bookstore can also order it from the distributor Ingram Spark, or print-on-demand if they have the equipment). The first chapter deals directly with the reason we celebrate Memorial Day: to honor those people who fought and died for us. Len Saunders, our main character, gets to recount the story of his brother Jack, who made the ultimate sacrifice. After you read this, watch Action in the North Atlantic, about the Merchant Marine sailors who braved German U-Boats like Jack did, to bring desperately-needed supplies to the Soviets.

This isn’t really a WW II book, but we do hear later how Len, a 17-year old boy, made his way to New York City by himself to find out what happened to his brother.

The story of Albert Kahn, the American architect who built the Stalingrad tractor factory, where some of the most bitter fighting happened, is all true. It’s hard to believe that the US actually cooperated with the Stalin regime and helped them industrialize.

================ Souvenirs =============

It was spring, 1992. Len was finally ready to get out of the frigid Midwest and move to California. His old friend Stan down the street had sold his house and moved to Miami with his son, leaving his (apparently) estranged wife behind, and that was the last straw for Len. That, plus the fact that the lawn mowing service raised its prices yet again, and there were rumors of another property tax increase in Bloomfield Hills. He was finally sick of it. He figured no one was going to buy a house in the winter, so he might as well dump it while the weather was good and the kids would be out of school soon.

Len was 67. He’d retired from Chrysler almost two years ago, and hadn’t really latched onto anything in his retirement that grabbed him. Detroit was going down the toilet and had been for 30 years, and no one was doing anything to stop it. His daughter Janet was making it big in Silicon Valley, he was divorced, and she was his only kid. Her new husband Walt had offered to let him live on his property in the Sierra. He could fish every day, go for hikes and have a dog to hike with him, and best of all, see her and Walt all the time! In fact, he’d already tried living there for a couple weeks and he loved it.

Janet was ecstatic, and also relieved. Now she wouldn’t have to worry about him taking care of that gigantic house and going up the stairs in his old age, and he’d be only three hours away. Walt started the process of getting permits for the father-in-law house he, Len, and Janet were going to build for him.

Len had a giant garage sale one Saturday, and everyone in the neighborhood knew that meant yet another long-time Detroiter was leaving. Pretty soon there’d be no one left that they knew anymore. This whole corner of Michigan was a one-industry town, and now that autos were a dying industry, everyone was bailing. No one’s kids wanted to live here after they finished college. They moved to Chicago, or New York, or California, and the parents moved to Florida. 

Jamie, a 16-year-old kid from the next block, came over and shook hands with him. He called him “Mr. Saunders” and said he was going to be studying World War II in his history class next year, and his father told him Len had some stories he really should hear. Len was busy dealing with buyers and told him to come back towards the end of the day when things quieted down. 

Around 3:30 Jamie came back with his dad. Len had gotten a couple lawn chairs and invited them to sit down.

Jamie’s dad Harry was someone Len had helped out on some project or other many years ago. He didn’t even remember what he’d told Harry about his time in the war, but apparently Harry did.

“So Jamie, you wanted to hear about the Big War, huh? Well, I’ll tell you what I can. I’m afraid I didn’t have a very exciting war, unlike your dad here!”

Harry smiled self-deprecatingly. “He’s sick of all my war stories!”

Jamie looked embarrassed. “You always tell the same ones, Dad! I bet there’s a lot more you haven’t told us yet!”

“You’re too young for those!” said Harry.

“Anyway, Jamie, your dad is probably remembering my older brother Jack’s experiences more than mine.”

“ ‘Jack’, that’s the name I couldn’t remember. This is important, Jamie. Listen up! I’ve forgotten most of this myself.”

Len grabbed a can of Bud out of his cooler and passed one to Harry. He gave Jamie a Coke. This was going to be a long story.

“So, does the name ‘Albert Kahn’ ring any bells for you, Jamie?” He shook his head.

“Well, Albert Kahn was the most famous architect in Detroit, or maybe in the whole country or even the world, if you just look at industrial buildings. He built the River Rouge plant for Ford, and almost all the car factories in Detroit, including Chrysler’s where I worked.”

“OK..” said Jamie, not sure where this was going.

“In the late 20’s, the new Communist government in Russia needed to build factories fast, but they didn’t know how. Who do you think they turned to?”

“Let me guess: Albert Kahn?”

“You’ve raised a smart boy here, Harry. Right, Albert Kahn. Now, does the name ‘Stalingrad’ mean anything to you?”

“I think we get to that second semester. Wasn’t there a big battle there or something?”

“A big battle!” laughed Len. “Yeah, I’d say it was a big battle. But we’re getting ahead of ourselves here.”

“One of the things that Kahn’s company built was a big tractor factory in Stalingrad, in about 1930.”

Harry interjected, “That’s the part that blows my mind. Americans helping the Communists! And you said Henry Ford was behind it, too, right?”

“Yeah, the Commies weren’t the bad guys yet. They even sent some of their engineers over to Detroit!”

Harry just shook his head. “Pay attention here, Jamie.”

Len continued, “I was only five when the deal first started, but Jack was eighteen, and he got a job with the Kahn company.”

“OK.”

“They sent him to Russia to work on the Stalingrad tractor factory. He was gone for over a year, and when he came back he didn’t want to talk about it much, or even tell us where he went.”

“How come?”

“Well, I guess the Russians were pretty secretive even then. You could be shot if you talked too much. Over time that attitude seeps into you.”

“Wow. Did he ever tell you any more?”

“Yeah, over time I managed to worm it out of him. He was pretty proud of that gigantic factory! He said he learned more from the Americans than the Russians, though.”

“Oh, yeah? Why’s that?”

“Well, he said the Russians had studied and memorized and always wanted to do everything exactly the way the books said. The Americans were more seat-of-the-pants, practical guys. They always used to argue with the Russians about that. I’m like Jack. He taught me everything I know about mechanics.”

Len continued, “So of course we got into the war in December 1941. I was too young to go, and Jack was too old, at least at first. Later on, the draft board got more desperate.”

Jamie was looking impatient. “So if Jack was too old, how is this about him?”

Harry said, “Be patient, boy. He’s getting there.”

“We were both sitting around at home while all the other guys were going off to war. You might not get to study this part, but the war was not going well for us at all in 1942. It was torture for Jack and me not to be part of it. At least I knew I could join up when I turned 18.”

“Are we almost to the good part?” Harry elbowed him hard.

“So they had the battle of Stalingrad, the Germans and the Russians, in late 1942, and Jack was obsessed with it. They were actually fighting in his factory! He knew every inch of it. It killed him that they were destroying it.”

“And so…?” prompted Jamie.

“And so he got it in his head that he wanted to go over there and help out! That was all he talked about.”

Harry interrupted. “That’s the part that gets me: actually wanting to be part of that meat grinder! If they even let him near it.”

“That’s what everyone told him. My parents, the guys at Kahn, everyone. But he wouldn’t listen. One day in October he disappeared.”

“So did he get to Stalingrad?”

Len looked like he’d just pulled a shade down over his eyes. His words came more slowly.

“We never saw him again. That was the worst thing for me and my parents.”

“Did you ever find out what happened?”

Len took even longer to answer.

“I finally couldn’t stand it. I figured I had maybe six months until my 18th birthday when I’d get drafted, and I was going to use the time to find out.”

“So what’d you do?”

“Well… I knew he couldn’t fly to Russia, so he must have taken a ship. I went to New York, and started asking around. Long story short, I ended up at the Merchant Marine hiring office. And they had his records!”

Jamie interrupted him. “Excuse me, Mr. Saunders, back up: you went to New York, by yourself?”

“Yep, I sure did.”

“How did you get by there?”

“Oh, it wasn’t that hard. All the men were off fighting the war, so there was lots of work.”

Jamie was seriously impressed. Len was on a roll. He thought maybe he had a reference Jamie would get:

“Hey, have you heard of that new Disney movie, ‘Newsies’?”

Jamie had. “Yeah, it’s kind of a flop, though, isn’t it?”

“I guess so. Anyhow, it’s about a newsboys strike in 1899, long before I went there, but selling papers on the streets was one of the things I did to make money.”

Jamie hadn’t seen the movie, so he let that pass.

“Anyhow: what’s ‘Merchant Marine’?”

“That’s the civilians who sail the cargo ships. Jack signed on to one of those ships headed for Russia.”

Jamie just waited for the rest of the story.

“Well, maybe you’ve heard of the U-Boats? Those were German submarines who hunted cargo ships like Jack’s.”

“Like in the movie Das Boot?”

Harry elbowed him again.

“Just like that movie, Jamie. Jack’s ship went down. Some survivors were rescued, but not Jack.”

Jamie didn’t know what to say, but this time he had more restraint and just waited.

“I figured maybe I could find some of his shipmates, so I hung around New York a few more months.”

“And did you find any?”

“I did. They all told me Jack was a great guy, did his job well, never fought with anyone. He really wanted to jump ship in Murmansk and get to Stalingrad, and they always told him he was nuts. He thought he could just go to the train station and buy a ticket!”

Len was tearing up, but he wiped his eyes and continued.

“I knew Mom and Dad would want to hear any little details about him, so I kept pressing. Finally, one of them, ‘Tom,’ I think his name was, told me a story that I can still remember word for word. I don’t even know if it was all true or not, but I knew my folks would want to hear it that way.”

“One night they were playing poker. Jack was losing, but he never complained. Suddenly the ship just exploded when the torpedo hit. It caught fire right away, the sirens sounded, the loudspeaker told them to abandon ship, and they all ran for the lifeboats.”

“All of them but Jack got into a boat. Someone noticed he was missing and ran back to look for him. There were flames and oily smoke everywhere.”

Harry and Jamie were transfixed.

“He came back dragging Jack. Apparently he’d tried to go down below to look for anyone who was trapped, and the fire and smoke just got him.”

“Was he still alive?”

Len just shook his head. “He wasn’t sure, but the other guys could tell he was dead. They put him in the lifeboat anyway so he could have a proper burial.”

“At that point, Tom put his hand on my arm, and said, ‘Your brother was a hero, Len.’ We were both crying.”

Harry wanted to pause for a few minutes, but Jamie was dying to hear the rest of the story.

“So they all got rescued?”

“Yeah, it was freezing cold, but they survived. Not Jack, of course.”

Jamie didn’t know what to say. Finally, “Thanks, Mr. Saunders.”

Len wiped his eyes again and said, “Well, Jamie, war’s not like in the movies. The rescue ship didn’t have facilities to keep dead bodies, so they gave him a burial at sea. Tom and all the other guys in the lifeboat stood next to the body as the chaplain read the service and they slid him over the side.”

“When I got back home, my own draft notice was waiting for me.”

Harry put a hand on Len’s arm. “That’s enough for today, Len. Jamie, I guess you’ve got a good story to tell your history class next year!” 

Harry shook Len’s hand. “Len, if I don’t see you again before you move…”

Len said, “Yeah, good luck to you too, Harry. And especially you, Jamie!”

Jamie shook his hand. “Thanks again, Mr. Saunders! Good luck in California.”

The crowds were all gone, and Len figured that was it. He’d have to take the rest of the stuff to the dump. Janet’s old Schwinn — he couldn’t imagine anyone wanted that heavy old thing, but someone gave him $10 for it. Some of the stuff had belonged to Betty, but if she hadn’t asked for it in the twenty or so years since the divorce, well, too late now.

He thought, “I’ve gotta tell Janet about that bike!” and called her. She couldn’t believe anyone wanted her old bike. Then he told her about the conversation with Jamie and Harry:

“Hey, you remember the story about your Uncle Jack?”

“Vaguely. Wasn’t he killed in the war?”

“More or less. He was on a cargo ship that got sunk by a U-Boat.”

“Oh yeah, now I remember. Why, what happened?”

He told her about how Jamie came over to hear his old war stories. She said,

“But you didn’t even leave the States!”

“Shhh! He didn’t get time to ask about that!”

She laughed, “What did you do again? Monitor aircraft production for the Army or something?”

“Hey, logistics won the war as much as the guys firing the guns!”

“And you must have done a great job at it! After all, we won.”

Len laughed and updated her on his progress in moving. She told him Walt was submitting his house plans to the county for approval tomorrow.

The rest of the night, he thought about his big move. Did he really want to spend the rest of his life fishing and visiting with Janet and Walt? It might get boring, but it wasn’t a bad life, all in all. Detroit was sure as hell no place to retire, and Florida didn’t appeal to him. California was expensive, but he was going to have a place to live that was almost free, and he’d have all the proceeds from selling his house, too.

Jack didn’t get to live this long; he barely reached his thirtieth birthday. What would he have done, if he’d survived the war? He might have gone to college and become a full-fledged architect for the Kahn outfit. Maybe eventually the draft would have caught up with him, and he’d have the GI Bill to fall back on, like Len did. If he survived.

Len thought about his own college experiences in Ann Arbor. He’d always been good with numbers, and in the war he found he really liked the accounting part of his job! The auto companies were actually building the airplanes and tanks and generally knew what they were doing, but the government was paying them. They got a lot of money for it, and someone had to keep them on the up-and-up. Len found that he actually liked doing that!

The civilians made fun of him as a “bean counter,” but the Army really appreciated what he did. So in college he got his degree in Accountancy. “You’ll always have a job in Accounting,” his dad used to say.

After college he got a job with Arthur Andersen, the big accounting firm. They put him on a few “fraud audits,” which meant swooping down on a company where they suspected embezzlement, and questioning every single piece of paper and every financial transaction. He absolutely loved it, especially when he found something and the bad guys got caught. They noticed his enthusiasm and the partners started asking for Len Saunders when they had a fraud audit coming up.

He remembered one big case, where a bunch of war profiteers kept up their thievery even after the war was over. Len ferreted out the phony invoices that sunk their case. They paid themselves, in a devious way they thought was safe, and Len figured out how their scheme worked. They went to prison. He’d seen some shady stuff during the war, where invoices were padded and non-existent employees drew paychecks, but he’d never quite managed to nab anyone.

It still rankled him that he wasn’t made a partner after that. He got an award, but that was it. When he came up for his “make partner or leave” review after eight years or so, he left and went to work at Chrysler. It turned out that no matter how great a job you did, if you didn’t bring in a lot of new business, you had no chance of being a partner. Being the guy who sends people to prison was not exactly the best way of selling your services!

Now at least Janet did seem to have that smoothness he lacked. He remembered one epic run-in he had with a VP, Harold Townsend was his name, and Mr. Townsend wanted him to include some revenue in one quarter that really belonged in the next, and Len just refused. He was sure that Townsend held a grudge and kept him from ever getting promoted again. He’d thought of leaving Chrysler, but hey, he had a family to support. 

Judging by her steady rise up the corporate ladder, Janet must not be shooting herself in the foot like that. He must have done something right with her! She didn’t have kids, though. His brother was dead, so the two of them were the last Saunders left, “Well, too late to do anything about that,” he thought. “Maybe Janet will make it to CEO someday!”

Janet. He thought back to Retirement Day and all the stuff that happened since then, and how he came to be leaving the state he’d lived in all his life.

Body cam footage 🎥 

“Officer I can’t scoot!”

Bodycam is wild. Charges later got dropped.

The footage shows officers interacting with JiDion @edpwatch_ (wearing a black Lyft shirt, light pants) after he and others were ordered off private property near a McDonald’s while confronting an alleged squatter situation. He is later arrested and struggles to get into the back of the police car due to his size.

•  JiDion: This is going to get dropped? Do you really think this is gonna get dropped?

•  Officer: You’re under arrest for being disorderly, not for being on the property.

text:
🕰️ WHEN PEACE ARRIVED, THE WEATHER TURNED, AND HISTORY REFUSED TO BEHAVE!

══════════════ ❧ ══════════════

THE WEIRDEST EVENTS IN HISTORY 🤯

══════════════ ❧ ══════════════

STRANGER THAN FICTION — NOVEMBER 11TH EDITION

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🕒 ESTIMATED READING TIME: 13 MINUTES

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🗺️ CONSPECTUS

📜 EPIGRAPH — A little truth to set the tone.

🎬 INTRO — Five stories. One very strange date.

❓ HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY — Test your instincts.

⭐️ MAIN EVENTS — Five moments when history got spectacularly weird.

🎙️ HARVEY’S CORNER — The rest of the story.

⚖️ CLOSING — The day, considered.

✅ QUIZ ANSWER — The answer revealed.

🍬 CANDY — One last sweet bite, with a look at tomorrow.

💋 SEND-OFF — Pass the madness along.

📚 SOURCES & FURTHER READING — Follow the evidence.

✒️ PUDD’NHEAD WILSON HAS THE LAST WORD — Mark Twain gets the final say.

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

📜 EPIGRAPH

“Truth is stranger than fiction, but it is because Fiction is obliged to stick to possibilities; Truth isn’t.” — Mark Twain, Following the Equator (1897).  ☄️

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🎬 INTRO

November 11 arrives every year dressed for a funeral and somehow still manages to trip over its own footnotes. It has earned the solemnity—ceremonies, silences, the whole respectful hush—but the history underneath it behaves like a drunk uncle at the wake. A boatload of strangers drafts emergency paperwork so they don’t immediately turn on one another; a court prices an enslaved man on the way to killing him; the agreement that ends a war politely leaves another six hours of shooting on the schedule; a country buries someone it cannot name; and a mild Midwestern morning decides, without warning, to become a killer blizzard. History, it seems, does not do “neat.”

Other dates show up with tidy labels and color-coordinated commemorations. November 11 prefers loose ends, bureaucratic afterthoughts, and weather that files no flight plan. The paperwork still matters. So does the silence that follows the guns. Common sense, as usual, has been delayed in transit and is currently arguing with the ticket agent.

Five stories. One date. Let’s watch what happens when history declines the invitation to behave itself.

Cue the chaos. Let’s roll. 💥

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

❓ HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY

On November 11, 1940, the Armistice Day Storm struck the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes region. The morning began relatively mild, but conditions deteriorated with astonishing speed.

Which detail best illustrates how deceptive the storm’s beginning was?

[A] The first snowflakes fell during a scheduled military parade.

[B] Duck hunters headed out in light clothing under mild, sunny skies before the weather turned deadly.

[C] The storm was forecast to be a hurricane but arrived as a heat wave.

[D] The Great Lakes froze solid before noon.

👇 (Answer at the end of the issue.)

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

⭐️ MAIN EVENTS

⛵ 1620 — THEY MISSED THEIR STOP, THE PASSENGERS STARTED MUTTERING ABOUT MUTINY, SO 41 MEN SIGNED A PAPER TO INVENT A GOVERNMENT WHILE STILL ROCKING ON THE BOAT 🇺🇸

Aboard the Mayflower, off Cape Cod | November 11, 1620

The date follows the English calendar then in use; in today's Gregorian calendar, it was November 21.

The Mayflower crossed the Atlantic intending to settle farther south, in territory covered by its English patent. Dangerous shoals and difficult conditions brought it to anchor off Cape Cod, well north of the intended destination.

That was more than a navigational inconvenience. Some passengers outside the Separatist congregation questioned whether they were still bound by the leaders who had organized the voyage. If they were outside the patent's territory, why obey the same leadership?

William Bradford later described “mutinous speeches” among some of the passengers. The prospect of a divided and leaderless settlement was not exactly an encouraging start to life in a new world.

On November 11, 1620, while still aboard the ship, 41 adult men signed an agreement to combine themselves into a “civil Body Politick.” They promised to create and obey laws for the general good of the colony. The document later became known as the Mayflower Compact.

It was not a modern constitution, nor did it establish universal democracy. Women, children, and many other passengers did not sign it. But it was a practical agreement to establish a common government when the group’s original legal arrangements no longer fit the circumstances.

The Mayflower had not reached its intended destination. Before building homes, the passengers had to decide who would make the rules.

🧩 TRIVIA: The original Mayflower Compact has not survived. Its wording is known through early printed versions and a handwritten copy preserved in William Bradford’s manuscript, Of Plimoth Plantation.

🐶 SPOT: Bradford’s manuscript does not call the document the “Mayflower Compact.” The familiar title was attached later; Bradford simply described the agreement and its signers.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The Mayflower Compact was born from a practical crisis, not a leisurely philosophical exercise. A group of passengers had landed outside the territory they expected to occupy, and some questioned the authority of their leaders. Before they could build a settlement, they needed a way to keep the people aboard one ship from becoming several competing factions.

───────────────

⚖️ 1831 — NAT TURNER: THE REBELLION, THE TRIAL, AND THE PRICE PUT ON A HUMAN LIFE 🇺🇸

Jerusalem, Southampton County, Virginia | November 11, 1831

In August 1831, an uprising led by Nat Turner shook Southampton County, Virginia. Turner was an enslaved preacher who believed he had been called to lead his people out of bondage. The revolt began on August 21 and spread through the county over the next two days.
Turner and his followers killed approximately 55 to 60 white people, including women and children. The militia crushed the uprising. The backlash was brutal: Black people who had taken no part were also killed, and Virginia tightened restrictions on Black education, assembly, and movement.

Turner evaded capture for more than two months. He was found on October 30, tried in Southampton County on November 5, and convicted. The surviving court record states that he was sentenced to be hanged on November 11.

Turner was executed that day in Jerusalem, the county seat. His revolt had been defeated, but the fear it generated among slaveholders helped fuel a wave of repression designed to prevent another uprising.

The rebellion remains the largest uprising of enslaved people in U.S. history. Its consequences reached far beyond the men who took part in it, touching the lives of Black communities throughout Virginia and the wider South.

🧩 TRIVIA: Virginia authorities offered a $500 reward for Turner’s capture and safe return to the Southampton County jail.

⚠️ IRONY: The surviving November 5 trial record assigned Turner a monetary value of $375 as enslaved property. He was being tried and sentenced as a human being while the legal system still treated him as property that could be priced. The contradiction was not incidental; it was built into the institution he had resisted.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Nat Turner’s execution did not end the story of the rebellion. The uprising was followed by collective punishment and harsher laws that targeted Black education, movement, and assembly. The court’s valuation of Turner is a stark reminder that the institution he resisted was embedded not only in private ownership but in the machinery of law.

───────────────

🕊️ 1918 — THE ARMISTICE: THE WAR ENDED AT ELEVEN—BUT NOT WHEN IT WAS SIGNED 🇫🇷

Forest of Compiègne, France | November 11, 1918

After more than four years of slaughter, the First World War was approaching its end. Germany’s military position had deteriorated, its allies had fallen away, and revolution was spreading at home. Kaiser Wilhelm II had abdicated and fled to the Netherlands. A new German government sent representatives to negotiate an end to the fighting.

In the early hours of November 11, the German delegation met Allied representatives in a railway carriage in the Forest of Compiègne, northeast of Paris. At 5:00 a.m. French time, the armistice was signed.
But the guns did not stop immediately.

The agreement specified that hostilities would cease at 11:00 a.m. French time. Six hours separated the signing from the ceasefire. The interval allowed the order to reach the armies along the front. Fighting continued while soldiers on both sides knew that an end had been agreed.

At 11:00 a.m., the guns finally fell silent along the Western Front. The date and hour—the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month—became a lasting symbol of remembrance.

The armistice was not a peace treaty. It stopped the fighting and required German forces to withdraw from occupied territories and surrender substantial military equipment. The Treaty of Versailles followed in 1919.

Relief was immense, but the final hours were not bloodless. Men continued to die until the ceasefire took effect. The battlefield had to obey the clock.

🧩 TRIVIA: The armistice required Germany to surrender 5,000 locomotives and 150,000 railway wagons, alongside vast quantities of artillery, machine guns, aircraft, and motor vehicles.

🐶 SPOT: American soldier Henry Gunther was killed at 10:59 a.m. on November 11, 1918, one minute before the ceasefire. He is widely identified as the last American soldier killed in action in World War I.

🔑 ESOTERIC: An armistice suspends military operations; it does not, by itself, create a formal state of peace. That distinction matters: the November 11 agreement stopped the fighting, while the formal peace settlement with Germany came later, through the Treaty of Versailles in 1919.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: November 11 marks the end of fighting on the Western Front, not the signing of a final peace treaty. The six-hour gap between signature and ceasefire is a sobering reminder that even when leaders have agreed to stop a war, the people at the front may still be ordered to fight—and die—until the clock says otherwise.

───────────────

🪖 1921 — THE UNKNOWN SOLDIER: A FUNERAL FOR THE MAN NO ONE COULD NAME 🇺🇸

Arlington National Cemetery, Virginia | November 11, 1921

Three years after the armistice, the United States gave one unidentified serviceman a state funeral. He represented the thousands of Americans whose remains could not be identified after the First World War.

Four unidentified American service members had been exhumed from military cemeteries in France and placed in identical caskets. On October 24, 1921, Sergeant Edward F. Younger was given the honor of selecting one. He walked among the caskets and placed a spray of white roses on the one chosen to represent the Unknown Soldier.

The remains were carried across the Atlantic aboard the USS Olympia, the celebrated warship that had served as Admiral George Dewey’s flagship during the Spanish-American War. After arriving in Washington, the Unknown lay in state in the Capitol Rotunda.

Approximately 90,000 people came to pay their respects.
On November 11, a horse-drawn caisson carried the casket through Washington and across the Potomac to Arlington National Cemetery. President Warren G. Harding presided over the ceremony at the Memorial Amphitheater. A nationwide two-minute silence marked the occasion. He placed the Medal of Honor on the casket, and foreign representatives presented their own nations’ decorations.

The permanent marble monument familiar today did not yet exist. The Unknown was first laid to rest in a temporary tomb, and the great sarcophagus was not completed until 1932.

The ceremony gave a nameless soldier a national identity—and made him represent everyone whose identity had been lost.

🧩 TRIVIA: France and Great Britain had each buried an unidentified soldier on Armistice Day 1920, a year before the United States held its own ceremony.

🌀 OBSCURE: Before the Unknown was interred, a two-inch layer of soil brought from France was placed beneath the coffin so that he would rest above the earth where he had fallen.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier honors an individual whose identity remains lost while representing thousands of families who never received the certainty of knowing where their loved ones lay. The ceremony transformed an absence into a national act of remembrance.

───────────────

🌨️ 1940 — THE ARMISTICE DAY STORM: WHEN A BEAUTIFUL MORNING TURNED FATAL 🇺🇸

Upper Midwest and Great Lakes, United States | November 11, 1940

The morning of November 11, 1940, did not look like the beginning of a disaster. Across much of the Upper Midwest, skies were blue and temperatures sat in the 40s and 50s Fahrenheit. Duck hunters, seeing pleasant conditions, headed for marshes and waterways in light clothing.

Then the weather changed.

A powerful low-pressure system moved northeast from the central United States, dragging a fierce cold front across the region. Winds strengthened, temperatures plunged, rain turned to sleet and then driving snow, and conditions deteriorated with frightening speed. The storm produced blizzard conditions across parts of the Dakotas, Minnesota, Iowa, and Wisconsin.

Twelve duck hunters were trapped on the Mississippi River between St. Paul and Prairie du Chien. They sought shelter on small islands, but the cold and exposure proved fatal. Elsewhere, motorists were caught in heavy snow and powerful winds. Snowdrifts reached extraordinary depths, and rescue efforts were complicated by ice that formed overnight.

The Great Lakes suffered their own catastrophe. Powerful southwest gales whipped Lake Michigan into dangerous seas. Three steamers sank, other vessels ran aground, and smaller craft were lost. Fifty-nine people died on Lake Michigan alone.

The storm claimed 154 lives across the region, including 49 in Minnesota, and killed thousands of cattle. A mild day had become a winter emergency.

The name “Armistice Day Storm” carries a cruel irony: a day of remembrance became a disaster for people far from shelter.

🧩 TRIVIA: The storm killed approximately one million turkeys across Wisconsin, Minnesota, and neighboring states.

🐶 SPOT: Snowdrifts reached 20 feet near Willmar, Minnesota, as gale-force winds piled snow across roads and fields.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The Armistice Day Storm is a warning about the danger of trusting a pleasant morning when conditions are changing rapidly. On November 11, 1940, the weather turned faster than many people could react—and the consequences were devastating on land and water alike.

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

🎙️ HARVEY’S CORNER

VIOLET JESSOP — MISS UNSINKABLE

Good day, everybody.

Some people spend a lifetime trying to avoid trouble. Violet Jessop spent much of hers working aboard ships that seemed determined to find it.

She was a stewardess, later a nurse, whose career placed her aboard three White Star sister ships: the Olympic, Titanic, and Britannic. All three encountered disaster while she was aboard.

Let’s start with the Olympic.

In September 1911, Violet was working aboard the Olympic when the great liner collided with the British warship HMS Hawke in the waters off the Isle of Wight. The Olympic was badly damaged and had to return for repairs. It did not sink, and neither did Violet. She went back to work.

Then came the Titanic.

Violet had not been especially eager to leave the Olympic for its new sister ship. Friends persuaded her that the maiden voyage would be an experience worth having. She joined the Titanic as a stewardess.

On April 14, 1912, the ship struck an iceberg. According to her memoir, Violet was ordered into a lifeboat so that passengers who did not understand English could see that it was safe to board. As the boat was lowered, an officer handed her a baby.

She survived the sinking and reached the Carpathia. In her memoir, Violet recalled that a woman rushed up, took the baby from her arms, and hurried away without a word. Violet’s memoir does not identify the child or record what happened afterward.

After surviving the Titanic, a sensible person might have chosen quieter work. Violet did not.

During the First World War, she served with the British Red Cross and worked aboard the Britannic, which had been converted into a hospital ship. On November 21, 1916, the Britannic struck a mine in the Aegean Sea near the Greek island of Kea.

The ship began to flood. As it listed, its enormous propellers rose toward the surface. Two lifeboats were drawn into the still-turning screws and destroyed.

Violet was among those who jumped into the water to escape. She was pulled beneath the ship and struck her head against its keel. She survived, but years later a doctor discovered that she had suffered a skull fracture.

The Britannic sank. Violet lived.

And then, in one of the most astonishing details of the story, she returned to sea. She continued working aboard ships for decades, retiring in 1950 after a career that had lasted more than forty years.

“Miss Unsinkable” can make her story sound like a joke about luck. It was not. She was a working woman caught in emergencies that cost others their lives.

She survived the Olympic collision, the Titanic disaster, and the sinking of the Britannic. But she was not a passenger collecting extraordinary vacation stories. She was a professional stewardess and wartime nurse, doing her duty when the ships around her failed.

Violet Constance Jessop died in 1971, aged 83.

Three ships. Two sinkings. One collision. One remarkable woman who kept going back to sea.

And now you know the rest of the story.

Good day!

—— ❦ ——

🧬 HUMAN

Violet Jessop’s own memoir, published after her death as Titanic Survivor, preserves her first-person recollections of the Titanic and Britannic disasters. Her account describes not only the terrifying moments at sea but also the ordinary working duties she continued to perform while the ships were in danger.

⚖️ CLOSING

November 11: a date with a solemn reputation and a remarkably complicated guest list.

It put William Bradford and a shipload of would-be settlers in a position where a signature was needed to prevent a new colony from becoming a floating argument. It brought Nat Turner to the gallows after a rebellion that shook the slaveholding South—and left behind a court record that priced a human life in dollars.

It ended the fighting on the Western Front, though not at the moment the armistice was signed. Six hours remained, and men continued to die until the clock reached eleven. Henry Gunther was among them, killed just one minute before the guns fell silent. Three years later, the nation buried an unidentified soldier with the honors due to a hero, giving a nameless grave a place in the national memory.

Then, in 1940, the same date delivered a storm that began under mild skies and ended with 154 people dead. Duck hunters went out expecting an ordinary day. The weather had other plans.

And somewhere in the middle of all that, Violet Jessop kept surviving ships that had no business making her career quite so eventful. She went back to sea, because apparently the ocean had not yet made its point.

November 11 is remembered for what it resolves and what it exposes—and it throws in a blizzard.

History can be solemn. It can be strange. And every so often, it can be downright unreasonable. 🌨️

─────────────── ◈ ────────────────

✅ QUIZ ANSWER: [B] Duck hunters headed out in light clothing under mild, sunny skies before the weather turned deadly.

The morning began with blue skies and temperatures in the 40s and 50s Fahrenheit. A powerful cold front then brought fierce winds, plunging temperatures, sleet, snow, and blizzard conditions. Twelve duck hunters became trapped on the Mississippi River, and the storm ultimately claimed 154 lives across the region.

The calendar keeps turning. Common sense remains conspicuously absent. 👀

‘An imperfect solution’ gains traction in data center fight | Kinnia Cheuk, Politico

Governors are turning to community benefit agreements as they scramble to address data center blowback without alienating tech giants.

Democratic governors have a new message for data center developers amid community backlash: Cut a deal.

Community benefit agreements are increasingly appearing in state strategies for handling the data center boom. In recent months, three Rust Belt governors — Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro, Illinois’ JB Pritzker and Michigan’s Gretchen Whitmer — have called on project developers to enter into legal agreements with communities that can cement pollution limits, hiring commitments and local investment promises.

“My message to data center developers is clear: if you can’t agree to our strict requirements and get the community where you want to build to say ‘yes,’ you’re not going to have the Commonwealth’s support either,” Shapiro said in a statement when he signed an executive order last month that features CBAs. “These are some of the biggest companies in the world — they can afford to be good neighbors, follow the rules, and do this right.”

CBAs first cropped up 25 years ago, when a coalition of Los Angeles community groups hammered out a deal with the developers of the Staples Center. That first-ever CBA traded promises of jobs and local investment for community support that helped secure city subsidies. Since then, communities across the U.S. have used versions of the legal agreement to secure economic benefits from a variety of developments.

Policymakers are now mulling mandates for such agreements. Shapiro signed an executive order last month ordering his state’s Department of Environmental Protection to only review permit applications for data center developers that have agreed to sign a CBA with their local community, among other requirements. Otherwise, DEP will not begin review until after all local approvals, including for zoning and land use, are secured.

The move was the latest sign that Shapiro, a likely 2028 presidential contender, has gone from a data center cheerleader to a vocal skeptic. He’s not alone. Both Democrats and Republicans are grappling with how to address a growing public backlash to the energy- and water-guzzling facilities, which are cropping up faster than political leaders and regulators can keep up.

CBAs appeal to moderate Democratic governors who are scrambling to address data center blowback without alienating the tech giants they hope can provide a much-needed boost to their local economies. But even progressives who support moratoriums on data centers, like Michigan Senate Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, have referenced CBAs as a way to protect communities from data centers’ possible impacts.

Abre’ Conner, director of the NAACP’s Center for Environmental and Climate Justice, said organizers of the group’s Stop Dirty Data Centers campaign quickly realized that some projects can’t be stopped by advocacy efforts — no matter how fervently communities oppose them.

CBAs can be “a tool in communities’ toolboxes” during negotiations when data center developments turn out to be inevitable, Conner said.

Experts say that the legal agreements are far from a cure-all. So far, only one community seems to have cut a deal with a data center developer.

The Data Center Coalition also argues that the vast majority of its members— including the likes of Google and Amazon — have voluntarily invested in communities beyond the jobs they create, like filling school budget gaps. Mandating CBAs before zoning or permitting, as some states are considering, could create delays and drive developments away, said Brad Tietz, the group’s director of government affairs in the Midwest.

“We’re in uncharted territory,” said Tietz. “Mandating something legislatively is far different than it occurring naturally between the local government and the company.”

But some politicians see CBAs as a stop-gap solution, providing relief for communities and serving as a model for responsible developers before other regulations are set in stone. That’s the idea behind a package of bills that Michigan state senators unveiled in June. The legislation, backed by Whitmer, would require local governments to reach a CBA with developers before moving forward with zoning approvals.

“Community benefits agreements will not solve all of the problems, but if you can put it together with strong regulations on data centers and the entire regulatory framework, then I do think that we’re in a stronger position to have members of our community feel that they are being heard right now,” said Michigan state Sen. Darrin Camilleri (D), assistant majority leader and the package’s primary sponsor.

(Re)building trust

Data centers’ sky high unpopularity has given many communities the power to demand environmental standards and investments from developers.

“Two years ago, communities really didn’t have much leverage against a Google or a Meta. But now we’re starting to see so many data centers that are canceled because of public defense, and so now communities really have a lot more leverage than they had in the past,” said Dana Kuhnline, program director at regional coalition ReImagine Appalachia.

At least 20 proposed data center projects were canceled after local pushback during the first three months of 2026, accounting for more than $41.7 billion in investment and 3.5 gigawatts of electricity demand, according to data from Heatmap.

The opposition has prompted a wave of local moratoriums and restrictions: Virginia has enacted a new energy consumption tax and New York has paused new data center construction for a year. In Illinois, lawmakers have proposed the POWER Act, which would require data center developers to enter into a CBA with a coalition of community-based organizations or a community advisory board formed by the municipal government.

Meagan Niebler, program director at the nonprofit law firm Fair Shake Environmental Legal Services, said more communities want to stop data centers entirely instead of reaching a deal.

But if developments continue to move forward, communities will be thinking about how to hold companies legally accountable and ensure protections with CBAs, said Niebler, who has collaborated with Midwest communities to ensure environmental protections in data center development.

Pennsylvania’s regulations and proposed laws in Illinois and Michigan would mandate that companies negotiate with communities until both sides agree. But nonmandatory CBAs depend heavily on a developer’s good faith effort.

It’s “very hard” to get large companies to a table for open dialogue with communities, and locals often need a lot of organizing and legal leverage to even get their foot in the door, Niebler said.

“There’s a lot of things that make it an imperfect solution, but an imperfect solution is still better than nothing,” said Liza Paudel, senior program manager for tech equity at the nonprofit Greenlining Institute.

The data center industry says their key concern is timing. Delays can significantly derail a project if local governments are slow to appoint community members to an advisory board to discuss contract terms — like the Illinois proposal would require — or if negotiations are stretched out indefinitely, Tietz said.

“What if you have a local government who’s interested, but obviously opposition rises, and then you’ve spent 10, 12 months negotiating for the project that is not even going to advance?” Tietz said.

Developers would have more confidence in the project if permitting could occur while the CBA is being negotiated, Tietz said. That could mean, for example, requiring an agreement to be reached before construction begins — rather than before a permit is issued.

States could alternatively offer incentives — such as tax breaks — to developers who reach community benefit agreements, he said.

Past programs emphasizing community engagement have had mixed results.

In 2021, the Biden-era Department of Energy required all clean energy projects funded by the Inflation Reduction Act to submit community benefit plans detailing how developers would engage in the local workforce and benefit disadvantaged communities. But the plans were not negotiated — and many residents complained that the process left community members without a role in any talks.

Projects that won grants often fell short of true community engagement, according to a former senior DOE official under then-President Joe Biden who was granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak by their current employer.

Many communities had “no idea” that any sort of benefits were promised to them, and the terms of the program were often drafted and implemented unilaterally on the developers’ side, the former official said.

“I never wanted it to be seen as the gold standard. We did a lot in a very constrained environment, but it wasn’t enough,” the official said.

For mandatory CBAs to work, they said, the community has to have the veto power to shut the project down.

Looking to Lancaster

You have to travel to the heart of Amish country to find the data center industry’s only CBA, according to research by the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University.

Chirisa Technology Parks and codeveloper Machine Investment Group have an agreement with the government of Lancaster, Pennsylvania, over two data center sites in the city, encompassing approximately 2 million square feet with at least 700 megawatts of planned capacity.

First proposed by then-mayor Danene Sorace, the agreement was formally executed in November. The company had already planned to adhere to certain environmental standards, so executives thought the CBA was a “great idea,” said David Kelly, chief technology officer at Chirisa.

Barry Handwerger, who drafted the agreement for Lancaster as city solicitor, said the city determined the bulk of the terms. Chirisa mainly met with the mayor’s office, though it held an open house for the community early on in the process.

The final agreement requires that Chirisa source all its power from clean energy sources, employ a closed loop cooling system that conserves water and adhere to a publicly disclosed municipal water use cap, noise limits and wastewater regulations. The company must submit annual environmental and operational reporting and make its power use public, said Handwerger. The agreement also holds Chirisa to investing $20 million into clean energy and sustainable development for the city.

If those requirements aren’t met, the company faces millions of dollars in penalties and permanent injunctions for breaches of nonfinancial commitments like noise limit violations.

Several state and local officials within and outside of Pennsylvania have reached out to City Council members to learn about the agreement, said Lancaster City Council President Ahmed Ahmed, who voted to pass the CBA.

The data center issue is a “very difficult topic” to discuss in the public forum, he said, but the CBA quelled residents’ anxieties on whether the project would use too much water or rely on fossil fuels.

The activist organization Lancaster Stands Up challenged the city’s approval of the Chirisa project, encouraging residents to express their concerns at City Council meetings. Some meetings drew 100 people to city hall, said Frank Arcoleo, a Lancaster resident and member of the group. Arcoleo appealed the zoning approval for the data centers in August but was ultimately unsuccessful.

The group also submitted detailed recommendations for the CBA, including requirements for renewable energy, noise limits and decommissioning. Arcoleo said nearly all of them made it into the final agreement.

“Had there been a little bit of public grousing and complaining about these data centers, but it went away, I think they wouldn’t have done anything,” he said.

Lancaster Stands Up, which is part of Pennsylvania Stands Up, has shared its documents and experience with other chapters of the organization, especially those involved in data center fights themselves, Arcoleo said.

“Where they’re winning, they’re stopping the data centers to begin with. Where they’re losing, they’re at least demanding that the community benefits agreement be at least as good as Lancaster’s,” he said.

Complementary solutions

CBAs are only one aspect of the major new strategies that states are rolling out for the data center boom.

Pennsylvania’s regulations, as well as the proposals from Illinois and Michigan, include provisions that protect ratepayers from bearing the cost of data center projects and prohibit developers from entering into certain nondisclosure agreements to maintain transparency.

Republican senators in Michigan say that the legislation is more talking points than substance. State Sen. Jim Runestad, assistant minority caucus chair of the Michigan Senate, has proposed a one-year moratorium on data centers. Absent a moratorium, developers may still be able to have their way over community’s needs, he said.

Mandating community benefits between local government and developers may mean that “some board, county board, city board, negotiates something for themselves, which may be a swimming pool close to the elected official’s backyard,” he said. “It’s all fluff.”

While CBAs can be valuable tools for some communities, blanket local zoning ordinances can provide many of its benefits, said Christina Libre, attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center.

Zoning ordinances ensure that all baseline considerations are taken into account every time a data center application comes before the locality, rather than relying on the goodwill of any individual developer to negotiate an agreement with the community, she said.

Possible ordinances could require all data center developments get city council approval, she said, or mandate pollution limits.

Lancaster began drafting a data center zoning ordinance only after Chirisa proposed building its data centers last spring. The ordinance passed this July, mandating noise mitigation plans, air quality testing, and water and power use reporting. The law also limits data center development to land zoned for suburban manufacturing, reducing land open to data centers from 200 potential parcels to only 16.

But Christopher Delfs, Lancaster’s director of economic development, still sees a role for CBAs in the future.

“Zoning is about regulation and what you can’t do, but a CBA is more creative about what you want a data center to achieve, like finding other ways for the city to realize its sustainability plan by investments in renewable energy, and other funds like the economic development and innovation funds,” he said.

Chirisa is currently partnering with the nonprofit Economic Development Co. of Lancaster County to determine how the financial commitments from Chirisa will be used, said EDC Lancaster County President Ezra Rothman. He hopes that Chirisa’s data centers won’t just be “server rooms” for Lancaster, but can help drive how the city’s schools and companies prepare for an AI future.

“Hopefully the agreement is a start, and the partnerships in our community can really become a model for leveraging the physical construction of a data center to drive innovation,” he said.

“There are many challenges that we face in our day. The world is literally in commotion.

Two months ago, I celebrated my eightieth birthday. This gives me a very long perspective on what is essential to provide protections. 

When Mary and I were still in our twenties in the 1960s, the turbulence, anger, and social unrest was similar to what we have experienced recently. We lived in the San Francisco Bay Area. 

In the face of this chaos, we were blessed to receive counsel from President Harold B. Lee, who was the president of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles at the time. We appreciated that counsel then and cherish it now.

President Lee’s counsel, in addition to following the prophet, was for both families and individuals. 

First, build Zion in your hearts and in your homes. 

Second, be a light on the hill and an example in your community. 

And third, focus your vision and goals on the ordinances and principles taught in the temple. 

President Lee promised that we would be protected if we followed these principles and that we could live anywhere in the world.

My challenge to you is to learn what is essential when the world is in commotion to protect and bless you and provide the happiness, peace, and success you desire. 

Please avoid detours and stumbling blocks that diminish this protection.

Despite the lack of righteousness in the world today, we live in a sacred, holy time!”

Quentin L. Cook
BYU Devotional; November 2020

Build Zion. 
Be a light. 
Focus your vision. 

We have been given EVERYTHING we need to be successful in navigating these last day challenges. Keep following the prophets- they do know the way!

Texas isn't exactly a retiree's paradise either.

Its effective property tax rate is TWICE California's, and life expectancy at birth is 2.1 years shorter.

California offers great weather, excellent medical centers, and no state income tax on Social Security benefits. But housing and long-term care are incredibly expensive.

Texas offers much more affordable homes and ZERO state income tax. But extreme heat, insurance costs, and property taxes still matter.

AND HERE'S WHAT YOU CAN'T IGNORE.

Selling your California home and moving to Texas could free up a LOT of money.

But leaving your family and friends behind comes at a different kind of cost.

Now imagine you have the EXACT SAME SAVINGS and the same Social Security benefits.

Where would you rather spend the next 20 years of your retirement?

🌴 CALIFORNIA or 🤠 TEXAS?

And if you already live in one of them, tell me why you'd NEVER move to the other.

text:
🧭 A DAY OF REMEMBRANCE, RECKONING & SELF-DETERMINATION

════════════════ ❧ ════════════════

ANNALS OF THE DAY 🪔

════════════════ ❧ ════════════════

A HISTORICAL CHRONICLE • NOVEMBER 11TH EDITION

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

⏱️ READING TIME: APPROXIMATELY 15–18 MINUTES

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🪔 EPIGRAPH

“History does not repeat itself, but it often leaves us the same questions to answer.” — Hodgepodgery, 2026

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

📑 TABLE OF CONTENTS

🪔 Epigraph — A thought to frame the day.

🔎 Intro — The stories and contradictions behind November 11.

🧭 Calendar Overview — The date, its place in the year, and its observances.

🏛️ Major Historical Events — Five consequential moments that changed the course of events.

🔬 Scientific, Technological & Cultural Milestones — Discoveries and innovations that changed how we see and experience the world.

🎂 Famous Birthdays — Notable people born on this date.

🥀 Memoriam — Remembering those whose lives ended on November 11.

🏟️ Sports Highlights — Records, milestones, and extraordinary sporting moments.

❓ History Quiz — A question to test your historical instincts.

🌎 Closing — A final reflection on the lessons of the past.

📣 There's More History Waiting! — Today's publication schedule.

🦉 The Stoic Mind — One thought from the Stoic tradition.

✅ Quiz Answer — The answer and its historical explanation.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🔎 INTRO

November 11 is a date when the world remembers the cost of war—and the complicated work of building peace. A ceasefire silenced the guns of the First World War; an unknown soldier was laid to rest in Arlington; and a new American state entered the Union. Elsewhere, a white-minority government defied Britain, Angola emerged from Portuguese colonial rule amid conflict, and a naval air raid demonstrated that aircraft carriers could change the balance of sea power.

The date brings remembrance, independence, invention, and the truth that freedom is not always equal. ⏳

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🧭 CALENDAR OVERVIEW ♏️

November 11 is the 315th day of the year in the Gregorian calendar (≈86.30% of 2026 completed). There are 50 days remaining, representing approximately 13.70% of the year. The year 2026 is a common year of 365 days. Today is Wednesday, falling in ISO week 46. The United States observes Veterans Day, honoring all who have served in its armed forces. The date is also marked as Armistice Day in several countries, while Poland celebrates National Independence Day, commemorating the restoration of its independence in 1918. Angola observes Independence Day, marking its independence from Portugal in 1975. 🫡

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🏛️ MAJOR HISTORICAL EVENTS

Five November 11 events reveal the price of war and the responsibilities that follow historic change.

—— ❦ ——

1889 — WASHINGTON BECOMES THE 42ND U.S. STATE 🌲

On November 11, 1889, President Benjamin Harrison issued the proclamation admitting Washington to the Union as the forty-second state. The territory's path to statehood had taken years of debate, constitutional drafting, and political negotiation. Washington's voters had approved a state constitution in October, and the final presidential proclamation completed the process.

The new state added a strategically important Pacific Northwest region to the growing United States.

🧩 TRIVIA: Washington was the last of four states admitted during November 1889, following North Dakota, South Dakota, and Montana.

🐶 SPOT: The final paperwork nearly stumbled at the finish line. The first copy of Washington's constitution sent to President Harrison was not properly signed by the territorial governor. A replacement had to be prepared and rushed to Washington, D.C., before the President could approve it.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A new chapter in a nation's history may begin with a grand proclamation—but getting there often depends on patient work and a signature in the right place.

—— ❦ ——

1918 — THE ARMISTICE BRINGS THE FIGHTING OF WORLD WAR I TO AN END 🕊️

At 11:00 a.m. on November 11, 1918—the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month—the armistice between the Allied powers and Germany took effect, bringing the fighting on the Western Front to a halt. The agreement had been signed earlier that morning in a railway carriage in the Forest of Compiègne, France.

After more than four years of industrialized slaughter, the guns fell silent. Millions had died, empires had shattered, and borders had been redrawn. The ceasefire did not itself create a final peace treaty; that came with the Treaty of Versailles, signed on June 28, 1919.

The date became Armistice Day, later known in the United States as Veterans Day.

🧩 TRIVIA: The armistice was signed at approximately 5:45 a.m. local time, but its terms specified that hostilities would cease at 11:00 a.m.—giving the agreement its unforgettable place in the calendar.

🐶 SPOT: The guns did not fall silent everywhere at the same instant the agreement was signed. Fighting continued until the appointed hour, and men were still being killed on the war's final morning.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: An armistice can stop the shooting, but it cannot immediately end grief, repair destruction, or guarantee that the peace will last.

—— ❦ ——

1921 — THE UNKNOWN SOLDIER IS LAID TO REST AT ARLINGTON ⚔️

On November 11, 1921, an unidentified American serviceman from World War I was buried in Arlington National Cemetery during a national ceremony led by President Warren G. Harding. The Unknown Soldier's casket traveled from the U.S. Capitol to Arlington in a horse-drawn caisson, accompanied by military units and a vast procession.

At the Memorial Amphitheater, Harding placed the Medal of Honor on the casket. Representatives of foreign governments presented their own decorations, turning the ceremony into an international expression of mourning for the dead of the Great War.

The Tomb honored those whose identities could never be recovered and offered families a place to grieve for loved ones with no known grave.

🧩 TRIVIA: The Unknown Soldier was selected from four unidentified American servicemen exhumed from military cemeteries in France. Army Sergeant Edward F. Younger made the selection by placing a spray of white roses on one of the caskets.

🐶 SPOT: The Unknown Soldier arrived in Washington aboard the protected cruiser USS Olympia, the same historic ship that had served as Admiral George Dewey's flagship at the 1898 Battle of Manila Bay.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A nation can honor the fallen by name, but it must also remember those whose names and final resting places were lost.

—— ❦ ——

1965 — RHODESIA'S WHITE-MINORITY GOVERNMENT DECLARES INDEPENDENCE ⚖️

On November 11, 1965, Rhodesian Prime Minister Ian Smith's government issued a Unilateral Declaration of Independence from Britain. The declaration was made by a white-minority administration that rejected British demands for a credible path toward majority rule.

Britain regarded the declaration as illegal, and the United Nations condemned the breakaway regime. International sanctions followed. The white-minority government maintained control for years, while the country endured mounting conflict and isolation. The crisis was not resolved until negotiations led to internationally recognized independence for Zimbabwe in 1980.

The episode exposed a contradiction of decolonization: a government could speak of independence while denying political equality to the majority.

🧩 TRIVIA: The declaration's opening deliberately echoed the language of the American Declaration of Independence—a striking borrowing by a government whose constitution denied equal political power to most Black Rhodesians.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Independence is not the same as freedom when political power remains reserved for a privileged minority.

—— ❦ ——

1975 — ANGOLA DECLARES INDEPENDENCE FROM PORTUGAL 🌍

On November 11, 1975, Angola became independent after centuries of Portuguese colonial rule and fourteen years of armed struggle. Portugal's withdrawal ended its formal colonial authority, but independence arrived in the middle of a bitter contest among rival Angolan movements seeking control of the new state.

The Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA) proclaimed the People's Republic of Angola in Luanda, while rival forces also claimed authority elsewhere. The competing movements were supported by outside powers, turning the struggle into a major Cold War battleground. Independence marked the end of colonial rule and the beginning of a devastating civil war.

🧩 TRIVIA: Portugal formally granted Angola independence on November 11, 1975, but the United States did not recognize the government proclaimed by the MPLA until May 19, 1993.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The end of colonial rule can open the door to self-government, but peace and political unity require work that independence alone cannot complete.

And so the pages of history turn—leaving lessons, warnings, and stories worth remembering. 📜

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🔬 SCIENTIFIC, TECHNOLOGICAL & CULTURAL MILESTONES

November 11 also changed how people travel, how navies fight, and who may serve as a priest in one of the world's oldest Christian institutions.

—— ❦ ——

1926 — AMERICA ADOPTS ITS NUMBERED HIGHWAY SYSTEM 🛣️

On November 11, 1926, the American Association of State Highway Officials approved a national system of numbered highways. The plan replaced a confusing patchwork of named trails and regional road designations with a coordinated system that made long-distance travel easier to navigate.

The familiar U.S. highway shields and route numbers helped travelers follow roads across state boundaries. It also laid groundwork for the later Interstate Highway System.

🧩 TRIVIA: In the numbering plan, even-numbered routes generally run east–west, while odd-numbered routes generally run north–south. The numbers also follow a broad geographic pattern across the country.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A simple shared system can connect distant communities and make a vast country feel easier to navigate.

—— ❦ ——

1940 — BRITISH AIRCRAFT STRIKE THE ITALIAN FLEET AT TARANTO ⚓

On the night of November 11–12, 1940, the Royal Navy launched Operation Judgment against the Italian fleet anchored at Taranto. Fairey Swordfish aircraft took off from the aircraft carrier HMS Illustrious and attacked warships in the harbor with torpedoes and bombs.

The raid damaged several Italian battleships and demonstrated the striking power of carrier-based naval aviation. It was a turning point in naval warfare: aircraft launched from a carrier could reach a heavily defended fleet in port and inflict devastating damage without a traditional surface-fleet engagement.

Taranto became a case study for naval planners, including Japanese officers preparing for Pearl Harbor.

🧩 TRIVIA: The attacking aircraft were slow, fabric-covered Fairey Swordfish biplanes—an old-fashioned-looking aircraft that proved unexpectedly effective against modern battleships.

🏆 FIRST: Taranto was the first major attack in which carrier-launched aircraft struck a major enemy fleet at anchor, demonstrating a new form of naval power.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Military technology does not always announce its arrival with a sleek new machine. Sometimes an outdated-looking aircraft changes the future of warfare.

—— ❦ ——

1992 — THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND APPROVES WOMEN FOR THE PRIESTHOOD ⛪

On November 11, 1992, the Church of England's General Synod approved the final legislation allowing women to become priests. The decision followed years of debate over women's roles in the church and marked a major change in the institution's modern history.

Parliamentary approval and Royal Assent followed in 1993; the first women were ordained in 1994.

🧩 TRIVIA: Angela Berners-Wilson became the first woman ordained to the priesthood in the Church of England, in March 1994, after the legislation had cleared the necessary stages.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Institutions change when long-standing boundaries are reconsidered—and when a vote is followed by the work of putting change into practice.

Here's to the curious minds, bold ideas, and remarkable discoveries that move humanity forward. 🚀

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎂 FAMOUS BIRTHDAYS

Today we celebrate a founding-era voice, a controversial military commander, a novelist who transformed his wartime trauma into literature, and performers whose work reached audiences around the world.

—— ❦ ——

1744 — ABIGAIL ADAMS ✒️

American First Lady, political adviser, and early advocate for women's rights Abigail Adams was born in Weymouth, Massachusetts. She brought an unusually independent intellect to public life and corresponded with her husband, John Adams, about the Revolution, government, and the future of the new nation.

🧩 TRIVIA: In a famous March 1776 letter to her husband, she urged the men drafting new laws to “Remember the Ladies” and not place unchecked power in the hands of husbands.

🐶 SPOT: Abigail had no formal schooling. At a time when most New England schools excluded girls, she educated herself by reading from her father's library.

—— ❦ ——

1885 — GEORGE S. PATTON 🎖️

American Army general George Smith Patton Jr. was born in San Gabriel, California. A flamboyant, aggressive, and often controversial commander, he became one of the best-known Allied generals of World War II, leading armored forces across North Africa, Sicily, France, and Germany.

🧩 TRIVIA: Before becoming a famous tank commander, Patton competed in the modern pentathlon at the 1912 Olympic Games in Stockholm, finishing fifth.

—— ❦ ——

1922 — KURT VONNEGUT 📚

American novelist and satirist Kurt Vonnegut was born in Indianapolis, Indiana. His books include Slaughterhouse-Five, Cat's Cradle, and Breakfast of Champions, blending dark humor, science fiction, and moral criticism.

🧩 TRIVIA: Vonnegut was a U.S. Army prisoner of war in Dresden during the February 1945 bombing. He and fellow prisoners survived in an underground meat locker, an experience that later became central to Slaughterhouse-Five.

—— ❦ ——

1925 — JONATHAN WINTERS 🎭

American comedian, actor, and improvisational performer Jonathan Winters was born in Bellbrook, Ohio. Known for his inventive characters and spontaneous comic imagination, he became a major influence on generations of comedians.

🧩 TRIVIA: Robin Williams openly described Winters as one of his greatest comic influences, and the two later appeared together on the television series Mork & Mindy.

—— ❦ ——

1962 — DEMI MOORE (age 64) 🎬

American actor and producer Demi Moore was born in Roswell, New Mexico. Her film career includes Ghost, A Few Good Men, Indecent Proposal, and G.I. Jane.

🧩 TRIVIA: Moore made Hollywood history when she was paid $12.5 million for Striptease, then the highest salary ever paid to a movie actress.

—— ❦ ——

1974 — LEONARDO DICAPRIO (age 52) 🎥

American actor and producer Leonardo DiCaprio was born in Los Angeles, California. His work includes Titanic, The Aviator, The Departed, The Wolf of Wall Street, and The Revenant.

🧩 TRIVIA: DiCaprio received his first Academy Award nomination at age 19 for his supporting performance in What's Eating Gilbert Grape.

Happy birthday to them all! 🎉

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🥀 MEMORIAM

We remember those who died on November 11 and the legacies they left in politics, public health, business, and entertainment.

—— ❦ ——

1938 — MARY MALLON, “TYPHOID MARY” (aged 69) 🕯️

Mary Mallon, the Irish-born cook whose case became one of the most famous and troubling episodes in American public-health history, died on North Brother Island in New York. Identified as a healthy carrier of Salmonella typhi, she was linked to outbreaks of typhoid fever in households where she worked. After returning to cooking despite public-health restrictions, she was confined for the final decades of her life.

Her story raises difficult questions about disease prevention, personal liberty, public responsibility, and the way a person's identity can be reduced to a label.

🧩 TRIVIA: Mallon spent approximately 26 years in isolation on North Brother Island, where she worked in the hospital laboratory and kitchen during her confinement.

—— ❦ ——

2004 — YASSER ARAFAT (aged 75) 🕊️

Yasser Arafat, chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organization and president of the Palestinian National Authority, died in a military hospital near Paris. A central and deeply controversial figure in modern Palestinian history, he led the PLO for decades and became a principal participant in the Oslo peace process.

In 1994, Arafat shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and Foreign Minister Shimon Peres for their efforts toward reconciliation in the Middle East. His death marked the end of an era in Palestinian politics.

🧩 TRIVIA: Arafat received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1994 alongside Rabin and Peres, three leaders whose participation in the Oslo process represented a historic, if ultimately incomplete, attempt at peace.

—— ❦ ——

2005 — PETER DRUCKER (aged 95) 📘

Austrian-born American writer, teacher, and management thinker Peter F. Drucker died at his home in Claremont, California, eight days before his 96th birthday. Often called the father of modern management, Drucker reshaped how businesses, public institutions, and nonprofit organizations thought about leadership, innovation, and the role of people in organizations.

His books influenced generations of executives and helped establish management as a serious field of study.

🧩 TRIVIA: Drucker wrote more than 30 books, and his 1946 study of General Motors, Concept of the Corporation, helped popularize the idea of decentralization in large organizations.

—— ❦ ——

2016 — ROBERT VAUGHN (aged 83) 🎬

American actor Robert Vaughn died in Danbury, Connecticut. He was best known for playing secret agent Napoleon Solo in the 1960s television series The Man from U.N.C.L.E. He also appeared in The Magnificent Seven and received an Academy Award nomination for The Young Philadelphians.

Vaughn was also a scholar and outspoken critic of the Hollywood blacklist.

🧩 TRIVIA: Vaughn won an Emmy Award in 1978 for his supporting performance in the television miniseries Washington: Behind Closed Doors.

In fond remembrance of them all. 🕯️

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🏟️ SPORTS HIGHLIGHTS

November 11 has produced an iconic performance by Jim Thorpe, an almost unbelievable college-football record, and the end of one of hockey's longest losing streaks.

—— ❦ ——

1911 — JIM THORPE LEADS CARLISLE TO A STUNNING UPSET OF HARVARD 🏈

On November 11, 1911, the Carlisle Indian Industrial School football team defeated nationally ranked Harvard 18–15 before approximately 25,000 spectators in Cambridge, Massachusetts. The legendary Jim Thorpe scored all 18 points for Carlisle: a touchdown, an extra point, and four field goals.

The victory foreshadowed Thorpe's two Olympic gold medals the following year.

🧩 TRIVIA: Thorpe's four field goals and touchdown accounted for every Carlisle point in the upset.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A single athlete can change the course of a game—and sometimes challenge the assumptions of an entire sporting establishment.

—— ❦ ——

1939 — TEXAS TECH AND CENTENARY SET A RECORD WITH 77 PUNTS 🌧️

On November 11, 1939, Texas Tech and Centenary College played to a 0–0 tie in Shreveport, Louisiana, in a torrential downpour. The muddy field and driving rain turned the game into a punting contest: the teams combined for an NCAA-record 77 punts.

Texas Tech punted 39 times and Centenary 38. The record remains one of the strangest statistical landmarks in college football history.

🧩 TRIVIA: Texas Tech's Charlie Calhoun punted 36 times for 1,318 yards, an individual single-game record that became nearly as extraordinary as the combined total.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Not every record is born from brilliance and perfect conditions. Sometimes history is made by two teams refusing to give an inch in the worst possible weather.

—— ❦ ——

1944 — THE NEW YORK RANGERS END A 25-GAME WINLESS STREAK 🏒

On November 11, 1944, the New York Rangers defeated the Detroit Red Wings 5–2, ending a 25-game NHL winless streak that had stretched across two seasons. The run included 21 losses and four ties, making it one of the league's most notorious slumps.

The victory ended months of frustration and entered hockey history.

🧩 TRIVIA: The streak stood at 0 wins, 21 losses, and 4 ties before the Rangers finally broke through against Detroit.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: In sport, sometimes the most satisfying victory is simply the one that ends the wait.

And that is November 11 on the sporting calendar: a day of individual brilliance, improbable records, and hard-earned relief.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

❓ HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY

On November 11, 1921, which U.S. president presided over the burial of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery?

[A] Woodrow Wilson

[B] Warren G. Harding

[C] Calvin Coolidge

[D] Herbert Hoover

Think it over before scrolling to the answer. 👀

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🌎 CLOSING

November 11 is often remembered through a single moment: the silence that followed the guns of the First World War. But the date's history is larger than an armistice.

It is also the day a nameless soldier was given a place of honor, Washington became a state, and Angola emerged from colonial rule. It reminds us that independence can be proclaimed without equality, that a ceasefire is not the same as lasting peace, and that remembrance must include the people whose names were never recovered.

The day also carries quieter achievements: a highway system that helped connect a continent, aircraft that transformed naval warfare, and a church vote that opened a door long closed to women.

History does not offer easy answers. It asks us to remember sacrifice without romanticizing war, to recognize freedom without ignoring injustice, and to understand that the work of building a better future begins after the ceremonies are over.

Honor those who served. Remember those who were lost. And never stop asking what kind of world their sacrifices were meant to make possible.

History has had its turn. Now go make yours. ✨

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

💋 SEND-OFF

If today's stories made you think, wonder, or see the past a little differently, pass the discoveries along. Share them with someone who loves history—or someone who has yet to discover just how extraordinary it can be.

Keep questioning. Keep discovering. The past always has another story to tell.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

📣 THERE'S MORE HISTORY WAITING!
