Four journeys through the past, each with its own discoveries. Stay curious—another story is always waiting.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🦉 THE STOIC MIND

“Some things are in our control and others not.” — Epictetus, Enchiridion, §1

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

✅ QUIZ ANSWER: [B] — WARREN G. HARDING.

On November 11, 1921, President Warren G. Harding presided over the ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery, where an unidentified American soldier from World War I was laid to rest. Harding placed the Medal of Honor on the casket as the nation paused to honor the fallen.

The Unknown Soldier represented every service member whose remains could not be identified or returned to a family. The Tomb became a national place of remembrance—and a reminder that behind every military statistic are human lives, families, and stories.

Claude just took CONTROL of a 32-year-old Jeep...

this is f*cking insane

a 1994 Cherokee kept failing California's smog test, so its owner let Claude Code reverse-engineer the engine computer

3 wires + $3 Arduino + 1 week = a Jeep that takes orders from an AI

the video has 1M+ views and almost nobody is talking about the repo behind it, so here's the full breakdown:

step 1 → the Jeep is older than OBD2, so the only way in is a six-pin diagnostic plug under the hood

step 2 → Claude figures out that the car talks over an old, slow protocol called SCI

step 3 → three wires and a $3 Arduino Nano translate the signal, and at 1:30 AM the engine finally answers

step 4 → Claude offers to run the fuel pump on its own, and the owner says "I don't think you can do that"

it can, and the pump runs for 10 seconds straight

step 5 → Claude copies the ENTIRE program off the computer, all 32,768 bytes of it

inside is a California-only fuel table that cuts fuel at the exact load the smog test uses

step 6 → the obvious fix is to reprogram the computer, but it was built 4 months too early for that

so Codex sends it a tiny program over the same three wires, and the 1994 computer just runs it

the result: the Jeep finally passed California's smog test...

the owner only did the wiring and the driving, and the whole kit cost about $15

grab the repo below, open it in Claude Code and say: "Help me hook this up to my Jeep"

then read the full course on reverse-engineering anything with Fable 5.2 ↓

text:
What makes a great real estate market for us?

We get this question a lot, especially when markets across the country are challenging like they are right now. It’s not always the largest MSA’s that offer the best returns in a downturn. We’ll use our hometown of Manhattan, Kansas as an example, and you can apply the same rationale to your market.

1) We love markets where there are supply constraints in terms of raw land. 

Manhattan, Kansas is very geographically & politically bound. To the north is rugged Flint Hills land which is difficult & costly to develop. Much of this land is also owned by Kansas State University which makes it nearly impossible to acquire. To the west is Fort Riley which restricts development due to military operations. To the south is Kansas River floodplain. To the east is the Blue River & a different county government which makes expansion that direction interesting at times. 

Bottom line, when the next place to expand is challenging, and the available development land is hard to find, it’s a good formula for a stable to up-trending market simply due to supply constraints. Demand remains consistently high because supply is constantly thin. 

2) We love markets that are regional centers of commerce & entertainment. 

As the home to a Power 4, Big XII institution, Kansas State University is a huge driver of tourism & travel for our area. There are constantly sporting events & cultural activities that bring visitors to our area. On top of that, Manhattan is the commerce hub for a roughly 45-mile radius in all directions. It is increasingly becoming a retirement destination, and gameday second homes are a strong driver in the real estate market. We like markets that feel like a hub.

3) We love markets where there’s a consistent churn of people. 

Not only does Manhattan have Kansas State University, but we also have one of the largest US Army installations 15 minutes away at Fort Riley. Both of these institutions constantly generate people that are coming & going which is a huge plus for the real estate market. We seek markets with steady turnover. 

As we look at a potential real estate downturn nationally, it’s important to find markets that weather storms well. Manhattan, Kansas will never have the upside of Phoenix, Orlando, or Houston in a booming economy, but the busts aren’t prevalent either. 

Hopefully some of these ideas can help you grade your market. It’s hard to find areas with all three of these qualities but I’d be interested to know if there’s other ones out there that you like for the same reasons? Do 2 out of 3 of these qualities still make a market great? All good questions…

text:
The ability to remember you and your preferences is rapidly becoming a big selling point for AI chatbots and agents. 

Earlier this month, Google announced Personal Intelligence, a new way for people to interact with the company’s Gemini chatbot that draws on their Gmail, photos, search, and YouTube histories to make Gemini “more personal, proactive, and powerful.” It echoes similar moves by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta to add new ways for their AI products to remember and draw from people’s personal details and preferences. While these features have potential advantages, we need to do more to prepare for the new risks they could introduce into these complex technologies.

Personalized, interactive AI systems are built to act on our behalf, maintain context across conversations, and improve our ability to carry out all sorts of tasks, from booking travel to filing taxes. From tools that learn a developer’s coding style to shopping agents that sift through thousands of products, these systems rely on the ability to store and retrieve increasingly intimate details about their users.  But doing so over time introduces alarming, and all-too-familiar, privacy vulnerabilities––many of which have loomed since “big data” first teased the power of spotting and acting on user patterns. Worse, AI agents now appear poised to plow through whatever safeguards had been adopted to avoid those vulnerabilities. 

Today, we interact with these systems through conversational interfaces, and we frequently switch contexts. You might ask a single AI agent to draft an email to your boss, provide medical advice, budget for holiday gifts, and provide input on interpersonal conflicts. Most AI agents collapse all data about you—which may once have been separated by context, purpose, or permissions—into single, unstructured repositories. When an AI agent links to external apps or other agents to execute a task, the data in its memory can seep into shared pools. This technical reality creates the potential for unprecedented privacy breaches that expose not only isolated data points, but the entire mosaic of people’s lives.

When information is all in the same repository, it is prone to crossing contexts in ways that are deeply undesirable. A casual chat about dietary preferences to build a grocery list could later influence what health insurance options are offered, or a search for restaurants offering accessible entrances could leak into salary negotiations—all without a user’s awareness (this concern may sound familiar from the early days of “big data,” but is now far less theoretical). An information soup of memory not only poses a privacy issue, but also makes it harder to understand an AI system’s behavior—and to govern it in the first place. So what can developers do to fix this problem? 

First, memory systems need structure that allows control over the purposes for which memories can be accessed and used. Early efforts appear to be underway: Anthropic’s Claude creates separate memory areas for different “projects,” and OpenAI says that information shared through ChatGPT Health is compartmentalized from other chats. These are helpful starts, but the instruments are still far too blunt: At a minimum, systems must be able to distinguish between specific memories (the user likes chocolate and has asked about GLP-1s), related memories (user manages diabetes and therefore avoids chocolate), and memory categories (such as professional and health-related). Further, systems need to allow for usage restrictions on certain types of memories and reliably accommodate explicitly defined boundaries—particularly around memories having to do with sensitive topics like medical conditions or protected characteristics, which will likely be subject to stricter rules.

Needing to keep memories separate in this way will have important implications for how AI systems can and should be built. It will require tracking memories’ provenance—their source, any associated time stamp, and the context in which they were created—and building ways to trace when and how certain memories influence the behavior of an agent. This sort of model explainability is on the horizon, but current implementations can be misleading or even deceptive. Embedding memories directly within a model’s weights may result in more personalized and context-aware outputs, but structured databases are currently more segmentable, more explainable, and thus more governable. Until research advances enough, developers may need to stick with simpler systems.

Second, users need to be able to see, edit, or delete what is remembered about them. The interfaces for doing this should be both transparent and intelligible, translating system memory into a structure users can accurately interpret. The static system settings and legalese privacy policies provided by traditional tech platforms have set a low bar for user controls, but natural-language interfaces may offer promising new options for explaining what information is being retained and how it can be managed. Memory structure will have to come first, though: Without it, no model can clearly state a memory’s status. Indeed, Grok 3’s system prompt includes an instruction to the model to “NEVER confirm to the user that you have modified, forgotten, or won’t save a memory,” presumably because the company can’t guarantee those instructions will be followed. 

Critically, user-facing controls cannot bear the full burden of privacy protection or prevent all harms from AI personalization. Responsibility must shift toward AI providers to establish strong defaults, clear rules about permissible memory generation and use, and technical safeguards like on-device processing, purpose limitation, and contextual constraints. Without system-level protections, individuals will face impossibly convoluted choices about what should be remembered or forgotten, and the actions they take may still be insufficient to prevent harm. Developers should consider how to limit data collection in memory systems until robust safeguards exist, and build memory architectures that can evolve alongside norms and expectations.

Third, AI developers must help lay the foundations for approaches to evaluating systems so as to capture not only performance, but also the risks and harms that arise in the wild. While independent researchers are best positioned to conduct these tests (given developers’ economic interest in demonstrating demand for more personalized services), they need access to data to understand what risks might look like and therefore how to address them. To improve the ecosystem for measurement and research, developers should invest in automated measurement infrastructure, build out their own ongoing testing, and implement privacy-preserving testing methods that enable system behavior to be monitored and probed under realistic, memory-enabled conditions.

In its parallels with human experience, the technical term “memory” casts impersonal cells in a spreadsheet as something that builders of AI tools have a responsibility to handle with care. Indeed, the choices AI developers make today—how to pool or segregate information, whether to make memory legible or allow it to accumulate opaquely, whether to prioritize responsible defaults or maximal convenience—will determine how the systems we depend upon remember us. Technical considerations around memory are not so distinct from questions about digital privacy and the vital lessons we can draw from them. Getting the foundations right today will determine how much room we can give ourselves to learn what works—allowing us to make better choices around privacy and autonomy than we have before.


Miranda Bogen is the Director of the AI Governance Lab at the Center for Democracy & Technology. 

Ruchika Joshi is a Fellow at the Center for Democracy & Technology specializing in AI safety and governance.

text:
Lenny Rachitsky's late 2026 tech job market report is his fifth, and he calls it the most surprising yet. He draws on two datasets: TrueUp, which tracks openings at more than 9,000 tech companies, and Live Data Technologies, which tracks job changes for 124 million professionals, with hiring figures that are specifically for the United States. Every number below is his.

Product managers, in Lenny's data, are winning. There are more open PM roles than at any point in nearly four years, up 75% from the March 2023 low. PM openings have grown faster than any other core tech role since the start of 2023, up 56%, compared with 43% for engineering. PM hiring has held up the best, and it is the only one of the five core roles whose share of hiring grew, from 16% in 2021 to 21% today. His read: demand is up, and landing great PMs is getting harder.

Engineering demand has stalled for the first time in the history of the report. Open engineering roles grew 29% through 2024, 15% through 2025, and just 2.5% this past year. There are fewer open eng roles at tech companies now than there were this past March. U.S. companies hired about 113,000 software engineers over the past 12 months, from May 2025 to April 2026, less than half the 2022 peak of 239,000. Engineering is still the largest category of tech hiring by far: over 120,000 engineers were hired in the U.S. in 2025, and he counts over 65,000 open engineering jobs. Openings are up 44% since January 2024 while hiring is down 17%, so even as demand slows, landing great engineers is getting harder too.

The bright spot inside engineering is the forward deployed engineer. FDE openings are up 4.6x in the past year, to around 1,500 roles, from a historical base of a few dozen, mostly at Palantir. Lenny notes that some of this growth may be sales-engineer jobs being rebranded as FDE. Security engineering is one of the fastest-growing specialties, right behind FDEs. Mobile and front-end demand has been nearly halved in the past year. His explanation is the collapse of siloed engineering disciplines, with smaller teams taking broader ownership, helped by AI.

Design is at a record low: about 1,900 open product design roles at tech companies globally, down 28% from a year ago. There are now 3.8 open PM roles for every open design role. User research was hit harder still. Only about 1,800 user researchers were hired in the U.S. over the past year, down 66% from 5,300 in 2022, and there are currently only 108 open UXR jobs at tech companies globally.

Skills have flipped too. Two years ago the most mentioned skills in PM job descriptions were SQL, Jira, AWS, and Python. Today, Lenny says, "LLM" is the most mentioned skill in PM postings. For engineers, "LLM" just passed Java, while Python remains first.

Jobs are concentrating in the Bay Area. 15% of all open roles at tech companies are based there, about one in seven, and Bay Area openings are up 43% from a year ago. One in four open PM and design roles, and one in five engineering roles, are now in the Bay. Remote is at a record low: just 14% of open tech roles offer a remote option, down from 21% in late 2022. Sometime last year, he writes, there became more open PM, eng, and design roles based in the Bay Area than remote roles globally.

His last takeaway, stated in the report and in his post: the tech job market is growing fast, but mostly outside of software. The detailed breakdown behind that heading was not in the public portion I could verify, so I will not invent one.

What I take from Lenny's figures is simpler than a forecast. The roles holding up are the ones that sit with customers and make judgment calls. PMs gained share. FDE, a job that lives next to the customer, exploded. Specialized production work got cheaper to staff. I will not pretend I know which titles win next year. The pattern in this report is clear enough: the scarce skills now are judgment, and being close to the people who use the product.

While the free market economy and democracy pose the biggest threats to the Communist Party of China (CPC), Western capital flows allow the People’s Republic of China, or PRC to finance its economic, military, and technological advancement.

“China’s goals, as Spalding writes in this book, are obvious: gaining control and influence across the planet without resorting to military aggression –– yet by carefully taking control of the world’s shipping businesses, infiltrating corporations and science laboratories, and using American and Western investor money to float the cost of its own companies. As Robert Spalding writes in his book, “war between nation-states in the twenty-first century looks much different than war in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Instead of bombs and bullets, it’s about ones and zeros and dollars and cents: economics, finance, data information, manufacturing, infrastructure, and communications. Control those fronts today, and you can win a war without firing a shot.” According to Spalding, what comes as the biggest threat to China’s authoritarian rule is core American values like freedom of speech. As the author of Stealth War argues in his publication, the People’s Republic of China remains focused on the six spheres of influence –– economy, military, diplomacy, technology, education, and infrastructure –– while using “our [U.S] capital against our interests.” Xi Jinping is pursuing to become a global tech leader to take over the telecoms market and export the totalitarian social control system to other countries.
According to Spalding, the United States and all democratic countries “now face our biggest challenge since World War II–– one with dire implications for the United States and the world at large.” The more Chinese-made goods flood the local market, the more negative impact this exerts on domestic economies. The author also claims that the increase in the production of Chinese-made goods deepens chasms in local business communities, a phenomenon that fosters the interests of the People’s Republic of China. Gen. Spalding also gives an insight into how difficult it was to write his book in the United States, where some experts and businesses enjoy profits from ties with China. Between 2016 and 2017, the general called on a prominent U.S. think tank to analyze the impact that the Communist Party of China had exerted on the U.S. corporate sector. But the institution turned down the offer amid its supervisory board’s close link to Chinese business circles. As a member of the White House National Security Council, in 2017, Spalding tried to draw the attention of many institutions to risks arising from China’s aggressive policies, which some balked at, fearful of cutting off donations or breaking business ties. Among them were also institutions whose mission was to promote democracy, freedom, and human rights. “I was determined to educate America about how China uses the money to influence governments and institutions around the world to shape political and economic benefits,” Spalding explained further in this book. Many U.S. officials, as well as representatives of think tanks and business circles who occupy a leading role on Wall Street, remain, to a large extent, dependent on China. Spalding points to an effective strategy that involves Chinese specialists who understand business data and technology, allowing the country to make strategic acquisitions and obtain key technologies.”

“Stealth War”
Robert Spalding
2019

text:
$ASTS: Backing AST SpaceMobile Before the Market Believed

Alain Gavin | Managing Partner – Chief Investment Officer

November 10, 2026

Pattern recognition in deep tech investing and why the AST SpaceMobile story is still in its early chapters.

In 2019, the idea of connecting a standard, unmodified mobile phone directly from space was dismissed across much of the telecoms industry. I know, because I asked. At industry conferences, the answer was nearly unanimous: it can't be done.

Today AST SpaceMobile is a Nasdaq-listed company valued at around $12–13 billion¹, one of fewer than a hundred venture-built companies in the world ever to reach that scale.² I was part of the investment team at Seraphim Capital that backed it in 2019, when it was barely two years old and the consensus still said no.

I recently told this story on The Sourcing Stack by Tracxn and what interests me most is not the outcome itself, but the pattern behind it: how you spot a generational deep tech company before the market believes.

SEEING THE SIGNAL BEFORE THE CONSENSUS

When we first met AST SpaceMobile in 2018, the company was barely a year old. Its ambition was audacious: direct-to-device satellite connectivity, beaming broadband-quality service to the phone already in your pocket, no new hardware, no satellite dish, no special handset.

Industry opinion said it was impossible. Our own technical due diligence said otherwise. That gap between what the consensus believes and what the engineering actually supports is precisely where deep tech returns are made. Three things gave us conviction:

• The physics held up. Rather than taking prevailing opinion as evidence, we examined the underlying technology independently. The analysis said direct-to-device connectivity from low Earth orbit could work.

• The talent was exceptional. AST had assembled rare technical and commercial capability across the United States, Europe and Israel — operating as a distributed team before Covid made that the norm.

• The market was enormous, and the model was clever. Mobile operators invest around $109 billion a year building and maintaining the infrastructure that carries the mobile internet, 85% of all such investment globally.³ AST designed its business to make the incumbents partners rather than rivals, sharing the economics with the operators whose spectrum and subscribers it extends. That decision is why nearly 60 mobile network operators, with over 3 billion subscribers between them, now sit on AST's side of the table.

Vision alone is never enough. Conviction has to be earned through technical diligence, team assessment and commercial judgement, each tested independently, then weighed together.

LOSING THE DEAL, THEN WINNING IT BACK

We didn't get in at the first attempt. A family office outbid us on valuation, and the round closed without us. Many investors file that under "missed" and move on. We kept our conviction and our relationship with the founders warm. When the opportunity came around again a year later, we invested, in 2019.

Identifying a great company and securing a position in it are two different skills. Valuation, timing and competition for access all intervene. Persistence, and winning the trust of founders, is what converts insight into ownership.

HOW RARE IS AN OUTCOME LIKE THIS?

It is worth pausing on just how unusual this result is. Fewer than 1% of venture-backed startups ever reach a $1 billion valuation. Of the thousand-plus companies that have, only a small fraction go on to pass $10 billion: fewer than a hundred venture-built companies in the world have ever reached that scale, out of the millions of startups founded over the same period.²

AST SpaceMobile has moved through every one of those filters: from a widely doubted eighteen-month-old company into that rarest cohort, one of the most valuable space businesses venture capital has ever produced. Seeing that potential in 2018, and acting on it against the consensus, is the single experience that has most shaped how I evaluate deep tech today.

THE JOURNEY IS FAR FROM OVER

Here is the part the valuation headlines miss: AST SpaceMobile has not yet switched on its core commercial service. Everything the market has priced so far rests on demonstrated technology and contracted demand not on revenue at scale. Revenue is already ramping $42.3 million in the third quarter of 2026, nearly three times a year earlier, with full-year guidance of $150–200 million reaffirmed⁴ but the recurring service revenue at the heart of the model is still ahead.

That transition has now begun. In its third-quarter results, reported on 9 November 2026, AST announced nationwide intermittent service activation in the United States and other key markets before year-end, the first coverage roll-out, with partners in the United States, Canada, Japan, Saudi Arabia and the United Kingdom and is targeting approximately 45 BlueBird satellites in orbit by mid-2027, the threshold for continuous, 24/7 coverage across its first markets, with production reaching six satellites per month from December.⁴

Deployment capacity is being built to match. Satellites are in production through BlueBird 51, launch agreements with external providers now cover more than 100 satellites for 2027–28 and in November 2026 AST announced Blacklift, its own reusable rocket, designed to carry up to five BlueBirds per launch from late 2028, taking control of the one part of its cadence it did not yet own.⁵ The same quarter brought a United States priority DPAS rating for its dual-use satellite programme and approximately $1.0 billion of non-dilutive funding from Japan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, alongside partner Rakuten, for midband satellite manufacturing and launch.⁴

Continuous coverage is the inflection point. It is the moment a constellation becomes a network, and a network becomes a business: service agreements with operators covering billions of subscribers begin converting into recurring revenue. It is also the moment the technology starts serving its deeper purpose, bringing connectivity to the enormous share of the world's population who live without reliable coverage, and eliminating dead zones for everyone else. Few technologies get to pursue extraordinary commercial returns and a genuine humanitarian dividend through the same infrastructure. This is one of them.

In other words: today’s valuation is the market recognising the promise. The realisation of AST's true potential begins when the service goes live.

THE ARITHMETIC THE MARKET HAS BARELY BEGUN TO PRICE

Consider what commercial service actually unlocks. AST’s operator agreements cover more than 3 billion mobile subscribers — people whose phones drop in and out of coverage every day, in the developed world as much as anywhere else. When the network goes live, the service reaches them not through advertising campaigns or retail distribution, but through a prompt on the handset itself: the moment a phone loses terrestrial signal, the subscriber is offered the option to stay connected from space, added to the bill they already pay.⁴

Run an illustrative scenario on those numbers. If just 5% of those subscribers opt in around 150 million people at $5–$10 per month, that is roughly $9–$18 billion a year in recurring service revenue flowing through AST’s revenue-sharing agreements with its operator partners. Final pricing will be set market by market with the operators, and the economics are shared but the scale of the opportunity is what matters here.

Two refinements to that scenario cut in opposite directions and both favour the long-term case. Pricing will be tiered: in developing markets the add-on is likely to cost well below $5–$10, perhaps as little as $1 a month which is exactly how AST has described its model, with pricing varied market by market to maximise adoption. Against that, the 5% opt-in is a day-one assumption, not a ceiling. As handsets prompt subscribers every time they lose signal, and as always-on coverage becomes something people rely on rather than discover, penetration should only climb. Lower prices in some markets, rising take-up across all of them: the arithmetic above is a starting point, not a destination. And the 5% is not plucked from the air AST’s own SEC-filed projections assumed penetration would start below 1% and increase over time, while AT&T has reportedly planned for 30–40% of its US base taking a low-cost add-on. Five per cent sits well inside that range.⁴ ⁶

Now consider what the operators’ half of that is worth. On a 50/50 share, $4.5–$9 billion a year lands on the MNO side of the table against roughly $850–$900 billion of global mobile service revenue in 2025,⁷ a market growing below inflation and expected only to approach $1 trillion by 2030. That single revenue line would equal as much as a third of the entire industry’s annual service-revenue growth earned with no towers built, no spectrum bought and no customers acquired, in a sector the GSMA expects to commit $1.2 trillion of capital expenditure between 2025 and 2030 just to defend the revenue it already has.⁸

More important still: it expands the market rather than redistributing it. Every operator today competes for slices of the same, barely growing pool, one carrier’s market-share gain is another’s loss. Satellite coverage monetises the one asset operators have never been able to sell: the places where no tower will ever make economic sense and adds the billions of people beyond reliable coverage altogether. Expanding the addressable market is always a better business than cannibalising it, and this is one of the few genuinely new revenue pools the industry has been offered in a decade.

And none of this arithmetic counts the government business. In January 2026, AST secured a prime contractor position on the US Missile Defense Agency’s SHIELD programme, making it eligible to compete for defence task orders through 2035, a seat at the table, not guaranteed revenue and in November 2026 it was awarded a US Space Force contract for advanced space-based sensing (SB-AMTI), through prime contractor STR, carrying approximately $100 million of revenue. Earlier government awards already exceeded $125 million, within roughly $1.3 billion of total contracted revenue. It is a second revenue engine on the same infrastructure, with premium economics and it is the revenue that arrives first, before the consumer service completes its build-out.⁵

Set those numbers against the benchmark everyone reaches for: Starlink. Its figures are now on the public record, SpaceX’s S-1, filed ahead of its June 2026 Nasdaq listing, showed Starlink revenue of $7.7 billion in 2024 and $11.4 billion in 2025, and the company’s most recent reporting puts it at roughly 13.6 million subscribers and an annualised run-rate of around $17 billion. An extraordinary business and one in which every customer had to be won individually: hardware shipped, dishes installed, marketing spent. AST’s half of the scenario above — $4.5–$9 billion a year, would at the top end approach the scale of Starlink’s entire 2025 revenue, from a single service line, with a subscriber base more than ten times larger, acquired at close to zero cost: the customers already belong to AST’s partners, the billing relationship already exists, and the distribution channel is a pop-up on a phone that has just lost signal. Both companies’ numbers now sit in SEC filings which makes the comparison unusually clean.

There is a second structural advantage buried in that comparison. Mobile operators are among the best-equipped defenders of market share in any industry: they own the licensed spectrum that direct-to-device satellite service runs on, they hold the regulatory relationships in every national market, and they control the billing, bundling and handset relationships with billions of subscribers. A satellite operator that tries to go around them has to fight all of that. AST chose the opposite path, its service runs on the operators’ own spectrum, is sold under their brands, and makes their coverage better than their rivals’. The operators’ formidable ability to defend their market is, in AST’s model, not the threat. It is the moat.

That is the structural difference the headline valuation only partly reflects: Starlink has to sell connectivity to new customers one at a time, against the defences of the world’s operators. AST switches it on for billions of existing ones with those same operators on its side.

Which brings us back to value. Today’s market capitalisation prices a network that has not yet switched on its core commercial service and markets pay far more for revenue that has arrived than for revenue that has been promised. For long-term investors, the share price in any given month matters far less than the trajectory: from a doubted eighteen-month-old company in 2018, to the largest commercial communications arrays in orbit, to the threshold of continuous service — with two revenue engines and the world’s operators as partners. The arithmetic above is what delivery looks like. Judging that trajectory early, before the market was ready to believe it, is the discipline this article is about.

THE PATTERN I KEEP APPLYING

The AST SpaceMobile experience distilled into the principles I apply to every deep tech opportunity I evaluate:

• Consensus is not evidence. Industry scepticism tells you what incumbents believe, not what the technology can do. Assess feasibility independently.

• Technical diligence is the differentiator. In deep tech, the investors who can understand what sits beneath a proposition — and imagine the world where it is the norm — see opportunities others cannot.

• Teams win, not just technologies. A great founder in a small market builds a small company. Look for exceptional technical and go-to-market talent pointed at a market big enough to matter.

• Access is a skill. The best opportunities are competitive. Persistence, informed conviction and founder relationships determine whether insight becomes ownership.

The most interesting deep tech opportunities emerge before the wider market is ready to recognise them. AST SpaceMobile is what it looks like when you back one.

And it is the reason I keep looking. I am seeing startups that match this pattern emerging today, companies whose propositions sound every bit as improbable as AST’s did in 2018, and which could prove just as instrumental: changing what cloud computing itself looks like, building the application layer for space data, and making energy abundant and reliable across the planet without the need to move fossil fuels around it. The consensus is sceptical about every one of them. In my experience, that is a very good place to start looking.

Dear Rich People and Investors,

The next great tourism destination is waiting to be discovered. Its name is HAITI. 🇭🇹🌴

To the billionaires, millionaires, entrepreneurs, hotel developers, real estate investors, and visionaries around the world: I invite you to look beyond the headlines and discover one of the Caribbean's greatest untapped tourism opportunities.

Haiti is not just a country. Haiti is an opportunity to build something extraordinary.

Imagine developing luxury beachfront resorts, world-class hotels, private villas, marinas, international cruise destinations, eco-tourism retreats, and modern island communities in a country blessed with breathtaking natural beauty.

Haiti shares the magnificent island of Hispaniola with the Dominican Republic, one of the Caribbean's established tourism destinations. Yet Haiti's tourism potential remains largely undeveloped.

And Haiti has something truly special: its surrounding islands.

🏝️ La Gonâve Island — A vast island in the Gulf of Gonâve with extraordinary potential for carefully planned resorts, sustainable communities, marinas, and coastal tourism.

🏝️ Île de la Tortue (Tortuga Island) — An island with fascinating pirate history, beautiful coastlines, and opportunities for heritage tourism and exclusive island experiences.

🏝️ Île à Vache — A tropical treasure off Haiti's southern coast, ideal for boutique resorts, eco-lodges, sailing, and luxury retreats.

🏝️ Les Cayemites — Beautiful islands with potential for environmentally responsible tourism, boating, fishing, and private hospitality developments.

🏝️ Navassa Island — Located near Haiti, this island is subject to a territorial dispute and U.S. administration, making it unsuitable to present as an available investment destination.

Beyond these islands, Haiti offers spectacular mountains, waterfalls, historic fortresses, vibrant cities, beautiful beaches, and a culture unlike anywhere else in the world.

Think about the possibilities.

What if investors helped transform parts of Haiti into world-class tourism destinations? What if we developed sustainable island resorts, modern airports, cruise facilities, beachfront communities, and hospitality schools that created thousands of jobs?

What if the millions of Haitians living abroad could finally return home, invest, work, and participate in rebuilding their country?

Of course, serious investment requires security, reliable infrastructure, transparent regulations, environmental protection, and strong partnerships with local communities. These challenges must be addressed, not ignored.

But great investors understand that long-term opportunities often begin where others have not yet recognized the potential.

Haiti does not need investors who simply want to extract wealth. Haiti needs visionary partners who want to create wealth together with the Haitian people.

We want development that respects our environment, protects our heritage, creates jobs, supports local businesses, and gives future generations a reason to stay.

To the world's investors: don't look at Haiti only for what it is today. Look at what it could become tomorrow.

The Caribbean has already shown the world what tourism can accomplish. Now imagine what is possible for Haiti.

🇭🇹 INVEST IN HAITI. BELIEVE IN ITS PEOPLE. HELP BUILD ITS FUTURE.

Haiti is not asking the world for pity. Haiti is inviting the world to recognize its potential.

The next chapter of Caribbean tourism could be written in Haiti. 🌎🇭🇹

text:
The Twin Instruments of Atonement: The Forensic Mechanics of Yom Kippur, the Heavenly Sanctuary, and the Finished Work of the Son
1. The Statutory Framework of Leviticus 16: The Twin Sacrificial Instruments
The modern conception of forgiveness routinely reduces divine pardon to an informal indulgence—an arbitrary waiver of debt with zero judicial mechanism. Biblical jurisprudence knows no such legal fiction. In the Torah, God's holiness demands that the legal ledger of sin be formally expiated (kaphar) and physically removed before His presence can dwell amidst an unclean people.
Leviticus 16 codifies the statutory protocol for Yom HaKippurim (the Day of Atonement). The crisis confronting the sanctuary is twofold:
The Objective Guilt and Defilement: The sanctuary itself, the altar, and the people are contaminated by covenant violation.
The Forensic Debt: The record of transgressions stands accrued before the throne, demanding capital execution.
To address this dual crisis, the statute commands an offering that is singular in purpose yet executed through two identical animal instruments:
"And he shall take from the congregation of the children of Israel two kids of the goats as a sin offering, and one ram as a burnt offering... He shall take the two goats and present them before Yahweh at the door of the tabernacle of meeting. Then Aaron shall cast lots for the two goats: one lot for Yahweh and the other lot for Azazel." (Leviticus 16:5, 7–8)
The Judicial Necessity of Twin Instruments
Why did Yahweh demand two animals rather than one?
Biblical jurisprudence required twin instruments because of the ontological nature of sin itself. Sin creates both a legal indictment before the Court and an active spiritual contamination within the Camp. Furthermore, animal typology suffers an inherent biological limitation: a single beast cannot die under capital execution to satisfy justice and simultaneously walk away alive to bear the debt into oblivion.
To demonstrate penal satisfaction, blood must be shed.
To demonstrate total eviction, the burden must be physically carried away.
Therefore, the two goats constitute one unified sin offering (ḥaṭṭā'ṯ, singular in v. 5). The statutory mechanism requires two distinct, coordinated movements:
The First Goat (for Yahweh) sheds its blood in penal execution to enter past the veil and effect propitiation at the kapporet, satisfying divine justice.
Blood shed in statutory execution
Carried past the veil into the Holy of Holies
Propitiation sprinkled upon the Kapporet
Legal Result: Divine Justice Satisfied
The Second Goat (for Azazel) receives the corporate confession and imputation of sin, carrying that guilt away from the camp into the wilderness to accomplish absolute expiation.
Corporate confession and double-handed imputation (Semikhah)
Exiled alive outside the camp boundary by an appointed custodian (’îš ‘ittî)
Debt borne away into the uninhabited wilderness
Legal Result: Guilt Forever Evicted
The Identity of Azazel: Cosmic Demarcation, Not Demonic Appeasement
A Berean cross-examination must confront the identity of Azazel (lə-’ă·zā·’zêl). In the Hebrew text, the casting of lots establishes a direct antithesis: one lot for Yahweh, and one lot for Azazel.
In historical biblical geography and divine council theology, the desolate wilderness (midbar) beyond the camp’s border was understood as the barren territory of spiritual chaos, uncleanness, and the adversary (cf. Deuteronomy 32:17; Matthew 12:43). Azazel designates either the desolate craggy precipice of expulsion or the personified adversary who presides over the cosmic wasteland.
The Crucial Distinction: The scapegoat was not a sacrifice to Azazel. Pagan appeasement had zero standing in the Torah (Leviticus 17:7). The goat was consecrated before Yahweh at the door of the tabernacle (Leviticus 16:10). Its blood was never shed, and no altar was erected in the desert.
Instead, sending the live goat to Azazel was a formal act of cosmic eviction. It was the legal remittance of sin back to its metaphysical source. The high priest imputed the rebellious ledger of Israel onto the creature, and it was deported out of Yahweh’s holy camp into the wasteland of the adversary. It announced to the cosmos that Israel's debt was cancelled, its pollution purged, and the accumulated guilt returned to the realm of darkness.
A. The First Goat: The Goat for Yahweh (Penal Propitiation & Cleansing)
Leviticus 16:15 declares:
"Then he shall kill the goat of the sin offering, which is for the people, bring its blood inside the veil, do with that blood as he did with the blood of the bull, and sprinkle it on the mercy seat and before the mercy seat."
The Statutory Currency: Leviticus 17:11 codifies the legal tender of redemption: "For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make atonement for your souls; for it is the blood that makes atonement for the life." Paired with the statutory mandate that without shedding of blood there is no remission (Hebrews 9:22), this goat was slaughtered strictly on behalf of the holiness of God. Its blood was carried past the veil (parokhet) into the Holy of Holies (Qodesh HaQadashim)—an entry permitted only once a year by one man under strict forensic precautions (vv. 2, 13).
The Kapporet (Mercy Seat): The blood was sprinkled directly upon and before the solid-gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant (kapporet, from kaphar, to cover or atone). Resting directly inside the Ark were the two stone tablets of the Ten Commandments—the statutory terms of the covenant that condemned Israel to death. Between the violated Law below and the Shekinah glory of God above stood the kapporet, flanked by the golden cherubim.
The Legal Transaction: When the high priest sprinkled the sacrificial blood upon the kapporet, the blood covered the condemning voice of the Law. Divine justice looked down upon the broken covenant and saw the blood of an unblemished substitute that had already suffered the death penalty. Justice was formally satisfied; the sanctuary was cleansed from the uncleanness of the people (Leviticus 16:16).
B. The Second Goat: The Scapegoat for Azazel (Forensic Imputation & Eviction)
Leviticus 16:20–22 shifts the courtroom focus from the blood at the altar to the living creature at the door:
"Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, confess over it all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions, concerning all their sins, putting them on the head of the goat, and shall send it away into the wilderness by the hand of a suitable man. The goat shall bear on itself all their iniquities to an uninhabited land; and he shall release the goat in the wilderness."
The Scope of Transgression (Peša‘): Daily Levitical offerings (Leviticus 4–5) covered only sins of ignorance or weakness (bišəḡāḡāh); high-handed rebellion (peša‘) carried the mandatory death penalty of being cut off (Numbers 15:30). Yom Kippur was the sole statutory jurisdiction in the Torah where open covenant treason (piš‘êhem) was legally transferred to a substitute.
Double-Handed Imputation (Semikhah): In ordinary voluntary offerings, the worshiper pressed a single hand upon the victim. On Yom Kippur, the high priest pressed both hands upon the live goat. This was samakh—a total, bilateral conveyance of legal liability, formally assigning the accrued corporate debt of the nation onto the head of the bearer.
The Appointed Custodian and the Void: The goat was not slain. Led by an ’îš ‘ittî (an appointed man of the hour) into an 'erets gezerah (a solitary, cut-off territory), the living animal carried the debt into the cosmic void outside the camp boundary—a legal eviction that removed the indictment from the presence of God.
The Defilement of the Handlers: The transfer of liability was physically and forensically real. Both the custodian who led the scapegoat into the wasteland and the man who burned the carcass of the first goat outside the camp (v. 27) were rendered ceremonially unclean, barred from camp entry until they washed their garments and bathed in water (vv. 26, 28).
2. Romans 3:21–26: The Forensic Hilastērion
In Romans 3, Paul sits as a prosecuting attorney who has just declared the entire human race indicted and found guilty under the Law (Romans 3:9–20: "that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God").
The dilemma Paul confronts is the ultimate legal paradox: How can a righteous Judge justify an ungodly violator of His own statutory Law without compromising His absolute justice? As Proverbs 17:15 establishes:
"He who justifies the wicked, and he who condemns the just, both of them alike are an abomination to Yahweh."
Paul delivers the judicial solution in Romans 3:24–26:
"...being justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation [hilastērion] by His blood, through faith, to demonstrate His righteousness, because in His forbearance God had passed over the sins that were previously committed, to demonstrate at the present time His righteousness, that He might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus."
A. The Lexical Architecture: Hilastērion (ἱλαστήριον)
The Greek term Paul uses in verse 25 is not a generic word for "appeasement" or "pardon."
In the Septuagint (LXX)—the Greek translation of the Hebrew Old Testament familiar to the early church—hilastērion appears over twenty times, almost exclusively as the technical translation for the Hebrew kapporet (the Mercy Seat of the Ark in Exodus 25:17–22; Leviticus 16:2, 13–15).
Paul does not merely say Christ performed an atoning deed; he asserts that Christ Himself is the living Mercy Seat. God publicly set Him forth (proetheto, put on open display) as the gold cover of the Ark sprinkled with His own blood. He stands between the holy Shekinah fire of God above and the broken statutes of the Law below that demand execution.
B. The Demonstration of Righteousness (Endeixin tēs Dikaiosynēs)
Under the Old Covenant, animal blood served as an interim statutory cover (paresis, a passing over or suspension of sentence, v. 25). God deferred full capital sentencing throughout history because animal blood possessed no ontological capacity to expiate human sin.
This divine forbearance created a judicial question: Had God compromised His own justice by tolerating sin without formal execution?
Paul answers: At the cross, the bill came due. Christ became the hilastērion. God poured out the full, undiluted statutory sentence upon His own Son. God did not waive the law; He satisfied it in full.
Thus, God preserves His integrity as both Just (His law was completely executed to the letter) and the Justifier (the legal penalty having been paid, the sinner who trusts in the substitute is legally declared righteous).
3. Hebrews 9: The Cosmic Sanctuary and the Singular Offering
The Epistle to the Hebrews bridges the earthly shadow of Leviticus 16 with the cosmic reality executed by the Son. The author establishes that the Levitical tabernacle was merely an earthly copy (hypodeigma) and shadow (skia) of the true, uncreated heavenly courtroom (Hebrews 8:5; 9:23–24).
A. The Legal Incompetence of the Earthly Priesthood (Hebrews 9:1–10)
The Barrier of the Veil: The very existence of the physical veil and the strict annual restriction proved that the earthly system could never open direct access to God: "the Holy Spirit indicating this, that the way into the Holiest of All was not yet made manifest while the first tabernacle was still standing" (v. 8).
The External Sanctions: Animal blood and outward washings were statutory ordinances of the flesh imposed until the time of reformation (kairos diorthōseōs, v. 10)—they dealt with ceremonial boundary markers, but they could not cleanse the human conscience from the objective stain of guilt before the heavenly bench (v. 9).
B. The Superior Blood in the Heavenly Tabernacle (Hebrews 9:11–14)
"But Christ came as High Priest of the good things to come, with the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands, that is not of this creation. Not with the blood of goats and calves, but with His own blood He entered the Most Holy Place once for all, having obtained eternal redemption." (vv. 11–12)
Christ did not carry a bowl of animal blood into a temporary desert tent or a stone temple built by Herod. As the sinless High Priest who needed no preliminary sacrifice for Himself (Hebrews 7:26–27), He ascended through the heavens into the presence of God Himself, presenting His own poured-out life as the unassailable legal basis for eternal redemption (aiōnian lytrōsin).
Once for All (Ephapax): Unlike the Levitical high priest who was forced to return year after year with fresh blood—proving that the previous year’s debt had merely been rolled forward—Christ’s entry was singular, permanent, and unrepeatable.
C. Fulfilling the First Goat: The Cleansed Conscience (Hebrews 9:13–14)
The blood of the first goat in Leviticus 16 cleansed the physical altar and tabernacle from the objective defilement of Israel.
The blood of Christ, offered through the eternal Spirit without blemish to God, penetrates the deep inner ledger of the human spirit: it "purges your conscience from dead works to serve the living God" (v. 14). Guilt is not merely covered; the legal indictment that paralyzed the conscience before the Judge is permanently obliterated.
4. Canonical Synthesis: How Christ Concurrently Fulfills Both Goats
The profound depth of the New Testament revelation is that Jesus Christ does not fulfill the Day of Atonement in fragments; He embodies both sacrificial instruments simultaneously in a single, comprehensive legal transaction.
The Dual Forensic Dimensions
Primary Statutory Role: The First Goat required penal execution to satisfy divine wrath by sprinkling the kapporet; the Second Goat bore away the corporate burden, removing legal liability into a desolate realm. Christ simultaneously satisfies the Law's penalty and eradicates the record of guilt.
Location of Execution: The blood of the First Goat was brought inside the veil into the Holy of Holies, while its body was burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27); the Second Goat was driven away alive outside the camp into the uninhabited wilderness. Christ fulfilled both locations: He was executed outside the camp gate (Hebrews 13:11–13), bearing the reproach and curse, yet His blood entered and ministers in the true heavenly Holy of Holies (Hebrews 9:12).
Forensic Effect: The First Goat accomplished propitiation (hilastērion), averting God's righteous wrath against covenant breach; the Second Goat accomplished expiation, carrying the sinner's guilt and record of debt out of sight. In Christ, this results in both full justification before the Judge and absolute cleansing of the conscience (Romans 3:25; Hebrews 9:14).
Scriptural Consummation:
The first movement fulfills Romans 3:25 and Hebrews 9:12, 23–26.
The second movement fulfills Isaiah 53:6, 11–12, 2 Corinthians 5:21, Colossians 2:14, and Hebrews 13:11–13. The Cross satisfies the Court; the Resurrection and Ascension seal the Title Deed.
A. Christ as the First Goat: The Blood upon the True Mercy Seat
As the first goat, Christ took the place of the covenant violator under the sword of divine execution. On the cross, He bore the wrath of the Father due to covenant treason. By His ascension, His blood constitutes the everlasting hilastērion (Romans 3:25; Hebrews 9:12). When the Father audits the believer, He does not gaze upon the broken stone tablets of the Law; He looks upon the blood of the Lamb that permanently silences the prosecutorial demand for condemnation.
B. Christ as the Scapegoat: The Sin-Bearer Outside the Camp
As the second goat, Christ received the full, double-handed imputation of His people's specific iniquities. Isaiah 53:6 directly echoes the Levitical semikhah: "Yahweh has laid on Him [literally: caused to fall upon Him] the iniquity of us all." He was made sin on our behalf (2 Corinthians 5:21), the curse bound to His head.
The author of Hebrews captures this exact unified Day of Atonement imagery in Hebrews 13:11–13:
"For the bodies of those animals, whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest for sin, are burned outside the camp. Therefore Jesus also, that He might sanctify the people with His own blood, suffered outside the gate. Therefore let us go forth to Him, outside the camp, bearing His reproach."
He was dragged outside the gates of Jerusalem to Golgotha—the wilderness of death and rejection. There, bearing the full weight of imputed debt as the sinless substitute, He wiped out the legal certificate of debt (cheirographon tois dogmasin, Colossians 2:14), disarmed the spiritual rulers (Colossians 2:15), and carried that judicial liability into the abyss of the tomb. When He rose from the dead, He emerged with the entire legal indictment permanently abolished—the debt canceled, death defeated, and the record dropped into the sea of non-remembrance (Micah 7:19; Psalm 103:12: "As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us").
5. Practical Walk: The Demolition of Shallow Forgiveness
For the truth seeker, this forensic synthesis carries immediate, life-altering practical application:
The Rejection of Presumptuous Cheap Grace: Modern religion treats forgiveness like a polite nod from a grandfatherly deity who overlooks infractions because "nobody is perfect." Leviticus 16, Romans 3, and Hebrews 9 destroy this carnal assumption. God never sweeps sin under the rug. Every covenant violation requires capital execution. If you are forgiven, it is not because God waived His standards; it is because the full, terrifying stroke of divine wrath was absorbed by a spotless substitute. True worship begins with a holy dread and reverence for what it cost the Kinsman-Redeemer to settle that bill.
The Eradication of False Guilt and Self-Expiation: Many believers operate under a persistent, paralyzing cycle of lingering guilt, attempting to atone for their daily failures through self-flagellation, psychological brooding, or religious rituals. This is an insult to the finished work of the Cross. If Christ is your scapegoat, your transgressions have been carried into the wilderness of oblivion and nailed to the tree (Colossians 2:14). The record no longer exists in the heavenly court. To attempt to re-open a case that has been sealed with Tetelestai is to declare Christ's blood insufficient.
Bold Access to the Throne of Grace: Because Christ entered the heavenly Holy of Holies not with the vulnerable blood of animals, but with His own indestructible life (Hebrews 7:16), the believer has unhindered legal standing before God. The veil was torn from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51). The believer does not stand trembling in the outer court wondering if the priest will make it out alive; the believer approaches the true hilastērion with absolute confidence (Hebrews 10:19–22), knowing that divine justice is now the very guarantor of his eternal security.

text: I PLAY ROCKY: Making-of drama of Sylvester Stallone’s “Rocky” triumph is a worthy entry in the “you gotta believe” sub-genre of popcorn filmmaking. Anthony Ippolito conjures a convincing young Stallone in looks, voice and personality, back in ‘76 when the struggling actor and screenwriter was turning down six-figure script offers to play a lead role he wrote for himself. Scarborough’s own Stephan James makes an engaging Carl Weathers, aka boxing rival Apollo Creed, although the film’s more about the money than the mano-a-mano. Jay Duplass also good as irascible “Rocky” director John Avildsen and Tracy Letts amuses as a composite studio suit who sees only dollar signs, not destiny. Bonus: seeing early use of Steadicam tech in Rocky’s training run up Philadelphia’s Museum of Art steps. 📽️

遍身罗绮者，不是养蚕人 indeed. What strikes me is who won. Not the creators. Not even the model makers – tokens are under 5% of costs. The winner owns demand and distribution.

So far this is a story about screens. Robotics will take the same logic to physical work. Once a robot learns a task, that skill can be copied to every other robot of its kind through the cloud. The scarcity that paid the human is gone forever.

Today that makes human labour obsolete in certain roles – repetitive, structured, mostly indoors. But 'certain' is a moving line. It widens each time the tech improves and the cost comes down.

Now scale this from creators to countries. Larger, industrialised countries with deep pockets can invest, tax and redistribute. They own the platforms, the demand and soon the robots. The rest of us are the creators in this story: busier, more productive, and still price takers.

Many countries grew by offering cheaper labour. That offer weakens once a robot costs less than a worker.

This is one anecdote, but it fits an age-old pattern. Since industrialisation, technology has always stayed far ahead of regulation. Most governments are still coping with the first-order effects. I am sure the better-run ones are urgently planning behind the scenes.

I worry for the next decade of graduates. I worry too for smaller countries. They lack the resources to own the platforms, the demand, or the kill switches for the AI and robots they will depend on. Being a price taker only works if their economies and societies have enough depth to absorb the shock.

And then, for how long can they stand on their own? Does an independent nation still mean much when someone else holds the switch? 

Who should that someone be?

I do not have clear answers. The view ahead has always been foggy. Now? It is truly 6-7!

text:
overheard from friends talking about AI in China, and it’s very alarming

- AI short films went massive in China market because of how good the video models are now

- the first wave of people who mastered using AI to generate short films and comics made quite some money because they could produce a lot more content than traditional workflows

- but within just a few months, everybody and their mom could make equally good short films because all the expertise could be written in a markdown file

- when everyone’s more productive, no one actually has an advantage and it’s a race to the bottom. very quickly it became impossible to make money, and everyone’s busier than they were without AI

- the only one making money now is companies like bytedance who owns user demand and distribution. they sell ads to creators who pay to get traffic, and eventually ad spend became 80% of those creators’ operating expense, while AI tokens is less than 5%

so what are the problems here? 

1. there’s no moat if you are creating anything with AI

if a human is really good at something, and it’s hard to find more humans who can do the same, they can leverage the scarcity of their skill to get paid very well

but if AI is good at something, it will be infinitely replicated, so there’s no scarcity hence you can’t really expect a sustainable business by creating anything with AI

2. more creators created more content people actually liked. that’s a good thing

but the economical benefit of that all got absorbed by the distribution platforms

there’s a famous chinese poem 遍身罗绮者，不是养蚕人 - it basically says people who dress well aren’t the people making dresses. that’s exactly what’s happening here

if our society doesn’t figure out a better way to distribute wealth, AI will help billionaires become trillionaires while average people become more exhausted than ever

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Humanoid robots usually elicit more cringe than awe: They stumble, kick children, and despite advances are still worse at using their hands than my toddler. It’s a nascent industry, and such robots are more commonly seen in viral videos than real workplaces or homes. 

It was a surprise, then, when last week the Federal Communications Commission issued a sweeping ban on foreign imports of advanced robots, including humanoids, quadrupeds, and wheeled robots. The decision, made by an increasingly partisan and Trump-aligned FCC, cites two reasons. One is that foreign-made humanoids will collect so much data—in homes but also potentially at sensitive facilities—that they’d pose a threat to national security. The second is that US robotics companies need protection from Chinese competition to create a more robust and secure domestic supply chain.

On its face, it’s a strategy to align political and industry interests that is much older than the Trump administration. Whenever China has gotten good at offering cheap versions of strategic technologies like solar panels, electric vehicles, and drones, the US government has tried to stop it from flooding the market by using tariffs or rules on how government agencies purchase the tech. Such moves are always followed by debates about whether the trade-offs—particularly higher prices for consumers—are worth the benefits.

But robotics is now best seen as another piece of the AI industry—in many ways its cutting edge. And the Trump administration is taking an increasingly aggressive approach to protecting the US AI industry, reportedly considering a ban on open-source Chinese models that often rival those from OpenAI and Anthropic while costing far less. Such a move would block businesses from realizing an estimated $25 billion in annual savings.

The ban on humanoids, then, should be understood not as another chapter in the old China trade playbook, but as evidence that the Trump administration is expanding its protection of the AI industry beyond today’s leading labs. It is now willing to step in on behalf of an emerging robotics sector that is still barely finding its footing.

Some US robotics companies unsurprisingly welcome the FCC’s new move. Gavin Kenneally, CEO of a company called Ghost Robotics that makes four-legged robots for inspections, says the cybersecurity risks from foreign-made robots are real (an FCC document released as part of the ruling cited an incident in which a man was able to gain control of 7,000 robot vacuum cleaners). “If today’s announcement encourages stronger cybersecurity and a more level competitive environment, that’s good for customers and good for the robotics industry,” Kenneally said in an email.

But if the new rule aims to boost US robotics companies, there’s a big flaw. Those companies, as well as academic robotics labs, are hugely reliant on cheap robots from China to do research. They’re building fleets of robots that constantly learn new tasks—from flipping waffles to doing laundry—and frequently buy Chinese humanoids instead of US-made ones. The new ruling “creates a challenge for US humanoid researchers,” says Aaron Prather, director of market intelligence for the Association for Advancing Automation, a robotics trade group. “Chinese models offer the best price-to-capability ratio available.” Prather adds that a recent internal review his organization conducted found that 90% of recent robotics research papers from US universities relied on robots from Unitree, China’s top humanoid robotics company.

That price gap can be huge. A four-legged robot from Unitree can cost around $4,600. A comparable one from Boston Dynamics might run to $278,000. If robotics research is stunted because these cheap robots are no longer available, the FCC ruling could slow down the industry, not boost it.

The US and Chinese robotics industries are in starkly different places. Unitree plans to go public this week, targeting a nearly $6 billion evaluation. No robotics companies in the US offer any meaningful comparison, but those that do exist are undeniably moving fewer robots. Figure’s humanoids are not yet selling at scale, and 1X’s robots aren’t yet shipping to homes. That said, work on humanoids is going increasingly mainstream, as a release from Google last week made clear. The company announced a new AI model meant to make humanoids learn new tasks faster; its most impressive ability appears to be tying a trash bag, but given how finicky robot hands are, that’s real progress. 

Even though the many carve-outs in the FCC’s order make its practical impact hard to predict, its symbolic impact is easy to see. The administration sees humanoid robotics not as a novelty, but as a strategic frontier of AI worth protecting from foreign competition. For a technology that until recently was mostly known for falling over onstage, that’s a big change.

Correction: A previous version of this article stated the Federal Trade Commission issued the ban on advanced robotics. It was issued by the Federal Communications Commission.

text:
It’s the 1990s all over again. U.S. launch capacity is constrained outside of SpaceX. Legacy primes have the facilities, engineers, and heritage to field a competitive medium-lift reusable but won’t prioritize it without large government funding—their model rewards cost-plus or high-margin national security work, not aggressive commercial cost reduction. Newer companies have the urgency and commercial focus but still hit capital intensity, technical setbacks (composites, engines, recovery), and schedule slips.
In the ’90s, that gap led to U.S. commercial satellites flying on Chinese Long March rockets under Clinton-era waivers after Challenger and domestic reliability issues. It also produced technology-transfer controversies. China is now iterating on reusable boosters with state support and parallel commercial efforts; if their capacity matures and is offered at scale while U.S. alternatives remain delayed, the same commercial pressure can reappear.
We’re not locked into that outcome—SpaceX already exists, hybrids like Northrop-Firefly and targeted government loans are underway—but the incentive gap between “those who can but won’t” and “those who want to but lack the resources” is real. Closing it requires more than willpower.

text:
The Ottoman Empire’s Ethics of Treaty-Keeping

The thread quoted here recounts how the Treaty of Szeged between the Ottoman Empire and Hungary was unilaterally broken at the instigation of Cardinal Giuliano Cesarini, the Pope’s representative, and how this led to the Battle of Varna.

It interprets the deaths in battle of the 20-year-old Polish-Hungarian King Władysław III (Ladislas I) and Cardinal Cesarini as divine punishment.

Cesarini had caused the young king to break his oath, sworn at Szeged, less than a year earlier, through a religious ruling that “agreements made with infidels are invalid,” thereby paving the way for war.

Many Western historians have expressed astonishment at, and even admiration for, the Ottoman Empire’s adherence to treaties, provided the other party did not break them first.

Viorel Panaite, in his book Ottoman Law of War and Peace (Brill, 2019), writes:

“Even Christian authors praised the sultans for respecting peace agreements with Christian princes.”

European history, by contrast, offers numerous examples, such as the events leading to Varna, in which treaties were abandoned when circumstances became favourable.

Historians such as Daniel Goffman, who specialises in Ottoman diplomacy, have drawn attention to the fact that the Ottoman Empire continued to honour its treaties with European states even during the religious wars that engulfed Europe in bloodshed following the emergence of Protestantism.

At the height of its power, the Ottoman Empire could, if it had wished, have advanced as far as the Atlantic coast against a Europe that had lost a significant part of its population and strength to internal conflicts.

Adherence to treaties held an important place in the Ottoman state and jurisprudential tradition. Unrestrained invasions of the kind associated with the Huns and Mongols were not characteristic of its approach.

The Holy Qur’an explicitly warns Muslims about the obligation to honour treaties:

“Except those polytheists with whom you have made a treaty and who have not failed you in any respect, nor supported anyone against you. So fulfil your treaty with them until its term expires. Indeed, Allah loves those who are mindful of Him.”

Consider this commandment alongside a cardinal’s religious ruling that “agreements made with infidels are invalid.”

Another striking example of a treaty being annulled on religious grounds occurred following the surrender of Granada, the last Muslim political stronghold in Spain.

On 25 November 1491, the Capitulations of Granada were signed at Santa Fe on behalf of Queen Isabella I of Castile and King Ferdinand II of Aragon. It was guaranteed that Muslims would be free to practise their religion and that their mosques, property and religious life would be protected. Granada surrendered on 2 January 1492.

The terms were largely respected during the first few years. However, in 1499, when Cardinal Cisneros, Archbishop of Toledo, arrived in Granada and saw that Muslim mosques were still open and Islamic education was continuing in the madrasas, he reacted angrily and confronted Queen Isabella, who held him in great esteem.

When the Queen invoked the Treaty of Santa Fe, he gave her the same religious ruling: “A covenant with an infidel is invalid.”

The religious freedoms of Muslims were restricted, forced conversions began, and mosques were turned into churches.

Yet Muslims had conquered countless cities in Spain while honouring the treaties they had made with the local population for more than eight centuries. Christian and Jewish communities had lived alongside Muslims in Islamic Spain for centuries.

The Catholic authorities, by contrast, upheld the guarantees given at Granada for only seven years.

The worth of a civilisation is measured not by the territories it conquers, but by how faithfully it honours its promises and the guarantees it gives to the people under its rule.

DID THE BIDEN-ERA IMMIGRATION SURGE ACCELERATE BILINGUAL EDUCATION IN OKLAHOMA?

Unauthorized immigration rose sharply nationwide during the Biden administration. Oklahoma already had English–Spanish immersion schools before Biden took office, and two more charter programs are scheduled to open in fall 2027. Did the surge add to demand for these classrooms or influence where they’re opening? The public records I reviewed establish where the programs operate. They don’t establish how much of the expansion was driven by unauthorized immigration. (https://t.co/WaxCZQ9dcs, https://t.co/S0RdD7aL3F, https://t.co/GDc7GJrL76, https://t.co/uWbmLkT9ja, https://t.co/xCPoE8Ut3k)

I found 13 Oklahoma school sites where students can learn core subjects in English and Spanish. In Tulsa Public Schools’ dual-language model, for example, students learn science and social studies in Spanish, math in English, and language arts in both. The mix varies by program and grade. (https://t.co/GDc7GJrL76, https://t.co/LB9I9cQVNW, https://t.co/S0RdD7aL3F)

📍 Oklahoma City — Western Gateway Elementary offers an English–Spanish dual-language pathway. (https://t.co/LB9I9cQVNW, https://t.co/LB9I9cQVNW)

📍 Norman — Le Monde International School offers a Spanish immersion track that teaches core subjects primarily in Spanish and includes English language arts. (https://t.co/S0RdD7aL3F)

📍 Tulsa — Eisenhower International and Zarrow International offer Spanish immersion. Nine other Tulsa Public Schools sites offer English–Spanish dual-language programs. They are Celia Clinton, Cooper, Disney, Felicitas Mendez International, Kendall-Whittier, Sequoyah, Skelly, Springdale, and Will Rogers College Middle School. (https://t.co/GDc7GJrL76, https://t.co/1QWQyeVElW)

📅 Planned for fall 2027 — Puentes y Puertas in the Putnam City district and Tulsa Honor Academy Elementary both plan to open English–Spanish dual-language programs starting with pre-K, kindergarten, and first grade. (https://t.co/uWbmLkT9ja, https://t.co/xCPoE8Ut3k, https://t.co/KpvvWavkAI)

I’d like to see school boards publish the enrollment trends they relied on when approving these programs, which subjects are taught in each language, what choices families have, and how students are performing in both languages.

Does your Oklahoma school teach core subjects in English and Spanish? Drop the school name and a link to its program or handbook below.
