text:
A Robot Demo Is Not a Result

This article first appeared in my newsletters on LinkedIn, from my interview with Dr. Saxena (@AshutoshSaxena_) of @TorqueAGI. The full interview is linked at the end.

Alyssa Christensen

"We judge results by what a customer can measure, in speed, throughput and savings, and we do not count a demonstration as a result," wrote Dr. Ashutosh Saxena, founder and CEO of TorqueAGI, in written follow-up answers supplied on October 30, 2026.

A robot on a construction site has to deal with the surface in front of it, the space around it and the people who share it. Conditions shift as the work progresses. A successful demonstration gives us a glimpse of what a machine can do, while a live job reveals what it can keep doing as those circumstances vary. That gap became the focus of my conversation with Dr. Saxena about TorqueAGI, the company he leads. Its product is an intelligence layer designed to help existing machines reason about the physical world and adapt to the tasks their operators need them to perform.

I spoke with him on October 23, 2026 after his representatives at Moat Global wrote to me about my article on human fragility and physical AI. I wanted to know what happens when software that can interpret a situation also has the ability to move something heavy, work at height or act beside a person. The opportunity is substantial: machines could take on more dangerous and repetitive duties while people set the goals and oversee the results. The practical questions concern how the system learns a task, what it has demonstrated and how its behavior is constrained when its understanding is incomplete. His interview and his written follow-up answers of a week later offer a useful account of that approach, along with several boundaries that matter when evaluating it.

Adaptability for machines already at work

TorqueAGI supplies intelligence to the companies that build and operate industrial machinery. Dr. Saxena described it in our interview as "an add-on to the existing robot software," with the aim of giving the hardware additional capabilities. In his written answers he said each customer runs a private model that starts from the company's base platform and learns within that site under that customer's procedures. The initial information includes a description of the machine and the job, current operating rules, equipment logs and order histories, followed by a small number of demonstrations. The firm then tests the system on the buyer's own premises against a chosen performance measure before widening its role. The intended value is easy to state: a unit should use what it knows about its task and surroundings to handle the ordinary variation in the work.

The product names reflect the settings TorqueAGI is pursuing. TorqueFlow covers warehouse and logistics tasks such as unloading, sorting, kitting and packing. TorqueFocus addresses inspection and quality control, with defect detection and measurement. TorqueField serves outdoor and heavy equipment, including agriculture, airports and construction. In his written responses of October 30, 2026 Dr. Saxena listed TorqueBuild for assembly as still in development. Those distinctions separate the work the company says it supports today from the capabilities it is continuing to build.

What a changing job site asks of a robot

A construction partnership makes the physical problem tangible. TorqueAGI's June 29, 2026 post describes the JLG subsidiary Canvas automating the mudding, sanding and painting of interior walls on active building sites. The manufacturer's page calls its RO2330 a "worker-controlled intelligent drywall machine," which keeps the person's role visible in the product itself. In the same announcement TorqueAGI credits its software with helping the robot reason about geometry, surfaces and forces as circumstances change. The collaboration illustrates the kind of challenge the startup is addressing, while the precise contribution of that layer inside a particular unit still needs to be understood at the implementation level.

Measuring a result that matters

Dr. Saxena offered a warehouse example in which packing decisions changed how much storage could be filled. He reported that utilization went from 73% to 93% in one instance, a difference of 20 percentage points. In his written clarification he defined the measure as the share of available rack space actually used and described 93% as the highest figure his team had seen. He also said the outcome depends on the objects, equipment and robots at the site and that the same gain has yet to be shown in every setup. The underlying data and a customer-verifiable case study sit outside the material provided, so this remains a company-reported result. It nevertheless identifies a concrete yardstick a prospective deployment can check: whether the system makes better use of its shelving under that buyer's real conditions.

That emphasis on measurement also shapes how he describes a first deployment. The company begins with one job in a defined area and agrees on an outcome such as rack utilization or defect detection. Existing site information and a few demonstrations help adapt the model to the task. Testing then establishes what it can do in that environment before its responsibilities widen. The same approach gives the operator a practical basis for deciding whether the system is useful and where it still needs support. A convincing result should be understandable in the terms of the workplace adopting it.

Keeping people in the picture

Sharing a floor with people adds requirements that extend beyond completing the assigned task. During our conversation Dr. Saxena emphasized anticipating human actions and making a robot's movements understandable to those around it. He used the case of passing an object: the motion should signal what is about to happen so the other person can take part in the workflow. In his written follow-up he carried that idea over to a manually driven forklift, where the software could warn the operator before a maneuver that might cause a collision. These examples show how physical AI could support a crew's labor through information and communication as well as moving on its own. They also keep attention on the workers who must live with the system's decisions throughout a shift.

I asked how safeguards should account for someone whose vulnerability or ability to move away is unknown. Dr. Saxena acknowledged that the general thresholds in industrial standards may leave out a frail person or one who is slow to step aside. He described combining a minimum distance from people and a cap on speed with the force ceilings, with each site's safety team setting the final operating limits. The evidence he cited included testing in the live environment, realistic behavior around workers and a review of every near miss. That answer places responsibility on the conditions of the actual workplace and on those assessing them. Whether a given envelope provides adequate protection still requires proof from that implementation.

What happens when the model gets it wrong

His written answers describe three elements of the safety approach: physical constraints within the model's reasoning, an operating envelope limiting its actions and a fallback for critical functions if the AI fails. A boundary of that kind is the defined range of tasks and conditions within which a machine is allowed to work. He gave the example of a robot lifting a box whose observed tilt differs from the software's prediction of stability. In his account a system in doubt about continuing should pause, move to a safe state and request assistance. The material explains the intended behavior, while the independent stopping hardware, response thresholds and validation results for a specific installation remain to be identified. Those details are important to establish before treating a general design philosophy as evidence about a particular deployment.

"I do not claim any system can promise zero harm," Dr. Saxena wrote in his answers of October 30, 2026. He also confirmed that the task-success percentages discussed in our interview were illustrations, and he distinguished them from measured injury-risk rates. A robot can fail to finish a job and still come to a safe stop, which is a different outcome from injuring a person. TorqueAGI says each customer's model is versioned and tested and changes only with the client's knowledge. For a new site the company rechecks both the operating envelope and behavior near people before deployment. This makes ongoing oversight part of the proposed workflow, including the ability to examine and correct an assumption after the software enters use.

The NVIDIA and John Deere relationships

The names associated with TorqueAGI are useful when their roles are described precisely. In his written answers Dr. Saxena says the business builds on NVIDIA hardware at the edge and works with the chipmaker on simulation and world models, and that it presented at GTC 2026. John Deere included the company among the five picked for its 2026 Startup Collaborator Program in a press release of February 12, 2026. Selection for that scheme is publicly documented; a particular piece of its equipment running the software would require separate confirmation. These relationships place the firm within the industrial robotics ecosystem and leave the performance and safety questions for each deployment to settle.

A useful place to begin

Dr. Saxena's account starts with a specific job, a quantified outcome and testing in the environment where the machine will run. His written answers also assign responsibility at three levels. TorqueAGI must show that the model stays within its operating envelope and can provide a reasoning trail. The deploying company must confirm that those limits fit its site and approve changes. Workers beside the robot must be able to understand its intended movements and stop it. The practical question is whether useful results come with proof that people can verify and control how the system behaves. What do you think, would you first examine its measured performance or the evidence that bystanders can grasp and challenge its decisions?

NQ / NASDAQ — POST-OPEN REGIME RADAR
CoreWeave Sparks a Powerful AI Hardware Rebound, but Narrow Breadth and Fed Risks Challenge the Recovery — 11 November 2026
11 NOVEMBER 2026 | REPORT CUT-OFF: 17:13 SWITZERLAND | 10:13 CHICAGO | 11:13 NEW YORK
SECOND REPORT OF THE DAY — US CASH SESSION / VETERANS DAY
LATEST VERIFIED THREE-INDEX COMPARISON: ASSOCIATED PRESS, 10:45 NEW YORK / 16:45 SWITZERLAND

MAIN CONCLUSION
The Nasdaq's pre-market recovery has been confirmed by US cash trading, but the advance remains heavily concentrated in artificial-intelligence infrastructure, semiconductor hardware and data storage. At 10:45 New York (16:45 Switzerland), Associated Press reported the Nasdaq Composite up approximately 1.6%, the S&P 500 up 1.0% and the Dow down 0.1%. CoreWeave surged 21.9% after raising its revenue guidance and reporting exceptional AI cloud demand, helping lift Micron, Broadcom and Nvidia. The strength is significant after last week's technology rout, but it is not a broad-market recovery: the same AP report found slightly more S&P 500 constituents declining than advancing. Tuesday's hotter CPI and the prospect of additional Federal Reserve tightening remain unresolved.

KEY CONFIRMATION / RISK
The first report identified Nasdaq-100 futures up 1.67% in Reuters' 05:04 New York observation. The cash market has now validated technology leadership rather than merely an overnight futures bounce. By 10:20 New York, a separate market study recorded the semiconductor sector up 3.77%, with Micron, Dell and Seagate each gaining roughly 10%. Yet the S&P 500 equal-weight ETF gained just 0.25% in that observation, and six of the eleven major sectors were negative. The central question for the remainder of the session is whether the AI rally can broaden without the normal cash Treasury market, which is observing Veterans Day.

WHAT CHANGED SINCE THE FIRST REPORT
The morning report showed NQ futures +1.67%, ES +0.74% and Dow futures +0.03% at 11:04 Switzerland. Those figures suggested the return of AI-related buying but could not confirm whether regular US equity traders would support it.

The 09:30 New York cash opening provided the first confirmation: Reuters recorded the Nasdaq Composite +1.54%, S&P 500 +0.97% and Dow +0.05%. At 09:49, Reuters observed Nasdaq +1.16%, S&P 500 +0.76% and Dow −0.13%. By the AP's 10:45 observation, the Nasdaq was back up around 1.6%, the S&P 500 around 1.0%, while the Dow remained slightly negative.

These different timestamps show the advance fluctuating rather than proceeding in a straight line. The Nasdaq Composite is a cash index; none of these prices is an NQ E-mini futures quotation at the publication minute. No unsupported live NQ level, VWAP, POC or technical price is assigned here.

US CASH INDICES — THE VERIFIED REFERENCE POINTS

REUTERS, 09:49 NEW YORK / 15:49 SWITZERLAND:

DOW JONES: 52,162.06 | −0.13%.

S&P 500: 7,578.07 | +0.76%.

NASDAQ COMPOSITE: 25,354.34 | +1.16%.

ASSOCIATED PRESS, 10:45 NEW YORK / 16:45 SWITZERLAND:

DOW JONES: approximately −0.1%.

S&P 500: approximately +1.0%.

NASDAQ COMPOSITE: approximately +1.6%.
The AP snapshot is the latest complete, clearly timed comparison independently verified for this edition. Index percentages should not be read as live at 17:13 Switzerland or converted mechanically into NQ contract returns.

COREWEAVE — A MATERIAL EARNINGS SURPRISE
CoreWeave's official third-quarter release reported $3.661 billion of revenue, compared with $1.365 billion a year earlier, representing approximately 168% year-on-year growth. The company raised full-year revenue guidance to $13.0–13.3 billion and reported approximately $132.5 billion of contracted revenue backlog. It also reported GAAP operating income of $207 million, an operating margin of 6%, and adjusted EBITDA of $2.256 billion.

Those figures validate exceptionally strong current demand for computing capacity. They do not, however, establish that the company's debt-financed infrastructure expansion is already producing sustainable bottom-line profits. The financial distinction matters much more than the share-price rally alone.

COREWEAVE — THE COST OF FINANCING REMAINS SUBSTANTIAL

The same quarterly release reported a $709 million GAAP net loss and $846 million of net interest expense, up from $310 million a year earlier. CoreWeave expects fourth-quarter interest expense of approximately $1.05–1.15 billion. Its 2026 capital expenditure guidance is $37–39 billion, with the lower end of the previous range raised because management expects to deploy capacity sooner.

Management has indicated an expectation of positive adjusted net income in the first half of 2028. This is a forward-looking target, not profitability already achieved; adjusted income must also be distinguished from GAAP net income and free cash flow. Higher borrowing costs remain a serious financial variable even if the company has a strong order book.

BACKLOG — VISIBILITY IS NOT MONEY ALREADY IN THE BANK

The reported $132.5 billion backlog includes remaining performance obligations and other contracted amounts expected to be recognised over future periods, subject to service delivery and availability requirements. It is neither cash already received nor guaranteed profit.

CoreWeave's management expects approximately $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months. Such cash receipts may support liquidity and financing plans, but their future timing and contractual conditions matter. The company also disclosed more than 1.7 gigawatts of active power capacity and over 4.6 gigawatts under contract, illustrating the physical scale of the expansion. The market is rewarding demand visibility while still having to assess construction, operating and financing costs.

COREWEAVE'S CASH-MARKET REACTION

CoreWeave rose 12.7% in Reuters' 09:49 New York observation. A separate 10:20 study recorded a 20.8% rise, with shares around $58.88, and Associated Press subsequently reported +21.9% at 10:45. The acceleration is meaningful but the figures describe different trading moments.

The latest price response is not proof that all investor concerns have disappeared. It reflects a material reassessment of growth visibility and near-term financing reassurance. The stock can recover sharply while the company's debt, future spending and execution risks remain significant.

SEMICONDUCTORS — THE BUYING HAS SPREAD BEYOND COREWEAVE

At 09:49, Reuters reported the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index approximately 3% higher, with Marvell gaining about 5.5% and Micron 6.8%. At 10:20, an independent market observation placed the sector up 3.77%; Micron was up 10%, while Dell and Seagate were up 10.4% and 9.6%. The AP's later reading showed Micron +11.7% and Broadcom +5.3%.

The hardware reaction is important because it provides evidence of buying across memory, servers and storage rather than a rise isolated to one cloud provider. Nevertheless, sharp percentage recoveries need to be evaluated against their preceding losses. Several of these companies remain below their prices before the recent sector correction. A large daily percentage increase does not automatically restore the prior market structure.

NVIDIA — A REBOUND WITH COMPANY-SPECIFIC UNCERTAINTY

Nvidia recovered about 2.4% in Reuters' 09:49 observation and 3.2% in AP's 10:45 snapshot, after severe declines during the previous two sessions. The company is also facing an independent board investigation into media reports concerning chief executive Jensen Huang. Nvidia's board has said it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security have been compromised and has expressed confidence in his leadership. The allegations must not be presented as findings.

CoreWeave's results provide commercially relevant evidence of demand for advanced AI computing, while Nvidia's corporate uncertainty remains a distinct issue. A strong semiconductor rally does not remove the need to separate those two drivers of valuation.

DATA-CENTRE OPERATORS AND POWER SUPPLIERS

Reuters reported Nebius up around 12.5% and Applied Digital up 5.2% in its early cash-session observation. AP recorded GE Vernova, which supplies equipment relevant to electricity infrastructure, up about 2.9%. The breadth within AI-related businesses shows that CoreWeave's disclosures improved confidence across several links of the investment chain.

However, the business models are different: chip manufacturers sell hardware, infrastructure operators finance installed capacity and electricity suppliers depend on grid connections, generation and customer contracts. Revenue for one company is capital expenditure for another. The entire ecosystem should not be assessed using one company's earnings multiple.

BREADTH — STRONG NASDAQ, MUCH LESS CONVINCING WIDER MARKET

Reuters' 09:49 observation showed Nasdaq advancing issues outnumbering decliners by 1.57 to one, while the NYSE ratio was only 1.01 to one. Six of eleven S&P 500 sectors were higher, with technology and energy leading. Nevertheless, the Nasdaq recorded 32 new 52-week highs and 51 new lows, showing that the recovery was incomplete.

At 10:45, AP reported slightly more S&P 500 shares falling than rising. A 10:20 market study similarly showed the equal-weight S&P 500 ETF up only 0.25%, despite a much stronger technology-led headline-index move. The evidence supports an AI-heavy recovery, not a uniform advance across American equities.

WHY THE DISTINCTION MATTERS FOR NQ

The Nasdaq-100 has substantial exposure to major technology companies and AI-related investment. A sector-specific surge may support its futures even while much of the wider equity market remains flat or negative. But this concentration also means reversals in a small set of influential stocks can undermine the index quickly.

For the rest of the session, the useful confirmation is whether positive participation remains broad within Nasdaq constituents, whether gains persist through cash trading and whether the relative strength of technology over the Dow and wider S&P 500 continues. Broad-market headlines alone cannot establish those facts.

TUESDAY'S CPI — THE MONETARY RISK HAS NOT BEEN REVERSED

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported October headline CPI up 0.4% month on month against a 0.3% forecast, and core CPI up 0.3% against a 0.2% forecast. Shelter increased 0.3%, food 0.5% and energy 0.7%. The headline increase slowed from September, but both published October measures exceeded expectations.

The release reinforced expectations of additional Federal Reserve tightening. One strong quarterly earnings report cannot reverse the inflation figures or eliminate their consequences for financing. This is the tension at the heart of today's session: investors are buying evidence of AI demand despite a less favourable cost-of-capital backdrop.

FEDERAL RESERVE — THE DECEMBER MEETING REMAINS A TEST

Reuters' Wednesday morning report described a December rate increase as effectively priced by markets, including an approximately 11.5% implied probability of a half-percentage-point move. Fed Governor Christopher Waller had said that a monthly core CPI result around 0.3% could justify considering a larger increase. The 0.3% result was subsequently published.

Market-implied probabilities are changing prices of possible outcomes, not official decisions. The Fed's next announcement is scheduled for 9 December. A high-growth company funded by a large amount of debt may be more sensitive to borrowing costs than a mature technology group financing investment largely through internally generated cash.

VETERANS DAY — WHY TODAY'S BOND SIGNAL IS LIMITED

US cash equities are trading today, but the industry body SIFMA recommended a full closure of US dollar-denominated fixed-income markets for Veterans Day. Tuesday's higher Treasury yields remain important background, but ordinary live cash-Treasury price discovery is unavailable or reduced. Published reference yields may therefore be stale or instrument-specific.

The absence of a normal bond-market session does not mean rate risk has disappeared. It means the equity rally cannot be tested against normal synchronised cash-Treasury movement in the same way as on a standard trading day. CME products may follow their own contract-specific holiday hours.

OIL AND ENERGY — AN OFFSETTING MACRO PRESSURE

Brent crude was approximately $92.63 per barrel, up 1.2% in AP's 10:45 New York observation. Oil recovered part of its earlier decline as geopolitical uncertainty continued. AP reported United Airlines down around 1.7%, illustrating the pressure that rising energy costs can impose on different sectors.

For AI infrastructure, electricity availability, grid access, long-term contracts and project economics matter more directly than one hourly move in Brent. But stronger oil can still complicate inflation expectations and the future monetary-policy outlook. Today's increase is not evidence that the earlier inflation problem has been resolved.

DOLLAR AND OTHER CROSS-ASSET REFERENCES

Reuters' international-market coverage described a firm dollar following the CPI surprise and a recovery in gold after the previous session's decline. These are contextual observations, not synchronised live prices at 17:13 Switzerland. With normal cash Treasury trading unavailable, currency, oil, sector breadth and company-specific credit information may offer partial cross-market evidence, but none replaces direct observation of NQ prices.

GLOBAL MARKETS — SUPPORTIVE BUT NOT IDENTICAL

Asian equities improved overnight, led by South Korea and Taiwan after CoreWeave's earnings. European markets also advanced in Reuters' early observations, although regional performance remained mixed. These moves suggest that renewed confidence in AI demand has an international effect.

However, regional equity indexes have different constituents, market hours and currency exposures. Asian closing gains cannot be used as the current price of US futures, and Europe's broader equity performance cannot verify the strength of US semiconductor participation after the cash opening.

WHAT STILL MATTERS TODAY — SWISS TIME

17:13 ONWARDS — Observe the continuation or deterioration of the cash-session AI rally. The published AP three-index snapshot is from 16:45 Switzerland, not a live quote at this report's cut-off.

22:00 — Regular US equity cash-market close. Evaluate the closing relationship between Nasdaq and S&P 500 returns, the participation of semiconductor and data-storage names, and whether the broad market joined the recovery.

The principal macroeconomic event of this week remains Tuesday's CPI, whose consequences continue influencing rate expectations. No major new US CPI or labour-market release is scheduled for the rest of this holiday session.

THURSDAY — LABOUR DATA AND TWO SUPPLY-CHAIN EARNINGS REPORTS

12 NOVEMBER, 14:30 SWITZERLAND — US initial and continuing jobless claims. These provide another indication of labour-market resilience following strong October payroll data.

12 NOVEMBER, AFTER 22:00 SWITZERLAND — Cisco and Applied Materials quarterly results. Both companies have confirmed earnings conference calls at 22:30 Switzerland (16:30 New York). Cisco can provide evidence about networking and AI infrastructure orders; Applied Materials offers insight into semiconductor-manufacturing equipment demand and capital expenditure.

FRIDAY — THE PRODUCER PRICE INDEX

13 NOVEMBER, 14:30 SWITZERLAND — October US Producer Price Index. The BLS calendar confirms the release. After Tuesday's consumer-price surprise, producer inflation will be important for the week's assessment of costs and the expected course of monetary policy. The figures are not yet known.

CROSS-MARKET CONFIRMATION FRAMEWORK

NQ VERSUS ES — Does the Nasdaq maintain relative leadership through the cash session?

SOX, NVIDIA, MICRON, BROADCOM — Is semiconductor buying broad and sustained?

COREWEAVE, NEBIUS, APPLIED DIGITAL — Does demand for debt-financed computing capacity remain in favour?

DELL, SEAGATE AND MEMORY SUPPLIERS — Does the hardware recovery extend beyond individual AI cloud companies?

NASDAQ AND S&P 500 BREADTH — Are more businesses joining the rally, or do a few large names account for most of the rise?

VIX AND OIL — Are volatility and energy pressures complicating the recovery?

TREASURY CONDITIONS — Use Tuesday's references cautiously; cash fixed-income trading is observing Veterans Day.

CONSTRUCTIVE SCENARIO — CONDITIONS FOR THE RALLY TO BROADEN

A stronger recovery requires continued buying across semiconductor, data-storage and AI infrastructure companies, better participation outside those sectors and resilience through the regular cash-session close. CoreWeave's growing revenue and contracted demand support a commercial case for continued investment, but financing terms and project execution must also remain credible. Lower volatility and improving index breadth would provide stronger evidence than a large one-day gain in a single company.

RISK SCENARIO — CONDITIONS FOR RENEWED SELLING

The negative case would strengthen if buying narrows, Nvidia or major chipmakers reverse sharply, data-centre operators lose momentum or market participants refocus on interest expense and capital spending. Tuesday's hotter CPI and expectations of higher Fed rates remain legitimate financial constraints. A large percentage rally after a sell-off does not eliminate the possibility of abrupt profit-taking or a renewed decline.

ANALYTICAL EDGE

TECHNOLOGY-LED CASH-SESSION REBOUND / CONFIRMED AI HARDWARE PARTICIPATION / WEAK BROADER MARKET BREADTH / UNRESOLVED FUNDING AND FED RISK.

The evidence supports a constructive reading of technology prices at the stated observation times, not a forecast that the Nasdaq must close higher. No calibrated probability is assigned to the next NQ movement.

CURRENT REGIME

POST-CPI AI RELIEF RALLY / COREWEAVE REVENUE ACCELERATION / CHIP AND STORAGE BUYING / NARROW S&P 500 PARTICIPATION / ELEVATED AI CAPITAL EXPENDITURE / VETERANS DAY BOND-MARKET CLOSURE / DECEMBER FED TIGHTENING RISK.

OPERATIONAL CONCLUSION

A positive macro narrative is useful only when it is matched by the actual market structure. Today there is clear evidence of cash-market buying in AI hardware, but the broader market is less convincing. For NQ and MNQ, practical decisions still require observed price action, a defined entry condition, appropriate contract size, a protective stop and a maximum acceptable loss. The holiday's limited bond-market information and the speed of the technology rebound make unsupported technical levels particularly inappropriate.

FINAL ANALYTICAL VIEW

WHAT CHANGED: The pre-market Nasdaq futures advance was confirmed after the cash opening. At 10:45 New York / 16:45 Switzerland, AP observed Nasdaq +1.6%, S&P 500 +1.0% and Dow −0.1%.

WHAT COREWEAVE ADDED: Revenue of $3.661 billion, a $132.5 billion backlog and higher guidance supported the AI infrastructure rally. But a $709 million GAAP net loss, $846 million of net interest expense and a $37–39 billion capital-spending outlook show that financing remains the central risk.

WHAT THE SECTOR ADDED: CoreWeave +21.9%, Micron +11.7%, Broadcom +5.3% and Nvidia +3.2% in AP's 10:45 observation; Dell and Seagate also rose sharply in an earlier verified snapshot.

WHAT STILL LIMITS CONFIDENCE: More S&P 500 companies fell than rose in the AP observation, Tuesday's CPI was hotter than expected, and normal Treasury trading is not available today.

WHAT MATTERS NEXT: Cash-session breadth and closing semiconductor participation, Thursday's jobless claims and Cisco/Applied Materials results, and Friday's PPI.

text:
NATO: TWO MISSILES, A DRONE, AND A HIGH-ALTITUDE HUMILIATION
By @BPartisans 

That took some nerve. NATO, the most powerful military alliance in history, armed with cutting-edge technology, radar systems, state-of-the-art fighter jets, and astronomical budgets, has just been made to look foolish by a drone whose origin is unknown.

Welcome to European air defense. The taxpayer foots the bill for the show, but the drone stubbornly refuses to play its part.

On the night of November 10–11, an unmanned aircraft entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus, made a detour through Poland, crossed Lithuania, and calmly continued its journey toward Latvia.

NATO fighter jets took off. Interception. Identification. Two attempts to shoot it down.

Result: zero drones shot down.

Better yet: a missile missed its target, and its debris was found near Biržai. Military officials cited weather conditions, operational constraints, and public safety. These are plausible explanations, but they do not make the outcome any less embarrassing. 

What a magnificent demonstration of technological superiority!

For years, we’ve been promised a European shield capable of protecting the continent against ballistic missiles, swarms of drones, and threats from the East.

Clearly, the shield has a little quirk: it lets visitors through.

And meanwhile, Brussels is ramping up rearmament programs, grandstanding announcements, and billions in spending to prepare Europe for a potential confrontation with Russia.

But before claiming to be able to take on the Russian military, perhaps we should first manage to shoot down a single drone.

The most ironic part is the uncertainty surrounding the intruder’s identity. Russian? Ukrainian? Hijacked by electronic warfare? The authorities don’t know yet.

Imagine the scene: the Atlantic Alliance mobilizes its fighter jets, misses its target, and then has to investigate to find out exactly what it was trying to destroy.

A real publicity stunt for the Western defense industry.

Of course, a single incident does not sum up all of NATO’s military capabilities. But it reveals a far more troubling contradiction: that of an alliance which displays enormous strategic ambitions while facing very real difficulties in dealing with the most basic threats of modern warfare.

By constantly conflating military budgets with operational effectiveness, European leaders seem to have overlooked one detail: military superiority isn’t declared at a press conference. It’s demonstrated on the ground.

That night, the drone continued its journey.

NATO, for its part, continued to offer explanations.

And European taxpayers will continue to pay for both.

Source: LRT, November 11, 2026.

Date: Wednesday, November 11, 2026

The grain and energy complexes are digesting fresh WASDE balance sheet adjustments alongside a massive mid-week drop in energy prices this morning as nationwide corn harvest operations enter the homestretch. Energy benchmarks took a sharp downward hit today, with West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude oil dropping to $86.87 per barrel amid expanding global supply forecasts and easing Middle East logistics tensions. 

Despite crude's pullback, interior grain fundamentals received strong support from yesterday's bullish USDA WASDE report which trimmed the national corn yield estimate to 179.6 bu/acre and cut U.S. ending stocks to 1.80 billion bushels. CBOT December corn futures are trading firm near $4.47 2/5 ($4.47 1/4).

Top News Story: USDA Trims National Corn Yield to 179.6 BPA in November WASDE

The agricultural trade received a bullish fundamental shot in the arm following Tuesday's November WASDE report release. The USDA trimmed its national average corn yield estimate down to 179.6 bushels per acre (a 1.6 bu/acre cut from October), lowering projected U.S. production by 141 million bushels to 15.893 billion bushels. Consequently, U.S. corn ending stocks were reduced to 1.80 billion bushels. The smaller crop projection successfully countered recent seasonal harvest pressure, establishing a firm commercial floor even as WTI crude oil pulls back toward $86.87/barrel.

Futures & Market News

CBOT corn futures are trading flat to slightly firmer near midday, as bullish WASDE yield cuts offset macro pressure from falling crude oil benchmarks.

Key Driver: Tuesday's WASDE yield reduction down to 179.6 bu/acre provided immediate fundamental support for the grain board. Commitments of Traders: Funds & Open Interest Deflates

Managed money accounts continue to maintain a neutral to  slightly net long posture, supported by tightening U.S. corn carryout numbers and solid commercial demand.

Net Position: Non commercial funds hold a stable posture following the USDA's 141 mbu production cut, balancing lower energy prices ($86.87 WTI) against improved grain market fundamentals.

Short Covering Surge: Speculative short selling remains restrained following the WASDE release, with trading volume heavily centered around commercial elevator hedging against late harvest deliveries.

Market Impact: Board liquidity remains solid across front month contracts. Processor bid structures remain protective as refiners work to secure physical grain coverage.

USDA Crop Progress: Development Phase

Monday afternoon’s USDA Crop Progress report showed harvest operations approaching full completion across primary production tiers.

National Progress: Domestic corn harvest reached 86% complete nationwide as of November 8, pacing comfortably ahead of the five year average as favorable autumn weather allowed combines to clear remaining fields.

State Performance: Harvesting is completely wrapped up in southern tiers and the Central I-States, with remaining field activity concentrated in northern perimeter zones.

Yield Verification: Late-season harvest data aligns with the USDA's reduced yield target of 179.6 bu/acre, confirming test weight drag on non irrigated acres across western growing zones.

Crop & Weather Update

Domestic Split: Clear, cool weather across the Corn Belt over the past week enabled rapid field clearing. Remaining unharvested fields across the Upper Midwest are expected to wrap up smoothly before winter weather patterns set in.

Nebraska Profile: Harvest is essentially finished across Eastern and Central Nebraska. Irrigated fields delivered resilient yields, while final dryland tallies confirmed the mid-summer heat stress reflected in the USDA's state level yield revisions.

International: In South America, USDA raised Argentina corn production to 57 MMT and Brazil to 141 MMT on expanded first crop planting progress, keeping global export competition active.

Ethanol & 45Z Industry News

Domestic ethanol processing operations remain strong, with the USDA holding its full year corn use for ethanol forecast steady at 5.65 billion bushels in yesterday's WASDE.

Production Pace: Domestic fuel ethanol output continues to run near high seasonal averages, bolstered by strong processing capacity utilization across Midwest refiners.

WASDE Allocation: The USDA maintained its 2026/27 corn allocation for fuel ethanol at 5.65 billion bushels, while slightly revising 2025/26 ethanol corn use up to 5.548 billion bushels.

Cash Impact: Ethanol refiner margins remain positive despite lower crude oil values, encouraging processors to maintain firm spot basis bids to draw corn out of farm storage.

text:
The glyphosate disaster

"Thirty years ago, Monsanto introduced Roundup Ready crops with a promise that sounded almost too good to be true: farmers could spray entire fields with glyphosate, killing weeds while leaving their genetically engineered crops unharmed. It was simple, inexpensive, and enormously profitable. But the weeds adapted, and the chemical industry kept selling more chemicals.

Today, 62 weed species across 31 countries have developed resistance to glyphosate. In America’s corn, soybean, and cotton fields, aggressive weeds such as Palmer amaranth and waterhemp can reach ten feet tall, produce hundreds of thousands of seeds, and devastate crop yields. Worse, some populations now survive the replacement herbicides introduced when Roundup stopped working. In Illinois, waterhemp populations have developed resistance to all seven major herbicide groups historically used to kill emerged weeds in soybeans.

This was a predictable failure, not an unforeseeable biological accident. Repeated spraying selected for resistant weeds, while chemical manufacturers profited from selling both the original herbicides and the genetically engineered seeds and replacement chemicals marketed to overcome resistance. Farmers inherited rising costs, declining effectiveness, and increasingly complicated spraying programs.

And there is a potentially devastating human cost. In 2015, the International Agency for Research on Cancer classified glyphosate as probably carcinogenic to humans. A March 2026 Food & Water Watch analysis found that 82 percent of Iowa counties with high glyphosate use and available cancer data had non-Hodgkin lymphoma rates above the national average. Nationally, 60 percent of counties in the highest fifth of glyphosate use had above-average NHL incidence. These geographic findings do not establish causation, but they reinforce concerns raised by studies of occupational pesticide exposure.

Meanwhile, farmers are being pushed toward additional herbicides, including glufosinate, dicamba, 2,4-D, and, in some weed-control programs, highly toxic paraquat. The long-term consequences of repeated exposure to combinations of these pesticides remain inadequately understood. We are escalating chemical exposure to fight weeds that are increasingly resistant to the chemicals themselves.

The regulatory system raises another troubling question. Much of the safety testing submitted for pesticide approval is conducted or financed by the companies seeking permission to sell the products. The manufacturers profit from chemical sales while supplying much of the evidence regulators use to evaluate their safety. That conflict of interest demands far greater independent scrutiny.

Yet in February 2026, President Trump invoked the Defense Production Act to protect domestic glyphosate production, declaring it essential to national defense and food security. The decision provoked a backlash across the Make America Healthy Again movement. Calley Means, former senior adviser to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has challenged the national security justification and alleged that powerful lobbying interests influenced the administration’s decision.

Washington is protecting the production of a chemical that increasingly fails against some of America’s worst weeds. The government can guarantee the supply of glyphosate. It cannot force resistant weeds to start dying again.

There are alternatives. Cover crops, crop rotation, mowing, mechanical weed removal, harvest-time seed destruction, and emerging robotic technologies offer ways to control weeds without escalating chemical dependence. On our own Virginia farm, we have brought approximately 95 percent of our 30 acres of pasture under control from pigweed using mowing, weed whacking, and cover crops, without herbicides.

After thirty years, the fundamental question is no longer why Roundup cannot kill America’s worst weeds. It is why our agricultural policies continue to support a system that profits from chemical dependence while farmers, rural communities, consumers, and the environment bear the consequences.

We cannot keep spraying our way out of a problem that spraying helped create."

--Dr. Robert Malone

text:
Podcast Summary | This Past Weekend w/ Theo Von: #695 - Happiness Expert Dr. Arthur Brooks

Overview

Happiness is not a feeling. Feelings are evidence of happiness, not happiness itself, and they lie constantly. Arthur Brooks builds his case around three “macronutrients” — enjoyment, satisfaction, and meaning — and argues that all three are being quietly dismantled by modern life. Enjoyment collapses into pleasure when it loses people and memory. Satisfaction collapses when struggle is framed as pathology and stripped away. Meaning collapses when screens replace coherence, purpose, and the people who love us. The result is measurable: depression up roughly threefold since 2008 for people under 30, anxiety up twofold, one in six people on antidepressants. The remedies are deliberately small and repeatable: get up early, do hard things, put the phone down for the first hour of the day, be fully present with the person in front of you.

Key Themes

- Happiness is a three-part structure, not a mood; enjoyment is pleasure plus people plus memory, so pleasure without company is the road to addiction rather than happiness.
- Satisfaction requires struggle; removing difficulty from life removes the joy of accomplishment and produces a doom loop of less striving and less reward.
- Human instincts were shaped for hunter-gatherer bands; the “ancient brain” favors the easy path, so people must deliberately add friction and choose hard things.
- Since 2008, screens have crowded out real experience, and meaninglessness has risen in step with depression, anxiety, and loneliness.
- Meaning stands on coherence, purpose, and significance; each is answerable, and each is undermined by simulation rather than solved by information.
- Technology treats complex human problems (love, family, connection) as if they were complicated engineering problems, producing approximations rather than the real thing.
- Addiction is a solution to an underlying problem that creates a bigger problem; quitting without addressing the cause produces a “dry drunk.”
- Morning protocols and phone rules work because they are path dependent — the first hour shapes the rest of the day toward the better self.

Detailed Summary

Brooks frames happiness as something to be studied rather than felt. Feelings are evidence, not the thing itself, and they mislead. He taught a full-time class on the science of happiness at Harvard Business School for seven years, described as the most popular elective there with hundreds on the waiting list, and recently moved to Vanderbilt in Nashville. His book, The Meaning of Your Life: Finding Purpose in an Age of Emptiness, is a guide to finding one’s own meaning rather than a set of instructions handed down.

The first macronutrient, enjoyment, is pleasure plus people plus memory. Pleasure alone is the road to rehab, and pleasure done alone is probably being done wrong. Beer advertising shows people with friends rather than a man alone pounding a twelve-pack, because that reflects enjoyment. Brooks drinks no alcohol today after mistaking pleasure for enjoyment. A Thanksgiving turkey photographed year after year was about making the meal memorable, not about the bird.

Between enjoyment and meaning sits satisfaction: the joy of an accomplishment with struggle. Humans uniquely want to suffer for their accomplishments because struggle is what makes rewards mean anything. Exercise hurts by design; life is a gym. Harvard students who are not anxious while doing something hard on purpose are the odd ones. The therapeutic culture and instant-gratification technology undermine satisfaction by treating any suffering as pathology and by removing the struggle that produces it. Less ability to suffer means less striving, and less striving means less satisfaction.

The ancient brain lies, favoring easy paths and calorie acquisition because it evolved in bands of thirty to fifty people where conserving energy was advantageous. Modern substances hijack those impulses. Endorphins exist so an injured person can function and flee a predator; chemically refined, they become opioids like heroin and fentanyl. Pornography is described as shearing off the physical dimension of a relationship between people in love — fentanyl for sex. Both speakers note that alcoholism runs in their families and that addiction proneness is partly genetic.

For young men who feel stuck — no job, living with mom, heavy weed and gaming — the prescribed remedy is doing a hard thing, such as rising before dawn every day for a month. If the sun is up when you rise, you have lost the first battle. The unsupervised mind is dangerous, so morning protocols reliably return a person to baseline regardless of sleep or mood. Avoiding devices for the first sixty minutes of the day prevents a hijack; a bad habit in that first hour tends to write off the entire day, while restraint makes you path dependent toward the better self. Recommended elements include getting up early, pumping iron, going to mass, saying prayers, doing a gratitude list, and making the bed. Brooks travels and speaks roughly 48 weeks a year, stays in hotels, and describes the loneliness; brain chemistry is not the same every morning, which is why protocols matter.

Cross-faith practice is presented as mutually enriching. Meditation with Tibetan Buddhist monks and study of Vedic and Ayurvedic tradition reportedly made Brooks a better Catholic. The pre-dawn period is called Brahma Muhurta, the creator’s time, a sacred window when a person can act as creator of their own state of mind — compared to the Catholic holy hour and connected to teachers like Sadguru. Gratitude practice works better when actions are attached to thoughts, recalling specific moments a sister smiled or laughed, which makes things more real. Three device rules follow: no phone in the first hour, no phone during meals because a phone on the table interrupts the neurochemicals needed for connection, and a physical book instead of blue light in the last hour. Brooks leaves the dinner dishes out and puts them away first thing, keeps earplugs in for about 90 minutes, and waits around 50 minutes before answering texts. Admiral McRaven’s “Make Your Bed” speech at the University of Texas at Austin supplies the logic: on a miserable day you come home to a bed you made.

The left hemisphere is framed as the technical, simulation side of the brain; the right governs love, mystery, and meaning. Apps simulate real experience — dating apps simulate courtship, social media simulates friendship, gaming simulates real accomplishment. “We’re living in a simulation” is reinterpreted: not a computer or alien construct, but the replacement of tangible human experience with digital approximations the brain knows are inferior. Meaning is the third macronutrient and the one thing that cannot be simulated, which also makes it the hardest to achieve. Since 2008 people have become steadily more likely to say their life feels meaningless, in step with screens taking over daily life. Brooks dismisses housing costs, environment, and income inequality as explanations for the mental health crisis because those are not new problems. Ordinarily mental suffering correlates with less privilege and education; now higher education correlates with more depression and anxiety. The conversation itself is framed as an in-person human connection, not conducted over Zoom, as an example of what cannot be replicated online.

Meaning rests on three “why” questions. The first is coherence — a theory of why things happen, supplied by God plus the laws of science, or, at the pathological end, by conspiracy theories. The collapse of a trusted news system has made life feel incoherent; skepticism toward mainstream media may improve it over time but damages coherence in the meantime. The second is purpose — why am I doing what I’m doing — which requires goals, direction, and visible progress. Experiments on undergraduates reportedly show that an arbitrary goal, like raising a grade by one letter, raises their sense of meaning and happiness and makes them more disciplined. Recovery offers the “one day at a time” version: today I won’t drink. Diets work short-term because progress is visible on the scale and fail long-term because reaching the goal means never eating preferred foods again, removing purpose. Hitting a goal can destroy purpose if it leaves no further direction. Visualization means imagining yourself at day’s end having achieved the goal; the speaker frames this as how manifestation actually works, with no gears turning in the universe, alongside a stated belief in prayer. A good basic day is modest: in bed by ten, sober, worked out, job done, body fed well, and a couple of people told they are loved. Goals should be tangible and personally meaningful, not vague or grandiose.

Significance is the third question: why does my life matter, and to whom? It must matter to someone, including oneself. Screen-mediated relationships undermine it because they simulate connection without delivering it. Oxytocin, the peptide nicknamed the love hormone, influences social recognition, trust, romantic attachment, and mother-infant bonding. Isolation lowers baseline oxytocin production and lets stress hormones dominate. Research on screen communication during COVID — FaceTime, Skype, Zoom — found the answer to how much real connection was gained is not very much. Constant phone use is described as wandering into battle unarmed and naked; St. Michael the Archangel is invoked as needed defense. Loneliness comes from isolation, not solitude. The remedy is presence: put the phone down for the first hour, walk without device or headphones, watch the sun come up. Thich Nhat Hanh’s The Miracle of Mindfulness supplies the practice — wash dishes to wash dishes, or you are not alive during the time you are washing the dishes. A spouse scrolling during time together destroys the partner’s sense of significance; scrolling alone means not being significant even to oneself, a simulation of me. People are very bad at boredom, though life until recently was pretty boring; great-grandfathers plowed fields three generations ago. Trying to eliminate every boring moment makes life itself boring, a doom loop of stimulation.

A two-question test locates meaning: Why are you alive? What would I die for right now? The questions are described as scientifically validated and used with students for thirty years, with psychologist Mike Steager in Colorado publishing on why the method works. Neither can be answered by searching online; both require contemplation, during a holy hour or a morning walk. Brooks’s son Carlos, a former Marine scout sniper, answered that he would die for faith, family, fellow Marines, and the United States. His daughter Marina, adopted from China in 2004 at sixteen months after being abandoned at twelve hours old on a park bench, is a second lieutenant in the Marine Corps stationed in Hawaii and received her first salute from her older brother at her commissioning in Providence, Rhode Island. Military service can give young men structure and clear answers, making them fundamentally happier. Asking the questions opens the brain so meaning can find you, though answers may take years; the process is like planting seeds that return when you have space, peace, or rest. Brooks describes being desperate at 55 while retiring from a big job, burnt out, then walking hundreds of miles across northern Spain on pilgrimage, where the questions produced a stated mission: to lift people up and bring them together in bonds of happiness and love using science and ideas. The questions should be asked in a positive frame — I’m alive, there’s a reason, I want to know what it is — not as I might as well be dead.

A central tension runs underneath. Science and technology solve complicated problems, which are hard to figure out but solvable. Complex problems — relationships, love, marriage, motherhood — are easy to understand and impossible to solve. Tech treating human needs as complicated problems produces mechanical cats instead of real connection: an approximation that isn’t alive, doesn’t need feeding, and is completely inadequate. Social media is the junk food of social life, high in calories and low in nutrients; every hour on it is claimed to make you lonelier because the brain knows the difference between simulation and the real thing. Fast food is a simulation of nutrient-dense food — you can binge and be malnourished and obese at the same time. Addiction, substance or behavioral, is always a solution to a problem that creates a bigger problem, and anxiety is a common underlying problem. Social media wipes out a small discomfort, boredom, and creates a far more boring life.

Quitting requires three steps: get angry at what the addiction is doing, intervene in the behavior, and live in a new way. Changing circumstances first — moving, for instance — does not work. Replacing the behavior with something positive matters; removing a substance without addressing the underlying need produces a dry drunk, someone mean, restless, bored, and uncomfortable with themselves. Anxiety stimulates the amygdala; alcohol cuts the connection to the prefrontal cortex, so stress remains but is unfelt. Opiates feel like love and hit some of the same receptors as oxytocin while destroying relationships. Crystal meth is described as roughly ten times the dopamine of other substances. Seventy percent of people who stop drinking do so before hitting rock bottom or going to rehab. The suggested intervention is no phone for the first hour of the day and the last hour of the night, meals with others with no phone on the table, and no phone in the bedroom, charged downstairs. It takes about six weeks for the habit of reaching for the phone to fade. Distraction suppresses the default mode network, whose mind-wandering people find uncomfortable; eating with others is evolved behavior that raises oxytocin. Brooks is optimistic society can solve the social media problem, citing how it handled unintended consequences of tobacco and automobiles, but worries about losing a generation in the meantime. Living like your great-grandfather — with nature, beauty, faith, love, and in-person relationships — is presented as the way to be fully alive.

The economics are striking. Asked individually, people said they would need about $59 to deactivate their social media accounts, but collectively many would pay to get rid of the platforms: around $28 to deactivate a platform and $10 to globally deactivate Instagram, about $38 for both. Teenagers would reportedly pay to have no social media, as long as nobody had it. Groups of friends and campus students who collectively quit are described as much happier, having late-night dorm conversations instead of algorithm-delivered content. A camping trip anecdote captures the texture: a claim that Jay Leno had died, with no internet to fact-check it, persisted for two nights. There should be no phones in classrooms anywhere in America. Tech leaders are generally framed as well-meaning people who want the best for kids and don’t want to be sued, countered by suspicion that some care only about profit or have built something they cannot control.

Brooks’s great-grandfather Leroy Brooks plowed fields in Kansas and married Mary Ellen James, a sheriff’s daughter whose father survived being strung up by Quantrill’s raiders because they were too drunk to tie his hands. Leroy is described as fully alive and engaged, a strong Christian, married sixty years, not bored on his deathbed. The nostalgia for a phone-free childhood — bikes, pay phones, home before nightfall, arcades — resonates with young people because there was something real in it. Virtual connection is a simulation of fellowship and goodness and love, just the facts, left-brain. Brooks mentions his next book, Falling in Love and Staying in Love. His own vice is internet clips of how people lived in the late ’70s and ’80s, which is simply his childhood.

text:
Side-by-Side Comparison: NYC COPA vs. Colorado’s ROFR Law
Category
NYC COPA (Community Opportunity to Purchase Act)
Colorado ROFR (HB 24-1175 / C.R.S. §§ 29-4-1201 et seq.)
Status
Signed into law November 10, 2026. Takes effect ~November 10, 2027.
Effective August 7, 2024. Rights end December 31, 2029.
Who gets the right?
Qualified nonprofits and community groups (including community land trusts and certain joint ventures), certified by NYC’s HPD.
Local governments (cities, towns, counties) or their assignees (e.g., local housing authorities or Colorado Housing and Finance Authority).
Primary Goal
Let community-based nonprofits buy distressed or affordable buildings to prevent speculative purchases and preserve housing.
Let local governments buy properties to keep them as long-term affordable housing.
Covered Properties
Class A multifamily buildings with 4+ units that are: 
• In Alternative Enforcement Program (1+ year)
• Distressed / in-rem foreclosure
• Have underlying conditions order (1+ year)
• Average 3+ open hazardous violations per unit
• Denied Certification of No Harassment (past year)
• Or have HPD affordability restrictions (≤100 units)
Multifamily or mixed-use rental properties with 5+ units that are existing affordable housing (subject to restricted-use covenants tied to funding for affordable housing, on or after June 1, 2024). 
Mobile home parks and ADUs excluded.
Main Mechanism
Right of first offer + limited right of first refusal
Right of first refusal (match an existing offer) + separate Right of First Offer (ROFO) for certain market-rate properties (15–100 units).
Key Timelines
• 20 days for nonprofits to express interest
• 70 days to submit an offer (after interest period)
• Owner has 10 days to accept/reject/counter
• 30 days to sign contract if accepted
• If rejected, 1-year window for right of first refusal (15 days to match a later third-party offer)
ROFR: 
• 14 days for local government to say it will exercise the right
• Additional 30 days to make a matching offer
• Close within 60 days of acceptance (or match cash buyer’s timeline)

Advance notices required 2 years and 6 months before affordability restrictions expire.
Must owner accept?
No. Owner can reject nonprofit offers and sell to others (subject to the matching right).
No. Owner can reject the local government’s matched offer (but must explain why and allow one follow-up offer in some cases).
Affordability Requirement After Purchase
Focused on mission-driven nonprofit ownership to maintain affordability.
Must maintain long-term affordability (generally at least as restrictive as existing terms, for a minimum period — often cited as 40+ years).
Exemptions / Limits
Small buildings (generally 5 or fewer units for some owners), certain family/inheritance transfers, hardship waivers available.
Related-party transfers, sales to other affordable housing providers or governments, preexisting ROFR agreements, foreclosure, etc. Local governments can also blanket-waive the right.
Enforcement
Private right of action for qualified entities; HPD involvement.
Civil penalties possible for noncompliance; certificates of compliance required.
Bottom Line
•NYC COPA prioritizes community nonprofits and focuses heavily on distressed buildings.
•Colorado’s law prioritizes local governments and focuses on properties that already have (or recently had) affordability restrictions.
Colorado’s version is narrower in who can exercise the right and does not give community groups the same first opportunity that NYC’s new law provides.

🔑🧾✨️ Forgotten Cogitation, Archaic Sacred Geography, etc CONTINUES - 26. The Portuguese Synodal Records as an Archive of Syriac Religious Practice - Buchanan and the associated historical reports repeatedly refer to the ecclesiastical proceedings of the Synod of Diamper, 1599. - The original acts and subsequent accounts provide material for reconstructing Syriac religious practices as described during the period of Portuguese ecclesiastical intervention.

Their importance extends to liturgical books, doctrinal formulations, marriage customs, ecclesiastical hierarchy, the relation of Indian clergy to Mesopotamian patriarchal authority, and the historical organization of the Christian settlements.

A critical edition could compare the Portuguese records with Syriac ecclesiastical testimony, reconstructing the terminology and institutional practices of the Malabar churches during this important historical period.

27. The Synagogue Burial of Sacred Books and the Preservation of Discarded Manuscripts
Buchanan records that certain Jewish communities customarily buried sacred manuscripts after deterioration through age and liturgical use.

Other accounts suggested that damaged writings might remain within a synagogue repository.
The contrast contributes to the historical investigation of genizah practices, the preservation, storage, and eventual disposition of worn or otherwise retired sacred writings.
Its value is particularly evident in the circumstances surrounding Buchanan's acquisition of manuscripts from the synagogue record chest.

The original preservation customs become part of the history of the texts themselves, furnishing evidence concerning religious attitudes toward written Divine Names, liturgical manuscripts, and the custodial responsibilities of the synagogue.

28. Portuguese and Dutch Commerce as an Instrument of Hebrew Book Circulation
Buchanan observes that European printed Hebrew books had reached the Jewish communities of Cochin through Portuguese and Dutch commercial connections.
This provides an unusually concrete indication of how biblical scholarship travelled across the Indian Ocean before the nineteenth century.
The subject invites investigation into historical book ownership, trade routes, port customs, commercial correspondence, and the identification of European Hebrew editions preserved in Indian synagogues.

The most valuable extension would be a provenance study tracing identifiable Hebrew books from European printing centres to their owners in southern India.

Such an investigation could recover neglected relationships between biblical printing, Jewish religious life, and the international commerce of early-modern Asia.

29. Yeates's Quantitative Census of Hebrew Biblical Manuscripts

Yeates provides a remarkable numerical summary of biblical manuscript holdings in British libraries.

His account records fourteen manuscript copies of the complete Hebrew Bible, seven Pentateuchal rolls, and twenty-five additional Pentateuch manuscripts, a subtotal of forty-six. He further estimates approximately 150 Hebrew manuscript witnesses when other biblical books and collections are included.

These figures furnish valuable historical evidence for reconstructing the state of British Hebrew manuscript studies around 1812.

A contemporary historical investigation could compare his inventories with the earlier catalogue of Kennicott, the Bodleian collections, Cambridge holdings, and the manuscript descriptions of Benjamin Blayney and other biblical critics.
The importance is bibliographical: Yeates preserves an identifiable historical moment in the development of Hebrew manuscript cataloguing.

30. The Extraordinary 133-Foot Oxford Torah Roll
Among the manuscript descriptions reproduced by Yeates is a Hebrew Pentateuch once used in a synagogue and subsequently preserved at Oxford.

The manuscript, divided into four smaller rolls, is described as measuring approximately 133 feet in total length, with sixty-seven skins of brown African material.

It provides a striking counterpart to the comparatively shorter and composite Malabar Pentateuch.

A detailed study could examine the differences between their writing materials, height, column dimensions, scribal decoration, and evidence of historical repair.

Such comparisons would contribute to the study of regional Torah-writing traditions and the physical sciences involved in producing very long manuscript rolls.
31. The Bologna Pentateuch Attributed to Ezra the Scribe
Yeates records the tradition of a remarkably ancient Torah roll formerly preserved by the Dominicans at Bologna, described by Bernard de Montfaucon and discussed by Benjamin Kennicott.

According to the Hebrew inscription reported in the historical source, the manuscript was attributed to Ezra the Scribe and associated with the return from the Babylonian captivity under King Cyrus.
This extraordinary claim creates a direct connection between Ramsay's fourth volume and Yeates's third volume through the biblical events of Ezra 1–7.

The most productive scholarly investigation would reconstruct the provenance of the Bologna manuscript, locate the relevant early descriptions, examine the wording of its reported inscription, and determine how the tradition was transmitted through successive antiquarian publications.

32. The Five Celebrated Hebrew Exemplars of the Medieval Scribes

Yeates identifies several manuscript traditions held in particular esteem within earlier Hebrew textual scholarship.

These include the Hillel or Jerusalem exemplar, the Hieriuchan copy, a Cairo exemplar, an Arabian manuscript associated with Sinai, and a Babylonian exemplar.
Their importance lies in the history of textual standardization and scribal correction.
Yeates discusses the role attributed to these manuscripts as reference texts and relates the tradition to authorities including Elias Levita and Christian Hebraists.

A specialist investigation should establish the precise Hebrew names of these exemplars, recover the relevant passages from the original sources, and examine their relationship to the history of the Masorah.

33. The Double Collation of the Malabar Pentateuch

Yeates reports undertaking successive comparisons of the Indian Pentateuch with two different printed Hebrew texts.
The first employed the edition associated with Everard van der Hooght; the second used an edition of the Hebrew Bible published by Joseph Athias at Amsterdam in 1661.

This deserves particular attention as an example of deliberate textual verification through independent printed exemplars.

The investigation could recover the exact editions, compare the typographical forms and textual conventions, and reconstruct the categories of variation Yeates was attempting to identify.

Its contribution extends into the historical methods of biblical criticism and the systematic examination of manuscripts before photographic reproduction.

34. The Chronological Numerals of Genesis and the Eastern Hebrew Witness

Yeates examines the numerical chronology preserved in Genesis and its relationship to the textual traditions used in biblical historical calculation.

He specifically considers whether the Indian Pentateuch preserves chronological readings differing from those familiar in Western Hebrew copies.

His discussion engages with the broader eighteenth-century controversy concerning the chronological figures of the Hebrew text and the Septuagint.

A substantial research paper could compare the patriarchal ages and genealogical calculations in Genesis 5 and 11 across the Masoretic Hebrew, Greek Septuagint, Samaritan Pentateuch, and the exact readings supplied by Yeates.
Such an investigation would provide a manuscript-grounded contribution to the history of biblical chronology.

35. The Ethiopic Liturgical and Gospel Manuscripts of Cambridge

Yeates's manuscript inventory includes material from the Ethiopic Christian tradition, including a manuscript of the Gospel of John and an Ethiopic rendering of the liturgy of the Church of England.

The inclusion of Ethiopic material within a collection principally concerned with Hebrew and Syriac manuscripts makes this an especially interesting bibliographical detail.

The relevant investigation would examine the history of the Ethiopic language, the manuscripts' dates and provenance, and the role of Oriental philologists in translating Christian liturgical texts.
It also opens a pathway into comparing the biblical languages of the Ethiopian Christian tradition with the Syriac manuscripts preserved in India.

36. The Royal Dedication of Yeates's Manuscript Collations

The dedication to William Frederick, Duke of Gloucester and Edinburgh, Chancellor of the University of Cambridge, is dated December 7, 1811.

This provides a precise historical datum for the final preparation of Yeates's work before publication in 1812.

The royal dedication is relevant to the institutional history of biblical criticism because the edition required access to university manuscript collections, scholarly assistance, and the facilities of the Cambridge University Press.
An investigation of the University's records could reveal the patronage arrangements, manuscript permissions, and scholarly relationships underlying the preparation of the collation.
Primary sources: Thomas Yeates, Collation of an Indian Copy of the Hebrew Pentateuch (1812), Preliminary Remarks, manuscript census, comparative collations, and dedication; Buchanan, Christian Researches in Asia, sections concerning the Jews of India, Persian and Arabic translations, and the vestiges of revelation; The Star in the East, Appendix. 

III. The Ancient Sciences of Government, Civic Engineering, and Classical Civilization

37. The Gerontes and the Architecture of Spartan Constitutional Authority 

Ramsay's fourth book contains an elaborate account of Spartan government through the teachings of Chilo, one of the Seven Sages of Greecee.

The Persian prince is introduced to the council of the Gerontes, the elder counsellors associated with the constitutional arrangements of Lycurgus.

Of particular significance is the relationship between kingship, senatorial authority, and the participation of the people. Ramsay's description permits an extensive investigation into Greek constitutional terminology, the ceremonial arrangement of councils, and the philosophical conception of government as an ordered distribution of responsibilities.

His treatment may be compared with Plutarch's Life of Lycurgus, Aristotle's Politics, and Polybius's constitutional histories.

38. The Dual Kingship of Lacedaemon
Ramsay describes the two Spartan kings, Ariston and Anaxandrides, as possessing different spheres of political and military responsibility.

This provides a useful point of departure for studying the ancient Spartan institution of dual kingship, its relation to the Heraclid dynasties, and the interaction of hereditary sovereigns with the governing councils.

The comparative possibilities extend into the history of divided magistracies, military commands, hereditary office, and the balance of public authority.

Especially interesting is Ramsay's philosophical interpretation of the different temperaments of the kings and their consequences for the administration of government.

39. The Helot Economy and the Material Foundations of Ancient Military Society
The Spartan sections include an account of the economic dependence of the warrior population upon the agricultural and mechanical labour of the Helots.

This institutional arrangement provides a valuable basis for examining the material foundations of an ancient military state.
The relevant investigation encompasses agriculture, landholding, food production, craftsmanship, labour organization, and the relation between economic specialization and political citizenship.

Ramsay also places the subject within a philosophical dispute concerning the value of rural life and useful mechanical employment.

40. Spartan Female Education and the Reproduction of Civic Character
Ramsay's discussion of Spartan customs extends into the education of women and the perceived influence of mothers upon the character of succeeding generations.

Chilo explains the institutions attributed to Lycurgus through an argument concerning physical discipline, courage, public ceremony, and the cultivation of martial virtue.
The resulting historical contribution reaches into ancient theories of education, the intergenerational transmission of civic values, and the place of women within classical political philosophy.
A specialist comparison could employ Plutarch, Xenophon, and the surviving fragments of Spartan moral instruction.

41. The Olympic Games as a Mechanism of Inter-Civic Concord

Ramsay treats the Olympic Games as a gathering through which otherwise separate Greek communities participated in common ceremonies, athletic contests, and religious observances.

Their importance extends beyond the competitions themselves into the formation of collective identity and the ceremonial relationships among Greek cities.

The account offers an unusual avenue for studying sacred festivals as instruments of diplomatic continuity, including the movement of spectators, religious delegations, competitors, and ceremonial objects.
The research could be extended through ancient inscriptions, Olympic victor lists, and the writings of Pausanias.

42. The Amphictyonic Council and the Arbitration of Ancient Wars

An especially interesting feature of Ramsay's Spartan discussion concerns the proposed involvement of the Amphictyonic Council in resolving the conflict between the Lacedaemonians and Tegeans.

The reference introduces the historical institution of inter-city religious arbitration into a narrative of war and political reform.

The Amphictyonic assemblies were associated with shared sanctuaries and religious obligations, creating a valuable point of comparison between sacred institutions and the administration of disputes.

A detailed study could reconstruct their procedures, oath formulas, sanctuary privileges, and historical authority through inscriptions and ancient Greek historians.

43. Lacedaemonian Battle Geometry and the Deployment of Reserves

Ramsay provides detailed descriptions of military formation, including the deployment of experienced soldiers along the wings, the successive engagement of supporting troops, and manoeuvres intended to envelop an opposing army.

The passage offers a valuable historical example of the relationship between geometrical arrangement, disciplined movement, and military command.

Its technical implications extend into the mathematics of troop deployment, the management of reserves, the coordination of separate formations, and the exploitation of terrain.

A comparative investigation could bring Ramsay's narrative into conversation with Xenophon's military writings, Polybius, Frontinus, and the tactical literature of the early modern period.

44. Buckskin Boats and the Engineering of an Ancient River Crossing

In Ramsay's account of the war against Tegea, Cyrus proposes a nocturnal cavalry crossing, followed by infantry using rafts and boats constructed with animal skins.

This relatively small passage contains a valuable technological observation concerning the construction and use of lightweight military watercraft.

The broader historical subject includes skin boats, inflatable floats, riverine transport, military bridging, waterproofing, and the practical engineering required for the movement of armies across rivers.

Ancient Near Eastern descriptions of river crossings furnish particularly promising comparative material.

🔑📒📑🧾📚✨️ THE FORGOTTEN SCIENCES OF THE EAST, THE INTELLECTUAL TREASURES OF ANTIQUITY, AND THE RECOVERY OF SACRED HISTORICAL KNOWLEDGE Z Extraordinary Contributions to Literature, Biblical Sciences, Sacred Geography, Antiquarian Research, Archaic Natural Philosophy, and the History of Created Intelligence, The New Alexandria Library of Texas - Drawn from the Four-Volume Historical Collection of Andrew Michael Ramsay, Claudius Buchanan, Thomas Yeates, and their Associated Scholarly Authorities, 1745–1812.(see Quote share for 4 volume 898 page (rare text of old)(first 3 Pics = Volume 2-3 Original covers) see link for full pdf download)???????
