The following contributions concentrate upon substantial historical particulars and specialist discoveries that received little or no attention in the preceding abstract and 84-term lexicon. They include forgotten investigators, neglected episodes, technical practices, obscure geographical records, institutional achievements, and remarkable intellectual constructions preserved throughout the original publications.

I. The Unexamined Intellectual Treasures of Oriental Christianity and Sacred Learning

1. The Royal Latin Correspondence of the Tranquebar Missionaries

Buchanan preserves letters from King George I of Great Britain to the missionaries Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Johann Ernst Gründler, whose work at Tranquebar occupied an important place in the early history of Protestant Christianity in India. These communications, originally written in Latin, belong to the international documentary history of religious patronage.

Their significance extends into royal diplomacy, ecclesiastical correspondence, and the literary reconstruction of early eighteenth-century missionary establishments. Particularly interesting is the relationship between monarchical patronage and the production of vernacular Christian literature.

A complete edition of the correspondence could compare the Latin diplomatic formulas, the original missionary records, and the accounts transmitted through the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, yielding a detailed history of royal involvement in the diffusion of biblical learning.

2. The Serfoji Memorial and the Royal Poetry of Tanjore 

An especially striking passage occurs in Buchanan's visit to Tanjore, where he describes sitting upon the granite slab covering the grave of the Reverend Christian Friedrich Schwartz (1726–1798).

Buchanan records that the epitaph was composed in English verse by Serfoji II, the Maharaja of Tanjore, and signed with the king's name.

 This remarkable memorial provides an unusual conjunction of Indian royal authorship, English commemorative poetry, Christian missionary history, and monumental inscription.
Its literary value increases when considered alongside the cultivated interests of the Tanjore court, its libraries, artistic traditions, and educational establishments. 

The monument invites exact transcription, epigraphic examination, and comparison with the royal correspondence concerning Schwartz.

3. Tamil Sermonic Stenography and the Reproduction of Oral Knowledge
Buchanan records a fascinating educational practice in which students transcribed Tamil sermons upon palm leaves, subsequently presenting their written work for examination.
This procedure represents a sophisticated form of religious knowledge transmission involving public discourse, rapid notation, manuscript production, memorization, repetition, and instruction.
The particular importance lies in the conversion of spoken theological discourse into portable handwritten literary evidence.
A specialist investigation could reconstruct the implements employed, the layout of the palm-leaf inscriptions, the shorthand conventions, the educational abilities of the students, and the relationship between Tamil literary culture and Christian preaching.
This is a particularly promising contribution to the neglected history of information recording and indigenous educational technologies.

4. Sattianaden and the Indigenous Intellectual History of Indian Christianity

Buchanan records his particular interest in hearing Sattianaden, an Indian Christian preacher associated with the Tanjore mission.
This notice invites substantial attention to the intellectual accomplishments of indigenous Christian teachers, whose contributions extended into preaching, interpretation, vernacular religious instruction, and the cultivation of local congregations.
A deeper historical apparatus should reconstruct Sattianaden's educational formation, theological vocabulary, linguistic abilities, preaching methods, and relationship with the European and Indian scholars of the Tranquebar and Tanjore establishments.
The significance of such an investigation lies in recovering individual intellectual histories from institutional records where native scholars frequently appear only in passing.

5. The Extraordinary Academic Constitution of Fort William College

Buchanan includes a detailed institutional register of the College of Fort William, founded on May 4, 1800, identifying its governors, council members, professors, examiners, and indigenous teachers.

The curriculum embraced Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, Hindustani, Bengali, Tamil, Greek, Latin, mathematics, French, and legal studies. The college employed more than fifty indigenous pundits, maulvis, and munshis, whose learning was indispensable to the instruction and translation enterprises.
The original account also states that nearly one hundred volumes of Oriental literature had been produced during the college's first several years.
This extraordinary institutional record makes possible a detailed reconstruction of the division of scholarly labour, the formation of multilingual libraries, the organization of manuscript translation, and the early history of collaborative Oriental philology.

6. The Forgotten Indigenous Translators of the First Oriental Gospel Editions

The names preserved in Buchanan's institutional records deserve exceptional attention.
Mirza Fitrut, associated with the Persian translation enterprise, and Meer Bahadur Ali, who held an important position in the Hindustani department, appear alongside European scholars involved in the preparation and supervision of biblical and linguistic publications.
Buchanan also names Thomas Jarrett in connection with Malay translation, William Hunter in Hindustani work, and Colebrooke in the Persian department.

The recovery of these individual scholarly contributions would significantly enlarge the history of Oriental translation. A specialist register should record their original-language names, offices, manuscripts, identifiable publications, correspondence, and the surviving printed works upon which their linguistic expertise was exercised.

7. The Lost Academic Disputations of Bengal
Buchanan's bibliography of Primitiæ Orientales preserves an extraordinary but little-discussed series of multilingual academic productions associated with Fort William College.
The volumes contain essays, theses, and formal disputations in Persian, Hindustani, Bengali, Arabic, and Sanskrit, including records of students delivering learned addresses before an assembled academic audience.
One particularly unusual entry concerns a Sanskrit declamation delivered by Clotworthy Gowan, described as the first public speech in that language by an Englishman before such an assembly.
These publications provide a valuable archive for examining early Oriental pronunciation, academic rhetoric, translation exercises, formal disputation, and the history of Sanskrit and Persian instruction in British India.

8. The Indian Ocean's Extraordinary Ecclesiastical Correspondence Network
Buchanan's account reveals a wide correspondence between the religious and educational establishments of Bengal, the Coromandel coast, Ceylon, Persia, Arabia, China, and Europe.
The network depended upon manuscript exchange, letters, diplomatic introductions, translation reports, printed specimens, and the assistance of scholars possessing knowledge of several languages.

Its investigation could reconstruct an extensive historical system of intellectual communication, identifying the places from which manuscripts originated and the individuals responsible for transmitting them.

Particularly valuable would be the comparison of the surviving correspondence of Henry Martyn, David Brown, William Carey, Joshua Marshman, Robert Morrison, and the scholars associated with the College of Fort William.

9. The Languages of Ancient Ceylon and the Recovery of Religious Instruction

Buchanan's investigations in Ceylon preserve observations concerning the religious conditions of communities spread between the northern and southern parts of the island.
His discussions of scriptural translation, local educational establishments, and the distinction between inherited religious affiliation and active instruction invite a detailed examination of the historical languages of the island.
A new research avenue concerns the relationship between Sinhala, Tamil, Portuguese, Dutch, and English in the transmission of Christian literature, together with the institutional history of teachers, churches, and printing establishments.
The subject could yield a precise chronology of the earliest regional Bible translations, catechisms, grammars, and schoolbooks.

10. The Emerald Ring of Travancore and Royal Protection of Learning

Among Buchanan's most remarkable personal recollections is his audience with the ruler of Travancore.

The sovereign presented him with an emerald ring as a token of friendship and authorization intended to facilitate his passage through the country, while directing the Dewan to furnish appropriate assistance.

This unusual artifact introduces a fascinating historical subject: the use of jewels, personal ornaments, and royal gifts as instruments of diplomatic recognition and practical protection.
The episode also concerns the acquisition of manuscript catalogues from Indian temple libraries. It therefore connects the history of royal regalia with antiquarian fieldwork, scholarly patronage, and the diplomatic procedures required to investigate restricted literary repositories.

11. The Royal Manuscript Catalogues of Rameswaram, Tanjore, and Travancore

Buchanan records his efforts to assemble catalogues of Sanskrit manuscripts preserved in the religious institutions and libraries of southern India.

He describes catalogues received through the rulers of Tanjore and Ramnad and a request to the sovereign of Travancore for similar records of the temple libraries of his dominions.
The importance of these inventories extends into the history of mathematics, astronomy, medicine, grammar, sacred architecture, ritual literature, and indigenous geographical learning.
A particularly worthwhile undertaking would be to locate the surviving catalogues, recover the original Sanskrit titles, and determine which manuscripts can be identified in present collections. 

Their historical arrangement may reveal early systems of knowledge classification.

12. The Extraordinary Neighbouring Sanctuaries of Cenotta

Buchanan records an encounter at Cenotta, where Jewish and Syrian Christian communities occupied the same locality, their places of worship standing in close proximity.
He visited the synagogue, purchased Hebrew manuscripts, and subsequently entered the neighbouring Christian church.
The event provides a remarkable example of the coexistence of distinct religious archives within the same settlement.
P
A detailed study could recover the historical geographical name, examine the architectural remains, identify the communal manuscript repositories, and reconstruct the political and social arrangements under which these religious communities maintained their institutions.
The episode holds particular value for the historical geography of biblical Judaism and Eastern Christianity in India.

13. Mar Dionysius and the Ecclesiastical Regalia of the Syrian Metropolitan

Buchanan's account of his meeting with Mar Dionysius, the Syrian Christian metropolitan at Cande-nad, preserves unusually vivid details of episcopal appearance and ceremonial dress.
The metropolitan wore dark red silk, a substantial golden cross suspended from his neck, and a long beard reaching below his girdle.
Such particulars contribute to the historical study of Syriac ecclesiastical vestments, insignia, episcopal representation, and regional traditions of religious authority.

An expanded investigation might compare these descriptions with the vestments represented in Syriac manuscripts, Eastern Christian paintings, historical church portraits, and the ecclesiastical practices of Mesopotamian communities.

14. The Forgotten Christian Kingship of Udiamper
Buchanan identifies Udiamper, or Diamper, as a historical residence associated with Beliarte, King of the Christians.

This unusual notice opens a promising research path into the political organization traditionally attributed to the early Christian communities of Malabar.

The site also possesses exceptional importance because of the Synod of Diamper convened under Archbishop Aleixo de Menezes in 1599.
A specialist investigation should examine the historical testimonies concerning Christian rulers, the relationship between ecclesiastical and political jurisdiction, and the regional institutions preceding Portuguese ecclesiastical intervention.
Its wider geographical significance emerges through the relationship of Udiamper to Angamaly, Cochin, and the mountain settlements of the Syrian Christians.

15. The Goa Inquisition as a Historical Architectural and Documentary Archive
Buchanan's observations at Old Goa preserve descriptions of ecclesiastical buildings, religious authorities, judicial procedures, and his attempts to investigate the institution of the Inquisition.
His account also engages with the earlier published testimony of Charles Dellon, whose imprisonment and descriptions of the tribunal had circulated in European literature.

The combined sources provide a valuable foundation for studying legal terminology, ecclesiastical administration, historical confinement architecture, manuscript testimony, and the geographical organization of Portuguese judicial institutions in Asia.
An exact examination of contemporary records could reconstruct the offices, chamber arrangements, legal instruments, and documentary practices associated with the tribunal.
16. The Forgotten Maritime Chaplaincy of the East India Fleets
Buchanan's proposal concerning religious provision aboard East India Company ships introduces an unusual subject in maritime ecclesiastical history.

He discusses the extraordinary duration of voyages, the uncertainties of navigation, the hazards encountered at sea, and the importance of organized religious instruction for passengers and crews.

His reference to the loss of seven East Indiamen provides a specific historical episode around which ship registers, maritime correspondence, casualty records, and contemporary accounts could be assembled.

The resulting research might reconstruct the religious life of vessels travelling between Europe, Africa, and Asia, particularly the place of chaplains, Bibles, prayers, and written devotional material within the maritime world.
Primary source: Claudius Buchanan, Christian Researches in Asia (1812), particularly the sections on Tanjore, Tranquebar, Ceylon, the Syrian churches, Travancore, Goa, and the College of Fort William; additional testimony in the appendix to The Star in the East. 

II. Neglected Philological, Archaeological, and Manuscript Discoveries

17. The Fifty-Five Churches and the Unwritten Malayalam Bible

Buchanan records discussions concerning the possibility of producing an accurate vernacular translation of Scripture for approximately fifty-five Syrian Christian churches.
A priest named Abraham explains the difficulties arising from the scarcity of complete biblical manuscripts and the labour required to reproduce them. The discussion reveals the practical relationship between ecclesiastical literacy, manuscript availability, and the survival of religious instruction.

Especially valuable is the suggestion that certain Syrian clergy possessed the linguistic competence to translate directly between Syriac and Malayalam. Their abilities make them important figures in the history of indigenous biblical philology.

This testimony contributes to the reconstruction of a premodern scholarly world in which the possession of a manuscript could determine the availability of scriptural learning throughout an entire community.

18. Henry Martyn's Persian and Arabic Translation Enterprise

The accounts concerning the Reverend Henry Martyn (1781–1812) and his associates preserve an important episode in the history of biblical linguistics.

Buchanan describes the translation activity of Nathaniel Sabat, including Persian Gospel translations and the preparation of Arabic biblical material.
The work involved difficulties of idiom, doctrinal precision, stylistic interpretation, and the difference between classical literary expression and contemporary linguistic usage.
Particularly valuable is the appearance of translation reports that record the reconsideration of drafts through consultation with additional scholars.
The surviving evidence provides a foundation for reconstructing an early system of collaborative textual revision, comparing the biblical source languages with Persian and Arabic expressions under discussion.

19. The Arabic Polyglot and the Historical Science of Readable Translation

Buchanan discusses the Arabic biblical text available through the Polyglot tradition and raises the importance of communicating Scripture in language intelligible to its intended readers.
This introduces a substantial field of historical linguistic investigation involving the distinction between classical Arabic, regional literary styles, and the registers employed in religious instruction.

A specialist study could compare the Arabic Gospels associated with the London Polyglot Bible, earlier Eastern Christian translations, and the productions of the nineteenth-century translation establishments.
Particular attention should be directed toward religious terminology, inherited Syriac expressions, grammatical variation, and the literary choices made when rendering Hebrew and Greek concepts into Arabic.

20. The Armenian Episcopal Council of 1662 and the Reproduction of the National Bible
Buchanan preserves an important account of Armenian bishops organizing the republication of Scripture during the seventeenth century.
He records a council assembled in 1662 to address the need for additional copies of the Armenian Bible, whose fifth-century translation was highly esteemed.

The Orientalist Mathurin Veyssière de La Croze famously characterized the Armenian translation as the Queen of Versions, an expression Buchanan reproduces.

The account invites investigation into the Armenian printing enterprise of Amsterdam, the production of the editions of 1666, 1668, and 1698, and the movement of these books through the Armenian mercantile communities of Asia.
This history provides a remarkable example of ecclesiastical self-preservation through organized printing, international commerce, and inherited linguistic scholarship.

21. The Rock-Cut Triad of Elephanta and an Early Archaeological Conservation Proposal

One of Buchanan's more extraordinary observations concerns the colossal carved figures within the cave temple of Elephanta, near Bombay.

He describes the three principal faces of the monumental sculpture as approximately five feet in length and records that the sanctuary and its images were excavated from the solid mountain.
Of particular importance is his proposal for preserving the historical fabric: reconstructing damaged pillars, securing their foundations, repairing sculptural elements through reference to earlier descriptions, clearing accumulated debris, and revealing the continuity between the rock floor and architectural supports.

The description possesses exceptional relevance to the history of rock-cut engineering, sacred sculptural iconography, monumental conservation, and the early documentation of Indian architectural antiquities.
His interpretation of the triadic symbolism also offers a valuable historical example of Christian comparative theological reflection upon Indian sacred imagery.

22. The Ancient Indian Doctrine of the Twice-Born and Its Early Christian Interpretation
Within his section on the vestiges of revelation in Asia, Buchanan examines religious language concerning an inward transformation of human understanding.

He refers to Indian texts describing the influence of divine illumination upon the mind and compares their religious vocabulary with the Christian doctrine of spiritual regeneration.
The concept of being twice-born, Sanskrit dvija (द्विज), occupies an important place in Indian religious and social terminology.

The passage provides a substantial avenue for investigating the reception of Sanskrit religious expressions within early Orientalist scholarship, together with the historical methods employed to compare religious initiation, spiritual illumination, and the biblical language of the new birth.
A source-level comparison should trace the precise Sanskrit writings available to Buchanan and the translations through which he encountered them.

23. The Syriac Era of Alexander and the Alternative Chronology of the Eastern Churches

An unusually important detail occurs in the appended investigations concerning the Syrian Christians: the employment of a chronological era reckoned from the period associated with Alexander the Great.

The source records a correspondence between the year 325 of the Christian era and the Syriac year 636.

This offers a particularly valuable avenue for biblical and ecclesiastical chronology because manuscript dates recorded through different chronological eras require exact conversion before their historical relationships can be reconstructed.

The study should examine the Seleucid era, Syriac manuscript colophons, regional calendrical practices, and the chronological terminology used by Eastern Christian scribes.
This is especially useful for establishing the dates of ecclesiastical correspondence, manuscript copying, episcopal successions, and historical events preserved in Syriac chronicles.

24. The Reported Indian Bishop at Nicaea
The appendix to The Star in the East refers to a bishop associated with India and the Council of Nicaea in A.D. 325.

The original investigators employ this historical testimony while considering the antiquity of Christian establishments beyond the Roman Empire.

This passage opens a research avenue into the episcopal lists of Nicaea, the geographical meanings of India in late antique ecclesiastical literature, and the surviving Greek, Latin, Syriac, and Armenian witnesses to early conciliar history.
An expanded documentary study could compare the names transmitted in conciliar manuscripts and trace the interpretation of the testimony through early-modern histories of Christianity in Asia.

The contribution is the recovery of a specific historical claim and its documentary transmission across the centuries.

25. The Alleged Mesopotamian Patriarchal Archives

The historical report appended to Buchanan's sermon contains an unusually interesting account of churches and manuscript repositories said to have survived in Mesopotamia.

The Celestial Government of Creation, the Noachic Dispersion of Sacred Wisdom, and the Extraordinary Survival of Divine Testimony among the Nations of the Ancient East - 

A Historical, Philological, Metaphysical, and Biblical Investigation - 

The extraordinary survival of a Hebrew Pentateuch assembled from thirty-four ancient writing skins, the rediscovery of Syriac biblical manuscripts among the Christian communities of southern India, the preservation of royal privileges upon engraved metallic tablets, and the remarkable prophetic designation of Cyrus by the God of Israel collectively illuminate an immense inheritance of sacred antiquity.

Within the four historical publications assembled for the New Alexandria Library of Texas, the scholar encounters a succession of remarkable testimonies extending from the earliest biblical generations through the civilizations of Chaldaea, Persia, Egypt, Phoenicia, Greece, and India. Their combined contents disclose an unusually fertile avenue for investigating the intellectual recollections of primeval mankind, the preservation of divine revelation throughout the dispersions of the nations, the origins and progress of ancient sacred learning, and the material instruments through which religious knowledge survived successive kingdoms, languages, and historical transformations.

The writings of the Dr. Chevalier Andrew Michael Ramsay, the Reverend & Professor/Doctor Claudius Buchanan, Thomas Yeates, and their associated historical investigators permit the examination of these subjects through sacred cosmography, comparative theology, Oriental philology, archaeological testimony, manuscript science, natural philosophy, and the historical interpretation of the providential government of God.

At the centre of Ramsay's Travels of Cyrus stands an elaborate reconstruction of the intellectual education of the Persian monarch, whose extraordinary destiny receives its highest theological significance from the prophecies of Isaiah. Ramsay conducts Cyrus through a succession of geographical and philosophical environments, each possessing a distinctive inheritance of religious institutions, royal legislation, intellectual disciplines, and traditions concerning the Supreme Being. 

The Persian and Median courts introduce the political foundations of empire; the teachings of Zoroaster extend into the invisible operations of nature; the Egyptian mysteries disclose an elaborate hierarchy of sacred signs and priestly instruction; the institutions of Sparta and Athens furnish investigations into legislation and political virtue; the Pythagorean discourses concern the immaterial faculties of the intellect; and the Phoenician histories preserve traditions of celestial rebellion, suffering, and restoration.

 This immense itinerary eventually brings the prince into Babylon, where the Hebrew witnesses Eleazar and Daniel expound the authority of Divine Revelation, the history of Creation, the Flood, the election of Israel, and the prophetic significance of Cyrus's approaching conquests. The arrangement allows Ramsay to interweave the religious inheritance of the nations with the biblical account of history under the sovereignty of the Almighty.[1]

Particularly magnificent is Ramsay's treatment of the three primordial conditions of the created order: original felicity, subsequent corruption, and the anticipated renovation of creation. In his preface and appended discourse, he associates these recollections with the religion of Noah and the diffusion of ancestral theological knowledge among the nations descending from the patriarchal generations.

 The intellectual consequences extend directly into Genesis 6–11, the genealogy of the sons of Noah, the confusion of languages at Babel, and the subsequent emergence of ancient kingdoms. Ramsay's comparative descriptions of (Heathen little g g*ds) Oro*azes, Mith*as, Arima*ius, Os*ris, Ho*us, Typ*on, Bel*s, and Ado*is(All defeated see Isaiah 46, 47 & Jeremiah 47-41 ) permit a historically attentive examination of the religious symbolism through which different civilizations represented spiritual agency, divine government, the entrance of disorder, and the hope of restoration. 

The research thereby opens a substantial avenue for examining the ancient prisca theologia, or primordial theology, through the surviving testimonies of Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Syriac, Persian, and Egyptian antiquity.

 Its implications become especially fruitful when Ramsay's comparisons are studied alongside Ralph Cudworth's True Intellectual System of the Universe (1678), a philosophical work expressly invoked within Ramsay's own scholarly apparatus.

The Persian instruction furnished by Zoroaster introduces another extraordinary intellectual stratum: the contemplation of living nature through its smallest visible and invisible operations. Ramsay considers the supposed internal preformation of seeds, the minute organization of vegetable fibres, the circulation of nutritive juices, the influence of atmospheric pressure upon plants, the transformations of insects, and the mechanisms by which animal life appears to sustain its manifold functions. He proceeds into the study of aerial disturbances, subterranean fires, salts, sulphurs, nitres, luminous phenomena, and the subtle medium through which the natural philosophers of his age sought to understand cohesion, motion, and sensation. 

His account of vegetal pipes, minute fluid passages, and innumerable exhalations issuing from plants supplies exceptional material for historical pneumatic botany, physiological microstructure, and the study of the minute anatomy of created beings. Even the smallest insect becomes an occasion for contemplating the intricacy of organic arrangement and the wisdom manifested through the proportions of its delicate members. Ramsay additionally introduces aerial Genii as imagined observers of the concealed operations of nature, bringing the historical vocabulary of invisible intelligences into conversation with the physical and botanical sciences.[2]

Egypt furnishes an equally remarkable theatre of hieroglyphical theology and sacred natural history. Ramsay describes an imposing symbolic arrangement containing a porphyry obelisk, a hawk, a winged celestial globe, a serpent, a crocodile concealed beneath the waters, a sphinx, the veiled figure of Is*s, and the silent Harpocrates. 

The theological exposition attributed to the priest Sonchis associates these figures with the intellectual interpretation of the divine attributes, the sensible manifestation of spiritual principles, and the government of the created universe. 

The hawk's extraordinary sight and rapid movement become emblems of intelligence and activity; the celestial globe indicates the encompassing heavens; and the surrounding figures invite examination of the symbolic functions assigned to animals, waters, and composite beings within the ancient religious imagination. 

The narrative further introduces Hermes Trismegistus,(descendant from Ham- Noah) whose reflections upon animal death, the movements of the stars, and the operations of his own understanding culminate in the intellectual apprehension of a First Mover. 

Such passages possess exceptional value for a specialist study of Egyptian sacred iconography, archaic zoological symbolism, ancient theories of consciousness, philosophical introspection, and the historical development of arguments concerning the Creator's sovereignty over visible and invisible nature.[3]

The Phoenician investigations carry these themes into a remarkable theology of celestial rebellion and intercession. Ramsay's seventh book presents a dramatic account of B*lus, Ura*ia, Ad*nis, and the disturbance of heavenly harmony, culminating in the suffering of an intercessory figure who descends among the afflicted inhabitants of the earth. Within this narrative, the Hydr* of L*rna, the Nem*an lion, the serpent Pyth*n, and other monstrous figures become expressions of the spiritual and moral disorder described through allegorical mythology. 

Ramsay expressly considers the ancient idea of a mediating divine agent whose sufferings participate in the restoration of the created order. The proximity of Phoenicia to the territories of Israel enlarges the possibilities for researching the historical transmission of religious narratives, the ancient meanings associated with Ad*nis and T*mmuz, the representation of sacred suffering, and the reception of eastern theological traditions within classical literature. 

The associated materials invite comparison with Ezekiel 8, the symbolism of the prophets, the ancient interpretation of divine judgment, and the biblical testimony concerning the restoration of creation.[4]

At Babylon the geographical, theological, and prophetical threads of the fourth volume attain their most magnificent convergence. Cyrus encounters the Hebrew sacred tradition through the discourses of Eleazar and Daniel, while the narrative introduces the historical recollections of the Flood, Abraham, Moses, the covenantal election of Israel, and the great empires under which the people of God endured captivity. 

The prophetic declarations of Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1–7 provide the essential foundation for understanding the remarkable naming and appointment of Cyrus. Ramsay's account of the prince's eventual recognition of the God of Israel culminates in the royal authorization to rebuild the Temple at Jerusalem, thereby joining the historical narratives of Ezra and Chronicles to the prophetic interpretation of empire. 

The intellectual scope of this section also reaches into the relation between Divine Foreknowledge and human liberty, the administration of spiritual intelligences, the meaning of sacrifice, and the promised manifestation of Emmanuel. 

These materials furnish a particularly substantial foundation for research into providential historiography, sacred kingship, angelological administration, prophetic chronology, and the theological interpretation of ancient imperial succession.[5]

The enlarged historical investigation acquires a distinctive documentary dimension through the travels of Claudius Buchanan among the religious communities of Asia. His observations extend through Bengal, the Coromandel coast, Tanjore, Travancore, Cochin, Quilon, Cranganore, and neighbouring regions, where the scholar encounters the physical repositories of sacred literary inheritance: synagogue record chests, church manuscripts, royal charters, temple libraries, palm-leaf writings, vernacular translations, and historical ecclesiastical establishments. Buchanan's enquiries concerning the Syrian Christians preserve an unusually valuable account of their clergy, their inherited liturgical language, their ecclesiastical connections with western Asia, and their possession of Syriac biblical manuscripts. 

The associated report of Richard Hall Kerr provides additional evidence concerning the institutions and religious conditions of the ancient churches of Cochin and Travancore. 

Together, these materials permit a detailed reconstruction of the geographic and intellectual corridors through which Christian learning moved between Mesopotamia, Persia, the Indian Ocean, and the western settlements of the Indian peninsula.

Among the most significant discoveries is the manuscript presented to Buchanan by the Syrian metropolitan, whose ancient Estrangela characters, substantial vellum, and surviving impressions of faded writing furnished a remarkable object for Oriental palaeography. The manuscripts associated with the same collection include Syriac scriptural books, writings attributed to Clement, and additional biblical literature preserved among the Eastern churches. 

These collections illuminate the long historical life of the Syriac language, ܠܫܢܐ ܣܘܪܝܝܐ (leššānā suryāyā), as a vehicle of theology, worship, scriptural translation, and ecclesiastical memory. The connection between Syriac and the Aramaic linguistic world of the New Testament supplies an especially fruitful field for examining biblical expressions, inherited religious titles, and the literary transmission of early Christian knowledge. 

The comparison may be enlarged through the manuscripts of Baruch, Susanna, Maccabees, Ecclesiasticus, and the Clementine traditions, each opening an additional textual pathway into the preservation of Christian antiquity.
The Hebrew manuscripts recovered among the Jewish communities of Cochin introduce an equally extraordinary documentary inheritance. Buchanan describes an ancient record chest containing discarded sacred books and fragments written upon parchment, goatskin, and other materials, a neglected repository from which important textual witnesses were recovered for scholarly study. Thomas Yeates subsequently subjected the Malabar Pentateuch to a detailed examination of its constituent skins, scribal hands, columns, repairs, ornamental letters, and textual variations. Its thirty-four joined skins and 117 columns preserve an exceptional field for studying the history of Hebrew textual transmission. 

The manuscript's characteristic tagin, unusual letters, scribal divisions, and distinctive treatment of traditional textual spaces invite exact comparison with the Masoretic literature and the great eighteenth-century collations of Benjamin Kennicott. Yeates's accompanying notices of Hebrew and Syriac manuscripts, including the writings associated with Gad the Seer, further extend the collection into the less familiar regions of Jewish literary history, prophetic pseudepigrapha, and the manuscript reception of writings associated with biblical persons.[6]

The Megillah of Ahasuerus introduces an additional treasure of biblical manuscript science. Yeates reproduces an unusual Hebrew recension of material corresponding to the Greek additions to Esther, including royal proclamations, sacred prayers, and the prophetic dream attributed to Mordecai. The account of two contending dragons and the transformation of a little fountain into a great river furnishes rich material for comparative apocalyptic hermeneutics, particularly in relation to Daniel, the Septuagint, and the prophetic imagery of Revelation. Its reported transmission from an exemplar associated with brazen tablets at Goa creates a further avenue into the history of engraved texts and synagogue archival traditions. Equally remarkable are the metallic charters described by Buchanan, including six Christian plates containing eleven engraved surfaces and Jewish records of royal privileges. Their unfamiliar characters, witness formulas, hereditary rights, and comparisons with Palmyrene and ancient Near Eastern scripts furnish an extensive field for historical epigraphy, the archaeology of religious institutions, and the reconstruction of political relationships between Indian sovereigns and eastern mercantile communities.[7]

Another important dimension emerges from Buchanan's enquiries into the libraries and learned establishments of India. 

His references to manuscript catalogues associated with Tanjore, Rameswaram, Travancore, and other centres disclose the existence of extensive regional literary repositories whose contents extended through sacred writings, grammar, astronomy, law, medicine, and other branches of indigenous scholarship. 

His notices concerning palm-leaf manuscripts, the educational practices of the Indian churches, and the multilingual enterprises of the College of Fort William reveal an important history of intellectual transmission through writing, teaching, translation, and printing. Particularly significant is the association of Sanskrit, Tamil, Malayalam, Bengali, Persian, Arabic, Hindustani, Hebrew, and Syriac scholarship within the broader undertaking of biblical translation. The historical enterprise may be examined as an intricate network of linguistic receptivity, manuscript collation, grammatical interpretation, and the republication of sacred knowledge among distant peoples.

The presence of Nicolas Fréret's chronological letter within Ramsay's fourth volume enriches the entire collection with an additional discipline: the historical synchronization of ancient monarchies. His comparison of Herodotus, Ctesias, Xenophon, Median kingship, Persian chronology, and Babylonian political history invites a systematic study of the chronological frameworks within which the life of Cyrus and the biblical narratives of the Exile were understood. 

This apparatus may be extended through the regnal histories of Nabonidus, Belshazzar, Darius, and Cyrus, the chronology of Daniel and Ezra, and the interpretations of ancient historians preserved by Josephus, Eusebius, and later Christian chronographers. Its inclusion provides a valuable means of relating the speculative geographical journey of Cyrus to the historical authorities upon which eighteenth-century scholars constructed their understanding of the ancient East.

The culminating contribution of the four-volume collection resides in the extraordinary opportunities it provides for the recovery of neglected historical evidence and the renewed intellectual examination of sacred antiquity under the sovereignty of God. 

The minute ornament of a Hebrew character, the impressions remaining in a faded Syriac manuscript, the engraved title of a Jewish witness, the construction of an Egyptian hieroglyph, the pneumatic circulation imagined within a blade of grass, the traditions of celestial intelligences preserved in ancient philosophy, and the prophetic naming of Cyrus become individual avenues of investigation within an immense historical inheritance. Their careful examination requires the scholar to scrutinize material particulars, perpend competing textual witnesses, lucubrate upon the surviving ancient authorities, and excogitate fresh connections among the sacred languages, historical chronicles, natural philosophy, theology, and archaeology. The preservation of these rare books offers a substantial foundation for recovering forgotten scholarship, identifying neglected manuscripts, reconstructing dispersed intellectual traditions, and advancing a more extensive historical understanding of the created world, the operations of human intelligence, and the continuing testimony of Divine Revelation throughout the generations of mankind.

[11:43:12 AM] It is great to be here. Mr. President, Mr. Vice President, thank you, Norman, as well for taking this day. And this is a day that is special. I want to remind you of a country that over 390 years ago understood what it meant to defend what we have. 390 years ago, our National Guard really stepped forward and said, you know, we came to this country expecting to find liberty and freedom in the pursuit of what we want and freedom to have that pursuit of happiness. It was not guaranteed to us. It was a pursuit. And they understood that the only way we could have a pursuit is to actually fight for that pursuit. 390 years went by, 251 years ago. We started as a country with our Navy and our Army and our Marines adding on as we went. And over the years, what would happen just as they did 390 years ago, they would leave from the farms, they would leave the shops, they would leave their homes, they would leave their families to go do for this country what this country had given to them, and that it was the way to live and a way to pursue life and happiness. And so throughout the ages, we have woke up on mornings like December 7th, 85 years ago, when everyone was just getting up for Sunday morning thinking it was going to be a normal day, and then we were attacked cowardly at Pearl Harbor. We follow through with years of war in Vietnam, we go through the Gulf War, and then we come into a date in September much like this in which we were attacked again. What is the same throughout history is that every time that this country needed someone, someone stood up. That someone is a veteran. That someone has a face and a name. That someone is the reason you are here today. It is the reason you can assemble peacefully. It is the reason you can vote. It is the reason that you have freedom of press and freedom of speech. It is the reason that you have the life that you live. So veterans today understand one thing. This country does not forget. This president does not forget. This administration remembers that the purpose of the VA is to take care of veterans, and that is all we do at the VA is put veterans first every day. And in the past years, we’ve made it easier to get your compensation, easier to go to the hospital. We’ve opened 47, Mr. President, new facilities since 2025. And we’ve also made it easier to actually follow the law. I know that’s a strange concept for some in this city, but the Mission Act said that our veterans could go into the community for care, as you signed into law, sir. And we’ve had a 26 percent increase in veterans not only getting direct care, but community care just in the last two years.
[11:46:15 AM] So veterans, this is a day for celebration. If you have raised your right hand, you have done something that approximately 96 percent of this country never has done. You raised your right hand and said, I’m willing to go. I’m willing to serve. I’m willing to be there. Or as my friend and colleague at the Department of War says, here I am. Send me. You are the best of America. You are what makes us the envy of the world and also what the rest of the world fears, because when veterans come down, the world knows if they’re an American coming, then help is on the way. There’s one last thing that I admit every time because there’s press here, that have seen this, and I’ve seen this start cropping up, and I have to say it all the time, that I am tired in a country where I see we’re giving veterans this, we’re giving veterans that, and haven’t we given them enough. I have one thing to say to this country and those naysayers: we do not give our veterans anything. They have earned everything that they have gotten, and we will not forget you. And now it is my great honor and pleasure to introduce the Vice President of the United States and a fellow veteran, Mr. J.D. Vance.

VICE PRESIDENT J.D. VANCE:
[11:47:49 AM] Well, thank you, Doug, and thanks to all of you for your service, and let me just be another voice that says to all of our nation’s veterans, to their families, to their friends, to their children, to everybody who has served the United States of America in uniform, but also to the people who made it possible for them to serve the United States in uniform. This is your day. Happy Veterans Day, my fellow veterans. We’re proud of you, and we’re never going to stop fighting for you.
[11:48:23 AM] So, 22 years before Abraham Lincoln was president, he observed that it was our veterans who were the memorial to generations past, to the wars that they fought and to the freedoms that they earned. And in his time he was talking about the generation of Revolutionary War veterans who had served their country honorably and they were passing away, and he likened it to a massive, beautiful forest where every day we would lose one or another giant, beautiful oak tree. Think about what those veterans represented. Before we had these beautiful monuments, before we had stone, the first memorial to our nation’s freedoms and the wars that made them possible were our veterans. You saw them in the friends that you served with. You saw them in the people who lost limbs. You saw them in the headstones that represented a life that had served their country honorably. We’re proud in this amazing city and this beautiful capital of ours. We’re proud of all these incredible monuments, but we know that the most important monuments to our generations who served in the military, our most important monuments are you. It is the people who had the courage and the willpower and the fight to put on the uniform. The greatest monument to America — it’s you all. It’s the fact that you served.
[11:50:02 AM] But just as in Lincoln’s time, some of those monuments were disappearing, one of the amazing responsibilities and the humbling responsibilities as a veteran is that we have to pick up the torch when one generation sets it down. Now, when I first started doing work with the generation of veterans in Vietnam, one of the things they told me, one of the most important things they took to heart, is that they did not want to leave the next generation of veterans behind. Anybody who’s talked to a veteran of Vietnam knows that they were fighting not just for their own generation, so that the government honored the promises that were made to the generation in Vietnam, they were also fighting so that the generations that fought in Iraq and Afghanistan — so that the government honored those promises as well. Because one of the most important things our veterans do is not just fight the war in front of them. As one veteran to the next, we are picking up that torch every single day. We will never leave our veterans behind, ladies and gentlemen. That is my most sacred promise to every person here today.
[11:51:24 AM] But just as in Lincoln’s time, he was witnessing that amazing Revolutionary War generation lose an oak tree every single day, so in our time, we are watching fewer and fewer World War II veterans who still remember what it was like to serve in one of our nation’s greatest and most historic triumphs in 251 years of proud history. And so I want to give a special shout-out to three World War II veterans who are here with us today, and I ask that they be recognized, and that is Dave Yoho, Clifford Richardson and Julian Smith. Thank you for your service, for fighting for this country.
[11:52:34 AM] Ladies and gentlemen, my fellow veterans, this is your day of course, and I want you to celebrate. I want you to have a good time. And in my family, our great tradition, because veterans eat free at Golden Corral, was to go to Golden Corral. We had one guy in the back standing up and clapping. But whatever your tradition is, I want you to enjoy this day, but I also want you to take some special commitment. Just as the generations of World War II veterans and the generation of Vietnam veterans fought for my generation of veterans, it is now our time to pick up the torch and to fight for the next generation of veterans. So yes, ladies and gentlemen, let’s celebrate our veterans, but I want every single veteran here, every single veteran in our country, to remember that our job is to fight for the next generation of veterans, and that is exactly what we’re going to do.
[11:53:50 AM] And because of that, I am proud to introduce a man who has fought for veterans every single step of his life in public service. A man who expanded health care benefits for our veterans and who demands that his administration honor its commitments to the veterans who served our country in uniform. He is our commander-in-chief, but most importantly today, he is a fighter for the nation’s veterans, and I am proud to fight right alongside him. Mr. President, Donald J. Trump, the 45th and 47th president of the United States.

PRESIDENT TRUMP:
[11:54:33 AM] Thank you very much.
[11:54:37 AM] Thank you very much. I want to just thank the Vice President. He's doing a fantastic job. We appreciate it very much. And we come today to these hallowed grounds, and they are indeed very special. Rolling hills that hold the names of our great heroes etched in stone to honor 250 years of service, valor, and sacrifice unsurpassed in all of the ages. On Veterans Day, we reaffirm our undying gratitude to every patriot who has answered the call of duty. We pay tribute to all of those who have won the wars and worn the uniform, who face the enemy, who have beaten the enemy at every turn, who have borne the burdens of fate and destiny to stand as our protection in battle. You are indeed our protection in battle. And we thank Almighty God for the noble warriors of the United States military who have always stepped forward so that America might always stay free. To every veteran here at Arlington and across the nation, today we render you the highest salute.
[11:55:54 AM] We offer you our deepest respect and love, and we pledge to you our utmost loyalty and devotion. Please join me in thanking every American veteran of the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, Coast Guard, and the United States Marine Corps. And we want to thank you very much. As we salute our veterans, let us also express our profound love and appreciation for our military families, past and present. They are amazing. Thank you very much. And they are really among the very best of our nation. We're honored to be joined as well by the First Lady of the United States. Thank you very much. Thank you. The Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth. I had a feeling that was going to happen. He's done a fantastic job. And he loves you and he protects you. He's all about you. Secretary of Veterans Affairs with a 92% approval rating, the job he's doing. That's pretty good. Maybe we'll get it up to 100 pretty soon, Doug.
[11:57:31 AM] Doug Collins, thank you, Doug. What a job. It's about 50 points higher than his predecessor, I must tell you. That's a big difference. Many members of my Cabinet, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Dan Cain, who's fantastic. Thank you very much, General. Thank you. And representatives of our amazing Veterans Service Organizations and the countless members of the United States Armed Forces who are with us today. Thank you all. We really respect and appreciate you. Thank you all. To inherit a free nation is among the rarest blessings that any people in history have ever known. To defend that freedom is among the hardest and highest obligations, one of the most difficult tasks imaginable. Across every generation, American liberty has been preserved by legions of selfless patriots who have raised their right hands and sworn an oath of flesh and blood for a cause whose full cost could not be measured in advance.
[11:58:49 AM] There was no way it was doable, they thought. In every era, they stood watch, they've held a line, they've held a charge bravely into the fray that few people would have wanted to do or could have done. It's something that lies between order and chaos, freedom and tyranny, civilization and barbarism, and good and evil. Exact opposite ends of the spectrum. Time and time again, for 250 years, the American warrior has returned victorious. Our republic has triumphed. And today our country is stronger than it has ever been before. A nation without heroes is like a sky without stars or a heaven without angels. But in America, we've never known that darkness because we have the men and women of America's armed forces, our guiding lights, our greatest heroes, and our guardian angels. At 19 years old, Jack Myers kissed his young bride and newborn son goodbye and went to serve as a gunner in the 692nd Tank Destroyer Battalion in World War II.
[12:00:11 PM] Brave people all. In the frostbitten winter of 1944, Corporal Myers found himself in the largest battle in American history, the Battle of the Bulge. For weeks, he and his unit fought in one of the most intense crucibles in the history of war to turn the enemy's final advance into an unbelievable and somewhat unexpected defeat. We thought it would have to go on much longer than that. It was an incredible moment in military history. Months later, Jack's battalion was among the first to liberate the Dachau concentration camp, coming face-to-face with the evil he risked his life to destroy. Today, Jack is a great-great-grandfather and is here to receive our nation's gratitude at 103 years old. Jack, Corporal Jack Myers, we are honored by your presence today. It's really something. You see how we all respect you, respect you so much. Thank you, and thank you for being here. U.S. Army Colonel Douglas Moore served as one of the famous dust-off medevac pilots in Vietnam.

America Today | Transcript: 2026 National Veterans Day Observance, Arlington National Cemetery
Wednesday, November 11, 2026

This is a complete transcript of the official program of the 73rd National Veterans Day Observance at Arlington National Cemetery, from the prelude and the President’s wreath laying at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier through remarks in the Memorial Amphitheater and the retirement of the colors.

Source: Transcribed by America Today from the Right Side Broadcasting Network from-the-start livestream of the ceremony, https://t.co/6qGrDiGt6v. Speaker identifications were cross-checked against stills from the Real America’s Voice White House pool feed (CH1), https://t.co/dlGtXHmudB and https://t.co/e46DyQu2lV. As of 12:42 PM ET, November 11, 2026, https://t.co/jmStNikDdi (briefings and statements, and the remarks page) had not published a 2026 ceremony transcript. White House Veterans Day videos and the Memorial Amphitheater photo gallery then listed on the site are dated November 11, 2025, and were not used.

Times are America/New_York (ET). The RSBN pre-show before the official program (approximately 10:00–10:45 AM ET) and RSBN commentary after the ceremony’s close are omitted. Musical selections are noted; lyrics are not fully transcribed. A short list of Veterans Day National Committee names was checked against the audio; residual uncertainty on a few proper names is noted in the report NOTES.

A CEREMONY OFFICIAL:
[10:45:26 AM] And now, distinguished guests, the United States Coast Guard Band and the Air Force Singing Sergeants will perform a salute to the armed forces of the United States of America. For our veterans in attendance, please stand, if able, when you hear your service song.
[10:45 AM] [Musical selection: a salute to the armed forces of the United States, United States Coast Guard Band and the Air Force Singing Sergeants.]
[10:49:49 AM] Please be seated. During the wreath-laying ceremony, you will hear the bugler playing Taps. Protocol for the occasion is to stand, if able, and render honors by placing your right hand over your heart or rendering a hand salute. Thank you.
[10:55:53 AM] The President of the United States has arrived and is being greeted by Vice President J.D. Vance and National Commander Norman T. Henninger, Jr.
[11:06:39 AM] The Armed Forces Honor Guard and United States Army Band are formed and waiting as the President of the United States moves to the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier to place the wreath.
[11:07 AM] [The President places a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Honors are rendered, including Taps.]
[11:13:17 AM] Distinguished guests, the wreath-laying ceremony is now complete. The Veterans Day program will begin momentarily. Please move to your seats.
[11:13:27 AM] [Musical selection: “The Battle Hymn of the Republic.”]
[11:19:23 AM] Distinguished guests, it is now my distinct privilege to introduce the members of the Veterans Day National Committee. The committee was formed by presidential order in 1954 to plan this annual observance and support other Veterans Day observances throughout the nation. Please hold your applause until I have introduced each special guest. If you’re able, please stand when your name is called.
[11:19:44 AM] Gary A. McClure, Noncommissioned Officers Association of the United States of America. Frank J. Peters, The American Legion. Francis Lowe, Military Order of the Purple Heart. Russ Miller, Marine Corps League. Michael H. Hoyer, Military Chaplains Association of the United States of America. Robert Thomas, Paralyzed Veterans of America. Donald Marks, Legion of Valor of the United States of America. Marlon Ruiz, Military Order of the World Wars. Kyle M. Carpenter, TREA, The Enlisted Association. Nicholas Dockery, Congressional Medal of Honor Society of the United States of America. John Donovan, Disabled American Veterans. Jim O’Brien, Military Officers Association of America. Christopher Mendoza Trung, Commissioned Officers Association of the United States Public Health Service. Keith A. Reed, Air Force Sergeants Association. Michael Stetz, Polish Legion of American Veterans of the United States of America. Harold Treber, Korean War Veterans Association of the United States. David Rodriguez, American GI Forum of the United States. Michael Rano, Catholic War Veterans. Wade Davis, Blinded Veterans Association. Selena Kanowitz, Jewish War Veterans of the United States of America. Thomas Burke, Vietnam Veterans of America. Corey Geisler, Veterans of Foreign Wars of the United States. Sharon Martin, Fleet Reserve Association. Sandy Voorhees, AMVETS.
[11:22:30 AM] The associate and emeritus members of the committee are also with us today. Associate and emeritus members, please stand. Ladies and gentlemen, please join me in recognizing our Veterans Day National Committee leadership with your applause.
[11:27:31 AM] Please stand, if you are able, for the arrival of the official party.
[11:27:52 AM] Distinguished guests, the President of the United States, accompanied by the Vice President, the host of today’s ceremony, the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, and today’s ceremony co-host, the National Commander of Army and Navy Union, United States of America.
[11:28:11 AM] Distinguished guests, please remain standing for the procession of our nation’s colors and those of our veteran service organizations. As we march on the colors, the United States Coast Guard Band will play the National Emblem March. Please place your right hand over your heart or render a hand salute.
[11:29:00 AM] [The colors are marched on. Musical selection: “National Emblem March,” United States Coast Guard Band.]
[11:34:28 AM] Distinguished guests, please remain standing for the invocation given by Chaplain Byron Singleton, Acting Executive Director of National Chaplain Service for the United States Department of Veterans Affairs.

CHAPLAIN BYRON SINGLETON:
[11:34:48 AM] Let us pray.
[11:34:49 AM] Almighty God, creator and sustainer of us all, we gather today on these sacred hills of Arlington, as we are surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses, U.S. veterans who have passed away and are now at peace. There are generations of brave men and women who answer the call of duty to serve and defend our great nation and to preserve our liberties, which we hold dear. This Veterans Day we gather to express deep gratitude for unselfish service, steadfast courage, and enduring sacrifice to defend our land and to protect our Constitution. Dear Lord, we bestow favor upon the millions of veterans in every state who donned the uniform of the U.S. Armed Forces. We humbly thank you, God, for using them as a shield of protection, despite the hardships that they may have endured during times of conflict, war, and peace. We are surrounded by many rows of white headstones, which are a stark reminder that each headstone represents a life lived and a story told in the fabric of U.S. history. We remember our deceased veterans and honor living veterans who walked away from the battlefield with invisible wounds of war. We beseech you to grant spiritual healing to those struggling with post-traumatic stress disorder and moral injury. As people of faith, we touch and agree for total restoration of the body, the soul, and spirit. We ask for a special blessing for the families who shared the burden of military service when they were separated because of deployment. Comfort those bereaved families and shower them with peace and joy. May your amazing grace, goodness, and mercy consume them. In God, we ask that may our gratitude be demonstrated by actions of love, compassion, and service to each other. Help us, O God, to be one nation under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all. We pray all of these things in the name of our God, who is holy. Amen.

A CEREMONY OFFICIAL:
[11:37:12 AM] Please be seated.
[11:37:13 AM] I am honored to introduce the 2026 National Veterans Day Observance co-host organization, the Army and Navy Union of the United States of America. The Army and Navy Union USA is America’s oldest active veterans organization, founded in 1886 in Cincinnati, Ohio, and incorporated in Hamilton County, Ohio, March 31, 1888. Its fundamental objective is to continue national defense and national security, promote, foster, encourage, and perpetuate fraternal comradeship among those who have seen honorable service or are presently serving honorably in the United States Armed Forces, and to continue the high ideals of patriotism, loyalty, justice, and service to the country, educating all others in these principles. Representing Army and Navy Union USA is National Commander Norman T. Henninger, Jr. Mr. Henninger is a Vietnam-era veteran of the United States Navy. He is a two-term national commander, originally serving from 1988 to 1989, and has been involved with the Veterans Day National Committee on and off for 37 years. Please join me in welcoming the National Commander of the Army and Navy Union USA and co-host of today’s ceremony, Mr. Norman Henninger, Jr., who will lead us in the Pledge of Allegiance and deliver remarks. Please stand for the Pledge of Allegiance.
[11:38:47 AM] [The Pledge of Allegiance is recited.]

NATIONAL COMMANDER NORMAN T. HENNINGER, JR.:
[11:39:08 AM] On behalf of the Army and Navy Union, United States of America, Incorporated, the National Veterans Day Committee, and the Department of Veterans Affairs, we welcome you to the 73rd National Veterans Day Observance here at Arlington National Cemetery.
[11:39:22 AM] As we celebrate this Veterans Day, let us reflect on the meaning and purpose of Veterans Day. It is important that we separate Veterans Day from Memorial Day, which was to honor those who gave their lives in the defense of our country. Veterans Day celebrates all who have served in the service of our nation, living or deceased, to protect the freedoms we as Americans enjoy today. Veterans Day was originally known as Armistice Day. President Woodrow Wilson proclaimed on November 11, 1919, the first Armistice Day, marking the anniversary of the cessation of hostilities in World War I, which occurred at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month. Then on June 1, 1954, Congress changed the name to Veterans Day, a day to honor American veterans of all wars. In 1954, a Veterans Day proclamation by President Dwight D. Eisenhower called for the formation of the Veterans Day National Committee, chaired by the Administrator of the Veterans Administration, which later became the Department of Veterans Affairs, to oversee the national planning and organizing of Veterans Day observances. The chair then called together leaders of the national veterans organizations and asked them to serve on this committee. As such, Veterans Day offers a time of reflection. For our older Americans, it may bring back memories of service or loved ones who have served. For future generations, it is an opportunity to gain experience from our history and prepare for our future. This Veterans Day, let us dedicate our lives to assisting veterans and their families in the times of need or in distress and to assist in the burial of such veterans whenever called upon to do so. When we see a veteran, extend your hand. Thank them for their service. They will appreciate it and it might just make you feel better also.
[11:42:11 AM] I am now honored to introduce the host of today’s ceremonies, our chair of the Veterans Day National Committee and the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, Douglas A. Collins. Mr. Secretary?

SECRETARY OF VETERANS AFFAIRS DOUGLAS A. COLLINS:
[11:42:18 AM] Please be seated.
[11:42:41 AM] Well, welcome everyone to Veterans Day. For all our veterans here serving today, I am a little partial, of course, for my 25-plus years almost in the Air Force, but also my Army brethren, my Navy brethren, Coast Guard, and Space Force. But I have a special shout out. I will be a little bit quieter for some in the audience. You may know who I’ve forgotten, so if this is going to be your opportunity. But somebody had a birthday yesterday. If you don’t have the Marines in the house, who’s going to bark? There we go.

(Continued in part 2 of 3)

Doctrine of Retention: There are moments when a state ceases to negotiate over a possession and begins to define itself by that possession. In Rezaei's interview with Al Mayadeen, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, did precisely that.

✲ Rezaei did not speak the language of compromise, he spoke the language of permanence.

'We will not allow even a single particle of enriched nuclear material to leave Iran' - This was not a bargaining position but a declaration of sovereignty, phrased in the smallest possible unit, a particle, to render the refusal absolute - 'No fraction would be surrendered. No quantity would be deemed insignificant enough to trade.'

✲ Rezaei then removed any ambiguity toward whom this message was directed - 'we've informed our Russian friends that the enriched materials will remain in Iran and that we will use them ourselves.'

Moscow had been presented, in Washington's imagination, as the repository, the neutral custodian to whom Iran's stockpile might be entrusted, Rezaei closed that imagination - 'the material would not be transferred, stored abroad, or placed u/foreign guardianship. The material would remain, and the material would be used, by Iran alone.'

✲ The justification Rezaei offered was not military, but civilizational.

'We need enriched materials for the purpose of designing ships and submarines powered by nuclear energy.'

✲ In the unabridged interview, he expanded the vision - nuclear-powered vessels, nuclear-powered submarines, and eventually small modular reactors to power the nation itself. Iran, in Rezaei's telling, is not clinging to a weapons programme but claiming the right to an energy future, to a navy that does not depend on foreign fuel, to a technological independence that no sanction can revoke.

The world reads this differently, and Rezaei knows this. The IAEA estimated Iran possessed 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to 60% - a level far beyond civilian necessity, when Is*ael and the United States struck Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025. Since then, inspectors have been unable to verify how much survived, or where the material now rests. Washington demands removal of the material as the price of peace while Tehran now answers - there is no price.

• Then came the second claim, quieter, yet no less consequential - we've reached an advanced level in the field of electronic warfare, which enables us to take control of American UAVs and land them safely.

• Iranian media rendered this claim as cyber warfare, the capacity to seize a drone in flight and compel the drone to descend intact. The claim remains unverified by independent sources. Yet the claim echoes recent IRGC Navy assertions of capturing American MQM-170 drones over the Strait of Hormuz by overriding their guidance, assertions US Central Command has denied. Whether true or not, the message is deliberate - American eyes in the sky are no longer untouchable.

• And finally, the strategic frame, where Rezaei confirmed there're no negotiations currently taking place b/w Tehran and Washington. Iran, Rezaei said, has presented Washington with 7-conditions and awaits a clear and direct response. Until those conditions are fulfilled, the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed.

• Among those conditions, Rezaei said, is an end to the war on all fronts across West Asia, particularly in Lebanon.

Any new American attack, Rezaei warned, will not be answered only at nearby bases. Any new American attack will be answered at distant bases as well, incl.those Iran has not yet struck, incl.some in Europe.

This is the weight behind the message. Rezaei, former commander of the IRGC and newly appointed SNSC secretary, had just met President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin on 5 Nov, carrying a message from Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.

Beyond the soundbites, the interview is not a series of isolated statements but a coherent doctrine, one where every answer draws a red line - Iran will retain enriched material as a marker of sovereignty, not as a bargaining chip. Iran will justify that retention as a necessity for national development, not as defiance. Iran will link the reopening of Hormuz to a wider settlement of war in the region, not to pressure or concession. And Iran will promise that any future strike will be met not with restraint, but with reach.

'Not a single particle leaves. Not a single condition is conceded. Not a single frontier, in Tehran's telling, is beyond Iran's grasp.'

In a post on TruthSocial, Trump said he had an excellent conversation with Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, PM of Qatar, about Iran.

He said Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, and others would prefer the status quo, a continuation of the Greatest Naval Blockade in History, and the new Operation Iron Gate, therefore, land and sea.

CENTCOM said the blockade has prevented more than $25 billion in Iranian crude oil exports.

US Disables Blockade-Running M/V Huda In Gulf Of Oman

CENTCOM statement on M/V Huda - CENTCOM forces disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, 7 Nov, after the ship's civilian crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to violate the naval blockade against Iran multiple times. A US military aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda, disabling the ship after CENTCOM forces directed the crew to abandon targeted spaces. The cargo vessel tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port.

Video: UNCLASSIFIED CENTCOM footage shows the precision stern strike.

text:
Today is Veterans' Day, an opportunity to reflect on the sacrifices made in the defense our our country. For 250 years, select Americans have felt a calling to service, inspired by the desire to contribute to something larger than themselves, to safeguard our national inheritance for future generations.

I believe this is a divine calling. Psalm 18:39 says that it is the Lord who "girded me with strength for battle" and "subdued under me those who rose up against me." It is a calling that I felt 6 years ago when I commissioned into the United States Navy and joined the distinguished ranks of our veterans.

Our veterans embody the very best of the American spirit -- determined yet selfless, smart yet unpretentious, strong yet kindhearted. The greatest blessing of my time in service was learning from their example, being surrounded by many of the most inspiring individuals this nation has to offer.

That calling is still with me today. Although off active duty, I am still a member of the Navy Reserves. I am also an attorney for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, where approximately one-third of our personnel are other veterans. After years projecting American power abroad, many of us felt that it was time to protect our own borders here at home.*

Indeed, veterans are the ones guaranteeing our national sovereignty and all the rights that come along with it. On this day, I am reminded of a poem from Father Denis Edward O'Brien, a U.S. Marine Corps veteran and priest:

"It is the Soldier, not the minister,
Who has given us freedom of religion.

It is the Soldier, not the reporter,
Who has given us freedom of the press.

It is the Soldier, not the poet
Who has given us freedom of speech.

It is the Soldier, not the campus organizer,
Who has given us freedom to protest.

It is the Soldier, not the lawyer,
Who has given us the right to a fair trial.

It is the Soldier, not the politician,
Who has given us the right to vote.

It is the Soldier who salutes the flag,
Who serves beneath the flag,
And whose coffin is draped by the flag,
Who gives a protester the freedom he abuses to burn that flag."

May we never forget their service or their sacrifice. Most importantly, we must strive to be worthy of that sacrifice, to preserve the America for which they served and fought. That is the best way to honor them. Our veterans should not have to face combat oversees only to see this country torn apart from within. Today, make that your pledge: that you will defend their legacy by fighting for our country here at home.

Stories of Service: Captain John S. McCain III, U.S. Navy

Born into a Navy family in 1936, John McCain followed in the footsteps of his father and grandfather, both four-star admirals. He graduated from the United States Naval Academy in 1958 and became a naval aviator, eventually deploying to Vietnam aboard the USS Forrestal.

On October 26, 1967, during his 23rd bombing mission over North Vietnam, McCain's A-4 Skyhawk was shot down over Hanoi. He ejected from the aircraft, suffering serious injuries, and was captured by North Vietnamese forces.

McCain spent five and a half years as a prisoner of war, enduring repeated torture, beatings, and solitary confinement. Despite being offered an opportunity for early release because of his father's position in the Navy, he refused to leave before his fellow prisoners, remaining committed to the military Code of Conduct.

Released in March 1973, McCain returned to the United States and continued his service in the Navy before retiring in 1981. He later served for more than three decades in Congress, including as a U.S. Senator from Arizona, and a nominee for President in 2008.

His life was defined by a commitment to service that extended well beyond the cockpit. His story is a reminder of the courage, resilience, and devotion to country that have defined generations of American sailors.

This Veterans Day, we remember Captain John McCain and all those who have served in defense of our nation. 🇺🇸

$CAE (CAE Inc.): 10Y Historical Avg ±8.1%, with a hotter 2-Year Average of ±10.1% (Last move: -4.9% vs. ±10.0% implied; historically beats implied in 8 of 16 reports, or 50%).

text:
This man purchased a $20 scratcher at a gas station in Roswell New Mexico.

It showed that he won $500,000.

The lottery told him that it was actually a misprint.

And gave him $100 worth of free tickets.

John Wines was 65 years old and retired from his heating and A/C repair business in Roswell, NM.

In December of 2014 he walked into a nearby Shell gas station and bought his weekly Powerball ticket.

Just because, he also bought a $20 Ruby 7s scratcher.

He sat in his car and immediately started scratching.

His winning numbers were 1 and 2.

He scratched five winning numbers, two showing $250,000 each, one for $75, one for $500, one for $50.

His total winnings turned out to be $500,625.

What was even stranger was the maximum prize on the card was $250,000. 

He doubled that.

When he went into the gas station and scanned the scratcher, the machine said it wasn't even a winner.

Then he called the New Mexico Lottery.

They replied acknowledging the flaw, reconstructing the ticket, and that of course wasn't a winner.

They offered compensation for the flawed ticket with $100 worth of free lottery tickets.

Wines told the story to reporters and was talking about how whenever he made a mistake in business, he paid for, the lottery system didn't care.

To most peoples surprise, he didn't sue.

Wines wife told him to forget about it.

He also came on Fox and Friends and said he'd given up pursuing the money.

After all, the New Mexico Lottery was pretty prepared.

They had disclaimers on tickets saying liability for misprinted tickets or disputes is limited to the refund of the retail sales price.

That would've been $20.
