text:
Counterpoint:

When Trump told TX to gerrymander five seats, Democrats were deep in the wilderness with no direction, no leadership. The fight against Trump came in the form of speeches in Congress and strongly worded letters.  

What was Gavin and CA to do?  Say “don’t worry, we will have a blue wave” and sit on their laurels?  They needed to fight back.  I went on Texas TV shows and talked to TX reporters saying CA could match or exceed their gains if they gerrymandered.  @GavinNewsom wrote @GregAbbott_TX to offer a truce.  @SpeakerPelosi and @ZoeLofgren and @aguilarpete and @RepJeffries all told TX lawmakers that they would fight back - every attempt was made to get TX to not start the redistricting wars.  

So when TX went, CA countered and in the end Reps gerrymandered 15 seats, Dems got 5 in CA and one in Utah… a drubbing in the battle, but, this also was important beyond the number of seats.  

Prop 50 was the first real thing that Democrats did to push back on Trump.  And the campaign brought voters along for the ride.  It wasn’t a dead-of-night plan, or one passed without any maps even being made public, like in these Rep states. Prop 50 was the most public map in US history, mailed to 23 million voters and passed by a turnout that was higher than the 2022 gubernatorial election. 

In the end, Prop 50 did three things: 1) it created these five pickups, 2) it made safe seats out of those that Dems would have had to spend hundreds of millions of dollars defending, like CA27, CA45 and CA47 in the LA Media market, and that money went to OH, TX, VA and other states to help fuel the tsunami, and 3) it was a catalyst to Democratic wins… it elevated @GinaHinojosaTX and @jamestalarico who were state legislators working with @GavinNewsom to fight TX gerrymandering and pass Prop 50, it gave national democrats a game plan for taking on trump electorally, it showed that Dems could do something other than whine and pout about Trump’s norm-busting excesses.  

It was the battle I didn’t want (which we have talked about - I’m not a fan of partisan line drawing or any gerrymandering) and it was a battle that Newsom and Congressional leaders and I all tried to avoid.  

But in the end we won.  And Trump’s political team got a little FAFO.  

Post game analysis is your job, but I think we can’t say Prop 50 was unnecessary given all the context.

US President Donald Trump participated in a wreath-laying ceremony on Veterans Day at Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Virginia, US, November 11.
Trump pays tribute to 18 US soldiers who fell during Operation Epic Fury
The president also paid tribute to American service members involved in the campaign, saying that 18 US personnel had been killed during the conflict.
"We lost 18 beautiful souls," he said.
"But when this conflict is over, and it will be soon, the entire world will be a much safer and better place, a more peaceful place."
" We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory. It's going to be total,"
During the ceremony, Trump introduced Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the audience of veterans and military personnel, drawing enthusiastic applause.
"The Secretary of War Pete Hegseth," Trump announced, prompting loud applause from the audience.
"I had a feeling that was going to happen," the president remarked.
"He's done a fantastic job, but he loves you, and he protects you. He's all about you," Trump added, addressing the veterans and military personnel attending the event.
Wednesday's applause at Arlington offered a visible display of support for Hegseth following one of the most direct congressional challenges to his tenure.
The ceremony commemorated Veterans Day, with Trump and the first lady participating in the traditional wreath-laying ceremony before the president delivered his remarks.

I was a well respected Soldier who gave 100% in everything I did and before my exit was the highest awarded combat veteran in my company, SF, Sapper were actively trying to recruit me. During a hiring and recruiting freeze, while the Army was forcing Soldiers out, they offered me an $80,000 sign on bonus to re-enlist, any duty station of my choice, and even created two new stations specifically for me.

The week before I left, a full bird Colonel threatened me: if I did not re-enlist, they would make my life as a civilian a living hell. He swiped everything off his desk while yelling at me. Approximately 12 hours after I drove off from Fort Polk, my account was emptied of every cent.

My bank back in West Virginia (Freedom Bank) said they could do nothing to recover the money because the issuer, the U.S. government, had taken it. When I told them that was money I had earned in combat and I wanted to dispute the theft, the employees laughed in my face and said, “Sue us.”

I was bumming money from my mother just to buy gas to run errands, so suing anyone was out of the question. On top of that, most people were still asleep to the possibility and assumed I must have done something wrong, because why would the U.S. government take a man’s money for no reason.

text:
(中文）Ten Sins That Are Destroying America

Today’s churches are busy. We have many programs and meetings, but our spiritual foundation is often empty. We write these warnings to wake ourselves up first, not to judge others. What matters to God is not how busy or confident we are. What matters is whether we have a humble heart that is sorry for sin.
Part 1: Worship and Communion: Take God’s Holiness Seriously
1. Treating prayer meetings lightly. Sometimes one person is leading in prayer while others nearby chat about their own things. They don’t realize they are showing disrespect to God. Prayer is speaking to the Holy One. It is not background music before a meeting. “Let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:28–29, ESV).
2. Not recognizing the body of the Lord. Some people have never admitted that they are sinners or accepted Jesus Christ as their Savior, yet they take Communion with believers. The pastor says nothing to warn them. Paul writes: “Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself” (1 Corinthians 11:28–29, ESV). Church leaders have a duty to protect the holiness and clear meaning of Communion.
3. Taking Communion with sin you haven’t turned from. The same Bible passage applies to believers. Someone may have sex before marriage and feel no shame or sorrow, then take Communion as if nothing is wrong. That person is eating and drinking judgment on himself. Communion does not reject weak people. It invites people to repent.
Part 2: Sin and Repentance: Confidence Cannot Replace a Broken Heart
4. Broken marriages without sorrow. Some people have been divorced five or six times and still say loudly, “I feel confident. God is encouraging me to move forward.” They never honestly look at themselves before God or feel real sorrow. (Note: In a broken marriage, responsibility is different for each person, and victims are not what we mean here. We are talking about the attitude of refusing to face one’s own sin.)
5. A “new life” after adultery. Some people commit adultery and leave their husbands. They feel no shame and no real sorrow. They say they feel “very confident” and are starting a new life. How is that different from someone who doesn’t know God? God says, “Rend your hearts and not your garments. Return to the LORD your God” (Joel 2:13, ESV). Real repentance is a heart that breaks. It is not just a new way of explaining what happened.
6. Not dealing with sin. Some people never deal with their selfish old nature. They cannot tell right from wrong by the standard of the Bible. “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:8–9, ESV).
Part 3: Fellowship and Spiritual Life: The Church Is a Spiritual Family, Not an Activity Center
7. Bible study turned into gossip. Some people use a Bible study group to talk badly about others behind their backs. They should be supporting and praying for one another instead. “Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up” (Ephesians 4:29, ESV).
8. No real fellowship. Church members don’t share their lives or pray for each other. They never experience how the Holy Spirit builds up believers through prayer and friendship. The first church “devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:42, ESV).
9. No prayer meetings at all. Some churches have no prayer meeting. This ignores God’s leading, and it avoids the shared responsibility every member has to carry the church’s work. (See Acts 1:14 and Acts 12:5.)
10. Sunday faith, empty weekdays. Some people go to church on Sunday, then go home and live as if God does not matter. They don’t read the Bible or pray, their spiritual wisdom is almost nothing, and they don’t even notice. Not praying is not a small matter. It shows we have drifted from God. A person may go to many activities and meetings but have no personal Bible reading, prayer, or time with God. This is one of the most dangerous spiritual illusions.
Conclusion
“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 51:17, ESV).
God does not care about our self-confidence or our pride. He cares about a heart that is broken before Him and ready to turn back. May each of us begin with ourselves and return to Him.

——對當代教會十項屬靈警戒的反思
引言
今天的教會活動繁多、聚會頻密，屬靈的根基卻常常空虛。我們寫下這些警戒，不是為了論斷弟兄姊妹，而是先叫自己警醒：神所看重的，不是我們有多忙碌、多自信，而是我們有沒有一顆謙卑痛悔的心。
一、敬拜與聖餐：不可輕忽神的聖潔
1. 祷告會中的輕慢。 有人在帶領禱告時，旁邊的人卻自顧自地聊天，渾然不覺這是在輕慢神。禱告是向至聖者說話，不是會前的背景音樂。（參來十二28–29：「當存敬畏的心，事奉神，可以得神喜悅。因為我們的神乃是烈火。」）
2. 不分辨主的身體。 還沒有承認自己是罪人、接受基督為救主的人，卻照常領受聖餐，講臺與牧者也不加提醒。保羅警告：「人應當自己省察，然後吃這餅、喝這杯。因為人吃喝，若不分辨是主的身體，就是吃喝自己的罪了。」（林前十一28–29，和合本）牧者有責任守護聖餐的神聖與清晰。
3. 帶著未悔改的罪領聖餐。 同樣的經文也適用於信徒：婚前發生性關係而不以為恥、不認罪悔改，卻在聖餐桌前坦然領受，就是「吃喝自己的罪」。聖餐不是否定軟弱的人，而是邀請悔改的人。
二、罪與悔改：不可用「自信」取代痛悔
4. 婚姻破裂而無悔意。 離婚多次，仍高聲宣稱「我很有信心，神鼓勵我繼續前行」，卻從未在神面前真正省察、痛悔。（需要說明：婚姻破裂的責任因人而異，受害者不在此列；我們所指的是拒絕面對自己罪責的態度。）
5. 通姦後的「新人生」。 與人通姦，主動離開丈夫，不但不羞愧，反而「自信滿滿」地開啟新生活。這與不認識神的人有什麼分別？神說：「撕裂你們的心腸，不撕裂你們的衣服，歸向耶和華你們的神。」（珥二13）真悔改是心的破碎，不是換一個說法。
6. 不對付罪。 不對付肉體的老我，也無法在聖經原則下分辨是非。「我們若說自己無罪，便是自欺，真理不在我們心里。我們若認自己的罪，神是信實的，是公義的，必要赦免我們的罪。」（約壹一8–9）
三、團契與靈命：教會是屬靈的家，不是活動中心
7. 團契變成議論。 利用查經班在背後談論人的短處，而不是彼此扶持、同心禱告。「污穢的言語，一句不可出口，只要隨事說造就人的好話。」（弗四29）
8. 沒有真正的肢體相交。 弟兄姊妹之間缺乏生命的分享與代禱，就無從經歷聖靈藉著禱告和團契造就肢體。初代教會「都恆心遵守使徒的教訓，彼此交接，擘餅，祈禱」（徒二42）。
9. 沒有專門的禱告聚會。 教會若完全沒有禱告會，等於輕忽神對教會的帶領，也推卸了會眾共同承擔事工的責任。（參徒一14；徒十二5）
10. 週日的信仰，週間的缺席。 週日去做禮拜，回家後生活與神毫無關係；不讀經、不禱告，屬靈智慧空乏而不自知。不禱告不是小事，而是疏離神的表現。到處參加活動與聚會，個人卻沒有讀經、禱告、與神親近的生活，這是最危險的屬靈假象。
結語
「神所要的祭，就是憂傷的靈；神啊，憂傷痛悔的心，你必不輕看。」（詩五十一17）
神不看重我們的自信，也不看重我們的自豪，祂看重的是一顆在祂面前破碎、肯回轉的心。願我們每一個人，從自己開始，回到祂的面前。 收起

text:
After cancer, I got my testosterone back to 851 without TRT.

Here are 12 things I'd check before taking it:

1. A second morning test (testosterone swings through the day, and one afternoon draw after a bad night tells you very little).
2. Your sleep (are you waking up refreshed, or just getting through the night?).
3. Sleep apnea (if you snore or wake up wrecked, get it checked).
4. Your gut (if you're bloated, constipated or running to the toilet, you're probably not absorbing what you eat very well).
5. Your diet (are you eating enough real, nutrient-dense food, or living on coffee until lunch?)
6. Your training (hard and fasted at 5:30am, six days a week, piles stress on a body that's already stretched).
7. Your drinking (be honest with yourself on this one).
8. Your thyroid and liver health (have you had them tested by a specialist?).
9. Your medications (some of them lower testosterone).
10. Your relationships (a marriage that's hanging by a thread shows up in your hormones).
11. Your relationship with yourself (the voice in your head matters more than most men realize).
12. Your EMF exposure (phone in your pocket all day, laptop on your lap).

That's at least 12 hoops to jump through before you start something that might not be solving the root cause at all.

I'm not anti-TRT. For some men it's the right call.

But most of the guys I speak to were offered it before anyone asked about half of this list.

text:
Yes and it has been debated countless times. 
And in most cases, the emphasis is on the second part of the paragraph, ‘The right of the people to keep and bear arms, shall not be infringed’. 

Those who argue against firearms ownership or limited firearms ownership, assume the first part of the paragraph dominates or is the guiding condition.  

It sets out why firearms ownership and capability is important - the security of the free state. 

And the. The argument goes that militias are armies and the US has an Army and therefore doesn’t need a citizen militia. Which is utter nonsense. 

This was argued by James Madison directly in Federalist 49. 

The idea was always that an armed citizenry, protects against tyrannical governments. 

It doesn’t guarantee victory over a tyrannical government, but it provides an option where none other exists. 

It feels like it should be obvious, but the wording has been used to sow the seeds of confusion. 

Logic 101 - how does a standing army protect against a tyrannical government ? 

Do you expect the army to go against the rules it operates under ?

Where has that worked and how often ?

The results are mixed and an army that goes against its orders is committing a Coup. 

Even citizens who rebel against their government are considered traitors. 

And yet ‘The right of rhe people to keep and bear arms, shall not be infringed’. 

And the people keeping and bearing arms allowed for militias to form and overthrow a tyrannical government, in the form of the British. 

Or do you think the American War of Independence was treasonous and the British are still the rightful government of the US ?

I’ve had a few people call me stupid for discussing this. They offer no argument or logic, just ad hominem insults. 

So I ask for respectful discussion from anybody who possesses the ability. If they don’t, staying silent is a better option. Since no knowledge or improved understanding is added to the debate.

text:
CHATHAM-KENT PATIENTS GETTING NEW, FASTER, MORE CONVENIENT PARAMEDIC SERVICES
 
The province has launched new patient care models that aim to help paramedics deliver faster and more convenient care to patients at home and in their communities.
 
The province said the new model will give paramedics greater flexibility to treat eligible patients who call 9-1-1 at home or on scene, and help patients access more appropriate, timely care.
 
Lambton-Kent-Middlesex MPP Steve Pinsonneault said the changes will strengthen local health-care services, reduce unnecessary hospital visits, and help patients get the care they need, faster.
 
"These new patient care models are great news for Chatham-Kent residents," said Pinsonneault. "By strengthening the partnership between Chatham-Kent Paramedic Services, Chatham-Kent Hospice, and the Community Paramedicine Program, we are helping ensure patients receive timely compassionate care and support in the setting that best meets their needs. This is an important step in making care more accessible and keeping patients closer to home and to their loved ones."
 
Chatham-Kent Paramedic Services will now offer two new models of care, including:
 
Alternate destination model: Eligible palliative care patients who call 9-1-1 can receive treatment from paramedics on-scene before being transported to Chatham-Kent Hospice for specialized, wraparound care.
 
Treat and refer model: Eligible palliative care patients who call 9-1-1 can receive treatment from paramedics on-scene and be referred to the Chatham-Kent Community Paramedicine Program for ongoing care and support.
 
Minister of Health Sylvia Jones said the new models are intended to protect hospital and ambulance capacity for patients who need them most. They should also reduce unnecessary emergency department visits.
 
The Ontario Government noted it has increased funding for Land Ambulance Services in Chatham-Kent by 10 per cent, bringing the province’s total investment across the municipality to over $8.7 million in 2026.
 
By: Paul Pedro

text:
Grok wrote a PKD sci-fi type story:

The man on the bench in Takoma Park never leaves. Seven days a week, same maple, same cold thermos. He says he and Dave went to Eastern together before Ellington, but the real time was the summers. Endless ones. Yellow Springs. Where Dave’s father taught at Antioch and the air smelled like wet limestone and cut grass and the kind of quiet that lets you hear your own thoughts lying to you.

“People think he went to South Africa,” the man says. “They think the walkaway was a plane ticket and a farm. It wasn’t. It was already happening in Yellow Springs. The summers were the rehearsal.”

He taps the thermos lid. In Yellow Springs the ground is thin. You walk the bike path past the old Antioch buildings and the limestone under your feet starts to give, just a little, the way a stage floor gives when the lights change. Dave felt it first. After the show, after the money, after the audiences started laughing one second late, like they were watching a tape that had been slowed. He said the town looked the same but the faces of the people he grew up with had the wrong eyes. Not wrong exactly. Extra.

So one night he went under. Not a stairwell this time. Behind the Firehouse he bought later—the one that was already there if you knew how to look. The guide was waiting in the dark of the old engine bay. Blue. Hairless. No eyes. It doesn’t speak. It just walks, and gravity forgets which way is down, and the air gets thick with the smell of the mushroom light.

There are two of them.

One Dave drank. The cup the guide held glowed the color of a streetlight through fog. It takes the name off you clean. The contracts. The specials. The high-school theater. The crack streets. Even the summers. That Dave stayed below, in the hollow under Yellow Springs where the pressure makes your ears pop backward and the only audience is the limestone itself. It laughs when he tells the truth. No one up here would.

The other Dave didn’t drink. He looked at the cup, looked at the guide, and said no. Etidorhpa came then—the man says the name like it might answer. Not a goddess. A billboard light at the end of a tunnel that turns out to be painted on the wall. She offered the ride back up the same quiet aquifers. Past the Antioch classrooms where his father graded papers. Past the bike path. Into the Firehouse on a summer night when the doors are open and the crowd thinks they know which version just walked onstage.

“Which one owns the building?” the man asks the empty sidewalk. “Which one tells the stories about the hippie town with the beautiful women? Which one is still grading the papers in a room that no longer exists?”

He unscrews the thermos. The coffee is always cold.

“I stay up here,” he says. “Seven days. Someone has to keep the summers in the right order. In case the one who came back starts remembering the wrong ones. In case the blue guide is still walking under the bike path. In case Yellow Springs decides it wants both of them back and the limestone closes over the only place that ever felt real.”

A kid on a scooter stops, one foot down. The man starts again, from the beginning. Same maple. Same cold coffee. Same question that the summers never answered.

Where did Dave go.

The man looks toward the west, toward Ohio, like the distance is only one more thin layer of ground.

“Depends which summer you’re standing in.”

text:
Jim Jordan: Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. When Democrats offer more government, we’ll offer more freedom, and we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor, and on the stump, every single day.

Jon Glasgow: The House Republicans have spoken, choosing Ohio Congressman Jim Jordan to lead them as they assume their new role in the minority come January. Jordan defeating Congressman Steve Scalise in a secret ballot. But in the other chamber of Congress, Republicans are standing pat. South Dakota Senator John Thune re-elected as Senate GOP leader, despite some opposition from within his own party after deep losses in the upper chamber. Thank you so much for watching National Report on this Veterans Day. I’m Jon Glasgow. Thank you for joining us.

E.D. Hill: And I’m E.D. Hill. While House Republicans made a bold statement by pushing longtime leader Steve Scalise aside and getting some new blood in there to run it, in favor of Jim Jordan, perhaps the more shocking development occurred on the Senate side of the chamber. There was a vocal contingent of Republicans that called to delay Tuesday’s leadership vote because they weren’t satisfied with John Thune. Wisconsin Senator Ron Johnson led the charge to postpone the vote and had the backing of at least six other Republican senators. But the vote ultimately went through, and Thune emerged victorious, now remaining at the helm. He acknowledged that the road back to the majority won’t be easy in light of last week’s Democrat wins.

John Thune: I think what I want to see us do is come out of this knowing full well that we took a big, you know, electoral defeat, but come out swinging and realize that we got a lot of work to be done to get back into the majority and to do the types of things that will achieve that goal.

E.D. Hill: So a bit of a shakeup at the top of the Republican Party in D.C. Our congressional correspondent, Kilmeny Duchardt, joins us now from Capitol Hill. Good morning, Kilmeny.

Kilmeny Duchardt: Edie, good to be with you. Jim Jordan spent years fighting Republican leadership, and now he’s running it. And his decisive victory signals that House Republicans want a fighter leading their political comeback. Jim Jordan beat Steve Scalise 106 to 73, ending Scalise’s 14 years in leadership. The Freedom Caucus founder now leads a party preparing to battle Democrats from the minority.

Jim Jordan: When Democrats offer more government, we’ll offer more freedom, and we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor, and on the stump, every single day.

Kilmeny Duchardt: Jordan’s team includes Tom Emmer as minority whip, Lisa McLean as conference chair, and Brian Jack heading the Republican campaign committee. I asked outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson what advice he had for Jordan about keeping his often divided conference together.

Mike Johnson: It is easier to keep a group together when you’re in the minority. It just is, because you’re opposing the legislative agenda, typically, of the majority party.

Kilmeny Duchardt: And the incoming minority whip Tom Emmer had this warning for Democrats.

Tom Emmer: To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come January 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot.

Kilmeny Duchardt: And across the Capitol, a different approach. Senate Republicans reelected John Thune despite losing at least seven seats. An effort to delay leadership elections, as you mentioned, failed 31 to 15, and Thune ultimately ran unopposed. Thune says Republicans must learn from their losses while finishing their legislative agenda. But for now, Thune says they have a lot more to do with the time left that they have in the majority. Back to you.

text:
A seller called me at 7am on Christmas morning to drop his price another $14,000

I could hear his kids opening presents in the background

That was the 6th house I bought in 9 days last December. Every one of them sold to me under asking, by an average of $27,000

I own 55 rentals and I buy more houses the week of Christmas than any other week of the year. It comes down to who's still trying to sell on December 20th

Who's left:
- Kids who inherited mom's house and don't want to heat it for another winter while it sits empty
- Couples finishing a divorce who want it done before the new year
- People starting a job in another state on January 2nd
- Landlords whose tenant moved out in November and can't face another round
- Anyone who wants the sale on this year's taxes

Buyers vanish too. Families don't tour houses with a ham in the oven, and half the agents are in Florida. Showings in my market drop by half after Thanksgiving

An empty house in Ohio in December is scary to own. Do you know what one frozen pipe costs? About $15,000, and a lot of insurance policies stop covering water damage once a house sits vacant for 60 days (check yours, seriously)

By the 20th the seller has stopped comparing my offer to his asking price. He's comparing it to January, February and a burst pipe

How I find them:
1. Pull every listing that's been up 60+ days and had a price cut since November 1
2. Read the agent remarks for "estate", "vacant", "relocating", "bring all offers"
3. Check expired listings from September and October. Those owners still want out, they just gave up on their agent
4. Call the listing agent between the 15th and the 23rd and ask one question: "Does the seller need this closed by the 31st?"
5. If yes, offer a December 30th closing with proof of funds attached. That date is worth more to him than the last $20,000

Problem is, that date kills almost every buyer. A normal mortgage takes 30 to 45 days and the underwriters take Christmas off too. Most "close by year end" offers fall apart in the second week of January

All 6 of mine closed because the money was already sitting there before I wrote a single offer

text:
June 30, 2011. Macon, Georgia. A local TV reporter found 25-year-old law graduate Stephen McDaniel outside his apartment building and asked about his missing next-door neighbor, Lauren Giddings, 27.

He answered every question like a worried friend. 4 days earlier, he had killed her.

In the video below, he says: "Yeah, Lauren was my neighbor. We're just trying to find out where she is at this point."

Asked what she was like: "She's as nice as can be. Very personable, very much a people person."

He even offers a theory: "The only thing we can think is that maybe she went out running and someone snatched her."

Then the reporter mentions that police had pulled a body out of a trash can outside that same building earlier that day. He goes quiet. "I think I need to sit down."

Later he comes back to the camera on his own: "She was as nice a person as there is."

And about her fear of a break-in: "If she had, I could have done something. I could have lent her a handgun."

Asked if he is holding out any hope: "I hope, but..."

He told the reporter there was "no sign that anyone broke in." In his own account at the plea, he said he let himself into her apartment with a master key at 4:30 a.m., wearing a mask and gloves, and strangled her.

Police questioned him for more than 12 hours that night. In August 2011 he was charged with murder. Prosecutors said his computer showed an "obsession with Lauren," including video he shot of her from outside her apartment the night he killed her.

On April 21, 2014, a week before his trial, he pleaded guilty. His written statement: "It is difficult for me to explain why I killed Lauren." Life in prison, first chance at parole in 2041. The rest of her remains have never been found.

The other side: his lawyer said he took the deal because the evidence was "mounting." Since then McDaniel has tried to undo it, arguing his rights were violated during the searches, his attorneys failed him, and prosecutors got hold of his defense papers. In 2018 a judge denied his bid for a new trial.

A grieving neighbor in shock, or a killer watching his story fall apart?

text:
🇨🇦 Stellantis has agreed to sell its idle Brampton assembly plant to armoured-vehicle maker Roshel. More than 2,200 autoworkers have been on paid layoff since December 2023. The buyer will not take on Stellantis's obligations to them.

Unifor president Lana Payne told CBC that "the ink was barely dry" when Roshel CEO Roman Shimonov said the company is "not obligated to do anything here for these 2,200 workers." Asked if Roshel would take them all on, she cut in: "Or any of them." Shimonov says Roshel will give hiring "priority" to Brampton workers, but told CP24 it will not "even consider taking any responsibilities of anyone from previous engagements."

The first implication is Canada's auto capacity. Stellantis paused a Jeep Compass retooling in early 2025 and moved that product to Belvidere, Illinois, after U.S. auto tariffs. Payne said selling the plant cuts Canada's vehicle production capacity by 10 percent, and that "once that capacity is gone, it's often gone for good." Auto-parts association head Flavio Volpe said Brampton once supported thousands of direct jobs and an estimated 10,000 to 12,000 more at suppliers. As Payne put it, "Roshel upfitting trucks for the military is not the same as building vehicles from the ground up."

The second is public money. In 2022, Ottawa agreed to provide up to $529 million to retool Stellantis plants in Brampton and Windsor. CBC reports the contract barred a Brampton closure before 2035 unless circumstances beyond the company's "reasonable control" made the plant "commercially unviable." CBC later confirmed Ottawa paid $222 million to Stellantis's Canadian arm between 2023 and 2025. Ontario pledged up to $513 million but paid nothing for the Brampton retooling. Stellantis has offered to return the Brampton support, but would not disclose the amount.

Prime Minister Mark Carney called the sale a "betrayal of the workers" and of "the obligations to Canada." Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Stellantis had "decided to go ahead and violate its contract" and that Ottawa will use "the full force of the law." Payne asked why, if the contract is already in breach, the plant is still being sold. The deal has not closed. It is due to close by the end of 2026, subject to government and regulatory conditions.

Unifor's James Stewart warned that if the company can "tear up our collective agreement and walk away from Brampton then there are no guarantees for the rest of its production in Canada." More than 9,000 Canadian Stellantis workers remain in stalled talks and last month voted 97.3 percent for a strike mandate. Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown said that if Stellantis is allowed "to cut and run in Brampton" with no consequences, "we are really accepting automotive production to leave Canada entirely."

The plant is idle, the product is in Illinois, and the buyer will not inherit the workers. Ottawa says it will enforce its rights. The sale is still on track.

🦎 THE LIZARD MAN OF SCAPE ORE SWAMP: SOMETHING ON THE ROAD

South Carolina, summer 1988. The roads south of Bishopville cut past fields and the dark edges of Scape Ore Swamp. It was the sort of place where a flat tire after midnight would be bad luck enough. According to seventeen-year-old Christopher Davis, what happened after he changed his tire was far worse.

Davis told authorities that a figure came toward his car from the darkness: towering, green and wet-looking, with red eyes and skin that reminded him of scales. He said it pursued his vehicle as he escaped. This was his account—not a confirmed sighting of an unknown animal—but it was enough to make a quiet stretch of Lee County famous.

Then came the damaged car. In July, Tom and Mary Waye reported finding their parked vehicle battered, with torn trim and damage under the hood. They suspected the same mysterious creature. Deputies investigated, and other residents told stories of encounters near the swamp. The physical damage was reported at the time; what caused it was never established as a reptilian monster.

By July 20, the strange story had reached national wire reports. Sheriff Liston Truesdale spoke with reporters, and the nickname “Lizard Man” spread far beyond Bishopville. Curiosity seekers arrived. A radio station even offered a spectacular reward for capturing the creature. What began as a handful of unsettling reports became a summer-long sensation.

But the story grew less certain under scrutiny. Some later claims were exposed as fabrications, and authorities considered ordinary animals—including a bear—as possible explanations. No verified biological evidence established that a seven-foot reptilian humanoid lived in Scape Ore Swamp. The original witnesses' descriptions, the vehicle damage, and the legend that grew around them are not the same thing.

Still, imagine that lonely roadside: a tire finally changed, the engine turning over, and a shape at the edge of the headlights that you cannot quite make sense of. Whether the Lizard Man was a mistaken identification, an elaborate story, or something else, the summer of 1988 left Bishopville with a legend that refuses to stay buried in the swamp.

text:
Happy Veterans Day! To all who have served, still with us or forward deployed -- Thank you. Today started as Armistice Day, marking the end of WWI on the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month. My great uncle, Ray Howard Aseltine, joined the Army at age 16 and fought in France under Gen. Pershing ... well, let's hear from him about his experience ... buckle up! (That's Ray on the left).
-------------
The first question people ask me when they discover I have been a prisoner of war is, “How did you feel when the Germans captured you?” All I can truthfully say is, “I just didn’t—” I wasn’t conscious of any feeling. I often wondered after I was in the prison camp why I didn’t kill myself before they got me. Well again, I just didn’t. It’s not a all easy to describe one’s feeling while a prisoner and I guess, on the whole, it’s better to forget one’s thoughts; for the worst kind of a ghastly night-mare is a beautiful fairytale compared to the horror of eight months spent in a German prison camp.

My home is in Michigan, but I was visiting in St.Louis when war was declared on Germany. The next day I enlisted as a member of the 18th Co. 5th Regiment, 2nd Division. I was sixteen but gave my age as nineteen and luck was with me. I was accepted. After four months training at Paris Island, South Carolina, we were sent across and there received six months of good, hard training in France. We were the first Marines over and the first to relieve the French. Our first fight was at Verdun.

On the 19th day of April, Lt. Brady sent ten men out on patrol to gather information. I was one of the ten. On No Man’s Land we ran across about one hundred Germans and a fierce fight took place and lasted about three-quarters of an hour. Sergeant Wichenbaugh was badly wounded but this did not prevent his carrying in a Lieutenant, who was in a serious condition and who died three days later. For this, Wichenbaug received the D. S. C. and the Crois de Guerre.

Eight of the ten boys were killed, leaving Gunnery Sergeant Butler and myself. We were wounded and taken prisoners. I had thirteen wounds in my leg. The Germans lined up to shoot us but reconsidered and took us prisoners in the hope of getting information from us. That was on April 19, 1918, at midnight. They walked us two solid days without food or sleep, then took us to a German officer where we were questioned day and night. We were put in a little room, just large enough to turn around in, and kept there eight days and fed once in twenty-four hours on bread and water. This was in Metz. We were then sent to Conflans and questioned steadily for one solid week. Then we were sent to punishment camps. I was sent to Darmstadt where I did three months hard laber on a diet of black bread, made of potatoes and sawdust, and a cup of acorn coffee. There we were fed twice a day. During this time the guards practiced every conceivable brutality; their favorite pastime being that of knocking down and beating the men who were slowly dying of starvation. There were about one hundred Americans at this prison camp. When we first arrived there the Germans took all our clothes, put the most awful things on us, including wooden shoes, and lined us up in front of what seemed to me like half of the German army; and there explained that this was the way the Americans were being sent over to fight – that they had no leather for shoes and no proper clothing.

Up to this time I had received no medical attention except paper bandages on my leg. A kind English boy dug the piece of grenade out of my leg with a pen knife. We worked about twelve hours a day. On a detail one day, while carrying a sack of potatoes (these sacks weighed two hundred pounds) a young fellow dropped from weakness. The German guard beat him to insensibility with his rifle. That was a common occurrence. On the streets the German children and women greeted us with sneers and would often spit at us. After three months here I was sent to the worse camp in Germany – Limburg, on the river Lahn. There the prisoners were made to work in coal mines, on the roads, and splitting rocks. I was among the latter. My prisoner companions, French and Russian. We were only fed once a day here – one slice of black bread and one cup of acorn coffee.

Our sleeping quarters were the very worst imaginable. We slept on wooden floors where it leaked in on us, when it rained, and we were lucky if we found a blanket to cover ourselves with. From five to ten died a day here of starvation and inhuman treatment. The rest of us were driven about crazy with fleas and cooties. One day I saw a starving Russian steal a raw potato from a wagon. He was immediately killed by a German who beat him to death with the butt of his rifle.
The men who worked in the coal mine began their work at five in the morning and continued until six at night; then they had one hour off and were sent back for four hours more of work. This they did without being given either change of clothes or soap with which to clean themselves. In the eight months I was a prisoner I was never given a change of clothing. My mother had been notified of my death at the time of my capture and four months later received word that I was a prisoner. She immediately sent me clothes and food but I never got a thing.

After two months of this horror, during which time I lost eighty pounds, I became so weakened that one day, while carrying the potato sack, I fell. A Russian guard sent me to a German hospital. Here I lay absolutely without medical aid of any sort. The hospital was little better than the prison camp. During one day and night there, twenty-three allies died of starvation. The Red Cross, acting from Berne, Switzerland, sent us thirty pound packages every week; but we were lucky if we got one a month of them. However, the fact that I am alive, I owe to the Red Cross and its help; and all that I can put into words is but a small portion of the gratitude I feel for that wonderful organization. The first piece of soap I had seen in Germany was received form the Red Cross. I was offered twenty-five marks (about five dollars in our money) by a German officer for a five-cent piece of Armour’s soap. I refused to sell it. When the Germans found these packages were coming regularly, they tried to become friendly in the hope of buying some food from us. The Red Cross sent me an entire outfit of clothing to this hospital.

During all these months I had to listen to the jeering remarks of Germans regarding the Allies and their boasts that only the Germans would win. We knew better and that kept our courage up. When the first news of the Armistice came, the Germans took it as a joke. Big riots took place in the streets of Goblenz, in which thousands of Germans were killed. After the signing the prisoners were turned loose and I went to Limburg. While out walking one day I was stopped by a German who asked me if I had forgotten him. I didn’t know, at the moment, that I had reason to remember him but he soon told me it was he who had taken me prisoner and showed me the photo of myself. He gave me the photo which I sent home to my mother. After leaving him I was accosted by an elderly German who seemed anxious to explain his great disappointment that America had been brought into the war. Germany and America should always have continued friends he explained. I gave him reasons for thinking otherwise but I can’t say I persuaded him to agree with me. He told me he had a beautiful daughter whom he would be glad to have me meet, and in the event of our marrying, he’d gladly taken me into business with him. He was a photographer. I suggested he photograph me at my happiest moment – leaving Germany. I returned to Metz where I saw the German prisoners receiving pay, being well fed and dressed, also provided with good sleeping quarters. I felt I would like to have put them through some of my experiences but I was so happy at being free that I didn’t let myself dwell much on the past. I was too much concerned with making plans for the future.

I got to Toule, France, the day before Thanksgiving and was sent to a Casual camp; from there to Savaney. I shall never forget my Thanksgiving dinner. It seemed I must be looking at a moving picture. I asked a fellow to hit me three times to see if I was awake. I was – and I nearly made myself sick eating. I arrived in New York on the 24th of January, 1919. We had a stormy voyage home but we got here, which is the thing I am certainly grateful for. I’ve been at the Riverside hospital for some time but I’m going home on a thirty day furlough – home to see the folks who have been waiting all these months. I am going back to school when I get my discharge from the army. There are about twenty-five of us alive of the three hundred in the 18th Co. We lost one of the bravest captains of the war, Captain Wass. It’s all over now and the suffering is only a memory but I wouldn’t give back one day of it all as my bit toward winning the Big Fight.

The American Dream is hard work and grace work

Once, while driving Uber, a passenger gave me a $100 tip for the first time in my life. it felt like a million dollars.

I rushed home and gave it as an offering to my wife, because I know it’s a seed, but then I was wondering when I would be able to give such a huge tip myself.

I applied to jobs again and again

If you believe in God, walk in His ways and seek His face, you will never be disappointed.

text:
Remote Texas

A young woman from New York was driving through a remote part of Texas when her car broke down.

An Indian dame riding by on horseback and offered to give her a lift to a nearby town.

She climbed up behind him on the horse and they rode off.

The  ride into town was uneventful except that every few minutes the Indian  would let out a loud whoop that echoed back from the surrounding hills.

When they arrived in town, he left her off at the local service station, yelled one final yahoo and rode off.

What did you do to get that Indian so excited, asked the service station attendant?

Nothing,  I merely sat behind him on the horse, put my arms around his waist and  held onto his saddle horn so I wouldn’t fall off.

Lady, the attendant said, don’t you know Indians always ride bareback?

text:
The Planet That Pulled a Cosmic Disappearing Act

For seven years, a scorching hot Jupiter roughly 1,000 light-years away regularly dimmed its star as it crossed in front of it. Then, in 2026, the transits simply stopped.

The planet hadn’t been destroyed or hidden by a cloud. It had tilted out of view.

TOI-2535 b is a gas giant that races around its star in just 8.25 days—ten times faster than Mercury orbits the Sun. UCLA astronomers, using data from NASA’s TESS telescope, watched its transits grow shorter, shallower, and more irregular (arriving up to six hours early or late) until they vanished entirely.

The culprit is an unseen neighboring planet. The two worlds are gravitationally tugging on each other so strongly that their orbits wobble like spinning tops. As TOI-2535 b’s path tilts, it no longer crosses our line of sight—the same geometry that makes total solar eclipses on Earth rare instead of monthly.

“This is the most extreme example we’ve seen,” the researchers note. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching.”

The planet is expected to swing back into view in 30 to 50 years. Its hidden companion may appear sooner. The discovery also offers a clue about how the hot Jupiter got so close to its star: the presence of a nearby neighbor suggests it migrated inward more gently through the disk rather than being violently flung onto an eccentric orbit.

It’s a rare, real-time view of planets actively reshaping each other’s paths.

text:
Ex-US Rep. Matt Gaetz accused of sex trafficking in federal suit

Two women say the former U.S. Representative and others offered money, drugs and travel in exchange for sex.

Two women sued former U.S. Representative Matt Gaetz and others Thursday, accusing them of using money, drugs and travel to exploit them as part of a sex trafficking scheme.

The complaint, filed Thursday in the Middle District of Florida, names Gaetz, former Seminole County Tax Collector Joel Greenberg, Christopher Dorworth and four Greenberg-affiliated businesses.

The women, who are not identified in the complaint, say that from 2017 through January 2019, Gaetz and Greenberg recruited them for sexual encounters and split expenses for drugs, hotel rooms and travel. 

They accuse Dorworth of knowingly participating in events at his home and claim Greenberg’s family businesses helped finance the operation.

“They were men of power, wealth, and privilege who used their positions not to protect the vulnerable but to prey upon them," the women say in their complaint.

They seek unspecified damages under the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Act.

Gaetz told The Guardian in a statement Thursday he looks forward to depositions to prove the accusations are false.

“The lawsuit relies almost exclusively on a congressional committee report that didn’t allow me to confront my accusers,” he said. “Now I will finally have that chance.”

TO SECRETARY MARCO RUBIO: I CAN WRAP THIS UP WITHIN A WEEK. THINK ABOUT WHO IS MISSING FROM YOUR SYMPHONY.

Mr. Secretary,
@SecRubio @rub

The most important part of my strategy is public accountability.

Nobody wants to be humiliated on the world stage. No leader wants the spotlight shining on their failures. No government wants its people and the international community asking why it is standing in the way of peace.

But you cannot begin by blaming the Houthis until you have dealt with Saudi Arabia.

That is where your accountability must begin.

Saudi Arabia must wash its hands of this war. Its leadership must agree to transfer coordination to Egypt, and the Yemeni government currently residing in Saudi Arabia must be relocated to Egypt.

I believe Prince Mohammed bin Salman will do everything possible to avoid the public humiliation of being identified as the leader obstructing peace. In my view, he bears responsibility for starting this war and for failing to bring Saudi Arabia's involvement to an end.

Make the responsibilities public. Make the consequences of refusing them public.

Once Saudi Arabia has agreed to disengage, the Houthis must be given a clear opportunity to negotiate.

They must publicly acknowledge that Yemen's future requires negotiations with the existing Yemeni government, even though that government has been operating outside the country.

They must begin discussing a constitutional agreement, a shared political future, and the responsibilities of both sides.

Only then can we determine who genuinely wants peace.

If the Houthis refuse after their sovereignty has been recognized and credible negotiations have been offered, their refusal must be made public.

They cannot continue demanding sovereignty while refusing to negotiate with their fellow Yemenis.

And they should understand that such a refusal risks reinforcing accusations that they are behaving like the Khawarij—a characterization with serious religious and historical implications.

But first, Mr. Secretary, you must deal with Saudi Arabia. You cannot demand accountability from one side while excusing the other.

And now let me tell you my favorite part of this entire strategy.

OMAN.

Sultan Qaboos left behind an extraordinary legacy of diplomacy, restraint, and peace.

That legacy means something.

Oman has an opportunity to honor that legacy by participating at the highest level in bringing Yemen's competing political forces together to negotiate their constitutional future.

This is about prestige. It is about responsibility. It is about demonstrating that the legacy of Sultan Qaboos continues to have meaning in the Muslim world.

You are the one who doesn't want to get an A+, Mr. Secretary.

You need someone who understands the blueprint, understands the parties, understands the Muslim world, and knows how to communicate the responsibilities that each participant must accept.

The person who designed the blueprint understands what needs to be said, what needs to be done, and how to bring the parties toward an agreement.

You can continue traveling, making statements, and holding meetings.

Or you can put the right people together, assign the responsibilities, and begin holding everyone accountable.

I believe I can help organize that process within a week.

The blueprint is on the table.

The responsibilities are clear.

The accountability framework is ready.

And the people of Yemen have waited long enough.

Something happened at my workplace last week that completely changed how I see our management.

One of my coworkers, a single mother named Denise, received a call from her son's school informing her that he had developed a high fever and needed to be picked up immediately.

She approached our manager, explained the situation, and asked permission to leave two hours early. She even offered to make up the hours the following morning.

His response was unbelievable.

He told her that personal problems were not the company's responsibility and that everybody had responsibilities outside work.

Denise tried explaining that she had nobody else available to collect her son. He simply told her that if she walked out, she shouldn't expect to have a job when she returned.

She left anyway.

The following morning, she received an email informing her that her employment had been terminated for abandoning her responsibilities.

text:
Pat Murphy accepted the National League Manager of the Year award last night from a hospital bed, in a green gown, two days after having his hip replaced.

No manager in the history of either league had ever won it three years running. Bobby Cox won three. Terry Francona won three. Dusty Baker won three. None of them did it three in a row.

He got 20 of the 30 first place votes.

What he had to say about all of it, from the bed, was mostly one word.

"I had the hip replaced, feel good and very grateful."

"But I am just super, super, super, super grateful."

Christian Yelich has a piece of advice for anybody joining the Milwaukee Brewers, and it is about food.

"If he ever offers you food, you say no."

This is because Murphy keeps food in his pockets. Yelich calls them Murph's pouch pancakes. Over the years his players have watched him produce a pancake, a waffle and an egg roll out of a hoodie.

In spring training of 2022 he told a rookie outfielder named Sal Frelick that he was the team's video guy.

Frelick believed him.

Murphy, as the video guy, then informed Frelick that Frelick's favorite player growing up, Dustin Pedroia, stinks. He did not mention that he had coached Pedroia at Arizona State.

He kept the whole thing going for about a week, until Frelick looked up at the first Cactus League game and saw the video guy walking out to home plate to exchange the lineup cards.

"Even now, half the stuff he says, I don't know if it's a joke or it's true."

In 2021 he told a rookie pitcher named Aaron Ashby to be ready to pinch run. Ashby started getting into full uniform and cleats early, game after game, waiting for it.

"Murph is very good at making it seem like he's serious."

Ashby finally pinch ran on September 5 of that year.

He gives everybody a name. Slim. Jack Jack. Pee Wee. Rock. Tito. Drumstick. Bruce. The team's media relations director eventually had to write up a glossary of them and hand it out to reporters so they could follow his press conferences.

He gets up at four or five in the morning, in season, and writes notes about the people around him rather than about lineups. He calls what he is after meaningful exchanges, which means looking at somebody and telling them what they are worth to you.

A sports psychologist named Harvey Dorfman gave him the line he has run his life on.

"Kids spell love T-I-M-E."

He has four children. The oldest is 39 and the youngest is 6. His son Kai, who plays in the minor leagues, went and got a tattoo of a photograph from 2005 of the two of them holding hands.

"That blew me away."

That is the man who said grateful four times into a camera last night, in a hospital gown, with a new hip and a trophy nobody had ever won three times running.

text:
The Parkman family went to the police the next day.

They offered a reward of $3,000 for finding him alive and printed 28,000 notices. Later they offered $1,000 for his body.

The city had about 120 newspapers and magazines, and the talk was everywhere. At first people blamed Irish immigrants.

City Marshal Francis Tukey had the Charles River and Boston Harbor dragged. Officers searched Parkman's buildings and the medical college, including the dissecting vaults, and found nothing.

On Sunday, Webster called on Parkman's brother, the Reverend Francis Parkman. He said he had met George on Friday and paid him $483.64 toward the debt.

Then he left. He never asked how the search was going.

Ephraim Littlefield was the college janitor. He and his wife lived in the basement, next door to Webster's laboratory.

He started to watch the professor. A few days before Parkman vanished, Webster had asked him a lot of questions about the dissecting vault. Now Webster kept his rooms bolted.

He gave Littlefield a turkey for Thanksgiving, which he had never done before. One day the laboratory furnace burned so hot that the wall on the other side was too hot to touch.

On Thanksgiving Day, with his wife keeping watch, Littlefield borrowed a hatchet, a drill, a crowbar and a chisel. He went down a tunnel under the building and started on the brick wall below Webster's private privy.

On Friday, 30 November, he broke through. By the light of his lantern he saw a human pelvis and parts of a leg.

Littlefield ran for one of the professors, who fetched the marshal. Officers went to Webster's house in Cambridge and took him to jail on a charge of murder.

When he heard what the janitor had found, Webster said, "That villain! I am a ruined man."

In his cell he swallowed strychnine. It only made him ill.

Over the next days the searchers found more remains in a tea chest in the laboratory, and in the furnace they found bone fragments and part of a jaw with false teeth.

Boston's upper class couldn't believe it. "Of course, we cannot believe Dr. Webster guilty, bad as the evidence looks," Fanny Longfellow, the poet's wife, wrote. "Many suspect the janitor."

text:
Under Obama and Biden, have they ever neglected U.S. Military Service Members: 
Answer: YES
Yes. There were documented failures, mismanagement, and inadequate support affecting active-duty service members and veterans under both the Obama and Biden administrations. These were not unique to those presidencies—VA care problems, barracks conditions, readiness shortfalls, and high suicide rates have been chronic across multiple administrations—but specific high-profile cases stand out.

Under Obama (2009–2017)
The most prominent example was the 2014 VA wait-times scandal. Officials at multiple VA facilities (notably Phoenix) maintained secret wait lists and falsified data to hide long delays for care. An Inspector General investigation confirmed systemic issues; veterans died while waiting (CNN and others reported at least 40 alleged deaths linked to Phoenix delays, with the IG finding that long waits contributed to some deaths).⁠Vox

Problems with inaccurate reporting and gaming of schedules were known earlier—including briefings to the Obama transition team—and dated back years (including under Bush). The benefits claims backlog also surged early in the administration as post-Iraq/Afghanistan claims rose, with some veterans waiting hundreds of days.⁠Revealnews

Accountability was limited: relatively few senior officials were fired despite widespread findings. Defense budget pressures and sequestration also contributed to readiness concerns in Obama’s later years, though overall defense spending remained substantial and the force was not broadly “depleted.”

Under Biden (2021–2025)
Afghanistan withdrawal (2021): The execution was chaotic. Thirteen U.S. service members were killed in the Abbey Gate suicide bombing at Kabul airport. Roughly $7 billion in equipment (aircraft, vehicles, weapons, night-vision gear, etc.) was left behind and fell into Taliban hands. Many Americans and Afghan allies were stranded. Gold Star families publicly criticized the administration’s handling and Biden’s demeanor at the dignified transfer. Congressional investigations and SIGAR reports highlighted poor planning, prioritization of optics, and failure to order a timely noncombatant evacuation. Both the Trump-era Doha deal and Biden’s decision to fully withdraw contributed, but the final collapse and deaths occurred under Biden’s execution.⁠https://t.co/GLh4Da3Rm4
COVID-19 vaccine mandate: DoD ordered vaccination in 2021. More than 8,000 service members were involuntarily separated for refusal (many with general/under-honorable characterizations that affected benefits). Religious and other exemptions were often denied. The mandate was later rescinded (2023). Subsequent administrations have moved to offer reinstatement, back pay, and discharge upgrades for those affected solely by the mandate.⁠White House
Recruiting and retention crisis: FY2022–2023 saw major shortfalls (Army missed goals by ~15–25%; Navy and Air Force also fell short). Contributing factors included low eligibility rates among youth (~23% qualified without waivers due to obesity, education, criminal records), declining propensity to serve, and post-COVID effects. Critics also pointed to DEI-focused messaging, “woke” policies, and the vaccine mandate as alienating traditional recruiting pools (e.g., veteran families). Numbers recovered in FY2024–2025 as standards were adjusted and other changes made.
Living conditions: A 2023 GAO report documented widespread substandard barracks conditions (mold, sewage overflows, pests, broken HVAC, inoperable locks/fire systems, privacy shortfalls) affecting thousands of junior enlisted. These issues have persisted for decades due to underfunding, poor oversight, and unreliable condition assessments; they are not solely attributable to one administration but continued under Biden.⁠Gao
Context and caveats
Military suicide rates have remained elevated across administrations (active-duty and veteran rates well above civilian averages; post-9/11 suicides exceed combat deaths in those wars). Readiness challenges with aging platforms, maintenance backlogs (e.g., submarines, aircraft), and industrial base capacity are multi-decade problems. VA care and claims processing issues long predate Obama and continued after.

Combat deaths were lower under Biden than under prior post-9/11 administrations primarily because major combat operations in Afghanistan ended. Claims of systematic “neglect” as deliberate policy are overstated; more accurate descriptions are chronic mismanagement, slow accountability, prioritization failures (e.g., on housing or VA access), and specific policy decisions with clear negative effects on troops and veterans.

Sources include GAO reports, VA IG findings, SIGAR, congressional investigations, Pentagon data, and contemporaneous reporting. Partisan commentary exists on both sides, but the core facts above are corroborated by official investigations and data.

text:
Honor a Veteran. Help a Veteran. Change a Life. 90 Days.

As a former U.S. Air Force fighter pilot, Veterans Day has always held special meaning for me. It's a day to honor the extraordinary men and women who have served our country and remember those who made the ultimate sacrifice.

But this year, I'd like to challenge all of us to do something more than simply say, "Thank you for your service."

Let's ask a different question: "How can I help?"

Following the tragic events of September 11, 2001, I witnessed something extraordinary. Americans from every walk of life came together to help their fellow citizens. They didn't wait to be asked. They saw a need and stepped forward.

I believe we need to bring that same spirit of service to the veterans living in our communities today.

Consider this sobering statistic: Approximately 18 American veterans die by suicide every single day. That's nearly 6,500 lives lost each year, according to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.

Some veterans are struggling with homelessness. Others are searching for meaningful employment. Some have jobs but are struggling to find their footing in civilian life. Others are battling physical injuries, emotional challenges, or a loss of purpose and connection.

And many are facing these challenges quietly.

We cannot solve these problems with a handshake and a "Thank you for your service."

But we CAN make a difference, one veteran at a time.

Here's my challenge:

Over the next 90 days, identify ONE veteran in your community whose life you can positively impact.

Maybe you can help a veteran find a job, make a professional introduction, offer mentorship, connect someone with resources, or simply invite a veteran to lunch and listen.

You don't need to change the world. You just need to make a difference in one person's world.

Imagine the impact if thousands of Americans made that commitment today.

Throughout my military and business careers, I've learned that good intentions are important, but execution is what produces results.

Gratitude is important. Action is what makes a difference.

I'm accepting this challenge myself, and I hope you'll join me.

Find one veteran in your community. Ask how you can help. And then follow through.

Ninety days from now, let's each be able to answer one simple question:

"Whose life did I make better?"

To my fellow veterans, thank you for your service. It was an honor to serve alongside you.

God Bless America.

Anthony "AB" Bourke
Proud U.S. Air Force Veteran

🇺🇸🚨 PALANTIR CEO WARNS AI COULD MAKE BILLIONAIRES 100 TIMES RICHER WHILE ORDINARY AMERICANS FALL BEHIND!

Alex Karp, the billionaire CEO of Palantir, has delivered a remarkable warning about the future of artificial intelligence and the growing divide between America's wealthy elite and everyone else.

His concern isn't simply that AI could eliminate jobs.

It's that the people developing the technology are becoming extraordinarily wealthy while telling ordinary Americans to prepare for a future in which their livelihoods may disappear.

And then, as Karp points out, those same executives suggest that society should depend on them to redistribute some of the wealth.

He describes AI as pouring gasoline onto a society already consumed by economic frustration.

Karp believes the technology could actually create more and better opportunities for working-class Americans.

But there's a catch.

While those workers might see modest improvements, some technology professionals and investors could become 10, 20 or even 50 times wealthier.

And that disparity, he warns, could generate a political backlash that ultimately damages the wealthy without meaningfully improving life for poorer Americans.

Karp also proposed a controversial 50% inheritance tax, linked to a requirement for the government to identify and eliminate waste before collecting the corresponding revenue.

His argument is that a society cannot remain stable indefinitely if billionaires become 100 times wealthier while everyone else experiences only marginal improvements.

He offered a simple example: a carpenter in Louisiana whose standard of living may not have changed substantially in 30 years, despite watching a small group accumulate extraordinary fortunes.

The most interesting part of Karp's warning is that it comes from someone who stands to benefit enormously from the very technological revolution he's criticizing.

And it raises a question that Silicon Valley cannot avoid forever.

What happens when artificial intelligence makes an economy dramatically more productive, but most of the financial rewards flow to people who were already wealthy?

AI could generate extraordinary prosperity.

But if the public sees technological progress primarily as another mechanism for concentrating wealth, the backlash may become as consequential as the technology itself.

The real challenge isn't just building more powerful AI. It's ensuring that ordinary people have a meaningful stake in the prosperity it creates.  https://t.co/0MJQmc6YYU
