text:
Climate- An opportunity for Democrats to shine.

 Noah Gordon

 Any vision for an effective climate policy must grapple with the hard truth about the United States’s climate record so far: it is one of failure. A grumpy foreign diplomat might describe the United States as the world’s largest oil and gas producer and historical emitter, a rich nation that has rejected the two most important climate treaties (Kyoto and Paris) and consistently failed to deliver climate finance to poorer countries. They would be correct. Of course, hardworking US diplomats have also helped secure important climate-related agreements—in Montreal (1987), Paris (2015), and beyond—and the country has achieved moderate emissions reductions. Yet the structural forces in favor of drilling for gas and oil and delivering short-term profits and shareholder value have outweighed efforts to reduce domestic emissions or meet the country’s obligations under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) treaty to help poorer countries. In Trump’s second term, we saw dramatic steps backward, with the United States going so far as to bully other countries into killing climate initiatives, such as an International Maritime Organization plan to place a global carbon levy on polluting ships. It will take more than a return to the Paris Agreement and the Biden-era status quo to set the United States on the right track in 2029 and beyond.  Three principles should guide the United States in developing climate policy for 2029: 

1. Do what you’re good at From the statements of some US analysts, one might think that the United States and China were neck-and-neck in a race to produce the technologies that could save the climate. The Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) was described as the “largest climate investment in history”—except presumably for the much larger Chinese investment. The Development Finance Corporation was sometimes described as a competitor6 or alternative to the Chinese Belt and Road initiative that, in fact, dwarfs it.

 Leading proposals bore names like the “Clean Energy Marshall Plan”:  effective marketing, yes, but overlooking the reality that developing countries are not lining up for loans to help them buy uncompetitive US-produced clean energy technologies. In fact, Chinese overseas investment in clean manufacturing from 2021 to 2025 surpassed the amount that the United States invested in Europe over the four years of the Marshall Plan, at a time when US manufacturing did actually lead the world. In other words, it was China that did the Green Marshall Plan. Washington’s inability to grasp the balance of clean energy power, like these reflexive claims to “leadership,” is a symptom of the US obsession with maintaining global hegemony.

 Policymakers must think more clearly about where the United States fits into the global climate puzzle. In 2029, the United States will not be the largest emitter, nor the most important cleantech producer, nor a trusted diplomatic partner that the world’s climate negotiators look to for leadership. But it will be a major emitter, a technological powerhouse, and potentially a crucial source of global aid. To start, US foreign deals and investments in the climate space need more focus. The Biden administration was on the right track with its emphasis on high-profile, multilateral projects like the Lobito Corridor, a G7 initiative to facilitate the export of minerals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia to the coast of Angola. One of the rare successes of the Trump administration has been the billions in finance it has committed to support non-Chinese rare earth production. Still, in general, previous US clean energy agreements with other countries have spread themselves too thin across large sectors (e.g., batteries or solar) rather than on specific areas where US firms can make a competitive offer (e.g., providing long-duration storage to fast-growing renewables markets like India). US agencies, such as the Development Finance Corporation and Export-Import Bank, should concentrate their firepower more strategically, enabling partner countries to buy US goods and services in those few cleantech areas in which the United States is globally competitive. Foremost among these areas is next-generation geothermal energy. This is currently a niche technology, but the International Energy Agency projects that it could supply “up to 15 percent of global electricity demand growth to 2050.” It also makes use of some of the same drilling technologies—and potentially, workers—that have made the United States the world’s gas superpower. There is a big potential export market here, notably in Europe, Japan, and Indonesia. US policymakers should also talk to European allies about ensuring reciprocal access to cleantech subsidies to boost producers in both regions in the face of Chinese competition.

 The US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) could support exports by subsidizing the cost of drilling in key foreign markets. The United States is very good at inventing new technologies, if not at commercializing them or driving down costs through gradual improvements in manufacturing—the “process innovation” at which China excels.16 The next US administration should launch a massive program for domestic energy research. The focus should be on breakthroughs that may well be deployed and manufactured elsewhere to mitigate the climate crisis: solid-state batteries, fusion, carbon removal, geologic hydrogen, alternative proteins, and low-carbon industrial products like steel and cement. These may not all be key climate solutions for the 2030s, and they are sideshows relative to the growth of renewables and lithium-ion batteries that are cutting emissions in the near term. But they are still crucial to longer-term efforts to meet the climate challenge. Such a research program would build on the legacy of past scientific initiatives like the Manhattan and Apollo projects or Operation Warp Speed. Given the likely state of global politics in 2029, it would also represent an olive branch to a global community scalded by the slashand-burn approach of Trump 2.0. Such a research program must also set aside significant resources to revive and revitalize international collaboration on clean energy: funded exchange programs for US and foreign scientists and new visa programs for foreign scientists, engineers, and electricians. US workers should benefit too, for example through the expanded training of electricians to work at home and abroad. Indeed, the shortage of trained electrical workers in the United States is exacerbating supply chain challenges for key grid components like power  transformers. The government should be facilitating learning trips for US workers to leading battery producers like South Korea, not scaring away foreigners with aggressive immigration raids against firms from allied countries. Korean investments in particular are vital for US electric vehicle (EV) production and for maintaining a domestic manufacturing base in a key industry. If there were a global coordinating body for the energy  transition—the type of planetary governance humans could probably pull together if we faced an invasion of alien humanoids rather than a gradual, faceless threat—it would ask the United States to do what it’s best at and leave other areas to other countries. The task of a new administration in 2029 is to keep this planetary perspective in mind as it balances the climate crisis with its other responsibilities to keep Americans safe and prosperous. 

Working with unions, climate activists, and community organizers to design policy will help both win elections and advance green economic populism once in office.

 2. Electrify

 If the world is to decarbonize fairly and effectively, it will have to achieve electrification. This means both increasing the share of final energy demand that is met by electricity and giving more people more access to electricity. Let’s start with the first meaning: 

swapping out molecules for electrons. Any effective climate foreign policy must have a strong domestic component because US emissions affect the global climate. Domestic policymakers are the ones who have to keep the promises that the diplomats make. 

US greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are keeping steady under the Trump administration at around 11 percent of the global total—yet as the biggest historical emitter, the United States has a responsibility to clean up its own mess. This is a moral responsibility and also a practical and strategic one, because foreign countries will shun initiatives and tariff products from a petrostate whose pollution is hurting their interests. The priority for domestic policy should be on effective climate interventions that also improve Americans’ health and economic situation in the near future. 

The rising price of electricity was a key issue in the November 2025 elections, with even conservative Democrats like New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill calling for price controls on utility  bills. Since power prices will likely keep rising as demand does, an effective policy should shift more of the costs of electrification from residential consumers to the giant companies building data centers. We can capitalize on the fact that the world’s richest companies are desperate for a stable grid with abundant power, for example by requiring them to commit to a fund that supports grid infrastructure.

 What other policies fit the bill? The Biden administration’s Clean School Bus Rebate Program, which replaced diesel buses with electric ones, was a good one. Similarly ambitious proposals, like replacing the HVAC system in every public school with a new system that would reduce fuel costs, improve air quality, kill airborne diseases, and keep students cool enough to think straight, should also be pursued. Incidentally, these systems would all use efficient heat pumps rather than gas furnaces. Let the climate deniers and combustion-addicted reactionaries campaign against hiring and training US electricians to fix the United States’s schools. Federal dollars should support any leapfrog technologies that may emerge from that US clean energy research program.

 Government demand and tax credits can pull forward US-made clean steel or long-duration energy storage technologies, like the zinc-based batteries manufactured by the Pennsylvania firm EOS Energy Enterprises, in which the Trump administration took a stake in November  2025. Indeed, the Trump administration’s aggressive moves to take equity stakes in lithium, steel, and rare earth firms have provided a blueprint for a type of state capitalism that climate progressives once only dreamed of; the door has never been so open for the US government to force oil and gas firms to clean up leaky, abandoned wells. When it comes to the second meaning of “electrification”—delivering power to the world’s people—the key is to avoid double standards and ditch invidious policies that the United States isn’t itself following. If the United States implements some kind of tariff based on the carbon content in imports, it should be sure to either exempt the poorest countries or recycle revenue to them. The United States should not put pressure on developing countries, even recipients of US aid money, to stop exploiting their own fossil fuel resources while the wealthy United States remains a petrostate.

 Washington should welcome the fact that energy access is growing around the world and willingly provide financing for foreign partners to deploy, for example, US-made virtual power plant software to help manage the electricity being generated by solar panels and stored on EVs made in Asia. The now-cancelled Power Africa project (led by USAID) included some excellent technical and financial support for power grids that should be restarted. If we help the world switch from molecules to electrons, decarbonization will follow.

 3. Cooperate with China—with guardrails Any climate foreign policy must also be a China policy. An effective climate policy will welcome China’s immense production of batteries and solar panels, without which humans would be in even greater danger. It is ludicrous to speak of an “overcapacity” of the Chinese solar panels that are bringing light to countries like Pakistan and South Africa. To criticize China’s unfair trade practices and undervalued currency, when it actually hurts US interests, not its massive production of cleantech as such. What’s the right balance? The United States should follow Canada and allow a small number of Chinese EVs to be imported into the country each year, up to a quota. This would put more pressure on the US automakers to deliver cheaper clean vehicles but also protect the US market enough to give domestic producers a chance to improve their EV offering. 

In this spirit, the United States should invite limited Chinese investment into the US battery and EV industry, permitting a few joint ventures with US firms on a pilot basis. But the United States must put conditions on foreign investments to require that Chinese firms hire local workers, use some domestic components, and share technologies, as the EU is attempting. If they’re allowed to, Chinese firms will use US factories for final assembly alone. In general, retaining tariffs on heavily subsidized Chinese cleantech, which raises the cost of the domestic transition, is an acceptable price to pay for strengthening US “green asset owners”46 vis-à-vis fossil asset owners. Reshaping the domestic political economy so that most of the country is incentivized to support an energy transition matters more than maximizing short-run efficiency. Moreover, the United States should not invite China into all sectors.

 Americans should bear the cost of developing a rare earth and critical minerals supply chain that cuts out China and protects the country from aggressive Chinese export controls, as permanent magnets are required not only for EVs and wind turbines but also for defense technologies. While progressives should welcome cheap Chinese solar panels, they should insist that the inverters to connect them to the grid are made by US allies, for reasons of security. It is hard to predict where US–China relations will be by January 2029. Even more so than President Nixon did, Trump can seek warmer relations with China without appearing weak, perhaps by cutting a deal with President Xi to drop US export controls in exchange for Chinese clean energy investment. But as they work to repair the damage the Trump regime has done to US democracy, progressives should resist the urge to outflank MAGA by being even tougher on the Chinese electrostate. Polling suggests that voters care more about having cheap, clean energy, than the geopolitical competition with China that so animated the Biden administration. A constructive, normal country Climate is a useful policy area in which to think about a broader, progressive, pro-peace foreign policy that doesn’t prioritize the pursuit of global hegemony. The United States is not a latent climate superpower that could produce the world’s electrotech if only the IRA were fully restored. It is a giant hydrocarbon producer and home to many citizens who stand to lose out, in a narrow economic sense, from falling demand for fossil fuels and the machines that burn them—even as they and their country would gain much more from humanity’s success in limiting the deadly overheating of the planet. 

The United States will not be the clean energy leader, not on a planet shared with China. But nor can it afford to give up on the field of clean energy altogether— that would be a tragedy for the world, whose ongoing clean energy transition would go even faster with the aid of the United States. What it can be is a country that plays its part in a collective global effort and pushes climate-saving technologies forward in a few select areas. That is what we should strive for. Because the United States, even after years of Trumpian sabotage of climate science and the clean energy economy, still has so much to give. It is still pushing forward promising next-generation geothermal technologies, still home to brilliant scientists working on clean industrial technologies, and to deep capital markets that could help these get to market.

 The climate challenge is open-ended: indeed, humans have not even finished the first phase of getting emissions to peak, let alone driven them to zero and started removing carbon from the atmosphere. So it’s far too early to give up. It is, though, time for the United States to find its place as a constructive, normal country in this space.

text:
$NNDM Q3 2026 earnings: Nano Dimension cuts spending, but legal claims widen its loss

Nano Dimension, a maker of industrial printing and electronics assembly machines, cut running costs, but one-off bills drained its cash. Sales outside Markforged, the unit it is selling to Stratasys, rose 42%. Staff cuts narrowed the loss excluding one-offs sharply. But operations used $24 million of cash, three times the year-ago amount, partly to exit a lease.

• Sales outside Markforged, the unit being sold: $𝟏𝟑.𝟑𝐌 (+42% from a year ago)
• Loss before interest, taxes, depreciation and one-offs: −$𝟒.𝟖𝐌 (−$16.6M a year ago)
• Cash, deposits and listed shares: $𝟑𝟗𝟔.𝟗𝐌 ($433.3M three months earlier)
• Full-year outlook: 𝐒𝐮𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 (since May 2026)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better, because the cost cuts chief executive Moshe Rozenbaum promised now show clearly in the results. Essemtec, its electronics assembly business, grew for a second quarter. The bad news: Nano agreed to cover $14.7 million of an activist investor's legal costs and reserved $6 million for a lawsuit.

The question now is what Nano does with its $397 million of cash and securities. Its new board can return much of it to shareholders, or buy a business, as an earlier board did with Desktop Metal before its bankruptcy. The first plan from the board's new capital allocation committee will tell.

[Model: Claude Opus 5.5. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐅𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐑𝐨𝐬𝐞
Nano Dimension sells industrial 3D printers through its Markforged unit and electronics assembly machines through Essemtec. Chief executive Moshe Rozenbaum lists "aggressively reducing our cost structure" among his priorities, and this quarter the numbers followed. Running costs excluding one-offs dropped to $19.8 million, the lowest level in at least five quarters.

• Running costs excluding one-offs: down 16.5% from last quarter and 32.2% from a year ago
• Administrative overhead: 21.4 percentage points lower as a share of revenue than a year ago
• Research and development: 14.5 percentage points lower as a share of revenue
• Loss before interest, taxes, depreciation and one-offs (adjusted EBITDA): $4.8 million, against $16.6 million a year ago

Most of the savings came from payroll. Nano said it now employs fewer people after mergers and asset sales, which cut research, sales and overhead spending alike. Payroll savings tend to last, so the lower cost base should carry into next year. But the group still loses money before one-offs.

What to watch: running costs excluding one-offs in the fourth quarter, when the Markforged sale is due to close. A figure well below $19.8 million would show that Nano shed Markforged's costs along with its sales.

🟢 concern eased — 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐰 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐚 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫
Essemtec, Nano's Swiss maker of machines that mount components and dispense materials onto circuit boards, carries the business Nano keeps after the Markforged sale. Sales outside Markforged rose about 42% from a year ago, after a 53% jump last quarter. That reverses the drop Nano reported earlier this year.

Nano said demand was "particularly strong across AI-related electronics manufacturing, aerospace and defense, space and satellite systems". Excluding AME, the 3D-printed electronics line Nano sold in April, underlying growth reached about 67% by our math. But the base was soft, because tariff worries held buyers back a year ago, Nano said.

What to watch: sales outside Markforged in the fourth quarter, against $14.6 million a year earlier. Growth against that tougher base would show Essemtec's gains do not rest on one weak comparison.

🟢 𝐍𝐚𝐧𝐨 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐎𝐰𝐧 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬
Nano paused share buybacks during its strategic review, and an analyst challenged that pause. Chief executive Moshe Rozenbaum now calls "returning capital to shareholders" one of the "central pillars of our strategy".

Nano bought 7.0 million shares for $11.1 million in the third quarter. After the quarter ended, it kept buying through early November and spent another $8.6 million. As a result, shares outstanding fell about 6% from a year ago, so each remaining share has a claim on more cash. But the spending also shrinks the money the new board could use for an acquisition.

What to watch: the first plan from the board's new Strategy and Capital Allocation Committee, chaired by director Nadav Kidron. A plan that sets the size of future returns would make the buybacks a standing policy.

🟢 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭
Several claims behind the positive case got no fresh numbers in these results, so they stand where they stood after the second quarter.

• Yearly cash savings of about $25 million that Nano targeted from asset sales and its lease exit: the first quarter without the headquarters lease begins in January 2027.
• Earn-out on AME and Fabrica, a line Nano had already shut: up to $10.5 million of extra payments tied to the buyer's sales, still carried at $2.9 million.
• Markforged's orders from defense and automakers: its sales rose 6.3% to $18.6 million, but the unit leaves with the Stratasys sale.
• A merger worth more than the cash: the short list of partners Nano described in May has produced no deal yet.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐔𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐝
Nano's release leads with its cuts to running costs, but the cash statement tells a different story. Operations used $24.1 million of cash in the third quarter, by our math. A year earlier, the same line showed an outflow of $7.9 million.

Part of the jump came from one decision. In July Nano paid $13.0 million to end its headquarters lease early, a deal it said removes about $38 million of future rent. Without that payment, operations still used $11.1 million, by our math, which tops the year-ago outflow.

Cash, deposits and listed shares fell $36.4 million in the quarter, to $396.9 million. Chief executive Moshe Rozenbaum promised a "leaner, more focused and financially stronger organization", but the cash figures do not show that yet. The Markforged sale should bring in $42.5 million, yet Nano has already spent or committed more than half of that since September.

What to watch: cash used by operations in the fourth quarter, excluding the October payment to activist investor Murchinson. An outflow below the year-ago $11.7 million would show the cost cuts finally reaching the cash statement.

🔴🔴 𝐋𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐥 𝐂𝐥𝐚𝐢𝐦𝐬 𝐀𝐝𝐝𝐞𝐝 $𝟐𝟏 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐬
In July Nano settled a board fight with Murchinson, an investor owning about 10% of its shares. Four directors left and three joined, including Moshe Rozenbaum, now chief executive. A month later Murchinson asked Nano to repay its legal and proxy costs.

A committee of two independent directors agreed to pay $14.7 million, citing "reducing uncertainty, avoiding further disruption". Nano also set aside $6.0 million for a suit by law firm Quinn Emanuel after a court refused to dismiss it. Former bondholders of Desktop Metal, a printer maker Nano bought and lost to bankruptcy in 2025, seek more than $115 million.

Nano said it will "vigorously defend itself against the claims". Independent directors approved the Murchinson payment, but the money went to the shareholder whose settlement brought in the current chief executive. So the charges hit the loss and also raise a question about who benefits from Nano's cash.

What to watch: the court ruling on Nano's August motion to dismiss the case brought by Desktop Metal's bankruptcy trustee. A loss there would add a claim for which Nano has set aside no money.

🔴 𝐀𝐬𝐢𝐚 𝐒𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐌𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫'𝐬 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡
Nano sold $15.0 million of goods in Asia-Pacific, nearly four times the year-ago level. That region now makes up 47% of revenue. Sales in Europe, the Middle East and Africa roughly halved, and the Americas slipped about 10%.

Nano did not say which product line or customers drove the Asian sales. Last quarter it said about $3.0 million of orders would arrive later because of production timing. Without them, revenue would have barely moved from the second quarter, by our math. So this quarter's growth may rest on a handful of large orders.

What to watch: Asia-Pacific sales in the fourth quarter. A drop back toward the $4.0 million Nano booked there a year earlier would mark this quarter's jump as a few one-time orders.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Several standing concerns got no new answer in these results, and Nano held no conference call where investors could ask about them.

• Full-year outlook: still suspended since May, so investors have no company target for sales or losses.
• Merger plans: the short list of merger and reverse-merger partners from May got no update; a new board committee now owns the decision.
• Accounting controls: Nano reported a control weakness in March and replaced auditor KPMG with PwC Israel in September; the filing gives no reason.
• Markforged write-down: Nano wrote off all $40.4 million of the unit's goodwill, the premium it paid over the assets, in the first quarter.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐍𝐚𝐧𝐨 𝐂𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐢𝐝𝐝𝐥𝐞 𝐄𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐟𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐭 𝐈𝐦𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥
Nano, an Israeli company run from Massachusetts, said fighting between the US, Israel and Iran since February had an immaterial effect on its results. Tariffs mattered more a year ago, when Nano said "demand was negatively impacted by tariff uncertainty". That soft base flatters this year's growth comparison.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑𝟎.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Inventory edged up 6.1% from last quarter. It sits 22.4% below a year ago. Against a quarter's sales, stock fell to 94% from 144% a year earlier. So Nano holds less stock for each dollar of sales, which frees cash, though the AME sale also took some stock off the books.

𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐𝟕.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Money customers owe Nano climbed 26% from a year ago, ahead of sales growth. Receivables now equal 87% of the quarter's revenue, against 82% a year earlier. Slower collection ties up cash that the cost cuts free elsewhere.

𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟓.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇄ reversing
Deferred revenue, cash customers paid for service Nano has not yet delivered, rose 16% from last quarter. The jump reverses most of the second-quarter drop, when Nano wrote off $1.2 million in the AME sale. The balance still sits about 1% below a year ago.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐮𝐥𝐥-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤: 𝐒𝐮𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Suspended (May 2026)
Unchanged. Nano still offers no full-year target for sales, margins or losses. It set a sales range of $130–140 million earlier this year, then dropped it in May. Sales for the first nine months reached $90.6 million. The Markforged sale will reshape any new target, because that unit supplies most of the revenue.

𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐚𝐬𝐲𝐬: $𝟒𝟐.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐧 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡; 𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧 𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from $42.5 million in cash; closing expected in the second half of 2026
Unchanged. Nano still expects Stratasys to buy Markforged, its industrial 3D-printer unit, for $42.5 million in cash, and now names the fourth quarter. The deal remains "subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals". Markforged supplied 58% of third-quarter sales, so the group that stays will be much smaller. Nano said earlier the sale cuts yearly cash burn by about $15 million.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐍𝐚𝐧𝐨 𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐡 𝐚 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐟𝐮𝐥𝐥-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤?
Nano has offered no targets since May. Once Markforged leaves, readers need a sales and loss range for the remaining business to judge whether the cost cuts go far enough.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫?
Markforged supplies most of the revenue, and Nano said selling it cuts yearly cash burn by about $15 million. A quarterly loss figure would show what the remaining business earns on its own.

𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐝𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐣𝐮𝐦𝐩 𝐢𝐧 𝐀𝐬𝐢𝐚𝐧 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬?
Asia-Pacific sales almost quadrupled and now make up nearly half of revenue. A breakdown by product line and customer would show whether that growth can repeat.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐨𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐬𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐭 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐛𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬?
The new Strategy and Capital Allocation Committee will weigh buybacks, payouts and acquisitions. Shareholders need to know how much cash the board plans to return, and when.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐰?
Service revenue, which includes maintenance contracts, dropped 15% from a year ago while product sales rose 30%. Nano did not explain the gap, which matters because service income usually recurs.

text:
Postpartum Psychosis or Murder? Three Massachusetts Mothers and the Insanity Defense.

Postpartum psychosis, maternal mental health, and the insanity defense are becoming central issues in three high-profile Massachusetts filicide cases. Seven children are dead, two mothers face potential retrials in 2027, and a third case is just beginning.

At the center of all three is the same legal question: When does severe mental illness negate criminal responsibility?

• Latarsha Sanders - Brockton, February 2018
Sanders stabbed her two sons, Marlon (8) and La'Son (5), to death.

• Lindsay Clancy - Duxbury, January 2023
Clancy strangled her three children, Cora (5), Dawson (3), and Callan (8 months), before attempting to take her own life.

• Janette MacAusland - Wellesley, April 2026
MacAusland is accused of drugging and strangling her children, Kai (7) and Ella (6), during a contentious divorce and custody dispute.

All three cases involve serious questions about mental illness and criminal responsibility. And now, attorneys representing Sanders and MacAusland are publicly referencing the Clancy case.

The Janette MacAusland Case

MacAusland, 49, allegedly killed her children on or about April 22, 2026.

On April 24, she arrived at her aunt's Vermont home with a severe, self-inflicted neck wound. According to investigators, she admitted killing her children and attempting to take her own life, explaining that she wanted all three of them to "go to God together."

Authorities subsequently discovered both children dead in their mother's bed.

The medical examiner determined that Kai and Ella died from mechanical asphyxia and the combined effects of several medications, including zolpidem (Ambien), lorazepam (Ativan), acetaminophen, and ibuprofen.

The killings occurred during a contentious divorce and custody dispute. MacAusland's husband filed for divorce in October 2025, seeking full custody of their children and control of the family home. On April 16, just days before the alleged killings, the couple agreed to involve a guardian ad litem to represent the children's best interests.

On November 3, MacAusland pleaded not guilty to two counts of first-degree murder in Norfolk Superior Court. She remains held without bail, with her next court date scheduled for December 16.

Her attorney, Joseph Krowski Jr., says she has a lengthy history of mental health conditions and treatment. He has not ruled out an insanity defense.

The Lindsay Clancy Connection

MacAusland's attorney is already drawing comparisons to the Clancy trial.

"This is not Lindsay Clancy 2.0," Krowski told reporters, explaining that although MacAusland's circumstances are different, Clancy's trial has opened a national conversation about whether the criminal justice system should treat severe mental illness differently.

He has urged Norfolk County prosecutors to reconsider their approach to the charges.

Robert F. Shaw Jr., who successfully appealed Latarsha Sanders' convictions, has also publicly discussed the Clancy case.

Shaw has questioned how prosecutors use a defendant's seemingly ordinary behavior before a killing to challenge claims of psychosis. He argues that jurors can struggle to understand severe mental illness, particularly when the prosecution offers explanations based on familiar emotions and behaviors.

Both attorneys are raising questions about how mental illness is understood and presented in criminal proceedings.

What Happens When These Cases Start Influencing Each Other?

The Clancy trial received enormous public attention. Sanders' convictions have already been overturned because jurors were denied psychiatric evidence relevant to her insanity defense. And now MacAusland's attorney is invoking Clancy before his client's trial has even begun.

I'll be watching to see whether the Sanders and MacAusland defenses raise some of the same maternal mental health issues explored during Clancy's trial, particularly postpartum depression and postpartum psychosis.

Will their attorneys challenge the mental health care system or examine the lack of support available to mothers struggling with severe psychiatric conditions? Will they call some of the same experts? And how much of the Clancy defense strategy will carry over into these cases?

If I were the Commonwealth, I'd be concerned about jury selection, particularly in the two Plymouth County cases, but in Norfolk County as well.

How many prospective jurors will already have formed opinions about these mothers, the psychiatric evidence, or whether mental illness negates criminal responsibility?

Could the publicity and public sentiment surrounding Clancy ultimately benefit Sanders or MacAusland?

And perhaps the bigger question: Does the Clancy trial help or hurt the next mother who claims insanity?

I suggest that you read.

A Declaration by the Representatives of the United Colonies of North-America, Now Met in Congress at Philadelphia, Setting Forth the Causes and Necessity of Their Taking Up Arms.

If it was possible for men, who exercise their reason to believe, that the divine Author of our existence intended a part of the human race to hold an absolute property in, and an unbounded power over others, marked out by his infinite goodness and wisdom, as the objects of a legal domination never rightfully resistible, however severe and oppressive, the inhabitants of these colonies might at least require from the parliament of Great-Britain some evidence, that this dreadful authority over them, has been granted to that body. But a reverance for our Creator, principles of humanity, and the dictates of common sense, must convince all those who reflect upon the subject, that government was instituted to promote the welfare of mankind, and ought to be administered for the attainment of that end. The legislature of Great-Britain, however, stimulated by an inordinate passion for a power not only unjustifiable, but which they know to be peculiarly reprobated by the very constitution of that kingdom, and desparate of success in any mode of contest, where regard should be had to truth, law, or right, have at length, deserting those, attempted to effect their cruel and impolitic purpose of enslaving these colonies by violence, and have thereby rendered it necessary for us to close with their last appeal from reason to arms. - Yet, however blinded that assembly may be, by their intemperate rage for unlimited domination, so to sight justice and the opinion of mankind, we esteem ourselves bound by obligations of respect to the rest of the world, to make known the justice of our cause.

Our forefathers, inhabitants of the island of Great-Britain, left their native land, to seek on these shores a residence for civil and religious freedom. At the expense of their blood, at the hazard of their fortunes, without the least charge to the country from which they removed, by unceasing labour, and an unconquerable spirit, they effected settlements in the distant and unhospitable wilds of America, then filled with numerous and warlike barbarians. -- Societies or governments, vested with perfect legislatures, were formed under charters from the crown, and an harmonious intercourse was established between the colonies and the kingdom from which they derived their origin. The mutual benefits of this union became in a short time so extraordinary, as to excite astonishment. It is universally confessed, that the amazing increase of the wealth, strength, and navigation of the realm, arose from this source; and the minister, who so wisely and successfully directed the measures of Great-Britain in the late war, publicly declared, that these colonies enabled her to triumph over her enemies. --Towards the conclusion of that war, it pleased our sovereign to make a change in his counsels. -- From that fatal movement, the affairs of the British empire began to fall into confusion, and gradually sliding from the summit of glorious prosperity, to which they had been advanced by the virtues and abilities of one man, are at length distracted by the convulsions, that now shake it to its deepest foundations. -- The new ministry finding the brave foes of Britain, though frequently defeated, yet still contending, took up the unfortunate idea of granting them a hasty peace, and then subduing her faithful friends.

These devoted colonies were judged to be in such a state, as to present victories without bloodshed, and all the easy emoluments of statuteable plunder. -- The uninterrupted tenor of their peaceable and respectful behaviour from the beginning of colonization, their dutiful, zealous, and useful services during the war, though so recently and amply acknowledged in the most honourable manner by his majesty, by the late king, and by parliament, could not save them from the meditated innovations. -- Parliament was influenced to adopt the pernicious project, and assuming a new power over them, have in the course of eleven years, given such decisive specimens of the spirit and consequences attending this power, as to leave no doubt concerning the effects of acquiescence under it. They have undertaken to give and grant our money without our consent, though we have ever exercised an exclusive right to dispose of our own property; statutes have been passed for extending the jurisdiction of courts of admiralty and vice-admiralty beyond their ancient limits; for depriving us of the accustomed and inestimable privilege of trial by jury, in cases affecting both life and property; for suspending the legislature of one of the colonies; for interdicting all commerce to the capital of another; and for altering fundamentally the form of government established by charter, and secured by acts of its own legislature solemnly confirmed by the crown; for exempting the "murderers" of colonists from legal trial, and in effect, from punishment; for erecting in a neighbouring province, acquired by the joint arms of Great-Britain and America, a despotism dangerous to our very existence; and for quartering soldiers upon the colonists in time of profound peace. It has also been resolved in parliament, that colonists charged with committing certain offences, shall be transported to England to be tried.

But why should we enumerate our injuries in detail? By one statute it is declared, that parliament can "of right make laws to bind us in all cases whatsoever." What is to defend us against so enormous, so unlimited a power? Not a single man of those who assume it, is chosen by us; or is subject to our control or influence; but, on the contrary, they are all of them exempt from the operation of such laws, and an American revenue, if not diverted from the ostensible purposes for which it is raised, would actually lighten their own burdens in proportion, as they increase ours. We saw the misery to which such despotism would reduce us. We for ten years incessantly and ineffectually besieged the throne as supplicants; we reasoned, we remonstrated with parliament, in the most mild and decent language.

Administration sensible that we should regard these oppressive measures as freemen ought to do, sent over fleets and armies to enforce them. The indignation of the Americans was roused, it is true; but it was the indignation of a virtuous, loyal, and affectionate people. A Congress of delegates from the United Colonies was assembled at Philadelphia, on the fifth day of last September. We resolved again to offer an humble and dutiful petition to the King, and also addressed our fellow-subjects of Great-Britain. We have pursued every temperate, every respectful measure; we have even proceeded to break off our commercial intercourse with our fellow-subjects, as the last peaceable admonition, that our attachment to no nation upon earth should supplant our attachment to liberty. -- This, we flattered ourselves, was the ultimate step of the controversy: but subsequent events have shewn, how vain was this hope of finding moderation in our enemies.

Several threatening expressions against the colonies were inserted in his majesty's speech; our petition, tho' we were told it was a decent one, and that his majesty had been pleased to receive it graciously, and to promise laying it before his parliament, was huddled into both houses among a bundle of American papers, and there neglected. The lords and commons in their address, in the month of February, said, that "a rebellion at that time actually existed within the province of Massachusetts-Bay; and that those concerned with it, had been countenanced and encouraged by unlawful combinations and engagements, entered into by his majesty's subjects in several of the other colonies; and therefore they besought his majesty, that he would take the most effectual measures to inforce due obediance to the laws and authority of the supreme legislature." -- Soon after, the commercial intercourse of whole colonies, with foreign countries, and with each other, was cut off by an act of parliament; by another several of them were intirely prohibited from the fisheries in the seas near their coasts, on which they always depended for their sustenance; and large reinforcements of ships and troops were immediately sent over to general Gage.

Fruitless were all the entreaties, arguments, and eloquence of an illustrious band of the most distinguished peers, and commoners, who nobly and strenuously asserted the justice of our cause, to stay, or even to mitigate the heedless fury with which these accumulated and unexampled outrages were hurried on. -- equally fruitless was the interference of the city of London, of Bristol, and many other respectable towns in our favor. Parliament adopted an insidious manoeuvre calculated to divide us, to establish a perpetual auction of taxations where colony should bid against colony, all of them uninformed what ransom would redeem their lives; and thus to extort from us, at the point of the bayonet, the unknown sums that should be sufficient to gratify, if possible to gratify, ministerial rapacity, with the miserable indulgence left to us of raising, in our own mode, the prescribed tribute. What terms more rigid and humiliating could have been dictated by remorseless victors to conquered enemies? in our circumstances to accept them, would be to deserve them.

Soon after the intelligence of these proceedings arrived on this continent, general Gage, who in the course of the last year had taken possession of the town of Boston, in the province of Massachusetts-Bay, and still occupied it a garrison, on the 19th day of April, sent out from that place a large detachment of his army, who made an unprovoked assault on the inhabitants of the said province, at the town of Lexington, as appears by the affidavits of a great number of persons, some of whom were officers and soldiers of that detachment, murdered eight of the inhabitants, and wounded many others. From thence the troops proceeded in warlike array to the town of Concord, where they set upon another party of the inhabitants of the same province, killing several and wounding more, until compelled to retreat by the country people suddenly assembled to repel this cruel aggression. Hostilities, thus commenced by the British troops, have been since prosecuted by them without regard to faith or reputation. -- The inhabitants of Boston being confined within that town by the general their governor, and having, in order to procure their dismission, entered into a treaty with him, it was stipulated that the said inhabitants having deposited their arms with their own magistrate, should have liberty to depart, taking with them their other effects. They accordingly delivered up their arms, but in open violation of honour, in defiance of the obligation of treaties, which even savage nations esteemed sacred, the governor ordered the arms deposited as aforesaid, that they might be preserved for their owners, to be seized by a body of soldiers; detained the greatest part of the inhabitants in the town, and compelled the few who were permitted to retire, to leave their most valuable effects behind.

By this perfidy wives are separated from their husbands, children from their parents, the aged and the sick from their relations and friends, who wish to attend and comfort them; and those who have been used to live in plenty and even elegance, are reduced to deplorable distress.

The general, further emulating his ministerial masters, by a proclamation bearing date on the 12th day of June, after venting the grossest falsehoods and calumnies against the good people of these colonies, proceeds to "declare them all, either by name or description, to be rebels and traitors, to supersede the course of the common law, and instead thereof to publish and order the use and exercise of the law martial." -- His troops have butchered our countrymen, have wantonly burnt Charlestown, besides a considerable number of houses in other places; our ships and vessels are seized; the necessary supplies of provisions are intercepted, and he is exerting his utmost power to spread destruction and devastation around him.

We have rceived certain intelligence, that general Carelton[Carleton], the governor of Canada, is instigating the people of that province and the Indians to fall upon us; and we have but too much reason to apprehend, that schemes have been formed to excite domestic enemies against us. In brief, a part of these colonies now feel, and all of them are sure of feeling, as far as the vengeance of administration can inflict them, the complicated calamities of fire, sword and famine. We are reduced to the alternative of chusing an unconditional submission to the tyranny of irritated ministers, or resistance by force. -- The latter is our choice. -- We have counted the cost of this contest, and find nothing so dreadful as voluntary slavery. -- Honour, justice, and humanity, forbid us tamely to surrender that freedom which we received from our gallant ancestors, and which our innocent posterity have a right to receive from us. We cannot endure the infamy and guilt of resigning succeeding generations to that wretchedness which inevitably awaits them, if we basely entail hereditary bondage upon them.

Our cause is just. Our union is perfect. Our internal resources are great, and, if necessary, foreign assistance is undoubtedly attainable. -- We gratefully acknowledge, as signal instances of the Divine favour towards us, that his Providence would not permit us to be called into this severe controversy, until we were grown up to our present strength, had been previously exercised in warlike operation, and possessed of the means of defending ourselves. With hearts fortified with these animating reflections, we most solemnly, before God and the world, declare, that, exerting the utmost energy of those powers, which our beneficent Creator hath graciously bestowed upon us, the arms we have been compelled by our enemies to assume, we will, in defiance of every hazard, with unabating firmness and perseverence, employ for the preservation of our liberties; being with one mind resolved to die freemen rather than to live slaves.

Lest this declaration should disquiet the minds of our friends and fellow-subjects in any part of the empire, we assure them that we mean not to dissolve that union which has so long and so happily subsisted between us, and which we sincerely wish to see restored. -- Necessity has not yet driven us into that desperate measure, or induced us to excite any other nation to war against them. -- We have not raised armies with ambitious designs of separating from Great-Britain, and establishing independent states. We fight not for glory or for conquest. We exhibit to mankind the remarkable spectacle of a people attacked by unprovoked enemies, without any imputation or even suspicion of offence. They boast of their privileges and civilization, and yet proffer no milder conditions than servitude or death.

In our own native land, in defence of the freedom that is our birthright, and which we ever enjoyed till the late violation of it -- for the protection of our property, acquired solely by the honest industry of our fore-fathers and ourselves, against violence actually offered, we have taken up arms. We shall lay them down when hostilities shall cease on the part of the aggressors, and all danger of their being renewed shall be removed, and not before.

With an humble confidence in the mercies of the supreme and impartial Judge and Ruler of the Universe, we most devoutly implore his divine goodness to protect us happily through this great conflict, to dispose our adversaries to reconciliation on reasonable terms, and thereby to relieve the empire from the calamities of civil war.

☆ Jennifer Chao, NEW Executive Director on Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs 

“Washington’s vibrant and growing Asian American and Pacific Islander communities are an integral part of our state’s identity,” Governor Ferguson said. “Jenifer Chao’s deep commitment to the community and extensive advocacy experience will be valuable additions to the Commission."

“I am honored to serve as the next Executive Director of CAPAA as we enter a new chapter,” Chao said. “As a Mien immigrant who has dedicated the past 27 years to public service, I understand how public policy can impact a community’s ability to thrive. I am excited to partner closely with our commissioners to advance equity for our Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander communities.”

“The Commission is absolutely thrilled to welcome Jenifer to the team,” CAPAA Chair Kendall Kosai said. “Jenifer’s deep understanding of community combined with her experience navigating complex institutional systems, positions her for success as CAPAA undergoes a period of planning and growth. The Commission looks forward to working together to ensure that all Native Hawaii/Pacific Islander and Asian/Asian American communities are represented in our state government.”

Chao received a Bachelor of Arts in Communications from the University of Washington. Before joining APICAT, Chao held various leadership roles at the City of Seattle, including Director of the Department of Neighborhoods, where she advanced community-centered governance. Chao began her public service career at Asian Counseling & Referral Service and Neighborhood House and partnered with community coalitions to advance the needs of immigrant, refugee, and historically underserved communities.

Nam Nguyen, a former CAPAA commissioner, has served as interim executive director of CAPAA since 2024. He took over for former executive director Toshiko Grace Hasegawa.

“I appreciate Nam Nguyen stepping in to lead the Commission during this transition,” Governor Ferguson said. “Thank you, Nam, for your service to the people of Washington state and our Asian, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander communities.”

☆ Cultural Events and Activities

The following are some activities you may want to check out HAPPENing:

Native American Heritage Month Events

Native American Heritage Month is celebrated each year in November and Native American Heritage Day is celebrated Nov. 27. It's a time of celebration and recognition — of the rich cultures and traditions of our Native and Indigenous communities — but also one of learning, reflection and dialogue. 

Here is a short list of events happening around our region:

Yakama Nation Veteran's Day Mini Pow Wow
3 - 8 PM, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026 - Toppenish Community Center, Toppenish, WA Join the Yakama Nation in honoring our veterans with a social pow wow and celebration. A Veterans Honoring Ceremony will be held. All dancers, community members, and veterans welcome. Cake/pop walks, social dances, concessions, and more.

REACH Museum's Drummers and Dancers event
10 AM and 1 PM, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026 - REACH Museum, Richland, WA Each year, the celebration showcases the rich cultural traditions of the Mid-Columbia River Region’s Indigenous communities through drumming, dancing, and traditional crafts. Visitors are invited to experience the sounds of the drum, the movement of dance, and the artistry of time-honored skills, while learning about the heritage and values that continue to shape Native communities today. More than a performance, this annual gathering offers our community the opportunity to connect with and appreciate the cultural diversity of the Mid-Columbia.

☆ Transgender Day of Remembrance: Honoring Lives and Building a More Inclusive Community

November 20 | Transgender Day of Remembrance

Each year on November 20, we observe Transgender Day of Remembrance (TDOR), a day dedicated to honoring and remembering transgender and gender-diverse individuals whose lives have been lost to anti-transgender violence.

This day offers an opportunity for us to pause, reflect, and recognize the importance of creating a world where every individual can live authentically, safely, and with dignity.

Behind every name remembered is a person with a story, a family, friends, dreams, and a future that mattered. As an organization, we recognize that fostering an environment of respect, acceptance, and belonging is not simply a statement of our values—it is an ongoing responsibility.

Why This Day Matters

Transgender and gender-diverse individuals continue to experience discrimination, harassment, and violence. Transgender Day of Remembrance reminds us that meaningful inclusion requires intentional action, empathy, education, and a commitment to standing against discrimination in all its forms.

How We Can Make a Difference

Each of us has a role in helping create a more welcoming and inclusive environment. We can:

▪︎ Lead with respect: Honor each person's identity, name, and pronouns.

▪︎ Practice empathy: Listen, learn, and seek to understand experiences different from our own.

▪︎ Speak up: Challenge discrimination, harmful assumptions, and exclusionary behaviors.

▪︎ Foster belonging: Help create spaces where everyone feels welcomed, supported, and valued.

▪︎ Continue learning: Take opportunities to build awareness and understanding of transgender and gender-diverse experiences.

Moving Forward Together

While November 20 is a day of remembrance, our commitment to inclusion must extend throughout the year. Building a culture of belonging means ensuring that our words, actions, policies, and everyday interactions reflect respect and dignity for all.

Today, we honor those we have lost, stand in solidarity with the transgender community, and reaffirm our commitment to creating an environment where everyone has the opportunity to feel safe, respected, and valued.

We remember. We honor. We stand together.

Because everyone deserves to live authentically, without fear, and with the dignity and respect they deserve.

Governor Ferguson Appoints Jennifer Chao to serve as Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs Executive Director

OLYMPIA – Today Governor Bob Ferguson announced the appointment of Jenifer Chao as executive director of the Washington State Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs. The appointment is effective Nov. 1.

The Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs (CAPAA) is a state agency tasked with improving the lives of Asian, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander residents in Washington State by ensuring their access to government, business, education and more. The commission includes an advisory board of 12 commissioners who are also appointed by the Governor.

The commission traces its origins to Governor Dan Evans, whose 1972 executive order created The Governor’s Asian Advisory Council. Two years later, the Legislature formally created the commission. In 1995, the name was changed to include Pacific Islanders and Native Hawaiians to reflect the broad diversity of the community.

Chao brings more than 25 years of experience in public policy, strategic leadership, and managing complex organizations. Most recently, she worked with the Asian Pacific Islander Coalition Advocating Together for Health (APICAT), a grassroots organization rooted in community.

text:
🏀FORT KNOX SEEKS EXIT FROM 5TH REGION, MEADE COUNTY WANTS RETURN TO 5TH REGION AS KHSAA WEIGHS BASKETBALL REALIGNMENT 🏀

Military base access restrictions, midnight returns from road games and competing regional interests could reshape basketball districts across central and western Kentucky.

Two neighboring Kentucky high schools are asking to change basketball regions, with potentially significant consequences for district membership, postseason competition and travel across three regions. Fort Knox wants to leave the 5th Region, while Meade County, a former member, is seeking a return from the 3rd Region. Both requests are scheduled for consideration Thursday, Nov. 12, by the Kentucky High School Athletic Association Board of Control.

The schools have presented different reasons for changing regions. Fort Knox cites restricted access through the military installation, altered transportation routes and anticipated military personnel reductions. Meade County reports that approximately 80% of its away regional contests require late-night travel, with student-athletes frequently returning home at or after midnight on school nights.

Fort Knox currently competes in the 17th District of the 5th Region and prefers a move to the 21st District in the 6th Region, although it remains open to the 11th District in the 3rd Region. Meade County, currently assigned to the 11th District, wants to rejoin the 17th District beginning with the 2027-28 school year.

The requests have been under consideration for months. According to the KHSAA, Fort Knox expressed interest in a regional move as early as June 2025. Formal correspondence from both schools was discussed at the board's February 19, 2026, meeting, followed by additional presentations in September. No action was taken at either meeting.

FORT KNOX: WHY THE PREFERRED DESTINATION CHANGED

Fort Knox's realignment proposal initially favored the 11th District in the 3rd Region. In a February 13 letter to KHSAA Commissioner Julian Tackett, then-athletic director Jackie Prather requested consideration for either the 11th District or the 21st District, with the 3rd Region preferred if Meade County returned to the 5th.

Prather indicated that Fort Knox was prepared to make the move as early as the 2026-27 school year. The school's subsequent submission, signed by athletic director Wes Arnold, revises that preference based on current travel conditions.

Arnold identifies the 21st District in the 6th Region as the more practical geographic fit, citing changes in how teams enter and exit Fort Knox. His argument centers on Wilson Gate in Radcliff, historically used by athletic teams traveling to Hardin County schools.

According to Arnold, reduced operating hours at Wilson Gate have forced teams to use Chaffee Gate more frequently. Located near the Meade County line, Chaffee Gate changes the routes teams must travel to reach schools in Hardin County and elsewhere.

Arnold compares Fairdale, a 21st District school approximately 22 miles from Fort Knox, with Central Hardin, a current district opponent approximately 21 to 22 miles away. Despite those similar distances, he reports that trips to Central Hardin often exceed 35 to 40 minutes because of gate restrictions, traffic congestion and additional traffic signals.

The comparison illustrates the central argument in Fort Knox's request: mileage alone does not accurately reflect the transportation challenges of a school located on an active military installation.

Arnold also contends that the proposed realignment would reduce unnecessary backtracking after teams leave the installation, creating more practical travel arrangements for athletes, coaches and families.

MILITARY RESTRUCTURING ADDS TO FORT KNOX'S CONCERNS

Fort Knox's submission connects the restricted gate operations to broader military personnel reductions associated with the Army Transformation Initiative.

Arnold's letter projected the loss of more than 1,200 Army-affiliated personnel from the installation. The submission specifically identified the planned October deactivation of the 19th Engineer Battalion, involving nearly 400 active-duty soldiers, and the deactivation process involving the Army Reserve Aviation Command headquarters.

Those figures and timelines come from the school's submission. The letter does not establish the final number of personnel who have departed or quantify the resulting change in Fort Knox High School enrollment.

Arnold anticipates that the restructuring will affect enrollment and installation services, including gate access. For basketball realignment purposes, the resulting transportation conditions are particularly relevant because KHSAA policy requires consideration of geography and actual travel routes.

Although the 6th Region is now Fort Knox's preference, Arnold has not ruled out the 3rd Region. His letter specifically acknowledges Meade County's request to return to the 5th and expresses willingness to accept an 11th District assignment if it better accommodates the overall alignment.

That flexibility could become important as the board considers the effects of moving multiple schools rather than treating Fort Knox's request as an isolated decision.

MEADE COUNTY: THE ACADEMIC COST OF LATE-NIGHT TRAVEL

Meade County's request focuses on the educational and operational consequences of remaining in the 3rd Region.

In its advocacy document for the 2027-28 school year, the school identifies itself as the only Eastern Time Zone member of a region whose remaining schools operate in Central Time.

That creates a scheduling disadvantage when Meade County travels west. A game beginning at 7 p.m. Central Time starts at 8 p.m. for students and families in Brandenburg, with the return trip adding to an already late evening.

According to Meade County's submission, approximately 80% of away regional contests involve late-night travel, frequently bringing student-athletes home at or after midnight on school nights.

The school argues that those schedules affect sleep, classroom preparation and readiness for the following school day. Its middle school athletic programs, by comparison, compete against geographically closer 5th Region schools, reducing travel demands.

Meade County also reports that travel distances and time-zone differences have contributed to canceled junior varsity and freshman contests. The school maintains that those cancellations limit playing opportunities and development for younger athletes.

The concerns extend to school transportation employees. Meade County says bus drivers regularly return late from athletic trips while still being responsible for early morning transportation assignments the following day.

THE NUMBERS BEHIND MEADE COUNTY'S REGIONAL REQUEST

Meade County's advocacy document includes a comparison of travel proximity between the 3rd and 5th regions.

According to the school's calculations, approximately 61% of 5th Region member schools are within a 100-mile round trip of Meade County. Only 29% of 3rd Region schools meet that same threshold.

The percentages are figures submitted by Meade County, rather than independently verified calculations. They nevertheless provide a measurable basis for the school's argument that the 5th Region offers a more geographically practical collection of opponents.

The school also reports difficulty securing 3rd Region officials willing to travel to Brandenburg, citing long distances and time-zone differences. Its submission suggests that an assignment involving closer schools could improve officiating availability and scheduling consistency.

Community participation is another concern. Meade County says extended trips reduce attendance by students, families, pep bands and cheerleaders, diminishing the atmosphere surrounding school athletic events.

Its advocacy document cites local workforce information indicating that many Meade County families and supporters work along the Interstate 65 corridor, including Elizabethtown, Fort Knox, Louisville and Southern Indiana. The school argues that 5th Region competition would better match those established travel and community patterns.

Meade County also points to its history as a former 5th Region member, emphasizing rivalries and geographic relationships with neighboring schools. Its submission expressly frames the requested move around academic impact, community experience and transportation safety rather than competitive advantage.

HOW THE REQUESTS COULD RESHAPE THREE REGIONS

The two schools' preferred destinations would directly affect the 17th District, which currently includes Central Hardin, Elizabethtown, Fort Knox, John Hardin and North Hardin.

If Meade County returns and Fort Knox departs, the district could retain five schools, substituting Meade County for Fort Knox. That would restore Meade County's district competition against its Hardin County neighbors while moving Fort Knox's basketball postseason into another region.

The consequences elsewhere depend on Fort Knox's eventual placement. Meade County's departure would reduce the 11th District from four schools to three unless another school were assigned to replace it.

Fort Knox's preferred move to the 21st District presents another consideration. That district is listed with five members in the KHSAA's published basketball alignment, meaning adding Fort Knox without another adjustment would create a six-school district.

KHSAA alignment policy identifies four or five teams as the preferred size for bracketed-sport districts, although exceptions are permitted. The board therefore must weigh the effects of each proposed move on surrounding schools, not simply the travel advantages sought by Fort Knox and Meade County.

A Fort Knox move into the 11th District could address the vacancy created by Meade County's departure. However, that outcome would differ from Fort Knox's revised preference for the 6th Region.

The situation also intersects with a separate request from Trinity of Whitesville, currently a 12th District school seeking a return to the 11th District if Meade County leaves. That request is listed separately on Thursday's agenda and has not been approved.

For the 3rd Region, the consequences could extend beyond losing Meade County. Depending on the board's decisions, district membership and postseason competition involving Breckinridge County, Frederick Fraize, Hancock County and other neighboring schools could change.

WHAT THE KHSAA MUST CONSIDER

The KHSAA's alignment and realignment policy identifies geographic proximity, specific travel routes and historical alignment as factors in assigning schools to districts and regions.

The policy states that geography is important but not the sole determinant. It also directs the board to consider the effects of proposed assignments on existing members and the organization of regional competition.

For non-classified sports such as basketball, enrollment, socioeconomic composition, school type and previous competitive success generally are excluded from alignment considerations, subject to the policy's stated exception concerning competitive history.

That distinction matters in both requests. Fort Knox's anticipated military personnel reductions provide context for changing installation operations, while Meade County's documented concerns focus primarily on travel, scheduling and student participation.

Basketball regional boundaries also serve as an initial geographic framework for other non-classified team sports under KHSAA policy. Changes approved in basketball could therefore influence future discussions involving baseball, soccer, softball and volleyball, although those sports would require their own alignment consideration.

The board has discretion to weigh the competing requests and potentially adopt arrangements different from either school's first preference.

WHAT HAPPENS THURSDAY?

The KHSAA Board of Control's full board work session is scheduled to begin at approximately 9:15 a.m. Eastern Time on Thursday, Nov. 12.

The agenda places the requests under the initial consideration of basketball alignment changes, with possible action following public comments and discussion. The board may approve, reject or defer individual requests.

Meade County has specified the 2027-28 school year in its submission. Although Fort Knox's February letter expressed willingness to move as early as 2026-27, its updated request does not establish a final implementation date.

The KHSAA also indicated in September that affected schools would have an opportunity to provide feedback before further consideration in November.

For Fort Knox, the outcome could determine whether its basketball program remains in the 5th Region or moves into the 3rd or 6th. For Meade County, it could determine whether a return to the 17th District ends the school's current time-zone and regional travel challenges.

The decision will also require the board to account for the schools left behind and the districts receiving new members.

Thursday's discussion therefore concerns more than two requests to change opponents. It presents a broader test of how the KHSAA balances geographic access, school transportation needs and district stability across three regions.

OFFICIAL DOCUMENTS AND SOURCES

Readers can review the schools' submissions, KHSAA policy and previous meeting reports through the following official links.

text:
Chase Branham is Indiana’s newest (and first) class of 2027 basketball commit. The 6-4, 185-pound guard from Rogersville, Missouri, officially signed his letter of intent with the Hoosiers on November 11, 2026, under coach Darian DeVries.
He is a consensus 4-star recruit ranked No. 25 by 247Sports, No. 28 by ESPN, and No. 38 by Rivals — making him the 10th-highest-ranked Hoosier recruit in the 247Sports era. He committed in September 2025 over offers that included Purdue, Missouri, Iowa, Tennessee, and others.
High school & AAU background
Branham spent his first three years at Logan-Rogersville High School in Missouri, where as a junior he averaged 21.5 points, 3.6 rebounds, 3.1 assists, and 2.2 steals while shooting 61.7% from the field, 41.1% from three, and 84.8% from the free-throw line. He led the Wildcats to the 2026 Class 4A state title, including a 31-point performance in a semifinal upset of traditional power Vashon. He earned MaxPreps Small-Town All-American honors.
He then transferred to national power La Lumiere School in La Porte, Indiana, for his senior season. On the AAU circuit with KC Run GMC (Under Armour), he posted strong scoring and efficiency numbers, earned All-UAA First Team recognition, and was named MVP of the Under Armour Next City Classic. He also attended USA Basketball Men’s Junior National Team minicamps in both 2025 and 2026.
Scouting profile
Branham is viewed as a dynamic, multi-level playmaker and combo guard who can create on the ball or play off it. He scores efficiently at all three levels, shoots well from deep (including off the dribble), and brings playmaking and defensive disruption. DeVries described him as “a dynamic playmaker that is effective at all three levels” who “continues to push himself to new levels” thanks to his work ethic, while also praising his character.
He is the son of Lori and Nick Branham, has siblings Brooke and Jake, and was born September 5, 2008. He is expected to arrive in Bloomington for the 2027-28 season.

text: Wise ,when it comes to receiving a large lump-sum payment in the United States, you have to look beyond the amount being offered and consider the tax implications. What someone actually takes home can vary significantly depending on their state of residence, total annual income, filing status, and the source of the payment. For example, someone living in New York City could face a substantial tax bill because they may be subject to federal income tax, New York State income tax, and additional city taxes. Depending on the circumstances, a considerable portion of that money could go toward taxes. On the other hand, states like Florida and Texas do not impose individual state income taxes, which can make a significant difference in the final amount received. However, that doesn't mean the payment is automatically tax-free, because federal taxes may still apply. If the lump sum is her only source of income, her overall tax liability could be considerably lower, depending on how the payment is classified. That's why it's important to understand the tax structure before deciding whether taking the money all at once is financially smarter than choosing another payment arrangement.

text:
Rowling’s casting rule left no room for Williams

J.K. Rowling set the nationality rule for the film adaptations, and Columbus agreed to it. The principal cast would be British and Irish, an approach enforced from 2001’s Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone onward. It applied even when a major American actor approached the director personally.

Casting director Janet Hirshenson described Williams’s approach to HuffPost UK in 2016. “Robin had called [Chris Columbus] because he really wanted to be in the movie, but it was a British-only edict,” she said. Williams himself confirmed to the New York Post in 2001 that there were “a couple” of Harry Potter roles he wanted, and that his nationality stood in the way. His interest went beyond a single phone call about Hagrid.

The films made narrow exceptions, but not for American stars

Williams was also interested in playing Remus Lupin, Columbus later said. Hagrid went instead to Robbie Coltrane, who played the character throughout the original film series. Columbus said the British and Irish casting approach helped preserve a “degree of authenticity.” We think the consistency of the rule gives Williams’s rejection particular weight, since the production applied it even to someone who clearly wanted in.

Williams was not the only American turned away. Rosie O’Donnell offered to play Molly Weasley for free and was refused on the same grounds. The films did cast actors from other countries when the characters called for it. French actor Clémence Poésy played Fleur Delacour, while Bulgarian actor Stanislav Ianevski played Viktor Krum, both characters written as foreign in the books.

Lithgow's casting shows how much the old rule still resonates:

Lithgow said he was surprised by the backlash to his casting, rather than by the offer of the part.

Addressing viewers who objected, he urged them to wait for the performance: "Better to form an opinion after seeing the work than writing it off as a fail well in advance," he told Deadline in April 2025.

The casting change takes nothing away from Coltrane's Hagrid or the films' long commitment to their original approach. We see HBO's decision to cast an American as Dumbledore as the clearest sign that the old rule belonged to the original films rather than the franchise itself.

text:
At 16, Brian Banks was one of the best high school linebackers in America. USC had offered him a full scholarship. Pete Carroll personally called him.

One afternoon at school he made out with a classmate. Consensual. By the end of the day he was in jail, charged with kidnapping and rape.

She said he dragged her into a stairwell. It never happened.

The DNA came back negative. His mother sold her house and her car to pay for a lawyer.

He couldn’t make bail. He spent a year behind bars waiting for trial.

His lawyer told him: plead no contest, or risk 41 years in prison. He was 17. He took the deal.

He did 5 years in prison. Then 5 more on parole. Registered sex offender. GPS monitor on his ankle. Couldn’t go near schools or parks. No one would hire him.

Meanwhile, the girl and her mother sued the school district for not keeping her safe. They won $1.5 million.

In 2011, a Facebook friend request popped up on his screen.

It was her.

She wanted to “let bygones be bygones.”

Brian went to a private investigator. They hid cameras in the office and invited her to talk. She came by bus.

On tape, she admitted it. He never raped her. He never kidnapped her.

Then she said she still wouldn’t tell prosecutors the truth. Because she’d have to give back the money.

In May 2012, a judge cleared his name. The hearing took less than a minute.

10 years of his life. Gone in one lie. Erased in 60 seconds.

A few days later his phone rang. “I’m looking for a linebacker. You know where I can find one?”

It was Pete Carroll. The same coach who recruited him 10 years earlier.

He finally signed with the NFL’s Atlanta Falcons. At 27. The dream he had at 16.

She was ordered to pay $2.6 million back.

What should happen to someone who steals 10 years of your life with one lie?
