text:
Erin Burnett: I want to go to John Ullyot first, though. He served as Hegseth’s Pentagon spokesman. He also served in the first Trump administration, and he’s now the author of a new book, The President Deserves Better. Paul Rieckhoff and Jamal Simmons are also here, familiar faces to everyone. John, I want to start with you. It’s interesting in the wake of what Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez just said, that these articles could come again. When you look at Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment, the ones that go through the specifics, you also conclude that guilty is the verdict.

John Ullyot: Well, look, it’s up to Congress, but he’s going to get impeached. Whether it’s now, before January, or in January itself after the Democrats take the gavel. To me, Erin, it’s not about impeachment. If you look at that news conference Hegseth did today, where he’s screaming at reporters and yelling across them, he looked like a Fox News fire-breather, frankly, or a cable-news fire-breather trying to get a point across. He makes it about himself, not about the troops. He actually likes this, having the focus on him. It’s as if he’s on a set at Fox News. What I say in the book is that the president deserves better than that. He was confirmed only 50–50, with Vance casting the tie vote. If I’m somebody like that, getting in on such a thin margin, then when I get in office I pivot from being a Fox News co-host and focus on bringing the volume down, figuring it out, talking to people, and not making it about myself. The president deserves better. I looked at that news conference today and I just say, hey, the president’s got two more years to go. He doesn’t need this headache.

Erin Burnett: You want Hegseth to resign, but I think you go even further. When you talk about making it about himself during the war, we had to look at him putting out videos of himself lifting weights and talking about testosterone tests for troops. You think he shouldn’t have taken the job to begin with?

John Ullyot: Yeah. Let’s say I’m on the transition. Just as a reminder, I was a senior adviser on President Trump’s campaign in 2016. That was the same time Pete Hegseth was calling him an armchair phony warrior. He was not backing the president when we were working in Trump Tower to get him elected. That’s number one. Number two, Hegseth knew, when he was offered the job, that he was a Minnesota National Guard major. We honor everybody’s service, no question about it, but he had no management experience. He’d also built a career as a bombastic guy on Fox News. That’s very helpful if you’re going up the ranks from contributor. If I were in his shoes—

Erin Burnett: Or on cable news, but not running the department.

John Ullyot: Yeah, not running the department. If the president came to me and said, “Hey, John, for all your service over the years, I want you to be my deputy attorney general,” I would say, “Mr. President, I get a big car and a big motorcade, but you might want to think about somebody with a law degree, because I’m not qualified for that.” That’s what I think—

Erin Burnett: That’s where Pete Hegseth stands.

John Ullyot: Secretary Hegseth should just say, “Look, I’m a Fox News host. I’m bombastic. I like to throw bombs. I’m not the unifying figure you need after President Biden, looking forward, and you would be better served with somebody else who’s better qualified.”

Erin Burnett: Paul, just to make the point, John was the Pentagon spokesperson for Hegseth. So it’s significant that you’re saying what you’re saying. We’re here tonight where this just failed. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is saying it failed for now. And by for now, I don’t mean January 3rd, when Democrats control. I think Thomas Massie could do it again and succeed.

Paul Rieckhoff: He should, because today is the Marine Corps birthday. Tomorrow is Veterans Day. Pete Hegseth never should have gotten the job. He should have long ago lost the job. Every day he’s in that job, he’s making our country less safe. He’s making it about him. He’s dragging our military down. Our enemies are celebrating every single day he’s in office, and this is about our national security. Yeah, the Democrats blew it tonight by not having enough people there to pass it, but they should bring it back tomorrow. Drop it on Veterans Day. You want to serve our veterans? You want to serve our military? Remove the number one problem facing our military, and it’s Hegseth. There’s bipartisan support for that now. He does want to make it about him. He wants to grandstand. He wants to amplify his profile, and he probably wants to run for president.

Erin Burnett: We’ve heard that that’s all but a sure thing from those close to him. I don’t know whether he will or not, but that reporting has been there. Jamal, what about what the congresswoman said? Where were those Democrats who caused the failure today? It’s a complicated rubric of math when it comes to the House and its votes.

Jamal Simmons: The Republicans have learned nothing since Election Day. They’re not changing course. You pick Stephen Miller to be the White House chief of staff. You pick Jim Jordan to be the minority leader in the House. That means they’re not changing course. They’re not listening to the voters. You know who has learned something? AOC. Think about how constructive she sounded. She didn’t throw bombs at her colleagues. She gave people grace to figure out where they were, and then she opened a path. I don’t know what’s up with people’s health, but by the way, I clocked in at my job when I worked at a restaurant. She got a lot of things in there. She made her point in a way that didn’t take anybody else down, and then she opened the door for the Democrats to act. Here’s what’s important about that. When you’ve got Jim Jordan being named minority leader, that means the Republicans are knuckling up. They’re getting ready to get into a fight, and now you get people like AOC saying, “I’m knuckling up too. If you guys want to do that, I’ll match you.”

John Ullyot: Yeah, Jamal is absolutely right that that sends a bad signal from the outset. I’ve worked with Stephen Miller, and he is obviously a hardliner on immigration, but he does know the Senate. He worked for Jeff Sessions from Alabama when he was there. I don’t know, but my hope is that he pivots, just like Hegseth didn’t pivot after barely getting confirmed. He didn’t pivot from being a Fox News fire-breather over to actually doing the job. I’m hoping Stephen Miller says, “Look, I’m no longer in charge of immigration. I have to make this president succeed and work with Democrats.” We’ll see. The jury’s out. The jury’s out. Now he’s in charge of everything, and hope is not a course of action. I think the reality is we’re in for a new phase of war. It’s going to be open combat between all sides, and this period, between now and January, is especially dangerous, because what this tells you is Hegseth is still there. The most important story in the world is still that Trump can do anything he wants with the most powerful military in the world, and nothing is stopping him. They didn’t slow him down today. They didn’t check him today. Forever war rolls on. It can include Cuba and anything else he wants, because he circled the wagons and closed the circle.

Erin Burnett: Well, it comes down to this. The CIA warned you multiple times that the CEO of the single most important company in the AI war against China is sleeping with what they say is a Chinese spy, and Trump chooses to do nothing about it. We don’t know the whys and the motives, but we know the basic scaffolding of the story.

Jamal Simmons: We do, because we also know the President of the United States has given information to Russians in the Oval Office that was supposed to be secure. We know that he met with Putin, came out of the meeting, and said, “I trust Putin more than I trust my intelligence officials.” So there are real questions about how the president feels about intelligence in general. The question for me about Stephen Miller is that it could also be that Donald Trump likes to negotiate from a position of strength, and Stephen Miller is like a loaded gun that you put on the table to let Democrats know that if we’re going to fight, I’ve got somebody I’m ready to fight with. Now perhaps there is a doorway open for the Democrats to negotiate. But the Democrats have to fight back too. They have to show Trump that they are willing to go just as tough as he is.

Erin Burnett: Yeah. Go ahead.

John Ullyot: President Trump has two years. Those of us who worked for him for over a decade now, off and on, in and out, first term, second term, we know he’s only got two years left as president. He’s already shown that maybe he wants to fight, be very combative, but at the end of the day I still think he can take a step back and say, “Hey, look, I want to work and get something done.” He’s always concerned about these legacy projects, like the ballroom. His true legacy is going to be whether he comes to the table and actually gets things done in a bipartisan way.

Erin Burnett: And does. Yeah.

John Ullyot: If you’re Hegseth, if you’re truly loyal, or anybody for that matter, Kristi Noem, for example, if you realize that you’re being a drag on the president, and if you’re loyal to him, then you owe it to the president to say, “It’s not about me. It’s about you. And I’ve become a distraction.”

Erin Burnett: When you write in your book, “The president deserves better,” Trump picked Hegseth.

John Ullyot: Right.

Erin Burnett: And there were people around him who warned him. Early on, with Signalgate and all of that, there were people who said—

John Ullyot: Right. I wrote an op-ed right after I left, and I said—

Erin Burnett: Why do you think Trump stands by him?

John Ullyot: I don’t think President Trump realizes how much of a drag Pete Hegseth is. You’ve had good things happening in the military up until the war in Iran. Ammunition stockpiles, everything else. Did you hear what Pete Hegseth said? It was all rosy. He was giving all the top lines. Most of what he was talking about could have happened no matter who was secretary of defense. It was CENTCOM. It was STRATCOM that did a lot of the actual attacks on Iran a year and a half ago. Bottom line, he’s making it as if he— recruiting was already going up when he first came into office. Dismantling identity-politics programs, that was across government.

Erin Burnett: But does Trump ever say, “Hey, wait a minute. This guy didn’t tell me the truth about the munitions. He didn’t tell me the truth about the U.S. bases. He didn’t tell me the truth about the aircraft carriers that are in the region”? It goes on and on and on.

Jamal Simmons: Right. So what Trump might be doing is establishing that I’m not going to do what the Democrats want, and then three days from now he asks him to find somewhere else to go. Here’s the real bottom line. The American people have said they want a change in direction, and right now the Republicans aren’t giving them that. That’s going to hurt every single other Republican who’s going to be up for reelection soon.

Paul Rieckhoff: And Trump doesn’t care. Trump doesn’t care. Maybe tonight was a victory for Hegseth.

Erin Burnett: All right, I got to leave it there.

Abby Phillip: Noah, I’m going to start with you. I have a lot of thoughts about this, because this was started by a Republican, a disgruntled Republican, and Donald Trump is right: Thomas Massie. This was sort of his last salvo before he leaves, exit stage left. He was not reelected. He was booted out in the primaries because of Donald Trump. So what was the point of this?

Noah Rothman: What was Thomas Massie’s point? Perhaps to get quite a lot of attention for Thomas Massie. Members of the Republican conference do have plenty of problems with Pete Hegseth. They probably have more problems with Thomas Massie, but that was irrespective. I think, most likely, the conference realized they didn’t want to spend whatever floor time they have left litigating an issue that Democrats are likely to litigate themselves when they take control of Congress. But the articles themselves were rather flawed. There were elements in there where they have Pete Hegseth dead to rights. The mishandling of classified information on the Signal chat: you got him. Mark Kelly, the suppression of his speech over a political dispute: hard to argue with that. The notion that we are kidnapping, the language that they use, a sovereign leader in the form of Nicolás Maduro: I don’t know. It sounds like we’re invalidating, for example, the effort that extricated Manuel Noriega from Panama. And beyond that, a lot of these are just bank shots at the president. The president ordered these orders, and he and Pete Hegseth executed them. If your problem is with the orders themselves, your problem is with the president and his subordinates.

Abby Phillip: Well, that is certainly something that was argued today by not only Pete Hegseth, but Marco Rubio. Let’s listen.

Pete Hegseth: Iran, the cartels, Maduro, Yemen. Every one was a lawful operation ordered by the commander in chief.

Marco Rubio: The president of the United States makes these decisions. Ultimately our job is to execute on the president’s orders. Everything that he’s done, he is executing on President Trump’s mission and what President Trump has said we should do.

Abby Phillip: Explain to me what you think that defense is about.

Christopher Hahn: That defense is, hey, Democrats, try to impeach the president. Go down in flames by doing that. Look, I’m not happy with the president. I’m surely not happy with Pete Hegseth. Pete Hegseth needs to go, and I think he will go. I think the president is going to fire him probably Thanksgiving week. So good luck, Pete. Enjoy your success for a little while. But ultimately what they’re saying is, bring it on, do another impeachment, lose the momentum that you gained in this election, and then really good luck in 2028.

Abby Phillip: You were shaking your head when he was talking.

Caroline Sunshine: Oh, yeah. Pete Hegseth is not going anywhere. He gave, at least by the president’s account, a phenomenal press conference today. He’s a fighter. He was tough. He’s a great communicator. Congress doesn’t have any balls, and they don’t care about ending wars. If they did, they would cut funding to Ukraine tomorrow. We all know they’re not going to do that. Congress is the only people to blame for not stopping this war. All of them had a vote. They could have voted to use the war powers. They all chose not to. They voted a couple of times. Clearly not enough. Even people who agreed with the war decided they were not going to exercise their authority on the war. Now, the charge against Pete Hegseth. First of all, a secretary of war has not been impeached since 1867. A hundred and fifty years. The charge against him is bogus. The charge is that he carried out unlawful military operations because there was no congressional authorization. But did we have any legal authority to go into Pakistan when we were getting Osama bin Laden? No. Did we have any legal authority to go get Noriega? No. Did we have any legal authority to go get Saddam Hussein in Iraq? We sure as hell did not. What they are saying is the American people might be anti-war, and they’ve spoken this election and said that they are, but the American people are pro-soldier. And what Congress is doing by picking this fight with Pete Hegseth is saying that if the orders he gave were all unlawful, then all of our men and women who carried out their longest deployments on the USS Abraham Lincoln, all of them who went to save our soldiers in Iran, are following unlawful orders.

Abby Phillip: Are you filibustering the table? She’s filibustering.

Caroline Sunshine: Yeah, I’m right.

Abby Phillip: No. Because you’re conflating a lot of things, first of all about the War Powers Act, but I don’t even want to debate that, because at the end of the day this motion failed. So why are we going to debate whether this was actually— it didn’t fail on the merits. It failed on a political, procedural matter. Debating that is something else. But what is interesting is this argument that somehow impeaching Pete Hegseth is hurting the troops. If you look at what the American people say, and this is across party lines, they just had a poll, November 6th to 9th, from Reuters/Ipsos. Support for Congress ending the Iran war: overall, 71 percent. Republicans, 51 percent. Democrats, 93 percent. Independents, 70 percent. The idea that Pete Hegseth is the same thing as the soldiers. Democrats could argue, and I’m someone who spent a lot of time with the military in the Middle East for many, many years, and what Democrats would tell you, in fact what they do say, is that they’re trying to protect the military from Pete Hegseth. So I’m just wondering what you see here.

Ashley Allison: I think we’re still experiencing folks in Washington, D.C., who haven’t caught up with the rest of the country, if I’m honest. Democrats and Republicans. Republicans could have actually voted to impeach. They would have had the votes as well, but they didn’t go with Massie. That is a failure of leadership on their part. And then there were some Democrats who didn’t show up. Eleven. And I think that they are—

Abby Phillip: Including Nancy Pelosi.

Ashley Allison: And I think they are trying to figure out the settlement of this earthquake that just happened in this country. Politically, the observation is that folks are still trying to recalibrate where their power is in Washington, D.C., as opposed to with the voters. The other thing is, what I heard Marco Rubio say, and what I heard Pete Hegseth say, is: I’m with the president, but in two seconds, if this anchor gets a little too heavy, which it already is, I’m out. I’m out. They are literally saying, this is not my fault. This is his fault. And I actually think the president is still trying to recalibrate where he is, because there’s a way that he’s like, wait, why is everybody paying attention to Hegseth? Is he more important than me? Come after me. I’m the guy. This is all just folks in Washington, not in the real world, in their bubble, in their D.C. circle.

Abby Phillip: Camille, you’re looking like you don’t buy that.

Kmele Foster: Well, I’m just not sure I heard the subtext you’re referring to there, that Rubio was hedging in a way to protect himself. I think they’ve made the best argument that they can, that ultimately the president is the one making these decisions. I do think that perhaps this is a little bit of a hope that they can bait Democrats into going after the president of the United States. But what else would you expect them to say? I think that’s the part that’s clear. If I could just continue to talk for a moment, it would be nice if we could have a conversation. Let’s take a look at the actual articles of impeachment, the particular things that are there. I think Noah is absolutely right. There are certain things that don’t wash quite as easily, but there are other things about which there are profoundly serious questions. Should the United States of America be in the business of simply murdering people who are traveling across the high seas, without any sort of approval from Congress, without any sort of authorization to commit war, without any sort of presentation of the evidence in public that says these people were actually headed to the United States? When they actually apprehend people, they hand them back over and then they’re simply let go. Why not interdict? Why not have conversations? Why not actually conduct a serious intelligence operation? This seems like an administration that is interested in simply running afoul of the law, or doing whatever they want. That is deeply concerning.

text:
Last month, I was back in Ottawa to keynote the @AsiaPacificFdn Indo-Pacific Forum 2026. And I am hugely grateful to @jeff_nankivell and his fantastic team for having me back for a second dance after I keynoted their annual event a few years ago.   

The first time around, in a speech subsequently rebroadcast on the @SinicaPodcast, I offered a rather dark view of U.S. policy and posture in Asia—and warned Canadians that they and other American allies would soon be in American crosshairs as Washington increasingly sharpened the contradictions for its closest partners in an effort to shrink their options. That warning, I think, turned out to be quite prescient. (And I note that I delivered it during the ostensibly "pro-alliances" Biden administration not the "anti-alliances" Trump administration.)     

So this time, I tried to do something a little bit different—offering an aspirationally hopeful view of optionality and what Canada and other third countries that are warily eyeing both the United States and China can do to shape Asia’s future in a forward-looking way.   One view of Asia's future is that it will be characterized and constrained largely by U.S.-China competition. And because @MarkJCarney and others have called for "middle powers" to unite, a lively debate has ensued about what is and isn't realistic for these countries and whether so-called middle power optionality is just pie in the sky.   

As I explain in this video of my keynote remarks, some of this debate confuses cause and effect. To my mind, optionality does NOT necessarily imply multipolarity. But it can be crucial to international rule-making—and a useful strategy for countries like Canada—if policy understands and embraces the distinction between "form" and "function." Bluntly put, forming middle power groups that then grope around for purpose isn't especially likely to yield anything at all. But functional coalitions that pool real capacity to solve real problems have real potential, especially when third players become first movers as standard setters and rule makers.

text:
The Real Play Behind Jensen Huang’s "Spy" Scandal: A Classic DC Two-for-One  Don't let the "Chinese spy" tabloid drama fool you. The real story behind Jensen Huang's affair scandal may have less to do with espionage than with pure Washington politics. 

US China hawks may be trying to pull off a classic "two birds, one stone" play.  First, they want to kneecap Jensen's influence in DC. Huang has successfully lobbied the Trump administration to ease export controls on high-end AI chips like the H200, a move that has drawn strong opposition from China hawks in both parties. Linking his affair to an executive at a firm suspected of chip smuggling offers a convenient way to undermine his credibility, raise questions about whether he could be compromised, and put pressure on the White House to tighten the screws on chip exports again.  

Second, they're pushing the "Chinese spies are everywhere" narrative to stir up security panic. Spinning a personal affair and a business compliance dispute into a "Chinese spy" story—without publicly presenting hard evidence—plays straight into Western fears. It smears China's image while giving Congress political ammunition to push for harsher tech restrictions and tighter controls on cross-border talent and business exchanges.  Look at the timing—it's hard not to raise questions. US intelligence reportedly knew about the matter more than a year ago, and Trump had reportedly been briefed on the intelligence concerns. Yet the story only broke in the press on October 29—just days before the midterms and weeks ahead of Trump's planned Asia trip, with Huang's participation in the delegation still under discussion. 

The timing, followed by Huang's November 8 statement, inevitably raises questions about why the information surfaced when it did. That "sit on it, then drop it at a politically convenient moment" pattern looks very much like classic DC selective leaking.  Look at who's leading the charge: Brian Mast @RepBrianMast , John Moolenaar @RepMoolenaar , and Rick Crawford @RepRickCrawford  Republican chairmen of the House Foreign Affairs, China, and Intelligence committees—who just demanded a closed-door briefing from Huang. 

Meanwhile, Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren @SenWarren has separately challenged Nvidia over its China-related chip exports. All four are longtime critics of Huang's China chip sales and Big Tech's lobbying power.  Forget the spy thriller narrative and look at what Jensen Huang's opponents in Washington may actually be trying to achieve. With the midterms now behind them and Democrats set to take control of Congress in the next session, the real tug-of-war over AI regulation and China chip policy between Trump and the incoming Democratic-led Congress is just getting started

text:
The Perfect Tax Code

A nurse finishes a shift. Her paycheck arrives with the taxes already taken out.

Jeff Bezos’s wealth grew by an estimated $99 billion between 2014 and 2018. He paid $973 million in personal federal taxes over those five years, according to ProPublica. That’s an enormous tax bill. It’s also less than one cent for every dollar his fortune grew. A nurse pays tax on what she earns before she gets to spend it. The two numbers measure different things. That’s the problem.

The tax code is very good at finding work. It’s much less interested in finding wealth.

I’d turn that around.

Let the nurse keep more of her paycheck. Same for the mechanic, the teacher, the person who took a chance and opened a small business. Make the first serious chunk of earned income tax-free. Cut the tax on ordinary wages. If somebody is working and still struggling, add to their pay.

Then go where the money is.

I don’t object to Bezos getting rich. He built something people use. The question is what happens once a fortune reaches a size where ownership itself produces billions more.

If that money is going into a new business, a factory, a treatment, housing, research, people learning a skill—good. Give it a tax advantage. Make it a real investment, with money spent and something built. Let the public see what it bought.

If it just sits in assets that keep rising, tax the gain. Tax it before taking another dollar from the nurse’s shift.

And close the exits. Don’t let the gain disappear at death. Don’t let someone borrow against a mountain of stock to fund his life and put off the tax forever. Count losses, too. Give owners of businesses that can’t easily be sold time to pay. Don’t charge twice on the same gain.

People will say that’s complicated. Of course it takes work to write the rules. We have managed to write plenty of complicated rules to protect fortunes. We can write some to tax them.

I’d treat land differently as well. A vacant lot becomes valuable because other people build a city around it. Tax more of that land value and less of the building somebody puts on it. Don’t force a person on a fixed income out of a home because the neighborhood got expensive. Collect the tax when the property changes hands.

And yes, tax enormous inheritances. A parent should be able to leave children secure. They don’t need to leave them command of an economy they did nothing to build.

Now here’s where I don’t trust Washington. The moment you offer a tax break for “productive investment,” every lobbyist in town shows up claiming his client is indispensable. So make every break public. Say who got it, what it cost and when it ends.

Did the hospital produce better care for less money? Did the school help children learn? Did the energy project deliver cheaper, reliable power? If the answer is no, end the break. I’m tired of paying for promises.

For most people, paying taxes should be boring. The government has your wage information already. Send a return with the numbers filled in. Let people check it, fix it and get on with their lives.

None of this excuses what government spends. We keep paying more for healthcare, education and defense while people who know how to do parts of the work better struggle to get in the door. Washington protects the old arrangement and borrows to cover the bill.

The people inside the arrangement get paid now. Everybody else pays later.

That’s the tax code I want: work gets a break. Vast wealth gets one when it actually builds something. Otherwise it pays before the nurse does.

text:
Phil Jackson reveals how he tried to shift Kobe Bryant’s mindset from chasing individual greatness to understanding the importance of winning championships as a team.

Jackson says he gave Kobe leadership books, including The Tao of Leadership and The Tao of Pooh, hoping to help him develop a broader understanding of leadership. He recalls Jerry West calling him during his first season with the Lakers after Kobe questioned how West and Elgin Baylor managed to average 30 points each on the same team. Kobe was concerned about the scoring gap between himself and Shaquille O’Neal, who was averaging 28 points while he was averaging 18.

Jackson recognized that Kobe was determined to become one of the greatest players ever, but wanted him to understand that individual achievements were not the ultimate measure of success. He repeatedly reminded Kobe that the real joy of basketball comes from winning a championship and experiencing that achievement together as a team.

He explains that winning a scoring title while the team struggles offers only limited success. For Jackson, the greatest reward comes when everyone contributes to a championship and gets to share that unforgettable moment together.

text:
Similarly, we must remember that this world is not our true home. With our first parents, we were cast out from Paradise because of Original Sin. Only through the mercy of Christ can we be restored. Recognizing our exile and its cause is the first step toward healing. If we do not acknowledge our spiritual leprosy, we will not cry out for the only cure: Jesus’ mercy.
One beautiful aspect of this story is that it reveals a second, deeper level of spiritual healing. The ten who cried out and were healed represent those who are baptized and remain in a state of grace, either by avoiding mortal sin or by being restored through sacramental confession and absolution. Yet only one, upon realizing he was healed, returned to give thanks to Jesus. The other nine did not.
The fact that only one returned suggests that most of us are best represented by the other nine. Just as an immature child expects his parents to feed and care for him, so we often expect God to forgive and restore us without giving proper thanks. If that is the extent of our spiritual lives, we remain immature. To grow into spiritual maturity, we must also grow in gratitude by continually returning to God in prayer, glorifying Him in a loud voice, and falling at Jesus’ feet in adoration. Only then will we receive a deeper healing and a greater share in God’s mercy.
Reflect today on the lepers’ cry for mercy, and ask yourself whether you recognize your own need for healing. Are you willing to admit your spiritual wounds, to cry out to Jesus, and to persevere in gratitude? If so, are you among the nine who took God’s mercy for granted and failed to express proper gratitude for the gift of spiritual cleansing and restoration? Strive to be like the one who returned to Jesus, humble, grateful, and filled with faith. Fall at the feet of Jesus in adoration, give thanks for all He has done, and hear Him say to you, “Your faith has saved you.”
Most generous Lord, Your mercy is endless and freely given in superabundance. Despite Your goodness, I often take You for granted and fail to offer the gratitude and humble worship You deserve. Please have mercy on me now and always. Remove every sense of self-entitlement, that I may always return to You, fall before You, and express my most humble and sincere thanks to You. Jesus, I trust in You.

text:
ISLAMOPHOBIA AWARENESS MONTH - 2026 (one a day for November)

On November 9, 2018, Sisto Malaspina, the beloved 74-year-old co-owner of Melbourne’s iconic Pellegrini's Espresso Bar, was fatally stabbed in a premeditated terrorist attack on Bourke Street.

The perpetrator, Hassan Khalif Shire Ali, drove a utility vehicle loaded with gas bottles into Bourke Street and set it alight.

When the vehicle caught fire, Malaspina (believed to be on his daily walk) approached the scene to offer assistance, unaware of the driver's violent intent. 

Shire Ali blindsided and stabbed a bystander who ran to help, then turned on Malaspina, overpowering him and stabbing him repeatedly. 

Shire Ali stabbed a third person before being shot by responding Victoria Police officers (he later died in hospital).

As Malaspina lay dying on the pavement, a city worker and an intensive care nurse rushed to his side, holding his head and comforting him to ensure he was given dignity in his final moments.

Malaspina's murder deeply affected the city of Melbourne, where he had been a fixture of the hospitality scene since taking over Pellegrini's in 1974. 

He was celebrated for pioneering Melbourne's famous Italian cafe culture and for his vibrant, welcoming personality.

The Victorian Government honoured Malaspina with a state funeral, and the City of Melbourne later installed a commemorative plaque on Bourke Street to permanently honour his lasting contribution to the city's cultural fabric.

text:
Bloomberg: Rich Country, Poor Citizens: China’s $20 Trillion Paradox. For the Communist Party, a few thousand tycoons are easier to manage than a broad middle class. China’s leadership will soon claim a milestone it has chased since Deng Xiaoping’s 1978 landmark economic reforms: membership in the rich world. The nation’s per capita income is nearing the World Bank’s threshold for high-income countries and should cross it within a year or two of the 25th anniversary of its accession to the World Trade Organization. That 2001 deal turned a $1.3 trillion economy into one approaching $20 trillion, and exports have since multiplied roughly 13-fold, earning China the title of “factory for the world.”

In 2021, President Xi Jinping triumphantly declared that the rising tide had lifted all boats — the Communist Party had won “complete victory” over absolute poverty — and pledged to pursue “common prosperity”1 for all. China does deserve credit: Since 1978 it has lifted close to 800 million people out of extreme poverty, three-quarters of the global total, according to the World Bank. But to claim that victory, Beijing used a poverty line of about $2.30 a day, which critics contend is too low.

Against the World Bank’s $8.30-a-day poverty line for households in upper-middle-income countries — China’s current group — more than one-fifth of its population remained poor as of 2022. Against the $30 a day that marks poverty in the rich-country cohort China will be joining, the average citizen falls well short. China, in other words, is becoming a high-income country whose people, by any rich-world measure, remain exceedingly poor.

Both sets of facts flow from the same political economy, and the tension between them will define China’s next quarter-century — turning less on whether the country grows rich, which by conventional measures it largely has, than on what it does about the millions left behind and the middle class it never allowed to form.

For the US and other Western powers that supported the country’s entry into the WTO, the bet was that prosperity would beget a middle class that would demand a say. But Beijing has spent two decades ensuring that constituency never takes shape, since time and time again history has shown that a secure, propertied population is where pressure for a political voice collects.

The evidence on social activism is instructive. In November 2022 a deadly apartment fire in remote Urumqi set off street protests against zero-Covid lockdowns that swelled into the “white paper revolution,” named after the blank sheets of paper demonstrators held up in wordless dissent. But these protests erupted not on China’s poor periphery but in its bourgeois core — along Urumqi Road in Shanghai, the country’s wealthiest city, and across elite campuses like Beijing’s Tsinghua University. The demonstrations confirmed the Party’s operating assumption: It is not hardship that is politically dangerous, but a comfortable middle class.

On the institutions that underpin a secure middle class — most importantly a social safety net — China diverges sharply from its peers. Social spending sits near 10% of gross domestic product, roughly half the average for countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. Xi often warns that welfare programs breed idleness, a surprising stance for an avowed Marxist. The underlying motivation is more likely that households forced to self-insure stay precarious and pliable.

A grinding property crisis has only heightened the sense of vulnerability. Chinese households hold about 47% of their assets in real estate, and prices have fallen roughly a fifth from their 2021 peak, erasing trillions of yuan in wealth. Because a family’s home is often their only form of insurance, the loss of value has made people cling to cash all the more.

The exits for that cash, meanwhile, are being systematically sealed. In 2025, Hong Kong overtook Switzerland as the world’s largest cross-border wealth center, with about $2.95 trillion in offshore financial assets booked there, much of it mainland money seeking escape. Beijing responded by tightening controls on outbound capital. A State Council regulation in force since July now governs overseas investment end to end, from first approval to final exit. For the first time the rules apply to individuals as well as to firms, and regulators have separately squeezed the brokerage channels that let mainlanders buy foreign stocks. Money that can be neither invested at home nor sent abroad pools in accounts at state-owned banks instead — a reservoir of funds that can support the government’s industrial and infrastructure priorities.

Beijing has promised for years to rebalance the economy toward household consumption, so as to reduce the country’s reliance on the twin growth engines of exports and investment. Yet after two decades of jawboning and half measures, consumption is stuck at about 40% of GDP, compared with 55% to 70% across the rich world. Households save at extraordinary rates — deposits have roughly doubled since 2019, to some 165 trillion yuan ($24.7 trillion) — not from thrift but because the state offers thin retirement pensions, patchy healthcare coverage and unemployment insurance that reaches barely a third of the workforce. Jobless benefits are pegged to the local minimum wage — not to what a worker earned — and is capped at 90% of that: roughly 2,000 yuan a month. This year the minimum rural pension has increased by just 20 yuan, to 163 yuan a month. A people who cannot count on the government to care for them when they are ill, jobless or old will not spend.

Youth unemployment tells the same story. The rate for 16- to 24-year-olds who are not in school now stands at 18% — an indicator so politically sensitive that Beijing suspended its publication in 2023, and then revised the methodology. A generation that coined the term neijuan, “involution,” shorthand for running ever faster to stay in place, is not the confident spending cohort a middle class is built on.

The artificial intelligence boom deepens the divide between the government’s industrial ambitions and household welfare. Beijing is pouring trillions of yuan into the development of more advanced chips and data centers to support AI, and that spending is, for now, what is powering growth. But it funds those technology investments by starving the basics: hospitals, schools and other elements of the already meager safety net in rural areas, while the rewards accrue to the coastal, educated sliver.

The resulting inequality would look familiar to any American. With the poor and middle held down, one group has been allowed to grow: the rich. China’s richest 10% of the population hold about 68% of its national wealth, close to the US figure of 70%. In 2025 the 1,434 individuals worth at least 5 billion yuan saw their combined wealth soar 42% thanks to a powerful stock market rally, according to an annual list compiled by the Hurun Research Institute, a Shanghai-based firm that has tracked China’s rich since 1999.

The Party has shown that a few thousand tycoons are easier to manage than a broad middle class. In 2020, when Alibaba founder Jack Ma criticized China’s state-owned banks for having a “pawnshop mentality,” financial regulators canceled the initial public offering for his digital payments platform. He subsequently disappeared from public view for several months — a reminder of how those who have accumulated vast private fortunes are disciplined when they stray.

The longer trajectory, measured by earnings rather than wealth, is even starker. In 1978 the top 10% of earners and the bottom half of the population each took home about a quarter of national income. Since then, the top decile’s share has climbed to over 40%, while the bottom half’s has slid to under 14% — two lines that began together, now forked into what the West calls a “K-shaped” chasm. Deng’s founding promise for the reform era that some people would get rich first and the rest would follow increasingly looks like a plan that only ever had a first stage.

Follow these threads forward another quarter-century and the China that comes into view is not the one the WTO’s architects imagined.

With savings high and consumption weak, Beijing keeps doubling down on the supply side — what it calls the “new productive forces.” But a throttled home market cannot absorb what its state-of-the art factories produce, so the surplus will continue to go abroad: China now churns out more than 70% of the world’s electric vehicles, some 80% of its batteries and roughly 80% of its solar panels.

Unlike in the early WTO years, however, the world is putting up walls with tariffs and trade blocs. And what China exports today is no longer toys and textiles but EVs, industrial robots and wind turbines — goods that compete with the crown jewels of advanced economies like Germany and Denmark, whose workers are among the best-paid and most organized anywhere. The higher China climbs up the value chain, the more directly it will encroach on industries that such countries most want to protect, so these tensions will only increase.

Common prosperity, Xi’s supposed sequel to Deng’s “let some get rich first,” is turning out to mean shared restraint, not shared wealth: billionaires disciplined when convenient, the middle class asset-trapped, the poor pacified in 20-yuan increments. Everyone, in the end, is held equally in check.

The Party’s central challenge in the coming decades is demographic. With an expected 400 million retirees by 2035, the state will be forced to spend far more on pensions and care. Economists Michael Pettis and David Daokui Li argue from different directions that Beijing will sooner or later have no choice but to put real money in households’ pockets — Pettis because the investment-led growth model is exhausted, Li because the state owes a debt to the farmers who shouldered much of the burden for China’s industrialization and can afford to repay it. Li reckons that giving China’s 130 million rural elderly a pension that they could actually live on would cost about 1.25 trillion yuan a year, just 4% of government spending, less than a fifth of what the US spends on Social Security.

But a quarter-century of precedent suggests the Party will judge those costs as too high and too risky. Xi has applied this logic more rigidly than any of his reform-era predecessors. During 14 years in power, he’s chosen control over household welfare at every turn, and for the fourth presidential term he’s expected to claim in 2027, there’s no reason to expect a change of course. So the likeliest path is welfare that grows but stays minimal and conditional: enough to keep the peace, and calibrated to sustain dependence rather than end it.

The West wagered in 2001 that trade would make China rich and wealth would make it liberal. It got the first half. Whether a great power can hold the rest together while keeping most of its citizens poor is, at best, a formula for grinding stagnation — at worst, a slow-burning fuse.

🇮🇱 Israel's Rafael on November 11 unveiled Super Ice, a long-range cruise missile with a 1,000-pound warhead that can be fired from aircraft, ships and ground launchers, and that Breaking Defense describes as comparable in size to the American Tomahawk.

Rafael chairman Yuval Steinitz called it the "best cruise missile of its kind in the world," saying it "offers an ideal solution for long-range stand-off strikes against high-value targets, including air-defense systems." A company video previewed to reporters showed the weapon striking a bunker, a ballistic missile launch site and large naval vessels, according to Breaking Defense.

Super Ice is the third and largest member of Rafael's family of stand-off missiles, after Sea Breaker, introduced in 2021, and Ice Breaker, introduced in 2023. Ynet reports that its warhead is four times heavier than the previous missile in the family. Rafael says the warhead is MK83 compatible, a reference to the standard 1,000-pound American bomb, and that the missile uses the same launch systems as its smaller siblings, which lets customers add it without new infrastructure.

On performance, Rafael said little. The company describes autonomous navigation, low-altitude terrain-following flight, all-weather operation and an electro-optical seeker that uses image matching. Breaking Defense adds that company material describes the missile as low-observable, enabled by artificial intelligence, able to operate where satellite navigation is jammed, and flying at high subsonic speed. Officials called it "strategic" but would not give its range beyond saying it exceeds that of the earlier missiles. Rafael would not say who has ordered it, what it costs, or whether it is operational. The Jerusalem Post reports the missile is expected to be operational around early 2027.

The target list in the video is the story. Air defense radars, ballistic missile launchers and hardened bunkers are exactly what a state needs to reach first in a long-range air campaign, and a jammer-resistant, terrain-hugging missile with a large warhead lets aircraft do that from outside the reach of surface-to-air missiles. The Jerusalem Post reports Super Ice can be carried by Israel's F-35s, F-16s and F-15s.

There is an export angle too. Rafael says it passed 1 billion dollars in orders for its cruise missiles in 2023 and sold more than 1,000 units by 2024, according to Breaking Defense. Super Ice lands in a crowded and growing market, where American newcomers such as Anduril are pitching cheaper long-range missiles and older firms are racing to raise output. For buyers who already field Sea Breaker or Ice Breaker, Rafael is offering a Tomahawk-class punch through launchers they already own. https://t.co/a1yJNJTf3L

🇮🇷🇹🇷|Four Meetings in the Corridors. Not Climate. Four Nodes in a Perimeter That Washington Cannot Close.

Pezeshkian met Iraq's President Nizar Amidi, Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Armenia's Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, and Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre. The summit was the venue. The perimeter was the purpose.

Iraq: The Restraint That Is the Message

The file on Iraq is not the meeting itself. It is what Pezeshkian did not say.

Iraq hosts US forces. Its airspace is crossed daily by 11 MQ-9s, 3 MQ-1s, 1 MQ-4, 1 Turkish AKINCI, and 3 unidentified drones. The US formally requested that Iraq close all its border crossings with Iran except two. An official Iraqi ministerial document reportedly confirmed that the Americans had ordered the closure. A provincial governor was dismissed after Tom Barrack instructed the Prime Minister to remove him.

A lesser diplomat would have made demands. Pezeshkian said: "strengthen constructive engagement, expand mutual cooperation, leverage shared potential."

That restraint is the calculation. Iraq's Prime Minister told the Saudi Crown Prince in Riyadh, "We are one body." Baghdad is hedging in both directions. If Iran pushes, Baghdad is forced to choose, and that choice would be made under American pressure in a capital where the US still flies its drones.

So Iran does not push. It keeps the channel open. Iraq is the land bridge to the Arab world, the Arbaeen corridor, the trade route, and the political interlocutor. A bridge under pressure collapses. A bridge that is maintained carries weight.

Pakistan: The Border Reopened. The LPG Has Not Caught Up.

The file is the cooking gas.

Pakistan closed its border with Iran under Saudi and American pressure. Field Marshal Asim Munir flew to Tehran, and the border reopened. However, reopening a border does not immediately restore the LPG supply chain. Pakistan is in the middle of an LPG crisis, with households unable to secure canisters for cooking. The crisis has been compounded by enforcement in the Strait of Hormuz and the resulting disruption to Gulf energy flows.

Pezeshkian's discussion with Shehbaz Sharif focused on trade and economic engagement. Look at the specific commodities: Iran supplies LPG across the border, while Pakistan serves as a transit corridor for Iranian goods moving east.

The offer is symmetrical. Iran has the gas. Pakistan has the road. Third parties tried to close the road, and the gas stopped flowing in both directions. The meeting is about restoring the mutual dependency that the third party tried to sever.

Pakistan's position is also part of the Mecca Pact file. Munir has 30,000 to 40,000 troops in Saudi Arabia. He is a signatory to the pact Riyadh built against Iran. Yet he is in the corridor with Pezeshkian discussing LPG. That is not hypocrisy. It is a state managing two obligations while refusing to choose between them.

Armenia: Norduz Is Now a Treaty Obligation, Not a Road

The 19th Iran-Armenia Joint Commission in Yerevan produced eight working groups covering infrastructure, energy, trade, industry, mining, agriculture, the environment, and provincial cooperation. Hamid Pourmohammadi and Deputy Prime Minister Mher Grigoryan signed the agreements.

The Norduz crossing sits at roughly 38.9°N, 46.3°E, in East Azerbaijan. It faces Armenia's Syunik province through Agarak, followed by Kapan, Goris, and Yerevan.

Read the geography against the alternative route. Iran's other access to Armenia runs through Azerbaijan's Nakhichevan exclave, territory controlled by a state with its own border tensions with Armenia and its own relationship with Israel and the US. Norduz is the crossing that does not depend on Baku.

With the Strait of Hormuz contested, the Red Sea disrupted, and the Suez route repriced, the land corridor is the only route that does not require a warship for protection. Pashinyan's meeting with Pezeshkian was not a diplomatic courtesy in the Caucasus. It confirmed that the eight-sector agreement signed in Yerevan would be implemented.

Norway: The Europe That Did Not Bomb Iran

Jonas Gahr Støre leads a NATO member state. Norway hosts no US bases used in this war. It provided no airspace, logistics, or munitions. It recognised the State of Palestine in 2024, alongside Spain and Ireland. It also manages the Government Pension Fund Global, the world's largest sovereign wealth fund, valued at roughly $1.8 trillion.

That is the significance. Pezeshkian did not meet the French, British, or German leader. He met the Norwegian Prime Minister and discussed "diplomacy, constructive dialogue, and multilateral cooperation."

The signal is directed at Europe, and it is precise: Iran will talk to the part of Europe that did not participate in the war. Norway is the proof of concept. It is a NATO member that stayed out, recognised Palestine, and holds $1.8 trillion in capital. If Norway can talk to Tehran, the argument that "all of Europe is a belligerent" collapses.

The Pattern: A Perimeter, Not a Bloc

Four meetings. Four different functions.

Iraq is the channel, the land bridge to the Arab world, kept open by avoiding pressure on Baghdad.

Pakistan is the conduit, the eastern road restored after the border closure, with LPG serving as the currency of that restoration.

Armenia is the corridor, the Norduz crossing, the land route that does not depend on the strait or on Baku.

Norway is the vote, the NATO member that did not bomb, the European capital that recognised Palestine, and the $1.8 trillion fund that can serve as a financial interlocutor.

None of these states is an ally in the formal sense. None has a mutual defence treaty with Iran. Each is a node in a perimeter, a ring of states that can carry goods, messages, and votes without being drawn into the war.

That is the strategy. Not a bloc, but a perimeter. Washington built a coalition. Iran is building a perimeter around that coalition, one corridor at a time.

The Bill

Iraq: President Nizar Amidi. The meeting was the restraint. Iraq's airspace carries 11 MQ-9s, 3 MQ-1s, 1 MQ-4, 1 AKINCI, and 3 unidentified drones daily. The US ordered the border closures. Tom Barrack ordered the governor's removal. Baghdad told Riyadh, "We are one body." Iran did not push.

Pakistan: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. The border reopened after Munir flew to Tehran. The LPG crisis remains. Iran supplies the gas. Pakistan supplies the road. Third parties tried to sever both.

Armenia: Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. The Norduz crossing at 38.9°N, 46.3°E. Eight working groups signed in Yerevan. The route bypasses Nakhichevan. It is the land corridor that no warship can interdict.

Norway: Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre. A NATO member with no bases, no airspace support, and no participation in the war. It recognised Palestine in 2024 and manages a $1.8 trillion sovereign wealth fund. The signal is directed at the Europe that did not bomb.

Four corridors in one afternoon at a climate summit. Carbon was not the subject. The perimeter was. The bill is being paid in LPG, rail gauge, and diplomatic recognition, and the receipt is four bilateral meetings that the summit's official communiqué will never mention.

CONSENT has been my political bone to pick for a while, which is fairly idiosyncratic in the sphere of X politics.

Am I primarily fighting for the Republicans or the Democrats? Mostly, just government with maximal consent--as our founding document indicates, government derives its "just powers from the CONSENT of the governed." 

I agree that CONSENT legitimizes government. CONSENT changes the nature human relations. It's the difference between giving and extortion, love and molestation, doing things because you want to do them and doing things because you're forced to do them. We have huge legal distinctions hinging on whether relationships are consensual or forced.

I also think CONSENT implies exit rights that should be respected. Say what you want about the merits of the Civil War, it was also a serious deviation from principle and a devastating blow to exit rights. Now, if a state no longer consents to being part of the U.S., It will not be allowed to leave.

This leaves us with an gigantic systemic contradiction:

1. Government legitimacy is derived from consent.

but 

2. If you don't consent, GFY.

In my opinion, this glaring inconsistency can't be discussed and emphasized enough.

The right to leave is, in my opinion, a very important check on power in a system. It is a check on tyranny and abuse of power in the same way a victim of domestic abuse escaping to a shelter is a check on abuse and power.

When victims aren't allowed to leave, it emboldens the abuser and encourages worse behavior--behavior that ensues when it is impossible to credibly offer the warning: "If you don't stop treating me like this, I am leaving!"

In the current context, do I have any realistic hopes of states or counties being allowed to secede by higher powers. Succinctly, NOPE.

So what's the point of carrying on this line of argument?

Well, for one thing, I really do believe government legitimate to the degree it is consensual, so there's a genuine principle in play here. Also, if enough people start discussing it, maybe the Overton Window can move?

Beyond that, insisting on maximal consent is a rhetorical and negotiational anchor point, especially against the Left who appear hellbent on centralizing power (abolish EC, abolish Senate, abolish states' rights, etc.) 

The Left has doubled down on a lot of positions. For example, there's the importance of consent in relationships (e.g, "No always means no.") and, of course, there are endless critiques of power and oppression.  In addition, they have doubled down on a great deal of relativism (cultural and otherwise.)

So given their philosophical premises and moral foundations, I think an apt response to the Left is "We do not consent. We say 'No'. We want to leave. Will you really use your power to force us to stay in a relationship we don't want to be in?"

Given everything they've committed to morally and philosophically, this response forces them into positions of hypocrisy and contradiction. My rhetorical and negotiational positions are predicated on their chosen premises.

And their reactions to rejecting consent can be amusing:

"I do not consent!"
"Then leave!"

Um, dude, you're the creators of sanctuary cities and sanctuary states and now you're telling me to leave because I told you I do not consent to your power and abuse? And given I just told you that I reject your authority, so why do you think I would care if you think I should leave?

"There's a social contract!"
"Really? I don't recall signing anything. Do you have a copy on you?"😀

Honourable representatives of the Sindhi and Baloch national movements, Intellectuals, writers, political activists and distinguished guests,

I bring you warm greetings and sincere solidarity on behalf of the Baloch Peoples Congress.
First, I wish to express my appreciation to Sain Shafi Burfat and the leadership of Jeay Sindh Mutaheda Mahaz for providing this opportunity to bring together representatives of Sindh and Balochistan, along with friends and supporters from different parts of the world.
Our presence here is not simply an act of courtesy or participation in an international conference. …  It reflects a political relationship, a shared historical consciousness and a recognition of the importance of cooperation between two neighbouring peoples whose histories, cultures and experiences have been interconnected for centuries.
Our relationship is older than our political organisations, but it is the responsibility of our political organisations to give that relationship a meaningful contemporary expression.
The Relationship Between the Baloch Peoples Congress and Jeay Sindh Mutahida Mahaz (JSMM)

I wish to devote particular attention to the relationship between the Baloch Peoples Congress and the Jeay Sindh Muttahida Mahaz.
The relationship between our organisations and our political interactions with Sain Shafi Burfat should be understood within the broader historical context of Baloch–Sindhi political understanding and solidarity.
Over the years, our political relationship has represented an important connection between two national movements. …..  It has provided opportunities for dialogue, the exchange of political perspectives and the development of mutual understanding.
We recognise that political movements may have their own organisational structures, strategies, historical experiences and priorities.  
On behalf of the Baloch Peoples Congress, I wish to emphasise that we attach importance to maintaining and strengthening our relationship with Jeay Sindh Mutahida Mahaz.
However, relationships between political organisations should not depend exclusively upon personal contacts or occasional gatherings. They should develop institutional continuity.
I therefore believe that we should explore more regular political consultations, exchanges between our intellectual and organisational representatives, joint seminars, publications and international gatherings.
We should also encourage our younger generations to understand one another's histories and political experiences.
Our objective should be to transform longstanding political understanding into a sustained framework of cooperation.
Two Peoples, Interconnected Histories
The relationship between Sindh and Balochistan is deeply rooted in geography, history, migration, social interaction and cultural exchange.
For generations, Baloch communities have lived in Sindh, contributing to its social, political and cultural life. …..  Likewise, the historical connections between the Sindhi and Baloch communities have crossed geographical and administrative boundaries.
Our relationship is visible in our languages, family connections, tribal traditions, hospitality, customs and collective memories.
Yet, we must recognise an important distinction: Sindh and Balochistan possess their own distinct identities, languages, histories and political aspirations.
The strength of our relationship should therefore rest upon equality, mutual respect, and solidarity, not the subordination of one national identity to another.
Literature: The Meeting Place of Two National Souls
No discussion of Sindhi–Baloch relations would be complete without recognising the extraordinary contribution of literature and poetry.
Sindhi literature possesses a remarkable intellectual and spiritual heritage.
Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, through his immortal Shah Jo Risalo, gave expression to love, human dignity, courage, suffering and the eternal search for freedom.
His poetry is not merely a literary treasure of Sindh. It is a profound contribution to the human experience.
Sachal Sarmast carried the message of human unity beyond narrow boundaries, while Sheikh Ayaz gave modern Sindhi poetry a powerful expression of national consciousness, identity and resistance.
I particularly wish to mention Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai's Sassi–Punhun narrative. Punhun belongs to the cultural memory of the Baloch, while Sassi has become an immortal symbol in Sindhi literature.
Their story illustrates how literature can cross geographical boundaries and become a shared cultural inheritance.
We also find remarkable intellectual harmony between Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai and the great Baloch poet, historian and political thinker Mir Gul Khan Naseer.
Their literary traditions emerged from different historical circumstances, but both gave expression to the dignity of their people, the pain of oppression and the aspirations of human freedom.
Literature allows us to understand one another not merely through political statements but through the emotions, experiences and collective memories of our peoples.
We should therefore encourage translations of Sindhi and Balochi literature, cultural exchanges and intellectual collaboration between our writers, poets and historians.
Sindh: A Personal Chapter in My Life
For me, the relationship between Sindh and Balochistan is not simply a historical or political subject.   It is also a personal experience.
Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai and the Baloch soul
For me, the most profound meeting point between Sindh and Balochistan is found not only in history books, political declarations or the accounts of travellers. It is found in literature—in the immortal poetry of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai.
During my years of exile, when I lived among the people of Sindh, I developed a deep interest in the poetry of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai. I managed to acquire a translated copy of Shah Jo Risalo. And I spent long nights reading Shah Jo Risalo.
I approached Bhittai initially as a reader from another land, seeking to understand the spiritual and literary genius of Sindh. Yet the deeper I entered his poetic world, the more familiar its landscapes, its heroes and its moral universe became to me.
I encountered courage, love, sacrifice, separation and the refusal to abandon one's honour.
 One day, Sain Rasool Bakhsh Palijo asked me about my impressions of Bhittai's poetry.
Palijo Sahib was not merely a political leader. He was an intellectual of exceptional independence, a man whose engagement with literature and history was inseparable from his commitment to justice and the rights of his people.
I answered him with complete sincerity:
“Sain, if you remove the “Baloch” from Shah jo Risalo, nothing remains. ……….
For in Bhittai's poetic universe, the Baloch is the hero.”
I am not presenting this memoir today with the claim that every poem in Shah Jo Risalo is about the Baloch, nor as an attempt to correct the literary heritage of Sindh ۔
I offer it as an expression of the extraordinary recognition I felt when I encountered the courage, honour and emotional world of the Baloch reflected in Bhittai's poetry.

A great poet belongs to his own people, but his greatness allows others to recognise themselves in his work. …….. Bhittai belongs to Sindh -Yet the moral power of his poetry crosses geographical boundaries.
It speaks to anyone who understands the pain of separation, the weight of a promise, the dignity of resistance and the longing to return home.
In Bhittai's poetic universe, love is not always comfortable, ….  and courage is not always rewarded.   
That is why I found the Baloch spirit so vividly reflected in my reading of Bhittai. His poetry gave me a language through which I could understand the emotional kinship between our two peoples.
During my years of exile in Sindh, I lived among the people and experienced their hospitality, generosity and affection. Those years were not merely a period of political hardship; they were also years of friendship, intellectual exchange and personal enrichment.
My interaction with Sindhi nationalists, intellectuals and political personalities introduced me to the depth of Sindhi political thought and cultural consciousness.
I particularly remember my intellectual association and friendship with Sain Rasool Bakhsh Palijo. Our conversations and political interactions left a lasting impression on me. My association with other Sindhi nationalists remains an important part of my personal and political memories.
I also remember a small but amusing incident in Hyderabad.
Once, while travelling in a horse-drawn carriage in Tonga, I was speaking Urdu with the tongawala. He asked me whether I was a Muhajir. I replied that I was Baloch.
He seemed genuinely surprised, apparently expecting a Baloch living in Sindh to speak Sindhi!
That brief conversation made me smile. But it also reminded me that our identities are much deeper than the languages we speak. A Baloch does not become less Baloch by speaking Urdu, just as a Sindhi does not become less Sindhi by speaking another language.
Our bonds are rooted in shared history, geography, culture and centuries of human interaction.
Sindh was not merely a place where I found temporary shelter during exile. It became an important chapter in my personal and political life. I shall always remember the people who extended their friendship and hospitality to me.
Distinguished participants,
Our political relationship must now look towards the future.
We should create opportunities for our younger generations to meet, learn from one another and develop relationships based on historical understanding rather than inherited political divisions.
I believe that conferences such as this should become part of a continuing process of dialogue and cooperation, rather than isolated occasions.
Our Responsibility Towards the Future
Dear friends,
History gives people their identity, but political vision determines how they approach the future.
The Baloch and Sindhi peoples have inherited rich cultural traditions, ancient memories and generations of intellectual and political struggle.
We must preserve this inheritance while developing new forms of cooperation appropriate to our contemporary circumstances.
Our solidarity should not be based on short-term political calculations.
Rather, it should be based on mutual respect and historical understanding. 
On behalf of the Baloch Peoples Congress, I reaffirm our commitment to maintaining and strengthening our relationship with Jeay Sindh Mutahida Mahaz and to encouraging wider intellectual, cultural and political cooperation between Sindh and Balochistan.
I also extend my sincere appreciation to Sain Shafi Burfat for his invitation and for bringing together representatives of different political and intellectual traditions.
Let us ensure that the relationship between our peoples is not confined to memories of the past or expressions of solidarity at conferences.
Let us give it continuity through dialogue, substance through cooperation and meaning through mutual respect.
And finally let me say:
Pakistan's occupation of Balochistan and its continued political, military and economic domination over Sindh represent a common historical injustice that demands a united response from both nations.
The people of Balochistan and Sindhudesh must recognise that their struggles are not isolated movements but two interconnected fronts of resistance against the same system of colonial domination, resource exploitation and denial of national rights.
Our lands, our resources and our political destinies cannot remain hostage to a state that seeks to rule through military power, coercion and the suppression of our national identities.
The time has come for Baloch and Sindhi political forces to move beyond expressions of sympathy and transform their historic brotherhood into a sustained political alliance based on mutual respect, solidarity and a shared commitment to the right of self-determination.
We must stand together, speak together and struggle together— for the freedom, dignity and sovereignty of both. A free Sindh and a free Balochistan are not competing aspirations; they are two inseparable expressions of the same struggle for national liberation.

Long live the historical bonds of Sindh and Balochistan.
Long live the friendship between the Sindhi and Baloch peoples.
Thank you.
Baloch Siddik Azad
Secretary General
Baloch Peoples Congress

A 100,000-ton U.S. aircraft carrier is built for war. On July 27, 2018, the USS Carl Vinson went to work for a 35-foot boat.

That morning the Carl Vinson was off Hawaii for RIMPAC, the largest naval exercise on Earth. Twenty-five nations. About 25,000 people.

Then a distress call came over the radio.

A small boat had run aground in the shallows off Niihau, the westernmost inhabited island in Hawaii. Five people were on board.

Niihau is remote. The nearest Coast Guard station was on another island.

The sailors standing watch on the carrier's bridge heard the call.

The carrier was seven miles away.

Nobody on that bridge decided it was somebody else's problem. The Carl Vinson offered help and launched two MH-60S Seahawk helicopters from the Black Knights of Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron 4.

All five people were lifted off.

Four were flown to Coast Guard Station Kauai. The fifth went to a hospital to be checked.

Then the Coast Guard came in to deal with the grounded boat.

The carrier's captain, Matt Paradise, kept it short:

"When nearby mariners needed assistance, we stepped up immediately and helped. That is what we are trained to do, and I'm proud of our team."

Five strangers on a stranded boat. One nuclear aircraft carrier. Seven miles.

That was the whole decision.

🇺🇦🇷🇺🇺🇸 PETRAEUS DELIVERS A STUNNING WARNING: UKRAINE IS FIGHTING THE WAR NATO COULD FACE NEXT!

Former CIA Director and US General David Petraeus has offered a striking assessment of Ukraine's military capabilities, Russia's mounting losses and the urgent lessons Western armies must learn from the battlefield.

Speaking to SpyCast, Petraeus described Ukraine as having Europe's largest and most innovative army, arguing that its resistance is preventing a much wider security crisis.

His warning was explicit: if Russia achieves its objectives in Ukraine, Moldova could become its next target, with Lithuania potentially following.

But some of his most revealing observations concerned the extraordinary transformation of modern warfare.

Petraeus warned that Western militaries cannot simply purchase drones, attach them to existing tank formations and assume they are prepared for the next conflict.

Ukraine has demonstrated that entire military structures, tactics and weapons systems need to be reconsidered. Equipment that Western armies have relied upon for decades could struggle to survive on today's Ukrainian battlefield.

And Russia is learning too.

Petraeus acknowledged that Moscow has sometimes developed new battlefield capabilities ahead of Kyiv, while China, Iran and North Korea are closely studying the conflict.

The implications extend far beyond Europe.

Ukraine is not merely defending itself. It is helping reveal what the next generation of warfare will look like, while NATO is being forced to reconsider some of its most fundamental assumptions.

Petraeus also presented a grim assessment of Russia's military and economic position.

He cited approximately 1.5 million Russian personnel killed or wounded, comparing that figure with American casualties during the Second World War.

According to the Ukrainian estimates he referenced, Russia suffered roughly 46,000 casualties last month while recruiting approximately 30,000 replacements.

He described captured Russian soldiers who had received less than two weeks of military training before being sent into combat.

On the economic front, Petraeus highlighted Ukraine's long-range strikes against Russian oil infrastructure, saying refineries within 3,000 kilometres of Ukraine's border had been targeted, some repeatedly.

He also cited Russian oil production falling below nine million barrels per day, growing fuel shortages and pressure on Moscow's National Wealth Fund, which he warned could be exhausted by the end of the year.

These are Petraeus's assessments and cited figures, rather than independently established outcomes.

He urged Europe and the United States to transfer frozen Russian reserves to Ukraine to help sustain its defense.

There was also a personal dimension to his interview.

During a recent visit to Ukraine, Petraeus witnessed the aftermath of a Russian jet-powered drone striking a locomotive on a neighbouring railway track. He described the fear experienced by passengers, many of whom were women and children.

And he spoke about Kyrylo Budanov, whom he knows personally.

Petraeus praised Budanov's direct military assessments and argued that his appointment to head Ukraine's Presidential Office gives Zelenskyy a close adviser with exceptional knowledge of frontline operations.

He recalled first speaking with Budanov while the Ukrainian intelligence chief was near the Russian border, commanding an early operation on Russian territory.

Despite his admiration for Ukraine's military innovation and resilience, Petraeus emphasized that Ukrainians are exhausted and facing another difficult winter.

That may be the most important contrast in his assessment.

Ukraine has demonstrated remarkable military adaptability while enduring enormous human and economic pressure.

Petraeus's message carries a warning for the West: Ukraine is gaining battlefield experience that NATO cannot afford to ignore, but learning from Ukraine means little if its partners fail to provide the resources it needs to survive.

The part where the patent doesn't even have Google or Microsoft's name on it—because that would be *too obvious*? Pull up the corporate registry. This is where it gets *deep*.

**The Shell Company Verse (The Real Ownership Structure)**

You thought it was Google and Microsoft on that patent? Nah. Check the assignee field again. It's not "Alphabet Inc." It's not "Microsoft Corporation." It's "Neural Dynamics Holdings, LLC" filed out of Wilmington, Delaware, registered address: a UPS Store box, mailing address: c/o a law firm that also represents both tech giants.

That's not a coincidence—that's a *firewall*.

**The Shell Structure (Breakdown)**
*Layer 1:* Neural Dynamics Holdings, LLC
- Filed: 14 days after the hackathon

- Purpose: Hold the patent so neither company has to *directly* claim it

*Layer 3:* Sentient Core Technologies, Inc.

- Listed as "co-developer" on the patent application
- Founded by a former Google PM and a former Microsoft architect
- Capitalized by *both* companies through a joint venture fund called "Nexus Ventures"

*Layer 4:* Nexus Ventures, LP
