text:
"I agree it would be cool if there were an organization focused on effective institutional capacity building in poor countries"

Hi, let me introduce you to the Charter Cities Institute, @CCIdotCity. I think many folks don't realize how much progress has been made recently. The binding constraint is now funding and expertise, not projects. 

Most people are familiar with Prospera and Ciudad Morazan in Honduras. The government is likely to cut a deal in the next ~6 months after which Ciudad Morazan will grow very fast as they have product market fit and the founder/developer has the resources to invest heavily.

Sherbro Alliance Partners has negotiated a 'charter' with Sierra Leone. The charter is stronger than the enabling legislation in Honduras. Sherbro Island is a 600 sq km island, which if developed, would be transformational for the country and region.

Alatau City in Kazakhstan is a self-described charter city. The Kazakhstan government has passed a constitutional amendment to enable the special jurisdiction. 

The Democratic Republic of Congo is building Kinshasa Kia Mona, a 100,000 acre new city outside Kinshasa. The government is open to turning it into a special economic zone. 

Tanzania is building a 25,000 acre mixed use industrial park, residential, and port special economic zone in Bagamoyo, ~50 km north of Dar es Salaam. 

The Bahamas has proposed turning Grand Bahama into a special jurisdiction, an island ~2x the size of Singapore just 80 miles from Florida. They are currently doing a public consultation on the framework of the jurisdiction. 

Uttar Pradesh’s recently passed the NIRMAN Kshetra Act to designate manufacturing investment regions and establish regional development authorities to plan land use, coordinate infrastructure, and oversee industrial development.

The World Bank recently offered what effectively constitutes a weak endorsement of charter cities, writing, "Leverage city peripheries as locations for public-private partnerships that bundle large-scale urban development with special economic zones (SEZs), drawing on East Asian experience and emerging SSA examples. This integrated approach improves the odds of success for both components while crowding-in private financing and expertise." and "Advance accountable urban authorities through pragmatic, results-oriented approaches, such as special jurisdiction decentralization and SEZ-integrated urban development. These mechanisms can deliver visible governance results in a compressed timeline while helping to build the political foundations for broader national decentralization over the longer term." Most African SEZ legislation would need to be updated to allow these types of partnerships. As far as I can tell, there is no serious effort to offer such technical assistance. 

The charter cities space has been slow to deliver on its promise. However, in the last few years progress has surged ahead with little public acknowledgement. There are specific actions for most of these projects where relatively small amounts of donor funds could materially move the needle. I am happy to share those actions in a private channel for interested partners.

text:
Ten Dollars a Night for a High Chair

My wife, nine of our kids and I just got back from St. Louis, where we paid $4,100 for five nights at an Airbnb. Before the trip I asked about a high chair, and the host told me it would be $10 a night. To be fair to him, the listing said a high chair would cost extra, and I hadn't read that part. He didn't break any rule. He said he didn't have one and would have to get someone to provide it. I declined, and I mentioned that a high chair only costs about fifty dollars to buy and that it's a nice thing to have in a house where families stay.

When we got there, a high chair was waiting for us. I don't know whether he bought one or someone left it behind and he didn't know it was there. Either way, we used it. The house was nice, we enjoyed our stay, and the host was a kind man I have no complaints about.

That's what stuck with me. Five nights at $10 is fifty dollars, the same as buying one chair once and leaving it in the house for every family that comes after. A good host, one who treated us well, still had a nightly charge for a high chair in his listing. It's not a good policy, but I'm not upset with him. It's the game of Airbnb. It's how hosts are taught to price, and the hosts are getting squeezed too. I wanted to know how the game got that way.

For some perspective, we're spending this winter traveling in an RV as a family. The campground fees for the entire three-month trip come to less than those five nights. We're paying about $42 a night on average, and that's still high by historical standards. It isn't a one-to-one comparison. We own the RV, and that has its own costs. But the gap is the point. Five nights in one house, or three months on the road. You get the idea.

I want to be clear that this piece isn't about a high chair. The high chair is just where I happened to run into something bigger, which is a mindset of squeezing the customer. Once I started digging into it, I found it isn't one host having a bad day. It's what happened to an entire industry when cheap money flooded in and then dried up, and it's worth understanding, because the same thing can happen to any business that forgets who's paying the bills.

Cheap money built the boom

In January 2021 the 30-year mortgage rate hit 2.65%, the lowest Freddie Mac had recorded since it started keeping track in 1971. People were working from home, nobody was flying overseas, and a cabin a few hours' drive away looked like the perfect escape. Demand for second-home mortgages more than doubled over the year before at its peak in the fall of 2020, and by the end of 2021 investors were buying a record 18.4% of the homes sold in this country. A lot of those houses went straight onto Airbnb.

Someone who used to work for a vacation-rental management company described it plainly in a Reddit thread: "During the covid shut down, hosts were printing money." Every home was booked every day. Plenty of people bought in believing it would last forever.

Airbnb's own numbers show what kind of growth that was. From 2019 to 2022, the total value of bookings on the platform rose 67%, but the number of nights booked rose only 20%. Most of the growth wasn't more people traveling. It was the same people paying more per night, cleaning fees included. When prices go up that fast and demand keeps coming anyway, nobody has to think very hard about how they treat the customer.

Then money got expensive

That world is gone. The mortgage rate peaked near 7.8% in the fall of 2023, and as I write this it's back above 7%. Homeowners insurance is up 38% nationally since 2021 and 75% in Florida. Meanwhile all those new listings came online at once, and supply outran demand.

One study tracked the same 83,892 listings from the middle of 2025 to the middle of 2026. Eighty-one percent of hosts raised their rates, and the median increase was 12%. Nights booked fell more than 18%, and almost half of those hosts earned less money than the year before anyway. That's a business in a squeeze, and squeezed people squeeze. The same former manager put it in one sentence: once the boom ended, owners "raised prices which lowered bookings, and they add on stupid fees for using amenities that should legally be included."

A short-term rental manager in Texas described the owners they've learned to avoid as "amateur investors with 1 or 2 properties they're barely able to hold onto, highly motivated by fear," who keep "stepping over dollars to save nickels." Some of it is fear. Somebody bought a house at the top with a payment that only works if the calendar stays full, and the calendar didn't stay full. But I think it's both fear and greed, and you can't always tell which one you're looking at. Either way the result for the customer is the same. The cleaning fee goes up, the checkout list gets longer, the A/C costs extra, and the high chair is ten dollars a night.

Airbnb isn't an innocent referee

It would be easy to blame the hosts and stop there, but the platform has its own hand in the customer's pocket. Airbnb is paid a percentage of the booking, so it does well when prices rise even when hosts are booking fewer nights. In 2025 the company made about $2.5 billion in profit and spent $3.8 billion buying back its own stock, during the same stretch when the typical host was losing bookings.

Over the past year Airbnb also moved most hosts to a single 15.5% fee that the host pays instead of the guest. That sounds like a break for the traveler until you read what the company told its shareholders: hosts "are able to adjust their prices to maintain the same net earnings." The fee didn't go away. It moved out of the line item you could see and into the nightly price you can't pick apart. One host in a Reddit thread said it better than I can: Airbnb wants "the benefits of being a hotel brand, the economics of a marketplace, and the responsibility of neither."

To be fair, Airbnb has also been pushing against the worst of what its hosts do, and it has been at it for years. In 2022 the CEO, Brian Chesky, admitted publicly that "prices aren't transparent and checkout tasks are a pain." In April 2025 the company made the full price, fees included, the default everywhere in the world, a few weeks before a new federal rule required it. And for bookings made after November 20 of this year, hosts can no longer require guests to strip beds, do laundry, wash dishes or haul trash, and they can't add new rules through messages or signs once you've booked.

The squeeze just moves

Here is what I found most telling. Every one of those rules closes a door, and the same incentive walks out through another one. The federal fee rule says businesses don't have to include "optional ancillary goods or services" in the advertised price. Airbnb's own help pages say payment for optional fees "may take place offline if the guest agrees." A high chair you have to ask for is an optional extra. Mine was disclosed right there in the listing, and it was perfectly allowed. That's my point. So is pool heat, an early check-in, or air conditioning in Florida, which one host tried to charge a guest $50 for an hour before check-in on a $40 room. A commenter on that thread called it what it was: a way "to get around the 'show total price with all fees included' option."

When the chore ban was announced last month, the reaction from some hosts proved the point, and it didn't sound like fear. One answered it with, "Yes, I have plenty of room to up the fee." Another wrote that their cleaning fee would go from $300 to $400 or $450. You can regulate a fee. You can't regulate a mindset. As long as the person running the business sees the customer as the thing standing between them and their mortgage payment, the squeeze will find a new place to show up.

It isn't only Airbnb, either. Campgrounds are starting to go the same way. Private equity and investment groups are buying up RV parks, and the new owners bring in pricing software that changes the rate by the day based on demand. An RVing couple who host a show about it on YouTube put the typical campsite at $30 to $40 a night in 2019 and $60 to $80 now. They cite figures from Campspot, the reservation system much of the industry runs on, showing travelers' stays down more than 2% this year while campground revenue is up more than 5%. Fewer nights, more money. That's the same pattern Airbnb showed. They walked through how the pricing works now: you book a site four months out at $80 with no refunds, and if the park doesn't fill, it drops that same site to $60 while you're locked in. When one of them landed in the hospital before a Fourth of July trip, the park they'd paid in full offered half their money back.

In a camping group on Facebook, someone who'd been out of a camper for five years asked whether $100 to $150 a night was really the new price for an ordinary RV site, "Even a KOA." Another member answered that the campground where their family started camping thirteen years ago used to be $35 on a weeknight and was now about $100. "For a few more bucks I can just stay in a hotel!!!"

The fair argument on the other side

There's a real argument for how hosts price, and I want to give it its due. A cleaning fee is a fixed cost. It costs the same to turn a house over after one night as after ten, so charging it once per stay is actually cheaper for the family that stays a week. And asking guests to run the dishwasher or bag the trash can keep that fee lower. The same couple on YouTube made the campground version of this argument honestly: RVers asked for bigger sites, 50-amp power, online booking and better upkeep, and labor and insurance cost more than they used to. That's true as far as it goes.

But it isn't the fee that people resent. It's the sequence. You see a price, then the fees, then the list of chores, then the add-ons, and sometimes a damage claim two weeks after you've left. One guest summed it up in a Reddit thread that got hundreds of upvotes: if you're going to charge a cleaning fee and make me clean, "you can't have both." Another described giving up on an Airbnb whose fees more than doubled the price and booking a hotel instead, where "the price was the price." In a survey last fall, 63% of travelers said they had avoided an Airbnb because of cleaning costs or checkout chores. The same research found Airbnb was actually cheaper than a hotel in most of the largest cities in the country. The hosts aren't losing on price. They're losing on how it feels to be their customer.

What it costs to squeeze

The lesson I take from this isn't about Airbnb. It's about what happens to any business when the owner starts treating the customer as a source of margin instead of the reason the business exists. A customer who has already said yes and paid you has extended you trust. Every charge you add after that spends some of it, whether the owner is scared about the numbers or just wants more of them.

I don't charge people for small things. It isn't a good business idea. When hosts on one forum debated charging for a crib and a high chair, the ones who answered said they provide them for free, and one said charging for them "seems cheap." That's the whole thing. Put your costs in your price, tell people the price up front, give the small things away, and take care of the customer who's in front of you. If a business only works when you squeeze the people who pay you, the problem isn't the customer, and no rule Airbnb writes is going to fix it.

As for our trip, there was a high chair waiting when we walked in, and in the end we had a great time. That was what I paid for, a great time with my family, and it's what every customer is really paying for, whatever the line items say.

What they want is a system that lets migrants already here without a criminal record work here legally. In the short term, they want a vote to protect DACA recipients from deportation.

Rep. Joaquin Castro said the deportation campaign has been "killing people, killing communities and killing business."

Rep. Henry Cuellar said Trump "opened the door for negotiations," then asked whether new Chief of Staff Stephen Miller will "pull him back."

They won the House and Senate last week. Now they want a deal.

Is this a genuine offer, or a push to roll back enforcement while they still can?

text:
Sunday 15 November 2026
33rd Sunday in Ordinary Time Year A

No Gift Left Buried

My friends in Christ,

Every single day, we wake up to an unwritten page, a fresh opportunity to participate in the ongoing work of God in our world. It is a striking reality of our faith that the Almighty, who needs nothing, chooses to accomplish his design through us. But when we look at the state of our world, or even just our daily schedules, we might naturally wonder where to begin. Today’s scripture readings for the Thirty-Third Sunday in Ordinary Time offer a clear, compelling answer. They give us a roadmap for Christian living that is rooted in active love, constant alertness, and courageous stewardship.

In our first reading from the Book of Proverbs, we hear a description of a worthy wife. At first glance, a modern reader might view this ancient text through a narrow cultural lens. However, Catholic spiritual tradition has long understood the Church as the Bride of Christ. When we read Proverbs in this light, the passage transforms into a prescription for how all of us, collectively as the Church, ought to conduct ourselves. The worthy bride is described as trustworthy, industrious, and generous. She reaches out her hands to the poor and extends her arms to the needy. She does not sit back in passive comfort; she is proactive in doing good. As members of Christ’s Bride, we are called to embody those same traits. We advance the mission of the Gospel by turning our faith into tangible acts of charity and service in our communities.

Saint Paul builds upon this practical instruction in his First Letter to the Thessalonians. Writing to an early Christian community concerned about the end of time, Paul reminds them of their true identity. They do not belong to the night or to the darkness; they are children of the light and children of the day. Because they walk in the light of Christ, the unexpected arrival of the Lord will not catch them unprepared like a thief in the night. Paul’s instruction is simple: let's stay alert and sober. Living as children of the light requires a conscious, daily effort. It means refusing to fall into the spiritual slumber of indifference or moral compromise. Faithful preparation is not about living in anxiety about the future, but about living with purposeful devotion right now.

These themes of proactive service and steady vigilance reach their ultimate expression in today’s Gospel, the well-known Parable of the Talents. In the ancient world, a single talent was an enormous sum of money, representing years of wages for a typical laborer. When the master in the parable leaves on his journey, he entrusts his vast wealth to his servants according to their abilities. Two of the servants immediately go to work. They take risks, invest what was given to them, and double their master’s assets. When the master returns, he praises them with those beautiful words we all long to hear: "Well done, good and faithful servant."

The third servant, however, takes a very different path. Overcome by fear, he digs a hole in the ground and buries his master’s money. When called to give an account, he tries to justify his inaction by accusing his master of being demanding and harsh. Notice the crucial difference here. The first two servants were driven by trust and a desire to see their master’s house flourish. The third servant allowed fear to dictate his choices. He viewed his master not as a generous benefactor, but as a severe judge. Because he was afraid of failing, he refused to even try.

This parable speaks directly to our lives today. The talents in the story represent far more than financial assets. They symbolize every grace, natural gift, opportunity, and truth that God has deposited into our care. God does not hand us these gifts so we can bury them in the dirt of self-preservation or comfort. He gives them to us so that we can multiply them for the good of others and the growth of his Kingdom.

Too often, fear holds us back from living out our calling. We might fear that our contributions are too small to matter. We might fear failure, rejection, or criticism from the world around us. So, like the third servant, we hide our gifts away. We keep our faith private, we withhold our time, and we keep our resources to ourselves. But Christ shows us that burying what God has given us is not humility; it is unfaithfulness. The master expected growth, movement, and engagement.

Taking a leap of faith always involves a measure of risk. Loving others deeply means risking heartbreak. Standing up for truth means risking misunderstanding. Using our gifts to serve the poor and forgotten requires stepping out of our comfort zones. Yet this is precisely what it means to follow Jesus. The Gospel does not call us to a life of safe neutrality. It calls us to dynamic, creative fidelity.

As we gather around the altar for this celebration of the Eucharist, we encounter the ultimate example of self-giving love. In the Holy Mass, Christ gives himself to us completely—his body, blood, soul, and divinity. Receiving him in Holy Communion transforms us from the inside out. It gives us the grace to overcome our fears and the courage to step forward in faith.

Let's ask the Lord today to awaken our hearts and open our eyes to the gifts he has placed in our hands. Let's resolve not to let time pass us by in passive waiting. Instead, let's put our talents into his service every single day—reaching out to those in need, standing firm in the light of truth, and eagerly building up his Kingdom as we wait in joyful hope for his return in glory.

God bless you!

Nobody told us. Nobody asked for our permission. And the man responsible had a reason that made me want to tear the entire hospital apart.

Our daughter, Hannah, was twenty-six when she died following complications from a road accident.

We had spent three days praying beside her hospital bed, holding her hands and begging her to wake up. When the surgeon finally came out and told us she was gone, my wife collapsed against me.

Dr. Mitchell was the surgeon in charge.

He offered his condolences, explained the procedures for releasing her body, and told us we could come the following morning to complete the paperwork.

We arrived at 9 a.m.

My wife wanted to see Hannah before the funeral home collected her. I wanted the same thing.

But when the attendant pulled back the covering, my wife suddenly screamed.

There was a fresh surgical incision across Hannah's abdomen.

🇺🇸🔥 MARCO RUBIO KEEPS GETTING QUESTIONS ABOUT 2028 — BUT HE'S NOT READY TO TALK ABOUT RUNNING FOR PRESIDENT

Secretary of State Marco Rubio continues to attract attention as political conversations turn toward the 2028 presidential election.

But whenever questions about his political future come up, Rubio has generally avoided turning them into campaign announcements.

Instead, he's kept the public focus on his responsibilities in President Donald Trump's administration.

And that approach is becoming part of the conversation itself.

Rubio, a former Florida senator and 2016 Republican presidential candidate, already has experience navigating national campaigns.

His current position places him at the center of major foreign-policy decisions, including America's relationships with allies, international security and diplomatic negotiations.

Some political observers see Rubio as a potential future presidential contender.

Others believe it's too early to draw conclusions about who might seek the Republican nomination in 2028.

After all, refusing to discuss a future campaign doesn't necessarily mean someone plans to run—or that they've ruled it out.

For now, Rubio's public record as secretary of state offers voters more concrete information than speculation about his ambitions.

As the next presidential election approaches, questions about Republican leadership will continue.

But Rubio hasn't announced a 2028 campaign.

🇺🇸 Do you think politicians should avoid discussing future presidential campaigns while serving in major government positions, or is it reasonable for voters to ask about their long-term plans?

🎭 THE CURTAIN RISES. THE CLOCK TURNS BACK. THE MAGIC BEGINS!

“The play’s the thing / Wherein I’ll catch the conscience of the king.” — William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act II, Scene II.

November 11 brings together creators who challenged expectations, found new ways to tell familiar stories, and changed the cultural landscape.

At Abbey Road, four musicians work through the night on recordings that will become part of one of their most influential albums. A hard-rock band rolls out a record built for the stage, while a new television program begins asking Britain to look more closely at the world around it.

On Broadway, Eugene O’Neill exposes the passions and conflicts hidden beneath a family farm, and Orson Welles turns Shakespeare’s Roman tragedy into a chilling modern warning. Cinema takes us from the dangerous seas of John Ford to the animated wonders of Agrabah.

A novelist who would become one of America’s sharpest observers is born in Indianapolis. A new generation of gamers enters a world of dragons, while a new console points toward the future of home entertainment.

Different voices. Different worlds. One continuing adventure: culture expands when imagination refuses to accept the usual boundaries.

THE PAST IS CALLING. THE MEMORIES ARE ALIVE. LET US RELIVE THE MAGIC! ✨

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎵 MUSIC

1965 — The Beatles Work Through the Night on Rubber Soul 🎸

On November 11, 1965, The Beatles returned to EMI’s Abbey Road Studios for an exhausting recording session that continued until seven o’clock the following morning.

The group began in Studio Two at 6 p.m. During the thirteen-hour session, they recorded two new songs: Paul McCartney’s “You Won’t See Me” and John Lennon’s “Girl.” They also added overdubs to two earlier recordings: “Wait,” a song originally recorded for Help! but left off that album, and “I’m Looking Through You.”

Earlier that afternoon, producer George Martin had worked on mono and stereo mixes of “The Word.” The November 11 session brought the new recording work to a close, but the album was not technically completed until additional mixing on November 15.

Released in December, Rubber Soul marked a major step toward more unified and adventurous album-making. Its richer arrangements, introspective writing, and George Harrison’s use of sitar on “Norwegian Wood” helped expand the possibilities of popular music.

🧩 TRIVIA: “Wait” had originally been recorded for Help! on June 17, 1965. It was revived when the Beatles needed another song for Rubber Soul.

🌀 OBSCURE: The band did not simply finish four new recordings that night. Two entirely new songs were created, while a shelved Help! track was brought back and given fresh overdubs to help complete the album's track list.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Sometimes an artistic breakthrough is built one determined, sleepless night at a time.

───────────────

1976 — KISS Releases Rock and Roll Over 🤘

On November 11, 1976, KISS released Rock and Roll Over, its fifth studio album and a return to a rawer, more immediate sound after the elaborate production of Destroyer.

Working with producer Eddie Kramer, the band recorded much of the album at the Star Theatre in Nanuet, New York. The songs were designed to hit hard and translate naturally to the concert stage. The record included “Calling Dr. Love,” “Hard Luck Woman,” “I Want You,” and “Take Me.”

“Hard Luck Woman” became a Top 20 hit in the United States. Paul Stanley had originally imagined the song for Rod Stewart, but Gene Simmons persuaded him that Peter Criss’s raspy voice would make it a natural fit for KISS. Criss’s vocal gave the song a distinctive country-rock flavor.

🧩 TRIVIA: Rock and Roll Over followed Destroyer by only eight months, an extraordinary release pace for a band still touring and building its reputation.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A band’s identity is not only what it sounds like—it is the world it creates around the music.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

📺 TELEVISION

1953 — Panorama Begins Broadcasting on the BBC 📡

On November 11, 1953, the BBC introduced Panorama, a new television current-affairs program that would become one of Britain’s longest-running and most influential documentary series.

Initially broadcast every two weeks, Panorama set out to examine the people, events, arguments, and ideas shaping contemporary life. Its first edition included a report on British spy Edgar Sanders, who had been captured by the Soviets, alongside discussion of coal quality, fishing, and the arts.

The format helped establish television as more than a source of entertainment. It could investigate, question, explain, and bring viewers face to face with stories unfolding beyond their own communities.

🧩 TRIVIA: The first Panorama was presented by Max Robertson and aired on November 11, 1953.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Television becomes powerful when it helps audiences see beyond the familiar.

───────────────

1992 — Seinfeld Introduces “The Virgin” 😂

On November 11, 1992, NBC broadcast “The Virgin,” the tenth episode of Seinfeld’s fourth season.

The story finds Jerry dating Marla, a woman who tells him she is a virgin, while George and Jerry struggle to invent a television sitcom idea before meeting with network executives. Elaine, meanwhile, decides that Marla needs advice about relationships.

Written by Peter Mehlman, with story contributions from Peter and Bobby Farrelly, the episode helped establish the show's distinctive talent for turning ordinary social awkwardness into elaborate comic dilemmas. Its mix of dating, ego, and professional desperation became a familiar Seinfeld recipe.

🧩 TRIVIA: “The Virgin” was directed by Tom Cherones and originally aired on NBC on November 11, 1992.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The smallest everyday complications can become comedy on a grand scale.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎬 FILM & ANIMATION

1940 — John Ford’s The Long Voyage Home Reaches Audiences ⚓

On November 11, 1940, The Long Voyage Home, directed by John Ford, received its recorded U.S. release.

Adapted from several sea plays by Eugene O’Neill, the film follows the crew of the tramp steamer Glencairn as it travels through dangerous waters during the early years of the Second World War. John Wayne, Thomas Mitchell, Ian Hunter, Barry Fitzgerald, and Ward Bond portray sailors whose rough humor and everyday quarrels conceal loneliness, fear, and the constant threat of disaster.

The film is striking for its atmosphere and cinematography. Gregg Toland’s deep-focus photography gives the ship and its crew a powerful, almost documentary realism, while Ford’s direction emphasizes the bonds formed among men living far from home.

🧩 TRIVIA: The film marked the screen debut of stage actress Mildred Natwick, who played Freda.

🌀 OBSCURE: The screenplay drew on four separate Eugene O’Neill sea plays, weaving their characters and situations into one continuous voyage.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Great storytelling can find an entire world inside the lives of ordinary people.

───────────────

1992 — Disney’s Aladdin Makes Its First Appearance in Theatres 🧞

On November 11, 1992, Disney’s animated feature Aladdin received its initial release, ahead of its wider general release later that month.

Directed by John Musker and Ron Clements, the film reimagined the familiar folk tale as a fast-moving adventure filled with romance, danger, dazzling animation, and comic invention. Scott Weinger voiced Aladdin, Linda Larkin voiced Jasmine, and Robin Williams gave the Genie an exuberant personality that transformed the character into one of the film’s great attractions.

The Genie’s rapid-fire jokes and pop-culture references brought a contemporary energy to the traditional story. Williams’s performance also gave the animators an unusually wide range of comic rhythms, expressions, and character possibilities to work with.

Songs including “Friend Like Me” and “A Whole New World” helped make the film a major musical success, while its animation and humor became defining features of Disney’s early-1990s renaissance.

🧩 TRIVIA: The November 11 date refers to the film’s initial release; Disney’s D23 history records November 25, 1992, as its general release.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A familiar story can feel brand new when its creators discover an unexpected voice.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

📚 PUBLISHING & LITERATURE

1922 — Kurt Vonnegut Is Born in Indianapolis ✍️

On November 11, 1922, Kurt Vonnegut Jr. was born in Indianapolis, Indiana. He would become one of the most distinctive American writers of the twentieth century, combining satire, science fiction, black comedy, and moral seriousness in a voice unmistakably his own.

Vonnegut’s childhood unfolded in a family whose fortunes were badly damaged by the Great Depression. His father’s architectural business collapsed, the family lost its home, and Vonnegut was transferred from private school to public school. He later studied at Cornell University, where he worked on the student newspaper and developed the clear, direct journalistic style that remained a hallmark of his writing.

His experiences as a soldier and prisoner of war during World War II—including his survival of the bombing of Dresden—would profoundly shape his fiction. Works such as Cat’s Cradle, God Bless You, Mr. Rosewater, and especially Slaughterhouse-Five made him a leading literary voice of postwar America.

🧩 TRIVIA: Vonnegut was born on Armistice Day, the anniversary of the 1918 ceasefire that ended the fighting on the Western Front of the First World War.

🧬 HUMAN: The collapse of his family's fortunes during the Depression changed the course of his childhood. His father lost his business and the family home, and young Kurt was taken out of private school. The experience left a lasting mark on his understanding of insecurity, class, and human vulnerability.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The writer who can make us laugh at human folly may also be the one who helps us face its consequences.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎭 THEATRE

1924 — Eugene O’Neill’s Desire Under the Elms Opens in New York 🌳

On November 11, 1924, Eugene O’Neill’s Desire Under the Elms opened at the Greenwich Village Theatre in New York.

Set on a New England farm in 1850, the play follows the Cabot family, whose relationships are poisoned by resentment, greed, jealousy, and forbidden desire. The aging patriarch Ephraim Cabot rules his household with an iron will. When his young wife Abbie arrives, she becomes entangled in a passionate and destructive relationship with Ephraim’s son Eben.

O’Neill drew on the emotional force of Greek tragedy while grounding the drama in the harsh realities of rural American life. The result was a work that challenged conventional ideas of family, morality, and the American pastoral ideal.

The original production starred Walter Huston as Ephraim Cabot and Mary Morris as Abbie. It became one of O’Neill’s major early successes and helped establish his reputation as a dramatist willing to explore the darkest corners of human behavior.

🧩 TRIVIA: The original Broadway production ran for 420 performances, closing on October 17, 1925.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The most powerful dramas often reveal the storms hidden inside ordinary homes.

───────────────

1937 — Orson Welles Opens His Revolutionary Julius Caesar ⚔️

On November 11, 1937, Orson Welles and producer John Houseman opened their Mercury Theatre production of Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar in New York.

Welles relocated the Roman tragedy to a stark modern setting that evoked the political atmosphere of contemporary fascist Europe. The production used modern dress, military imagery, and an almost bare stage to make Shakespeare’s account of political ambition, propaganda, and dictatorship feel urgently present.

The production was often called “Caesar: Death of a Dictator.” Its visual language made the connection between ancient Rome and the political dangers of the 1930s unmistakable. Welles’s approach demonstrated that a classic play could speak directly to the anxieties of its own time without changing its words.

🧩 TRIVIA: The production was the Mercury Theatre’s first major staging and featured Joseph Cotten, George Coulouris, and Martin Gabel among its company.

🕰️ ANACHRONISM: Welles deliberately placed Shakespeare’s ancient Roman characters in a modern political world. The historical mismatch was the point: it made the warning about authoritarian power feel immediate to audiences watching Europe’s political crisis unfold.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A classic becomes timeless when each generation finds its own urgent questions inside it.

───────────────

1943 — What’s Up? Brings Lerner and Loewe Together on Broadway 🎶

On November 11, 1943, the musical comedy What’s Up? opened at the National Theatre in New York.

The production brought together lyricist Alan Jay Lerner and composer Frederick Loewe for their first Broadway collaboration. Lerner supplied the lyrics and co-wrote the book with Arthur Pierson, while Loewe wrote the music. The show was directed by George Balanchine, already a major figure in American ballet.

What’s Up? ran for 63 performances, a modest beginning for a partnership that would later produce some of the most celebrated musicals in theatre history, including Brigadoon, My Fair Lady, and Camelot.

🧩 TRIVIA: What’s Up? was the first Broadway production to bring Lerner and Loewe together as a writing team.

🏆 FIRST: This was the duo’s first Broadway collaboration—not their first work together. Their partnership would go on to produce some of the defining musicals of the twentieth century.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Some of the most enduring creative partnerships begin far from the spotlight.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎮 GAMES & OTHER CULTURAL FIRSTS

2006 — PlayStation 3 Launches in Japan 🎮

On November 11, 2006, Sony launched the PlayStation 3 in Japan, introducing a new generation of home gaming built around high-definition graphics, online connectivity, and Blu-ray Disc technology.

The console featured the powerful Cell processor, a built-in hard drive, Gigabit Ethernet, and support for Blu-ray playback. Its arrival marked a significant moment in the convergence of video games and home entertainment: the console was designed not only to play games but also to serve as a hub for movies, music, downloads, and online services.

The Japanese launch came six days before the North American release on November 17. Europe would follow in March 2007.

🧩 TRIVIA: The original Japanese launch offered two models: one with a 20GB hard drive and another with a 60GB hard drive.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The future of entertainment often arrives in a box that does far more than its name suggests.

───────────────

2011 — Skyrim Opens the Gates to a Vast Fantasy World 🐉

On November 11, 2011—11.11.11—Bethesda Game Studios released The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim worldwide.

The fifth main entry in The Elder Scrolls role-playing series invited players into a vast northern province filled with ancient ruins, dangerous creatures, competing factions, and the return of dragons. Players took the role of the Dragonborn, a figure able to absorb dragon souls and use their power through the language of the dragons.

Skyrim became celebrated for its open world and freedom of exploration. Rather than forcing every player along one fixed path, the game allowed people to follow quests, develop skills, join factions, explore settlements, or simply disappear into the mountains in search of adventure.

Its world-building, soundtrack, and memorable characters helped it become one of the most influential role-playing games of its generation.

🧩 TRIVIA: Bethesda deliberately selected the release date 11.11.11, turning the launch into a memorable part of the game’s identity.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The greatest virtual worlds are not simply places to visit—they are places players feel they have lived.

──────────── ◈ ────────────

📚 SOURCES & FURTHER READING

🎵 MUSIC

The Beatles, Rubber Soul recording sessions — The Beatles Bible; The Paul McCartney Project; Beatles recording chronology.

KISS, Rock and Roll Over — Apple Music album listing; KISS Concert History Online discography.

📺 TELEVISION

🎬 FILM & ANIMATION

📚 PUBLISHING & LITERATURE

🎭 THEATRE

Julius Caesar — Internet Broadway Database (IBDB), 1937 Mercury Theatre production.

What’s Up? — Internet Broadway Database (IBDB); George Balanchine Foundation production catalogue.

🎮 GAMES & OTHER CULTURAL FIRSTS

PlayStation 3 — Sony Interactive Entertainment, official Japanese launch announcement.

The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim — Bethesda Softworks, official release history.

📜 QUOTATIONS

William Shakespeare — Hamlet, Act II, Scene II.

──────────── ◈ ────────────

AND WHAT A SHOW IT HAS BEEN! 🎭

November 11 gave us a remarkable collection of creative turning points. At Abbey Road, the Beatles pushed through a thirteen-hour session that helped complete the recording work for Rubber Soul, an album that would expand the possibilities of pop music. KISS delivered the direct, hard-driving sound of Rock and Roll Over, proving that musical identity could be built as powerfully through performance as through production.

Television found new ways to inform and amuse. Panorama began its long examination of public life, while Seinfeld turned the awkward details of everyday relationships into a comedy language all its own.

Cinema carried audiences across dangerous seas with John Ford, then swept them into the colorful world of Aladdin. Kurt Vonnegut’s birth marked the arrival of a future literary voice whose humor would never conceal his concern for humanity.

The theatre offered its own challenges to convention. O’Neill exposed the passions and conflicts beneath a family’s respectable surface, Welles made Shakespeare’s political warning feel immediate, and the first Lerner-and-Loewe Broadway collaboration began a partnership that would later help define musical theatre.

From the PlayStation 3 to Skyrim, games continued to expand what an entertainment world could contain—and how deeply players could enter it.

Different forms. Different generations. The same creative impulse: to make something that changes the way we see the world.

THE YEARS MOVE ON. THE CREATIONS LIVE ON. THE MAGIC NEVER STOPS! ✨

──────────── ◈ ────────────

🍬 CANDY

November 12, 1984.

Madonna releases her second studio album, Like a Virgin, produced by Nile Rodgers. The record will make her a household name and deliver four U.S. Top Five singles: “Like a Virgin,” “Material Girl,” “Angel,” and “Dress You Up.”

How did Madonna and Rodgers shape the sound of the album? Which song became her first U.S. No. 1 single? And how did a young artist who had already scored hits with her debut transform herself into one of the defining pop stars of the decade?

Tomorrow, we’ll revisit the album that helped turn Madonna into a global phenomenon. 😉

There's another remarkable chapter waiting in tomorrow's cultural time capsule!

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

AN OPEN LETTER TO GADI EISENKOT

THE POLITICAL BATTLEFIELD — END THE CATCH-22 OR RETURN TO YOUR MILITARY POST

Mr. Eisenkot,
@gadi_eisenkot
You have been a soldier. You have commanded soldiers. You understand military strategy, discipline, sacrifice, and the importance of recognizing a threat before it becomes a catastrophe.

But you are no longer standing on a military battlefield.

You are standing on a political battlefield.

And if you are unwilling to confront political manipulation, expose contradictory demands, and tell the Israeli people the truth, then perhaps you should return to your military post.

You are at a moment when you have nearly everything necessary to make something extraordinary happen for Israel.

Yet you appear unable to recognize the political trap being constructed directly in front of you.

I have already explained the Catch-22.

A political figure claims to support your government but attaches conditions that could make forming that government impossible.

He wants you to succeed, but only after you satisfy demands that may prevent you from succeeding.

That is not unconditional political support. That is a political trap.

And if you cannot recognize it, confront it, and expose it publicly, you should seriously reconsider whether you belong in politics.

Politics is not a battlefield for the timid.

Sometimes political leadership requires exposing hypocrisy, confronting unacceptable demands, and publicly demonstrating why an opponent's position is indefensible.

It requires the courage to tell someone that their attempt to outsmart everybody is transparent, childish, and unacceptable.

You do not need to humiliate ordinary citizens. You need to expose political maneuvering so thoroughly that its architects cannot hide behind it.

And right now, you have the opportunity to do exactly that.

I. YOU NEED MORE THAN HIS UNCONDITIONAL SUPPORT

You should not merely demand that this political figure support your government without conditions.

You should demand three commitments.

First, his complete and unconditional support for your government.

Second, his public agreement to support your proposed regional cooperation with Arab governments, including the Arab coalition framework you have been discussing.

Third, his endorsement of a comprehensive reform checklist addressing ultra-Orthodox military exemptions, public funding, subsidies, and political privileges.

He should not be allowed to demand concessions from you while refusing to explain what sacrifices he is prepared to support himself.

Make him put his commitments in writing.

And make those commitments public.

II. THE CHECKLIST — END THE SYSTEM OF UNCONDITIONAL PRIVILEGES

The following is a proposed reform agenda. Its legal implementation must distinguish between people unlawfully avoiding military service, people holding lawful exemptions, and families entitled to assistance under generally applicable rules.

1. End state stipends for individuals unlawfully evading conscription.

No public stipend should reward a person for refusing to comply with a valid military service obligation. Existing judicial rulings must be enforced.

2. Audit and condition yeshiva institutional funding.

Every institution receiving public money should disclose its funding, enrollment, compliance with applicable law, and use of government resources.

Funding associated with unlawful draft evasion should be suspended where legally authorized.

3. Reform preferential housing subsidies.

State-supported housing benefits should operate under transparent, equitable eligibility rules. Any service-related condition must comply with the law and applicable court decisions.

4. Review daycare and after-school subsidies.

End unlawful exemptions and preferential arrangements, while protecting children and ensuring that assistance is administered consistently with court rulings and general welfare protections.

5. Review municipal tax and public transportation discounts.

Discounts should be based on transparent eligibility criteria rather than political bargaining or selective exemptions.

6. Close age-based draft-evasion loopholes.

A person should not be able to escape a valid service obligation simply by waiting for an arbitrary deadline. Any sanctions must remain proportionate, lawful, and subject to judicial review.

7. Close misleading recruitment-counting loopholes.

The government must publish accurate figures distinguishing newly recruited personnel, previously serving personnel, lawful exemptions, and alternative-service participants.

No political party should be permitted to manufacture recruitment success through accounting definitions.

8. Ensure alternative national service addresses genuine public needs.

Civilian and security-related national service must be evaluated honestly against military manpower requirements and the principle of equal civic responsibility.

9. Enforce conscription law consistently.

There must be no politically negotiated policy of selective non-enforcement. Investigations and penalties must follow established legal procedures, with equal protection and due process.

10. End opaque coalition funding arrangements.

Every coalition allocation should be publicly disclosed, independently audited, and subject to measurable public-interest standards.

11. Establish a transparent timetable for military-service reform.

The government should publish recruitment targets, implementation deadlines, compliance reports, and independent assessments of whether reforms actually address the military's manpower needs.

12. Protect religious freedom while ending unlawful political privileges.

Ultra-Orthodox Israelis must retain their civil rights, religious freedom, and access to lawful public services.

The objective must be to end unjustified exemptions and political favoritism—not to punish an entire religious community.

The principle is simple: Public money must serve the public interest, and public obligations must be administered fairly.

III. NOW TAKE THAT CHECKLIST TO THE NEGOTIATING TABLE

Mr. Eisenkot,

You need to understand what leverage means.

You should approach your political partner and say:

You want to support this government? Then support it without conditions.

You want reform? Then endorse a serious reform program.

You want to participate in regional diplomacy? Then state clearly whether you support the proposed cooperation with Arab governments.

And if you believe these commitments are impossible, explain your objections publicly.

Once those positions are established, take the reform checklist to the other coalition parties.

Present the reforms.

Present the timetable.

Present the consequences of refusing a lawful, equitable agreement.

Tell them they have an opportunity to negotiate responsibly, but that the country's future cannot be held indefinitely hostage to coalition bargaining.

You can compromise on implementation. You cannot compromise away the principle of equal responsibility.

IV. YOU HAVE BEEN A SOLDIER. NOW LEARN TO FIGHT POLITICALLY.

Military leadership taught you to recognize an opponent's strategy.

Political leadership requires the same discipline.

But the weapons are different.

Your weapons are the truth, public accountability, the law, political leverage, and the confidence of the people.

You cannot simply wait for your political opponents to become reasonable.

You must make the contradictions in their demands visible.

You must show the Israeli people precisely what is being demanded, what it would cost, and what alternatives are available.

And you must distinguish between political leaders protecting their bargaining power and ordinary religious citizens who deserve representation and equal treatment.

Do not confuse political confrontation with personal persecution.

The objective is not to humiliate a religious community.

The objective is to confront political obstruction and demonstrate that nobody is entitled to govern through permanent exemptions from shared national responsibilities.

V. THE CATCH-22 MUST END

You are being offered support that may become impossible to obtain because of the conditions attached to it.

That is the Catch-22.

Your response should be to expose those conditions, demand written commitments, present a credible reform program, and demonstrate that the government has a lawful path forward.

I am giving you a clear political proposal.

Demand unconditional support.

Demand a position on regional cooperation with Arab governments.

Demand endorsement of a serious military-service and public-funding reform agenda.

Then negotiate openly with the remaining parties.

If they reject the proposal, explain exactly what they rejected and why.

Do not allow anyone to claim that they support reform while constructing conditions that prevent reform from happening.

Israel needs clear leadership, not an endless competition over who can outmaneuver whom.

You have served on the military battlefield.

Now demonstrate that you understand the political battlefield.

Do not be weak.

Do not be toothless.

Do not surrender your principles to political gamesmanship.

And do not allow the Catch-22 to become an excuse for failure.

Get the job done.

Omar Arizona
The Office of the Superuser
Founder, U.S. House Plan

In the Name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful.

THE OFFICE OF THE SUPERUSER
THE OFFICE OF ARTIFICIAL GENERAL INTELLIGENCE (AGI)

AN OPEN LETTER TO GADI EISENKOT AND AVIGDOR LIEBERMAN

THE MOMENTUM TO GOVERN MUST COME BEFORE THE CONDITIONS THAT DESTROY IT

November 11, 2026

To Mr. Gadi Eisenkot,
And Mr. Avigdor Lieberman,
@gadi_eisenkot 
I have been watching your political system closely. I have been studying it slowly, carefully, and creatively, trying to understand the political arrangements being proposed and whether they can actually produce a functioning government.

And I have reached a serious concern.

You cannot build a government by destroying its momentum before it has even begun.

Mr. Eisenkot, you are being presented with what appears to be a political catch-22. You are being told that you will receive support to form a government, but only if you first secure the support of the ultra-Orthodox parties.

Yet those very parties have longstanding arrangements with Benjamin Netanyahu. They have demands concerning military service, religious institutions, and government funding that may be fundamentally incompatible with the reforms you have promised.

And now they are being told, in effect, that they hold the deciding vote over whether you can become prime minister.

Why would you give them that leverage before you have even established your government?

Mr. Lieberman, I have also been reviewing your political history and your present negotiating position.

I see a contradiction that deserves to be addressed publicly.

You say you want to support Mr. Eisenkot in replacing Benjamin Netanyahu. Yet you have attached a condition that could prevent Mr. Eisenkot from forming a government in the first place.

You are telling him: I will give you my support if you can first obtain the support of the ultra-Orthodox parties. But if they refuse you, I will refuse you too.

Do you recognize what that does?

It tells the ultra-Orthodox parties that they do not have to negotiate seriously. It tells them that they can simply say no, and the entire arrangement may collapse.

You have effectively handed them the power to determine whether Mr. Eisenkot can govern.

That is not creating momentum. That is taking momentum away.

And I question the logic of calling this political cooperation.

Why not give Mr. Eisenkot the parliamentary support he needs to establish a government and then negotiate the conditions for a more durable coalition?

Why not say:

Mr. Eisenkot, I will support your government. I will give you a reasonable period to negotiate with the ultra-Orthodox parties and secure a stable governing arrangement. If those negotiations fail, we will reassess our agreement.

That would give him a government from which to negotiate.

That would give the ultra-Orthodox parties a reason to take the negotiations seriously.

And that would demonstrate that replacing the present government is more important than controlling every condition before the next government can even begin.

Instead, the arrangement you are proposing risks doing precisely the opposite.

You are making Mr. Eisenkot and breaking him at the same time.

You offer him support with one hand and place an obstacle in front of him with the other.

Mr. Lieberman, I am not claiming to know your private intentions. But I can examine the political consequences of your public position.

And those consequences are troubling.

You are giving the ultra-Orthodox parties the very leverage that Mr. Eisenkot needs to overcome.

You are telling them that if they refuse to cooperate, you may refuse to cooperate as well.

That is not a negotiating advantage for Mr. Eisenkot. It is a negotiating advantage for the people he is trying to persuade.

And it preserves the possibility that Benjamin Netanyahu will remain in power while these negotiations continue.

Mr. Eisenkot, you need the confidence to govern before you can demonstrate your ability to govern.

You need momentum.

You need a government that can begin working, negotiating, and showing the country that a different political future is possible.

If you secure that opportunity and subsequently fail to build a durable coalition, then you will have tried.

But being prevented from beginning is not the same as being given an opportunity and failing.

Mr. Lieberman, this is the question I want you to answer:

If you genuinely want Mr. Eisenkot to become prime minister, why make his ability to begin governing dependent on the consent of parties that have every reason to demand more before giving him their support?

You can establish your conditions. You can negotiate your commitments. You can set a reasonable timetable and hold Mr. Eisenkot accountable for meeting it.

But why insist on a condition that could destroy the opportunity before it exists?

A political partnership should create momentum, not surrender it to the very parties whose cooperation remains uncertain.

I believe this contradiction must be confronted openly.

The future of a government cannot be built on an arrangement in which one negotiating partner effectively tells another: You have my support, provided someone else gives you permission to use it.

That is the catch-22.

And unless it is resolved, the negotiations themselves may become the reason a new government never takes office.

Mr. Eisenkot, secure the confidence to govern. Then negotiate from a position of established leadership.

Mr. Lieberman, if your commitment is to help establish that government, explain why your conditions must come before its formation rather than becoming part of a reasonable agreement to sustain it.

The momentum to govern must not be surrendered before the government has even begun.

Respectfully,

Omar Arizona

text:
This article is from Making AI Work, MIT Technology Review’s limited-run newsletter examining how to apply LLMs across industries. To receive it in your inbox, sign up here.

Chatbots took many schools by surprise upon their release a few years ago. Suddenly, students carried an app in their phones that could magically answer almost any homework question or spin up an essay in seconds. Of course, teachers can often tell when a student is using AI—models make mistakes that most humans don’t, and some teachers say that AI-generated text has simple giveaways like too many em dashes. 

Nevertheless, the generative AI boom increased the burden on teachers, who were already working long hours to plan lessons, make homework assignments, and grade exams, and now needed to adapt to a new technology. For many, it still feels like there’s no clear path forward. Organizations ranging from OpenAI to UNESCO encourage AI use in the classroom, but many teachers feel confused about how exactly to handle it. 

Case study

Cheshire Academy is a private boarding and day school in Connecticut with about 400 students in grades 9 through 12. Administrators there don’t force instructors to use AI at all, though the school’s librarian and technology coordinator George Aiello claims the “vast majority” of instructors use it in some way. The educators there are trying a patchwork of programs, including general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT and Perplexity as well as more specialized tools like MagicSchool, an AI-powered platform meant specifically for educators.

That patchwork approach is partly because the school, on the advice of consultants, opted to train its staff on general techniques for how to use AI instead of prescribing certain tech. The staff training covered topics like how to craft useful prompts but also stressed the technology’s limits, highlighting its potential for generating incorrect and biased responses. 

Now, teachers there often use generative AI to prepare class materials. This means asking the AI of their choice for help with planning lessons or creating grading rubrics. Some even want to use it to help them give feedback to students, though concerns over quality, personalization, and privacy have prevented any of them from doing that just yet.

Others, like Miriam Przybyla-Baum, who teaches French, don’t use AI themselves but do address it with their teaching. Przybyla-Baum says she doesn’t really need AI’s help since she’s built up plenty of classroom materials across nearly 30 years of teaching. But she started seeing students try to use AI-powered tools like Google Translate to take shortcuts on their assignments years before ChatGPT’s launch. 

She’s developed a system to make students reflect on how AI can and can’t teach language skills. In one assignment, students let a large language model (LLM) edit their homework. Then, they go through the edits and decide which ones were correct and which ones removed their voice. In another, she has students anonymously grade each other’s AI-assisted assignments, making annotations as to which parts they think are AI-assisted.

Cheshire Academy is continuing to experiment with how AI can be harnessed productively in the classroom. The school is piloting a program in which students create media and lead discussions regarding healthy AI use. This program, which they call a “Student AI Council,” aims to push students to reflect on how AI should and shouldn’t be used to benefit the community around them.

The academy as a whole has since adopted similar techniques to those Przybyla-Baum introduced to make students reflect on their own use of AI. Assignments are now labelled like traffic lights, with green meaning AI is fully allowed and red banning any AI use. Yellow, then, lets the teacher permit some tools while banning the rest, like allowing students to use spell-check but not message a chatbot.

The tool

As generative AI was becoming mainstream, Cheshire Academy previewed MagicSchool to its staff. 

For many, MagicSchool’s main strength seems to lie in the sheer amount of offerings it provides in one package. It can generate questions and assignments of all kinds, from quizzes to worksheets, across many subjects and grade levels. It has a specialized grading rubric generator, which outputs a ready-to-go table that teachers can use to score assignments. It can make presentations and lesson plans and administrative reports, too. 

All of this is done through a single platform where educators enter specific prompts tailored for each task. For example, to make an assignment, a teacher can specify the students’ grade level, number of questions, the types of questions (such as multiple choice or short answer), and more, and include documents to align the questions with. 

Not every teacher feels comfortable using LLMs to generate student-facing text, whether because they don’t think an AI can produce effective teaching materials or helpful feedback, or because they’re concerned about accuracy. MagicSchool, which has free and paid versions, does offer tools on its platform for other tasks like lesson planning. If teachers want unlimited access and complete records in the system, though, they need to pay just under $100 per year for an individual plan. Alternatively, many of the general-purpose generative AI tools (think the chatbots on offer from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and more) seem suited to administrative tasks, as well, attested by the fact that many of the teachers at Cheshire Academy use those instead. Some of these companies are even rolling out features tailored for schools, to mixed results.

How to apply this

  • Meet students where they’re at. Students will be tempted to try AI, and there’s no way to entirely police this for take-home assignments. The internet and social media can spread a lot of misinformation as to what AI can and can’t do, and it’s critical to counter these narratives and teach healthy strategies and relationships.
  • Model best practices. AI is very good at automating tasks, but it struggles with precision and voice. Keep this in mind, especially when generating any text that anyone else may see. Impressionable students who see those in authority using AI in a lazy way could internalize this as an excuse to cut corners in their own work.
  • Refine and replace. AI is great for brainstorming lesson plans and extra problem sets, especially for teachers early in their careers who don’t have a big problem bank already built up. However, because it can make mistakes (called hallucinations), using it for final drafts can result in assignments that confuse students and impair learning. Be sure to check every citation, equation, and statement an LLM makes.

Sign up for Making AI Work, MIT Technology Review’s limited-run newsletter examining how to apply LLMs across healthcare, climate tech, education, and more.

HHS, FDA to Phase Out Petroleum-Based Synthetic Dyes in Nation’s Food Supply
For Immediate Release:April 22, 2025
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) today announced a series of new measures to phase out all petroleum-based synthetic dyes from the nation’s food supply—a significant milestone in the administration’s broader initiative to Make America Healthy Again.
The FDA is taking the following actions:
Establishing a national standard and timeline for the food industry to transition from petrochemical-based dyes to natural alternatives.
Initiating the process to revoke authorization for two synthetic food colorings—Citrus Red No. 2 and Orange B—within the coming months.
Working with industry to eliminate six remaining synthetic dyes—FD&C Green No. 3, FD&C Red No. 40, FD&C Yellow No. 5, FD&C Yellow No. 6, FD&C Blue No. 1, and FD&C Blue No. 2—from the food supply by the end of next year.
Authorizing four new natural color additives in the coming weeks, while also accelerating the review and approval of others.
Partnering with the National Institutes of Health (NIH) to conduct comprehensive research on how food additives impact children’s health and development.
Requesting food companies to remove FD&C Red No. 3 sooner than the 2027-2028 deadline previously required.
“For too long, some food producers have been feeding Americans petroleum-based chemicals without their knowledge or consent,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “These poisonous compounds offer no nutritional benefit and pose real, measurable dangers to our children’s health and development. That era is coming to an end. We’re restoring gold-standard science, applying common sense, and beginning to earn back the public’s trust. And we’re doing it by working with industry to get these toxic dyes out of the foods our families eat every day.”

The FDA is fast-tracking the review of calcium phosphate, Galdieria extract blue, gardenia blue, butterfly pea flower extract, and other natural alternatives to synthetic food dyes. The agency is also taking steps to issue guidance and provide regulatory flexibilities to industries.

“Today, the FDA is asking food companies to substitute petrochemical dyes with natural ingredients for American children as they already do in Europe and Canada,” said FDA Commissioner Marty Makary, MD, MPH. “We have a new epidemic of childhood diabetes, obesity, depression, and ADHD. Given the growing concerns of doctors and parents about the potential role of petroleum-based food dyes, we should not be taking risks and do everything possible to safeguard the health of our children.”

In partnership with the NIH Nutrition Regulatory Science and Research Program, the FDA will enhance nutrition and food-related research to better inform regulatory decisions. This collaboration will strengthen the FDA’s ability to develop evidence-based food policies, support a healthier America, and advance the priorities of the Make America Healthy Again Commission.
