text:
This is VERY lengthy but I thought it might interest some, particularly today.

"In the summer of 2024, I visited Thiepval in Northern France where stands a war memorial dedicated to those killed on the Somme during World War One and for whom there is no known grave.

Remembered there amongst the 72,311 British and South African officers and men who died and whose names are etched on that memorial is Private Joseph Fraser, a family member whose own story I have shared a little of before.

Joseph was, "presumed killed" in the autumn of 1916 aged just 21, during a battle for an area known as High Wood. He remains one of those known simply as “the missing”.

Shortly after returning to England, I spent an evening at a lecture given by RAF veteran @JohnNicholRAF , during which he told the story of the "Unknown Warrior", a World War One soldier recovered from the battlefields of France and who today represents all those British military lost to war.

That lecture and the book which accompanied it was to take me on an unexpected journey of my own, one that had started just weeks earlier beneath the steps of a memorial at Thiepval.

From time to time I travel to London, journeys made in the hope of capturing through the lens of a camera a little of life there. Witnessing those moments that draw so many; the protest, the celebration; and those thankfully rare occasions of national grief and mourning.

But during more recent visits, I passed those journeys lost in the pages of John's book, distracted from the London of today and focused more on its past, our past.

I don't intend to repeat the stories within his book; and as wonderful and recommended a read as it is, today I will simply share my own much shorter one.

Many of us have stood at the Cenotaph on Armistice Sunday, some of you and deservedly so, have been very much part of the ceremony itself. A ceremony that drives an ineffable sense of pride in our Nation’s Armed Forces. But who of us really knows that Cenotaphs own tale, that white Portland stone standing at the heart of our nation, I for one did not.
How, in those early days after World War One, had the idea of this single emblem around which the nation could gather evolved.

It was a question I became so gripped by I found myself travelling beyond the pages of a book, to a small almost forgotten piece of railway history in the Sussex countryside, the Highlands of Scotland and eventually to the very Cenotaph itself.

Those who on Armistice Day have watched our old soldiers march proudly past that Cenotaph know it presents a powerful image. In recent years I have made the journey more often, drawn perhaps by the realisation that those ranks of men and women who passed under its shadow in years gone by have now, but for a few, joined those whom we solemnly commemorate there.

Like their World War One brothers, the last of the brave men and women of World War Two will also soon be lost to us; the inevitable passing of an irreplaceable generation. A thought that gently echoes through the consciousness of the crowds who have come together to salute them.

But the Cenotaph is so much more than a place for us today to simply gather and to remember.
From 11th November 1918 at 11am, the end of World War One, "The Great War", there was no single point at which to grieve for those who had sacrificed a loved one to it. Their soldier simply lost forever in the mud of France, or buried together in graves, the names of those within unknown or unrecorded.

However, the enormity of the task of repatriating the dead soon saw it become Government policy that those lost to war would not be brought home. Thus, except for a few wealthy or determined individuals who took matters into their own hands and recovered their loved ones, the dead would remain where they fought and died.

Despite this decision, the Government of the day was still acutely aware of the growing calls for something to bring comfort and closure to families and sometimes entire communities, who in that early post-war period were attempting to rebuild their lives without familiar faces and voices around them.

A plan was therefore put into place to exhume some of those killed, reinterring them in recognised War graves near where they had been lost to battle; large military cemeteries, which remain today throughout Europe. British soldiers, often lying alongside their allies; and where families could perhaps one day hope to visit.
Bu it soon became clear that this too was an almost impossible task. One taking its toll on the physical and mental health of those involved, men already scarred by war, so the plan was soon abandoned.

There was however amongst those grappling with this issue one man, the Reverend David Railton, a man who perhaps more than many knew the pain being felt across the nation. So many husbands' fathers and sons lost; their families to whom he now ministered in peacetime, turning to him, desperate for news and for comfort.

The name David Railton is though itself oddly almost lost in time, yet it is one that played such a significant part in the story.

David Railton understood the horrors of war for good reason; he had witnessed that horror close up. As an Army Chaplain, he spent his war giving solace to the dying and offering prayer for the dead. A man recognised for his own courage in bringing back wounded men from the field of battle, acts of valour that in 1916 saw him awarded the Military Cross.

Reverend Railton refused to carry a weapon, instead he faced his war armed with a bible and a Union flag brought from his own home, a reminder of why men would risk so much woven into its very fabric. A flag he now used to cover the dead in a final prayer, or in those rare moments of calm, as a makeshift altar cloth from where he would perform simple religious services for men huddled together in the mud churned trenches of the Somme. Trenches that had now become their home. A flag that still today holds a significant place in his and their story.

My journeys to London end at Victoria station, it was on one such journey, deep in John Nichol's book that I learnt of the Reverend David Railton and his part in the story of the Unknown Warrior.

The Unknown Warrior: The body of a fallen British soldier, one of four men removed of rank and insignia, carried on the 7th of November 1920 to the chapel of St Pol sur Ternoise in the Pas de Calais, France. One man from each of the four major battle fronts of Aisne, the Somme, Arras and Ypres. British soldiers brought together to perform one final duty for the nation.

The task and method of selecting the man who would become the Unknown Warrior now fell to Brigadier General Louis Wyatt, Commander of forces in France and Flanders. A process itself shrouded in military secrecy.

Despite many theories about that process, apart from publishing one letter assuring the nation of the randomness of his choice, it was a secret Louis Wyatt took to his own grave many years later.

The coffin in which the man chosen had been laid by Wyatt and his aide Lieutenant Colonel Edward Gell, was now placed into a larger iron banded casket. A casket carved from English oak and designed for this one purpose. Oak cut from the trees of the Royal Palace of Hampton Court. A connection perhaps to the King in whose name he fought and for the nation he had died.

The Unknown Warrior lay briefly in that chapel at Saint-Pol, the other three men, like all who had died and were now represented by this one man, surrendered back to the French earth from which they had been taken just days before. They themselves, whether by design or not, remain in unknown graves.

On 10th November 1920 at 10.30am, with the church bells of Boulogne ringing out and led by one thousand French school children, the Unknown Warrior, placed upon a French military wagon drawn by six black horses, travelled for one final time over the French earth that had so recently embraced him.

Under the salute of the Supreme Allied Commander of the Western Front, French General Ferdinand Foch, he was carried with full military ceremony onto the deck of the British Royal Navy Destroyer HMS Verdun.
Safe in her care and escorted by 6 other Royal Navy Destroyers, the Unknown Warrior at last crossed the sea toward home, a sea that in the years before had brought him toward this moment.

When those awaiting the arrival of that solemn flotilla sighted its approach, the guns of Dover castle fired a 19-gun salute to announce his return. A salute normally reserved for a Field Marshall.

The oak casket, upon which had now been placed a powerfully symbolic Crusader sword, continued its journey by train carriage toward London. The same carriage which just 18 months earlier had
carried home English nurse Edith Cavell, shot by a German firing squad in 1915 for helping 200 allied soldiers escape from Belgium into neutral Holland.
But now it carried the Unknown Warrior, arriving at platform 8 Victoria Station on the evening of 10th November 1920. Here he would remain overnight, guarded by representatives of the armed services, before making his final journey toward the Cenotaph, Westminster Abbey and into history.

Apparently, the news of his arrival saw the railway embankments lined with people, many of whom had undoubtedly lost loved ones, all now hoping to catch a glance at the returning Warrior.

As I read that chapter and my own train rattled toward Victoria, I wondered if I were now travelling along the same tracks that his journey had taken him and had those ancient English Oaks rushing past my window bore silent witness to that moment.

Then when the skyline of London came into sight, a very different London from that of 1920, I could not help but imagine those faces staring silently on, each lost in that single moment of hope, was this their own soldier, home at last.

Stepping onto the station at Victoria I crossed to platform 8, where for the first time I saw, affixed to a station column, a plaque, large, wooden framed with prominent white wording upon a black canvas, words remembering that moment over a century before when at 8.32pm on 10th November 1920 the Unknown Warrior arrived.

Back in 1918 the state had wrestled with the issue of what to do for so many families who had lost their loved ones. It also sensed in a post war Britain, unsettled times and growing frustration.

A government and a Monarch that had an eye fixed firmly on the inevitable change war had brought to Europe. Changes that had so recently seen King George V own cousin Tsar Nicholas II and his entire family slaughtered by a Russia in revolution.

David Railton had no such distractions, from as early as 1916 he had written to the military Commander of the British Expeditionary Force, Western Front, Field Marshall Douglas Haig, raising this issue. It is said his letter, looking ahead to the cost of rebuilding peace and restoring a nation's soul, went unanswered.
Now after the end of the war, still troubled by his own thoughts on how poorly the state had responded, he was increasingly hearing those same concerns from the families in his congregations, families who still turned to him for answers.

David Railton took that message to those at the very heart of his own church, a church which in that period held much sway with the state itself. It was here at last that he found a powerful and sympathetic ear. His words also soon reached the Dean of Westminster Abbey, the Right Reverend Herbert Ryle, a man who understood like no other the power of ceremony within the walls of his Abbey.

Their combined voices soon had the machinery of the State listening, and that State acted with uncharacteristic speed. The idea of one man, David Railton, was now the focus of the Government of the day. Chance at last for so many to find comfort and hope of recovery in each other, in one soldier and in a single white Portland stone.

By late 1920 David Railton’s vision of an Unknown Warrior and a Cenotaph at which to remember all warriors had become a reality.

Now on the morning of 11th November 1920, the Unknown Warrior’s comrades carried him toward his final resting place. And at 11am before a nation in silence, under the gaze of those gathered, that Unknown Warrior arrived before his Cenotaph.

In parish churches or family homes across the Cities, towns and villages of the Kingdom the nation could at last join together at the homecoming of their own lost soldier.

There are many historical pictures of the gun carriage upon which the Unknown Warrior arrived at the Cenotaph, a Cenotaph on that day draped in two huge Union Jacks; a scene movingly recreated for VE Day 2025, and at which in 1920 regardless of status, King or subject, all there bowed their heads in silent respect for this one man. But, if you look closely at any of those images, covering that oak coffin is another flag.

In a touching acknowledgement by the nation of the work of David Railton, his flag, a flag with which he had covered the dead on those fields of battle, now lay over one final warrior, his warrior.

Before leaving that day in 1920; as the Unknown Warrior was laid to his final rest within Westminster Abbey before a humbled King, also gathered around him were the invited one thousand mothers and wives who had lost sons or husbands. Women together in what must have been an inescapable moment of deep pride and intense grief, surrounded and supported in that moment by the combined ranks of an honour guard of 76 Victoria Cross holders.

David Railton retired in 1945 and settled in the highlands of Scotland where he lived until his own death. I don't know why he chose to move so far from his life on the South coast of England, though as I stood at his grave in the small churchyard of St Brides in North Ballachulish on an early evening in June and looked out to where the loch met the mountains and the mountains the sky, I wondered, now no longer distracted by his ministry, did the peace of this place offer him some respite from the memories of the featureless flat landscape and grey skies of Northern France of all those years before.

Memories of a war-torn shattered earth on which he witnessed so much. Had he at last found a place of solitude and of calm, a chance perhaps to restore some of the faith that must have been tested by each equally war-torn shattered soul who had lain beneath his flag.

Many years later his own grandson spoke guardedly about the impact of war upon his grandfather; an impact David Railton may one day have shared. But, if it were a search for peace or the renewal of faith, then I hope he found both in measure for fate was to now play its part.

On the 30th of June 1955 whilst travelling to Scotland from Sussex and as the train on which he travelled approached Fort William station, David Railton left his seat and stood in the carriage corridor. As he did so, the train crossed a junction point, the latch on the door against which he leant or had stumbled failed, and he fell from the train onto the track below, where at the age of 70 his remarkable life ended.

It is difficult to find any reason for comfort in that tragic moment, except I think, perhaps in an odd and moving irony, in that death he was at last to share one final connection to the story of his Unknown Warrior.

David Railton, who had been so instrumental in one man’s journey and our nation's history, was now himself carried to a railway station and where, like his warrior who had laid overnight at Victoria station, retired Army Chaplain the Reverend David Railton Military Cross lay at the station of Fort William until he too was to start his journey toward his own final resting place.

And so, my little story has now travelled almost full circle, from that sunny French morning standing for the first time at the steps of Thiepval memorial under the name of a family member lost still on the Somme, to laying a single poppy at the grave of the Reverend David Railton in a small churchyard deep in the Scottish Highlands.

David Railton whose humanity, vision and passion saw the nations warriors brought home in one man, a man who now rests amongst Kings: That husband that father that son.

Last year at the 11th hour I again stood at the Cenotaph and in those few sacred moments when the Nation fell silent I thought not only of those lost to war; of Joseph Fraser aged 21, of family and friend, but of the Reverend David Railton MC and his Cenotaph.

But I still had one more visit to make, Westminster Abbey, where at the feet of the Unknown Warrior, under the flag of David Railton, a flag once stained with the blood of our nation, I allowed myself to wonder; for a moment anyway.
                         ***************************
“Until the day break and the shadows flee away”.

The South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty (Rarotonga Treaty) Consultative Committee Meeting convened yesterday at the Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat in Suva, Fiji.

Chaired by New Zealand, Committee Members shared updates on regional nuclear issues and agreed on arrangements for the upcoming Second Meeting of States Parties to the Treaty on 8 December and the commemoration of the Treaty’s 40th anniversary of its entry into force on 9 December 2026 at the Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat.

The meeting also heard an update from the Republic of the Marshall Islands as Chair of the CROP Taskforce on Nuclear Legacy Issues in the Pacific.

The 40th anniversary of the Treaty’s entry into force next month offers the Pacific region an opportunity to reaffirm its commitment to regional peace and security, including through the engagement of the next generation of Pacific leaders under the Youth Leader Fund for a World without Nuclear Weapons – Pacific Edition (YLF Pacific) programme.

(14:05) There needed to be an outlet that would call out right from wrong, that would stand up against the people like Donald Trump and the vote suppressors, that if it were happening today, would call out what happened to James Chaney and Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner in unequivocal terms, and call them out for the heroes that they were then and are today.
(14:39) So, for the first time, Democracy Docket has sent journalists to cover a post-election case. Like, even in 2020, it didn't do that. Democracy Docket journalists are on the ground right now in the state of Mississippi, bringing this information to you directly. I am doing these live streams to bring you this information as well as what's going on in the rest of the country directly.
(15:05) While much of the legacy media continues to treat the race in Mississippi as a horse race between a Democrat and a Republican. I am proud that the coverage that Democracy Docket has offered is about what this fundamentally is, a story about democracy and freedom, about free and fair elections and voter suppression, about election workers doing the best they can when you have a state that has election rules written by people who didn't want to make it easy for you to vote or for those election officials to do their jobs.
(15:33) Democracy has no reason to sugarcoat that. No reason to dress it up. No reason to make it seem pretty. No reason to curry favor with and tell a both sides story where there isn't one. I am as sure as anything that in the coming days, Scott Colom will be declared the winner and his election will be certified. And I fully expect that when he takes office in January, he will become one of the most critical voices in the fight for voting rights, not just for black Americans, not just in the deep south, but for everyone from coast to coast,
(16:06) from north to south. Look, Donald Trump and his cronies, they're going to keep fighting. They're going to keep attacking our democracy. They're going to keep attacking our elections. That is unavoidable. And every time the legacy media tries to sell you a counternarrative that somehow Donald Trump has changed his stripes, that somehow Donald Trump will accept the elections, I call it out that it's not true. It's not going to be. It is a lie.
(16:33) The legacy media is like Charlie Brown with a football over and over again. I'll go back after this election to doing what I do. I'll be back in court. I'll be litigating voting in election cases in states and in counties on laws that you've never heard of that are not capturing the nation's attention and don't seem all that important.
(17:00) One of those cases a few years ago involved the Republican National Committee trying to make it impossible for the state of Mississippi to count mail-in ballots if they're postmarked by election day but received afterwards. I saw this lawsuit and said we have to be involved. Our clients want us to be involved. Our clients hired us and retained us to fight for this fight.

(17:53) Last spring, the United States Supreme Court held down handed down the decision in Watson versus Republican National Committee, and we won. Their mail-in ballots will count because the Republican party failed and justice and law prevailed.

text:
🇺🇲 🇷🇺 🇪🇺 Scoop: Washington asks Putin to write a new security offer for Europe, with "symmetrical steps" to calm the continent

The Trump administration wants Vladimir Putin to put his demands for Europe's security on paper, and to say what Russia would give in return. According to Axios, citing two sources with knowledge of the matter, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner asked Russian negotiators in Abu Dhabi to submit a new proposal for a future security agreement with Europe. 

The sources say Russia's team told the room that Putin launched the invasion because President Biden never answered his 2021 letter on security. Kushner and Witkoff replied that the world has changed since 2021 and asked Moscow to draft a fresh offer that lays out its concerns and also the "symmetrical steps" it would take to de-escalate and reassure Europe it will not attack again.

Kushner described the message publicly after the talks. "We told the Russians, they have their desires and fears, but they have to provide different de-escalation and different proposals as well, if they want Europe to be able to receive those proposals in a good way."

The envoys meet Putin in Moscow on Thursday morning, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told TASS, and Axios says they will repeat the request there. They also want Putin to let European representatives join the next round of Russia-Ukraine talks. Moscow has refused so far. Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said after Abu Dhabi that he did not understand what could be discussed with European leaders, while also saying Russia wants a broader security deal with Europe as part of ending the war. "In Ukraine, an abscess has simply burst," he said. "The entire body needs to be treated."

The sources told Axios that European officials in Abu Dhabi agreed to work on both tracks at once, the war and the wider architecture, while insisting that final decisions on European security come only after the war ends. A source familiar with White House thinking said Washington will not sign a security deal with Russia unless Europe and Ukraine are on board, and will not give Moscow a veto over Europe's security choices.

Why it matters: for years the US rejected Russia's demands to limit NATO and pull back forces from Eastern Europe. Washington now appears open to discussing them in some form. Europeans are deeply suspicious, and their leaders gather in Dublin on Thursday as Witkoff and Kushner fly there from Moscow to see Zelensky.

text:
Dr. Strangelove Now Speaks German. Paris Is Terrified.

A deterrent only works if the other side knows the rules, and France has just admitted to the Financial Times that Europe's newest one doesn't have any.

On the morning Europe layed its wreaths for the last great war it sleepwalked into, six people close to the talks between Paris and Berlin let the Financial Times know, in the careful language of officials who understand exactly what they are admitting, that the next one could begin with a German missile and a Russian officer who has a few minutes to guess what it means. One French official warned that Europe could "get to the nuclear threshold without realizing," which is a sentence that deserves to be carved over the door of every chancellery on the continent. Armistice Day, of all days.

Stanley Kubrick filmed Dr. Strangelove in 1964 and called it a comedy. The whole plot turns on a deterrent that fails because nobody bothered to tell the other side how it works, while Dr. Strangelove himself, the German scientist advising the President in the War Room, explains the logic of it all after the bombers have already left. 62 years later the script has been picked up in Europe and recast with a French president who fancies himself as le petit roi and a German chancellor who arrived via the BlackRock boardroom, and this time nobody is laughing. Least of all the French.

Because what Paris is asking for, once you strip away the diplomatic upholstery, is that Berlin's doctrine for "deep precision strikes" be tied to French nuclear strategy before the hardware shows up, and the reason offered by one source is that France has a nuclear "grammar and vocabulary" that Germany lacks. Translation: the only capital in the EU with its finger on a real button has read the German shopping list and reached for the defibrillator.
And the list is something to behold. 

Berlin has pledged €780 billion for defence through 2030, with roughly €12 billion going to a long-range arsenal that includes nearly €3.4 billion of American Tomahawks on mobile Typhon launchers and a classified missile project with the British that could be in service by 2034. The ranges run from 500 km to beyond 2,000, Berlin to Moscow is about 1,600, and nobody in the Russian General Staff needs that arithmetic explained to them.
The cast is as revealing as the catalogue. 

Merz has promised "the strongest conventional army in Europe," Pistorius has handed the Bundeswehr the first (suicidal) military strategy in its history with Russia written in as the main threat and 2039 (just in time for the Centennial!) as the deadline and the general chosen to run the whole machine from February is Christian Freuding, the officer who spent the war coordinating Germany's military aid to Ukraine. So here is a question from the cheap seats, Herr Merz. You have the range, the Ill gotten money stolen from Germans without a mandate for world war, the general and the deadline…. and by your closest ally's own account you do not have one published line explaining when you would fire, since no joint doctrine exists. What exactly is Moscow supposed to assume?

99 Luftballons, remixed
We have been in this cinema before. In November 1983 the Pershing IIs were arriving in West Germany with a flight time to Soviet command centres measured in minutes, a NATO exercise called Able Archer had convinced part of the Soviet leadership that the real thing might be hiding inside it, and a German pop song about a handful of balloons mistaken for an attack was climbing the charts across the West. The ground launched cruise missile parked in Europe in those years was an early Tomahawk with a nuclear warhead, Germany is now buying Tomahawks and Putin drew the Pershing comparison himself back in 2024. It took the INF Treaty to get the continent out of that trap and it took Washington walking out of the treaty in 2019 to put it back in. Brilliantly stupid and suicidal. 

Continue reading on our substack👇🏻

text:
Russian ambassador Alexander Darchiev dies suddenly at 66

Alexander Darchiev, Russia’s ambassador to the United States, has died suddenly at the age of 66, according to the Russian Foreign Ministry as reported by Al Jazeera. His death ends the tenure of a diplomat whose work focused on relations with North America, including the United States and Canada. Moscow did not release further information about the circumstances of his death. The ministry’s announcement therefore gives his age and describes the death as sudden, while leaving its cause and other details unstated. Darchiev’s appointment to the US ambassadorship was reported in March 2025 by the South China Morning Post. The Guardian placed the appointment shortly after Donald Trump returned to power. The South China Morning Post described Darchiev’s period in the role as one and a half years. Those reported details do not align neatly: the stated appointment month and the reported length of service are both presented in the source material, without further explanation of the timing. The central point of agreement across the reports is that Darchiev died suddenly at 66. The accounts differ, however, over when he served as Russia’s ambassador to Canada. Al Jazeera and the South China Morning Post give a period from 2014 to 2021, while The Guardian gives a period from 2021 to 2024. The available accounts do not resolve that difference, so neither date range can be treated here as a settled common account. The Canadian dates matter to the account of his career because they affect how his diplomatic assignments are placed in sequence. The reported ranges overlap at 2021, but the reports otherwise assign different years to his tenure. Separately, The Guardian says Darchiev led the Foreign Ministry’s North America department from 2014 to 2020. Al Jazeera reports that he returned to that department as director in 2010 and held the position again until the year before its report, a description that does not itself settle the disagreement over his Canadian service.

Darchiev’s career in diplomacy began in 1992, when he entered the service and became a first secretary and head of the Foreign Ministry’s North America department, according to Al Jazeera. The same account records an assignment as an adviser at Russia’s embassy in the United States in 1997. It also says he worked at that embassy as minister-counsellor from 2005 through 2010. These postings show that his later appointment as ambassador followed earlier work in the same bilateral relationship, though the facts do not describe the responsibilities of each role in detail. After his embassy service as minister-counsellor, Al Jazeera says Darchiev returned to the Foreign Ministry’s North America department in 2010 as its director. The account says he held that post again until the year before the report, without specifying that year in the fact provided. The Guardian’s separate account places him at the head of the department between 2014 and 2020. These descriptions identify extended work on North America, but they supply different levels of detail and should not be merged into a single uninterrupted timetable. The Foreign Ministry characterized Darchiev as a diplomat of distinction, an experienced leader and a considerate colleague. It also said he had worked in an especially important part of Russian foreign policy. Those are the ministry’s assessments, rather than independently detailed descriptions of his duties. Al Jazeera identifies his specialty as Russia-US relations, placing the ministry’s broader characterization alongside a specific area of expertise. The ministry’s public statement, as reported by Al Jazeera, announced the death and offered praise for Darchiev’s professional qualities. Moscow supplied no additional information about what had happened. The facts provided do not record another official account of the death or explain whether further information was expected. The distinction is important: the reported announcement establishes the ministry’s description of the death, but it does not provide a cause or a fuller account of the circumstances.

Darchiev also made a public comment on Russia’s action against Ukraine. Al Jazeera reports that in 2022 he called that move a “necessary measure.” The phrase records his characterization at that time, but the fact provided does not give the surrounding remarks or explain the grounds he offered. It therefore establishes what he said about the action without supporting a broader account of his position beyond that description. The biographical account also traces Darchiev’s family background to diplomatic service. Al Jazeera says he was born to Nikita Ivanovich Darchiev, who served as a minister-counsellor at the Russian Embassy in Hungary. The information identifies his father’s role and location, but does not state how that background shaped Darchiev’s own career. His own reported service, by contrast, includes posts in the United States, leadership in the Foreign Ministry’s North America department and an ambassadorship in Washington. Taken together, the available reports describe a diplomat whose work repeatedly involved North American affairs, from early Foreign Ministry responsibilities to service at Russia’s embassy in the United States and, later, appointment as ambassador there. They also report his earlier Canadian ambassadorship, while disagreeing about its dates. The ministry’s announcement supplies the immediate change: Darchiev died suddenly at 66, with no further details from Moscow. The accounts establish the broad outline of his career and the official response, but leave both the circumstances of his death and the disputed Canadian chronology unresolved.

text:
I have carefully examined the research by James Jackson and Mathias Larsen. Their study offers some useful observations about China's EV industry, but I have serious reservations about their decision to explain China's development model through the concept of "eco-authoritarianism".
First, the authors appear to conflate two different questions: whether a state possesses the capacity to pursue long-term industrial strategies, and how that state's political system should be categorised.
China's EV development has undoubtedly involved long-term central planning, local government experimentation, financial resource allocation and infrastructure investment. But these developments primarily demonstrate the state's capacity to organise industrial transformation. They cannot all be adequately explained by a single political label.
Second, the authors underestimate the role of markets and businesses themselves.
China's EV industry includes companies such as BYD, Geely, NIO, XPeng and Li Auto, competing across battery technology, intelligent driving, manufacturing processes, product positioning and cost efficiency. These companies are not simply waiting for government production instructions. They are developing technologies and business models in response to actual market competition.
A separate 2026 study published in The China Journal also examines the rise of China's EV industry through strategic alliances between local governments and private capital, highlighting the important contribution of private manufacturers to innovation and market expansion.

This demonstrates that China's industrial development is considerably more complex than a simple top-down command structure.
Third, the methodology deserves scrutiny.
The paper relies primarily on 15 expert interviews conducted between 2022 and 2025, alongside policy documents. The authors themselves acknowledge that these interviews provide interpretative evidence rather than a statistically representative account of all industry participants.
Building a broad theoretical explanation of China's political economy on such a limited qualitative sample requires considerable caution.
Interestingly, the paper also acknowledges that the Chinese government faces limitations in addressing price wars, duplicated investment and excess capacity. This demonstrates that China's economy is not a machine that the government can manipulate at will. Corporate decisions, market forces and local interests all matter.
I would therefore put a fundamental question to the authors:

If China has developed an integrated battery supply chain through long-term industrial planning, achieved technological progress through corporate competition, reduced EV costs through large-scale manufacturing and accelerated the global transition towards cleaner transportation, why must these achievements first be explained through a politically loaded conceptual framework?
Western governments also use industrial subsidies, tax incentives, public procurement and strategic investment to support domestic industries. Government participation in economic development, by itself, is not sufficient evidence for any particular political classification.
Academic research should recognise that different countries can pursue different development models and apply equally rigorous standards when examining their industrial policies.
Studying China should not mean using political labels as substitutes for serious analysis. Good scholarship should explain how China achieved what it did, rather than assigning a label first and then interpreting every achievement through that label.

It genuinely reads like a manual for good governance that Western governments should be studying instead of slapping a scary label on.

text:
I've listed all 46 REPEAL PROVISIONS in Rep. Donna Howard's (D) Child Sacrifice Initiative, HB 126.

Think I'm being dramatic? Read them for yourselves.

HB 126 would repeal decades of landmark Texas laws protecting preborn children, infants born alive following abortions, parental rights, women's health, and children from pediatric gender modification.

Some provisions repeal individual statutes. Others eliminate entire chapters of Texas law.

Below are all 46 repeal provisions, in the order they appear in HB 126, with a brief explanation of what each would eliminate.

PARENTAL RIGHTS, NEWBORN PROTECTIONS, AND TAXPAYER FUNDING

1. Civil Practice & Remedies Code §30.022 — Repeals special attorney-fee rules governing lawsuits challenging Texas abortion restrictions or limits on taxpayer funding for abortion providers.

2. Civil Practice & Remedies Code Chapter 74, Subchapter L — Repeals provisions classifying certain civil actions against physicians and healthcare providers for violations of abortion laws as healthcare liability claims subject to specific procedural requirements.

3. Education Code §38.063(e-1) — Repeals restrictions on school-based health grants going to nonprofit organizations providing reproductive or contraceptive services, counseling, or referrals, or affiliated with licensed abortion facilities.

4. Family Code Chapter 33 — Repeals parental notification and consent requirements for unemancipated minors seeking abortions, including judicial bypass procedures and medical emergency exceptions.

5. Family Code §151.002 — BORN-ALIVE INFANT PROTECTIONS — Repeals explicit statutory protections guaranteeing infants born alive following abortions or premature births the same legal rights as other newborns. Current law requires lifesaving medical care, including immediate hospital transfer following an attempted abortion, and establishes civil penalties of at least $100,000 and third-degree felony consequences for violations. These protections were strengthened by HB 16 in 2019.

6. Government Code §311.036 — Repeals provisions preventing the implied repeal of existing abortion restrictions, preserving local governments' authority to enact stricter abortion regulations, and requiring abortion statutes to be treated as severable.

7. Government Code Chapter 2273 — Repeals restrictions on state and local governments using taxpayer resources in transactions with abortion providers, affiliates, and organizations facilitating abortions. Also eliminates associated civil enforcement remedies.

8. Health & Safety Code §32.005 — Repeals restrictions on using public funds administered through Texas's Maternal and Infant Health Improvement Program to provide abortions, except when the mother's life is endangered.

9. Health & Safety Code Chapter 54 — THRIVING TEXAS FAMILIES — Repeals the Thriving Texas Families Program established by SB 24, which provides pregnancy support, parenting education, adoption resources, material assistance, housing referrals, and other services for pregnant women and families. Also repeals restrictions on abortion-related and family-planning services within the program's provider network and requirements for provider accountability.

PEDIATRIC GENDER MODIFICATION AND ABORTION PROHIBITIONS

10. Health & Safety Code Chapter 161, Subchapter X (redesignated Subchapter Y) — SB 14 — Repeals Texas's landmark prohibition on pediatric gender modification surgeries, puberty blockers, and cross-sex hormones for minors, subject to limited medical exceptions. Also repeals restrictions on public funding and state health plan coverage, along with professional licensing consequences for violations.

11. Health & Safety Code Chapter 170A — TEXAS ABORTION TRIGGER BAN — Repeals Texas's abortion trigger ban, which prohibits performing, inducing, or attempting abortions except under limited circumstances involving life-threatening physical conditions. Current law establishes criminal penalties, civil penalties of at least $100,000 per violation, and professional licensing consequences.

12. Health & Safety Code §§171.002(2), (3), (4) — Repeals statutory definitions of abortion provider, medical emergency, and sonogram used in Texas abortion regulations.

WOMEN'S HEALTH AND ABORTION REPORTING

13. Health & Safety Code §171.0031 — Repeals requirements that abortion providers maintain hospital admitting privileges within 30 miles, provide patients with 24-hour emergency contact information, and identify nearby hospitals for emergency care. Current law establishes Class A misdemeanor penalties for violations.

14. Health & Safety Code §171.004 — Repeals the requirement that abortions performed at 16 weeks of gestation or later take place in a licensed ambulatory surgical center or hospital rather than a physician's office or other clinic.

15. Health & Safety Code §171.005 — Repeals provisions directing the Texas Health and Human Services Commission to enforce Chapter 171 abortion regulations, except the Texas Heartbeat Act, which uses private civil enforcement.

16. Health & Safety Code §171.006 (HB 13) — Repeals requirements for physicians and healthcare facilities to report abortion complications, including hemorrhage, infection, organ damage, and infants born alive following abortions. Also repeals specified reporting deadlines and civil penalties for noncompliance.

17. Health & Safety Code §171.006 (HB 215) — Repeals requirements for physicians performing abortions on minors to document and report how the abortion was authorized, including parental consent, judicial authorization, or the minor's independent legal authority. Also repeals associated confidentiality provisions.

18. Health & Safety Code §171.008 — Repeals requirements for physicians to document whether abortions were performed because of medical emergencies, to preserve women's health, or for other reasons, and to maintain those records.

INFORMED CONSENT, SONOGRAMS, AND FETAL DEVELOPMENT

19. Health & Safety Code §171.012 — Repeals informed consent requirements, including disclosure of abortion risks, the preborn child's gestational age, pregnancy assistance, and alternatives to abortion. Also repeals sonogram requirements, explanations of detectable fetal heart activity, signed consent forms, and the 24-hour waiting period, subject to statutory exceptions.

20. Health & Safety Code §171.0121 — Repeals requirements to retain signed informed consent certifications in patients' medical records for at least seven years, or until age 21 for minors when that is later.

21. Health & Safety Code §171.0122 — Repeals provisions allowing women to decline viewing informational materials or sonogram images and hearing fetal heart sounds. Current law also permits women to decline certain verbal explanations under specified circumstances, including sexual assault, incest, certain judicial bypass cases, and irreversible fetal abnormalities, without penalty.

22. Health & Safety Code §171.0123 — Repeals requirements to provide women continuing their pregnancies with information about establishing legal paternity, obtaining child support, and understanding parental responsibilities.

23. Health & Safety Code §171.0124 — Repeals provisions allowing physicians to bypass standard informed consent, sonogram, and waiting-period requirements during medical emergencies, together with requirements to document the emergency and report the medical condition to the state within 30 days.

24. Health & Safety Code §171.013 — Repeals requirements to provide state-developed informational materials before abortions, including applicable 24-hour or 72-hour advance-delivery requirements and options for online review.

25. Health & Safety Code §171.014 — Repeals requirements for Texas to publish and annually review informational materials explaining abortion risks, fetal development, pregnancy assistance, and adoption alternatives. Current law requires English and Spanish materials and a state-maintained website with privacy protections.

26. Health & Safety Code §171.015 — Repeals requirements to identify organizations assisting women during pregnancy, childbirth, and child-rearing, including adoption agencies and free sonogram providers. Also repeals the 24-hour toll-free referral number and restrictions on including abortion providers and affiliates in those referrals.

27. Health & Safety Code §171.016 — Repeals requirements for state informational materials to describe the unborn child's anatomical and physiological development, including the possibility of survival, at two-week intervals throughout pregnancy, with realistic color illustrations.

28. Health & Safety Code §171.017 — Repeals provisions allowing informed consent waiting periods for minors to run concurrently with parental notification periods rather than consecutively.

29. Health & Safety Code §171.018 — Repeals criminal penalties for physicians who intentionally violate informed consent, sonogram, and waiting-period requirements. Current law provides misdemeanor penalties with fines of up to $10,000.

MAJOR ABORTION RESTRICTIONS AND FACILITY STANDARDS

30. Health & Safety Code Chapter 171, Subchapters C–H — Repeals multiple major Texas abortion laws and their enforcement mechanisms, including:

The prohibition on abortions at or after 20 weeks post-fertilization.
Restrictions on abortion-inducing drugs.
The prohibition on partial-birth abortions.
The prohibition on dismemberment abortions.
The Texas Heartbeat Act and its private civil enforcement mechanism.
Associated criminal and civil penalties.
Human trafficking training requirements for certain healthcare personnel.

31. Health & Safety Code §241.007 — Repeals requirements for hospitals to comply with pre-abortion sonogram and informed consent laws, including explanations of detectable fetal heart activity and applicable waiting periods.

32. Health & Safety Code §243.017 — Repeals requirements for ambulatory surgical centers to comply with pre-abortion sonogram and informed consent laws.

33. Health & Safety Code Chapter 245 — ABORTION FACILITY LICENSING — Repeals Texas's abortion facility licensing and inspection framework, including minimum health and safety standards, physician oversight, abortion reporting, and patient confidentiality requirements. Also repeals associated licensing actions and administrative, civil, and criminal enforcement penalties.

34. Health & Safety Code §285.202 — Repeals restrictions on hospital districts using district tax revenues to finance abortions while receiving state funding, except in medical emergencies. Also repeals requirements to document emergencies, report medical conditions within 30 days, and retain records for seven years or longer for minors.

35. Health & Safety Code Chapter 697 — FETAL REMAINS — Repeals requirements for the dignified disposition of embryonic and fetal remains through burial, cremation, or other approved methods rather than treatment as pathological waste. Also repeals burial and cremation assistance programs and licensing penalties for violations.

TAXPAYER FUNDING, INSURANCE, AND PEDIATRIC GENDER MODIFICATION

36. Human Resources Code §32.024(c-1) — Repeals restrictions on using certain Texas women's healthcare program funds to perform or promote elective abortions. Also repeals prohibitions on contracting with organizations that perform or promote elective abortions or are affiliated with those organizations.

37. Human Resources Code §32.024(pp) — SB 14 — Repeals restrictions on Texas Medicaid coverage for pediatric gender modification procedures prohibited under SB 14, including gender-transition surgeries, puberty blockers, and cross-sex hormones for minors, subject to statutory medical exceptions.

38. Insurance Code §1218.003 — Repeals an exception allowing health insurance coverage for medically necessary emergency abortions without the separate coverage and premium requirements applicable to elective abortions.

39. Insurance Code §1218.005 — Repeals requirements for insurers offering elective abortion coverage to calculate premiums sufficient to cover those abortions and prohibitions on offsetting costs against projected savings from other healthcare services.

40. Insurance Code §1218.006 — Repeals requirements to notify insurance enrollees that elective abortion coverage is optional, separate from other health benefits, and requires an additional premium. Also repeals notification of the right to purchase coverage without elective abortion benefits.

41. Insurance Code Title 8, Subtitle M — Repeals restrictions on elective abortion coverage in qualified health insurance plans offered through Affordable Care Act exchanges, while permitting separate optional or supplemental abortion coverage outside the exchanges.

CONSCIENCE PROTECTIONS, TELEMEDICINE, AND MEDICAL LICENSING

42. Occupations Code Chapter 103 — HEALTHCARE CONSCIENCE PROTECTIONS — Repeals protections preventing healthcare professionals from being compelled to participate directly or indirectly in abortions. Also repeals protections against employment and educational discrimination, legal remedies including reinstatement and back pay, and protections for private healthcare facilities, subject to an exception when the mother's life is immediately endangered.

43. Occupations Code §111.005(c) — Repeals restrictions on establishing practitioner-patient relationships through telemedicine for prescribing abortion-inducing drugs or other drugs and devices intended to terminate pregnancies.

44. Occupations Code §164.055 — Repeals Texas Medical Board disciplinary and licensing provisions for physicians violating specified abortion laws, including denial of licenses and renewals. Also repeals related sanctions and provisions protecting physicians exercising reasonable medical judgment in qualifying pregnancy complications.

45. Occupations Code §164.0551 — Repeals professional requirements for physicians to comply with pre-abortion sonogram and informed consent laws, including explanations of detectable fetal heart activity, waiting periods, and statutory exceptions.

46. Revised Statutes Title 71, Chapter 6½ — HISTORIC TEXAS ABORTION PROHIBITIONS — Repeals longstanding criminal prohibitions against performing, attempting, or assisting in abortions, including penalties for providing abortion-inducing drugs, causing a woman's death during an abortion, and destroying an unborn child during birth. Current law includes an exception for medical emergencies.

Aside from these repeals, HB 126 also proposes changes elsewhere in Texas law, including redefining abortion as a medical procedure.

Read the complete HB 126 policy analysis from Protect Childhood Initiative. (In the comments.)

Source: Protect Childhood Initiative, HB 126 Policy Brief, Section 9 repeal table, pages 3–6.

text:
Sensitiveness

1. A single severe glance from our employer or superior is enough to make us anxious. If it is accompanied by a word of rebuke we are thoroughly upset. Why should this be so? It is because we are lacking in the fundamental virtue of humility. We want to keep up appearances and to be held in high regard. If we are frustrated in this ambition, we suffer inwardly.

All this is quite natural, but on this natural foundation we must build the virtue of humility and the desire to serve God alone. If we possess this virtue, we shall continue to be sensitive to insults and humiliations but our suffering will be sanctified and will be meritorious in the sight of God.

We are all pleased when we are praised by others and are hurt when we are criticised, because our natural inclinations are never destroyed. Our sensitivity, however, can be moderated and brought under the control of right reason, whose guide should be the rule of virtue. It is worth reflecting on what the “Imitation of Christ” has to say in this regard.

“Whenever a man desireth anything inordinately, straight-away he is disquieted within himself. The proud and the covetous are never at rest; the poor and humble in spirit pass their life in abundance of peace. The man who is not yet perfectly dead to self is soon tempted and overcome in little and paltry things. He that is weak in spirit, and in a certain manner as yet carnal, and inclined to things of sense, cannot without difficulty sever himself wholly from earthly desires. And therefore he is often sad when he does withdraw himself; and besides, he is easily moved to anger if anyone thwarts him. And, if he has pursued his inclination, forthwith he is burdened with remorse of conscience for having gone after his passion, which helped him not at all to the peace he looked for. It is by resisting the passions, therefore, and not by serving them, that true peace of heart is to be found. Peace, therefore, is not in the heart of the carnal man, nor in the man who is devoted to outward things, but in the fervent and spiritual man.” (Bk. 1, c.6)

“Continual peace dwelleth with the humble, but in the heart of the proud is frequent envy and indignation.” (Ibid., c. 7, v.3)

2. Our wounded feelings sometimes give rise to an external explosion in the form of bitter and offensive remarks. These always create disharmony and have various unfortunate after-effects.

It is fatal to lose control over ourselves. A man who has surrendered to anger and resentment does not weigh his words and is not responsible for his actions. When the fit has passed, he is left with a sense of humiliation because of his lack of moderation and must suffer the consequences both before God and before his fellow-men in his domestic and social environment. “When the angry man has calmed down,” Seneca truly observed, “he is angry with himself.” “Let anger be foreign to us,'' said Cicero, “for an angry man is incapable of acting correctly or prudently. Anything which is done in a state of agitation cannot be done properly nor can it meet with the approval of the bystanders.” (De Off., I, 38)

Let us meditate also on these apt quotations from Sacred Scripture. “A mild answer calms wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” (Prov. 15:1) “An ill-tempered man stirs up strife, but a patient man allays discord.” (Prov. 15:18)

3. Let us form the following resolutions: (1) Never to speak or never to make a decision in a moment of anger. (2) To wait until we have regained full self-control and serenity before we make any statement or perform any action. (3) Never to be disturbed by the unpleasant remarks or behaviour of others in our regard. Considering that the Saints actually looked for humiliations and penances, the least we should do is accept those God sends us and offer them to Him. (Antonio Cardinal Bacci)

text:
What does complete surrender to God mean in Christianity? 🔥

It means laying down your own will, plans, and control and fully yielding them to God. Like an army that surrenders in battle, you stop resisting, give up your rights to run your life, and let Him take over. It’s not partial or conditional. God wants all of you. 🔥

This begins when you accept Jesus as both Savior and Lord. From there it becomes a daily posture. You offer yourself as a living sacrifice in response to God’s mercy. You trust Him with all your heart and stop leaning on your own understanding. You deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Jesus every day. The goal is the reality of Galatians 2:20: it is no longer you who live, but Christ who lives in you. 🔥

Jesus Himself modeled it in Gethsemane when He prayed, “Not my will, but Yours be done.” Billy Graham often described it as the total surrender of your mind, heart, body, and will to the Lordship of Christ. You hold nothing back that you’re aware of. It is active trust, not passive resignation. You still make decisions and take responsibility, but you hold everything with open hands and let God’s will lead. 🔥

The paradox is real. The more you surrender your life to Him, the freer and more at peace you become. Your old self-centered nature is gradually replaced by one that reflects Christ. It is both a decisive moment and an ongoing walk, and it leads to the deepest human fulfillment. 🔥♥️🔥♥️🔥

text:
Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs fought on the Axis side in the Second World War. In Burma and north-eastern India, the Indian National Army fought alongside Japan against British and Allied troops. Its commanders included Prem Kumar Sahgal, a Hindu, Shah Nawaz Khan, a Muslim, and Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon, a Sikh. All three had been officers in the British Indian Army. After the war, all three were convicted at Delhi’s Red Fort of waging war against the King.

In Europe, Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs served Nazi Germany in the Free India Legion, formed under Subhas Chandra Bose. The Legion guarded the Atlantic Wall in occupied France and passed into Waffen-SS control in August 1944. During its retreat towards Germany, its men fought the French Resistance.

In the Balkans, the  Bosnian Muslim Handschar Division of the Waffen-SS fought Yugoslav Partisans. Hajj Amin al-Husayni, the former Mufti of Jerusalem, helped recruit men for the division and addressed its military imams. In October 1944, German intelligence dropped a five-man German-Arab sabotage team into the Jordan Valley. The team was intercepted before it could carry out its mission. Under interrogation, members said al-Husayni had personally briefed them.

Wartime treachery had an earlier chapter. In February 1915, Kartar Singh Sarabha, a Sikh, and Rash Behari Bose and Vishnu Ganesh Pingle, both Hindus, helped organise the Ghadar plot to provoke a mutiny within the British Indian Army. The plot was uncovered and Sarabha was later executed. Indian conspirators also worked with German officials on the Annie Larsen–Maverick scheme to ship arms to India for a rebellion. The shipment failed.

In Singapore, the mutiny went ahead. On 15th February 1915, Muslim soldiers of the 5th Light Infantry turned on their officers, attacked civilians and sabotaged infrastructure. Around 47 people were killed, most of them British.

Indian recruits who joined the Allied war effort for the pay, food and pension enlisted out of self-interest, not patriotic duty to Britain. In the Great War, the army paid 11 rupees a month and recruiters held out the promise of land. In the Second World War, service offered a steady wage, two square meals a day and standing in a man’s village. When farming began to pay better in Punjab, the army found it harder to recruit.

IN 2019, SHE BECAME THE FIRST HAUSA/FULANI MUSLIM WOMAN AND THE FIRST INDIGENE OF KATSINA STATE TO ATTAIN THE RANK OF SENIOR ADVOCATE OF NIGERIA. IN 2020, SHE BECAME A HIGH COURT JUDGE. MEET JUSTICE SAFIYA UMAR BADAMASI.

© Michael Ugah

For many Nigerian lawyers, becoming a Senior Advocate of Nigeria is the crowning achievement of a career at the Bar.

But for Safiya Umar Badamasi, taking silk was followed almost immediately by another remarkable decision: accepting appointment as a High Court judge.

Her journey deserves telling.

Born on 12 June 1968 in Malumfashi, Katsina State, she attended Aya Primary School in Funtua and Federal Government Girls’ College, Bakori.

She was good at History and Literature. A guidance and counselling teacher recognised those strengths and encouraged her to study law. Sometimes, a teacher’s advice can help shape an entire life.

She obtained a Diploma in Law in 1987. Between 1989 and 1990, she worked as an Assistant Tourism Officer in the Katsina State Ministry of Commerce and Tourism.

She subsequently transferred to the Ministry of Justice and studied law at Bayero University, Kano, between 1991 and 1995. In 1998, she was called to the Nigerian Bar.

Within the Katsina State Ministry of Justice, she built a substantial career in litigation and public service. She served as Director of Public Prosecutions from 2007 to 2018, before becoming Solicitor-General and Permanent Secretary in November 2018.

Then came 2019.

Approximately 21 years after her call to the Bar, she became a Senior Advocate of Nigeria—the first Hausa/Fulani Muslim woman to attain the rank.

And her distinction went beyond being the first woman from her state.

As reported by The Nation on 15 October 2019, the Chairman of the Nigerian Bar Association, Katsina Branch, Mr. A. A. Ahmed, expressly stated:

“Safiya Badamasi Umar (SAN) is the first indigene of Katsina State to earn the prestigious (SAN) rank.”

Her response to that achievement was particularly striking. She expressed her intention to remain in Katsina, contribute to her state and groom younger lawyers.

Then, on 7 May 2020, she was sworn in as a judge of the Katsina State High Court.

A SAN becoming a High Court judge was so unusual that her appointment generated debate among lawyers. Some reportedly described it as a “wasted slot.”

But why should accepting responsibility for administering justice diminish a lawyer’s achievement?

The High Court is where witnesses testify, evidence is tested, facts are established and decisions affecting people’s liberty, livelihoods and property are made. It deserves experienced lawyers willing to serve.

From an Assistant Tourism Officer to a litigation officer, Director of Public Prosecutions, Solicitor-General, Senior Advocate of Nigeria and High Court judge, Safiya Badamasi’s journey offers plenty to reflect on.

And somewhere in that story is a schoolteacher who saw promise in a young girl who enjoyed History and Literature.

© Michael Ugah

text:
MY DAUGHTER INVITED ME TO HER WEDDING, BUT I WAS NOT ALLOWED TO SIT WITH THE FAMILY

My name is Patricia and I live in Baltimore, Maryland. I'm 56, and I never thought I'd see the day my own daughter would make me feel like a stranger at her wedding.

I raised Amanda mostly on my own. Her father, Michael, left when she was six. He moved to another state, started a new relationship, and slowly faded out of our lives. I worked two jobs so Amanda would never go without anything important. By day I worked in a hospital cafeteria, and in the evenings I cleaned offices. Some nights I was so tired I could barely get my shoes off, but whenever Amanda needed something for school, I found a way. I never reminded her of what it cost me. I figured that's just what mothers do.

When Amanda was 24, she met Ryan. He was polite, hardworking, and came from a wealthy family. I was happy when she told me they were getting married.
The trouble started when I met Ryan's mother, Eleanor. The first thing she asked me was what I did for a living. When I told her I worked in a hospital cafeteria, she smiled politely and went right back to talking about her family's businesses with Amanda. I didn't think much of it then.

But over time I noticed she treated me differently. She'd go over the wedding plans with Amanda and Ryan without including me. Whenever I offered to help pay for something, she'd say they already had it covered.

One afternoon Amanda called to say Eleanor had recommended a wedding planner. I asked if I could meet the planner too.
"Mom, please don't make things difficult," she said. "Ryan's family is handling most of the arrangements."
That hurt, but I swallowed it. I didn't want to be the mother who caused problems before her daughter's wedding.
A few weeks later the invitation came, and I got excited and started thinking about what dress to wear. Then Amanda called again. She said there'd be a special seating arrangement. Ryan's parents would sit at the main family table, and I'd be seated with some distant relatives and family friends.

I asked why. She said Ryan's parents were hosting the reception and wanted the main table set up their way.
"I'm your mother," I reminded her.
There was a silence, and then she said, "Mom, please understand. I don't want any drama on my wedding day."
I ended the call without arguing.
On the wedding day I got there early, wearing a blue dress I'd saved up for. I'd even paid for my own hotel room so I wouldn't put anyone out. When I walked into the reception hall, I saw Eleanor sitting beside her husband, with Ryan and Amanda close by. I checked the seating chart and found my name near the back of the room.

I tried to tell myself it didn't matter. I was there to celebrate my daughter, not compete with anybody.
The real embarrassment came during the family photographs. The photographer called for the parents of the bride and groom, and Eleanor and her husband stepped up beside the newlyweds. I waited for someone to call me. Nobody did.

Eventually I walked over and asked if they wanted me in the picture.
Eleanor looked at me and said, "Oh, we've already taken the immediate family pictures. We can do another one later."
I looked at Amanda, waiting for her to say something. She just smiled awkwardly and turned back to the photographer.
Something broke inside me.

I walked outside and sat down on a bench near the parking lot. I wasn't upset because I wanted attention. I was hurt because the little girl I raised seemed embarrassed to stand next to me.
After about twenty minutes Amanda came out and asked where I'd gone. I told her I wasn't disappearing. I was trying to understand why her husband's family seemed to matter more than the woman who raised her.

She got defensive and said I was making her special day about me.
"Amanda," I said, "I didn't ask for a special seat. I didn't ask you to announce my sacrifices. I just wanted to stand next to my daughter for one photograph."

UPDATE: Jordan Wins Minority Leader 106-73

House Republicans elected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio as minority leader for the next Congress on Tuesday in a closed-door secret ballot. He defeated Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana 106 to 73, according to sources in the room.

Speaker Mike Johnson had said last week he would not seek a leadership post after the party's midterm losses. Democrats are projected to hold the House majority when the 120th Congress convenes in January.

Jordan chairs the House Judiciary Committee and co-founded the House Freedom Caucus. He will lead the minority conference starting in January.

The same vote elected Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota as minority whip over Rep. August Pfluger of Texas, 103 to 76. Conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan kept her post.

Jordan said after the vote that House Republicans will fight for American families and offer more freedom.

text:
This Veterans Day, one Michigan place offers a window into the immense effort behind wartime service: Willow Run.

By March 1944, Ford’s bomber plant was producing completed B-24 aircraft at a pace of about one every 63 minutes. The Henry Ford’s collection records the plant’s 6,000th bomber on September 9 of that year.

That production figure describes the cadence of a huge assembly operation. It does not mean a single aircraft was built from raw materials in just over an hour. The distinction helps us appreciate the real achievement: many stages of work, materials and people coordinated across an enormous system.

Historic photographs make the scale visible, but they also invite us to look for the workers within it. Michigan’s industrial story is inseparable from the people whose skills and labor supported those serving overseas.

Take a moment with the museum’s Willow Run record, and with the service stories your own family or community has preserved.

History: https://t.co/qzwaNeXcKJ

text:
The University of Michigan has several notable museums, including the University of Michigan Museum of Art, the University of Michigan Museum of Natural History, and the Kelsey Museum of Archaeology. Each museum offers unique collections and exhibits, making them significant cultural and educational resources in Ann Arbor.

I used to take the train from Detroit's beautiful train station to Ann Arbor at 6AM.  Get there around 8AM.  Go to the several of the museums.  Get McDonalds.  Come back on the train.  Take the DDOT buses back to Moross and Harper and Semta bus home.   

They are worth spending a day touring.  

My wife and I visited the museums on campus in 2016.  Just after our daughter was born.   We were amazed that almost all of the students looked normal.   Signs welcoming the US military on campus.   Some of the students told us the left wing nut jobs are not in this part of the campus.  They are by the Triangle and UofM Hospital.   

We were in the Kelsey Museum of Archaeology.   I was explaining everything to a group of students on the periods of the dinosaurs.   Their professor walked in and invited us to see his collection not on display.   My wife rolled her eyes.   We took our children back to see them a few years ago.  I convinced our children they were making velociraptors in the one lab and during Hell Week they release 3 on campus.   The staff were laughing.  One said they would if they could.

I don't know what happen to it in 10 years.

The ASP jump in AI data-center CW lasers shows how quickly value is moving upstream. Industry estimates range from USD 3–4 for 70 mW lasers to USD 15–20 for 120–150 mW NPO products and as much as USD 50–75 for 400 mW UHP lasers used in CPO. Traditional telecom laser chips once sold for only USD 0.20–0.50. Some CPO laser products may carry gross margins above 60%.

Among the main names, $COHR offers the most balanced setup, supported by its new USD 20B long-term agreement. $LITE still has strong fundamentals, although the proposed $MRVL acquisition has created a valuation overhang.

$AAOI has strong order visibility, but delivery and DSP supply remain the main concerns. Its three-year 1.6T agreement could generate USD 1B–1.5B, depending on customer demand and execution. $SIVE is targeting annual capacity of more than 100M CW DFB lasers by Q4 2027, but qualification and management communication are still holding back the valuation.

Demand is real, but most AI optical stocks are still moving together. Execution will decide which names eventually break away from the group.

text:
DOUBLEDOWN INTERACTIVE $DDI Q3'26 — EBITDA MARGIN EXPANDS TO 42.7%, BUT PROFITS FALL 44% AS A $16.25 CASH TENDER OFFER TAKES CENTRE STAGE.
DoubleDown delivered stronger operating profitability despite declining revenue. What caught my attention was the rapid shift towards direct-to-consumer sales, improving margins and the proposed acquisition of minority ADS holdings by controlling shareholder DoubleU Games.
THE NUMBERS
🔹 Revenue: $94.3M (-1.6% YoY)
🔹 Earnings Per ADS: $0.37 (vs $0.66 LY) 🔴
🔹 Net Profit Attributable to Shareholders: $18.4M (-43.9% YoY)
🔹 Operating Profit: $37.5M (vs $35.0M LY) 🟢
🔹 Adjusted EBITDA: $40.2M (+7.2% YoY)
🔹 Adjusted EBITDA Margin: 42.7% (vs 39.1% LY) 🟢
🔹 Operating Cash Flow: $23.6M (vs $33.4M LY) 🔴
BUSINESS PERFORMANCE
🔹 Social Casino Revenue: $76.8M (-3.5% YoY)
🔹 iGaming Revenue: $17.4M (+7.4% YoY)
🔹 Direct-to-Consumer Revenue: $44.6M (vs $16.6M LY)
🔹 DTC Share of Social Casino Revenue: 58.0% (vs 20.9% LY)
🔹 Payer Conversion: 9.5% (vs 7.8% LY)
🔹 Revenue Per Daily Active User: $1.44 (vs $1.39 LY)
FY26 OUTLOOK
🔹 No formal numerical revenue or EPS guidance provided.
🔹 Management continues prioritising direct-to-consumer expansion, operating efficiency and strategic acquisitions.
CORPORATE DEVELOPMENT
🔹 DoubleU Games launched an all-cash tender offer at $16.25 per ADS.
🔹 The offer targets ADSs not already owned by DoubleU Games and its affiliates.
🔹 DoubleDown's board recommends acceptance.
🔹 Completion remains subject to tender and minority-shareholder approval conditions.
🔹 Aggregate Net Cash Position: Approximately $545M.
WHAT'S CHANGING
The biggest operational development is DoubleDown's shift towards direct-to-consumer distribution.
DTC revenue increased sharply, reducing reliance on third-party platforms and helping lift adjusted EBITDA margins by 360 basis points.
But the underlying growth picture remains mixed. Social casino revenue declined, while foreign-exchange losses and higher taxes weighed on reported earnings.
MY TAKE
I like the economics behind DoubleDown's direct-to-consumer strategy.
Generating more revenue through company-owned channels reduces platform fees and supports stronger operating margins, even when overall revenue growth is weak.
But I wouldn't overlook the 44% decline in attributable profit or the reduction in operating cash flow.
The $16.25 tender offer also changes the investment discussion. Shareholders now need to consider the offer price, completion conditions and potential remaining upside rather than analysing the business purely as a long-term standalone investment.
For me, the improving operating margins are encouraging, but revenue growth and cash conversion still matter.
WHAT MATTERS NEXT
Can DoubleDown sustain its higher DTC margins, stabilise social casino revenue and restore cash flow growth?
And will the $16.25-per-ADS tender offer successfully complete?
Those are now the two most important developments I'm watching.
