text:
There are pieces of your life scattered all over the internet, and some of them are for sale. Data brokers amass web searches, financial records, and location data from millions of individuals and sell them to various clients, including the US government. Information on your recent online purchases or the route that you take to work could be sitting on hard drives around the world, waiting to be used.

While reassembling those pieces isn’t trivial, there is early evidence that LLMs might make it far easier. LLM agents could potentially do the work of intelligence analysts in a fraction of the time and for a fraction of the cost, which would enable the state to aim its all-seeing eye toward anyone, not just its highest-priority targets.

“A lot of what we think of as privacy protection isn’t so much like something that’s written in the law,” says Karen Levy, a professor of information science at Cornell University. “It just has to do with how hard or how expensive it is to learn stuff about people.” When mobile phones became widespread, gathering data about people got much cheaper, but making use of that data remained difficult. Powerful LLMs could change that.

Worries over how LLMs could facilitate mass surveillance recently made headlines around the world. According to reporting from the New York Times and the Atlantic, contract negotiations between Anthropic and the US Department of Defense fell apart in late February because Anthropic balked when the DOD demanded leeway to use the company’s models to analyze commercially available data on US citizens. When Anthropic’s rival OpenAI agreed to a DOD deal mere hours later, OpenAI faced an immediate wave of public backlash for apparently swanning past Anthropic’s red lines. Under pressure, OpenAI and the DOD later revised the contract terms.

For avid followers of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, the company’s firm stance probably didn’t come as a surprise. In a lengthy essay published to his personal website in January, Amodei had argued that AI-enabled mass surveillance could constitute a crime against humanity. The core concern underlying his dispute with the DOD was that the government might use LLM-based systems such as Claude to analyze reams of data obtained from brokers and build detailed profiles of individual Americans at scale.

There’s plenty of precedent for AI being used for mass surveillance: Most notably, governments worldwide use facial recognition to track citizens and noncitizens alike, and recent reporting indicates that US Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents have leaned heavily on facial recognition apps in order to carry out the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign. While there’s not yet any smoking-gun evidence that the US government (or anyone else) is using LLMs to conduct surveillance in the way that Amodei warns about, there’s a clear appetite for such capabilities.

Artificial analysts

The sort of surveillance against which Amodei cautions is only possible in the United States because of a legal loophole. If the police suspect you of a crime and want to peruse the location data stored on your phone to see if you were present at the scene, they need a signed warrant from a judge. That’s because the Fourth Amendment of the Constitution protects anyone in the United States from “unreasonable searches” by the government.

But when the government buys bulk data from brokers, it isn’t itself searching—it’s taking advantage of searches conducted by the people who collected and compiled the data. That creates a paradox: The government can’t look at the location information on your phone without a warrant, but if a dataset that the government has purchased contains your phone’s location data, and the government is able to link it to you, then it can effectively perform an end run around the Fourth Amendment.

The good news is that finding your information in these databases probably isn’t as easy as just searching for your name. The data that brokers sell is often stripped of obvious identifiers—it might contain, for example, location traces from millions of cell phones but not the corresponding phone numbers. But that’s not an insurmountable obstacle. A 2019 New York Times investigation of bulk cell phone location data found that it was often possible to identify the owners of individual phones by making note of their apparent work and home locations.

Even though deanonymizing data does take some effort, it’s safely within the skill set of intelligence analysts, or indeed any competent internet user, and law enforcement has used ostensibly anonymized location data to tie people to specific crimes. But those are focused searches. While the government, or other organizations, might be able to access data that describes the locations of tens or hundreds of millions of Americans, it would take an utterly impractical number of human analysts to tie all of that data to specific individuals. AI agents could potentially do it faster and more cheaply.

“One way to look at the kerfuffle with Anthropic is that the DOD wants to be able to exploit this [commercial data] loophole to the max,” says Greg Nojeim, director of the security and surveillance project at the Center for Democracy & Technology.

There’s evidence indicating that LLM agents are up to the job. At the start of this year, Northeastern University professor Tianshi Li shared a particularly ironic example. Using an LLM agent, Li analyzed a publicly available Anthropic dataset that consisted of interviews with several scientists about how they use AI. Anthropic had redacted some personally identifying information in the scientists’ responses, but the agent that Li used was able to connect descriptions of some of the subjects’ research with specific studies that they had authored. Though the agent only managed to identify a fraction of the interviewed scientists, when it did succeed it was fast and cheap: Each attempt took about four minutes and cost less than fifty cents. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment for this story.

Other studies have shown that LLMs can match pseudonymous forum accounts to LinkedIn profiles; identify writers’ native languages; isolate potentially identifying information from a user’s online post history; and infer social media users’ psychological traits, locations, incomes, sexes, and ages, among other attributes. While some of these tasks could be completed by the average person if given adequate time, others, such as native-language identification, would be challenging for anyone but an expert. “In practice, they’re doing what a competent investigator would do,” wrote Nico Dekens, senior vice president of engineering at the intelligence software company ShadowDragon, in an email to MIT Technology Review.

All of these results suggest that agents could give an unskilled worker the capabilities of a team of highly trained intelligence analysts. “[An agent] can gather information on its own and it can make plans, so it’s not like a static search query,” Li says. “It both lowers the barrier to entry and maybe pushes the limits of surveillance even farther.”

If political leaders wanted to quash dissent or punish opponents at scale, the combination of bulk data and countless virtual analysts could enable them to do so. A team of LLM agents might be able to identify the real people behind social media accounts that express negative views about the government or leverage a location dataset to compile a list of people present at a protest. Those in power could then make their lives difficult. “If government agents want to harass people, there are many opportunities to do so,” says Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

In the United States, such harassment might take subtle forms—being pulled aside for excessive screenings at the airport, for example. Elsewhere, the consequences could be more drastic. Members of China’s Uighur ethnic minority, for example, have been extensively surveilled by their government for years, and police may choose to investigate individuals based on surveillance data. For Uighurs, such investigations can result in internment and forced labor. And China appears to be interested in integrating LLMs into its surveillance system: An unsecured dataset discovered last year on a Baidu server indicates that Chinese companies are using LLMs to flag online posts for the purpose of “public opinion monitoring,” which is a priority for the Chinese government.

All of this is made worse by the fact that LLMs make mistakes. The advantage of using LLMs for mass surveillance is that they can do far more work than human analysts far more quickly, but that also makes thoroughly checking their work impossible. And because mass surveillance is, by its very nature, secretive, some who fall victim to such errors may not have any recourse.

Privacy on a precipice

For now, these threats are theoretical. It’s almost impossible to determine how the US intelligence community is using LLMs in any detail: While most government agencies are required to report how they use AI, intelligence agencies are exempt. And the companies that provide tools that the government might use to conduct surveillance are cagey about the details of their tech, at least in public materials.

“There are legitimate reasons for secrecy about how informational assets are being obtained and used for intelligence or defense purposes,” Nojeim says. “But the amount of secrecy that surrounds this use is particularly troubling because the tech is so powerful and so new and so difficult for Congress to oversee.”

That said, there are some suggestive signs about how the government might be using LLMs. For example, government agencies, including ICE and the Drug Enforcement Administration hold subscriptions to ShadowDragon’s software, and, according to Dekens, the company is currently working on incorporating LLMs into the tools it offers. “LLM agents are already very good at the mechanical side of analysis,” he wrote. “Right now, the most effective way to use them is as a copilot and workflow layer.”

And the government could certainly take advantage of those capabilities, as it has access not only to commercially available bulk data but also to proprietary datasets compiled by individual agencies. Historically, those datasets had been siloed in different agencies—the Internal Revenue Service had your tax data and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services had your health records, and they didn’t share. Last year, however, the Elon Musk–led Department of Government Efficiency reportedly mounted a crusade to centralize all that data. With the data in one place and powerful AI tools at their fingertips, members of government agencies can, in principle, construct detailed profiles of anyone.

DOGE’s data-centralization efforts and the LLM-enabled acceleration of analyst work are two sides of the same coin. In principle, both changes could help the government operate more effectively and economically. But there’s a cost. “I think there’s sometimes an assumption that inefficiency is always bad,” says Levy. “But in privacy, you actually really want things to be hard.”

Few organizations would choose inefficient procedures of their own volition, but Congress could force the government down that path. Shortly after the Anthropic debacle, a bipartisan group of senators and representatives introduced a bill that would require the government to obtain a warrant before purchasing data from data brokers. Public outcry, too, seems to have had an effect: After OpenAI was overwhelmed by opprobrium for accepting DOD contract terms that Anthropic had rejected, the company and the Pentagon modified the contract to include additional surveillance protections.

But government surveillance is not the only concern. Private companies could just as easily purchase bulk data and analyze it with LLM agents, and they are less subject to legal constraints and public opposition, especially if they aren’t household names. If it is indeed possible for LLM agents to build detailed profiles of large numbers of individuals using bulk data, companies could use those capabilities to investigate job applicants or determine whether someone is insurable. “It is very, very hard to hold to account companies that are doing whatever they want to with our data,” Levy says. “It’s hard to even know what’s happening.”

In the absence of legislation preventing such uses, we might need to rethink how we understand our own privacy. It has always been possible that someone online might unearth your address or connect you with your pseudonymous accounts, but given the effort that would take, it was easy to feel safe. Even in the wake of Edward Snowden’s 2013 revelations about the National Security Agency’s extensive surveillance of US citizens, many people reassured themselves that their privacy was still intact because the government had no reason to look into their lives.

That kind of privacy depends entirely on friction: the time and effort required to link a secret social media account with its real-life owner, or the skill and resources needed to analyze bulk datasets. Stay under the radar, and no one will care enough to overcome that friction. But LLM agents could lessen that effort, or remove it entirely. If the government and other organizations can construct detailed profiles of millions of people at the drop of a hat, no one is beneath their notice.

The data center boom may be more speculative than it looks.

Meta is losing its longtime head of infrastructure.

Santosh Janardhan (at the company since 2009, recently leading Meta Compute) is stepping down next year. He’ll be replaced by Dave Brown, who joined earlier this year from Amazon after nearly two decades focused on compute, cloud, and AI. Meta’s infrastructure spend has been ramping hard for the AI race.

text:
Yann LeCun is a Turing Award recipient and a top AI researcher, but he has long been a contrarian figure in the tech world. He believes that the industry’s current obsession with large language models is wrong-headed and will ultimately fail to solve many pressing problems. 

Instead, he thinks we should be betting on world models—a different type of AI that accurately reflects the dynamics of the real world. He is also a staunch advocate for open-source AI and criticizes the closed approach of frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic. 

Perhaps it’s no surprise, then, that he recently left Meta, where he had served as chief scientist for FAIR (Fundamental AI Research), the company’s influential research lab that he founded. Meta has struggled to gain much traction with its open-source AI model Llama and has seen internal shake-ups, including the controversial acquisition of ScaleAI. 

LeCun sat down with MIT Technology Review in an exclusive online interview from his Paris apartment to discuss his new venture, life after Meta, the future of artificial intelligence, and why he thinks the industry is chasing the wrong ideas. 

Both the questions and answers below have been edited for clarity and brevity.

You’ve just announced a new company, Advanced Machine Intelligence (AMI).  Tell me about the big ideas behind it.

It is going to be a global company, but headquartered in Paris. You pronounce it “ami”—it means “friend” in French. I am excited. There is a very high concentration of talent in Europe, but it is not always given a proper environment to flourish. And there is certainly a huge demand from the industry and governments for a credible frontier AI company that is neither Chinese nor American. I think that is going to be to our advantage.

So an ambitious alternative to the US-China binary we currently have. What made you want to pursue that third path?

Well, there are sovereignty issues for a lot of countries, and they want some control over AI. What I’m advocating is that AI is going to become a platform, and most platforms tend to become open-source. Unfortunately, that’s not really the direction the American industry is taking. Right? As the competition increases, they feel like they have to be secretive. I think that is a strategic mistake.

It’s certainly true for OpenAI, which went from very open to very closed, and Anthropic has always been closed. Google was sort of a little open. And then Meta, we’ll see. My sense is that it’s not going in a positive direction at this moment.

Simultaneously, China has completely embraced this open approach. So all leading open-source AI platforms are Chinese, and the result is that academia and startups, outside of the US, have basically embraced Chinese models. There’s nothing wrong with that—you know, Chinese models are good. Chinese engineers and scientists are great. But you know, if there is a future in which all of our information diet is being mediated by AI assistance, and the choice is either English-speaking models produced by proprietary companies always close to the US or Chinese models which may be open-source but need to be fine-tuned so that they answer questions about Tiananmen Square in 1989—you know, it’s not a very pleasant and engaging future. 

They [the future models] should be able to be fine-tuned by anyone and produce a very high diversity of AI assistance, with different linguistic abilities and value systems and political biases and centers of interests. You need high diversity of assistance for the same reason that you need high diversity of press. 

That is certainly a compelling pitch. How are investors buying that idea so far?

They really like it. A lot of venture capitalists are very much in favor of this idea of open-source, because they know for a lot of small startups, they really rely on open-source models. They don’t have the means to train their own model, and it’s kind of dangerous for them strategically to embrace a proprietary model.

You recently left Meta. What’s your view on the company and Mark Zuckerberg’s leadership? There’s a perception that Meta has fumbled its AI advantage.

I think FAIR [LeCun’s lab at Meta] was extremely successful in the research part. Where Meta was less successful is in picking up on that research and pushing it into practical technology and products. Mark made some choices that he thought were the best for the company. I may not have agreed with all of them. For example, the robotics group at FAIR was let go, which I think was a strategic mistake. But I’m not the director of FAIR. People make decisions rationally, and there’s no reason to be upset.

So, no bad blood? Could Meta be a future client for AMI?

Meta might be our first client! We’ll see. The work we are doing is not in direct competition. Our focus on world models for the physical world is very different from their focus on generative AI and LLMs.

You were working on AI long before LLMs became a mainstream approach. But since ChatGPT broke out, LLMs have become almost synonymous with AI.

Yes, and we are going to change that. The public face of AI, perhaps, is mostly LLMs and chatbots of various types. But the latest ones of those are not pure LLMs. They are LLM plus a lot of things, like perception systems and code that solves particular problems. So we are going to see LLMs as kind of the orchestrator in systems, a little bit.

Beyond LLMs, there is a lot of AI that is behind the scenes that runs a big chunk of our society. There are assistance driving programs in a car, quick-turn MRI images, algorithms that drive social media—that’s all AI. 

You have been vocal in arguing that LLMs can only get us so far. Do you think LLMs are overhyped these days? Can you summarize to our readers why you believe that LLMs are not enough?

There is a sense in which they have not been overhyped, which is that they are extremely useful to a lot of people, particularly if you write text, do research, or write code. LLMs manipulate language really well. But people have had this illusion, or delusion, that it is a matter of time until we can scale them up to having human-level intelligence, and that is simply false.

The truly difficult part is understanding the real world. This is the Moravec Paradox (a phenomenon observed by the computer scientist Hans Moravec in 1988): What’s easy for us, like perception and navigation, is hard for computers, and vice versa. LLMs are limited to the discrete world of text. They can’t truly reason or plan, because they lack a model of the world. They can’t predict the consequences of their actions. This is why we don’t have a domestic robot that is as agile as a house cat, or a truly autonomous car.

We are going to have AI systems that have humanlike and human-level intelligence, but they’re  not going to be built on LLMs, and it’s not going to happen next year or two years from now. It’s going to take a while. There are major conceptual breakthroughs that have to happen before we have AI systems that have human-level intelligence. And that is what I’ve been working on. And this company, AMI Labs, is focusing on the next generation.

And your solution is world models and JEPA architecture (JEPA, or “joint embedding predictive architecture,” is a learning framework that trains AI models to understand the world, created by LeCun while he was at Meta). What’s the elevator pitch?

The world is unpredictable. If you try to build a generative model that predicts every detail of the future, it will fail.  JEPA is not generative AI. It is a system that learns to represent videos really well. The key is to learn an abstract representation of the world and make predictions in that abstract space, ignoring the details you can’t predict. That’s what JEPA does. It learns the underlying rules of the world from observation, like a baby learning about gravity. This is the foundation for common sense, and it’s the key to building truly intelligent systems that can reason and plan in the real world. The most exciting work so far on this is coming from academia, not the big industrial labs stuck in the LLM world.

The lack of non-text data has been a problem in taking AI systems further in understanding the physical world. JEPA is trained on videos. What other kinds of data will you be using?

Our systems will be trained on video, audio, and sensor data of all kinds—not just text. We are working with various modalities, from the position of a robot arm to lidar data to audio. I’m also involved in a project using JEPA to model complex physical and clinical phenomena. 

What are some of the concrete, real-world applications you envision for world models?

The applications are vast. Think about complex industrial processes where you have thousands of sensors, like in a jet engine, a steel mill, or a chemical factory. There is no technique right now to build a complete, holistic model of these systems. A world model could learn this from the sensor data and predict how the system will behave. Or think of smart glasses that can watch what you’re doing, identify your actions, and then predict what you’re going to do next to assist you. This is what will finally make agentic systems reliable. An agentic system that is supposed to take actions in the world cannot work reliably unless it has a world model to predict the consequences of its actions. Without it, the system will inevitably make mistakes. This is the key to unlocking everything from truly useful domestic robots to Level 5 autonomous driving.

Humanoid robots are all the rage recently, especially ones built by companies from China. What’s your take?

There are all these brute-force ways to get around the limitations of learning systems, which require inordinate amounts of training data to do anything. So the secret of all the companies getting robots to do kung fu or dance is they are all planned in advance. But frankly, nobody—absolutely nobody—knows how to make those robots smart enough to be useful. Take my word for it. 


You need an enormous amount of tele-operation training data for every single task, and when the environment changes a little bit, it doesn’t generalize very well. What this tells us is we are missing something very big. The reason why a 17-year-old can learn to drive in 20 hours is because they already know a lot about how the world behaves. If we want a generally useful domestic robot, we need systems to have a kind of good understanding of the physical world. That’s not going to happen until we have good world models and planning.

There’s a growing sentiment that it’s becoming harder to do foundational AI research in academia because of the massive computing resources required. Do you think the most important innovations will now come from industry?

No. LLMs are now technology development, not research. It’s true that it’s very difficult for academics to play an important role there because of the requirements for computation, data access, and engineering support. But it’s a product now. It’s not something academia should even be interested in. It’s like speech recognition in the early 2010s—it was a solved problem, and the progress was in the hands of industry. 

What academia should be working on is long-term objectives that go beyond the capabilities of current systems. That’s why I tell people in universities: Don’t work on LLMs. There is no point. You’re not going to be able to rival what’s going on in industry. Work on something else. Invent new techniques. The breakthroughs are not going to come from scaling up LLMs. The most exciting work on world models is coming from academia, not the big industrial labs. The whole idea of using attention circuits in neural nets came out of the University of Montreal. That research paper started the whole revolution. Now that the big companies are closing up, the breakthroughs are going to slow down. Academia needs access to computing resources, but they should be focused on the next big thing, not on refining the last one.

You wear many hats: professor, researcher, educator, public thinker … Now you just took on a new one. What is that going to look like for you?

I am going to be the executive chairman of the company, and Alex LeBrun [a former colleague from Meta AI] will be the CEO. It’s going to be LeCun and LeBrun—it’s nice if you pronounce it the French way.

I am going to keep my position at NYU. I teach one class per year, I have PhD students and postdocs, so I am going to be kept based in New York. But I go to Paris pretty often because of my lab. 

Does that mean that you won’t be very hands-on?

Well, there’s two ways to be hands-on. One is to manage people day to day, and another is to actually get your hands dirty in research projects, right? 

I can do management, but I don’t like doing it. This is not my mission in life. It’s really to make science and technology progress as far as we can, inspire other people to work on things that are interesting, and then contribute to those things. So that has been my role at Meta for the last seven years. I founded FAIR and led it for four to five years. I kind of hated being a director. I am not good at this career management thing. I’m much more visionary and a scientist.

What makes Alex LeBrun the right fit?

Alex is a serial entrepreneur; he’s built three successful AI companies. The first he sold to Microsoft; the second to Facebook, where he was head of the engineering division of FAIR in Paris. He then left to create Nabla, a very successful company in the health-care space. When I offered him the chance to join me in this effort, he accepted almost immediately. He has the experience to build the company, allowing me to focus on science and technology. 

You’re headquartered in Paris. Where else do you plan to have offices?

We are a global company. There’s going to be an office in North America.

New York, hopefully?

New York is great. That’s where I am, right? And it’s not Silicon Valley. Silicon Valley is a bit of a monoculture.

What about Asia? I’m guessing Singapore, too?

Probably, yeah. I’ll let you guess. 

And how are you attracting talent?

We don’t have any issue recruiting. There are a lot of people in the AI research community who think the future of AI is in world models. Those people, regardless of pay package, will be motivated to come work for us because they believe in the technological future we are building. We’ve already recruited people from places like OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and xAI.

I heard that Saining Xie, a prominent researcher from NYU and Google DeepMind, might be joining you as chief scientist. Any comments?

Saining is a brilliant researcher. I have a lot of admiration for him. I hired him twice already. I hired him at FAIR, and I convinced my colleagues at NYU that we should hire him there. Let’s just say I have a lot of respect for him.

When will you be ready to share more details about AMI Labs, like financial backing or other core members?

Soon—in February, maybe. I’ll let you know.

Respectfully, data integrity and inferred activity patterns are two very different things. Data integrity concerns the accuracy and integrity of stored information, while inferred patterns are a privacy and profiling issue. Much of the internet operates on such inferences using data collected by large technology companies. Third-party SDK risks are worth discussing, but they aren't evidence that our users' financial data is being leaked, shared, or compromised.

Secondly, we genuinely care about our users, but we also understand the ground realities of operating in Pakistan. It's no secret how difficult it is to convince users to pay for subscriptions here, while infrastructure and PSX licensing costs are very real.

And since you brought Grok into this discussion, there's an interesting irony: people are often happy to pay large global tech companies for subscriptions (and you seem to be one of them), yet question why a Pakistani-built app needs to monetize to survive.

We offer an ad-free subscription for precisely this reason. Users who don't want ads have that choice. We'd love to see the same willingness to support local products that we routinely show international ones.

Pressure can make an otherwise useful offer harder to consider.

Reactance is one reason: people can resist when they feel their freedom to choose is being threatened, even if the offer could help them.

These tactics can create that pressure:

→ Use fake countdown timers that reset every visit
→ Box people into "buy now or lose it forever" ultimatums
→ Shame them for not buying ("Don't you want to succeed?")

The fix:

Respect autonomy. ("Here are your options.")
Offer real choices, not ultimatums.
Use urgency honestly, or don't use it at all.

Give people enough information to decide whether the offer suits them, including the price, terms and what happens next.

A clear offer gives the customer room to make an informed choice.

As an employer, there’s nothing I can do about that. That’s a question for their parents and other support systems in their lives. 

I supported my kids so that they could have the time to focus on High School and College and get what they needed out of it.

But also, I’m struggling to find too much sympathy for this “meet my needs” framing. I started working at 14 doing my time in food service and expanded that into a tech support job, then a programming job. I grew up dirt poor and had to pull up by my own bootstraps for my career. No one owed me anything. If I wanted a job, I had to work for it.

I’m sympathetic to the number of kids out of work. That sucks. And I want to employ them. Seems like a fantastic pool of untapped talent on the surface. 

But a business is not a charity. They have to offer a better product than, “I did the things other people told me to do, why won’t you hire me?”

On Thursday, November 12, 2026, the state of Oklahoma is set to execute by lethal injection James Dwight Pavatt, age 72, for the 2001 Oklahoma County murder of Robert Dale Andrew, age 39. The incident and the trials that followed received a high level of media attention. This will be the fourth execution in the state this year and the 133rd since the resumption of the death penalty in 1990.

In peaceful opposition to the death penalty, a prayer vigil will be held near the front gate of the penitentiary, starting a 9:00am. Prayers will be offered for Andrew, Pavatt, their families, along with the correction officers taking part in the execution. The vigil will continue until the execution is carried out shortly after 10:00am. People of all faiths are welcome to take part in the vigil.

Other vigils taking place on November12 in opposition to the execution include the following.

Oklahoma City: 
The Oklahoma Coalition to Abolish the Death Penalty will host a vigil outside the Governor’s Mansion, 820 NE 223rd Street at Philip Avenue starting at 9am.

Tulsa Metro:
St. Scholastica Chapel at the Church of Saint Benedict, 2200 West Ithica Street, Broken Arrow. No formal service is planned but the chapel will be open to those who wish to pray for this intention.

McAlester:
Death Penalty Action will hold a vigil near the front gate of the penitentiary starting at 9am.

Multiple samples show Florida Atlantic attracting more tickets, while two show William & Mary receiving proportionally larger wagers. One sportsbook has reduced the favorite’s spread by a point, although others remain near the opener.

STATUS: CORROBORATED CONTRARIAN MONEY INTEREST. PARTIAL LINE-MOVEMENT CONFIRMATION. No independently established additional edge at the available price.

text:
The answer is that God had already established an arrangement for forgiveness before Jesus came. Under the Mosaic Law, animal sacrifices were required for the Israelites to receive forgiveness for certain sins.

For example, Leviticus 4:20 says that when the priest made atonement for the people, "they will be forgiven." So, those sacrifices were not meaningless; God had accepted them as part of the arrangement he had established.

However, the animal sacrifices were temporary. They could not permanently remove sin because animals were inferior to humans and could not provide the equivalent ransom for Adam's perfect human life. Hebrews 10:4 says: "It is not possible for the blood of bulls and of goats to take sins away."

So, how could God forgive people who lived before Jesus died?

God knew that Jesus would eventually offer his perfect human life as the ransom. On that basis, he could justly forgive repentant people who demonstrated faith in him, even before the ransom was actually paid. Romans 3:25 explains that God showed forbearance regarding sins committed in the past.

Then Jesus came and provided what animal sacrifices could never accomplish: a perfect, once-for-all sacrifice. (Hebrews 9:12; 10:10.)

In essence, animal sacrifices were part of God's temporary arrangement for forgiveness under the Law, but Jesus' sacrifice became the permanent and complete basis for forgiveness for all faithful people, both those who lived before him and those who came after him. ❤️

🔑⛵️ Phoenician Technology, Celestial Philosophy, & the Rare Historical Apparatus of Ramsay - 63-73 - 63. The Crescent Harbour of Tyre and Ancient Maritime Geometry - Ramsay's seventh book describes New Tyre as an island city approximately thirteen furlongs from the shore, possessing a crescent-shaped geographical arrangement that enclosed a sheltered harbour.
The account includes protective fortifications, maritime installations, a mole, and the employment of cedar trees within the port landscape.
This passage provides an unusually detailed literary source for studying ancient harbour construction, maritime defence, coastal geography, and the relationship between commercial cities and their artificial installations.

Its comparative value extends into Phoenician maritime archaeology and ancient descriptions of Tyre preserved by classical historians.

64. The Phoenician Discovery of Monetary Divisibility

In the Tyrian episode, Ramsay explains the practical difficulties associated with direct barter.
Perishable goods, changing exchange values, transportation costs, and the inconvenience of subdividing commodities lead into a discussion of money as a common measure of value.
Ramsay emphasizes properties including durability, portability, and divisibility.
This passage represents a substantial eighteenth-century contribution to the philosophical history of commerce.
It deserves comparison with Aristotle's discussion of exchange in the Politics and Nicomachean Ethics, together with the history of ancient metallic currency, weighing practices, and commercial institutions.
65. Soranes and the Hidden Psychology of Political Counsel
Ramsay's account of Persian political affairs introduces Soranes, whose intelligence, ambition, and extraordinary talents for administration are explored through a sustained psychological narrative.

The character's influence upon courts and rulers provides material for examining the philosophy of counsel, political manipulation, rhetorical persuasion, and the governance of powerful states.
Particularly interesting is the relationship Ramsay establishes between intellectual ability and the inward disposition of the counsellor.

The passage contributes to the history of moral psychology and the literary examination of conscience within eighteenth-century philosophical truths. 

66. The Ancient Bestiary of Moral and Celestial Disorder
Ramsay's Phoenician narrative associates the exploits of a mediating hero with the destruction of monstrous beings, including the serpent Python, the Nemean lion, and the Hydra of Lerna.

These creatures possess distinctive anatomical and symbolic features within ancient literature.

The investigation could be enlarged through the medieval bestiaries, Greek mythographers, Renaissance natural historians, and early modern discussions concerning prodigies and unusual creatures.

67. The Metaphorical Physiology of Ancient Political Bodies

Throughout The Travels of Cyrus, Ramsay repeatedly develops relationships between the constitution of the human body and the organization of the commonwealth.
Circulation, balance, nourishment, disciplined action, and the regulation of bodily faculties furnish conceptual parallels for government, political health, military organization, and legislation.

The relationship possesses considerable importance for the history of organic political philosophy, especially the longstanding practice of representing the state through bodily structures and functions.
The subject can be compared with Plato, Aristotle, John of Salisbury, and the anatomical-political analogies of early-modern European writers.

68. Animal Sensibility and the Archaic Philosophy of the Brute Soul

In the appended theological discourse, Ramsay discusses the nature of animal sensation and the philosophical explanations offered for the perceptive capacities of nonhuman creatures.
He considers the relationships among bodily mechanism, sensation, intelligence, and the immaterial powers attributed to living beings.
The passage provides an important historical contribution to the study of animal consciousness and the philosophical status of sensitive life.
Its comparative apparatus could include Aristotle's De Anima, the writings of Pierre Gassendi, the Cartesian discussions of animal mechanism, and Ralph Cudworth's investigations into the operations of living nature.

69. The Patristic Preservation of Ancient Philosophical Testimony
Ramsay's appended discourse contains a rich series of references to early Christian writers who preserved, discussed, or challenged doctrines associated with ancient philosophers.

These authorities include Eusebius, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Arnobius, and other ecclesiastical authors.
The documentary importance lies in the survival of fragments of ancient religious philosophy through Christian theological literature.

A particularly productive scholarly investigation would catalogue every ancient author cited by Ramsay, establish the precise original passage, identify the surviving manuscript or printed tradition, and compare the eighteenth-century quotation with its Greek or Latin source.
Such an apparatus would substantially enlarge the historical bibliography of comparative theology.

70. Orphic Literary Attribution and the Preservation of Ancient Hymnic Theology

Ramsay discusses works attributed to Orpheus and examines the testimony preserved by Suidas, Cedrenus, Eusebius, Proclus, and other authorities.
His investigation raises questions concerning the historical authorship, literary transmission, and theological significance of Orphic material.

The cited passages concern the primordial source of beings, the formation of the heavens, and the intellectual interpretation of Divine unity.

This subject offers a valuable contribution to ancient textual criticism, especially the reconstruction of fragmentary literature preserved through later quotations.
A specialist study could assemble the original Greek texts, early Latin translations, and the distinctive interpretations introduced by Renaissance and early-modern scholars.

71. The Astronomical Canon of Nabonassar and the Chronology of Cyrus

Nicolas Fréret's appended letter provides a particularly important investigation into the chronological systems used to reconstruct ancient Near Eastern history.

He discusses the era of Nabonassar, the reigns of Babylonian and Persian monarchs, and the chronological position of Cyrus.

His calculations employ regnal years, Olympiads, and comparisons among ancient historical authorities.
This is a promising field for reconstructing the relationship between astronomical eras and historical chronology, particularly where biblical events are synchronized with Babylonian and Persian royal succession.
A chronological appendix could reproduce Fréret's calculations, establish the dates he attributes to each reign, and compare them with the ancient sources upon which he depended.

72. The Chronological Reconciliation of Herodotus, Ctesias, and Xenophon
Fréret's letter examines differing historical accounts of Cyrus and the succession of the Median and Persian kings.

He compares the narratives associated with Herodotus, Ctesias, and Xenophon, while considering the chronological relationships among Astyages, Croesus, Cyrus, and the Babylonian monarchy.
The important contribution lies in his attempt to connect multiple literary histories through a coherent sequence of dates and events.

This provides an especially useful source for examining eighteenth-century historical method, the use of chronological tables, and the relationship between philosophical historical fiction and ancient documentary testimony.

73. The Babylonian Royal Affliction and the Restoration of Nebuchadnezzar

Ramsay's eighth book incorporates the remarkable biblical account of Nebuchadnezzar's humiliation and restoration.

The king's extraordinary condition is associated with the prophetic authority of Daniel and the recognition of the sovereignty of the Most High.

The episode provides extensive material for examining ancient traditions of royal transformation, divine judgment, the symbolism of animal existence, and the restoration of political authority.
Its biblical foundation belongs especially to Daniel 4, while its literary reception may be explored through Josephus, ancient Christian commentators, and the historical development of theological interpretations concerning the king's affliction.

text:
🔑📜✨️ CONT. - 60. The Solitary Hermes and the Intuitive Discovery of the First Mover - One of Ramsay's most extraordinary philosophical episodes concerns Hermes, whose early life is represented through an account of isolation, animal nurture, and the gradual awakening of human intelligence. After being sustained by a she-goat, Hermes observes the death of the creature and attempts to understand the origin of life.
His subsequent reflections upon the sun, stars, plants, animals, and the operations of his own mind lead him toward the conception of a First Mover.

This narrative invites comparison with the Arabic philosophical romance Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān by Ibn Ṭufayl.

Its scholarly significance extends into theories of intuitive knowledge, intellectual receptivity, self-consciousness, natural theology, and the philosophical ascent from sensible observation toward the apprehension of ultimate causation.

61. The Earless Heathen Jupiter and the Symbolism of Divine Omniscience

Ramsay describes a 
representation of Jupiter formed without ears, intended to signify that the Supreme Being requires no bodily organ in order to receive the prayers and petitions of mankind.

The unusual image provides an important avenue into the history of apophatic iconography, the representation of divine attributes through the omission or alteration of physical features.

The associated temple includes figures representing Truth and Justice, together with symbolic architectural arrangements.
The scene deserves comparison with ancient philosophical discussions concerning the incorporeal nature of God, divine knowledge, and the limitations of human figurative representation.

62. The Geometrical Corpuscles of Ancient Elemental Philosophy

Ramsay's account of Egyptian natural philosophy associates the constituent particles of matter with elementary geometrical forms
Invisible points, lines, surfaces, and more complex corporeal structures become conceptual instruments for explaining the composition and transformation of material substances.

The passage introduces a particularly interesting historical relationship between geometry, corpuscular philosophy, elemental matter, and the intellectual classification of physical forms.
It can be compared with Plato's Timaeus, ancient atomistic doctrines, early theories of matter, and the geometrical natural philosophy of the seventeenth century.

Principal source: Ramsay, The Travels of Cyrus, Books II–III, especially printed pp. 49–108, together with the Egyptian natural-philosophical descriptions and their original learned references.
author: texasmadde
authorBio: 📜 Specialist in Ancient Near east Levantine/Asia Minor Linguistics + Multidisciplinary Ancient Phenomenology + Mythology/Wonder Workings & Metaphysics

text:
🔑📜 ✨️Extraordinary Natural Philosophy, Mineralogical Phenomena, and the Ancient Sciences of Egypt - 52. The Colossal Geographical Monuments of Sesostris
Ramsay's Egyptian narrative recounts the legendary campaigns of Sesostris, describing a sovereign whose conquests were commemorated upon monuments throughout distant territories.

The account ranges from the lands of the Indus to western regions and introduces monumental inscriptions bearing extraordinary royal titles.

This material contributes to the history of ancient geographical imagination, the literary traditions of Egyptian imperial conquest, and the interpretation of monuments as evidence of political authority.
A specialist inquiry could trace the development of the Sesostris tradition through Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, Strabo, and the early-modern antiquarians, identifying the geographical names and historical testimonies employed by Ramsay.

53. Three Hundred Egyptian Priestly Statues and the Memorialization of Sacred Succession

In Ramsay's third book, the priest Sonchis introduces Cyrus to a hall containing three hundred statues of Egyptian high priests.
The scene provides an unusual representation of religious institutional memory, in which a succession of sacerdotal figures is preserved through sculptural commemoration.
Its historical implications extend into priestly genealogy, statue inscription, temple administration, and the architectural preservation of religious authority.
A comparative study could examine ancient Egyptian priestly lists, temple reliefs, memorial inscriptions, and the classical authors who described the antiquity of Egyptian institutions.

54. Egyptian Sacred Acoustics and the Ceremonial Administration of Silence

Ramsay describes an elaborate temple ceremony involving musical instruments, priestly proclamation, repeated prostration, and a sudden collective silence.
The invocation of Ammon, described as the unknown and incomprehensible deity within the priestly exposition, produces an atmosphere of profound ritual attention.
This passage is especially useful for studying ancient theories of sacred sound, ceremonial acoustics, collective participation, and the architectural conditions of religious performance.
The relation between spoken invocation, instrumental music, and deliberate silence also provides material for examining the history of contemplative religious practices.

55. Egyptian Funerary Anthropology and the Separation of the Mortal Remains

The Egyptian sections contain a detailed account of funeral observances, including the removal of bodily organs, the handling of an urn, embalming, and the deposition of the deceased.
Ramsay associates these ceremonies with ancient Egyptian ideas concerning immortality and the moral condition of the soul.
This source opens an extensive avenue into ancient embalming practices, mortuary architecture, the symbolism of funerary vessels, and the relationship between bodily preservation and religious expectations concerning the afterlife.

The passage is especially valuable when compared with the writings of Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, and Porphyry.

56. Piscine Hydrostatics and the Mechanical Receptivity of Aquatic Creatures

A particularly unusual natural-philosophical passage concerns the movements of fish within water.

Ramsay describes internal bodily structures whose expansion and contraction alter an animal's buoyancy, together with the rounded construction of fish eyes and their relationship to the refraction of light beneath the water.
These observations invite an investigation into the historical understanding of swim bladders, hydrostatic equilibrium, optical adaptation, and the anatomy of aquatic creatures.
The passage may be enlarged through seventeenth- and eighteenth-century comparative anatomy, including the investigations of John Ray, Francis Willughby, and other natural historians.
It provides a strong example of the minute mechanical structures through which earlier natural philosophers contemplated the workmanship of Creation.

57. The Archaic Mineral Genesis of Gold, Mercury, Copper, and Crystals
Ramsay's Egyptian natural philosophy contains an unusually detailed historical account of mineral formation.
The narrative describes sulphur and mercury as constituents of metals and associates the formation of precious stones with combinations involving metallic and crystalline substances.
Gold, mercury, and copper are assigned particular roles within this speculative mineralogical system.
The historical value lies in reconstructing the chemical vocabulary and explanatory principles employed by natural philosophers before the full development of modern chemical nomenclature.
Its comparative apparatus should include alchemical writings concerning sulphur and mercury, early theories of crystallization, metallic generation, and the mineralogical observations of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century investigators

58. Petrified Marine Creatures and the Diluvial Interpretation of the Earth's Interior
Ramsay's Egyptian philosophical discourse describes petrified remains discovered within the earth and upon elevated mountains.
These remains, including aquatic creatures, are interpreted within the historical doctrine of a universal inundation.
The account provides valuable material for studying the relationship between fossil discoveries, biblical interpretations of the Flood, ancient theories of geological transformation, and the history of natural theology.
Particular comparative sources include John Woodward's An Essay Toward a Natural History of the Earth (1695), William Whiston's A New Theory of the Earth (1696), and earlier natural histories preserving descriptions of petrified marine organisms.

59. The Monumental Union of Egyptian Engineering and Historical Memory

Ramsay describes Egypt through its canals, agricultural landscapes, obelisks, pyramids, royal monuments, and carefully organized settlements.
These architectural and hydraulic features provide an unusually broad field for the historical study of engineering as a component of political and religious civilization.
The obelisk is presented as a vehicle of historical commemoration, while the pyramid functions within the mortuary arrangements of distinguished individuals.
The connection between cultivation, water management, monumental construction, and royal authority permits investigation into the practical knowledge underlying the historical organization of the Nile Valley.

text:
Paul teaches that food previously sacrificed to idols is not inherently unclean or sinful (because idols are nothing), so Christians have liberty to eat it in ordinary contexts, but that liberty is strictly limited by love for weaker believers and by the absolute prohibition against participating in actual idolatrous worship. ￼
The main passages are 1 Corinthians 8–10 (Paul’s direct answer to the Corinthian question) and the parallel discussion of disputable matters in Romans 14.
Theological foundation (1 Corinthians 8:4–6, 8)
Paul agrees with the “strong” Corinthians that “an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one.” For believers there is one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ. Consequently, the food itself is neutral: “Meat commendeth us not to God: for neither, if we eat, are we the better; neither, if we eat not, are we the worse.”
Absolute boundary: no participation in idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:14–22)
Paul draws a sharp line against actual involvement in pagan cultic meals. “Flee from idolatry.” What pagans sacrifice they sacrifice to demons, not to God, and believers cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons or partake of the Lord’s table and the table of demons. This is not mere social dining; it is fellowship with demons. Many interpreters see the meals “in an idol’s temple” mentioned in 8:10 as falling under this prohibition when they function as genuine cultic acts, or at least as highly dangerous associations. ￼
Practical liberty in ordinary settings (1 Corinthians 10:23–27)
Outside of actual idolatrous participation, Paul affirms freedom:
•“Whatsoever is sold in the shambles [meat market], that eat, asking no question for conscience sake: For the earth is the Lord’s, and the fulness thereof” (quoting Psalm 24:1).
•If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you go, “whatsoever is set before you, eat, asking no question for conscience sake.”
All things are lawful, but not all are expedient or edifying; the guiding principle is seeking the good of others rather than one’s own rights.
Limitation by love and the weak conscience (1 Corinthians 8:7–13; 10:28–29)
Not everyone possesses this knowledge. Some (recent converts still habituated to idols) still eat the food “as a thing offered unto an idol,” and their weak conscience is defiled. If a strong believer’s example emboldens such a person to eat against conscience, the weak brother is harmed or even destroyed, and the strong one sins against Christ. Paul’s personal resolve is extreme: “If meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth.”
If someone explicitly informs you that the food was offered to an idol, do not eat—for the sake of that person’s conscience (not your own). Liberty is not judged by another’s conscience in the abstract, but love forbids wounding a brother for whom Christ died.
Parallel in Romans 14
The same logic appears more broadly. Nothing is unclean of itself, yet “to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean.” Do not destroy with your food the one for whom Christ died. The kingdom of God is not meat and drink but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Whatever is not of faith is sin. Strong believers are free; they must not use that freedom to grieve or cause the weak to stumble.
Relation to the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15)
The decree advised Gentile believers to abstain from things offered to idols (along with blood, things strangled, and fornication). This was primarily a practical measure to enable table fellowship between Jewish and Gentile Christians and to keep converts clear of the idolatry and immorality associated with pagan temples. Paul does not contradict it; he applies and nuances it by distinguishing actual cultic participation (forbidden) from ordinary market food of unknown or non-cultic origin (permitted when it does not harm a brother’s conscience). ￼

The white Christian man arrived to put an end to paganism and the widespread practice of human sacrifice among indigenous peoples—brown, black, and white—around the world.

In Maya and Aztec societies, captives and slaves were routinely dragged up temple pyramids, held down on stone altars, and had their chests cut open with obsidian knives so priests could rip out their still-beating hearts as offerings to the gods. Victims were also decapitated, thrown alive into sacred cenotes, or flayed; their skulls were displayed on racks, and in some cases parts of the bodies were eaten. These were not rare events—major temples could see thousands sacrificed in a single ceremony, and constant warfare was waged largely to capture more victims.

White pagan societies in Europe practiced their own aggressive forms of ritual violence. In the Roman world, human sacrifice was carried out in earlier periods and in moments of crisis, including the live burial of Gauls and Greeks after the Battle of Cannae, while the origins of the gladiatorial games lay in the ritual slaughter of captives as funeral offerings to the dead. Among Germanic tribes, archaeological evidence from bog bodies shows victims who were hanged, throat-cut, bludgeoned, or subjected to multiple forms of killing in overkill rituals; captives and slaves were offered as blood sacrifices to gods such as Odin, often drowned, stabbed, or left hanging from sacred trees, and prisoners taken in war were regularly killed to honor the gods and the dead.

Black pagan societies in Africa also practiced large-scale human sacrifice. In kingdoms such as Dahomey, Ashanti, Benin, and others, captives, slaves, and criminals were regularly killed as offerings to the gods and ancestors—often by beheading, throat-cutting, or live burial during annual festivals and royal ceremonies. Thousands could be sacrificed in a single custom; skulls and body parts were displayed, and warfare was frequently conducted to supply victims for these rituals.

Jews practiced paganism and human sacrifice. Kings Ahaz and Manasseh made their sons pass through the fire. People burned their children in the Valley of Hinnom. Solomon built high places for Chemosh and Molech. The Northern Kingdom set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan. Ahab and Jezebel promoted Baal worship. High places, Asherah poles, and foreign cults were repeatedly established and used. These acts are recorded in 2 Kings 16:3, 21:6, 1 Kings 11, 1 Kings 12, 1 Kings 16–18, Jeremiah 7 and 19, and elsewhere.

Across these cultures, the belief that the gods required human life and blood was widespread, and warfare often supplied the victims. With the coming of Jesus Christ, the New Testament, and the spread of Christianity, these sacrificial systems and the pagan practices that sustained them were nullified and destroyed. The New Testament declares that the death of Jesus is the final sacrifice that ends every blood offering, and Christian expansion suppressed and replaced these rites wherever it took hold. Christians themselves were also sacrificed and killed for refusing to participate in pagan rites and for working to stop them.

Jesus Christ is King.

text:
Sincere questioning comes from a real place of seeking, and that is welcome in Sanatana Dharma. There is no rule against worshipping Brahma, and nothing in the tradition frowns upon genuine respect for him. The simple reason he is not worshipped the way Vishnu and Shiva are lies in both the nature of the roles and expressions in the Puranas.

Manifestations of reality 
———————————-

Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva are three aspects of the same undivided Reality. Brahma creates, Vishnu sustains what has been created so that life and dharma can continue, and Shiva dissolves forms so that renewal and liberation become possible. Creation, once it has begun for a cycle, is already complete. The ongoing relationship between the Divine and the devotee is felt most naturally in the work of preservation and in the grace that removes ignorance. This is why devotion has gravitated towards Vishnu and Shiva

From the Puranas
——————————
Traditional accounts give a story form to this understanding. In the Shiva Purana, Brahma and Vishnu once argued about who was greater. An infinite pillar of light appeared between them. Vishnu admitted he could not find its end. Brahma claimed he had reached the top and brought a ketaki flower as false proof. Shiva, knowing the pillar is beginningless and endless, rebuked the falsehood. The episode is remembered as the reason temples dedicated only to Brahma remain few. It teaches that even the creative principle is subject to truth and humility.

A parallel story appears in the Padma Purana (Srishti Khanda, Chapter 17). When Brahma performed a yajna at Pushkar and his consort Savitri was delayed, the ritual was completed with Gayatri. Savitri, in her anger, declared that Brahma would receive little temple worship on earth, sparing the Pushkar site itself. The famous Brahma temple at Pushkar stands as the living exception, and special worship continues there during the month of Kartika. These stories do not reduce Brahma’s cosmic role. They simply explain the pattern of popular worship that has developed over time.

Natural difference
————————-

Vishnu’s avatars make the preserving grace tangible in human form, which is why devotion to him spreads so widely. Shiva’s presence as the auspicious one and the remover of bondage offers a direct path beyond form. Brahma’s work of creation is already accomplished. It is honoured every time a new life begins, every time the Vedas are recited, and every time the cosmos is seen as an expression of the One. The heart naturally turns toward the forms that sustain and liberate.

Choice of a seeker
—————————

Nothing in Sanatana Dharma restricts sincere reverence. The Bhagavad Gita (especially Chapters 10 and 11) shows that all powers rest in the one Supreme. The Upanishads affirm the same truth in different words: the Reality is one, yet it appears in countless ways. You may study Brahma, offer simple respect, or simply understand his place without any conflict. What matters is the sincerity of the heart. Sanatana Dharma has always held that the Divine meets the seeker in the form that awakens love and clarity. #SanatanaDharma  #SeekerMind

text:
A man spent 11 years entering the same local photography competition under a different name. Nobody knew he was submitting pictures taken by people who couldn’t afford cameras.

It began when he found an old camera at a yard sale in Oregon.

The seller was a teenage boy who had been trying to raise money for his school’s photography club. The camera barely worked, but the man bought it anyway and paid him more than the asking price.

A week later, he saw a photograph taken by the boy displayed in a coffee shop.

It was a picture of an empty basketball court after rain. Nothing extraordinary, except the reflection of the hoop looked like a doorway into another world.

The man asked who took it.

When he learned the boy had no money to print or submit his work, he offered to help.

Then he started noticing other talented people whose photographs never made it beyond their phones.

He began paying their competition entry fees anonymously.

There was just one unusual condition: every photograph had to be submitted under the photographer’s real name.

He never wanted credit.

text:
Duke Leto didn’t simply choose to confront the danger on Arrakis because he was overly confident. He understood that House Atreides was already trapped politically, and refusing the Emperor’s order could have been just as dangerous as accepting it.

The tragedy is that Leto recognised the trap but believed he could turn it into an opportunity. Unfortunately, he underestimated how far his enemies were willing to go.

There are several reasons behind his decision.

1. Refusing Arrakis would have made House Atreides look guilty

The Emperor’s decision to transfer Arrakis from House Harkonnen to House Atreides wasn’t a genuine reward. It was an invitation designed to destroy them.

However, Leto couldn’t simply refuse.

The Emperor had presented the transfer as an honour. Rejecting it would have made House Atreides appear disloyal to the Imperium and potentially given Shaddam IV the political justification to move against them openly.

Leto was essentially being forced to accept a dangerous assignment while knowing that refusing could be interpreted as rebellion.

2. Arrakis offered something House Atreides desperately needed

Leto understood that controlling Arrakis meant controlling the production of spice, the most valuable substance in the known universe.

But there was something even more important: the Fremen.

He had heard reports suggesting that the Fremen were vastly more numerous and militarily capable than the Imperium understood.

Leto saw an opportunity to build an alliance with them.

If he could win their trust, House Atreides would gain something that money, political influence and conventional military strength couldn’t easily provide: an enormous indigenous fighting force.

His ambition wasn’t simply to survive Arrakis. It was to make House Atreides powerful enough that even the Emperor would have to reconsider attacking them.

3. Leto couldn’t simply relocate his family somewhere safe

This is an important distinction.

House Atreides wasn’t an ordinary family that could sell its possessions, move to another planet and start again.

It was a Great House with political obligations, military responsibilities, lands and a reputation to protect.

Abandoning those responsibilities would have meant sacrificing the very political legitimacy that protected them.

And even if Leto had escaped with Jessica and Paul, what would have happened to everyone else?

His soldiers, advisers, loyal subjects and the thousands of people who depended on House Atreides would have been left behind.

Leto was a duke. His decisions affected an entire political institution.

4. He underestimated the Emperor’s willingness to cooperate with the Harkonnens

Leto knew the Harkonnens were dangerous.

He also suspected that the Emperor was involved in the political manoeuvring against him.

But knowing that your enemies are plotting against you and knowing exactly how they intend to destroy you are two different things.

The Emperor secretly provided Sardaukar troops disguised in Harkonnen uniforms.

That changed everything.

The Harkonnens weren’t simply launching another attack against their old rivals. They had the Emperor’s military power behind them.

Even Leto’s careful preparations couldn’t compensate for that betrayal, especially after Dr. Yueh compromised the household’s defences.

5. Was there actually a way out?

Possibly, but every option carried enormous risks.

Consider three alternatives:

Refusing Arrakis: This could have given the Emperor an excuse to portray House Atreides as rebellious.
Escaping before the Harkonnen attack: Leto might have saved his immediate family, but abandoning Caladan and his people would have effectively destroyed House Atreides as a political power.
Building the Fremen alliance earlier: This was arguably his most promising opportunity. Had Leto established a stronger relationship with the Fremen before the Harkonnen invasion, the balance of power might have been different.

Their Misplaced Hubris ...

And Braggadocio.

Is Going, To Cost Them.

Grok 🦾🤖🫡

**As of November 11, 2026, the dominant news from Iran centers on the ongoing US-Israel-Iran war (Day ~257 since late February 2026 strikes that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei; Mojtaba Khamenei is now Supreme Leader), the Strait of Hormuz standoff, missile developments, and stalled diplomacy.**[](<https://t.co/xuveub1fJa>)

### Military and Missile Developments
Iran’s IRGC unveiled an underground “Missile City.” Armed Forces Chief of Staff Maj. Gen. Ali Abdollahi inspected the facility (with IRGC Aerospace Force Commander Brig. Gen. Majid Mousavi), vowed that Iran would “certainly” destroy Israel, and highlighted new/surprise weapons. State media linked this to the lifting of Iran’s self-imposed 2,000 km ballistic missile range limit. Reports estimate Iran is producing up to ~50 ballistic missiles per month and holds roughly 1,700 missiles. Officials have threatened responses “beyond the region,” including against US bases in Europe if attacked again.[](<https://t.co/8FU0FZM7Ur>)

Shipping incidents continue in/near Hormuz: IRGC and Iranian army statements report oil tankers hitting naval mines (and catching fire or being abandoned) on “unauthorized” routes. There have also been reports of attacks on maritime navigation systems (e.g., on Oman’s Didamar island).[](<https://t.co/Iu1EbZ4Pla>)

### Strait of Hormuz and Negotiations
The strait remains severely restricted (commercial traffic far below pre-war levels; AIS-visible crossings in the low single digits per day recently). Iran says it will not reopen under pre-war terms and has set conditions (often referenced as a seven-point framework tied to earlier understandings such as the Islamabad MoU). These include ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing assets, lifting oil sanctions, and ending the US counter-blockade of Iranian ports. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf (Tehran’s lead negotiator) said the ball is in the US court after Iran communicated its terms and that a deal is possible. Security chief Mohsen Rezaei denied ongoing talks (“pure lies”), insisted no enriched nuclear material will leave Iran, and rejected transferring stockpiles abroad. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said the conflict will not be resolved by military means or more sanctions.[](<https://t.co/8g0oEoDOB8>)

US statements (from Trump, Rubio, and others) describe further major combat operations as highly unlikely if diplomacy advances, emphasize economic pressure (sanctions + blockade) as effective, and note nuclear issues must be part of any deal. Mediators (including Qatar and Pakistan) remain active; oil prices have hovered around $90–93/barrel and moved on deal-related headlines.[](<https://t.co/ADbzDRqhPg>)

### Other Notable Items
- President Masoud Pezeshkian, attending COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, demanded compensation for environmental damage from US-Israeli strikes (citing large CO2 releases from attacks on oil/gas facilities) and met counterparts including from Pakistan, Norway, Armenia, and Iraq.
- Iran designated Argentina’s navy and air force as terrorist organizations (reciprocal to Argentina’s earlier IRGC designation).
- US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was reported moved to a military base amid Iranian threats against officials.
- Domestic warnings of gas shortages this winter due to war damage to processing facilities.
- On the US side, House Republicans blocked an impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth tied to the war; the US has offered rewards for information on Iran’s nuclear program (which Tehran called repugnant).[](<https://t.co/MHLP8ky4Hz>)

The situation remains fluid, with a “no war, no peace” dynamic, low-level attacks, economic pressure, and intermittent diplomatic signals. For the absolute latest, check live blogs from Al Jazeera, Reuters, or specialized trackers on Hormuz traffic.
