text:
Author's Note — Happy Veterans Day!

This year, rather than write a conventional commemorative post, I decided to offer a short story in honor of the Silent Service, particularly those submariners who never returned from their final patrols.

This story also accompanies my musical rendition of Der Toten Erwachen (see the pinned comment), whose haunting imagery of the dead beneath the sea helped inspire it.

The characters and events are fictional, but the tradition of remembering lost submarines as "still on patrol" is very real. May we never forget those who gave their lives in service.

----------------------------------------------------------
No Orders to Return

A tale of the men still on patrol

I. The Last Dive

Philippine Sea — October 1944

The fourth depth charge knocked Samuel Voss from his chair.

His headphones flew from his head, and he struck the deck with sufficient force to drive the breath from his lungs. Somewhere aft, a pipe burst. The lights flickered, went out, and returned in the dim red glow of the emergency lamps.

"Report!"

The captain's voice carried through the control room.

"After engine room reports flooding!"

"Secure the compartment!"

"Can't reach the valve, sir!"

Voss struggled to his feet. His ears were ringing, and for several seconds he could hear little beyond the confused shouting and the prolonged groaning of the submarine's hull.

Another explosion.

"Four hundred feet!"

The submarine was descending.

"Blow main ballast!"

There was a violent shudder.

Nothing followed.

"Five hundred feet!"

Lieutenant Commander Peter Alden called for a damage report. Nobody answered from the after engine room.

"Five hundred fifty!"

Voss found himself thinking of the morning he had left home. His mother had stood beside the kitchen window, holding a cup of coffee, and had reminded him not to forget his scarf.

It had been July, and the scarf was still in his bag.

He remembered laughing at her.

"Six hundred feet!"

The hull began to scream.

A terrible, prolonged shriek passed through the submarine, followed by a succession of sharp metallic cracks.

Someone shouted that they were losing the forward bulkhead.

Voss closed his eyes.

I'm sorry, Mother.

Then the world came apart.

Somebody was coughing.

Voss opened his eyes.

He lay upon the deck, one hand beneath his chest and the other stretched toward the sound gear.

The lights were burning.

The deck was level. The gauges were intact. He could hear the familiar hum of the electric motors.

Somewhere forward, a sailor laughed nervously.

"Jesus Christ. That was close."

Voss got to his feet.

He found Captain Alden standing beside the depth gauge.

"Sir?"

The captain did not answer.

Voss followed his gaze.

The needle had passed beyond the final numbered marking and come to rest against its stop.

"Did we make it, sir?"

Alden looked at him.

For the first time since Voss had known him, the captain seemed uncertain what to say.

"Return to your station."

"Aye, sir."

"And Voss? Not a word of this until we know what happened."

Voss returned to the sound gear.

There were no propellers. No distant detonations. Not even the familiar murmur of the sea.

Then, somewhere far beneath the boat, he heard a bell.

It sounded three times.

He turned toward the control room.

"Captain?"

II. All Hands Accounted For

The muster began twenty minutes later.

Seventy-three men were accounted for. Eight were missing.

All eight had been stationed aft when the compartment flooded.

Chief Petty Officer Brennan accompanied the captain to the watertight door.

"Those boys were on the other side, sir. Collins and the rest. We shut it when the water got too bad."

"You're certain?"

"I heard them shouting."

The captain placed one hand upon the door.

Then somebody knocked.

Three sharp blows sounded against the steel.

Brennan stepped backward.

"Good God."

"Who's there?" Alden called.

"Collins, sir! There's eight of us back here! Can you get this damned door open?"

Brennan stared at the captain.

"Sir, that compartment was flooded."

"I know."

"We can't open it."

"Check the pressure."

An engineer examined the instruments.

"Normal pressure, sir. No water indicated."

Brennan shook his head.

"That's impossible."

"Open it."

The mechanism turned. The men stood aside, expecting a rush of water.

There was none.

Collins emerged first, followed by seven other sailors. Their clothes were damp, their faces pale, and they seemed thoroughly irritated.

"About damned time! We thought you fellows had forgotten us."

Nobody answered.

The captain looked past them. The machinery stood intact. Even the light fixtures shattered during the attack appeared undamaged.

"Collins. What happened after we shut the door?"

"Water was coming in something awful, sir. Then there was a tremendous noise, and I figured we'd had it. Next thing I knew, everything was quiet."

"How long were you waiting?"

"Ten minutes, maybe."

"Did you lose consciousness?"

"Couldn't tell you, sir."

Alden regarded him for several seconds.

"Very well. Report to the medical officer."

The sailors departed.

Brennan remained.

"Captain, those men couldn't have survived."

"No."

"Then what in God's name happened?"

The captain looked into the undamaged compartment.

"I believe we'd better make another count."

The second muster accounted for every man aboard.

Alden entered the result in his logbook.

October 1944. Enemy attack. Severe damage sustained. Circumstances of subsequent recovery unknown. All hands accounted for.

He read the final sentence twice.

He remembered the hull collapsing. He remembered the certainty of death.

And he remembered nothing afterward.

For nearly an hour he remained alone.

Then he closed the logbook and returned to the control room.

"Prepare to surface."

But the submarine would not surface.

Her engines answered perfectly. The diving planes functioned. The ballast tanks operated normally.

Yet every ascent ended at approximately one hundred and twenty feet.

No manipulation of the controls could bring her higher.

The captain ordered the periscope raised. Through its eyepiece he saw nothing but dark water.

For three days, according to the clocks, the engineers searched for damage.

They found none.

Finally, Alden ordered them to proceed toward their assigned station.

"We'll attend to repairs when circumstances permit."

Nobody questioned him.

The submarine was operational. Their captain had given them orders.

There was comfort in that.

III. The Years Between

Voss did not remember the fourth day.

He remembered going to bed after his watch and waking when Brennan called him back to the listening station.

The clock suggested several hours had passed.

He felt as though he had closed his eyes only moments before.

Later, he remembered another watch which seemed to last an entire week.

Such peculiarities were familiar enough aboard submarines. Without daylight, one day could seem interminable while another disappeared unnoticed.

But aboard the Copperfin, time gradually ceased to possess any dependable meaning.

The sailors maintained their watches. They ate in the mess, played cards, argued over baseball, and complained about the coffee.

Sometimes somebody asked how long they had been at sea.

Nobody could answer.

The captain maintained his log as faithfully as possible, although occasionally he discovered entries he could not remember writing.

Some bore dates separated by years.

He learned not to dwell upon them.

The first strange contact came through the sound gear.

Voss heard the creaking of heavy timbers, followed by the clattering of chains and the unmistakable striking of a ship's bell.

"Chief, I think it's a sailing ship."

Brennan stared at him.

"Down here?"

"I know how it sounds."

The chief took the spare headphones.

There came another bell, followed by what might have been human voices.

"That's damned peculiar," Brennan admitted.

The captain listened without speaking.

Then another sound intruded.

A long, dragging noise, accompanied by a deep resonance unlike any machinery Voss had encountered.

Its bearing seemed to change without its growing nearer or farther away.

Suddenly there came a tremendous report.

A cannon.

Then another.

The old vessel was firing a broadside.

The dragging noise changed direction. The guns continued for several minutes, then ceased.

The bell sounded three times.

And the vessel passed into silence.

They encountered other ships afterward.

Once Voss heard the slow beating of a drum, accompanied by the rhythmic striking of what sounded like hundreds of oars.

Another time he heard wooden pumps laboring, with sailors shouting in a language he did not recognize.

Sometimes bells answered one another.

Occasionally there was cannon fire.

He could not explain how such sounds reached them from depths at which no wooden vessel could survive.

Eventually, he ceased asking.

There were enough inexplicable things aboard the Copperfin.

The next remarkable contact was enormous.

Its machinery produced a continuous vibration unlike anything Voss had heard aboard a merchantman.

"Chief, I've got a big ship."

"How big?"

"Bigger than anything I've ever heard."

Brennan listened.

"Sounds like a whole damned factory."

For nearly an hour they followed its slow passage overhead.

Then Voss heard something peculiar.

A small splash. A brief succession of metallic noises.

And music.

He adjusted his receiver.

"Chief, I think somebody's playing a song."

"On the hydrophones?"

"Yes."

Brennan listened.

There was a guitar, the rhythmic clapping of hands, and two oddly enthusiastic cries.

"Ho! Hey!"

Then a man's voice began singing.

The music continued for several seconds before wavering into a peculiar electronic buzzing.

And it stopped.

"Lost it," Voss reported.

"Ship still there?"

"Yes, Chief. Just the music's gone."

"Probably turned it off."

"Probably."

Neither man knew that a passenger aboard the vessel had dropped a telephone overboard, its music continuing briefly as it sank.

Voss wondered what sort of passenger ship could produce such extraordinary machinery.

Perhaps the Navy had developed something new while they were away.

Whatever the explanation, he hoped somebody would tell him what that music had been when they finally returned to port.

It had been rather catchy.

IV. The Singing

The first indication of trouble came seventeen minutes after three.

Voss heard a prolonged scraping noise beneath the sound of the passenger vessel.

It resembled a heavy chain being dragged across the floor of some enormous chamber.

He reported the contact.

Captain Alden arrived presently, wearing his old service sweater.

"Movement?"

"Slow, sir. Bearing steady, as near as I can tell."

"Range?"

"Can't say."

The captain listened for nearly a minute.

"Any singing?"

Voss hesitated.

"Sir?"

"Have you heard singing?"

"No, sir."

"If you do, report it immediately."

A low vibration passed through the hull.

The scraping grew louder.

"Sir, I think it's coming closer."

"I know."

There was something in Alden's expression that Voss had never seen before.

He looked frightened.

The captain placed a hand upon his shoulder.

"Listen carefully, son. If you hear anything resembling a human voice, remove the headphones. You are not to answer it, whatever it says."

"Yes, sir."

"Whatever it says."

At that moment, the scraping ceased.

For several seconds there was silence.

Then Voss heard a woman singing.

There were no words, only a soft, sorrowful melody rising and falling through the darkness.

He did not recognize the tune.

But he knew the voice.

It was his mother's.

He knew the gentle uncertainty with which she approached the higher notes. He knew the little breath she drew before completing a phrase.

He had not heard her voice since leaving home.

The captain saw his expression and reached for the headphones.

But Voss had already begun to cry.

"Mother?"

Alden tore the headset from his ears.

The melody continued.

Not through the headphones.

Through the hull.

Every man aboard could hear it.

The crew assembled in the control room.

One sailor claimed to have heard his wife calling through the ventilation system.

Another heard his father.

Collins reported hearing his younger brother laughing beyond a watertight door.

The captain gave his orders.

"No man is to answer any voice originating outside this vessel. All hands will remain at their stations."

The executive officer approached him privately.

"Captain, what is happening?"

"I wish I knew."

"Sir, what are we?"

Alden regarded him.

For a moment he seemed ready to answer.

Instead, he said:

"We are the crew of the United States submarine Copperfin. Our duty is to this vessel and to one another. That much has not changed."

Then the scraping returned.

Voss listened.

The great passenger ship continued overhead.

But beneath it, another sound was rising.

A slow, tremendous pulsation.

Each pulse seemed to shake the surrounding water.

The singing began again.

And now the scraping was moving toward the passenger vessel.

"Captain!"

Alden turned.

"Sir, I think it's going after the ship!"

V. General Quarters

The captain ordered general quarters.

The familiar alarm sounded throughout the submarine.

Men hurried to their stations.

Voss listened desperately.

The passenger vessel continued upon its course, its machinery steady and untroubled.

Whatever approached it produced a noise that seemed to originate from several directions at once.

Then came a bell.

Three strokes.

Voss straightened.

"Captain. Another contact."

"Where?"

"Port side. I think it's that sailing ship, sir."

Alden took the spare headphones.

There was the creaking of timber, the muffled movement of heavy equipment, and faint voices.

Then the bell sounded again.

Three strokes.

A pause.

Three more.

The scraping grew louder.

Suddenly a cannon fired.

Then another.

The old vessel was engaging the thing beneath the passenger ship.

Alden turned toward the torpedo officer.

"Prepare tubes one and two."

The executive officer stared at him.

"Sir, what exactly are we firing at?"

"Something is attacking that passenger vessel."

"How can you be certain?"

The captain listened to the distant cannonade.

"Because somebody else has already opened fire."

The Copperfin maneuvered toward the sound.

The old ship's guns continued firing, accompanied by the deep impacts of something moving through the water.

Every time the vibration passed through the hull, men reported hearing voices.

Parents. Wives. Children.

Voss's mother returned.

"Samuel."

He shut his eyes.

"Samuel, come home."

He could almost see her standing beside the kitchen window.

The sunlight. The coffee.

The scarf he had forgotten to wear.

"Samuel, you've been away long enough."

"Voss!"

The captain seized his shoulder.

"Your report!"

Voss forced himself to listen.

The passenger vessel was still moving.

The old ship was firing.

And the scraping was rising toward the machinery overhead.

"Sir, it's almost beneath them!"

"Range?"

"I can't tell!"

"Best estimate!"

The scraping changed direction.

Another cannon fired.

Then a second.

The old vessel was drawing the contact away.

Only slightly.

But enough.

"Sir, I have a bearing!"

"Tube one. Stand by."

The torpedo officer repeated the order.

"Captain, we haven't got a firing solution!"

"I know."

"We may miss entirely!"

"Then God help us. Fire one!"

The torpedo departed its tube.

Voss heard its machinery begin to run.

Several seconds later, there came a tremendous explosion.

The submarine shuddered.

Somebody cheered.

Then the scraping returned.

Louder.

Much louder.

The singing ceased.

A violent impact passed through the hull, throwing Voss against his chair.

For an instant he heard the pressure hull collapsing again.

The dreadful sound of their final dive.

Then the old vessel's guns opened fire.

A full broadside.

The noise rolled through the ocean like thunder.

Voss seized his headphones.

"Captain! It's going for the other ship!"

"Tube two! Ready?"

"Ready, sir!"

"Voss! Bearing!"

He listened.

The old vessel was firing repeatedly.

There were shouts and the frantic striking of a bell.

Then the unmistakable groaning of timbers under enormous strain.

"One-four-two!"

"Fire two!"

The second torpedo ran.

The singing returned.

Not his mother's voice this time.

A multitude of voices.

Some pleaded.

Others laughed.

One screamed.

Then came a deep, dull detonation.

The scraping stopped.

So did the voices.

For several seconds there was nothing but the distant machinery of the passenger ship.

Then the bell sounded.

Once.

Twice.

Three times.

The Copperfin remained motionless.

"Voss?"

"Sir?"

"Any contact?"

He listened.

The old vessel was still there.

Its timbers creaked faintly. Somewhere aboard, men moved heavy equipment.

But the dreadful noise was gone.

"No, sir."

"Is it destroyed?"

Voss hesitated.

"I can't tell, sir."

The captain listened to the silence.

"Very well."

He turned toward the control room.

"Passenger vessel?"

"Still moving, sir."

"Any indication of damage?"

"None, sir."

The captain nodded.

"Secure from battle stations."

The order passed through the submarine.

Men returned to their duties.

Alden remained beside Voss.

Eventually, the bell sounded once more.

Three strokes.

Then the old ship began to move away.

The captain listened until it had nearly disappeared.

"Good hunting," he said quietly.

VI. Still on Patrol

The submarine resumed her course.

There was no damage to report.

The burst pipe had repaired itself. The lights functioned normally. The vessel answered her controls as faithfully as ever.

The torpedo officer reported that tubes one and two were loaded, though no order to reload had been given.

Nobody could explain how.

Nobody particularly wished to discuss it.

The captain returned to his cabin.

He opened the logbook.

There were pages upon pages of entries.

Some were dated in October 1944.

Others belonged to years he scarcely remembered.

He found reports of strange vessels, unidentified contacts, and encounters which had passed almost entirely from his recollection.

Then he came upon the final entry.

November 11, 2026.

The date was written in his own handwriting.

He could not remember writing it, nor could he imagine how he had learned the year.

Beneath it were four words.

Still on patrol, sir.

The captain stared at the page.

For a long while he remained seated.

Then he closed the book and returned to the control room.

Voss was at the listening station.

"Anything to report?" Alden asked.

"No, sir."

"Good."

The young sailor hesitated.

"Captain?"

"Yes?"

"How long have we been out?"

Alden considered the question.

"Longer than we expected, son."

"How much longer?"

The captain looked at him.

"My log says it's November of twenty twenty-six."

Voss stared.

"That can't be right."

"I know."

"But that's..."

"Eighty-two years."

The young sailor looked down at his hands.

For several moments he said nothing.

Then, very quietly:

"My mother..."

The captain placed a hand upon his shoulder.

"I know, son."

Voss swallowed.

"Sir, do you suppose anybody remembers us?"

The captain did not answer immediately.

He thought of his wife, and of the daughter who had been three years old when he departed on his final patrol.

He wondered what had become of them.

"I should think so," he said at last.

Then a faint crackle came from the radio.

The operator looked up.

"Captain, I'm receiving something."

"From whom?"

"I don't know, sir."

The radio had yielded no intelligible transmission since their final dive. Now a voice emerged through the static, clear enough to be understood despite the impossible depth.

"...those who gave their lives in service to their country..."

The captain approached the receiver.

"...and to the officers and men of the submarines which never returned..."

There was a pause.

Then the sound of a bell.

Alden closed his eyes.

The voice continued.

"They remain, as ever, still on patrol."

The transmission faded.

The radio operator adjusted his controls.

Nothing returned.

For a long while, nobody spoke.

Then Voss removed his headphones.

"They remember us, sir."

Alden nodded.

"Yes, son."

He placed one hand upon the young sailor's shoulder.

"They remember."

Far above them, the passenger ship continued upon its voyage.

None aboard had heard the cannonade, the singing, or the struggle beneath the waves.

Nor did they know that an American submarine, lost in October 1944, had expended two torpedoes in their defense.

Below, the men of the Copperfin returned to their stations.

Their watches continued. Their captain maintained his log.

And when the darkness stirred again, they would be ready.

They had received no orders to return.

They were still on patrol.

text:
Anthropic's IPO could now raise more money than SpaceX ever did.

Bloomberg says the IPO plus a private placement could reach $90.4 billion. SpaceX's biggest raise was $85 billion. An AI lab is about to out-raise the rocket company.

The target valuation is back at $1.5 trillion. Shares priced at $70 to $78. Up to 825 million shares, about $64.4 billion from the IPO alone. Orders are running several times the shares on offer.

Seven founders are each selling about $250 million of stock. Each one keeps roughly $18 billion. Microsoft has already committed at least $47.2 billion through June 2033. New deals with Microsoft and Google top $10 billion.

People keep asking if AI is a bubble. The order book is answering with numbers that beat SpaceX.

When the lab raises more than the rockets, what exactly are we still calling a bubble?
